Note: Review based on enhanced edition of game which is much improved over original release.
Overview: Sots2 is a grand 4x stratergy game that is increadibly deep and complex.  You have to grow and run your empire, controlling trade, colonization, stimulus, research, ship design and fully 3D, fully controllable space combat. Ship design and weapon placement makes a big difference in combat, and tactics, direction etc is very important in space combat.  Those looking for a deep strategic game with fully controllable Space Combat will not go wrong here.
Pros: Very deep, lots of control over empire from stimulus, colonization, research, base construction and upgrades. Unlike many other in the genre, space combat is fully controllable.  You control everything and controlling if your ships focus on broadside or frontal attacks makes a big difference, as does how you outfit your ship and where you place your weapons.  Overall very satisfying. The inclusion of an ingame chat system that allows you to speak to other players is very useful for getting player advice.  Also, the game looks great graphically.
Cons: Complete lack of tuturial is a major annoyance.  I had to watch a (highly recommended) youtube tutorial to make heads or tails of the game.  Considering how complex it is, can be very hard for new players to get into it.  Also, the game still suffers from crashes.  Final con is that Diplomacy is not that well implemented, which is fine for those warmongers among us, but those that want to play a more diplomatic game might be dissapointed.
Summary: If you want a deep, good looking 4x will excellent combat, then look not further than Sots2.

A gorgeous casual point-and-click adventure with many puzzles -- some too easy, but some challenging, original, and fun! There are also a handful of simple hidden-object scenes, but it's not a true hidden-object game.
The hand-crafted scenes are wonderful, bright and intricate, with an astonishing attention to little, delightful details. Even the items you pick up are carefully drawn. Everywhere you look is inspiration! (Even the protagonist sometimes exclaims: “Wow, what an amazing view!") The game also features very good facial animation for the characters, and excellent voice acting -- unfortunately a rarity in this genre.
The story is a weak, but you likely be too focused on the many cute and cuddly creatures inhabiting Nearwood to pay attention to it.
Those looking for challenging puzzle adventures might be disappointed, but if you play this one on expert mode it will at least make you think a bit.

I already got a copy of this game in a PlayStation Network sale earlier this year and I bought it again because it made me feel really good and happy the whole time I was playing it and I want to support the developer who did that for me.
Ugh. What a nerd.
Anyway, this game is sort of like if the pixel art worlds viewed from a slightly oblique top-down perspective which were a dominant presentation method for action-adventure games and RPG's during the 16-bit era were never usurped by 3D environments and polygonal graphics. By which I mean, it doesn't feel like a self-consciously nostalgia-laced throwback to the 2D era like many other indie games, but like the result of years of evolution in 2D game design and pixel art, culminating in this beautiful, visceral and mysterious experience.
The most direct comparison I can make is with top-down Zelda games like A Link To The Past or The Minish Cap, but with a heavier focus on exploration and (especially) combat, rather than on puzzle-solving, narrative and RPG elements. This focus on getting the combat and the feel of moving in the world absolutely perfect pays off, creating an experience that in many ways is far more satisfying than any of these classic Zelda titles. Link's controls can feel a bit clunky in those games, sometimes making it seemingly impossible to avoid being hit, whereas The Drifter becomes like some sort of perfect ninja assassin in your hands, and every time an enemy attack lands it feels like your fault. And while the RPG elements aren't as important here, they're still intelligently implemented with the combat emphasis in mind. In Drifter it is totally possible to finish the game with your starting equipment only and no upgrades, so the focus in the design of many unlockable items and skills is on simply adding a bit of variety to the ways you can kill enemies and in a few cases just making the Drifter *cooler* which I, as a shallow person, appreciate.
It's also just a beautiful game, a feast for the senses. Some of the most beautiful pixel art I've ever seen brings to life an utterly unique and truly original game world, aided by an amazing soundtrack from Disasterpeace, who also did the music for Fez as well as the film It Follows.
Your mileage may vary somewhat however. This is in some ways a game that can be described using the lazy shorthand of "it's a bit like Dark Souls". That is, the story is obscured from as much as it's told to you and the emphasis is on atmosphere and creating a mood rather than conveying any sort of coherent narrative; what you're actually supposed to be doing and almost all of the RPG systems involved are barely explained to you if at all, and you can only discover these things by exploring (or simply by Googling, which is perfectly legitimate if it makes the game more fun for you in my opinion); and it's hard. Not frustratingly hard in my opinion due to impeccable controls & enemy design as well as frequent checkpointing, but the combat does demand a little bit of practice to get good at it, and in some respects it's a game that does demand that you be at least fairly decent at games if you want to get to the end of it.
In some respects it almost feels like this game was designed with me in mind so you can take the next part with a grain of salt if you like, but in my opinion this is a masterpiece, the best indie game of all time, and for me it's a no-brainer that this was the game of the year for 2016.

This is truly an amazing product with nothing quite like it out there.
The good:
It has so many things to do in it that it's hard to know where to start.
I guess a good choice would be the 'Learn a song' mode which is the core of the game. I imagine that this is the reason why most people buy it, it was for me at least. It does a very good job at progressively increasing the difficulty on you. It starts off with very few of the most important notes just so that you get a feel of where your hands should be at any particular moment. It gradually increases the difficulty as you go along. This works very well, however sometimes it increases the difficulty by a whole lot but you can easily decrease it manually using the riff repeater.
Session mode is a really neat improvisation sandbox. You have a 'virtual band' that follows your lead and it does a really good job at it. This is very hard to explain because it's very different than the learn a song mode in that you tell the game what to play and not the other way around.
To help you learn to play, you have some lessons that do a very good job at explaining different concepts and some come with a 'try it' session so you can practice what you just learned.
If lessons bore you, you have these mini games that teach you chords, scales, chord progressions, string skipping, volume control and so on. They have a great way of teaching you because it doesn't feel like you're learning but rather playing a game and the guitar is just a controller.
The bad:
The waiting time in between mini games is really annoying. I'm pretty new at this so my typical session with them lasts about 20-40 seconds and the game intro+ending+scores (basically how long you have to wait in between games) is about 30 seconds, others feel like over a minute. It would be great if you could skip this and just retry instantly.
Also, some notes don't register properly depending on the mini game.
As an example of my configuration, using scale racer on the pentatonic major scale, when i used the bridge pickup everything registered properly until i got back to the root and wanted to start over, it just wouldn't register the first note unless I hit it like 4 times. Changing the pickup configuration to bridge + neck, the previous issue was fixed, however, another note on a different string wouldn't register. The only way that it worked well in this particular game was if i only used the neck pickup.
But different minigames respond differently to different configurations, Star chords for instance works best with neck+bridge in my experience and i've never gotten return to castle chords to work well. I have to perform 'Am' about 5 times before it registers it.
Overall, i think that this is a great purchase and a lot of people that I showed Rocksmith to were very impressed by it.

While not a great Resident Evil game it is a good TPS, albeit a flawed one.
I will start with the positives, first and foremost it's just a lot of fun to play as the combat is truly fantastic, apart from the cover system which is quite terrible so I never used it. There's endless ways to kill the enemy, including the always fun to execute melee finishers. The monsters take visible damage as you shoot them which I loved, bits of their body will fly off as you focus them and it just adds something to the combat which I appreciated. The game doesn't have an Oscar winning story but it keeps you interested, if you've ever played a Resident Evil game you know what's going to happen, as it always happens. The voice work is done well, although hurt by the script which isn't great at best, it's very cheesy and almost cringe-worthy at times but that's a staple of Resident Evil games at this point. Also I'll say that I had no technical issues, the game ran at a solid 60fps throughout on max settings, I know performance was an issue in the past but it's certainly not now on appropriate hardware.
As for negatives, the biggest for me was the length of the game, it truly overstayed its welcome, at 22 hours it feels very long and fatigue kicked in around the 15 hours mark. I would have enjoyed the game a lot more had they trimmed the fat and sliced off at least 5 hours, it would have been a more enjoyable game for it, I can think of a few sections that could be shortened or just removed entirely. By the end I was struggling to find motivation to finish it, and I dropped my overall rating from a 7 to a 6 as it just dragged on too much, the reduction in score was also due to the fact that Ada's campaign was poor almost throughout and as I played it last it left a sour taste in my mouth after I finished the game. Another gripe were the unskippable cutscenes, no one likes them, so please stop using them devs! Another dev favourite that we all hate are QTEs and the game is littered with them, so be prepared to die if you don't press A + X within a split second of it popping up on the screen.
Overall I did enjoy it for the most part but it definitely wore me down by the end, would I recommend it? Yes, but only when on sale and only if you feel you can endure the boring chapters as to enjoy the good ones. I should also mention the game is heavily co-op focused, you can play solo with an AI companion but the game is far more fun with a friend, or even a random online player although those are rare these days.

Are you looking for a truly terrible game? A game so clichéd that you are upset when the characters don’t put on sunglasses after their one liners? Where you can visit America’s only 1000 year old Church, filled with eastern European zombies, only a short bus ride from Washington D.C? Where enemies don’t die? Ever? Where the control scheme is one of the most convolutedly set up disasters it makes the Titanic look good? Where character backstory and development is best fleshed out while fighting mutating enemies on a horizontal elevator overlooking the abyss? Where the timeline is so hard to track you need an aboriginal hunter to help you out?
Then look no further than Resident Evil 6! This game features the cutting edge in game advancement, being a series of quick time events spliced with cut scenes you can die in! Tired of fair or evenly spread check points? Don’t worry about it. Tired of being able to gauge the length of a level? Not a problem. Tired of beating a boss in a grueling checkpoint-less fight only to never see him again? Forget-about-it. Resident Evil 6 is your answer to all these problems and more; yours for the excessive price of $29.99.

This game was honestly MUCH better than I expected.
1. Head-scratching but not punishing level-navigation puzzles coupled with generous checkpoints and respawns, like Fez.
2. A pretty cool cast of characters with different abilities, all necessary to beat the level, like Lost Vikings.
3. Witty, silly narration with a story that's much deeper than you think it'll be, like Portal 2 or The Stanley Parable.
This game is not really going to challenge anyone. Even the achievements are plainly visible in the levels, so it's easy to get 100% completion. But the great "cast of characters", the easy-going puzzle rooms, and the heartwarming underlying story make it one of my new favorite "relax, have a beer, and play for an hour" games. No real replay value, but I'll probably revisit it every year or so just because it's easy to get through (4ish hours?) and it makes me smile.

I played since launch on xbox for probably 200 hours before I switched to PC awhile ago, man the difference is undeniable. Obviously coming from playing For Honor in 30fps to 60fps makes the game incredibly smoother. The quick timing of parries seems a tiny bit longer almost it's so crisp. I love the combat in this game, in duels mostly.. Dominion is a circus.
The game works fine in duels and brawls. 4v4 game modes still have some network issues but guess what? Dedicated servers are coming next month(January) and from what I've heard from people who played the beta dedicated servers, they sound really good. The main reason this game has any negativity is because of the peer-to-peer networking, once that's taken away the game will be solid. Hell I hope they continue the IP into the future.
From launch until now I think the dev's have handled making steel easier to obtain very well. When the game first came out it was horribly slow to grind steel just playing games, now you can log on and do 2 easy orders for basically 1000 steel. You don't have to sit there and play for hours but if you do, you actually feel rewarded now. Yes, there is kind of a notion towards you purchasing steel but it's not thrown in your face like earlier or with other games. No Dawning here. You can actually earn things like mythic outfits just by playing now, it's easy, you can do it.
There's nothing much I really need to say about the gameplay. If you like melee style or old school fighting games this game is for you. The combat is intense- outside of getting 4v1'ed in dominion.. Seriously though, it's an adrenaline kick to the face when your duel goes down to the wire and you come out on top. Also since the launch of the game, we've gotten skill rankings and ranked game modes. This is what people were calling for when I remember playing on xbox, and I'm really glad to see ranked game modes. Completely awesome tournament style ranked duels and ranking systems so you don't get paired up against a rep 30 Lawbringer when you're playing a rep 0 level 1 Orochi. Because that actually did used to happen.
You might see a whole lot of negative reviews for this game, but they all have a relative pattern, and a time and date. Any reviews you see about the servers being bad and the connections are horrible are going to be immidiately inaccurate now. Dedicated servers are going to push this game to what we were really expecting when we wanted For Honor to release. The game itself is amazing! Once the dedicated servers come, there's nothing left to cry about except you being bad.

Crysis 2 is a pretty neat & fairly well-done FPS which still looks pretty good for its age. It is a sci-fi shooter set in a futuristic New York dystopia that has been attacked by terrorists. The main character of the game has been branded an enemy of the state & is hunted by agents of the government as well as by terrorist organizations. In this context you are the hero of a fairly small team which exists as part of the government but is being pursued as well & you have to try to clear your name & enact your revenge.
There are a few antagonists that are allowed to sort of do their thing in this game world. There is a sour & bitter radio dj that says offensive things on the radio that is allowed to exist in the game & has small voice parts throughout, talking about terrorist attacks & hackers & all that kind of stuff. That is tolerated but considered annoying by the so-called "main players" & military commanders who give the orders & pay the employees in this game. A solitary sports reporter follows the team of militants as well (from a safe distance, of course), sort of talking about what they do and imitating them, kind of like a sidekick or a recruiter or, as they might say in Minnesota, a gopher. These "antagonist" characters are set up as a foil for the main team of guys to demolish over the course of the campaign, & are cannon fodder
The gameplay is fairly standard shooter fare, which, incidentally, I enjoy, so yeah it's pretty fun stuff. Takes maybe 5-10 hours to complete the campaign entirely & I believe there is a multiplayer mode. They definitely maximize the whole superhuman hero soldier thing. I'm sure, or perhaps i should say, I'm CERTAIN that Cevat Yerli, lead dev over at Crytek UK, is super duper proud of Crysis 2 & how well-received it has been.
Setting: Much of the action takes place on various construction sites, as well as a dumpy factory, a scary office, a religious temple & what seems to be some sort of police headquarters. Also an airport baggage claim area and some ruined city streets. There is also at least one scene in an alien space-ship.
I'd say the game it most reminds me of is CoD: IW, as well as of course Crysis 1, which ALSO is fairly well-done & works fairly good. They did turn up the "cheesiness" in the original Crysis, as I recall. Aliens: Colonial Marines comes to mind as well as a similar title to this. The video game is similar to Half Life 2, which is considered a classic of its time period, which is the mid-2000's. Half-Life 2 is from Valve Inc, the makers of the STEAM video game purchase service. I guess this game is sort of like the Deus Ex franchise, so the word on the street goes. Not a follower of the Deus Ex franchise.
On another note, I do believe that they at Valve Inc are mostly involved with STEAM & connected products & do not make video games at this point in time, which is sad. It would be nice to see a Half-Life 3 at some point in the future. Pony Island is an extremely fun and original game. Never in my life have I played a game where you're stuck in hell and your punishment for the things you've done is to play a boring pony game for the rest of your existance. The goal of the game is to find a way to crash the game and escape hell. It's a very fun concept and is extremely well executed. The game has a great sense of humour much like Undertale, so if you like Undertale's sort of humour you'll laugh a lot at this game. The game is a puzzle game which means it has some good puzzles that are actually quite tricky, which is nice (Papyrus approves).
The thing I didn't like very much about this game was the music. I bought the soundtrack and I must say some of the songs in this game were ot that good at all (though I do love the main theme). Another thing that bugged me was the pony levels themselves. They were very repetetive and there were quite a lot of them during the adventure mode section, which slows the game down quite a lot.
Other than that, I think the game is in my opinion flawless. It's everything I love about indie games. It's creative, original, funny, clever, and just a good time. If you're looking for a fun experience like nothing else, pick this game up.

I felt like getting one or two casual games so I'd have something I could turn my mind off while I play and just relax with. I found this game on sale for $2.50 so I thought I'd give it a try, since it had beautiful art. It's kind of like a point and click adventure story where you solve a variety of puzzles, put objects together, and help fix things to save this fairy tale style magical realm from an evil darkness that was unleashed when your character's father stopped time by accident when trying to save his wife from a deadly illness and ended up freezing himself and the time lords in the process. The story is a bit of a stretch, but it feels natural within the atmosphere in the game. There are hidden object game parts, but not many, there is a good variety of puzzles most of which are pretty easy and simple. Quite a few of them require trial and error, but really easy to figure out trial and error, if that makes sense. There was only two puzzles that I felt took me a while to figure out, and only one puzzle did I use one of my skips for, but mostly because I was tired and wanted to move on so I could go to bed at the time (lol).There is a timer so if it's taken you a certain amount of time to solve the puzzle it'll allow you to skip it except for the hidden object parts which the timer allows you a hint instead. If you don't want to use a skip but are stuck, on the bottom right hand corner of the screen there's a guide button that provides a walkthrough, so you can see just one step ahead to get your gears moving. But to be honest, 99% of the game is very simple. The sound and art is beautiful and relaxing and getting objectives completed feels satisfying even if it's not that difficult, and the entire mood and atmosphere of the game is what sells it IMO. I love it, it's a good refresher from all those frustrating competitive games. The voice acting isn't very good at all but it's listenable and to be honest I expect these games to have bad voice acting. My only regret is that the voice acting isn't bad enough to be hilarious, but it's not bad enough to really hate it so I guess that's fine too haha. Overall, it took me four and a half hours to complete the main chapter before I got to the bonus chapters. So it's pretty short, but for these games longer would probably mean it outstays its welcome. I'm not sure if it's worth the full price of $15 (if I remember that correctly) but I'm always hesitant to spend money on casual style games because I'm a terrible person. But it was more than worth the $2.50 and I highly enjoyed my playthrough, definitely more solid than many other games of this genre I've played in the past.

The music and sound are also great, and the voice acting is good. The game very much succeeds in creating a beautiful and vivid fairytale-like atmosphere.
The gameplay mostly consists of puzzles and minigames, with a few very simple HO-type scenes. I have to say I was very pleasantly surprised by the puzzles in this game - they are very different and imaginative, not repetitive at all, and not the exact same puzzles and mechanics you see in most HOG or adventure games. While most of them are not extremely challenging, they are smart and very, very fun to play.
There is a tad bit more back-and-forth than I'd like between the great number of areas of the game, but at least it's quite obvious and logical where you should be going when you find a new item. I played in hard mode, so I don't know if this would be easier with the use of the map, but I found it was sometimes easy to forget in which of the previous ten areas the lock for the key you just found was located. But I did enjoy the variety of beautiful areas, and, again, the navigation made sense and the game did not suffer from a case of magically appearing objects and HO areas that a lot of games do. Another small criticism is that the controls of a couple of the puzzles seemed a bit fiddly and/or buggy (the rotating hourglass puzzle in particular comes to mind), but it was more of a rare, mild annoyance than a serious problem.
Gameplay in hard mode is 4-5 hours, including the bonus chapter, which is decent. There is a lot of content (areas, puzzles, etc) so the game felt very satisfying. I wish the game included achievements as well, but it's not such a big thing I guess.
The story of the game is nothing amazing, quite flimsy and cliche, but the setting and atmosphere are beautiful and interesting enough to make up for it. I have to admit that there were moments when some dialogue or story bits made me roll my eyes, most notably the part where a whole gnome village was left to languish because all the men had been kidnapped, leaving the women and children alone in the village, so there was apparently no one around to find food or repair things.
In conclusion, despite the few small flaws and flimsy story, I greatly enjoyed this game. The gorgeous art and interesting, unique puzzles more than made up for anything else.

I won't reiterate on the launch story of this game, although I was there to witness it all. It is largely stable now and very much enjoyable, though probably not the easiest game to get into.
First of all I'd like to mention one thing that drew me to this series of games: it's the great universe it depicts. It's a universe filled with races as detailed, likable and integral in their portrayal, as one could expect from an RPG. And it’s not simple the backstory from a manual: I liked very much how it seeped into little details in the game from drives to voices to event reports. It shows that the authors cared about their world and the species that populate it, and Sword of the Stars is the only game where I liked all of the different races.
It is also not a lifeless universe where only the major empires dwell. From silicoid swarms to grand menaces, there are always greater forces at work. Minor events influence your decisions early game, while aforementioned grand menaces may shape the entire match later on. I have witnessed everyone in a multiplayer game banding together to deal with a swarm of planet-sized self-replicating machines that have already stripped a good chunk of the map clean of all resources, and it’s the unexpected that makes many games memorable.
These events are also part of the story, with many of them heralding the introduction of new races over the years, and shaping existing factions.
It gets me to the third thing that I like about this game: replayability. It is paramount to 4x games in general, and Sword of the Stars goes further than most in this field. Besides events that I've talked about that help make each game memorable, there are different ways to travel among the stars for different races and randomized research tree. The latter may sound like a hindrance, but I found it to add immensely to the uniqueness of each game. It doesn't allow you to cherry-pick some kind of best combination and stick to it in every game, and when luck is not on your side, it provides for some challenge in overcoming your opponents despite the shortcomings of technology available to you.
The tech tree really links with the great ship customization. Beyond the great visual design of ships for different races, the game goes beyond three cannons that improve with new technologies. Further research provides a plethora of new options for each race in a system of soft counters. It means that a certain technology may be better against another, but not to the point where a fleet equipped with the former will curb-stomp a fleet built around the latter regardless of tactics employed. A clever selection of technologies provide you with an advantage, but rarely an overwhelming one.
What I said so far may sound like I consider SotS2 the best game ever created, and I apparently hold it in rather high regard. However, the Achilles heel of this game as it is now is mediocre AI, which is not really surprising in a game like this. It does a decent job now in adapting to your strategy and keeping its empire going and expanding. However its behavior in tactical combat is not really diverse, and it choices in diplomacy sometimes seem awkward and inconsistent. As my experience with the game grew I found the need to arrange some serious odds against me to make up for AI mediocrity.
Multiplayer can alleviate the previous concern quite a bit, and the game really shines online, but each game is so long you rarely can expect to finish it in one evening, and have to arrange for successive sessions which is not always possible. When a person leaves, AI takes over his empire, but like I said, it does mediocre job at best. Multiplayer also took a blow from GameSpy shutdown, so you have to arrange games through a global chat, which is nice, but not actually the most convenient way to handle multiplayer.
After all is said and done, Sword of the Stars 2 remains one of the best space 4x games in my opinion, and definitely an unique flower that I hope will continue to bloom and give fruit.

.

There isn't much can be said about the game's visuals asides from that they're amazingly well done. Pretty much the same thing can be said about the game's audio. The visual and audio can be adjusted in the game's option menu.
There are three different game difficulty modes to choose from: Casual, Normal and Expert.
There are interactive items in the game, they're marked with a symbol, but sometimes these interactive items do require extra items before they can be interact with.
The interactive map allows the player to fast travel between each location quickly. It also indicates something of interest can be done at certain location.  Please note that the map isn't given immediately when the game started. Also, the teleportation amulet automatically recharges itself after being used.
Most of the hidden object scenes consists of fragment items, placing items back. Some of them do require little or no interaction.
Most of the game's puzzles are rather easy to solve without much difficulty. For most of these puzzles there's a reset button. However, there's definitely a skip button, for all of the puzzles. These two features are only present in "Casual" game difficulty mode.
There are small creatures collectibles in the game called Snoop-Sees. They're scattered throughout the game.
Since this is a collector's edition game, there's a bonus chapter, but it can be unlocked only after the main story of the game's completed. The bonus chapter is the sequel to the main story.
There's a built-in strategy guide for the game. It can be access anytime during gameplay.
In the extra content section: Soundtracks, Concept Art, Wallpapers and Snoopedia.
[Please note that Snoopedia can't be accessed until some of its' collectibles are found.]
Final thoughts, I definitely enjoying playing this game all the way through to the end. As for the replay value I would say it's low. I would recommend this game but not at the full price.

Wow, I wasn't expecting this kind of beauty in display and quality in gameplay when I got
- a FROG, or fragmented object game - in a bundle some time ago. I was bored and looking for a "snack" game, which I'd be able to play with minimum mental capacity. Aside the story being purely lame and the ending being anticlimactic,
's been a feast within its genre.
The curtain opens up for us to meet Jane Lockwood, the only daughter of Nathan and Elizabeth Lockwood. Apparently, Jane's mother died out of a sickness and her father disappeared mysteriously just after, leaving Jane to be raised by her aunt. Growing up with many strange dreams of a magical realm, Jane finally decides to go back to the house that she lived with her parents when she was little, to learn more about her past.
There, a strange little man - either a gnome or a goblin - named Fey welcomes her back and invites her to the mysterious realm of Nearwood: a fairy realm that apparently little Jane and her parents lived in when she was younger. As a quite expected outcome, Jane seems to be the hero that Nearwood's been waiting for. Only she will be able to reveal the mystery of her past and mend the damage done to the realm!
Okay, after swimming in the sea of clichés that stands as a storyline, we should talk about the display: OMG, visuals are plain marvelous in this game!!! Beautiful effects, gorgeous backgrounds in vibrant colors and lovely character designs as if it's all just out of a fairytale book. Environment design being always unique and imaginative,
manages to set a light and magical tone for you to experience. Added with quite elaborate character designs and good voice acting, this silly magical realm is worthy for you to experience even for the sake of art only.
Nothing stands out much for the gameplay though, but we wouldn't expect anything imaginative from a HOG/FROG at this point. We know what we are getting ourselves into when we are buying a HOG: we run around in a predetermined area, collect items, solve some puzzles and call it a day by completing a cheesy story. Oh, wait: puzzles ARE imaginative and interesting, most of them being quite challenging! If you'd refuse skipping puzzles and complete the brief bonus chapter,
offers you a 4-5 hour gameplay which is quite fair.
This is a lovely game for you to kill a couple of hours, admire some lovely scenery and call it a day. Hey, if you have kids, I'd vouch for the game being kid friendly too. After your second hour and 40th snoopsee - a fluffy and mischievous creature that infests all
- you'd feel that you are 8 years old again.

A very deep and satisfying 4x SciFi game with a TBS strategic mode and RTS tactical mode which alternates bursts of action with slow-paced decision-making.
Pros:
- Very deep 4x strategic and tactical gameplay
- AI auto-resolution of battles & single-player battle speed control
- Interesting, modular ship design; design attributes
- Ships range from tiny to very large, and all sizes remain potentially useful throughout the game
- Fleet, supply, trade, sensor sphere mechanics
- 3D Political map
- Stealth ships, minefields, shields, beam weapons, psionics, space stations, asteroid bombardment, random menaces, diplomacy
- Good story background
- Varied races, with deep gameplay-level differences
- A huge and randomised tech tree
- Dedicated developer support, constant patch releases, good community tutorials
- Integrated global in-game chat
- Other games in the same universe expand upon the story
- Lots of references to other Science Fiction works
Cons:
- There are still some bugs and minor unimplemented features
- Takes a lot of memory, sometimes slowing down the game on older systems
- Some features could use some polishing, especially the more obscure menus and UI widgets
- AI diplomacy still 'feels a bit off'
- No story-driven campaign

Still, I won't deny enjoying its cutesy-horror style. And while your overall movement speed is fairly slow, I like how maneuverable your kitty is, with double-jumps, wall-jumps and air-dashes giving you plenty of options for navigating the (very easy) obstacle courses.
If you're looking for an extremely casual platformer with just a pinch of moodiness, maybe this would be worth it at a sale price. If you want a short, simple platformer that's actually a challenge however, maybe give LOVE a try instead. And if you want a game that will satisfy you for any extended period of time, definitely look elsewhere.

I have been enjoying this game sense September, its extremely fun for me, but theres something I have been noticing in reviews sense the quest change, miss information. So, I will be bringing in everyones favorite subject, Math, to show you all that the change, was actually VERY good.
Before the change to the quests, you, on average, would get 50-70 gold a day, and this number fluctuated because you never had an always set number, the quests were either 20-30 gold for completing them.
Now after the changes, we now will always have 2 quests, 1 which tells you to play a certain faction 4 times for 20 gold (Not win, just play), and a 50 gold quest, which on average will be completed in only 8 games, and you are able to complete these quests simultaneously, so on average you will be spending 8 games on the game to finish all your quests.
So after the change, you will ALWAYS get 70 gold a day if you play 8 games a day on average, but it doesn't stop there, as you get 20 gold for your first win of the day, and 15 gold every time you win 3 games.
So in 8 games, if you are able to win 6/8 of them, you will be getting an extra 50 gold for just winning games.
So, 20 + 20 + 15 + 15 + 50 = 120 gold a day.
That is much more than what you would get before the quest change was made.
Now if you play a full week, 8 games a day, and you do not spend a single gold, you will be getting 120 X 7 = 840 Gold a week.
So, solely from playing the game daily, for maybe 2 hours a day, you equivilantly have made 10 dollars for absolutely free. (10 dollars because 7 orbs in the armory costs 9.99 if you pay in real life cash)
Note: I am not garanteeing you will always get that much gold a day, sometimes you have good days and other times you have bad times when it comes to matchups, this is solely through calculations on what your best day would be.

Thomas Was Alone is a thought-provoking puzzle platformer created from the mind of Mike Bithel. The game originally started as a flash game back in 2010, before slowly making its way to Steam and  console systems a few years later.  As the player, you control Thomas-AT-23-6-12, or Thomas for short, an artificial polygon that has taken on a form of free thinking and is now questioning the world around him. As you progress the levels, you'll encounter and control several other characters, each with their own shape, narrated personality and unique ability to help you guide your way to the end of each level.
The story takes place within a computer mainframe that is run by a company known as "Artificial Life Solutions". Due to a glitch in the mainframe or some other unknown error, several of the polygon AI have become suddenly self-aware and see the computer mainframe as the world in which they live. Each newly aware shape takes on a different personality: some more eager than the rest, one a little more scared than the others, while one is just worried about being used for her ability and another just wants to be a superhero.  While every character is narrated by a single person (Danny Wallace), each personality is as different as the shapes they come in; Mr. Wallace does a phenomenal job.
Each shape's ability needs to be used to some degree to reach the end of the level: some jump higher than others, some float in water, some are tall, some are small, some defy gravity...etc. It is your job to guide these guys to the end. As you progress the story, you'll meet a new cast of characters, new puzzles to solve and more about the world Thomas and gang live in. There's a bit more to the story than first impressions realize and it's an intriguing story to flesh out over the course of the game. In total, there are ten segments of the game to play through, each with ten levels per segment.
The difficulty of Thomas Was Alone consists of a very fine, gradual learning curve. The game does not suffer from issues of spiking difficulties or unfair level design, which gives the game a very mellow tone alongside the pleasant narration, making it a fun experience, not a frustrating one. I'm not the greatest platformer around, so if I can do it, you can too. ^_-
In the end, Thomas Was Alone is a light-hearted joy to experience. I'd dive more into the plot, but I don't  want give away spoilers for those that have yet to play the game and have been lucky enough to not spoil it for themselves. You'll have to find out what has happened to Thomas and his friends, how have they become sentient, what are the "shifters", what's the pixel cloud about and who are the "Architects?
There's always something a game can improve on, but I feel hard-pressed to pinpoint what exactly I would change about this one. The positives truly do outshine any issues I did experience while playing it.


Overall, Thomas Was Alone is a gem. I purchased this game on a whim a while ago based on other reviewers and was pleasantly surprised with it. The story is charming, the levels are fun, the characters are unique and interesting (even as colorful shapes that don't speak) and it all flows so seamlessly together. There are very few games I play more than once, especially when I complete them entirely, but Thomas Was Alone is definitely one of them. Check it out if you have not done so already! It's worth the try.

Thomas Was Alone is a course of maps you have to complete with geometric shapes. Each shape has different abilities to help guide through the levels. It's a quite simplistic game really. The game rely on responsive and excellent gameplay.
You have to work with your buddies to achieve the goal. Once you did you progress to the next one. It has no cutscenes, so it's pretty much jump-to-action and it sort of reminds me of the old internet puzzle games. The game takes around 4-5 hours to complete, but since the game wasn't particularly hard, it has a high replayability value, since you can always come back a year later and have the exact same experience.
The graphics are very minimalistic. It is almost like an old Atari 2600 game, where you have to imagine what the characters and levels look like. Back when a white dot was bomb and you can have the same experience with this game. Its a big pixelated masterpiece.
The only voice you will hear throughtout the story is the narrator, who explains who Thomas is and why he is alone. He has that kind of
voice and humor, which makes you stop and actually listen. The soundtrack is beautiful, calm music mixed with 8 bit tunes. It makes the experience so much more enjoyable.

I'm giving " Nearwood - Collector's Edition" another of my grudging recommendations.  Technically, the game is pretty good:  good graphics and excellent voice acting are the big positives.  For minor negatives, there were a couple of puzzles with issues in the main game.  At one point, you have to set a clock.  But, unless I missed something, there's nothing that tells you what to set it to.  Looking at the Guide and some walkthroughs gives an answer.  But, the hints are given for a 12 hour clock and the clock is a 24 hour one.  Yet, the answer works.  Then there's a set of constellations you're supposed to show.  There's no indication anywhere what the constellations are supposed to look like.  So, you're just randomly rotating stars until something takes.
The big problem, though,  is the intended audience.  The story is written for children.  Young children.  Most of the puzzles are simple enough for them.  But, there are several puzzles that are hard.  Really hard.  So, if you play the game with your child, it'll be fine most of the time.  But, at other times, it'll be too hard.  If you play it by yourself (as an adult), the silly story will irritate you, the simple puzzles might bore you, and the difficult ones might frustrate you.  So, again, there's an audience mis-match.
I got a total of 5.5 hours out of the game (4.2 hours in the main game and another 1.3 hours in the bonus chapter).  So, by my measure, the game is a bit overpriced at it's current list price of about $10.

Short and sweet: Dont buy the game, dont support the devolopers. The game has had a year of patches and features are still non-functional, the AI is laughable, and there are still bugs and crashes.
The Nitty Gritty: The developers put out the game as a steaming mess, almost every feature in the game non-functional. Literally, every feature, from combat to building to trading to diplomacy. Everything was horrendous. After a year and a 'free' expansion, the game still has features and techs that don't function. Unfortunately, the rate of patches and updates released for it has slowed, as the developer has essentially run out of money to fund it, instead having to turn to other games to try and garner the neccessary funds to continue releasing patches.
In essence, the game is a traditional turn-based 4x, with a focus on combat rather than the micro-management of an empire. Credit given where it is due, the combat is pretty, with satisfying weapons and ships that look great when they go boom. The game uses an armor-matrix system instead of health to determine the damage ships take, with boxes of armor mitigating damage till weapons penetrate the hull, and even then you have to hit something critical to put the ship out of commision. Of course, its hard to tell what the critical hits actually do, because it provides little information in game, forcing you to go to an external wiki.
The tech tree is satisfying, with tons of different options and plenty of weapons, enforcing the focus on fighting. You can construct stations and devote them to each of the various trees to help you develop techs faster, giving you an edge on the opponent, but it can get expensive quick. Stations are also fairly easy to kill, so must be defended. For veterans of the original game, the tech tree doesnt go much higher than antimatter, but is diverse enough to make you want to see everything in it. The addition of battle riders, smaller ships carried into battle by larger ones, is welcome, though the interface for working with them is frustrating, making you assign them to each ship capable of carrying them, rather than just filling them up. Micromanagement where there should be an option to bypass it makes the game frustrating in several situations like this, especially when its in referance to a bunch of ships that are going to get blown away and have to be replaced every battle.
The UI is usable, with everything fairly clear and easy to understand. Everything is controlled by sliders, allowing you to easily dedicate your empire to production or research, while still allowing you to drill down and make planets do specific tasks for you. The Empire Overview is another section that could use some more explanation, as some of the sliders seem arbitrary but serve purposes, such as the ones relating to security. Most of the complexity in the interface could be easily served by a tutorial, which the game lacks, instead relying on an overlay which you can toggle which is supposed to point out how everything works.
As of this writing, most things are functional, with combat not crashing all the time, trade working as intended, and the interface being usable, if not sometimes cryptic. However, the AI is still lacking any challenge at all to a human player, end of turn times are still bad, and diplomacy is still in what essentially appears to be place-holder graphics, with little to no built-in explanation of what anything does. Several technologies are not working, with vague descriptions of what they should do. The developers have done a good job of making it playable, and for that I applaud them, but the state of the game at release  was unforgiveable and should not be forgotten.
Overall, the game is playable and moderately fun, with combat being the highlight of the game. Lousy AI makes it rather repetitive unfortunately, because it forces you to fight over every single planet they own. Diplomacy is still cryptic, and turn times are still a little long, but you can now get through an entire game from start to finish. I recommend playing it with your friends if at all, because that is the only challenge you will get with it, and the only way the diplomacy makes any sense. The unfortunate reality of having to have the wiki open in another window at all times is frustrating, because all the information should be given in game, but is not.
I still do not recommend buying it, even with the developers attempts to make good by their players, because it was unnacceptable to launch it in such a state, and judging by the rate of updates now, it will never be in a complete state. If you dont mind learning the interface and stumbling through things, then you can find some enjoyment in it.

A good game that seemingly got screwed by the "kitchen sink" effect. Very ambitious of a game - 3d tactical space battles that don't feel like a cheese fest or "just get everything as close as possible and fire away". There's not much rock-paper-scissors stuff - though you can adapt your ships and tactics, there's no guarentee that it'll be a completely effective counter to your enemies. On top of that, even though the races share the same tech trees, each get a few 'race specific' techs, and you're not even guaranteed to be able to research every technology - some trees may be almost completely unobtainable without salvaging the enemy's ships. Save game files are in SQLite, so grabbing an editor can help with situations where something has gone haywire - which does happen occasionally.

This game was terrible when it started because the game was full of bugs and it was still in alpha stage (not even beta!) when they released it. The company basically had runned out of money to continue so they released the game as is to get money to keep developping the game! Well 2 years later, they kept their promise, which is a rarity in the games company world! and now the game is great! The bugs are pretty much gone, the new faction the loa is pretty original and well, if you like deep space strategy, this game is up your alley.
The only thing is that the learning curve is pretty steep for a newcomer. Put the game on EASY difficulty and don't worry if you still get beaten up the first or second game. Just explore the tek tree, which change each game you play and depends in part on the faction you play! No mini-maxing here, you have to play with the tek you got! Also, the tek description is often imprecise in indicating what it does It does not give you hard numbers. For example, you get a laser but is it better than bullets? The damage number says the laser is inferior but in an actual battle, against drones and missiles, the laser is more useful. Against ships, it hit like a wet noodle which is fun to eat but not so much to beat a ship with! ;-) Thats why you need a few games at first to feel out what the tek actually do, especially the combat ones. But you get the hang of it pretty fast unless you're brain damaged or something. If you are, then what the heck are you playing this game for?
You can customize your ships to your heart content, each faction has a unique mode of travel through space, which means a different strategy for each faction. They even got different toughness of their ship. Also different speed.
The ai is pretty tought. If you let it expand too much, you're going to get screwed pretty fast, but if you expand too much,  you're also going to be in a rough place! Hehehehe! The 'Hard' difficulty is for insane megalomaniac who micromanage the hairs on their butts to manage to eck out a win. It's THAT tought.
There are also a boatload of random encounters, that you can adjust how much of them you want, from none at all to one knocking on your door every turns! And they range from mere annoyance to mega dangerous crap in your pant system killer who basically eradicate your system from the universe! That one is pretty ouch! But how much you laugh when you see it go into your ennemies territory! hehehe
So all in all, now a great game to play.

I have a very difficult time pressing "no," on my recommendation, because I really do want to like this game. I loved the first Sword of the Stars, and had a lot of faith in Kerberos, even with the botched launch of this title. With that being said, though, even as someone who enjoys grand strategy games, I can just not seem to get into this particular game even after racking up almost 90 hours with it. From an ergonomic standpoint, there are just far too many clicks to do any one thing. Rather than just selecting a fleet and sending it somewhere, you have to use a mission system which can only deploy a fleet to a designated system for a few turns at a time. It's impossible to simply park a fleet in a system and have it keep things safe, without also owning that system. Even then... it's a little frustrating.
I get what that's supposed to accomplish; I understand the mechanic of linking deployment patterns to a "real" military, but I prefer the more abstracted version in the previous game. On top of that, station construction is completely tedious; most turns I skip it completely because it's simply boring to click through dozens of systems with several bases each, trying to remember which system had the weapons lab and which had the power plant lab, etc.
Graphically, it's stunning in space combat. The ship design option is nice, though again a little tedious in some cases. Combat, like I said, looks good, but is vary annoying to run through because of the user interface and the massive scope of planetary systems -- sometimes it takes several turns to even encounter an enemy, and yet the game makes the combat take quite a long time. Randomized research is nice.
Turn times are awful, even on an i7 Ivybridge. Make sure you've got something on Netflix to keep you busy.
I'm sure a lot of people will try to say that I'm just not hardcore enough to like this game, but... Well, perhaps that's true. I don't have the patience to sort through many, many menus to do simple tasks, and I'm frustrated by wait times and the AI's inability to pose a challenge, along with the developers' very poor documentation (along with a surly community manager...). I will give it to them, in terms of spirit -- they tried very hard. Unfortunately, I think we're just going to have to wait for SOTS III for them to get back to the glory of the original game.

To play a 6 or more player map WILL result in unbelievable turn times, so much so that I took to reading an ebook between turns after a few hundred turns.  I was up to a minute plus after a few hundred turns, ie 60 mins of waiting per 60 turns... I had a black edition AMD machine 6 cores 3.8ghz, 16gb ddr3 1600mhz ram, ssd install drive and a £380 graphics card. Who the hell was it designed for? As the majority with dual core processors in the 3ghz range and 4gb ram must love 1v1 i guess.
So.. I very begrudgingly give it a thumbs up (Edit- see below for change) for the dedication shown in trying to patch it on an up until recently regular schedule. The potential for this game is outstanding, it has not sadly reached that potential. Ill still be checking back on this periodically which says something in itself.

A good Railroad simulator.
It is extremely user friendly compared to Railroad Tycoon 1 and 2, but it feels smaller (maps) and the rules are much more visible here.
You connect towns, deliver goods based on suppy and demand. Towns can level up over time when you do so, which allows you building additional manufacture plant (up to 3). Game tells you which town supplies goods and how many, so it is really a simple task, compared to RRT 1 and 2, where you had to know which building needs what and had to check what ammounts are available.
You can buy and sell stock to take over enemies if you play vs AI or multiplayer.
Patents and new locomotives are unlocked over time. You can colour the trains, build tracks by drgging them.
Overall I liked the game but SOMEHOW this feels more like a toy compared to old RRT games.
7/10 for me. Still recommended, not many simulation games like this gets made and it was a decent job.

Video version of this review:
This is a platform game where you solve puzzles, collect coins and keys, bring children to their ghosts, or souls, or whatever they are, and defeat mice and cat zombies.
You meet up with your ghost mom and she tells you she’s proud of you for collecting so many pennies. Okay, so that’s all you have to say to me? Nothing important at all? Not even an objective? Well, getting to the end of this haunted house is basically the only objective you have. Oh, also, childish misspelling. If that doesn’t make a high quality game, I don’t know what does.
The game starts off rather easy. I got through the first half of the game with almost no problems. These puzzles are hardly even a challenge. Although it does get harder in the second half, with spikes added to walls, and cat ghosts tucked away in a space you need to go through. It’s kinda like Mario, where you have to lure the ghosts away by making them follow you, and then slipping past them.
It’s not exactly the most interesting game to play, due to the slightly lower level of challenge than I am used to. But hey, at least it has cute cats.
The one thing I really don’t like about this game is the wall jumping. You can’t seem to jump immediately after you touch the wall again. In order to go faster up the wall you have to actually wait half a second after touching the wall before you press the jump button again. It’s kinda ridiculous.
I had a fair bit of trouble figuring out how to beat the final boss. You can’t attack her for whatever reason while she’s stirring up her brew in the toilet. Every time you try, you get hurt. What you actually have to do is let her shoot the ground with her magic. This makes an enemy appear, and you have to kill it. You have to do this three times before a key appears, which leads to the locked up child, and you have to bring her to her ghost thing. Then the enemy ghosts disappear and the witch starts flying around on her spoon. Now you can attack her.
Like I said, it’s not particularly interesting. It’s only 45 minutes long, but it’s not really a bad game. I’ll still recommend this. I mean, it has cute cats. That’s a thing.

The Original Crysis was an excellent adventure, full of tactical options, interesting (although simple) plot, and unique mechanics, all brought together by an amazing engine. Sadly, Crysis 2 seems to drop EVERY ball it was handed.
The plot is almost non-existant, as if they wrote five minutes of story and dragged it out over eight hours. Half the game they don't even tell you what's going on. They put you in this super suit and just expect you to walk from point A to B for four hours, killing people who try to kill you.
The tactical options are all there, but they shove them down your throat, telling you that there are new tactical options available every checkpoint, literally marking where you should stealth or snipe from effectively. It takes the decision making process out completely, and the whole game plays like a tutorial.
Even the engine seems less impressive than the original game, with poor AI and meager graphics.
I loved the first game, but this entry turned me off of the series entirely. Do yourself a favor, just enjoy the Original game, and steer clear of this mess.

After playing this for a while, quitting for a year and coming back it's basically same♥♥♥♥♥♥different toilet.
Let me be fair and say that the game is overall better than it was at release, and a year ago. It's "decent" fun at times now for sure, and the base gameplay is initally interesting. Very cool idea on paper with some fantastic animation and sound work.
But it's so marred with bull♥♥♥♥♥♥that it's hard to genuinely have fun and not just get irritated.
WORST ISSUES: #1 Gameplay Balance:
This game feels like it was not balanced for 1v1 or 4v4. It feels like they never comitted to either. Overal, it's very spammy and cheesy. Many heroes will just abuse 1 sequence of vortex unblockables to try to kill you as fast as possible. Or you will be grab spammed and thrown off ledges. The latter isn't really an issue once you get better and consistently grapple-break, but for new players it's going to be frustrating and something you have to get used to.
4v4 gameplay boils down to roaming with your team mates and gang- rap ing the other players to take objectives. But the game feels so clunky and ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ whenever mutltiple players are involved that it's just frustrating rather than fun or engaging.
Often times you will be going for an execution or a punish on a grounded opponent just to get whacked in the back of the head and interrupted by an enemy or your own team mate. (yes there is mild Team damage)
It's such a common occurence but it almost never feels natural or fair. The combat was clearly made with 1v1 in mind as the focus, so when forced to fight multiple enemies, it's a mashy♥♥♥♥♥♥fest.
Revenge mechanic is supposed to balance this but it only serves to make the combat that much more random feeling and volatile. Which may work sometimes to help you turtle and buy time, but it isn't fun.
1v1 isn't much better. Because some heroes were designed with 1v1 in mind while others pale in comparison.
For example, Valkyrie and Centurion are god mode with their mix-ups and free damage flow charts from basically landing one hit, while characters like Conq and Lawbringer are slow, low damage garbo and have to work way too hard to beat everyone else. It doesn't help that the DLC heroes are ungodly powerful compared to everything else for the most part. Probably to try to get you to buy them.
XP and Steel payout for 1v1 duels is also low, so it's not a viable way to level/grind compared to Dominion/4v4..which brings me to ..
#2 Progression:
Because the progression system requires you to grind for so long just to get one character prestiged enough to get blue/purple gear (Without it you will be stomped by stronger players), you have VERY little incentive to switch around and play different heroes. You will be back to level 1 with poop gear and spend another 30-80 hours (without boosts) getting reamed, even if you are decently skilled.
After about 60 hours of mostly playing conquerer, he's still not at prestige 3 which is the minimum to start unlocking purple gear. Most of that time spent without "Champion Status" XP/Steel boosts of course.
The fact that a $60 game requires you to have to buy the season pass and a bunch of boosts just to unlock the content and play competitively is baffling and stupid beyond reason. This feels like a free to play game in many aspects, but not in a good way.
-Connection isssues aren't nearly as bad as they used to be, though match making is still pretty slow at times and is prone to disconnecting.
TLDR: I'd be able to overlook a lot of the issues if this was free to play..but it's not. This game is not worth $60 at all. For $60 you are buying into a F2P-esque, grindy experience that punishes you for being low leveled/geared or switching characters.
I admit there is some personal bias here coming from playing more balanced Fighting games like Tekken and SF5, but what fun I had was often marred by glaring balance issues, low skill ceiling/cheesy combat mechanics and unstable and slow/spotty connections with the servers/ P2P opponents.
R6 Siege has the same issues with how long it takes to unlock stuff, but at least that game is only $15 now despite initially being like $40.
I can't honestly recommend getting this game unless it goes free to play or gets drastically reduced in price. And even then...prepare to grind for many hours or shovel out more money for the season pass benefits.

Pony Island advertises itself as a horror game, essentially using the "Pony Island" aesthetic as juxtapostion to make itself that much creepier.  From the steam page all the way through the game, Pony Island tries to put more beneath the surface than is immediately apparent.  However, while this brilliantly acontributes to the games unsettling atmosphere early on in the game, the story reaches beyond the skill of the writing, resulting in a dissapointing and ultimately skippable experience.
Your main gameplay will consist of playing Pony Island, which requires increasingly precise jumping and aiming of your ranged attack, and the Coding sections, in which you solve puzzles in your quest against the game itself.
I enjoyed playing this game. I enjoyed it quite a lot.  But my pleasant feelings drained quickly as the game concludes.
The developer was clearly not content with leaving the story as it was, and tries to reach for "meta commentary" that is neither consistent with the game's lore nor interesting.  Aside from some oddly humourous asides, the game has no more to say about video games than Undertale, and does so in a much less entertaining fashion, mainly due to the lack of meaningfull interaction with any interesting characters.
The game is cheap and will give you a few hours of enjoyment.  However if you are anything like me, the clear potential lost [edit: ad hominem attack was here] will take more away than the good begining ever gave.  Regardless of whether youre looking for puzzles, horror, or meta medium commentary, you would be better off looking elsewhere.

Recommended for the hardcore 4X fan only.
This game had THE worst launch I've ever seen (and I was there for Anarchy Online's launch).  When this came out, nothing worked.  Even the game option menus were disabled!  It was a total and absolute rip-off where completing a game was downright impossible.  But the developers worked HARD on the game after launch and have gotten this game on its feet.
This is the most detailed 4X game I've ever played.  The star map is actually 3D and when battles happen you don't just roll some dice, you actually play the battles out in an RTS-style interface.  Ship customization is done by picking from different section types then selecting weapons and special equipment for those sections.  There's a pretty vast selection of equipment to pick from, too.
The big controversial part of this game for me is the mission system.  When you tell a fleet to go do something (scout, patrol, whatever) in most games the fleet will go, do whatever it's supposed to do, and stay there.  In SotS2, the fleet will go out, do whatever it's supposed to do for a few turns, then return home.  You can change where 'home' is for a fleet but you can't select unpopulated planets for that.  On the one hand, this makes sense to me.  There are only so many peanut butter sandwiches you can store on a ship so it makes sense that they need to come back and restock.  On the other hand, it slows the pace of the game down and adds complexity.  I still can't decide if the extra realism is worth it.
The most enjoyable feature of the old SotS game is, IMHO, the variety in races and that translates over to SotS 2 just fine.  You can't make custom races but each race is VERY different than the others.  The method of propulsion is different, technology strenghts and weaknesses are different, some races can mount more weapons than others, and so on.  When you get right down to it, switching between the Liir and the Humans in this game will give you much more different gameplay than building a custom race in most games.
So I recommend the game but only to the serious 4X enthusiasts looking for a lot of depth.  If you're new the genre then you should probably stick with Civilization or Endless Space.  If you come out of those games wanting a lot more detail then this might be your game.
P.S.  Star Fleet Battles fans - you'll find your swordfish drones and plasma shotguns waiting for you.  Enjoy.

As an avid player of Hidden Object Games, I have certain preferences and pet peeves. Nearwood satisfies almost all of my preferences: beautiful art, a main character with a personality who is not unfathomably illogical, multiple puzzle types, a skip button, side collectibles (SNOOP-SEES FTW), and a plethora of unbelievably adorable creatures. But really though, that cat-thing in the gnome workshop. My heart stopped.

The trailer here poorly represents what ended up being one of the very best games in this genre I've ever played. The art is absolutely stunning, the voice acting is very well done, the puzzles are thoughtful and entertaining, the soundtrack is amazing, and the storyline is solid.
It's not actually "Hidden Object" - there were only a couple of "hidden parts" puzzles and zero HO puzzles. It's average in length (my full play-through took 5 hours, which is pretty standard), though I found the bonus chapter to be a bit shorter than is standard for this type of game. (But hey, it's a bonus chapter.) I also found the ending to be a bit abrupt.
This game is a fantastical story, not horror. Zero jump scares, which I appreciated very much. Good drama without feeling overdone, characters I could identify with, and omg the cuteness of the animals is out of control!
I have played dozens of this kind of game, and Nearwood is at the top of the class. If this genre is your thing, you will absolutely love this game. I highly, highly recommend it!

While I'm generally not a major fan of Call of Duty titles, Black Ops III is a great game to have in your collection if you enjoy FPS shooters on PC. Why? Black Ops III is the only AAA shooter on PC that supports BOTH local split-screen multiplayer AND the steam workshop to easily download and install mods (whether maps, weapons, game modes, or the like). These features alone make the game a great title to have to play with friends, and to play for a long time with its substantial community mod support.
In addition to those features, Black Ops III is just a downright fun game to play with lots of different (default) modes to keep you entertained. Black Ops III includes... Standard Campaign, a separate "Nightmares" Zombies Campaign, a "Freerun" arcade mode, the "Dead Ops Arcade II" top-down style arcade shooter, the standard Zombies wave survival mode and standard online multiplayer/matchmaking. Not only are all these fun and interesting, but local split-screen is supported in every one of them.
While there are definitely some cons to this game - most notably the overpowered aim-assist for controllers which is incredibly annoying to play against online, as well as some weapon balance issues - the cons are largely outweighed by the many features that Treyarch incorporated into the game.
Definitely recommend you pick up this title when you find it on sale.

Beat interface is counterintuitive.
I've played a lot of rhythm games before this - Dance Dance Revolution, Beatmania, Pump It Up, Rhythm Tengoku/Heaven, etc.
One of the primary aspects of a Rhythm Game is should it have a very straightforward interface - it should be obvious at what point in the beat you're supposed to press the button to get a proper ranking.  There's no feedback from the game if you push the button in tune with the beat, and auto-failing after a mis-press is extremely poor game design for a rhythm game.  Most other rhythm games have some sort of life meter that gives you room for error should you miss a beat or *almost* get it right.  The two concentric circles you have for your beat meter do not seem to be in flow with the music.  This game seems to have taken the "Nintendo hard" difficulty of game design by making you lose and only providing checkpoints halfway through a song, this is incompatible with the genre.
As another reviewer put, the default music lacks variety - too much EDM, not enough other songs that are iconic to the genre (techno, trance, etc.)
I'm surprised this game has a hardcore mode considering the default mode appears to be *the* hardcore mode.
If you want a game that has a great soundtrack that also makes you move/platform to a rhythm, get BitTrip Runner and its sequel.  It too has "you die you start over" difficulty but it's way more intuitive and better paced than this game.

I didn't get caught up in Hearthstone. I've played M:tG competitively for something like 20 years now, and the F2P digital CCG was a phenomenon I just wasn't interested in. Duelyst, though, does have my attention.
By combining the strategic element (deckbuilding) and the tactical element (sequencing) of a CCG with the movement and positioning of a tabletop wargame, Duelyst manages to be more than the sum of its parts. This strange alchemical concoction of disparate game types scratches an itch I didn't know I had. The presentation, too, is nothing to sneeze at: the pixel art style is executed as well here as I've ever seen it.
September 2017 Update: Many recent Steam reviews whinge about microtransactions or claim that the game is "pay to win". I'll be honest: I don't like the Bandai/Namco deal at all, and I wish that Counterplay had found a publisher that wasn't looking to "optimize" their revenue by using a mobile-esque currency model that doesn't map money spent exactly onto items received.
That being said, going so far as to call the game "pay to win" is a bit ridiculous. You are talking about a game that is very up front about it's "collectible" element. You don't start on an even playing field to established players, so you have two options:
1. Spend maybe $50 on Orbs and read a Reddit thread on disenchanting, then build a top-tier competitive deck, or maybe even two (depending on what you opened).
2. Grind your way up the ladder with basic cards, learn the mechanics, and craft your way to a top-tier competitive deck.
These are your choices in basically every digital (or paper, for that matter) CCG to one degree or another. It's an essential, core component of experiences like this. So if you're not about collecting things, maybe don't play games that revolve around doing just that?

I'll start this review by saying the Linux (Ubuntu 14.4, Ubuntu kernel 4.5 Wily, most recent stable version) version of this is plagued with bugs. about a quarter of a second of input lag, screen tearing, music plays even when muted, audio stuttering, windowed mode barely works, and I can't adjust the resolution.
I occasionally have audio stuttering on certain ALSA applications, so there is a chance that's what's causing the audio to stutter.
The story isn't the best. You play as multiple different cubes and rectangles of different sizes. These characters are actually AI who have become sentient, and are trying to escape deletion. The story is cute, but forgettable, and it certainly isn't bad.
The graphics are actually really nice in my opinion. While they aren't supre impressive, they look great. The mix of mainly squareish geometry, water, and lighting system work together really really well and everything just looks beautiful. A fun little game you'll probably sink lots of hours into.
- Big variety of developer created maps and endless amount of community made maps, some of which are bound to make you go "How in the hell did he manage to pull that off??"
- A big variety of visual customization that can be bought with in-game currency(cheese you gather on maps) as well as the option to pay for all of it with premium currency.
- Expansive skill trees that will make your experience as a Shaman(Help those mice get to the cheese!) unique. Invest skill points in various building pieces to make sturdy structures the mice can safely cross. Or maybe you're even more risky and want to invest into a mass teleport. Safe to say not everyone will make it to cheese and back. Finally, if the hard Shaman job got to you - all those mice not wanting to go back into the mouse hole, even though you got them their cheese, or simply refuse to grab it - invest in some cannonballs and send those that got out of line flying out of the map!
- Although the game seems simple at first glimpse, there is a lot of skill involved and sometimes it may get very competitive. The statistics, beside counting the mice you saved as shaman, cheese you brought as shaman, cheese you brought as a normal mouse are also counting cheese you brought first on the map. And to be that first one you'll have to put all you skills to use. Timing, risking it, special techniques such as wall jumping(wj) and corner jumping(cj, also sometimes reffering to cannon jumping) and much more.
To practice in the basic techniques there are special bootcamp maps. To get to the cheese with these you'll have to pull off such things you didn't even know were possible. Be aware though - there's a long way full of frustration and mistakes that are gonna be made until you learn it all and finally get to the cheese. There is also no Shaman in bootcamp to help you.
- Various fun minigames you can participate in to earn cheese.
- Lots of events and updates, adding more and more content, some of which is event-exclusive.
- The game also has lots of social elements to it. From simple emotions to show how you're feeling to the mice around you, to chat window under the map. With chat comes the usual Friend List and Ignore List to make your socialization a bit easier. There are tribes(guilds) you can create or join. There are language specific servers also.
I personally spent more than a hundred(if not couple hundred) hours in it and been playing it since 2010, well before it arrived on Steam.
Overall this game is a great time sink and I recommend for you to at least give it a go, since it's a free and small(weight-wise) game!

Sid Meier's Railroad Tycoon was the third game I ever purchased back in the 1800's, no, I'm kidding (Though it feels like it at times.) I actually purchased it in 1990 not long after acquiring my first desktop PC. I have played the series religiously since. I have roughly 100 hours in this game in the original 2006 disc retail box version. It certainly isn't a successor to the venerable Railroad Tycoon III, but it's still quite enjoyable if you realize this going in. The game is more of a "beer & pretzels" type real time strategy game with an emphasis  on attracting more casual type gamers. The game has a charming art style more akin to an HO or N scale model train layout than the ostensible real world look of the previous Railroad Tycoon games.
Industry acquisitions and playing the stock market against other AI railroad barons seem to have become more important in this title with train consists and railroad track signaling unfortunately taking a back seat. Being able to build your own train consists is possible (and necessary), but the importance seems to have been watered down compared to previous titles. Manual signaling has been removed altogether. The scenarios and their variety are adequate, but pale dim in comparison to Railroad Tycoon III. Firaxis encouraged fans to build maps and scenarios to add to the scenarios available. These additional scenarios can still be found on fansites. The game originally included multiplayer. Be advised, this feature has been truncated from the game entirely. The Steam version of Sid Meier's Railroads! has no multiplayer feature whatsover.
My boxed version would not run on Windows Vista without crashing to the desktop continually. It runs on my current iteration of Windows 7 64-bit, but there is a known bug concerning multi-core processors the game doesn't like. I noticed specifically when building long stretches of track I would get crashes to the desktop. I've played the Steam version for over two dozen hours as of this writing, and I rarely get a desktop crash anymore.
I miss the previous versions of Sid Meier's wonderful railroad games, but oddly, this one has become my favorite of the series. Despite its lack of seriousness, it's still challenging. The game exudes Sid Meier's influence in every pixel. It's colorful art style blooms beautifully, and the sound design which has been lovingly crafted really adds to the ambience. Music from each time period sets the tone and changes along with the times. Zooming in to view the busy animations of each industry and city building is the icing on the cake.
Very easy casual game.
