It's no easy feat to try and one-up one of the most immersive FPS shooters whose graphical prowess is so great that it's still used as a benchmark for modern computers almost a decade later. But due to the stiflingly hasty nature of game development, the sequel suffers from crippling linearity and environments that just don't have the same sheen as its older brother. But, again, in the time frame of crysis being the only game that people talked about, this was made an acceptable sequel back in the day because of significant improvements to player combat. But now? No. If you've played the first one, you're likely going to play the best out of them all.
Some aspects that stuck out to me in a great way was the flexible cover system that allows you to fully peer around objects in the first person perspective ala Time Crisis, or Call of Juarez: Bound in Blood. A customizable upgrading system for your abilities would also incentivize progression, but the enemies and environments just became too predictable. What good is a combat system if the obstacles are stale and not worth overcoming? It just got to the point for me where I just cloaked my way through combat intensive areas just to speed through it.
If you've enjoyed Crysis, great. You might find a few hours of enjoyment from its sequels. But in 2017, there's just better and more inventive FPS single player games out there. Far Cry, Battlefield, Dishonored, Wolfenstein, to name a few. This game was only meant to satiate the juvenile tastes of people who wanted more of the same.

Spooky Cats is meant to be a cute platformer with a "spooky" theme. That's exactly what it claims to be, and that's exactly what it is. I can't fault it on that.
What I can fault it on is almost everything else. The art style is at the very least consistent, but there are only a handful of platform textures used throughout the game, and none of them are particularly visually pleasing. (There are cloud platforms in this, but because they're not perfectly rectangular platforms, I think a bit on the edges are uncollidable, making them look bigger than they really are.) The music consists of two (I don't remember a third, maybe there was?) songs of vastly different styles: one was a sort of ambient "spooky" one, while the other was something you'd more expect in a hardcore platformer.
Gameplay wise, it's pretty simple. You have a double jump, wall jumps, and a roll attack. I had some trouble getting wall jumps to work consistently. Jumping on enemies or rolling into them kills them...except for one floating white enemy cat. There's also another white enemy cat that looks almost identical, except that it runs on the ground, so telling the difference between the two can be difficult at times. Not that there's much punishment for it: you have three hearts that serve as health, and you have to lose them all before being forced to restart the level. Not that any of the levels get particularly tough, even near the end.
Speaking of the end, you can reach that in 30 minutes, maybe less.
In the end, Spooky Cats isn't a terrible game, but it is incredibly mediocre. When there are so many good games out there, even at the price range that Spooky Cats is available at (or even free Flash games!), I find it impossible to recommend Spooky Cats.

If you like the HOG genre, you'll enjoy this game - if you also love heavy fantasy and dreamlike visuals, you will LOVE this game.
Nearwood is definitely a cut above the average on many levels with it's excellent voice acting (voice acting alone can be uncommon), stunning graphics, pleasant music, and well-designed map/hint system. The HOGs had a really nice amount of variety, themed goals, and beautiful art. No cut-and-clip photos here!  The other puzzles ran a nice gamut of difficulties, and this game went for the gusto with having actual 'boss battle' puzzles!
If I was to have any complaint, it would be on how they animated faces for this. It worked overall, but there'd be moments when characters would look downright uncanny or unintentionally creepy. I think it would have worked better if instead of mapping a whole face over a 3d model, they had 'layered' the portions of the face to come up with a more woodcut or conventional sort of animation. As it is the faces do distort weirdly a time or two.
But that's just one nitpick about an otherwise utterly gorgeous game. This is well worth the cost - happy hunting!

It’s hard to find any other fragmented hidden object game that looks better than Nearwood, but the gameplay and plot has serious design flaws.

On the surface Nearwood looks like the poster child of fragmented object games. The excellent voice acting and the highly detailed, absolutely stunning painted graphics all promise to enchant you as soon as you hit the Play button. Sadly this beauty is skin deep.
The story is as stock as it gets: you arrive in a clichéd fairy land tortured by a clichéd zero-dimensional evil to find a clichéd relic which can deal with this menace. Same in the bonus chapter with an added cartoonish over-the-top villain monologue.
The puzzles and fragmented object scenes offer a great variety both in types and difficulty, but there are a few questionable design choices. For example the fast travel option needs to be recharged, making the map useless; and the final (match-three) puzzle is actually based on sheer luck with the promise of many retries.
Still, Nearwood is an astonishingly gorgeous game that is worth to be played just for the looks alone. Just don’t expect much more from it.

Dear diary,
I didn't expect to get emotionally invested in a bunch of quadrangles, but here we are.

On the surface it looks to be a bare-bones platformer with rudementary graphics delivered with a fancy and evocative narrative that is almost ironically suggesting of something much "deeper" than blocks on a screen.
While that's close to describing Thomas Was Alone, it misses something pretty important. Beyond serving as a zero-effort art style, the simple geometry this world and its characters are made up of has been utilized in such a way that it offers some genuinely unique platforming gameplay elements which I've never seen done before. The result is a game that's often much more brain teasing than dexterity testing, although there are spots that will require those years of platforming experience you've accumulated. I was quite fascinated by the way simple shapes could fit together to make new gameplay that actually wouldn't have worked had the game been about something other than talking rectangles.
The top-notch narrative does elevate the experience in the end. It takes a simple (though very clever), relatively short game and makes it memorable. Very worth your time.

A lot of people are probably going to be confused at why i have so many hours logged in this game yet im giving it a not reccomended rating, the main reason for that is because i have more been using this game as a makeshift amplifier, rather than the way it was intended. This game is a great way to learn how to play to an extent.  and this review is based on my personal experiences. this is not my reccomendation for your primary go to way of learning how to play Here is why:
1. the game is designed around a notes or tablature style of learning and when you are playing individual notes, it doesnt tell you what the name of the note actually is, this is really troublesome if you are planning to use this program to learn to play the bass guitar. you really should learn at least a few scales before you start to just play songs.
2. you get so used to playing the songs that you do learn to the backing tracks provided. i will explain why this is a problem after point number three.
3. the game actually makes it sound like you are playing than you actually are, and often times you can just hit random notes during a guitar solo of a song and at least get a good enough portion of it recognized as right that the game still gives you a good rating on that section.  the reason that these two are a problem is that when you go to play a song that you think you learned and think that you can play outside the game, be it showing off your newfound skill to friends or just jamming at a guitar store, you will instantly realize that you have no idea what you are doing and that you have been learning the wrong thing the whole time.
that said, the game is good i would say for those that already have some prior knowledge of how to play a guitar as it does give you a real time look at what notes are played where if you know your fretboard well enough already.  if you actually are looking to learn to play the guitar or bass, i suggest your best option is to invest in an actual music tutor.  that way you learn the right way first.  it may be more expensive that way, but it puts you better off in the long run.

Despite being pretty unknown Crimson Trigger is actually a really good game and definitely a much,MUCH better "Megaman" game than Mighty Number 9.
I raccomand this hidden gem to all the fans of challenging action platformers.

Crimson Trigger is a platformer/action/adventure type of game that is very similar to Megaman series.
At the start, players will be given a choice between 2 characters with different skills.
You get thrown into the game fairly quickly, with some backstory and cut-scenes.
The learning curve is easy and straightforward, fans of the megaman series will find the gameplay similar, whereas new players will quickly adapt to the game.
Each "area" will consist of a range of different monsters, hidden power-ups and unique bosses. There is also an added feature of an EXP bar, which allow your characters to level up as you get more kills. This recharges your health bar to full, with increase in health/mana/damage.
At the base, there is also an added customisable menu to allow you to swap out abilities or certain equipment for the upcoming battles.
I have to point out, even though the learning curve is easy, the game's difficulty is a challenge, even on "normal" mode. Bosses might have standard patterns but they can be really challenging at times.
+++ The Good +++
1) Beautiful drawn art, 3d models of characters and monsters.
2) Music fits well with the game, fast-paced and keeps you going.
3) Platformer + RPG, character progression with level-ups and ability customisation
4) There is replayability based on different characters and boss fighting strategies.
--- The Bad ---
1) Keyboard controls are a little clunky, might take a while to get used to it
2) Difficulty can be really challenging even on "normal" mode.
3) Backstory is a bit lacking and abrupt. It could work better with more cutscenes and a more polished storyline.
In conclusion, Crimson Trigger is decent, with nicely drawn art and engaging gameplay.
This game will appeal more to platformer fans who don't really care much about the story, love a challenge and just wanna jump into the action immediately.
Final Score : 7 / 10

I played through this game twice, once for story and once for completion.
It is not actually a HOG in the traditional sense; it is an extremely casual point-and-click adventure that happens to mix in a handful of HOG-like elements.
Gameplay consists of:
1. Object-based puzzles (find an object, then use it where it's needed).
2. Mini-games that utilize rotating discs, matching, pattern recognition, mazes, and other simple challenges.
3. FROG puzzles (fractured object I-spy puzzles).
4. Recipes (combine several components together to create a new item).
5. A global I-spy puzzle that requires you to spot 111 "Snoop-see" creatures across both the main game and bonus mission in order to unlock pages of a book.
This game did several things right.  The artwork is beautiful (almost Jim Henson-esque), the mini-games are fresh and creative, the adventure puzzles are intuitive, the music and voice-acting are decent, and the FROG puzzles are challenging but not frustrating.
It is a good gateway game for those new to the genre.  They do a great job of providing constructive feedback to players, and they include both a hint system and a complete walkthrough (including Snoop-see locations) for anyone who is struggling.  Additionally, on easier difficulties, the game map shows points of interest, and allows you to teleport to any screen.  As an extra little bone to players, the pages unlocked by the Snoop-see hunt provide visual clues to the game's puzzle solutions.
I would have liked them to have a stronger story hook, and to use the dialogue more effectively (the start of the game is especially slogged down with cutscenes).  I also would have liked a bit more variety in the object-based puzzles; you can only collect so many keys, handles, triangles, and seals before it starts to feel repetitious.
Another thing that bugged me was the need for precision when using objects.  If you don't interact with the right hot spot, the puzzle will not recognize the required solution.
One special note: players who are colour-blind will have difficulty with the mini-games, as many of them require colour recognition to solve.  This is a major concern because the mini-games are a rather large component of the gameplay.
Overall, I would give this game a 7/10.  It was more child-like than I expected, and there weren't really any true HOG puzzles, but the art was pretty and the mini-games were fun.  It is a decent casual game to waste a few hours with, although I wish I had earned a few steam playing cards or achievements for playing.

I have to admit that I've only recently gotten into these types of games so I bought the "Sinister Bundle" while it was on sale as it was a great value so my review may have some what may seem as petty complaints to more seasoned players.
Anyways, overall this game was entertainingly worthwhile with a few setbacks.
Story:
+ standard "girl looking for her parent(s)" fare, nothing groundbreaking but not entirely throwaway either as the fantasy elements and art are vibrant and inviting.
- Pretty much all the creatures/characters are just "there," You find an item for them (or even do nothing at all) and that's the end of them. I wished that some of them got more use, whether appearing later on in the game with another need/puzzle or even just a quick story scene.
+/- I found the ending to come at a reasonable point but it could be viewed as abrupt.
Gameplay:
- I played on expert difficulty as I don't like the flashy help and hints, but that was a big mistake and wholly not recommended for 1st playthroughs as many interactive areas are too hidden and not easily recognizable. So unless you want to waste energy clicking everywhere on the screen then I'd recommend at most the 2nd difficulty. I didn't see an option to change it mid-game so I continued on, so a lot of my time was spent going back and forth trying to find the last item of a set needed to progress and tapping like mad (I only resorted to using the in-game guide once towards the end and I was disgusted at how unobvious the spot was).
+/- Some puzzles were a complete pushover while others had more a involved challenge. But as others have said, the rules and need of some of them aren't immediately clear, to which the prospect of figuring out on your own will either excite or frustrate you (you're helper Fey does pop up with a "?" button which I assume will explain things but I never bothered with it).
+ Items found are only needed in areas 1 - 3 areas away so no crazy backtracking.
- I played on a tablet pc, which did work well, but sometimes trying to use an item on the correct area wouldn't register correctly and needed a few extra tries. I'm not sure if the tablet touch had something to do with it or there were very specific spots that needed to be hit but it was annoying.
- Other than a couple of mixing puzzles, there's no manipulation of items. I would've liked to have seen some combining and such things.
Extras:
+ Promo art and soundtrack and others. Nice set of stuff so I can't complain.
In the end, many of my gripes are pretty minor and personal so it's still easily recommendable. Thumbs up!

Now before I begin this, I want you to know that I've played around 20 hidden object games in the last couple months so I am well versed in this genre.
Nearwood blew me away. It is one of the most visually stunning hidden object games out there. I was excited everytime I accessed a new area - every scene is beautiful. The characters and creatures look great. Some of the animals are the cutest I've seen. Voice acting is better than average for this genre. The puzzles range from very easy to "ack, this is hurting my brain" but you can skip any of them, if you so desire. The length of Nearwood, especially with the bonus game, is longer than most hidden object games. And there is a very cool "boss battle" that most puzzle games lack. I do have to warn you, the hidden object aspect of the game is limited and when you hit them, you're only searching for specific item parts. However, the game is SO good that the lack of "normal" hidden object areas didn't bother me in the least. I really could go on and on about how much I enjoyed playing this. This game is finally in a playable state.
When it first came out, over a year ago now, It was an unplayable mess of memory loops and unfinished coding...
However after a lot of work by a dedicated company, the game has flourished and is actually very enjoyable.
A large and randomized tech tree ensures a long, unpredictable game, plenty of ways to customize your ship's loadout make for interesting battles and the 3D nature of the game, coupled with the different types of FTL travel, make defending a complex and enjoyble task.
The species are varied and follow from the original title, each with their own strengths and weaknesses and, as previously mentioned, their own FTL travel techniques.
Bad points are finite, but there are a few I'd like to raise:
1) The game still sucks memory like a hungry zombie with a straw, and can be quite sluggish at endgame with lower end computers
2) The diplomacy is a little underdeveloped still, and I can't remember an ally that hasn't stabbed me in the back as soon as a weakness was revealed to them.
But overall, Good game and worth the money if you're into the 4x games.

A lot of people will tell you to not buy this game, and they would be right.  It is unfinished, and was left to die.  The combat isn't great or easy to learn, the ship design can crash often, and will be extremely annoying at times.  This being said, if you can get the game for $10 or less, it is a bargain deal, and you should immediately get it.  The research tree is a lot of fun, where you may research tech that has a % to go right, or wrong.  You could research that super weapon in 10 turns, 100 turns, or never.  And this changes EVERY match, some techs will be 100% one match, and you'll never research them another.  Faction diversity, ship diversity, battles, they are purely amazing.  You'll wonder why I recommend this game, and simply, the reason it failed isn't because of poor design values, but rather because of the developer losing faith.  The game itself has flaws, but is still fun and interesting.  Travel between systems changes depending on what faction you are.  The Hivers that have the slowest ship travel time, have gates, that take forever to move into positon, one per area, the reason for this is because they have some of the biggest mobility I have ever seen.  They can instantly transport from one side of the universe to the next, by taking a gate at their homeworld, they can repel an attack, or assault an enemy, instantly.  If you build a gate at your staging area (a system you mass troops in a strategy game), and then build a corresponding gate near your enemy base, will take forever to get there though, you can instantaneously mobilize your troops to attack, or defend any system with a gate, you can move reinforcements, or colonizing units, etc.  Each faction differs, the slave takers bore their way through space and leave a trail for their ships to follow, which is one of the fastest (minus Hiver teleport) if not the fastest method of travel, however their boreholes decay over time.  The humans are the most balanced, they can fly from system to system at a rather decent rate, and have no decay, but must follow the paths between the stars to do this (predetermined paths vs creating a path).  There are even more factions.   Planetary invasions are fun.  You can research a shuttle to invade (pretty much a must), design ships for firing on planets, or even research bio plagues (including zombie plague), equip them to a ship, and fire the plague onto the planet, and laugh as after the battle, their colony slowly dies.  Its definitely not going to win any game of the year awards, and has many issues, but if you can get it cheap enough on sale, then it is definitely worth a look.

Originally, I was going to not recommend
, but then I realized it was almost midnight because I had been playing it for 3 hours straight to get to the end. Yes, the plot suffers from open-to-interpretation-osis, but the narrator is phenomenal, getting me inside the thoughts and feelings of sentient pixels. The puzzles are hard without being obtuse. The characters are charming. I could recommend this game for the uniqueness of the experience alone.
is a game with enough heart and charm to win me over despite the flaws in it's storytelling. A fun and absorbing experience.
The immersive story of selflessness an pursuit of purpose bwas marred by vague narrative. I was left scratching my head as to exactly what the characters are, and the plot blurbs every 10 levels are too removed from context to make connections to the story unless you go online and look it up. The levels start to wear on for too long, and at least 10 complex levels towards the end look like they could be the "last" one. When the last level finally arrives, the ending comes out of nowhere and I was left very dissatisfied. Part of this dissatisfaction came because the characters at the end are different from the ones at the beginning, so I felt like the journey of neither set of characters was ever really finished. This was really disappointing as the game starts off incredibly immersive, and did a great job getting me to care about some rectangles. The plot was just too lazily written out in blurbs between levels that it never came together in the end.  That said, despite that I didn't know what the characters were trying to do, I wanted them to do it. It takes pretty strong characters to do that.
As for the puzzles, they were well constructed. I enjoyed the variety without odd mechanics coming out of left field. The controls felt sloppy. I had to press the jump button about half a second before I had to jump. I was using an Xbox One controller to play, so it may be better on keyboard.
An imperfect, but enjoyable experience.

Some people may complain about the difficulty spike between the generic enemies and the bosses of each area, which there definitely is, but the bosses themselves aren't ridiculously hard.
The story is somewhat vague and is only conveyed visually, but the game does this very impressively. Instructions and guidance on how to proceed are similarly sparse, but your goals are made simple enough to understand easily, and mechanics are combat-related and can be figured out quickly.
It's a masterpiece.

There's a lot of depth here, and if you undestand what you want to accomplish, it's a great tool. Don't, however, think that RockSmith with obviate the need for guitar instruction.
For example, let's look at Session Mode. This is one of the most useful tools for learning guitar I've ever seen. But only if you have enough of a theory background to understand why it's so great. And a plan for using it to better your playing.
You need to understand some basics. What is a "root" of a scale? What is a scale? Why are there mulitple types of scales? What is different about them, and why? If you don't have any theoretical background, or a teacher who can guide you through the theory, just memorizing the Pentatonic Minor scale and its five shapes isn't going to be that rewarding. But if you understand how the patterns help map out the fretboard and provide you with a context for playing certain types of music, having Session Mode to help you memorize the patterns is a huge help. Knowing when to use a pattern, and when to break the pattern for musical effect, that's practice and experience.
The same can be said for the song learning modes. I find, personally, that the "simplified" versions of songs that are started with often lead me to mistakes farther down the line. A fingering that makes sense when I'm playing 20% of the notes in a song often doesn't carry over to the full song. And the full song typically has patterns that make sense in context, and chord voicings I wouldn't think of using unless I'm in the context of that particular point in the song with my hand already playing something else. There's usually a reason that the original composer picked those chords, and often it's locality or simplicity of transition. Not always, obviously. But the default simplified verison of the songs often server me poorly for getting to the full song.
For me, it's much better to have the full song played at a slower speed, and work on getting the progression right and speeding up. That's not the defualt, though. And unless you have enough context to know how you best learn, you're not going to know how to tweak the Song Repeater to maximize your practice sessions.
So as an adjunct to learning guitar, either with a teacher (which I recommend) or theory books, Rocksmith is fantastic. I can't recommend it highly enough. At the cost of less than a couple of lessons, you get practice help, play-along bands with dynamic arrangement, great games to focus on specifics, and a lot of good music. Just don't expect Rocksmith to teach you how to play guitar. It's a tool, and like all tools, it's about learning the strengths and weaknesses of the tool and how you apply the tool that ultimately determines what value you get from the tool.
If you want to learn guitar, buy a decent guitar, Rocksmith 2014, and get a teacher or mentor or community to help direct your practice sessions with Rocksmith towards playing what you want to play.

I really wanted to like this. I was a huge fan of Heroes of Might and Magic III, spending untold hours play and replaying it. So when I saw this and heard that it was "basically a HOMM MMO" (almost a palindrome!), I thought, I'm in! I was curious to see what they would have to give up from the HOMM concept to make it online, immediately thinking of things that would be tricky to get working. Oh well, I thought, I'll see how it turned out. It didn't really dampen my enthusiasm.
When I started playing, it brought me back, even though it felt a bit like a cheesy, dollar-store ripoff of the real thing. It still had most of the basics down and was still a lot of fun. The units didn't stack, but since there was PvP, I figured that would make some sense. In fact, the first time I was attacked by another player, I was really grateful for the attempt at balance, particularly since they had attacked while I was AFK on a phone call. (Tip: If you're playing this and need to go AFK, log out first.) I don't know how long I was gone, but my opponent's melee units were halfway across the field and his ranged had already done some damage to one of my ranged, but I feel pretty good about the fact that I won anyway. The next two people who attacked me were a bit higher level and I lost those, but I did well enough that I had hopes to get better. Anyway, as in HOMM, if you have units all of the same 'type', they get bonuses. I don't remember what that is, but I never saw anything like being able to attack twice due to morale, so I don't think it was that. Probably for the best. Interestingly, you interact with your units outside of battle as cards, each one having a charge, which is a number on the card representing the unit's 'lives', which are added to every time you get another card of the same unit.
Outside of battle is a bit strange. As others have mentioned, you don't have a town in this game and as far as I could tell there weren't any you could conquer. This makes the concept of controlling resources seem a little pointless, and for the most part, they're only used for upgrading your spells and raising the level of your units. One obviously necessary departure from  the HOMM gameplay is movement. Whereas HOMM had your hero only able to move a certain amount in a 'day' that you had to carefully manage, this game gives you a whole lot of action points and every thing you do only takes one to three of them. This feels jarring if you're an HOMM fan, particularly when you can spend one action point to go all the way across the map to the mana well and refill your mana... after
battle.
That brings me to where I started to realize that the gameplay in this was far, far shallower than HOMM and that took a whole lot of the fun out of it. The multiplayer experience of that kind of game is best when you have people physically present, either in person or through a network, each player waiting their turn at which point the other players wait for theirs, unless there's a battle, in which both players take their turns. It's difficult to point out one big thing that ruins the feeling and the fun. It was a lot of little things. Things like your ranged units being able to move and
. You can't enjoy the feeling of being so much more powerful than a wandering unit that it asks to join you. Your ability to pretty much do as much as you like without worrying about time management and distance traveled and whether you're travelling on a road or through various terrains. Only having five units at most make the battles less interesting. No towns means no sieges. Being able to replenish your mana at any time, over and over again, taking out a good amount of the challenge. And many, many other little things like these.
I'm not blaming the developers so much. I think they've done pretty much the best you can do in making this kind of game an MMO. And with the work they've and some tweaking, I'd love to see a single player/multiplayer hotseat/network real-time turn-taking version of this. Considering how much the original has fallen, it could be nice to have a good one. The trouble is that this kind of game just doesn't seem to work well as an MMO. There are things I guess you just have to do in order to make it work that thins out the gameplay and makes it very repetitive.
For what it's worth, this is definitely not pay-to-win, but had it turned out better, I'd have been happy occasionally spending a little, just to support the game. As it is, the developers have made something really solid in a lot of ways and the community is great, so I might purchase something regardless just to give a little support despite not being able to recommend this, which I hate.
Maybe there are ways to improve it. I'll probably come back from time to time to see if they find those ways. And again, if they made something single player with the issues I've mentioned (and others) resolved, it would be an easy buy for me.

The game isn't easy, not by a long shot; You need map awareness, callouts, decent aim/crosshair placement, communication, and most importantly, patience.
Ranked mode is toxic as hell, unless you have your own squad. Otherwise, you could possibly get teamkilled at the start of every round for making a mistake the round before.
It's not even the most realistic experience like some people like to assume. Just because a game has some beautifully rendered and modelled guns doesn't mean they're gonna be 100% true to their nature.
But that aside, this game has been constantly updated through the years. Say what you will about Ubisoft, but they're still making fresh, new content for this game for two years strong. Players who are just now getting the game can still compete with players that have purchased DLC, and on top of that, they can play on all of the maps as well.
The loot drop system is purely cosmetic, and none of the items exactly grant benefits over players that don't have the same gun skin.
And Ubisoft is still taking steps in the right direction, listening to the community about what the most glaring issues are (like netcode and reporting toxicity).
Rainow Six Siege isn't perfect, nor will it ever be. But it's still pretty damn good.

An incredible way of learning songs. I've been playing guitar on and off for past 6 years, without too much progress. Learning songs by playing this game is much more interesting and keeps you more motivated, as you are just playing a game. The "Learn a Song" mode is simply incredible. Songs are cut up into many parts, each of which you can go back to, have it loop over and over, slow down if you'd like to have it broken down more. There's "Session" mode  which allows you to set up a jam session with a great backtrack which can further be customized. Base game and dlc's were all on sale when I bought them and I'm definitely looking forward to putting hours upon hours into Rocksmith mastering songs. This isn't necessarily only a game, it's a great tool for musicians looking to improve.

Not only one of the best free to play games on steam but probably one of the best games on steam all together.
Incredibly deep yet incredibly simple turn based strategy game.
Alot of people will try to compare this to hearthstone and they would he right to. Their are alot of similarities. How ever, using a grid system instead of 2 sides of a board to place your cards adds an unrivalled level of depth.
The way they have balanced the cards has created a system where there is multiple win conditions, and multiple ways to achieve each win condition.
Every faction (class) has 2 generals with different bloodline spells (your classes  spell) creating multiple play styles for each faction. Yet some how they have managed to get every playstyle for every faction to feel unique and compliment the lore and look of the faction.
The ladders seasons reset at the end of every month giving substantial rewards, and the game seems to be very generous in terms of card packs, gold and spirit (dust) rewards.
Because of these things, strategy plays a much more important role then draw or calibre of deck. Almost every game is challenging and rewarding. And unlike hearthstone where it was easy to play "optimally" and lost to either bad card draws or better decks, in Duelyst, every game I lose is because I make mistakes. And whats incredible is how often you can make mistakes and how you can actively see then cost you every game.
TLDR; Incredible game, And there is no reason not to try it.

Transformice is a fun platforming game with people that will either help you to your goal or help you perish.

The initial release of Sword of the Stars II was possibly the most shambolic release of a game I have ever seen, it made Master of Orion 3 look like a masterpiece of finished product.
A year on, and free to people who didn't take up the refund offer on the original, the Enhanced Edition finally shows what Sword of the Stars II should have been on release - a worthy successor to the ground-breaking original. It took them a while, but they got there in the end.
There's still a few rough edges, and some of the easy accessibility of the original is gone, but the sequel shows that they're still willing to challenge some of the design conventions that 4X games all-too-often find themselves blindly defaulting to.

If you haven't played Sword of the Stars, your brain will leap straight from your cranium and ooze across the carpet in a desperate bid to escape. In either case, space dolphins. And I hate them.

Consider this game if you're looking for a 4x space title that is a bit deeper than something like, say, Endless Space. Customization of ships is amazing, letting you select weapons for your ships (from 3 different categories -- energy, ballistic, and missiles -- and then there are types -- Beams, Pulse Lasers, Plasma Cannons for Energy, etc.) and putting YOU in charge of placing them on where you need them -- no "lol I'm gonna add ten Level 5 cannons, k I'm done designing!" And yes, you will need to pay attention to this sort of stuff -- combat is 3D rendered on a semi-2D plane (there are 3 different vertical planes ships can go to to avoid collision), and weapon placement matters.
Don't mind the Metacritic score, it comes from reviews from when the game was a terrible, buggy mess. It has been much improved over the past year, and is more than playable.

CTU tries to create a similar experience to SWAT 4. Unfortunately it fails doing so for the most part. The game is not terrible and can potentially be fun with friends, but it's not the tactical shooter I was waiting for.
The game has a good variety of different mechanics (Snake cam, various grenade types, leaning). Unfortunately most of them are not very well implemented. This is especially true for the movement: It is "floaty" meaning that you continue moving after releasing the key (even in "walk" mode). In general the controls feels unresponsive and clunky.
The level design is actually decent. You have multiple ways to go and different angles to cover. Potentially creating interesing tactical decisions. The biggest downside is, that there are only 4 different maps for the single player (+ 4 tutorial missions). There is a map editor in the game but it's in beta and is very bare bones. It has Steam Workshop integration however and a few people created maps already.
The AI is in my opinion the most important part for a tactical shooter especially the one for your teammates. Unfortunately this is the weakest part of the game. You can order your squad mates to either go to a specific point or to follow you around. The first option is very finnicky if you try to make them face a specific direction. When following they sometimes get stuck (on terrain or on each other) but it works for the most part.
It gets bad when you try to open and clear a room. Their positioning in front of a door is terrible. When you tell to "Open and Clear" they will make one step into the doorframe and engage the first enemy in sight (which is usually the one diagonally across) blocking line of sight for you. Sometimes they bug out and attempt to clear the room they were coming from (doing a 180° turn in the door frame).
If you give the order to "Open, Flash and Clear" they open the door (while not being in cover at all) and throw a flash greande in the room (which is ridiculously underpowered btw). If they don't see an enemy right away they will wait for the flash to go off and then attempt to clear the room. If they see an enemy though they will move into the room and try to engage him getting flashed by their own grenade.
The enemy AI is pretty bad as well and you get away with just run and gunning if you don't care for score (arresting people gives way more score than killing them).
I think the game can be reasonable fun if you play it in co-op and restrict yourself to not play optimally and instead coordinate proper door breaches and stuff. The SP experience is very lackluster, though. Definitely not the game I was hoping for.

My husband and I both LOVE this game. There's a lot of depth to the game that really makes it challenging! When you first start up, it's best to follow the tutorial just so you know the controls. Then, see how much money you can make by shipping the correct goods to the right city--but watch for in case a town develops into a city and wants new items! You can also build/purchase a company in different cities so that you can earn even more profits. Playing with AI or other players adds a whole new level to the game when you can't use or build onto others' railroads. Instead, you have to lay your tracks around or over their tracks to get to where you need to go. Playing with another human is fun as well; hubby and I quickly found that you can force players to pay an outrageous amount of money for something they really want--or something they don't want you to get. At the same time, if you buy a company on their rail tracks, they can simply stop shipping items to your company--and you lose all the potential profits you could be making. If you make enough money, you can purchase the stocks of other players, and potentially buy out their company. Be careful about if you choose to liquidate them or merge them.... Liquidation adds all of monetary value of their stuff the the monetary value of your stocks---not to your bank account. However, if you do choose to merge their company with yours (allowing you to combine your tracks, edit theirs, and so on), you'll find that the AI tends to be rather stupid and make money--somehow--from shipping a train full of magic nothing back and forth between two cities which requires a lot of poking around to make all their stuff actually profitable for you. lol.
If you like management strategy games--this is definitely worth giving a try!

The Crysis series is one that needs little to no introduction; even if you haven't played the games, you've probably heard about how brutal they are to run on PC. Although, that really only applies to the first release of the franchise, seeing as Crysis 2 can run on more or less the same recommended specs as its predecessor, which came four years earlier. In 2011, the Crytek team decided to continue the storyline of their landmark series, Crysis 2 picks up three years after its sophomore counterpart left off.
The year is 2023, and New York City has become infected by an unknown virus. It turns out that the origin of the plague is extra-terrestrial, and has been spread via the use of capsules by the Ceph; the name finally given to the hostile alien race. Knocking at death's door, a marine known only as Alcatraz is saved by Prophet, one of the team members from the original Crysis. As Prophet has become infected with the Ceph virus, he gives his upgraded Nanosuit 2 to Alcatraz, and then dispatches himself from the world. It's up to Alcatraz to stop the Ceph invasion, and finish what Prophet started.
It's an interesting choice that Crytek decided to forgo using Nomad as the protagonist for Crysis 2, seeing as he was the main character for the first game. Alcatraz is given no voice, and no back story, leaving players to feel as if it is them that has been placed within the Nanosuit instead. This is a pretty great feature, since it means that you do not need to play the first title to enjoy and understand what's happening in this sequel. Even though none of the characters are very well fleshed out, the story is solid, engaging, and it proves to be thought provoking as little twists and turns are revealed throughout the game's 19 chapters.
Where the first Crysis was semi-open world thanks to its massive maps and plethora of routes that could be taken to reach any primary or optional objectives, Crysis 2 is made up of a linear, closed-world environment with only primary missions. This makes the gaming experience much less tactical than its predecessor, although there are moments that will require you to decide on whether or not to take a stealth approach. Even though the title is much more enclosed this time around, Crytek have managed to make the world still feel enormous, thanks to vividly detailed maps that have an immersive depth to them. There's also extra exploration incentives, as players can find collectibles such as souvineres, dogtags, car keys, and e-mail documents, that will unlock bonus content.
With great attention to detail, you will notice subtle things such as a Wall St. street sign, the stock market, the Statue of Liberty, and tons of other landmarks that really make you feel like you're in a war ravaged New York City. As you progress throughout the game, the city becomes more and more derelict, with buildings collapsing left and right, to bridges faltering while you're on them, to just general debris littering the streets. Though not as significantly advanced as the first Crysis was for its time, all of the graphics here still look amazing; they're on par with Call of Duty: Advanced Warfare, which was released in 2014. As opposed to its predecessor, this installment in the franchise has excellent optimization that sees to it that 60 FPS is achievable through the whole game, thanks to the closed maps and downplay of tessellation.
The gameplay for Crysis 2 is excellent; the guns feel heavy and sturdy, as does Alcatraz. You can feel the connectivity in every shot you fire, and taking down the bad guys feels really satisfying. This time around, there's a larger arsenal of weapons at your disposal, but there's less of an emphasis on attachments and modifications for the guns. Instead, the game focuses more on upgrading the Nanosuit with the use of Nano Catalyst, which basically act like credits, that are earned from massacring Ceph. There are four different categories of suit upgrades, each with multiple upgrades that can be bought; though only one upgrade per category can be active at any given time. As well, Crytek removed the "maximum speed" aspect of the armor, but left in the ability to activate stronger defense, and the invisibility cloak.
Crytek have done it again, Crysis 2 is an amazing follow-up to its predecessor. Though not as graphically advanced, the crumbling world of New York City is beautifully mangled, brilliantly detailed, and stunningly immersive; the addition of collectibles gives players an added exploration incentive. The gameplay has never felt so solid before, and any FPS fan will agree that this title has a great sturdy feel to it. The implementation of Nanosuit upgrades will keep players engaged with the Ceph, rather than rushing past them as could be done in the first Crysis. To add icing and a cherry to the cake, the story is well worth paying attention to, and the soundtrack is simply incredible. The best part is, you can jump right into Crysis 2 without any prior knowledge of the franchise. Definitely still one of the best FPS games on the market today.

I thought Resident Evil 5 was lackluster, but it's 24 karat gold compared to this game. It feels like it had a massive budget, and yet whoever designed it was clearly out of their mind.
Not content to make it a basic action/horror game, they decided to add such fun things as: exploration through boring, hard to navigate areas with a terrible camera angle. Annoying stealth sections and tacked-on racing sequences that wil instakill you if you mess up, retaining an over the shoulder camera angle that makes it impossible to steer despite the fact that you're piloting a vehicle. Jump scares. Zombies that don't die after falling 40,000 feet. People that don't die after falling 100 feet. Vehicles coming from behind that will instakill you with no warning. And that's just in the first part of the game!
Meanwhile, they added a dumb skill point system that forces you to run around collecting gigantic chess pieces to gain combat abilities and power, ruining any sort of suspenseful mood that might be in the game and breaking the suspension of disbelief.
The thing is, I really like Resident Evil 4's action because I was never a horror fan, but I can appreciate a slow paced and strategic game that requires exploration. But this game totally throws the strengths of the Resident Evil series out the window and completely hinges on the series' weaknesses, it is now no different from every other mediocre third person shooter with linear levels.
I got it because I had a friend willing to play it with, and it's fun in that regard, but if you want to play it alone, don't do it unless you're desperate.

This is a really neat strategy game.
Yes, it has cards and decks, and they do add some randomness to it. However, I see it more as a turn-based strategy game using cards to add randomness. And for those who don't tend to like card games because they find the RNG frustrating, this game helps mitigate the RNG (mitigate, not eliminate) by allowing you to trade out one card per turn.
The board and units' placements upon it make it much more complicated than something like Hearthstone, or even Faeria, another turn based strategy game with card stuff going on. I'd actually place Faeria closer to Hearthstone and other CCGs than Duelyst is, by a pretty solid margin.

The game was tons of fun when they were all sorts of skill-levels and playstyles going on at once. Some people thought through every single move they made, and others just went balls and against wall. The game was extremely accesible when everyone was new to the game, but that is unfortunately no longer the case. Everyone that still plays the game regularly has been doing so since launch, and it shows. Whenever I try to play an online game, no matter how many bot matches I used to warm up, I just get completely♥♥♥♥♥♥on. The game is also no longe diverse in playstyles. Everyone plays extremely aggressive, and it no longer feels like the same game. I couldn't keep up with playing the game as I got busy with schoolwork and other games, and when I came back for some casual matches I just got slapped in the face with loss after loss after loss. The game has changed to what it originally was. If you enjoy games like Tekken or Mortal Kombat, then For Honor might've been up your alley with what it has become if it wasn't for the fact that the games learning curve has become larger than OG mudbone's peener with the fact that the game only has hardcore players active anymore. This game really could have been something special, but you'd have to have been playing since launch to even enjoy it anymore.

Hyper Light Drifter has been my favorite game of all time. The gameplay has that difficulty in the beginning, and soon, after cautious approach or death, the gameplay becomes easier and more manageable.
Timing is key in this game, the enemies mostly have easily telegraphed attacks and simple patterns, but can become overwhelming if given time. The boss fights are amazing, they were difficult enough to warrant several deaths, but were easy enough to create a strategy and work through it with enough health to last throughout the game.
The exploration in the world is phenomenal as well, while the game has a linear goal of capturing 4 pink crystals in 4 zones and defeat the zone boss. The amount of hidden areas in each zone grant it more diverse ways to conquer each zone. Some hidden areas are more easily discoverable than others, however the small details in each zone is incredible.
The overall gameplay was unbelievable, out of all the pixelated games I have played, on steam and off steam, this one takes the cake in beginning frustration mixed with quick adaptibility and satisfying victories in every area of gameplay. The combat is fluid, being able to slash close combat, while taking enemies out from a far using the blaster and other weapons make boss fights and the regular fights interesting and new each playthrough.
The lore of the world and the story behind the protagonist and the planet are really interesting! Without going into too much detail, the way you learn of the lore is through the stories shared through images rather than words kept me rapt in attention, instead of reading a paragraph from an NPC, he showed me three images that I could interpret myself.
The cinematics were beautiful, the ending gave me tears of joy, having ended an amazing adventure today. Personally, I have never cried before about video games, however, the cinematics, and the bond with the world were something new and beautiful.
10/10 would be my vote on this game, I highly recommend it to anyone who enjoys pixelated graphics, timing-based combat, and lore.

Beautiful art, great music, interesting, rich world, a vague, poetic plot of dark magic and gods told through pictures... all of it is mesmerizing.  But what really makes this game so special is the combat.  The flow of the combat.  It is precise, and sharp, and smooth, and ♥♥♥♥ing impossible.  Until is isn't.  You learn.  You find the rhythms, and you feel like a jedi or Neo, expertly slicing through a room of 30 enemies.  But what's great here is that it isn't like most other hack and slash or metroidvania games, where you get more and more powerful to hack through those 30 guys, do more damage, etc.  You get a couple more attack options, you get a couple more heals per life, but your base attack never does more damage.  You get better.  The game makes you find a flow in combat somewhere between dark souls, hack & slash, and bullet hell, but with a style all its own.  It's beautiful.
Edit: played a lot of games over the last couple years - this is the first I felt the need to review.  It's a masterpiece and deserves some solid recognition.

I've always loved business simulations and the kid version of me loves trains. Even though I have both of those things in me, I just didn't like the thought of a railroad tycoon type of game even if it is from the great Sid Meier.
After playing it though, its an enjoyable little game with a competitive element (if you chose). You chose the era to start and era to end the game. The game basically consists of you connecting resources, supply and demand. Resources get generated, such as oil, grapes, crops, livestock, minerals and so on. Then you connect them to towns that need them. A town will have one of three things demanding these resources. You setup the tracks, then make a train route to bring them in. It is just that simple. The towns will grow into cities. When they take the resources, based on what buildings they have, such as livestock and crops will turn into food. Minerals will turn into gold and so on. Then you export them to other towns that need them. The towns will grow into cities and get more buildings and need more resources for you to bring them. New towns will generate too.
The real twist here is a competitive element (if you have AI opponents). Even in single player, you can have up to 3 AI opponents (or no competition). A game of Monopoly really. You can buy stock in the other companies. You can sell your own stock for money. You don't just get money doing routes. You also get money buying facilities in towns and cities. However, when you try to buy them, you'll end up bidding against the AI competition if you have any. You can also construct facilities yourself for a flat fee if there are any available lots in a town or city.
This means, you can play Monopoly and never actually build a railroad. There's a buzz buying out your competition, but I never really felt all that threatened by them, even with all of their tracks around me. The twist of having stock and buying buildings makes the game a lot of fun in a game that wouldn't warrant replays. It is always the same map, BUT there is an option to randomize the land and cities which is very nice.
With all of that said, its a fun, relaxing, yet competitive game (if you have AI or do multi-player), but the only downside is, there's not much variety here. Once you've played one full game, you've played it all. There are victory conditions, but they're not front and center, so there's no focus on it. At $10, if you're into Monopoly style games, or railroading in general, give it a go. Otherwise, wait for a sale.

After a few hours of playing it, I'd say this game is pretty fun, quite fills a gap in the era of turn-based strategy games. This is almost only about battles, so if you want a game where a dense series of few-minute battles follow each other then you will like it. On the other hand if you want something with complex quests, story and game world then this game is not for you.
Pros:
- it loads & runs quickly even on mediocre hardware
- simple to learn, no complex game world, limited number of unit types
- the battles are fun (if you like Heroes3-style battles)
- I don't feel it to be pay-to-win (with money you can progress faster but no money-only feature, and the game is enjoyable without paying)
Cons:
- 2D retro graphics (not everybody likes it)
- lack of in-game help and documentation, and the UI needs improvements in general
- not much configuration options on the settings pane
To sum up, this game is for you if you like battles in  turn-based strategy games, but you don't want things like city building, overcomplicated game rules or complex game world. This is something you can play for hours, but also when you have only 5 minutes for gaming.

Wow is all I can say. Crysis, 2, and 3, are all amazing games, they are action packed, and engerizing. The crysis series is one of those types of games that will make you think alot. It is amazing.

The Crysis series involves a power suit that enhances specific abilities e.g. invisible stealth mode, armor defense mode, etc.
Crysis 2 allowed for customization of the power suit. You can basically unlock specific abilities for your own playstyle, and those abilities can be turned on/off without cost after unlocking.
The FPS aspect was alright. I'm more of a strategy/stealth player, so I did appreciate those times when I could just avoid all the encounters.
Certain boss fights or events could be surmounted via brute-force tactics. You go in, learn the patterns of enemies or weaknesses of bosses, die, and update your strategy. Death and reload happen very quickly so you're not really taken out of the action. Although I did like that aspect of the game, brute-forcing through boss battles isn't really fun for me.
If you're into FPS, I think this is a good title to play.

This game is the result of the total sum of everything that plagues modern first person shooters on top of it being poorly designed. From a game mechanics standpoint, the game uses what made the first Crysis such a fun and engaging game, except stripping down full control of your Nanosuit abilities for no other reason than to make the game accessible to play on a controller, AKA the game got consolized (ironically, as if the infamous “Press Start to begin” mistake in the multiplayer demo days wasn't clear enough).
That doesn't necessarily make a video game bad. What makes Crysis 2 such a bad video game is what follows:
1) The AI. In my 25+ years of gaming, I have NEVER, EVER played a video game that has an asinine AI behavior like the one this game has. The enemy spot you they will start engaging you and firing at you even if there was a huge building separating you and that said enemy. What is weird about that, you say? The enemy will actually start shooting the wall, as in, he will act as he have a clear line of sight on you. Sometime he will start throwing grenades at you resulting in him blowing either himself or his squad mates.
When an enemy will start to rush you, they will sometimes run towards you, stop momentarily, a take an X amount of degree turn and start shooting at you.
Not only that, the AI sometimes will go to his idle non-encounter behavior even in the middle of a gunfight. That will happen in almost every encounter, and that's not fun.
You would expect something like that happening in an early access title from an unknown and small developer, not a triple A game developer that also has contracts building military simulators.
2)Poorly designed enemy encounters. Every section you have multiple choices ranges from running and gunning, silently taking down enemies, sneaking your way out of the combat area or a combination of all of them. In paper, that sound like the game had a lot of options to make the gameplay itself engaging, but it is not.
When going run and gun, the enemies will go engage you in combat (with their ♥♥♥♥♥♥ AI behavior as noted before). Once you clear the half a dozen or so enemies around you new enemies will start spawning. The problem? The reinforcements will spawn from random locations, ranging from spawning at the very beginning of the section you are in to spawning literally a few inches behind you, which puts you in a lot of situations that I'm sure that the developers themselves didn't test, at all. Going for silent kills and sneaky-sneaky will get boring too thanks to the the bad enemy placement and poorly designed levels and encounters.
TL;DR: Play the first Crysis and pretend the series ended there.

Mercenaries is by far my favourite mode especially no mercy (huge L4d fan) and it really comes alive playing online with a partner.  So onto the singleplayer
Leon campaign - enjoyable, very similar in the first few chapters to re2
Chris - think Gears of war, enjoyable again, very over the top and good fun

Hyper Light Drifter has been my favorite game of all time. The gameplay has that difficulty in the beginning, and soon, after cautious approach or death, the gameplay becomes easier and more manageable.
Timing is key in this game, the enemies mostly have easily telegraphed attacks and simple patterns, but can become overwhelming if given time. The boss fights are amazing, they were difficult enough to warrant several deaths, but were easy enough to create a strategy and work through it with enough health to last throughout the game.
The exploration in the world is phenomenal as well, while the game has a linear goal of capturing 4 pink crystals in 4 zones and defeat the zone boss. The amount of hidden areas in each zone grant it more diverse ways to conquer each zone. Some hidden areas are more easily discoverable than others, however the small details in each zone is incredible.
The overall gameplay was unbelievable, out of all the pixelated games I have played, on steam and off steam, this one takes the cake in beginning frustration mixed with quick adaptibility and satisfying victories in every area of gameplay. The combat is fluid, being able to slash close combat, while taking enemies out from a far using the blaster and other weapons make boss fights and the regular fights interesting and new each playthrough.
The lore of the world and the story behind the protagonist and the planet are really interesting! Without going into too much detail, the way you learn of the lore is through the stories shared through images rather than words kept me rapt in attention, instead of reading a paragraph from an NPC, he showed me three images that I could interpret myself.
The cinematics were beautiful, the ending gave me tears of joy, having ended an amazing adventure today. Personally, I have never cried before about video games, however, the cinematics, and the bond with the world were something new and beautiful.
10/10 would be my vote on this game, I highly recommend it to anyone who enjoys pixelated graphics, timing-based combat, and lore.

Beautiful art, great music, interesting, rich world, a vague, poetic plot of dark magic and gods told through pictures... all of it is mesmerizing.  But what really makes this game so special is the combat.  The flow of the combat.  It is precise, and sharp, and smooth, and ♥♥♥♥ing impossible.  Until is isn't.  You learn.  You find the rhythms, and you feel like a jedi or Neo, expertly slicing through a room of 30 enemies.  But what's great here is that it isn't like most other hack and slash or metroidvania games, where you get more and more powerful to hack through those 30 guys, do more damage, etc.  You get a couple more attack options, you get a couple more heals per life, but your base attack never does more damage.  You get better.  The game makes you find a flow in combat somewhere between dark souls, hack & slash, and bullet hell, but with a style all its own.  It's beautiful.
Edit: played a lot of games over the last couple years - this is the first I felt the need to review.  It's a masterpiece and deserves some solid recognition.

The Soulsborne Series is hands down my absolute
game series of all time, and will remain so, but Hyper Light Drifter is the first and only game that has ever left me
speechless while playing it.
Perhaps that's a little bit over-dramatic, but from the moment I first started playing, I was IMMEDIATELY stricken by the beauty of the environment, the music, the character design, the fluidity of the combat... It was gorgeous, every element of it, and that feeling of awe didn't diminish even slightly as I progressed through the game and eventually beat it.
The art style is without a doubt insanely beautiful.  It's detailed and pretty without being over the top, and each zone tells its story without a lot of fussing around.  That being said, at times the pixel style makes it a tad difficult to tell what's going on, especially in
Despite that, each zone feels completely unique, with ncredibly strong atmosphere that makes you want to just stand around and admire the world you're in.
The combat is also, in my personal opinion, just about flawless.  It's fluid and fast-paced with the same level of unforgiving difficulty one might find in a Souls game.  Coming from the Souls games, I found it easy to acclimate to, but those who aren't used to such games might find it particularly challenging, especially with the isometric nature of the game world.  It's easy to learn, but
hard to master - and that kind of gameplay isn't for everyone.
The only negative thing I might say about HLD is the vagueness of the story.  Don't get me wrong, I VERY much appreciate when games don't spoon-feed their plots and lore to you.  That being said, HLD takes that concept...
far.  Even coming off of the Souls games I found it very difficult to pick up the overarching plot on my first playthrough.  It took me
runs of the game, studying the environment and the characters and such very hard, before I had a decent understanding of the game's lore.  And while I'm personally fine with that level of deep searching, I also understand that other people may just want to play it once or twice casually - and the fact of the matter is that they WON'T get the full plot with that kind of playthrough.  Keep that in mind when considering playing the game.
Overall, this game is ABSOLUTELY one of my favorites of all time. I would highly recommend it to people who want an experience similar to that of Soulsborne - A beautiful, well-made world with a challenging but rewarding difficulty level.

CTU is obviously trying to be a successor to SWAT 4 and Rainbow Six 3. Which is great, we need a modern take on both games. Unfortunatly CTU falls short like all the other games that have tried.
First of all, CTU seems to be using the default Unity character controller. This leads to "slippery" momentum based movement that feels just plain bad.
It ships with very few missions on top of the unskippable tutorial missions.
Poor pathfinding caused my ai teammates to get stuck on closed doors while they tried to reach me on the other side of the building many times.
Settings don't seem to save after closing and relaunching the game.
It's not all bad though. CTU has a few features that would have been welcomed in other games such as Takedown Red Sabre.
There's career progression in the form of recruiting new officers and purchasing different equipment, including a shield which was missing from SWAT 4.
There's a map editor. So if a large enough community forms, the lack of official missions could be fixed.
You can lean while walking, and leaning causes your character to "step out" making it really easy to check a corner.
CTU allows you to play a "run and gun" style, or a slower "no casualties" style, and rewards you more for arrests over kills. This is nice to see in a police themed game.
Overall, there's a lot of potential here, but it's not worth it at it's current price and still needs a lot of work and polish. I would be a lot more hesitant to give this a thumbs down if it was an early access title. Keep looking SWAT players.

The Soulsborne Series is hands down my absolute
game series of all time, and will remain so, but Hyper Light Drifter is the first and only game that has ever left me
speechless while playing it.
Perhaps that's a little bit over-dramatic, but from the moment I first started playing, I was IMMEDIATELY stricken by the beauty of the environment, the music, the character design, the fluidity of the combat... It was gorgeous, every element of it, and that feeling of awe didn't diminish even slightly as I progressed through the game and eventually beat it.
The art style is without a doubt insanely beautiful.  It's detailed and pretty without being over the top, and each zone tells its story without a lot of fussing around.  That being said, at times the pixel style makes it a tad difficult to tell what's going on, especially in
Despite that, each zone feels completely unique, with ncredibly strong atmosphere that makes you want to just stand around and admire the world you're in.
The combat is also, in my personal opinion, just about flawless.  It's fluid and fast-paced with the same level of unforgiving difficulty one might find in a Souls game.  Coming from the Souls games, I found it easy to acclimate to, but those who aren't used to such games might find it particularly challenging, especially with the isometric nature of the game world.  It's easy to learn, but
hard to master - and that kind of gameplay isn't for everyone.
The only negative thing I might say about HLD is the vagueness of the story.  Don't get me wrong, I VERY much appreciate when games don't spoon-feed their plots and lore to you.  That being said, HLD takes that concept...
far.  Even coming off of the Souls games I found it very difficult to pick up the overarching plot on my first playthrough.  It took me
runs of the game, studying the environment and the characters and such very hard, before I had a decent understanding of the game's lore. I currently have over 1,000hours in this game.
Here a list of things within the game on a scale of 1-10
Individual race design- 8/10 (each race still feels completely unique and fresh like they did in the first game)
Artificial Intelligent race design- 10/10 (this was actually done flawlessly and very unique compared to
other artificial intelligent races created in the same and even other sci-fi genres. It's a very fresh new look on AI playable races)
Story- 2/10 (there is no story, other than the lore you get from either the forums or within the encyclopedia their really nothing else.)
Tech Tree- 9/10 (the randomized tech forest with several branches and seven overall main weapon types, no matter what game you play against AI or other Human Opponents, the odds of running exactly the same weapon types is very slim after you reach turn 100)
Unit Health vs DPS -9/10 (basically this mean how unit health is dealt vs the weapon damage that it
takes. Unlike most Turn Based Strategy games SotS 2 contains a Real Time combat, so it already starts off with an advantage verse other turn based strat games. However with the inclusion of the ship matrix system which mimics physical armor depth and resistance. The game surpasses even the most advanced real time strategy game. In fact I would have to say this is the first time I scene a videogame of anytype properly model a vehicle or units armor in a way that it actually makes logical sense. However there are some downsides, for starters I don't feel weapons do enough DPS to the armor matrix in many cases some high end weapons just wont kill an enemy unit. In fact their are very few weapons that do enough damage to completely penetrate a CR armor matrix in one shot even at end game. On the flip side their are tons of weapons that are left "obsolete" once you reach Leviathans or even Dreadnoughts with AA so all around the matrix system is amazing, but weapon balancing could be better. Battles really do feel slow in many cases unless your focus firing with all your units. Leaves a lot of strategy left in the background to pick up dust.)
Game Length- 7/10 (It is a Turn Based Strategy Game, so it obvious that a single match could last
several days if not weeks depending on size and level of strategy of both the player and the Ai. So if I go on just length this game will get a 10/10 in this category way to easily, just because of its genre alone. However the problem I run into is the "fun" factor, in fact I can't really blame this particular game for this, since so many turn based games run into this problem. "The Clean Up Turns" around turns 200 to 300 you should if you a modest player and your playing at 100% eco and research with standard starting systems and 4 players, you will run into the clean up turns within this turn bracket. Basically Clean Up Turns is when your literally doing nothing, you have overpowered your opposition and steamrolling through their systems, it just gets boring the AI makes no attempt at counter attacking and even on the off chance they do, they don't succeed. Now verse a human player you will generally run into the point during this process where the Human player just quits. This is a good thing as it completely eliminates the Clean Up Turns. The Ai really needs an option at some point where they just cant go on any longer and they succeed from the game, whether this should cause the Ai's systems to separate into their provinces and become multiple Ai players or not, just to make it more interesting and stop the boredom of this clean up turns or just have it end the game all together. Either way something needs to be done about this, because reaching this point to often is the reason why I left so many other turn based strategy games. Just finishing the match is not fun after a certain point.)
Textures and Effects- 9/10 (the game is beautiful it really is)
Re-playability- 8/10 (after 1000 hours into this game, yes it has a ton of re-playability. Otherwise I
wouldn't have so many hours into the game. Even though it not being worked on 24/7 by its development team, it doesn't have to be. Randoms alone increase re-playability exponentially. On top of that modding "which I do a lot of" makes the game seem dynamic and different every time you change or add something new to its already complicated but fun dynamics which are in place and very solid. It could use some help though, like an expansion or two in order to mesh everything together and create a completely solid slap for modders to build from in order to create more dynamic events for the sandbox matches which are very much almost always enjoyable.)
I would give the total score of this game....
8/10
that would be my final verdict after factoring in everything I said above. The game is good in single player, its multi player can be a bit buggy still, but people do play it and have fun (although it can be a hassle)  so all around the game is worth its weight in USD (considering the USA economic issues though.... I think the game will always be worth its weight in USD... haha I make bad jokes)
, but yea it is worth the buy. Pick it up if you like Turn Based Strategy games.. or just like ships with pretty lasers shooting each other, both are good reasons!

Despite its age, there aren't many games that can be classified in the same category as Railroads.
To describe the mechanics of the game, you start with a number of cities, each with a supply, demand, and number of industries. As a railroad engineer, you connect cities by connecting them with railroads, buying trains, and designing trade routes. By using industries to convert resources to products, and then selling those products to larger cities, victory can be achieved in a number of virtual decades. Mutliplayer, unfortunately, is dead, which is sad because it would be an intriguing concept to have several players working together (or against eachother) to build up the largest stockpile of funds as cities are connected in a web of railroads.
This game is addicting, there's plenty of scenarios to play through, and plenty of maps to use. Furthermore, by randomizing cities descriptions and locations, there's a near-endless amount of ways this game can be played.
For the current price, there's no reason why a fan of Sid Meier shouldn't have this in their collection. Get it!

I dunno. It's not a bad game. It might be the two reviews I read that ruined it for me. The two snippets I got were about "thinking outside the box" and "just go in blind, you'll get the most enjoyment that way," which to me seem like definite good signs when I'm looking to buy a game. I was excited, and ready to be hit over the head with something brilliant. I played through it in one sitting, and I finished feeling pretty underwhelmed. At the end of the game, you're encouraged to delete the game from your HDD once you're done playing it. My reaction to this encouragement was, "don't mind if I do," and that was that.
So the game, of course, is not about ponies. The title of "Pony Island" is part of the overly cheerful facade that the game literally immediately tears down the instant you start. You're going on a journey with the goal of figuring out what exactly is going on, all while playing through some minigames and fighting the big baddie. But this process is painfully linear. If you think to do something that seems like it wasn't part of the intended linear path, you're typically rewarded with a ticket (tickets don't do anything other than net you Steam achievements) or some tongue-in-cheek joke. And then you hop right back on that path because you've gotten your reward for straying from it. I have nothing against linear storylines where the player doesn't interact with anything going on, and that method has worked fine for other games. But if there's going to be a linear and uninteractive story, it has to be good. And it is not good - it is mediocre. The plot is straightforward and unengaging. I found myself feeling apathetic when moments meant to evoke a response came up. Maybe I was just in a bad mood or feeling grumpy or something, but the story just didn't work for me.
And the gameplay is awful. The two core gameplay elements - a "hacking" puzzle and a hurdle-jumping platformer - are painfully boring. You can figure out what you need to do in a matter of seconds for both of them, and then you have to spend a minute or two executing that plan. If you mess up, you get to enjoy going all the way back to the start. Over the course of the game, new elements are added to these games as an effort to keep things fresh, but both minigames are so one-dimensional that it takes all of 15 seconds to have a solid understanding of what was just added, and then you're back to the grind. Now to be fair, the gameplay is clearly not the focus of this game. You're not buying the game to have fun jumping hurdles or solving rudimentary puzzles. You're buying the game for the rest of what's packed into it. But the literal and metaphorical hurdle-jumping of the gameplay just takes up so much time that it's hard to forgive it for being so dull, even if it's not the focus of the game.
I really wanted to like this game. I just can't. It doesn't do anything new, and it doesn't improve on what has already been done. It's not bad, but it's not good either. It's meh. A resounding meh.
