I have never played a Crysis game before nor do I have that much experience with storybased shooters on a regular basis. This also is a first impressions type of review that I shall update when I finished the game. I realise that the game is out for a few years now so the "First Impressions" wont matter all that much to you but I cannot just put out a half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥review of a game I barely played, so instead I will write my first impressions down.
=| Review |=
After loading the game for the first time, it stopped loading and I had to restart the game. After a restart however it seemed like everything was fine and it loaded up right quick. With the usual logos popping up that got annoying in Metro already. That sidehit out of the way, no big problems after this occured. Saying this I should also mention that a few people seemed to have problem with the steam installation. Enough problems for another user to post a discussion on the matter that it would be easier to activate your key on origin and download it from there. That being said, the gameplay awaits.
[Warning. The following content of the review may or may not contain spoilers. Read at your own risk.]
As I hop into the game I am greeted with real life cutscenes and soon after the first intro part of the game. I am a Marine and I am supposed to save a grand man because he seems to be important to, I honestly have no Idea. I know that they talked about Aliens and that is all that was stuck in my head. That and the behavior of one member of the team acting like a total dumbass on a team of trained professionals. But instead of actually getting on land we are being attacked by an unknown force. Most likely Aliens as I assume. We have to get out and the usual intro mission stuff kicks in. Duck, Run, Hold this to open door and get out only to get the team shot and you being the sole survivor. And then I am greeted with a quite awesome cutscene with quite awesome music.
But of course, getting shot by a alien Drone (?) also has its benefits. Because now a man in a cool looking armor scares the thing that attacked you away and carries you to safety. You wont get to know him for all that long because as soon as you wake up, you not only wear his armor but also see him dead on the floor. As you pick up his gun you are greeted with what will be your mission and information about the armor. The information is broad and not explained in detail as the game wants you to learn it in active combat, which I prefer greatly. It gives you little points in the game that dont break away from the immersion (due to the fact that the tutorials are portraied by the suits interface and AI) and gives you small tutorals on how to go into stealth mode, how to activate armor and how to use the suits visor. From there it is all you and how you play the game.
And here we go towards the gameplay. Apart from the usual small tutorials the game runs very nicely. My PC not being the best gaming PC to be had I dont have a full on 60fps but I also dont know if that even is a thing for the game. For all I know, it could be capped at 30 as some games do. If so, please let me know in the comments so I may correct the review for that matter. Going through on scenario after another I finally reach a bigger street with a bunch of enemies all over the place. I thought that I would just die there and not get through it in one try. Seems like I thought wrong as it was easier than I thought. The enemies after all are not bulletsponges and grenades can make the journey through the city also a fairly enjoyable one at that. Sure you will scare off all the birds but if you see one of those alien cockroaches, I am sure that you are happy about that as the aliens will have to feast on human flesh instead of those birdies. Oh wait, its equaly bad. Well at least you saved one being for now.
Getting through the first part of the campaign was rather easy to say the least. I am playing on Normal difficulty and find it still challenging enough. Now having entered the second part (just after loading) and getting to fight my first enemies in the new area I immediately died. And that is where I stopped to write this review.
Now to a thing that happens to not only confuse me but also upset me. You know, optimisation is a huge issue when it goes to games of this scale. And I am not talking about games that just lag like hell. No, the game runs fairly smooth all things considered. But no matter if that is the case, the optimisation of the game could be better. You cannot fully adjust your sensitivity to one specific number but have to choose between 5-10-15 and so on up to 100. The cutscenes as well seem to have a higher sensitivity when looking around which can be a tad confusing as well. That aside the main controlls are also kind of not complete for that matter. Of course the game tells you what you have to use in combat, ingame but there is no way (or at least I couldnt find one) to remap those controlls. No option to remap stealth or armor function. And bloody hell can people stop putting crouch on C? Who uses C anyways? Jokes aside, that can still cause little issues while playing when you can barely pay any attention because everything looks god damn amazing and you are overwhelmed by it.
The last thing I want to mention, which is a thing that annoyed me with GTAV as well. Graphical settings. The game (for me) turned on its lowest settings. That is just fine for me but there is a little problem there. Lowest, isnt "lowest". Lowest is "high". There are no options to choose Low graphical settings which seems to be a bit confusing for such grand titles. Because for GTAV, even if it says that you can run it on the lowest possible settings, that is about all you can do. Playing it is another thing that cannot be done for that matter. But of course this isnt GTAV (which still is a good game) and its playable no matter what. Its just that these are the things that I happen to find out while playing it for about an hour. And that is all.
Thank you for reading.

Coming from the original Crysis, I actually disliked the opening to this game a lot. However after sticking with the game, it grew on me and I have to say I probably prefer Crysis 2 to the original for afew things:
- Story: Much better than the original and is expanded on in Crysis 2. We learn more about the Ceph and have more encounters with them over the original game and many more Ceph variant enemies to fight.
- Fluid Controls: The controls are much more user friendly than the original. Yes you can remap but the way the suit handles far better in this game.
- Graphics: Improved and the game is still beautiful in 2017. The game has some stunning scenes and based in NYC,
- Gunplay: A larger variety of weapons and most feel unique and handle in their own way.
What I disliked:
- Linear: The game is very linear compared to the original. Much more on-rails shooter. I can only assume this was a design choice since Crysis 2 was 'consilized'.
- Some 30fps animations: I noticed some animations in the game seem to be locked to 30fps. Firing/Reloading with certain weapons such as the Shotgun has noticeable judder and can be distracting.
- Game mainly takes place in NYC and some levels/map design don't do a good job in making the feel of each level unique. Can get slightly repetitive at times.
I would recommend a playthrough of Crysis 2 for Crysis fans and whilst Crysis 2 does improve on some fronts for the franchise, I still think the original Crysis series remain more true to core gameplay and map design, so newcommers make sure to not miss out on the original!

Thomas was... alright.
FOCUS OF THE GAME:
- PUZZLE PLATFORMING:
The game plays around with different types of blocks with different types of mechanics and asks you to solve platforming puzzles with it. They're alright, though more often tedious than actual brain teasers.
- CORKY NARRATIVE:
The story isn't very good (it's a bit confused, jumping from character arc to forced character arc and often not knowing where or how to end something). But the story doesn't seem to be the focus as much as the narrative, the way the story is told. In this case, by a 'charming' Brit exploring the personality developments of the blocks, rather than only focusing on the story developments. I like the idea here, and I'm sure a lot of people will love the cuddly vibe the narrative gives, but I was personally a little itched at times by the game wanting to be 'charming' a bit... too much.
- MINIMALIST AESTHETIC:
Of course, the reason I came to play this game was all this talk by game designers about how this game tries to tell a story with only rectangles. They seem to have tried very hard to tell an 'inspirational' story about companionship, sacrifice and artificial intelligence fighting to be free from the system, complete with 'inspirational' soundtrack. I didn't feel very inspired, but if anything, I'm glad to have played the game to see the experiment in action.
SHOULD YOU BUY IT?
It's a short game, and far from being my favourite. Buy it only if you feel you will be emotionally moved by it, because there's not much to see in the gameplay department. And of course, if you're interested in talking about game design, you can add the Thomas Was Alone experiment to your vocabulary for only a few bucks and hours.
I PLAYED THIS GAME FOR: 4 hours (finished + all achievements)
I WOULD PAY FOR THIS GAME: €4. Wait for the sale.

I'll level with you, this game tears me apart. And this is a long review, so please bear with me.
(tl;dr This game takes work on your part and it has problems, but its worth it if you can give it that chance)
To start off, I am a huge history nerd, and as soon as I even heard someone was making this game, I was all on board.
I have participated in every Alpha, Beta, Public and Private Tests prior to it's release. I noticed in every stage what was wrong with the game, from heroes to Peer to Peer (P2P), and I gave Ubisoft that feedback at every opportunity they gave me. I've played this with mouse and keyboard, and many different controllers. I have tried every hero, learned their moves to certain degree, tracked good and bad matchups. The whole 9 yards. I have given this game every angle it can get. And I still go back to it.
Why? Because, apart from Chivalry (which I also have put hundreds oh hours on), there just simply is nothing else like it out there.
I don't play fighting games usually. Heck, I stopped playing Super Smash Bros after Melee. They just aren't my thing. But For Honor got me to stick with it and learn. And so learn I did, for a very, very, very long time.
Grinding and practicing are nothing new to me, nor is maining a hero. My experience with League of Legends will attest to that. But to play this game well, this is what it asks of you. Play the tutorials, all of them. Play the story, then play it again on Realistic to learn attack animations. Play custom games against Level 3 bots, who are no slouches, for 99 rounds, on all maps, against every hero. Go into endless duels and practice your dodges, parries, combos... everything.
Then go into matches, play against real people, learn their attack patterns and counters, and do that for hundreds of games, for dozens of hours. You will get better, I gauruntee it.
And even then, I'm still just an average player, who still needs to get good. So yes, this game asks alot from you.
I had friends when I started playing this game, but they eventually fizzled out because in the end it can be much for some.
But with the game itself, there are real problems. Dominion is an interesting concept, but Team Ganks are a real and regular occurance. Revenge, the only mechanic you have as defense against such scenarios, can only help so much. On top of that, connectivity issues are commonplace, at least for me. It's better in duels, but otherwise lag can be a real problem, especially in a fighting game with frames of reaction time.  With P2P, it was always going to be a problem, so I wasn't surprised when the game lost its player base by the end of Season 1. As a result now, mathmaking times are horrendously long, and sometimes unfair to newer players. Hopefully that will improve with dedicated servers, which at the time of this writing, were announced to release during the current Season 4, although they have yet to do so.
I personally don't think there are any heroes that are absolutely busted, I have found always at least one way to beat them or counter them. There is strategy involved, yours won't work everytime, but neither will theirs. Like I said earlier, if you take the time to learn the game, it's much more enjoyable.
I am annoyed by the gear having value in the game. Aesthetically, they are amazing. And while they have improved Steel (the games currency) income to at least 800-2000 a day, if you give the missions a fair go, gear upgrades and cosmetics like effects, ornaments, outfits, and executions are extremely expensive. While I never have had to purchase DLC heroes, I think all heoroes should be free, dont limit the player to how they want to play and learn and practice.
Believe me when I say I have put more than 300 hours in this game, regardless of what Steam says. I want this game to do well. And I think they are trying to do that, because the creators really put alot of love and effort into making this game a reality, and a beautiful one at that.
I paid my $100 dollars to pre-order, and even today I still don't regret it.
But I am not you. You have to make that decision. This game is decidedly unique, you won't easily find another game that can do for you what this game can, no matter how broken it may appear to be.
If you like that learning curve and challenge, by all means get this game, test your mettle.
If you like the history and the thematics and the aesthetics, get this game, because no other game has done it better. I know some people say the story mode wasn't very good, but I personally enjoyed it and often return to it just for the experiences and the epic battles and duels.
But if you don't like those things, if you don't want to put in the work to get the most of this game, don't buy it. Plenty of others come in and buy it and give up because they notice the same problems I did when I played the alpha. You already know, everyone knows, whats wrong with this game, even before they buy it. You adding to that list accomplishes nothing.
This game is not for everyone, and not everyone gives it the chances it deserves. If you can give it that chance, then I recommend this game for you, specifically, and no one else.

If Crysis was known for one thing, it was amazing graphics, the game felt imbalanced, had bizarre difficulty spikes, and felt more like a tech demo than an actual game.
Crysis 2 swaps the lush jungle for the war-torn streets of New York, where a killer virus is destroying civilization and a gooey race of alien invaders known as the Ceph are wrecking everything in sight. As US Marine Alcatraz, your job is to step into a superpowered Nanosuit and wipe out not only the Ceph, but the CELL private army that wants to take you down.
Almost as soon as the player gets a gun, the improvements over the original Crysis are clear. Strength and Speed are now passive abilities -- they'll automatically kick in if you charge melee attacks or start to sprint. Armor used to be the passive default option for the Suit, but is now an activated ability, along with stealth.
Activing Stealth and Armor won't drain your suit's energy within milliseconds, allowing you enough time to navigate to an advantageous position or absorb heavy fire.
The levels feel smaller than Crysis', but they are better designed and the action is far tighter, with consistent pacing and a natural flow from battle to battle. Before each fight, you can scope into the territory to mark enemies, ammo crates, and tactical options.
Most of the unique weapons aren't all that useful in an actual fight, so you'll likely want to stick to the dull assault and sniper rifle combo, which is a shame.
Crysis 2 is ostensibly Modern Warfare with sci-fi gadgets, it's a pretty damn good Modern Warfare with sci-fi gadgets.
As the game progresses, players can specialize and get access to more unique abilities - such as decoy devices that project holograms of players and draw enemy fire.
Multiplayer is "good". But I did not play it very much..

Hyper Light Drifter is a rough gem. It's certainly beautiful, and at its core it's a fun and rewarding experience. Unfortunately it's marred by intentional design choices which hold it back from being considered anywhere close to perfect.
To start, the visual design is absolutely stunning. The beautiful pixel art is the primary draw, and the world portrayed is crafted to perfection through the art, with most rooms created to feel real and vast. The smooth spritework is another plus, giving the living creatures and environments a genuine quality beyond the likes of even SNES RPG classics.
Besides the visuals is where things get inconsistent. Hyper Light Drifter is known first for its beautiful visuals, and second for its clear and distinct lack of any dialogue or words whatsoever, save for a few little prompts to explain only the most rudimentary game mechanics. I feel that this was a misstep, and not the simplistic brilliance it is touted as. Certain game concepts are fine with this restriction, such as how you gradually discover the way the currency and upgrades systems work, or simply the discovery of what direction you're supposed to take your quest.
However, it also becomes downright arcane at certain points. Exactly how outfits, swords, and the sprite which follows you around differ to one another is never explained at all. More importantly, this choice impacts the story in a way that results in a plot that unfortunately comes across as largely nonsensical. Whatever the world is supposed to be is either so complex that pictures don't properly describe it, or simply not made clear enough to identify what is of importance and what is not. The ability to interact with NPCs, but not have them say anything of value (barring the occasional slideshow which does the absolute minimum to explain the plight of a region) makes their existence pointless.
That isn't to say there aren't plenty of moments of dialogue-free storytelling. Each individual zone has a story to tell, and you become invested enough to see them through, from the genocide going on in the east to the mysterious facility hidden beneath the region southward, all explained through visual cues. It works. They are, however, seemingly irrelevant to whatever quest you yourself are playing out.
The gameplay fares much better. Combat is satisfying, if incredibly punishing. The incentive to switch between sword and firearm gives fighting a solid rhythm, even if the screen can become downright chaotic and the actual animations forcing a rigid window to input commands. Often times combat will feel less like a reflex-based response to how combat unfolds, and more one of constant situational awareness. Coupling that with one of the most miserable and restrictive dodging systems I've seen in an action game, there usually seems to be only one or two 'correct' ways through a fight, and the challenge comes from figuring out exactly what that way is. Were combat to be made more fluid, it would likely take some of the game's steep challenge away, but at the very least the dodging is far too unreliable.
The need for situational awareness extends to how you explore the world, as well. There is a consistent pattern to what secret rooms look like, and they are in an overwhelming abundance throughout Hyper Light Drifter. You need to know what to look for, and though experience with games like Metroid may assist you in searching for those inconsistencies in the environment, be prepared to scour through with a fine-toothed comb to reach 100%.
Finally, the music. Disasterpeace crafts a soundtrack that delivers excellent ambiance which really makes you feel the weight of the world around you. Unfortunately, that's about all it does. The music really does seem to drone on and on nearly everywhere, and it's more like listening to an effect rather than a distinct track. It's definitely a stylistic choice, and it's one I don't agree with. Having melody in certain instances such as boss fights would not have broken the immersion the game so wants to retain.
Ultimately, Hyper Light Drifter is definitely not a bad game, but it does seem like certain deliberate choices made to set it apart only served to weigh it down. From its awkward silence, to rigid gameplay, to its droning soundtrack, there is a lot which doesn't gel with the larger package. Thankfully, the core is a lovingly-crafted, brutally challenging, and very memorable game that will certainly stick with you long after you've finished, and push you into making repeat trips along the gorgeous journey which Hyper Light Drifter offers.

A lot of these reviews are obviously sarcastic. Here's one that isn't. Sure, Spooky Cats looks like a flash game and it's repetitive--but it's also easy to play, fun, cute, and affordable. The music is very adequate, though limited (3 tracks looped). Because of the simple graphics, even low-grade PCs can run Spooky Cats. My laptop isn't exactly a warrior and, sadly, quite a lot of games in my Steam library don't run well on it...so it's nice to have simple games like Spooky Cats (as well as more advanced retro titles like Hotline Miami, Eversion etc) that I know I'll be able to play.
And most importantly--I grew up on platformers, so I have a keen eye for them. Spooky Cats is the bare basics in that familiar, run-and-jump sort of way, and that's not a bad thing. The controls are very responsive and glitch free, something I can't say for a lot of indie platofrmers on Steam. Don't expect Fez, but at $3 dollars you can't really go wrong with a title like Spooky Cats. It makes a great in-between game for breaks from those more hardcore titles.

This isn't survival horror, plain and simple. The only survival horror you get is when you play the first 2 chapters of Leon's campaign, that's it.
Overall, Resident Evil 6 was one of the biggest dissapointments of 2012. The game isn't bad, gameplay wise it's great. But it's story and everything else is pretty bad. Capcom tried so hard to make this a great Resi game for the fans by adding all these returning characters like Leon and Sherry, instead the game suffered greatly by it's mediocre story and terrible segments. The fact that you can carry every weapon in the game that you find at once completely destroys the whole survival horror aspect. The ability to dodge at will without quicktime events, and the improved movement in general, is a great addition, but it's not without it's flaws. The strict movment in past games was made because it made the game felt more tense. It generated fear of not being able to dodge anything, and you knowing you had to take out what was in front of you or you'd get hit and you only have yourself to blame. In Resi 6, all that is thrown out the window thanks to the new movement. It further solidifies itself as an action game rather than a horror game, which we all know is NOT what Resident Evil is ment to be.
Overall, I'd have to give Resident Evil 6 a
. I wouldn't recommend this game if you're new to the series. Start with Resident Evil 4 instead, or even better, start with the original Resident Evil.
There's just no excuse for RE6 to have controls as bad as the original RE,  I'm done with Capcom, they will never see another dollar from me.

The normal difficulty is hard enough that you'll have to make multiple attempts at things while learning how new enemies fuction but it's not so hard you want to rip your hair out. The story is left very open and is without dialouge which gives it this very ethereal, atmospheric vibe. It's also definitely a bit spooky at times and gets my heart pumping when I descend into the depths of the underground and the music takes a sinister turn. The sound track overall is mesmerizing, the enemies are fun to fight, the story (while vague) reels me in, and aside from the map being a bit confusing at first I have no problems with this game. There's a lot of people crying in the negative reviews about this but I actually like that the developers don't do much hand holding. 10/10 would recommend.

As much as I love music/rhythm games, I can't say that this is one of them.
Mostly because it's more frustrating than fun, and it feels unfinished in some points.
First of all, there is no resolution option on the menu. You gotta use Launch Options through Steam properties, and that's not how it's supposed to be. Also, when I try to bind keys for my Xbox 360 controller, it kinda doesn't recognize the controller buttons, so I had to use JoyToKey in order to use my controller.
Second, you can't use your own music. I know the music that comes within the game is amazing, but if I can't listen to my own library, 50% of the fun is lost for me. You can actually create a level and uses your own music, but it only supports .ogg music. We are still living the .mp3 age, so I don't think that was a good format decision.
And finally, the difficulty!
I managed to beat games like Barrier X, after alot of tries, and of course I rage on games like that all the time.
But this one starts way too hard, in my opinion.
Right at the 20 seconds into a track you will have to press it like 100 times per second, the game says you have limited "hearts", but there is no onscreen information of how many times you messed up. So you just end up dying again, and again, and again.
The arcs come together in bunches, but how we are supposed to count how many times we gotta press the button, if they blend with each other?
It's not a question of "get good". I think the game should have settings for casual players, like difficult levels, and/or different layouts for how the arcs appear on the screen, because the way it is at this moment, it's too hard and frustrating.
But it stills has potential if they work on this properly. Just saying.

The thing about Railroads! is that it is simple, yet addictive. I played this shortly after release and couldn't stop, even though it had the strangest limitations - take the inability to build several independent railroads on one map as an example. Despite its oversimplified character and rather controversial artstyle (though beautiful it looks more like a Toys'R'Us display than a real railroad) it provides good exercise in imagination and the purest of joys - that of building your own tracks and setting your own trains on them to then watch how majestically they deliver cargo and passengers. That itself is enough to really have a blast with the game. Add some nice economic elements and not to shabby AI competition and you have got yourself a nice purchase. Definitely recommend.

I've enjoyed this game a lot, but it has its glitches, and they are considerable.
(1) I crash to desktop (CTD) about once an hour, maybe once every two. Inexplicably. This is common.
(2) Despite having multiple maps/scenarios, after about an hour on each map, the economy is simplistic.
(3) Route mapping for the train tracks is... odd.
Despite these issues, I really enjoy this game. I'm a sucker for sim/strategy games, though. And I guess I've got a soft spot for model railroads -- who knew?
The CTD is apparently pretty common. Auto-save every minute makes this an annoyance rather than a non-playable issue.
The economy being so simple is annoying, but is an essential element of the gameplay. i.e.: this city needs this good - send it there. That's the point! It would be oddly restrictive if the objectives swapped around.
I cannot abide some of the weird and usually arbitrary route mapping issues. I don't understand why every route must exist alongside or connected to a previously connected Primary Route. What is the gameplay mechanic that necessitates building routes alongside your already-existant rail routes? This is strange to me; it seems that if you want to invest in a new depot in a new city and build a new line to a new resource, you should just be able to.
Apart from these issues, I still recommend the game if you're a sim/strategy/builder fan. For $10? Puh-leeze. You'll spend more on your next meal at Chipotle. Spend 20 hours or so enjoying this little gem. You won't play hundreds of hours, but you'll enjoy the time you do spend playing it.

For reference, I also own this game on 360 so time played isn't total. Also, when it comes to RE I've played every one with the exception of the rail shooters; so I would like to think I'm pretty familiar with the series as a whole.
RE6 is not a good "Resident Evil" game in the sense that it lacks the spookiness of the original. A lot of people disown 4,5, and 6 because of that aspect. I can't say you're wrong for thinking that, but I can say that mindset is everything when it comes to enjoyment. RE6 is a fun game. I played the 360 version mostly solo, and I played PC exclusively Co-Op. I've had quite a few laughs over the absurdity of the gameplay, or the cheesy cutscenes. And that's the key; don't think of this as a survival horror game. RE6 is an 3rd person action shooter, with a few "horror" elements. As long as you don't go into this game expecting 'Spooky Spencer Mansion Mysteries pt.6', you can enjoy the game.
The highlight for me, as usual with 4 and 5, is Mercenaries. There's a handful of characters, a few game modes (that aren't very active because there isn't a huge online community anymore), a small number of unlocks (1 costume each, 1 "special" character), and a handful of stages each with their own "boss" enemy. It's fast-pace fun, and it doesn't disappoint.
Get the game if you want some ridiculous action fun, with some throwbacks to the history of the series.

I think the creators had an interesting goal in mind, which as the description says is your applying for asylum in a strange and foriegn city. The game gets this across very quickly and that is to its credit. From the first moment, you feel like your in an alien world and I found myself enjoying the actual game world throughout my short time in it. That being said, I got pretty tired with the overall experience pretty quickly. I believe this could be interpreted as the creators accomplishing their goal, as the objective is to confound and confuse you. However, I would say the game doesn't hit the mark, as the game play mechanics simply don't stand up.
The game will confound you, but in the wrong way. The game mechanics boil down to, walk into a room, get information, read information and do exactly what the it says to progress. There is no self-discovery, no aha moments, at no point did I ever feel confusion at trying to understand instruction given to me an unfamiliar way. The game could perhaps have took some clues from older point and click adventures, which give almost no information and thrive on self-discovery through trial and error. This is not a new experience, and I think the game needed to ground itself a bit more in what has been done. Instead, the mechanics don't match the central themes of the game. You quickly discover that you can ignore anything that is confusing, as long as you simply walk everywhere and click on everything, the game will tell you exactly what you need to do.
The theme is there, the tone is there, the art style really worked for me. What was lacking was the game mechanics. I appreciate what the creators did, I think its very clever and the end hit home for me. However, the game play itself was not enough for me to consider it a good game. It feels like they needed to go through more iterations of design before calling it the final product. The game play feels like it is far below what is possible to do while maintaing the themes and emotions they were aiming for, even on a budget.

The normal difficulty is hard enough that you'll have to make multiple attempts at things while learning how new enemies fuction but it's not so hard you want to rip your hair out. The story is left very open and is without dialouge which gives it this very ethereal, atmospheric vibe. It's also definitely a bit spooky at times and gets my heart pumping when I descend into the depths of the underground and the music takes a sinister turn. The sound track overall is mesmerizing, the enemies are fun to fight, the story (while vague) reels me in, and aside from the map being a bit confusing at first I have no problems with this game. There's a lot of people crying in the negative reviews about this but I actually like that the developers don't do much hand holding. 10/10 would recommend.

Ugh.  I'm a big Sid Meier fan, and played a great deal of Railroad Tycoon 1 and 2, but this thing is a grave disappointment.  The gameplay is excessively easy; run some track and trains, money pours in, woop.  There's little need to fine-tune your trains or manifests, or even plan ahead.  The graphics are dated by modern standards of course but not bad, but cartoonish; all bright colors and everything lit as if by a spotlight.  Mountains are vastly exaggerated, making it hard to see routes.  Economics is limited; there seems to be no limit to how much of a good you can send to one city, so there's little need to search out new markets.  You can't issue stock, merge with other companies, or even take out a freakin' loan!  There's no march of technology: auto factories in the 1830s?!  The UI is OK, but a little click-happy; basic keyboard shortcuts like Esc to close a window aren't always implemented.
Quibbling aside, there are two deal-breakers: first, the maps are small, a fraction of the size of RR1 or RR2.  They're also cramped, packed with towns and industries.  There's no lonely prairie where trains rumble on for miles between stops.  Games are short.  It really lacks any epic feel.  This is killer because there are only a handful of maps to play, and a handful of goals to achieve on each.  Having played four short games, I've seen about everything there is to see.
Second, the tracks.  Laying single track is fine; the program automatically adds tunnels, bridges, and overpasses reasonably well.  HOWEVER, hit the double track button and you get your own personal demon from hell to torment you.  The simplest operations now require careful planning and possibly some build-it-and-delete-it cycles.  Trains will take the wrong track and fail to recognize tracks that exist.  Nothing's more maddening than carefully laying out track, buying a train, setting up the route... and seeing that the train won't return to the first station, because it thinks it can only go one way on a certain arbitrary segment of track... somewhere.  Except maybe having that happen over, and over, and over again.
Oh, and it's already crashed.
So what's good?  Station management is simpler; you no longer have to worry about exactly catching all of a city's industries, build a station and it just works.  Trains won't get stalled to 1 MPH on steep slopes.  For an RR1 or RR2 fan, it's all very familiar, the learning curve is tiny (don't bother with the tutorial, just start a game).  Some maps have custom industries, like wineries and fromageries in France, a cute touch.  The "patents" system is kinda cool - you bid against the other players in a brief open auction for a ten-year bonus of some sort.  When laying track in a city, the buildings will rearrange themselves to make room, at no cost, which is hugely refreshing compared to the massive PITA that could be in RRT2, where you sometimes had to demolish chunks of a city at great expense so your railroad could catch the city and cross the river.
This thing was half-baked when it was released, and never brought up to speed.  I'm tempted to try RR3; as long as it's halfway stable, it's sure to be better than this.

I want to recommend this game. Believe me, I do. If zombies were its own game for like 20 or 30 bucks then I would recommend that. However, there are quite a few glaring flaws that require me to not recommend this.
For one, the multiplayer is absolutely horrendous. The boost jumping makes every firefight an absolute chore. With the amount of mobility it isn't a surprise when people start using the most overpowered weapons that Treyarch refuses to nerf (looking at you Brecci). Other than that the Multiplayer is as bland as its ever been, with the exception and addition of "classes" that have special abilities, some of which are obviously more powerful than the other. Basically, its your average Call of Duty multiplayer with boost jump and balance issues.
The campaign is an absolute mind♥♥♥♥ but is pretty interesting when you understand it I guess? It was pretty bland, the "customization" you are allowed is laughable at best not like it matters. Nothing really to say. Except the campaign has nothing to do with the previous Black Ops games. That was unfortunate.
The zombies is the only thing that is stopping me from crushing this game. It is an extreme deviation from the original zombies formula. Piggybacking off the new storyline created by the Origin map, the new zombies maps put a very large focus on puzzles and gathering parts to craft new weapons or easter egg components. If you liked zombies because it was an arcadish casual game mode, you probably won't like this new one. Treyarch fully recognized zombies in this installment as zombies is much harder than the old formula. However, I can't help but notice the lost potential. There were a lot of game modes for zombies in Black Ops 2 that honestly should have returned in the third installment.
EDIT: ZOMBIES CHRONICLES HAS RELEASED, ZOMBIE PLAYERS REJOICE! It is the thing that was missing from this iteration of zombies this whole time! I can safely recommend this game, but only if you can get a good deal on it. Maybe the upcoming steam summer sale?

So take Hearthstone, and give it a tactical layer. That's basically Duelyst, where positioning is king alongside good cardplay and overall strategy. Add top notch pixel-art animations and overall art direction, this is a game I have unhesitantly paid money towards - and will when budget allows and they continue to keep my goodwill. With 5 factions to choose from and 2 Generals each with their own abilities, there are plenty of niches to play Duelyst with.
It also helps there's less RNG apart from your card draw, and even that is ameliorated by the fact you can Replace - basically cyce one card out back into your deck for another, which helps when you have a bad draw. RNG is predominantly in random summoning placement which can make or make some plays, as well as some Mythic/Legendaries with unique abilities.
Their microtransaction model is again like Hearthstone, buying packs and cosmetics with real money or earned "Spirit". This is a translated version of my original slovak review. It's pretty long, so here's a TL;DR:
If you want to try something different OR if you liked Stanley Parable, this is a must buy, imho.
____________________________________________
Disclaimer: Key provided by the developer for review purposes.
It's hard to write a completely spoiler-free review for this game, since basically everything is a spoiler here. Have you seen description on Pony Island's steam page? Well, that's a spoiler, too…right? Anyway, I haven't read anything more than that before I jumped into it…that, and also I knew there will be a couple of weird twists along the way. Would my experience with Pony Island differ substantialy, if I didn't know even that much, I wonder? Well, honestly, I probably wouldn't give a rats♥♥♥♥♥about it, like anyone who doesn't care about unicorns (btw, why are they called ponies nowadays? someone please explain this to me…please.)
Long story short, your goal is to figure out who you are, why has Satan inprisoned you in his game and how to set yourself free. Gameplay consists of nothing more, than…well..a set of minigames. It doesn't sound particularly interesting, does it? Two of the minigames you'll encounter the most are the hacking puzzle minigame, and the runner segment, where you have to jump over obstacles, as one does. And to be honest…these are terrible, especially the runner one. It's absolutely primitive, it doesn't present player any real challenge, and therefore, it can't be rewarding. There's nothing to these things. Nothing.
…And that's the point, isn't it? After all, you're a prisoner of devil's machine. The game is supposed to be your eternal torment. The real genius of Pony Island lies in the narrative that connects these elements, providing experience that you've maybe never went through in a videogame before.
I wrote "maybe" there. It's not that long ago, when a lot of people were excited about a similar game - Stanley Parable. (I guess I could mention Undertale here, but I won't since I haven't played it…). Stanley Parable, the game that was consistently breaking the fourth wall, adressing the player, refererencing itself and the its creators. The choices presented to the player were merely an illusion. It was provokative and urged us to ask ourselves: is this a videogame? What is a videogame, exactly? What do we really expect from videogames?
After playing Pony Island for the first few minutes, Stanley came to mind. It uses similar tricks, which are still pretty novel, even though other games have attempted/used these before. "Breaking of the fourth wall" as a term is adherent to theater and cinematography, but the way Pony Island (or similar games) can utilize these principles is something, that is only possible thanks to interactive nature of videogames.
Pony Island is very linear, it guides you to where it wants you to be. It let's you see the glimpses of story every now and then. There's more to it than it seems at first glance. You'll quickly figure out there something more outside of the devils game, despite him trying the best he can to stop you. In your attempts to escape, you'll have to destroy a couple of core files of the game. That's where afformentioned hacking minigame comes into play. It's not terrible, but it isn't really challenging. It's OK, I guess.
However, the important thing is…hacking makes you a cheater. And let's be frank here, cheating feels good, doesn't it? It's thrilling. A little bit of cheating is fine…just a little bit.  You're cheating against the devil himself! Isn't that incredible? HELL YEAH it is! (heh)
There's a chatch, though.
Devil sees you. He knows what you're up to.
As you progress, a lot of tricks and surprises await. Some of them are incredibly clever, but even the cheapest tricks don't feel…as cheap? It is very clear that the developer is fully aware how lazy and cheap they are. He's just messing with you, he winks at you. And that makes all the difference.
He's making fun of game mechanics we know, and generally, the things that we've learned to expect from videogames. Pony Island uses them to progress the story, while constantly mocking you and crushing your expectations. That's why I think that people have to have some experience with videogames to really enjoy this one. I'd say it is kind of a "minimal requirement" you have to meet, otherwise it's pointless.
It's a pretty short experience, where it will take you roughly 3 hours to get through the main thing. You won't know the whole truth by the end of it though, so there's some replayability for you. A good thing is you can access a specific part (or as they are called here, "acts"), instead of playing the whole thing through. But after you've seen most of the game, it's just not that great anymore, you know. The element of surprise is mostly gone, although there are still some surprises left. I guess my main gripe with Pony Island is that even though there still stuff to explore in the game, I just don't feel the drive to complete it. I'm glad I'm done with those repetitive, godawful runner segments. It's over. Finally…I'm free…
Speaking of runner segments, the is the real Pony Island… Yes, I understand that that was the punishment I had to go through. I get it…but still, I feel like there was too much of it, and that it was the weakest link. On the other hand, these repetitive and boring segments dumbed me down enough to get surprised again and again, when game actually did something cool. The more I think about it, I realise how devilishly briliant (ok, I'm done with puns, I promise) design decision that is…but still, I'm torn on it. Is this my punishment too? Is this the real punishment?
It doesn't matter. The fact alone that I'm forced to question my own opinion makes Pony Island more interesting title than it has any right to be. It's not flawless, but I'm not sure if it's reasonable to expect perfection from a 5$ experimental indie game. There were moments when I felt like Pony Island set the bar too high for itself. I knew it could do better, because I was already spoiled. Pony Island spoiled me, and than let me down. He never called me back, even when he promissed he would.
Was all of that by design? I don't know, but I felt like it was breaking the immersion. Was that the point? I don't know. I just don't..I don't know anything anymore…
Conclusion
If you're not sure if 5$ is a reasonable amount to pay for a anusual 3 hours long experience, I can't solve that problem for you. If you've read the whole thing through, at this point, you should already have an idea if you'd enjoy this game or not. But what I'm sure about is that if you're looking for a game with great gameplay and replayability, this isn't the one to buy. You only buy this game if you want to experience something different, surprising and mindboggling. Pony Island is great even at times when it's the most boring thing you could possibly play, and that's a hard thing to pull off I feel.
There are games where you feel smart when you find a solution to a problem, or overcome some obstacle. Pony Island is the game where you feel like it's creator wants you to know that he is smart, because he probably is.
In Soviet Russia, Pony Island plays you.
Overall score: 8.5
+ presentation
+ intelligent and witty narrative
+ unique experience
+ everything has a purpose
+ consistently surprising
- lack of motivation after completing the main part (this is probably a personal thing)
- linearity
- one too many runner segments

Well, this certainly was an experience. I'm still undecided on exactly what sort of experience it was, but it definitely was an experience.
This game handles atmosphere surprisingly well. It also messes with you in somewhat unexpected ways. All in all, if you are willing to accept the game's looks, it is a very interesting adventure to consume.
Past that... Unfortunately, it's also the kind of game where the less you know about it when heading in, the better the experience you will likely have, so I don't want to start discussing particular aspects of the game.

Think of this 4-hour narrative indie game like you would a movie ticket - five dollars up front for an evening of solid entertainment. Are all the meta gags groundbreaking for the medium? No - Portal, The Stanley Parable and Undertale all did it better. Still, you'll appreciate the labor of love that went into this project. It's a meta-game about game programming and development. Programmers, chipheads and vaporwave fans alike will appreciate all the subtle nods to Windows 95, Atari, Arcades, Nintendo, Programming, Creepypasta, Terrible Flash Games, and the myriad glitches inherent to all software.
I do have one incredibly autistic nitpick that just bugged me, and that's the game's "zeroes and ones" motif - actual base-2 binary dumps are usually abbreviated as base-16 hexadecimal strings because it's slightly more readable than the raw pulses read by machines. Every Hollywood hacker movie gets it wrong, though.
Pony Island is not without much bigger problems, unforunately. The pony-jumping, whether by design or otherwise, wears out its welcome fast after just so many iterations. The two constant games at work here boil down to a flappy bird-esque timed rail jumper, and what can best be described as a programming minigame. None of the programming puzzles will make your head explode or require a particularly trained mind, save for Louie's last "Puzzle Break", which I found to be a massive difficulty spike requiring way too many steps and variables to juggle around - you practically need to draw out each step on graph paper. Maybe it's easier if you're well versed in programming or just have a really good memory, but the sheer difficulty of that last puzzle broke the game's pacing for me. I had to look up the solution on YouTube, and even following a walkthrough required me to write each step down over several grids. There's one last puzzle after that, but it's essentially a breather. Still, after wasting an hour on that last one, I was NOT in the mood for any more programming puzzles. I guess your mileage may vary, but I can't be alone in struggling with that one.
Another, lesser thing that tripped me up was trying to guess a "Pay Attention and Remember This" riddle on the last Core. I simply was not listening for the solution the guardian gave out earlier, and unfortunately it's given out right before a checkpoint when there's a lot of distractions going on, so I had to look up the solution on YouTube, again. Surely I can't be the only one who was caught off guard? How did this get by playtesters?! I get that it's supposed to test your mental savvy but this kind of 4-hour game really should be completable by the masses without having to break out a strategy guide. It's not a super-hardcore "git gud" game like Fighters, Dark Souls or Dwarf Fortress.
EDIT: Turns out I made an honest-to-god mistake and got too easily distracted. The passphrase actually flashes below him after the checkpoint for a good 3 seconds. It's no less noticable than those "I love Paris in the the spring" mind tricks designed to mildly screw with you. I was just too incompetent to notice before I pulled up a strategy guide. There's no strikeout markup on Steam but consider the above paragraph void.
*** SPOILERS FOLLOW ***
All gripes aside, the ending was pretty cathartic - it left me satisfied for the evening I invested into it. Although before the final escape, I was still pretty confused if Satan was dead after a previous "Final Fight" following the second core file deletion, or if God was a greater evil than Satan pulling the strings a la Shin Megami Tensei, or if the lost soul was going to betray me, but none of those cliched tinfoil twists I half-expected came to fruition. Satan is the villain through and through.
As for the tickets, there's a bonus fight at the end for collecting them all. Not much of a "True Ending", just an extra. It's really not worth your time. There's no big replay value here aside from little tidbits. You're better off viewing the bonus stuff you missed on YouTube. Don't let this game's one-trick pony wear itself out and negatively taint your memory of it through even more repetitious search for that last lousy point. This isn't necessarily a bad thing, but Pony Island has about as much replay value as The Stanley Parable, which is to say, next to none at all. It seems the developers were aware of this, as they literally tell you to delete the game from your hard drive when it's all over. I won't knock the game for being honest about itself. It's a charming little disposable experience for one or two sittings, well worth its meager asking price - moreso than the vast majority of forgettable Hollywood reboots with much less artistic merit than this game. All in all, Pony Island rises above the Sturgeon's Law tide of trendy 8-bit amateur garbage trying to ape Fez or Undertale (themselves heavily inspired by Super Paper Mario and Earthbound, respectively), without breaking any real ground for the medium.

WORTH THE $1 PRICE... but... This game feels far too much like an Early Access title.
I bought the game for myself and two firends while it is on sale.  I had my eye on this game for a while, however, i never bought it until recently. I'm a huge fan of rhythm games. However, there is so much that this one lacks.
First, I will say this game has a tremendous amount of potential. It's the only reason why I'm not refunding the game. (Though i wouldn't get much back anyway). But i feel like the most joy-killing aspect of the game is the lack of difficulty and handicap adjustment. Unlike many games where you can regenerate your health after missing or mispressing notes, you don't get that in this game. Instead you are allowed an annoyingly limited number of mistakes. I'm talking from 5-8. That's something i feel needs to be addressed. Sure maybe I lack skill, but shouldn't I be able to get better while simultaneously enjoying the game? I can't even progress through the first 10 seconds of some songs due to the lack of health regeneration. Perhaps add an easy difficulty that allows us more mistakes? Once we develope the skills needed, we can take on harder difficulties. That's how I found my way around DJ Max, after all.
My next point is more opinionated than factual. But I don't get much of a satisfying note comfirmation. The notes don't burst upon catching them. Imagine guitar hero or Rock  Band. Notice how the notes burst and explode when you hit them on time, right? Such a thing doesn't exist in this game. I find the overall layout of the gamelay interface a bit confusing all together.
The game is also poorly optimized. I can't even adjust the resolution. The game forces me to lay  in Fullscreen. My laptop heats like a grill while the game is running. Thankfully theres an upcoming update addressing this issue, but its been over four months since this update was announced.
I don't want the devs to feel discouraged. I was part of a game that recieved reviews similar to mine and the project was shut down. I don't' feel this game should share the same fate. That's why I'm keeping the game, while hoping that the upcoming update makes this game more fun to play.

Black Ops 3 may have mixed reviews on Steam, but I would suggest to at least consider it. I haven’t played Infinite Warfare, but after playing Advanced Warfare I can safely say that if you wanted to play one of the futuristic COD’s, just to see what they were about, I would recommend Black Ops 3 over Advanced Warfare completely. Let me explain why, but also warn you of some of the things that might turn you off from the game.
Black Ops 3 campaign is incredibly long for a modern COD game. Maybe it was because I played it by myself or it was just me, but it took me easily 10 hours to beat the campaign. The last time a COD campaign took me that long was the first two games in the franchise. It’s a refreshing change of pace in regards of time spent. The gameplay aspect of the campaign is in top form, in such a way that it simply outclasses Advanced Warfare. While Advanced Warfare gave  you a double jump and a grappling hook. There really wasn’t that many opportunities in the campaign to use it all that much. And while wall running still has little to no use in Black Ops, Treyarch decided to focus on Special Abilities that are split into three different class sets. One set is purely a cacophony of destruction, the other focuses more on you agility, and the last one focuses on hacking your enemies. All of them are incredibly useful and if you know how to use them, they add a nice mix to the old COD formula. There’s quite a few times where a few firefights were either made easier or more manageable with these abilities. And so this creates a fun dynamic that leaves a lot of room for experimentation.
Now the story of Black Ops 3 is where it falters the most. It takes quite a long while to get going and until it does it almost feels as if every mission is a new episode in a procedural show and not until that last 3-4 levels does it become more serialized. While I understand that this allows for the story threads to build up to a big reveal. The payoff isn’t all that satisfying. In the interest of not spoiling anything, let’s just say that Black Ops 3’s story isn’t as smart as it thinks its nor is it anything you haven’t seen before. What’s worse is that game ends a bit unceremoniously, which left me confused as to whether or not it’s something that’ll continue in a possible Black Ops 4 or if it just ended. The good thing is that all the story threads are tied up, so if there’s never a sequel there won’t be any thing lost.
Black Ops 3 rounds off its grand offerings with three more single player modes. Free Run, Nightmares, and Dead Ops Arcade 2. Each of one of these modes are fun and challenging. Nightmares almost put a “What If ?” Like scenario in the story’s campaign that is not that interesting, but sure is fun to play. Unfortunately, it does go through the same levels and environments as the main campaign, but it’s still a welcome addition. Dead Ops is a fun top down shooter, whose length of entertainment will simply rely on whether or not it’s the kind of game you like. Also Free Run adds a Mirror’s Edge like time trials that are fun to go through. All of this is ultimately what makes me recommend Black Ops 3 over Advanced Warfare, because it simply has much more bang for your buck and it’s all fun in it’s own right. I’d even recommend it over Infinite Warfare if it turns out that the game has the same dearth of content as Advanced Warfare before it.
Now a bit more about some of the negatives. I do believe they are important, since it might just be the thing that helps you to hold off for now or reassures you that it’s okay to go all in. Black Ops 3 has performance issues. That is fact, however at least in my system which compromises a Windows 10 OS, an i7 3820, and a GTX 970, the issues weren’t incredibly detrimental. When there are a whole ton of effects the game runs slowly, but the only level that I had significant frame rate drops was the second, which has a whole host of weather effects, shadows, water and all that. For the most part the levels of the rest of the campaign stayed at 60fps with the occasional drop in performance when things got real hectic. However I must warn you that I had to modify a few config files to get it to run smoothly. If you don’t mind editing an ini then great, but if you do I would hold off. Also to get into more negative things, the story is not all that great, although there is one level that really stands out and calls back to the previous Black OPs games and even the older WWII shooters and it does end up to be quite a treat. It doesn’t make up for the stories shortcomings.  Since the dialogue is mostly cringe worthy, albeit delivered about as well as someone could hope for and the actors do the best they can with what’s given. Lastly, the game is a bit repetitive and if that’s not your thing there’s that.
All in all, Black Ops 3 is game that simply is too much fun for me not to recommend. As I said, it may have mixed reviews, but I would decide for yourself if it’s the game for you. It surprasses the other Black Ops games on a technical and gameplay design level, but not necessarily on a story level. The saga of the Mason’s is far more engrossing than this story. However it’s a game that gives you a lot of bang for your buck, and if ever on sale or in the future when it’s performance issues are no longer an issue, it’s definitely worth the price of admission.

If you want to try something different OR if you liked Stanley Parable, this is a must buy, imho.
____________________________________________
Disclaimer: Key provided by the developer for review purposes.
It's hard to write a completely spoiler-free review for this game, since basically everything is a spoiler here. Have you seen description on Pony Island's steam page? Well, that's a spoiler, too…right? Anyway, I haven't read anything more than that before I jumped into it…that, and also I knew there will be a couple of weird twists along the way. Would my experience with Pony Island differ substantialy, if I didn't know even that much, I wonder? Well, honestly, I probably wouldn't give a rats♥♥♥♥♥about it, like anyone who doesn't care about unicorns (btw, why are they called ponies nowadays? someone please explain this to me…please.)
Long story short, your goal is to figure out who you are, why has Satan inprisoned you in his game and how to set yourself free. Gameplay consists of nothing more, than…well..a set of minigames. It doesn't sound particularly interesting, does it? Two of the minigames you'll encounter the most are the hacking puzzle minigame, and the runner segment, where you have to jump over obstacles, as one does. And to be honest…these are terrible, especially the runner one. It's absolutely primitive, it doesn't present player any real challenge, and therefore, it can't be rewarding. There's nothing to these things. Nothing.
…And that's the point, isn't it? After all, you're a prisoner of devil's machine. The game is supposed to be your eternal torment. The real genius of Pony Island lies in the narrative that connects these elements, providing experience that you've maybe never went through in a videogame before.
I wrote "maybe" there. It's not that long ago, when a lot of people were excited about a similar game - Stanley Parable. (I guess I could mention Undertale here, but I won't since I haven't played it…). Stanley Parable, the game that was consistently breaking the fourth wall, adressing the player, refererencing itself and the its creators. The choices presented to the player were merely an illusion. It was provokative and urged us to ask ourselves: is this a videogame? What is a videogame, exactly? What do we really expect from videogames?
After playing Pony Island for the first few minutes, Stanley came to mind. It uses similar tricks, which are still pretty novel, even though other games have attempted/used these before. "Breaking of the fourth wall" as a term is adherent to theater and cinematography, but the way Pony Island (or similar games) can utilize these principles is something, that is only possible thanks to interactive nature of videogames.
Pony Island is very linear, it guides you to where it wants you to be. It let's you see the glimpses of story every now and then. There's more to it than it seems at first glance. You'll quickly figure out there something more outside of the devils game, despite him trying the best he can to stop you. In your attempts to escape, you'll have to destroy a couple of core files of the game. That's where afformentioned hacking minigame comes into play. It's not terrible, but it isn't really challenging. It's OK, I guess.
However, the important thing is…hacking makes you a cheater. And let's be frank here, cheating feels good, doesn't it? It's thrilling. A little bit of cheating is fine…just a little bit.  You're cheating against the devil himself! Isn't that incredible? HELL YEAH it is! (heh)
There's a chatch, though.
Devil sees you. He knows what you're up to.
As you progress, a lot of tricks and surprises await. Some of them are incredibly clever, but even the cheapest tricks don't feel…as cheap? It is very clear that the developer is fully aware how lazy and cheap they are. He's just messing with you, he winks at you. And that makes all the difference.
He's making fun of game mechanics we know, and generally, the things that we've learned to expect from videogames. Pony Island uses them to progress the story, while constantly mocking you and crushing your expectations. That's why I think that people have to have some experience with videogames to really enjoy this one. I'd say it is kind of a "minimal requirement" you have to meet, otherwise it's pointless.
It's a pretty short experience, where it will take you roughly 3 hours to get through the main thing. You won't know the whole truth by the end of it though, so there's some replayability for you. A good thing is you can access a specific part (or as they are called here, "acts"), instead of playing the whole thing through. But after you've seen most of the game, it's just not that great anymore, you know. The element of surprise is mostly gone, although there are still some surprises left. I guess my main gripe with Pony Island is that even though there still stuff to explore in the game, I just don't feel the drive to complete it. I'm glad I'm done with those repetitive, godawful runner segments. It's over. Finally…I'm free…
Speaking of runner segments, the is the real Pony Island… Yes, I understand that that was the punishment I had to go through. I get it…but still, I feel like there was too much of it, and that it was the weakest link. On the other hand, these repetitive and boring segments dumbed me down enough to get surprised again and again, when game actually did something cool. The more I think about it, I realise how devilishly briliant (ok, I'm done with puns, I promise) design decision that is…but still, I'm torn on it. Is this my punishment too? Is this the real punishment?
It doesn't matter. The fact alone that I'm forced to question my own opinion makes Pony Island more interesting title than it has any right to be. It's not flawless, but I'm not sure if it's reasonable to expect perfection from a 5$ experimental indie game. There were moments when I felt like Pony Island set the bar too high for itself. I knew it could do better, because I was already spoiled. Pony Island spoiled me, and than let me down. He never called me back, even when he promissed he would.
Was all of that by design? I don't know, but I felt like it was breaking the immersion. Was that the point? I don't know. I just don't..I don't know anything anymore…
Conclusion
If you're not sure if 5$ is a reasonable amount to pay for a anusual 3 hours long experience, I can't solve that problem for you. If you've read the whole thing through, at this point, you should already have an idea if you'd enjoy this game or not. But what I'm sure about is that if you're looking for a game with great gameplay and replayability, this isn't the one to buy. You only buy this game if you want to experience something different, surprising and mindboggling. Pony Island is great even at times when it's the most boring thing you could possibly play, and that's a hard thing to pull off I feel.
There are games where you feel smart when you find a solution to a problem, or overcome some obstacle. Pony Island is the game where you feel like it's creator wants you to know that he is smart, because he probably is.
In Soviet Russia, Pony Island plays you.
Overall score: 8.5
+ presentation
+ intelligent and witty narrative
+ unique experience
+ everything has a purpose
+ consistently surprising
- lack of motivation after completing the main part (this is probably a personal thing)
- linearity

Well, this certainly was an experience. I'm still undecided on exactly what sort of experience it was, but it definitely was an experience.
This game handles atmosphere surprisingly well. It also messes with you in somewhat unexpected ways. All in all, if you are willing to accept the game's looks, it is a very interesting adventure to consume.
Past that... Unfortunately, it's also the kind of game where the less you know about it when heading in, the better the experience you will likely have, so I don't want to start discussing particular aspects of the game.
And, honestly, it's well priced. If it was even $10, I may have been more cautious in recommending it, but... For the $5, you get a nice bite-sized experience that you'll ingest, complete, mull a few things over for a bit, and then move on.

Think of this 4-hour narrative indie game like you would a movie ticket - five dollars up front for an evening of solid entertainment. Are all the meta gags groundbreaking for the medium? No - Portal, The Stanley Parable and Undertale all did it better. Still, you'll appreciate the labor of love that went into this project. It's a meta-game about game programming and development. Programmers, chipheads and vaporwave fans alike will appreciate all the subtle nods to Windows 95, Atari, Arcades, Nintendo, Programming, Creepypasta, Terrible Flash Games, and the myriad glitches inherent to all software.
I do have one incredibly autistic nitpick that just bugged me, and that's the game's "zeroes and ones" motif - actual base-2 binary dumps are usually abbreviated as base-16 hexadecimal strings because it's slightly more readable than the raw pulses read by machines. Every Hollywood hacker movie gets it wrong, though.
Pony Island is not without much bigger problems, unforunately. The pony-jumping, whether by design or otherwise, wears out its welcome fast after just so many iterations. The two constant games at work here boil down to a flappy bird-esque timed rail jumper, and what can best be described as a programming minigame. None of the programming puzzles will make your head explode or require a particularly trained mind, save for Louie's last "Puzzle Break", which I found to be a massive difficulty spike requiring way too many steps and variables to juggle around - you practically need to draw out each step on graph paper. Maybe it's easier if you're well versed in programming or just have a really good memory, but the sheer difficulty of that last puzzle broke the game's pacing for me. I had to look up the solution on YouTube, and even following a walkthrough required me to write each step down over several grids. There's one last puzzle after that, but it's essentially a breather. Still, after wasting an hour on that last one, I was NOT in the mood for any more programming puzzles. I guess your mileage may vary, but I can't be alone in struggling with that one.
Another, lesser thing that tripped me up was trying to guess a "Pay Attention and Remember This" riddle on the last Core. I simply was not listening for the solution the guardian gave out earlier, and unfortunately it's given out right before a checkpoint when there's a lot of distractions going on, so I had to look up the solution on YouTube, again. Surely I can't be the only one who was caught off guard? How did this get by playtesters?! I get that it's supposed to test your mental savvy but this kind of 4-hour game really should be completable by the masses without having to break out a strategy guide. It's not a super-hardcore "git gud" game like Fighters, Dark Souls or Dwarf Fortress.
EDIT: Turns out I made an honest-to-god mistake and got too easily distracted. The passphrase actually flashes below him after the checkpoint for a good 3 seconds. It's no less noticable than those "I love Paris in the the spring" mind tricks designed to mildly screw with you. I was just too incompetent to notice before I pulled up a strategy guide. There's no strikeout markup on Steam but consider the above paragraph void.
*** SPOILERS FOLLOW ***
All gripes aside, the ending was pretty cathartic - it left me satisfied for the evening I invested into it. Although before the final escape, I was still pretty confused if Satan was dead after a previous "Final Fight" following the second core file deletion, or if God was a greater evil than Satan pulling the strings a la Shin Megami Tensei, or if the lost soul was going to betray me, but none of those cliched tinfoil twists I half-expected came to fruition. Satan is the villain through and through.
As for the tickets, there's a bonus fight at the end for collecting them all. Not much of a "True Ending", just an extra. It's really not worth your time. There's no big replay value here aside from little tidbits. You're better off viewing the bonus stuff you missed on YouTube. Don't let this game's one-trick pony wear itself out and negatively taint your memory of it through even more repetitious search for that last lousy point. This isn't necessarily a bad thing, but Pony Island has about as much replay value as The Stanley Parable, which is to say, next to none at all. It seems the developers were aware of this, as they literally tell you to delete the game from your hard drive when it's all over. I won't knock the game for being honest about itself. It's a charming little disposable experience for one or two sittings, well worth its meager asking price - moreso than the vast majority of forgettable Hollywood reboots with much less artistic merit than this game. All in all, Pony Island rises above the Sturgeon's Law tide of trendy 8-bit amateur garbage trying to ape Fez or Undertale (themselves heavily inspired by Super Paper Mario and Earthbound, respectively), without breaking any real ground for the medium.

Crysis 2 is a thoroughly entertaining romp-especially when played on a gaming oriented PC hooked up to a large screen with some dope audio. The story is so-so and the writing hilariously poor at times, it is the technology though that really shines, Cry Engine 2 when paired with the Direct X11 based overhaul that came about in 2012 is quite thrilling. It is comparable to blasting through a hollywood blockbuster, the audio/visual effects and overall atmosphere are so rich that you'll forgive the identikit enemies and senseless story in serach of the next epic and hugely satisfying shootout.
A very different animal to the first game and not half as clever by design, one of gamings guilty pleasures. Combat scenarios usually offer several options with many alternative tactics possible, stealth kills, heavy weapons, sniping etc almost 80% of the time though the game demands a no holds barred guns blazing approach.
It's a power trip fantasy not far removed from Duke Nukem Forever in my eyes. Limited replayability even with the gorgeous graphics but absolutely worth at least one play through. The wrecked beauty asthetic of New York is still a landmark achievement in gaming fidelity. The AI is generally quite smart on the higher settings and very quick to react, combat feels weighted and fluid with all of the weapons and modifications providing excellent feedback, nano suit mods is nice and well implemented addition.
A very handome game indeed and several thousand times better then the abysmal third title. Buy it, play it, enjoy it.

Sid Meier's Railroads! is a very fun simulation/strategy game that reminds of the Railroad Tycoon series. I have to say that the gameplay and graphics are cleaner and friendlier than RT2 and RT3. You deliver goods from production points on the map to/from cities and between one another. The scenarios take place across the US and Europe with a series of objectives to complete during each time period. I really enjoy playing against the computer players while trying to buy out their railroad as I conquer the map. Ultimately, this is an engaging title that will make you wonder where the hours went- just like many other Sid Meier's games.

It’s not really “about” the contemporary refugee crisis - it’s more like the kind of nightmare you might have after watching a documentary about it and eating too much cheese.
Buildings, language, logic and gameplay are warped into unfamiliar, intimidating dimensions, and their opaque rules represent your main challenge and adversary in the game. The story is rich with the oppressive mood and ironic humour that Orwell and Kafka are famous for, and the style draws from Expressionism and Absurdism as well as cyberpunk dystopias.
The game can be a bit oblique at explaining itself - it didn’t even seem to have a menu or interface. But that consistent feeling of alienation and confusion you share with your character is the whole point. Beneath its presentation, the game isn’t actually that complicated and can be completed in an hour.
If you’re interested in story, atmosphere, general weirdness, and what games can be to create an experience, then this will reward you. It’s short, strange, ominous and bewildering, and if you can imagine that being a good thing then it’s probably worth your time.

Generally, the tutorial is pretty amazing. Author knows exactly when viewer might have a question and covers entire proccess very thorougly. Despite watching hundreds of similar tutorials on the web, this is the only one truly made UWV unwrapping logical and simple. So generally, I recommend this tutorial to everyone who has a general grasp of 3ds Max and beginner (or higher) skill of box modelling.
But also - what I learned or thought while watching this tutorial:
* If everyone would put such insane, almost autistic attention into modelling and texturing as show in this video, games would each take 50 years to complete. I cannot believe there's a software company boss who pays by the hour and lets any modeller spend such time and work on a single weapon model. But as a tutorial, it's perfect, of course.
* UWV Unwrapping is a thing human beings SHOULD NOT DO. I still don't understand why those guys at Autodesk keep adding tools to do it manually instead of - I don't know - writing a proper algorithm to solve this computational question that's been up and badly handled since 1996. Or if it's really that hard mathematically, maybe let learning computers get crack at this?
When author of this video started unwrapping various bolts and nuts, it seriously made me cringe. I repeat, letting humans still do this manually is serious waste of talent and lifetime.
* Physically-based texturing and amazing procedural systems like Substance Painter demonstrated in this tutorial probably single-handedly wipe most of knowledge of old-school modellers. This tutorial hardly uses any photoshop at all. But I think it's good. This tutorial sets a good case to prove this.
* Doing basically everything using shortcuts makes cramped, horrible case of failed UI design (of 3ds Max) that's only gone worse, year by year -- almost tolerable. As author does and encourages watchers to do.
So yeah, I highly recommend to watch this if you have any interest in box-modelling, modelling in general or curiosity how far we've come in tools and tehnique past 15 years.
