First of all, I would like to point out that I've actually spent more time on this tutorial than Steam is actually showing...
Here's a pic on my progress so far:
I'm currently in Part 2.2, giving the lower reciever some detail (as you can see, it's just a block right now, as I'm writting this).
So, let's get into the review:
_____________________________________________
If I had to describe this tutorial with one word, that word would be: "Wow". This tutorial easily exceeds any tutorial I've seen. It's definitely a lot better than any of the Digital Tutors/3dMotive/3DBuzz tutorials I've seen.
Tim provides everything one could've ask for... He even shows us his shortcuts for certain modifiers that you will need to use throughout this tutorial (thank you so much for those shortcuts, BTW). It teaches you ways of modelling both macro and micro details (letters, numbers, serial numbers, etc), Texture Baking, UV Unwrapping/Mapping (which is pretty hard if you don't know how to approach it), how to create PBR textures (which is a huge plus, since PBR makes the model looks a lot more realistic) and much more.
I've learned so much already. From how to approach certain objects/parts from a different angle to finally knowing what smoothing groups are for. I've been 3D modelling for what, half an year now?- and I can tell you that if this tutorial was available when I started modelling, my skills would be a lot more developed than they are today. This tutorial has tought me certain workflows that I would never even think of, and I haven't even started on both Lower and Upper Receiver (which looks to be the most difficult part). I can't wait to get there are see how Tim approaches those details of the weapon.
I have to give Tim props on his choice in modelling the AKM instead of any other gun. The AKM has a lot of different shapes. Shapes that need to be tackled with different approaches/techniques. He also tells the viewer everything he's doing. This might not seem like something huge, but believe me, it is.
If you've seen a lot of tutorials, you've probably run into the problem of looking at your model for a second, and when you look back that the tutorial, the Tutor has already done something completely different and didn't tell you what it was, forcing you to go back and watching what he did. It's pretty frustrating if it's happening constantly, and makes you not want to continue with the tutorial. This doesn't really happen in this tutorial because Tim's constantly telling you what he's doing.
This is an incredible tutorial. It teaches you everything you need to know about modelling hard surface objects.
I really hope to see more tutorials from Tim Bergholz. If you were on defense about this tutorial, just buy it. It will be the best tutorial you have ever seen.

Terrible game. There's a lot of content, but it's stretched thin. Has multiple campaigns with quite a bit of recycled content in each one. Makes you watch the same long cutscenes repeatedly. Controls are awful and inventory management is unintuitive and clunky. The melee combat is frustrating; moves are supposed to be contextual so when you go to strike an enemy on the ground you should stomp on them, but sometimes your character will decide to swing the air above them instead. I was in a coop game where my partner had a zombie pin him on the ground, so I turned around and repeatedly roundhouse kicked the air above the zombie while it ate his face off. The button to run is the same button to climb ladders and jump up or down ledges so you will frequently do one thing when you meant to do another. It has bad checkpointing so you'll replay tedious sections repeatedly. It's full of unecessary and annoying quicktime events that cause instant game overs, far more than any other Resident Evil game. It also has a major bug in Jake's campaign that halts progression in coop that requires a workaround to continue progression.
The worst part of the game is it frequently takes away control to make you look at something the game wants to tell you is important, unfortunately the enemies don't stop when this happens so the game is full of cheap deaths where you will be killed by an enemy that approached you and jumped on you during a cutscene. See a zombie approaching you? No problem, I'll just take out my shotgun... no the game wants me to look at some random door that I would've found myself... and I'm on the ground with the zombie on top of me and I'm dead.
The game is full of heavily scripted sequences. The game wants you to conserve ammo, but it is also full of scripted encounters with bosses with high health pools, and shooting them will either damage them or not depending on whether or not you're in a scripted sequence or not. It is beyond frustrating to use half your ammo on a boss only to realise that you can't actually damage him yet because the game hadn't decided you're at the scripted point in which you can. Once you have played these encounters out a few times you will begin to wonder every time you reach a boss whether you should shoot him or not or wait for a truck to run him over (often the correct decision). It doesn't just affect bosses but normal enemies. During quicktime events your partner will often not be able to do anything to help you. In my coop game a zombie grabbed my partner and slowly killed him over the course of about half a minute. During that time I unloaded half my shotgun ammo into him, a zombie type we had encountered before and typically took two rounds to take down. But because the game decided the only important thing was whether he passed the quicktime event, that zombie was invincible. You will also run into zombies lying on the ground numerous times that you know are obvious threats. You can shoot them but your bullets will have no impact. Even though you know they're a threat, you have to walk past them where they will  stand up and are only then able to be damaged.
The coop is poor compared to Resident Evil 5 or other coop games. There is no resource sharing so if your partner runs out of ammo and you have a ton, that person is just going to have to go on a punching spree until they find some more. You can't give first aid kits or medical supplies to your partner either, although you can use them on them. This is such a basic feature and it was important in Resident Evil 5, so its omission here is glaring.
It doesn't play like a survival horror game; I don't have any problem with that in itself but the game is trying to be an action game instead. When you compare it to other action games it doesn't hold up well at all. If you are considering buying this game, get Gears or War, Bulletstorm, Spec Ops: The Line, or one of the newer Tomb Raider games. Or Resident Evil 4. They're all significantly better than this game and tread the same ground.

I recently finished Thomas Was Alone, one of the most moving games in recent memory. It claims to be "a game about friendship, and jumping", but I also found sacrifice to be a central theme.
Genre-wise, it's a puzzle-platformer where you must make characters with different abilities collaborate, à la The Lost Vikings. This cooperation mechanic ties in very well with the game's themes. None of the levels is particularly hard, which I felt was the right choice because this game, thank god, is about something more than hand-eye coordination.
Plot-wise, every few levels we get to read a short fragment --- something like newspaper clippings from the future --- from which we must piece together the story. It adds mystery and makes it impossible to put the game down once we start to get it; we simply must know what happens next! I won't spoil any of it.
Aesthetically, TWA makes two contrasting choices that work amazingly well together.
Visually, it is minimalist in the extreme --- the main characters are literally rectangles of different shapes and sizes, and the environment consists almost exclusively of black polygons (there's water sometimes). This makes a lot of sense because the characters are AIs inside a computer, and it often works to great effect: the visual depictions of sacrifice are heartbreaking in their simplicity.
In terms of sound though, TWA embraces complexity. The excellent and often hilarious narration imbues these mere rectangles with more personality than can be found in 90% of games out there.
And then there's the soundtrack; the absolutely GLORIOUS soundtrack.
David Housden's masterpiece (created specifically for TWA) isn't just the most moving, well thought-out, complex and layered videogame soundtrack I've come across. It's some of the best music I've ever heard, period. It mixes analog instruments (strings, piano, winds) with more electronic sounds representing the AIs. These recurring "blip" motifs lend a structural cohesion to the whole rivaling that of any classical piece.
The soundtrack can even be appreciated without having played the game; you can find it on YouTube. Just listen to the hesitant dissonances of "Lost" --- like an electronic, distorted version of the adagio in Mozart's Gran Partita; they give way to the dramatic percussion of "A Time for Change", and then to the thrilling climax of "Escape", a piece that really gets your blood flowing when it comes on in the game. After I finished the game I listened to the soundtrack for weeks!

There are two types of video games. Those built for singleplayer, and those built for multiplayer. Many have stunning graphics, beautiful stories, and envigorating mechanics, but once the story is done, there's no drive to continue playing. The game experience, while memorable, is not prolonged, and the game's experience ends with the final boss.
Then there's games like Rainbow Six, who focus on creating a unique and ever-changing multiplayer experience. The game is diverse in mechanic, and heavily reliant on team and player composition. When you start a match, you have the option of choosing any variety of Operators, as the playable characters are called. Each of these characters have a unique ability and weapon set they can use that provide them advantages in shooting, pushing and preventing pushes, gathering intel, and♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥your enemies off. This aspect of the game, paired with the various maps, gamemodes, and objective locations - not to mention the differing skill level of every player - provides a unique and ever changing experience every single time you hit play. The Operators aren't free - in order to unlock a new one, you have to pay the equivalent of ~a week's worth of grinding. Many look at this as tedious, but I think of it as fantastic. This mechanic of the game provides you the feeling of satisfaction you get from clearing the final boss in a singleplayer style game; You play through the filler stages, some easy and some knee weakeningly impossible, but you prevail. You now have enough items to throw at the final boss that it dies, and you get the reward item. You now have a great toy to fight through the following filler stages with, and three months from now, the dev team will release another two bosses for you to conquer, and a new arena for you to fight on.
Rainbow Six:Siege is a prime example of a playable game. There is always going to be an opponent better than you, and there's always going to be a new strategy for you to learn. It has kept me entertained for six hundred hours of my life, and I expect it will keep me entertained for 600 more. I highly suggest Rainbow as a game for anybody that wants to kill time.

This is got to be the most tactical and awesome pixal art game I've played yet. Choose between Lynor, Songhai, Vetruvian, Abyssian, Magmar or Vanar decks to create a very fast grid turn based tactics game. It really is a fast, intense game. You learn quickly to play all you got and fast. Each deck is 40 cards of artifacts, spells and creatures. The deck themes are very much based on just that theme and nuetral creatures usually drop off once you can fill your whole deck with the themes. Each one has a VERY specific playing style and 2 types of generals. Generals lead the army and pretty much determine your style and tactics. Generals have bloodborn spells, ( spells that they only can cast and get every few turns.) Each one like the deck theme and general are very diffrent and change the gameplay. There is no missmatching decks but custom deck creation is possible. Unlock new cards for each factions deck by playing that deck and leveling it up. Also to unlock is profile pictures and emoticons. Yes, emoticans are able to be used by your general profile hub during gameplay to express if your impressed by your opponants last move, or if your not and think there being cheecky.  Also to unlock with gold and spirit points is spirit orbs( new cards).  Gold and spirit points and such are earned through dailies and quests and challanges. Challanges are neat little senarios that they put up for you so you can figure out how to do something ( usually kill an enemy general ) in a move or less. Sometimes they are hard and require some thought and actually READING every little things abilities to take full advantage of. Like I said the game moves fast and hard. Now try all the deck factions in solo challanges to learn abilities and unlock that loot or do practice vs AI mode, or ranked play to earn well, more loot. Gauntlet draft is they typical TCG , build a deck and see how well you do with it thus earning loot according too. There is no music to the game really but the sound effects and pixal art is deffinantly that. ART. Its really well done and exciting to see what happens on the playing board. Be prepaired to lose and the learning curve is steep, EVERY DECK HAS KILL CARDS. Be expected to get nuked if cards are drawn/played right. BUT have fun and see just how good you can make your factions deck and genral do in DUELYST.

This game is fantastic. It fixes a lot of issues that other card games have in terms of skill, and RNG. Each turn you get a free mulligan which is send a card to from your hand to your deck then draw a card. This adds plenty of consistency to your decks which would otherwise brick possibly harder, allowing you to get a much smoother curve overall unless your deck is really bad which is your own fault :/
Additionally, the skill aspect of having the control units on a tactical board allows for you to outplay people, just by knowing how to position properly. You can very easily see the difference in a players skill, just by how they are placing their units. This additionally helps deal with people who "netdeck" and use the flavour of the month decks. Sure, they have a bunch of cards which could be really good but they are still garbage and will probably lose if you are good.
Each month you get a ton of free cards just for placing in ranked. This is very beneficial to casual players as you can build your collection easier. Additionally, card drop rates for this game are very nice and fair. You get a legendary in about 1 out of every 4 packs. Extremely generous card drops. Also, you get plenty of cards for just playing a particular faction which will help out your deck. Finally, the starter cards they give you are pretty solid. There are some really good common neutrals which you can pick up to help fill your decks until you start specializing more heavily into a particular playstyle you enjoy.
Highly recommend this game to anyone who enjoys tcgs/ccgs

I've first played this in beta (~a year ago) and spent a decent amount of time and money on it playing through the standalone client.
I can recommend this game if you're a casual gamer and just want to try something different, the spacial aspect of the game adds a super fun and interesting layer to deckbuilding (refreshingly non-RNG-y) and piloting, but I can not recommend this game if you don't enjoy hyper-aggressive cancer.
When I last played the game, admittedly this was a couple of months ago (I did minor research for this review, nothing much at all seems changed in terms of top tier decks), I mostly played Tempo Lyonar (Argeon) and had great success with it, simply because it can outlast Burnhai and outtempo a lot of midrange decks, but sometimes due to the nature of movement and RNG, you just get burned down way too fast, you get slowed down immensely by insanely overbudgeted taunts, or other such joys. On the flipside of this, there is so much removal...games in Duelyst constructed often feel like a seesaw of tempo, massive swings in either direction all of the time.
Personally, the absolutely mental stat budgets were the biggest dealbreaker, and made the game feel very poorly balanced. There are some nice archetypes in the game, but they're usually either ineffective or super cheesy. Gauntlet (arena) felt awful, for the stat budgets exacerbate the imbalance between classes in arena even more, I have both flown through virtually unopposed and been crushed like a bug, with little to no possible consistency, worse than in any other TCG I have played (HS, ES:L, Eternal, Magic Duels).
If you'd like to play a game with a good ingame(!)-community, with a nice new spin on the genre but a TON of gimmicks, give this a try.
Did I enjoy myself to a level that matches my spending? Not really, I found the experience hugely unpleasant overall.

NORTH, heres my verdict..

+ Interesting storyline, however quite vague. (1pts)
+ They almost hit the nail on the head with providing a weird atmosphere in the game, even though its let down by the frame drops and awkward movement. (1pts)
+ Arguably you'd get your moneys worth with this, depending what you're looking for in a game. $2.39NZD for 30-50 minutes of gameplay. (1pts)

- Unskippable intro sequence. (0pts)
- Game is locked at 30fps and I experienced frame drops to 15-20fps in certain areas. (2pts)
- Very vague objective. (2pts)
- No escape menu or saves, if you crash or need to change resolution like I did you have to start from the beginning. You're also left with ugly motion blur & bloom effects. Not a huge issue due to the game being short but I'd imagine anyone that crashed near the end wouldnt bother replaying. (1pts)
- Navigation is awkward, FOV seems too zoomed in and the map is often too dark in some places to see slopes/stairs. I don't know if this was "intended" for the feel of the game but I didn't like it. (1pts)
I had absolutely no idea what to do in this part, so I have to say overall it wasn't that well executed.
(total -3pts)
The negatives outweigh the positives for this game. I wont say whether to buy it or not, but hopefully this has given some sort of insight.

In this sub-genre of dark, atmospheric, surreal indie walking-sims, NORTH is the gold standard.
If you're looking for a gameplay-heavy experience then look elsewhere, and I'd be lying if I said the game's non-existent budget couldn't be felt in its sluggish controls and slight performance issues.
But these slight problems in no way detract from the game's many strengths, including its beautiful art-style, interesting and cleverly conveyed story, great soundtrack, and immersive world.
If you're even slightly interested in this style of game, then play NORTH right now! You won't regret it.

At face value it's a relaxing, passive first person exploration game with a vibrant color palette, hypnotic electronic beats, and a lovely art direction. Like the flame to a moth, that's what drove me to it. However, what lies deeper is equally as beautiful: a thought provoking plot centered around existentialism and how it relates to other forms of philosophy and the various arts and humanities. Both its narrative and its audiovisuals are bastions of and for creativity.

It's a surreal immersion into another world.  It asks questions no other game would.   I highly recommend experiencing it.   It's Ultraworld.  But is it real?
Find everything for more answers... and more questions.

The textbook example of a pretentious indie project, an "interactive adventure" (I can't call it a game, my mind just won't let me) on par with stellar projects like "Gone Home" and "Walking simulator 983: Now with social commentary."
Cliche'd questions, cliche'd dillemas.
The game tries really hard to appear deep, but there is no suspense of disbelief big enough to keep this thing going.
"Hurf durf I'm totally an AI who made a game as soon as I became self aware, now help me solve some existential questions."
The visuals looked good at first, but everything's so movie-grain saturated, so filled with glare and bloom then my eyes cannot stand looking at it without tearing up.
The OST is an assortment of electronic blurbs and weak attempts to pander to the TRON atmosphere, I suppose. Done quite poorly.
Zero gameplay whatsoever.
Go from point A to point B, listen to a boring siloloquy which is supposed to stir some sort of questions in the mind of the player, proceed onwards.
The problem is - for people who have no interest in this kind of things, the game will seem boring due to lack of interactivity. For people who know even a tiniest bit about AIs from mass media the game will seem boring, since it's exploiting the same tropes that premate all the blockbusters about robots these days. The only audience who can probably appreciate it are hipsters, but goddamn screw those people.
To sum it up,
If I wanted to be educated about AIs and their problems, I'd much rather read Azimov than play this.

Artsy, psychedelic, first person exploratory narrative adventure with an internal philosophical debate that you are a part of. A game that will make you question who you are and what you are playing. There aren't many games that can actually stimulate all parts of the brain while playing but this one get's as close as possible. Focus hard enough and you will be able to feel the colors and taste the soundtrack!

hint, cough..  Colorful, vibrant, eye-pleasing. Yet, there is only so much to do in ULTRAWORLD.  There is no action.  No combat.

note: it is crash-tastic on Windows 7 and 8, but there is a very easy fix mentioned in the forums that takes care of it.

The game is a definitve setback from the older Railroad Tycoons.
* The routing of trains is awful. One basically has to build an own track per train or they will lock up (or one has to play with easy routing)
* The 3D interface makes it very difficult to lay track as one likes it. And more often than one would expect switches will not work. I managed to had a whole track in a station unuseable for mysterious reasons. Routing wouldn't use it, Trains could not be set in there.
* The 3D look is also more like a model railway than a real one. Especially the way height is overscaled looks ludicrious (the Western US seemingly mainly consists of peaks and valeys). Also one can only zoom out very slightly, giving no good overview of the landscape.
* The economy model is quite simpel. Lots of X delivered somewhere => Price of X decrease slightly everywhere (if the fluctuations were even caused by delivery action). You can overdeliver a good to an industry (exhausting its storage capacity so it is thrown away) and still get full pay.
* The differences between the engines are quite simple. One isn't even told their climbing abilities.
* And finally if one wins a scenario (at least if one does it an age earlier than expected) the game crashes to desktop.
The older Tycoons were better. A more realistic, albeit more abstract model of railway management is e.g. "Rails across America".

I bought it for the campaign, and I'm glad I did. I consider this the best game in the Call Of Duty series so far. The game has a decent story, gives you plenty of weapons to choose from, the option of several levels of difficulty, and provides a fairly varied assortment of enemies to shoot at.
My GTX 980Ti had no problem running this game on max settings synced at 60FPS. That being said, I did experience occasional stuttering (during some cutaway scenes), and 2 or 3 crashes during intense battles. Not sure about the cause, but I did notice that other people are complaining about the same issues on PC.
Also there's an annoying glitch where you can't pick up RPG's using the "X" button on your controller. I spent a frustrating half an hour of trying to figure out WTF is going on and whether I'm missing something, before I eventually googled it and found out that you have to press "left D-pad" instead, and then it was all good from there on.
Anyway, minor technical issues aside, I enjoyed the game, and replayed a few missions more than once. Treyarch always made the best COD games, and this one is no exception. I would definitely recommend it for the campaign.

Thomas Was Alone is beautifully realised puzzle platformer, which brings something a little different to the genre without straying too far from what works. The game revolves around a number of geometric characters (or "AIs"), each of whom have their own quirks you'll need to utilise to get to the end of each level. For me it's this cast of characters which is the game's biggest pull; level progression treats you to their adorably narrated story, and the soundtrack is absolutely stunning too. Yet despite all these positives, the game has a number of issues that really took away from the overall experience.
My biggest is that Thomas Was Alone reaches a logical conclusion about seventy levels in, in a way which felt climactic enough to be end-game. Yet instead of it naturally ending there you're suddenly foisted another thirty or fourty levels of stuff-you've-already-done, with completely different characters you're given no time to care about. It felt wrong when compared to the beautifully unravelling story you've just played through, and considering the technical issues you will have inevitably battled with to reach this first "ending" anyway (including music tracks layering up on each other indefinitely, characters flying off moving platforms or getting stuck on the environment, and a particular puzzle mechanic which only adds difficulty through poor implementation), Thomas Was Alone had outstayed its welcome by that point for me.
That being said I've given Thomas Was Alone a thumbs up, as the overall concept is great and I love how the fantastic narration not only drives the game, but gives personalities and depth to what are essentially a collection of shapes. Technical issues slowly add up to make completing it unenjoyable towards the end, but I'd still recommend it as a fun puzzle-platformer and even moreso to people who enjoy a great story.

A puzzle-platformer where neither the puzzles nor platforming are anything remarkable. In fact, they tended to work against one another. Often I would recognize a solution quickly but executing it became a tedious task. Constantly switching between the different blocks became a tiring experience.
I was initially warm to the idea of an abstract shape given character by clever narration, but it just wasn't clever or funny enough for me to care. Well voiced, but not especially well written. In my time playing, the narration was mostly spent stating the obvious.
I was blown away by the compelling narrative and (mostly) tight controls. It's a simple game, beautifully done.

Cons:
This game is a really cool idea but it's so terribly programmed.
The controls are unresponsive and the physics are completely broken.  The friction is horribly high and the collision is broken to the point where you can abuse it to get past levels early.  Half the time I can't even tell if I'm exploiting a bug or playing it how it's supposed to be played.
Also, there's some bug, seemingly with the particles for the water and the spinning square thing, that makes an infinite loop and it slows the game down really, really badly if you play it all in one sitting.  I 100%ed it in about 3 hours without stopping but around 2 hours in, the game was running at less than 10 FPS after starting out fine.  Once I restarted the game, it fixed it, but it's completely unplayable until you do so.
All that aside, the story is kind of cool, I guess, but it's just a really weird hipster-arthouse type thing which is honestly pretty lame.  I get the gist of the story and what it was supposed to represent or whatever, but it's just dumb.
There are some levels where you can get yourself stuck like right next to the exit and you're forced to start over.  There are also some levels without checkpoints that are really long and if you die you're just screwed.
The game isn't even fun.  It's just something to do.  It's not hard, but the levels are so tedious and it's really frustrating if the lack of controller response kills you and you have to restart the 20 minute long level.
Pros:
The art and narration are done really well.  This would have been better as a movie than a game.  Or at least like a Stanley Parable kind of game.
Also you can get all the achievements in less than 3 hours and you can get them all in one playthrough.

Jazzpunk is a very... unique game. Unique in the sense that it takes a 'lolrandom' approach to humour and actually manages to pull it off. The comedy harkens back to shows like Monty Python and the Young Ones, but with added pop culture references.
This comedy is reinforced in every aspect of the game, and even the characters in-game look like they belong on a bathroom door (something not gone unnoticed). Sound is used well to reinforce this humour, using trumpets and so on to make it reminiscent of cartoons, Looney Tunes in particular.
The actual gameplay part of Jazzpunk is negligible, and the few moments of traditional gameplay exists to serve the humour, usually taking form as part of a reference to other games. That said, these sections provide good breaks for pacing. Aside from those sections it's mostly an classic adventure game, you collect things so you can get past obstacles and you discover additional objects which have hidden uses.
It was a little shorter than I thought it would be, I expected another level or two. But the more that I think about it the more happy I become with its length, as humour has a tendency to be short lived regardless of quality.
To be honest, this entire game devolves into its humour; with everything else being superflous. If you enjoy memetic humour then you'll enjoy this game. If it turns you off then don't even bother. This is comedy first and game second, but it does the comedy well.
John Woo and Michael Scott sat down and wrote a script together. That script was made into a game. This is not that game. This is Necrophone Games game.

Cities: Skylines is a game that did not disappoint me at all. If you are a fan of games such as Sim City and/or Planet Coaster, I highly doubt you won't like Cities: Skylines. It is probably the best city-creator game I have ever played.
First off, the community is super creative. New mods and assets are uploaded to the Workshop each day. The mods add a lot to the game and the assets help you to further customize your city to your liking. You can also downloads maps to build your city on and save games of cities that other players have created.
Secondly, the game itself is addicting. You can play normal mode, where there is a budget and you have to learn to manage your money and sometimes even take loans, or you can play with an unlimited budget and create your city without limitations. This allows players that want a challenge to have a gamemode of their own, and players (like me) that just want to create the city of their dreams. It's one of those games that you get so involved in that you lose track of time. The longer you play and the more experienced you get, the more amount of time you spend on detailing and doing simple things such as making the road perfectly straight or perfectly curved.
Now, there are a few things that do bug me:
Deathwaves. I don't think I'm the only one that experiences this, but if I am, I would like to know why. Basically, there will be times where the death icon appears above nearly every building in the city. Your population may decrease a bit, but the thing that really annoys me is that it takes a while for these waves to pass. Your graveyards can get full and there's ambulances going around everywhere and it's really just annoying.
Abandoned buildings don't automatically demolish. Luckily, there is a mod for this, but just in plain vanilla, you have to manually.
Finally, the DLCs should already be part of the vanilla game. $15 for a night effect? No thanks.
Despite these few problems, the game is still great. I've invested quite a bit of time into this game and will continue playing it. Recommended.

Cities: Skylines is an improvement on the genre. If you are making the jump from Simcity 4 to Cities: Skylines, then you will be shocked by how much the road building; traffic simulation; and zoning have improved. Gone are the days of those rigid grid streets with cars being generated as you simply move the camera around. Gone are the days where plots have to be in a grid. You are free to build as you please, even weird shapes that look really ugly! Cars are persistent and try to reach fixed destinations that their drivers have (work, shopping, etc). You'll definitely never go back to Simcity 4 again, except maybe to blow up your cities.

I've first played this in beta (~a year ago) and spent a decent amount of time and money on it playing through the standalone client.
I can recommend this game if you're a casual gamer and just want to try something different, the spacial aspect of the game adds a super fun and interesting layer to deckbuilding (refreshingly non-RNG-y) and piloting, but I can not recommend this game if you don't enjoy hyper-aggressive cancer.
When I last played the game, admittedly this was a couple of months ago (I did minor research for this review, nothing much at all seems changed in terms of top tier decks), I mostly played Tempo Lyonar (Argeon) and had great success with it, simply because it can outlast Burnhai and outtempo a lot of midrange decks, but sometimes due to the nature of movement and RNG, you just get burned down way too fast, you get slowed down immensely by insanely overbudgeted taunts, or other such joys. On the flipside of this, there is so much removal...games in Duelyst constructed often feel like a seesaw of tempo, massive swings in either direction all of the time.
Personally, the absolutely mental stat budgets were the biggest dealbreaker, and made the game feel very poorly balanced. There are some nice archetypes in the game, but they're usually either ineffective or super cheesy. Gauntlet (arena) felt awful, for the stat budgets exacerbate the imbalance between classes in arena even more, I have both flown through virtually unopposed and been crushed like a bug, with little to no possible consistency, worse than in any other TCG I have played (HS, ES:L, Eternal, Magic Duels).
If you'd like to play a game with a good ingame(!)-community, with a nice new spin on the genre but a TON of gimmicks, give this a try.

Reviews here have been pretty negative, partly due to connecting this game to "immigrant issues". I say, leave that aside, take a few good stepe back and see the picture - It's a cyberpunk game with dark graphics, pretty good sci fi elements (seems like "people" in the game are significantly different physically from "us humans", to the point they might think a  "human" is severly disfigured), there's this whole weird church thing going on and there's this whole "mother" thing that probably generates energy somehow. It all gives you the alienation of sci fi, combined with the feeling there's a story behind this world and why it is the way it is.
Cons:
The graphics are outdated at best and feel flat.
If for some reason you exit the game, your computer restarts, it crashes - You have to start from the beginning.
Pros:
The whole "go to the post box and send a letter to get a clue\explanation on what just happened" mechanic is a nice way to go around just bluntly giving the player clues that break the experience in a way. It does force you to go send a letter after almost everything you do, though.

As buggy and laggy as North undeniably is, it is a wonderful allegorical game with a laudable message. I was truly immersed in the cold, detatched city where the main character finds himself. Experiencing just 0.1% of the frustration and helplessness that asylum seekers and refugees must feel makes this game easily worth its tiny price tag. Oh, and the music is great.

Kinda disapointed.
The visual aspect of the game is really good, the music is nice and parts of the concept are cool but that's about it.
I started with the tutorial to have some info but you'll have more info in the "tips" thing. But that still won't be enough. It took me some time to realise you have different number of lives depending on the map but the only way to know that is to fail a song. Then I also discovered 1h in the game that the central sphere is the indicator to how many lives are left. It's visually nice, but not very practical (the difference between blue light and white light is really small ><).
Now about the "rythm" part, I've been quite disappointed. I'm not a rythm game pro, but I do enjoy them and play some. But this is way off a rythm game, because the rythm doesn't matter. You can press the notes in any order and at any point so you just have to make sure you press them. It seems you'll have the right "rythm" when pressing them in order when they are at the scale of the center circle but it seems you get absolutely no reward for that.
Also, I find the scoring quite off putting. I've not investigated much about that but from what I read, you don't have any bonus / penalty for following / missing the rythm. And the thing is, you don't know how you're doing until you get to the score screen.
But I think the thing that annoyed me the most is that "Failed" screen. It appears for about 2s every time you fail. And you might fail a lot. I don't mind die and retry games, I do like some of them. But when I die, I want to be able to retry quickly and not wait for some ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t animation. For one song I did retry approx. 100 times I think, that means more than 3 minutes of game just staring at this "Failed" screen. That's way too much. And you also get this animation if you press escape while playing, so no way to juste restart quickly.
In the end, I feel like the core gameplay is flawed. Making a "rythm" game where the rythm doesn't matter... well, that doesn't make sense ? Also the 1 life (mostly) thing is a bit frustrating when it's so easy to miss on a quick succession of notes. Even if the core gameplay is not reworked, some stuff could be improved to make the game a bit more enjoyable.
I hesitated between recommending the game or not, because I still enjoyed parts of it. But in my opinion, it's too flawed in it's current state for me to recommend it. I hope to see some improvments in the future!

I bought it for the campaign, and I'm glad I did. I consider this the best game in the Call Of Duty series so far. The game has a decent story, gives you plenty of weapons to choose from, the option of several levels of difficulty, and provides a fairly varied assortment of enemies to shoot at.
My GTX 980Ti had no problem running this game on max settings synced at 60FPS. That being said, I did experience occasional stuttering (during some cutaway scenes), and 2 or 3 crashes during intense battles. Not sure about the cause, but I did notice that other people are complaining about the same issues on PC.
Also there's an annoying glitch where you can't pick up RPG's using the "X" button on your controller. I spent a frustrating half an hour of trying to figure out WTF is going on and whether I'm missing something, before I eventually googled it and found out that you have to press "left D-pad" instead, and then it was all good from there on.
Anyway, minor technical issues aside, I enjoyed the game, and replayed a few missions more than once. Treyarch always made the best COD games, and this one is no exception. I would definitely recommend it for the campaign.

This game is a massive disappointment to me. So much so that when it crashed (1.5 hours later) it was a relief.
The most frustrating thing is the brain dead train routing. My trains spent most of their time staring each other down, neither moving, even though there was a perfectly good piece of track right next to them and one of them was parked on the switch.
In a related frustration, signals seem to pop up like weeds. Only really thorny and with deep roots, so you can't actually get them out. These signals allowed my idiot trains to blissfully drive past the switch, resulting in the starting contest previously mentioned.
It is also impossible to make a station longer, meaning if a train sticks out it will still trigger the station's signal causing the whole track leading up to that to stop.
The stock market mechanic is basic and fairly boring. My biggest complaint is that you have to wait ~3 seconds between every buy/sell attempt, meaning you can't just totally dump a company if their stock starts dropping and you can't pick up a bunch when it's cheap.
The lack of ability to form a monopoly was also irritating. If I own an industry, I should be able to tell it to not ship goods to my competitors, and even to not buy their raw materials. Or at least pay them a rediculously low rate.
My final complaint is the size of the map. I had assumed that something the size of New England would contain more than a few cities and be large enough that I wouldn't encounter my opponents for a long time. Instead, I was surprised to find myself covering a full quarter of the board after having connected only two cities and my opponents building heavily in my territory.

After few played scenarios it seems to be an absolute masterpiece. Guaranteed Sid Meier quality! It's not like Civilization that takes a lifetime to finish.

If you're a fan of OpenTTD, Railroad Tycoon 2, RRT3 or similar games: I do not recommend this game. It's style over substance.
Having just played Railroads (I stopped when it crashed) I can't believe this has so many positive reviews on Steam and magazines via Metacritic. It came out in 2007, but OpenTTD was more than alive at that time and far superior.
This game is brain-dead. It's a train network game, except you can't properly adjust the train network!
The auto-track placement and the complete lack of manual signals ruins this game. You get signals where you don't want signals and you can't remove them. The signals do nothing more than claim the section of track from here to the next signal, but that doesn't work when the game is placing a million pointless signals. It doesn't matter if you always make sure to use the green 'extend' rather than the yellow 'fork' placement. The game still produces insane signal placement. I had one stretch of nice smooth track with a signal at either end. I use the "double up" button and double up the entire length and now suddenly I have 6 signals right next to each other in the middle of the track, which was pointless and just messed everything up if I wanted to try and share that line. Creating passing places is also extremely difficult and trains will often just blunder their way down the track until two are in a head-to-head deadlock either side of the signals. There's no way to reverse the train so the only solution is to nuke the train and buy it again.
Also: the fully stocked train is usually the same length as the track between the resource producer and consumer! There's no room for maneuver, which further exacerbates the no-passing-places and signalling problem.
Because of the stupid signals and the uber long trains, you basically have to dedicated a line to each train. Trains cannot share track. I find that pretty demented and it basically reduces the game down to laying a track, build some stations, placing a track to exclusively dominate a section of track and then simply sitting back and watching. There's no real decision making. You can't sit their endlessly tweaking a track for extra efficiency as you can in OpenTTD.
Also: The track-layer is also really finicky. When trying to create branches I often ended up with lots of tiny bits of track that took me ages to delete because it perfectly overlaps the other bit of track. Given that "lay track" is one of the 3 primary things you can do, it gets annoying fast.

Amazing graphics, smooth combat, addicting gameplay. My only gripe with this game is the fact that there are very hidden things that are vital to your progression in the game such as pathways obscured by foliage and such. Because this game has pixel graphics, you're forced to hug the wall to find any doorways. Apart from that, this game is very solid.

Solid mechanics and a progression system that's simple and intuitive. The story is what you make it, anything from a personal journey to dieties and war.
I wasn't sure what the heck was going on for the first hour or 2, but I kind of stopped caring since the game was just fun to play. The combat is solid and unforgiving, its fast paced and weighty. The dashing was fun and can get really crazy if you're fully upgraded. The bosses really gave me some trouble the first time through, but this is one of those games that make you realize how awesome you've become on the second playthrough.
The sound design is part in what makes the game so enjoyable. The music can be daunting over huge landscapes and become very aggressive and fast paced when engaging enemies. The soundtrack fits the asthetic to a T. Character designs were amazing, but I would've like to see more interactions between characters in each area, maybe side quests that award upgrades.
The story is abstract, but there are hints everywhere. If you really pay attention, its pretty dark and you're character goes through hell. My one complaint is the over reliance of wall hugging. This game tries to give hints into where all of its secret areas are by having enemies come through invisible walls and little markings on the floor, but it's not enough. To find everything, you sort of have to run along side every wall that's even remotely suspicious, and even then you'll still miss stuff. Ledges too.
9/10.

On the face of it this is just a puzzle platformer involving blocks in different shapes and colours which have different abilities. The puzzles aren't particularly tough, but are generally fun. That's all the game would be if you were to play it with the sound off and skip reading any of the text the game shows on screen.
All of which of course goes to show that you shouldn't judge a game by its screenshots. Because the narration, and the little blurbs between the different stages, turn this into a compelling narrative and turn simple coloured quadrilaterals into characters. In what seemed like a matter of seconds it seemed natural for me to refer to a simple red rectangle by name.
The incredible handling of both narration and narrative have made Thomas Was Alone one of the most compelling experiences I've ever had in gaming.

Thomas Was Alone is a clever, little puzzle platformer. You start as Thomas a red rectangle that can jump. Along the way you make some new friends with different colors and abilities. Some are small and can't jump as high, others help everyone jump farther. The goal is to traverse the level by getting all the shapes to the appropriate portal.
The platforming of the game is tight and feels good. It never gets too difficult either. A few levels require some faster jumping, but in general it's pretty forgiving. In fact, in most places it's not forgiving there will be mid-level saves. If you're coming from something like Super Meat Boy, this will be a walk in the park.
The puzzles are simple and there's rarely an "A-ha!" moment. This isn't to say they're not well done, but don't expect anything mind bending. This much more of a platformer than a puzzle game. There are a few moments where the game makes clever use of it's mechanics to create some of the funner puzzles.
The story actually makes you care about Thomas and the other characters. The story is entertaining and the voice over narative is charming.
The game is on the shorter side. I beat the main campaign in under four hours including the level 10 bonus missions and only missed two achievements. The game length is spot on for this type of game since it doesn't overstay it's welcome.

You came here to read a review? Wrong place, because I'll give you a recipe for how to make cookies
Chocolate Chip Cookies
Ingredients:
-2 cups all-purpose flour
-1/2 cup cocoa powder
-1 teaspoon baking soda
-1 cup softened butter
-3/4 cup white sugar
-3/4 cup packed brown sugar
-2 eggs
-1 teaspoon vanilla extract
-2 cups semisweet chocolate chips
Preheat oven to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C). Whisk together the flour, cocoa powder, and baking soda.
Beat the butter, white sugar, and brown sugar with an electric mixer in a large bowl until smooth. Beat in one egg until completely incorporated. Beat in the last egg along with the vanilla. Mix in the flour mixture until just incorporated. Fold in the chocolate chips; mixing just enough to evenly combine. Drop by heaped teaspoonfuls onto ungreased baking sheets.
Bake in the preheated oven until the edges are golden, 9 to 12 minutes. Allow the cookies to cool on the baking sheet for 1 minute before removing to a wire rack to cool completely.

"Listen to music and match all notes."
Despite the description, you don't have match notes to the music. This isn't a rhyhm game, but a music game.
As a rhythm game enthusiast and high difficulty player, I wouldn't recommend this one if you are looking for a real rhythm game.
It is quite nice and fun for it's price (got it for less than 1€ on sale), but as some sort of arcade time-killing game, not as real rhythm game. Note scoring is bad, you get full score for each note as long as it is on the screen, no matter if it's on the judgement line (i feel bad for even calling it as a "judgement line", as i said, the circle which indicates the right place where player should hit the note has nothing to do with scoring).
It was still fun to play for a few minutes, but after a moment it got boring. I've also tried the map editor to make my own song chart, but I gave up shortly after, because it is quite bad as well; there isn't any BPM sync or snap grid to help syncing notes with music precisely (well, I think lack of BPM meter can be good for not experienced people); also, it is quite hard to read.
Pros:
+Cheap, especially on sale
+Good for time killing
+Has editor
+Not really bad when not counted as a rhythm game
Cons:
+Bad scoring system
+Editor isn't really great
+Not a rhythm game
Well, I suppose if you're looking for a cheap time killer when you have nothing to do then it's fine, but seriously if you want a rhythm game then go somewhere else.

(Contains spoilers.)
NORTH is an experimental, atmospheric, unsettling game. It's short and frightening, not so much in a horror sense (although there are certainly horror elements here), but more in an existential sense. The problems it deals with are at their core very real and modern. All of this had me drawing comparisons to the free game the static speaks my name. Both deal with complex, contemporary humanitarian issues by rendering the player confused and increasingly hopeless. It puts you in the shoes of someone trying to cope with a miserable situation, and in the end without anyone to pull you out, getting lost in that misery.
NORTH's ending is a gut-punch, if a little cliche. The player spends the entire game trying to attain legal asylum in a cold and unwelcoming city of the North, and at each progress point they send a letter to their sister who still lives in the war-torn South. The letters are really the only way for the player to understand what is happening to the protagonist. They're a struggled attempt to make sense of the environment and the puzzles they are being forced to solve. They're also the only source of backstory for the protagonist, letting us know where he came from, why he's here, and that he still has family who were left behind. The lettters are vitally important to both the player and the protaginist in these ways, allowing you to both log your progress through the game by recording your difficulties and to maintain contact with the one person who may be actually sympathetic to your plight.
Then in the final sequence, right after you've proven your value enough to be granted asylum, the overlords of the North reveal that they have been confiscating and reading every single one of the letters you sent. "For security purposes." There's a point I wish I had screenshot where you're commanded to "Right click to feel the irony," and doing so triggers the sounds of derisive laughter. Therein lies the sinful cliche, a moment when the player's already present genuine emotions get a bit soured by the game's attempt at driving home its point. It's a "Press R to pay respects" moment.
But NORTH quickly recovers by closing on another letter, one clearly written not by the protagonist but rather by the North's government. It paints the picture of a man whose struggles in the city were his own fault for being ignorant, but who has ultimately triumphed over his shortcomings and become a happy and productive citizen of a civilization that is better than the South in every conceivable way. The letter concludes with an encouragement to his sister to join him in his newfound safety and fulfillment. Sinister icing on a cake of betrayal. The final title sequence plays, but this time instead of glowing white letters, we see the word "NORTH" presented in stark black on a dimming screen.
This back-and-forth of moving, nuanced storytelling and heavy-handed design choices are pretty consistent throughout the game. NORTH has a problem of telling instead of showing. While the point of the game is to disorient players by giving them an alien landscape and bizarre objectives, its protagonist is somehow able to make impossibly better sense of things. The letters become Outlands' way of overcorrecting for this. You move around in the game, click a few things, and then read a letter that explains exactly what just happened and tells you what you need to do next in not-so-subtle red lettering. If this game is supposed to make us feel like a refugee, then why is the player's experience not congruent with the protagonist's? NORTH was built with the potential to be an appropriately frustrating puzzle game but instead developed into a vaguely-challenging walkthrough.
Evey with all of this criticism, I have to give this game a thumbs up. It's egregiously rare for video games to tackle serious issues in a serious way. The refugee crisis is such a prevalent and ubiquitous international problem that ignoring it as modern media has is a massively shameful decision. NORTH is not shy about its subject matter. It's not so metaphorical that one could get away with dismissing it as being about something else. That the protagonist is openly gay and has been persecuted in the South because of this is an unexpected but realistic contribution to the seldomn-told video game narrative of the oppressed. As a bisexual brown woman, this unapologetic multifaceted representation is what sold me on NORTH.
If you're looking for a gaming experience that dives boldly into the relatively uncharted waters of deep and complex social issues, I highly recommend you add this to your collection.

North is an atmospheric First-Person, allegorical science fiction exploration game with simple puzzles and gameplay. The main theme it explores is the contemporary refugee crisis--from a western perspective I'd presume-- seen from the viewpoint of a refugee arriving in a foreign culture. The player character we control is a refugee that have just arrived in a stable city where he seeks asylum and citizenship. We follow him in said process as he periodically sends letters back to his sister telling her of his progress. The inhabitants of this dystopian society are represented as alienesque people that speak a language that we as players and the character we control don't understand. At one point we have to pass a test in the police station; it consists of selecting which short movies are appropriate and which are not, and while the whole test and the correct answer are absurd seen from our perspective from the real world. It functions naturally within the narrative to mold the player character into a potential citizen as a most noble cog in the machinery that is this city. Just like the test for Danish citizenship, at least a few years ago, consisted of a questionnaire based on more or less borderline pointless rote learning, in order to mold them into being part of a specific power structure.
In the ending sequence of the game the player character shifted viewpoint in a way that came about as rather jarring to me, as though the developer ran out of time.  Regardless the games overall ambience, with its hyperbolically allegorical Science fiction setting wrapped in a dark cityscape and accompanying synthpop soundscape intrigued me for the first part of the game. At least it isn't sordid entertainment even if the game in its finished result is a bit rough and iffy. It breaks noble grounds for a modest indie computer game within the gaming sphere.

NORTH is a game that does not truly have a vision, or at least so it seems. It wavers or oscillates between both emotional states and maturity-levels in its attempt to posit some kind of critique or view of the refugee crisis. What's even worse is the unfortunate idea that it doesn't even remain consistent in its view. The main body of the game presents a nightmare view of being a refugee, a Kafkaesque alienation from the society one is in, but it ends in reconciliation, with the supposed refugee acquiescing. And not in a “what other choice is there?” of some kind of pragmatical mindset, but a jarring leap from the idea of this new society being Orwellian and invasive to it being better than the “fiery desert”, at least, thus alleviating the anxiety in regards to the surveillance, suspicion, lack of love and so on. I did not, however, follow the game's road from the former to the latter, and I struggle to see how this game in any way is “Dealing with the issue of the contemporary refugee crisis”.
I don't necessarily think this is an awful idea or is not worth pursuing, games as news is a proper concept, and games as empathetic structures, or as conveyors of elements of empathy are what I foresee, and have experienced, as among the more potent mediums when it comes to putting you in somebody else's shoes, since that is more or less what is done. And within that model this game does not necessarily fail, it is just inconsistent. It conveys the idea of being in a foreign place somewhat well, albeit in a childish and naive way. The language is incomprehensible, the customs are tedious and confusing, people view you with suspicion solely due to the fact that you are different. But the obverse of what affects YOU negatively is the insight into how your own presuppositions, or your own pre-judgements affect how you view this new culture and how that serves to distance you and alienate yourself by virtue of these pre-judgements. People are blurred out and indistinct, overweight people are disgusting amorphous blobs, working is slavery, and so on. This is where the game contradicts itself even when it remains consistent in its overall view. The end result becomes a fairly hypocritical mindset where you are at once looking for the approbation of a different culture of your cultural heritage as you disapprove of the customs in this new, supposedly weird, world.
Nothing about this is in reality particularly shocking or uncommon, but it makes the game say not much at all, or actually deal with a problem. There is no direction or voice that can be gleamed from this experience, at least from what I could gather. It expresses what is putative fact. It shows a great deal of naivety and immaturity in dealing with the subject. I believe this is in part due to the effort to gamify this topic. It doesn't uncover the core of these issues to the point where it would be possible to create a game-mechanic out of it proper, it never truly conveys the felt impossibility of changing circumstances, appealing to bureaucrats or the State more than with slight discomfort or inconvenience. There is the confounding nature of settling into a new place with new rules, and it reinforces that idea through ambiguity and oblique explanations. It hints at an understanding of the bureaucratic absurdity of modern society, but again, in a very unexciting way, devoid of nuance. It feels very much like a critique of a world that is not yet understood or have been experienced in a genuine manner by the one who is critiquing. Especially when the critique falls into acquiescence and reticence. The complete disavowal of a point of view through silence or acceptance of a new order seems to completely negate the points raised beforehand. Points that moreover have had to been valid to some extent to have felt necessary to bring up or especially in this case when a game has been created around it.
Here we have to ask what NORTH is trying to do. I am not a refugee, so how can I understand this issue enough to fill in the gaps of what the game is not explaining to me? Is the queerness of the game meant to put me in the shoes of a refugee in a new country? Is this what explains the abstract architecture? The non-language? I can comment on these things because they are obvious, but what about the less obvious parts? In what sense does anatomy have a reason to be part of this game's presentation? Why is my home broken and filled with strange pictures? Many scenes of the game were to me strictly nonsensical, many times to such a degree as to make it funny. But fun never seemed to be the goal of this game, thus deeming many parts of it a failure, in my eyes.
Failure can be fun, though, as I'm sure most people have a sense of. Things can be so bad that they become good, which is the premise of a lot of ironic enjoyment. But I do not think I enjoyed this game, unfortunately. I appreciate the effort of trying something like this, and I think with a matured mindset, something like this could be very interesting. If it was more personal, even, it would be more interesting. What is in NORTH seems largely to base itself on baseless ideas of conspiracies. An idea of self-importance and arrogance that is necessary to overcome if you are to partake in any society, at least if you are an everyday person. One is simply reterritorialized by the end of NORTH, as opposed to becoming-nomadic, or becoming-child, in the sense of not being opposed to the new.
I regret playing this, in a way. It's an upsetting view of the world without the excitement that comes with understanding the way the cogs interact of a mechanism, or the parts of a machinic beast. It's sad in that it is ignorant and silly when it tries to be profound. It's sad in how it paints a world that doesn't exist. I'd recommend reading Kafka instead, his stories are closer to being universally human, he writes with force and excitement, through the drabness of any subject matter. Even the depressing can be exciting if expressed with competence, solely due to the vividness and vivacity that the expression has the capacity to evoke in the imagination. NORTH as a game seems confused and weak in its expression, but it's a valiant attempt. One that perhaps adumbrates a future of more exciting and heartfelt expression from Outlands.

i've tried pretty much all the F2P collectible card games on steam, (and blizzard's hearthstone) and duelyst by far is the only one i play.
the other CCGs didn't capture me for either of these reasons:
-very high skill ceiling, too much of a grind to get cards, not enough players, too generic, p2w, too much RNG involved.
but lets talk about duelyst.
-6 factions, each faction has 2 different 'general's, or heros.  so you choose a faction, then 1 of the 2 general, then build up your deck with a mix of faction specific cards and neutral cards.  nothing really different from other CCGs except that it is played on a grid.  go see a youtube vid on the gameplay; easier to see it in motion.
-very generous in gaining ingame currency to be able to get more cards.  i never felt i had to use real money since the daily quests give you lots of ingame currency, especially if you compare them to other CCGs
-most of the legendary cards are either very situational, or they only really fit into a particular faction's synergy.  so don't be thinking that just because you are a new player and lack legendary cards, that you are fighting an uphill battle.
-you are ranked (obviously), and majority of time only play within your ranking, from lowest to highest is bronze, silver, gold, diamond, and finally S-rank.   season restarts every month.  depending on the high rank you achieved, you will get a reward based on it.  once you reach a new rank, you can't go down to the lower rank.  your rank is account based; not faction based.
along with the generous ingame currency rewards, i feel like the difficulty, or skill ceiling is just right, at least for me.  not so complex that it turns me off, but also not so casually easy and RNG based.
no matter the time of day/night, you will wait no longer than 30 seconds to get a match.  the playerbase is small , but its solid.  the average waiting time for me is 10 seconds.
of course it can be frustrating reach a new rank and then just lose after lose.  but the official dueylst forum is filled w/helpful people, and the devs do chat on the forums.   its F2P, and i believe it will be coming on mobile, xbox 1, and PS4 in the near future.

Jazzpunk is a cultural tour-de-force that has overwhelmed me at every turn.

It's certainly a different flavor of humor that Jazzpunk serves up, and I'm pretty sure I like it. Some strange post-post future where everyone's not-secretly a robot and popular culture is some puzzlingly foreign potpourri. I got a number of laughs from the experience, and some sort of sense of abandon. Complete the area's task whenever you like! Take the time to explore, find all the bizarre humor that's hidden just out of sight for you to find it, in mailboxes, down a side alley, in a corner of the bar.
Of course, such a dense concentration of the substance known as Jokes leaves the game a bit short. My playtime as of writing is 2.5 hours, and that's at, I would guess, 85% completion. I also felt, as I continued on, that perhaps there was a bit of frontloading, that the areas after the first felt a bit too empty in comparison. It might also be that the initial novelty of the experience had worn off, and I had simply gotten more used to the absurdity around me.
But hey, the 2.5 hours certainly felt like more than that. It may be short, but it is potent.

Just beat this game in 11 hours. I didn't 100% it, and I think a decent chunk of that time was spent when I accidentally left the game running once. Anyways, visually it's stunning. The pixel art is very well done, and the color choices are great. Sometimes it can be a little hard to tell what something is though because of the art direction. The soundtrack is pretty, often very relaxing. Gameplay-wise it could get a bit repetitive at times, but I think for what it was going for it didn't overstay it's welcome. I think the options to upgrade all sorts of things (like your sword, drift, med pack limit, grenade limit, etc) was well done, my favorite upgrade was the charge attack. There are collectibles placed in secret places you have to save up a lot of in order to upgrade things, so it rewards the player from being percetive which is cool. The bosses were fun to fight, and pretty challenging. Each one had a bunch of attack patterns and it took multiple tries but not too many tries to win, if that makes sense. The story is extremely vague, I'll probably try to figure it out later when I'm not so sleepy. My biggest complaint is that I often had trouble figuring out where to go next. In one specific case, I wasted a couple hours trying to figure out where I needed to go, and when I finally looked it up it was a secret passageway through what looked like a normal wall, except an enemy came out of it, but it was so subtly done I have no idea how I was supposed to figure it out. There were some minor bugs too, like I glitched through a wall once, a checkpoint only working once when it should've worked multiple times, etc. Also, be careful if you're wearing headphones because if you play at a normal volume, 95% of the time you will be fine but that 5% (during cutscenes) it likes to blast your speakers for some reason. NPCs communicate with really pretty pictures of story elements instead of text, which I thought was a great idea. And the game doesn't hold your hand through a boring tutorial. All in all, I'd reccomend this game, I had a lot of fun.

Smirking Indie hipster offering with an one rose tinted eye firmly on the "Good old days" of gaming. Frustrating and repetitive in equal measure (just like proper 80's games), but not due to some ungrasped esoteric game design theory on my part, rather due to the reductive nature of the genre.
HLD is a retro (old fashioned) 2D 3rd person action game where you roam around a big map equipped with a sword n' gun. You battle evil sprites learning their attack patterns until you get to the big boss where you must learn his attack pattern. He has a big health bar and 3-4 patterns. And thats it. No really thats it. Gaming at it's purist or most puerile. But hey it's got cool art direction right?
Unfortunatley the art direction is actually confusing when it comes to stuff like telling what direction your character is facing and what is traversable scenery and what is actually a drop to your death. So expect those old school thrills like getting stuck because you didn't reach the part of the screen which triggers the scrolling code to reveal the way ahead.
The main draw here is the combat.There's a steep learning curve but it's rewarding when mastered. I felt the occassions where an unfair death reared it's head to be more often than in something like Hotline Miami. Especially when the screen is full of projectile spam or when enemies swarm in confined spaces.
Retro design elements abound, such as the dreaded return of indestructible turrets, instant death crushers and of course tiresome punishment checkpoints meaning repeating and repeating and repeating sections previously cleared areas.
Charming and challenging but still failing in all the ways old school games did when they ruled the roost. Those that do not learn from their mistakes are doomed to repeat them, that is the mantra of old school game design but Hyper Light Drifter is more guilty than anyone of not grasping that concept.
6/10 Good old fashioned gaming but nothing really interesting for gaming veterans.
One of the most touching gaming experiences ever, all without a single spoken word. This plays like a modernized, fast paced legend of zelda game.

Hyper Light Drifter is an incredibly atmospheric journey in a mysterious alien world. The soundtrack conveys the mood perfectly and really fits in with the overall theme of the game. HLD has a bit of a legend of Zelda feel to it as you are free to go wherever you want and the game does not hold your hand with waypoints. The story is told entirely through images and you must use your imagination to try and interpret what is happening. Exploring the world is very fun as there are secrets everywhere, including new guns and outfits which offer a variety of effects. The combat is fast paced and fluid as the Drifter can chain quick dashes, slash to reflect enemy projectiles, and return fire with 1 of 6 unique guns. Slashing enemies refills your ammo and using all of these abilities together makes for an incredibly satisfying experience. There are also a few challenge modes like boss rush, hoarde mode, and NG+ for added replayability. There is even local co-op which works quite well. If you are looking for an adventure in a stunning environment with tight controls I highly recommend Hyper Light Drifter.

If you like your retro games, this one is for you. Gives you a beautiful looking world to explore backed up by an excellent soundtrack. The controls take a little getting used to, but once you do you will be stylishly nipping behind enemies and popping them in the back of the head with the shotgun in no time. Once you've completed it there's even more modes to play through and even more difficulty to challenge yourself with.

(Disclosure and so forth: I was looking to buy this game anyway, between the low price and the themes addressed, but I was lucky enough to get it offered to me on Keymailer to cover. So here we are.)
Discussing NORTH isn't the easiest thing to do. It's not so much the subject matter at hand, the perils of refugee immigration, as it is the game itself. I loved NORTH, but there's only so much game there to talk about, and it's fairly easy to spoil. That said, it does a decent job with its small scope of offering some perspective.
NORTH's title comes from the game's setting: you fill the shoes of a refugee who's fled persecution in the shattered lands of the south in the hopes of a better life for yourself and the family you left behind. Things don't seem particularly great, between the living conditions, the hoops lined up for you to jump through to attain citizenship, and the sheer mystery of being in an unknown place with an unknown language holding you back. The game lets you run through all of this blind, just interacting with things whenever prompts present themselves, or you can pay attention to the letters you send home to your sister for some solid guidance. It's an interesting system, and acts more as a hint system if you end up playing it like a player, or provides an angle of empathy (and an advantage) if you take the time to keep in touch before rushing into things.
Gameplay iss mostly a brief wander through a small chunk of NORTH's city, with the occasional puzzle. The city itself, while simply rendered, does a good job of feeling strange and inhospitable, even after it's revealed you and your fellow refugees aren't so un-strange yourselves. Black, unfeeling masses rise above you but still form into places where locals and foreigners alike might gather in a more bustling environment, making the city feel at least a little lived in despite the eerie quiet. Between this and what you learn of the south from the game's narrative, a stark contrast is built that emphasizes the sort of culture clash those fleeing for their lives often encounter in the real world.
The puzzles/minigames you need to finish to progress are fairly straightforward, though often have a hidden element or two that your letters home are invaluable for discovering. Becoming naturalized doesn't take all that long either way, so this is a quick play, but enough to fit the price (if you're one of those dollars-to-playtime folk).
My favorite things about NORTH are the soundtrack, which jumps from style to style suddenly but not too jarringly depending on what's happening, and how it did an okay job of encapsulating refugee status in such a neat little package. There were also some interesting visual takes, especially with some of the architecture, that left me wondering if they were intentional. There were some dangling threads I felt could've been explored just a bit more, but again, this seems like a pretty compact little game, and there wouldn't have been much room for follow-up.
All in all, I recommend giving NORTH a chance. At $2, it's already cheaper than food at full price, offers a few trading cards on top of that, and gives you a few things to think about if you see it through. I really want to get my hands on the soundtrack, though.

Fantastic game. Basically chess where everyone (collects and) chooses a custom set of pieces. Faster than chess though and with much more variety.
I've been quite obsessed with this game. Pro and cons:
+ Matches are challenging; a lot of tactical considerations need to be made constantly. A replay function helps to review and learn from mistakes.
+ Six factions with many many possible styles and archetypes to play.
+ Little randomness.
+ Deck building is challenging and fun, can also be skipped by simply copying a deck from the internet.
+ Very fair free-to-play model (to be honest I actually invested money. 10$). You can get quite far without investing any money. By doing quests you can get about one card pack each day with good drop rates of rare cards.
+ Very helpful community, close to zero abusive behavior.
+ The match-making system works very well, matches are found quickly.
+ Well-done tutorial.
+ Gorgeous pixel art and sound/music.
+ The developers maintain the game actively and listen to community feedback.
+ For parents: can be played with only one hand (touchpad or mouse). Being away from keyboard for a minute if real-life calls is usually ok. Matches are usually fast (5-10min).
+ Good interface in-match.
- Very little single-player content.
- Quite demanding for a pixel art game (<30 FPS on my laptop with Intel HD Graphics first generation, but doing fine on later generations), however for most people that won't be an issue I guess.
- Awkward interface in deck building / card pool management.
- Very little statistics, but there are some community mods for that.
For veterans from Magic the Gathering:
+ Forget all problems involving mana. Here you get mana for free; each round your pool increases. One less random factor to care about, but definitely doesn't make the game trivial as there are ways to manipulate the mana curve.
+ Much less worrying about picking a good hand, because you get to mulligan two cards at the beginning (while seeing who your opponent will be, allowing strategic decisions already), and you can replace a card for free every turn (guaranteed not drawing the same card)!
+ There's a proper board which leads to more tactical depth.
+ A match is quickly found.
- Obviously not as many cards as MtG, but that's the same for most CCGs out there.
