Smirking Indie hipster offering with an one rose tinted eye firmly on the "Good old days" of gaming. Frustrating and repetitive in equal measure (just like proper 80's games), but not due to some ungrasped esoteric game design theory on my part, rather due to the reductive nature of the genre.
HLD is a retro (old fashioned) 2D 3rd person action game where you roam around a big map equipped with a sword n' gun. You battle evil sprites learning their attack patterns until you get to the big boss where you must learn his attack pattern. He has a big health bar and 3-4 patterns. And thats it. No really thats it. Gaming at it's purist or most puerile. But hey it's got cool art direction right?
Unfortunatley the art direction is actually confusing when it comes to stuff like telling what direction your character is facing and what is traversable scenery and what is actually a drop to your death. So expect those old school thrills like getting stuck because you didn't reach the part of the screen which triggers the scrolling code to reveal the way ahead.
The main draw here is the combat.There's a steep learning curve but it's rewarding when mastered. I felt the occassions where an unfair death reared it's head to be more often than in something like Hotline Miami. Especially when the screen is full of projectile spam or when enemies swarm in confined spaces.
Retro design elements abound, such as the dreaded return of indestructible turrets, instant death crushers and of course tiresome punishment checkpoints meaning repeating and repeating and repeating sections previously cleared areas.
Charming and challenging but still failing in all the ways old school games did when they ruled the roost. Those that do not learn from their mistakes are doomed to repeat them, that is the mantra of old school game design but Hyper Light Drifter is more guilty than anyone of not grasping that concept.
6/10 Good old fashioned gaming but nothing really interesting for gaming veterans.
One of the most touching gaming experiences ever, all without a single spoken word. This plays like a modernized, fast paced legend of zelda game.

Hyper Light Drifter is an incredibly atmospheric journey in a mysterious alien world. The soundtrack conveys the mood perfectly and really fits in with the overall theme of the game. HLD has a bit of a legend of Zelda feel to it as you are free to go wherever you want and the game does not hold your hand with waypoints. The story is told entirely through images and you must use your imagination to try and interpret what is happening. Exploring the world is very fun as there are secrets everywhere, including new guns and outfits which offer a variety of effects. The combat is fast paced and fluid as the Drifter can chain quick dashes, slash to reflect enemy projectiles, and return fire with 1 of 6 unique guns. Slashing enemies refills your ammo and using all of these abilities together makes for an incredibly satisfying experience. There are also a few challenge modes like boss rush, hoarde mode, and NG+ for added replayability. There is even local co-op which works quite well. If you are looking for an adventure in a stunning environment with tight controls I highly recommend Hyper Light Drifter.

If you like your retro games, this one is for you. Gives you a beautiful looking world to explore backed up by an excellent soundtrack. The controls take a little getting used to, but once you do you will be stylishly nipping behind enemies and popping them in the back of the head with the shotgun in no time. Once you've completed it there's even more modes to play through and even more difficulty to challenge yourself with.
10/10.

With the first one, you cant walk off without getting hit by the spikes. Later, they place 2 unkillable enemies in the places where you need to walkthrough. Meaning, you have to wat about 20 seconds to lure them out, then run through. Any illusion of diffuliculty is from the devs overplacing the unkillable enemies or over usage of spikes.
The introduction of trampolines, late in the game, is completly unesscary. Its used well on one level, but then completly forgotten. However, the level it was used well, was actually an ok one.

Thomas was alone, but now I feel alone
(Which is ironic because my name is Thomas)

Thomas Was Alone is a "video game" in that you control a character and advance through levels to reach the end.
More accurately, Thomas Was Alone is a rudimentary platformer used as a vehicle for a narration (A so-called Interactive Experience). You control a varying number of rectangles, each with their own abilities and """""personalities""""" which are explained to you by a narrator as the story progresses.
The problem is that the chosen method of storytelling is inefective and frankly laughable at points. Imagine a movie wherein none of the characters ever speak or carry out actions on their own. Instead, a narrator tells you what each person says and does. And the characters are blocks. Isn't there a "show, don't tell" principle for visual media?
These shortcomings could be forgiven if the gameplay was satisfactory. It is not. For the first 75% of the "game," the levels are so painfully simple that you'll feel as if the developer forgot to add challenges. Only in its closing moments does the game have somewhat difficult puzzles that require planning and strategy.
How this game is so critically praised is beyond me. It does not work as a game, and it doesn't work as a story.

It's late 2016, putting this game at up to 5 years old, and it still shines. Before I go too far, read the last paragraph on the complaints of linearity.
Crytek have an amazing grasp of engine technology, juicing more visual prowess, AI and performance from a PC than many other games on the market, and it helps drive an amazing game.
The setting is a well-realised New York City in the near future, with an alien attack ongoing, and several parties trying to vie for power to eliminate this threat and the various enemies in their own agendas. The story is excellent, and well acted (personally, this is my favourite SC/shooter/Super suit game - Sorry HL2), visually stunning (although a few updates now would truly put it back atop - it still is beautiful though, surprisingly so) through great texturing and lighting, and wonderful set pieces (Times Square in the soaking rain has a boss battle which oozes atmosphere, and the final level is a breathtaking idea, I won't ruin it), excellent sound (atmospheric, and great voice work), and liquid performance and controls to run it.
This game jumps from £6 to £12 (figure out your own currency, folks), and it's very much worth it at either price - a much treasured gem in your collection.
Now many people call this game "linear", compared to the first game. Honestly, you do run through streets, which feel like gauntlets, but every location has a number of options for stealth, attack and supply routes through (using your visor to plan & scan), the only real difference is that you can't wander off AS FAR. The first game was just as linear, it just had "wider" areas to explore, but still required you to end up at the same space to perform the same actions, from within the same level. So yeah, it may feel enclosed, but the only difference is a little less space to mess around with.
I highly recommend this game. Crytek make (or did) make fantastic stuff, and this is one of the best.
But can your PC run it? There's fun in the question before you even select "campaign".
Oh finally, you may want to read up a little on the events of the first game if you never played. Some self-referencing from the start throughout can leave you questioning things.

For Honor... A "special" game I would say, as many other people would too. Where do I start? Well let's with the bad I guess...
Cons:
Optimization
For Honor has poor optimization and will only run on really good computers. I have a GTX 950M and an Intel-i7 and I have to put it on low graphics and low resolution for 60 FPS.
Story
The story is OK+ but I couldn't give it more than that, with weak characters. it feels like an extended tutorial rather than a campaign.
P2P
The biggest the problem the game has as of right now is it's P2P connection system, often crashing and disconnecting, which I think why a lot of players left the game...
Now we got to the fun part, the "Pros". Believe me when I say the game has a lot of those.
Gameplay
Wow, this game's mechanics are one of the best I've ever seen! Offering a great variety of combos, moves, and special abillites that really enhance the experience. Also introducing a revolutionary fighting system that is easy to learn but hard to master, which only adds to some of the things I will talk about in a bit. The game also introduses an execution system that lets you, the player to perform cool yet brutal finishing moves on your opponent to regain health and to prevent their teamates to revive them.
Proggression
This game has on of the best, if not the BEST proggression system I've ever thing! For Honor consists of 3 factions: Knights, Vikings and Samurai, with each of these factions having history's greates warriors at their disposal. The game has 18 unique heroes to choose, each having their own rank/level, which give the player a lot to play for. The game also have a lot of loot that can be obtained through playing, and the more you proggress, the better the loot is!
Graphics
For Honor is beautiful! It has some stunning graphics, that really adds to the player's exprience, with detailed maps and heroes, to the small yet important details. For Honor some of the best graphical features known to date!
Now last but not least, the reason I still this game...
Mirco Transactions
I just thought that I should put it out there that all micro transactions in the game are for cosmetic reasons only, and does not limit your experience as a player.
Thrill
This game has something in it that justs makes you want more! Every time I hop on the game, enter a game session, choose a hero that I want to play with, and watch the intro I get that feeling, a feeling of greatness, of glory! The game makes sure to deliver some amazing sound effects to give you the feeling that YOU are a legendary and a deadly warrior. Going 1v1 against a player, and having the stare down to see who goes first, it's amazing! The game is very intense, and it will make sure you know it from the second you start your first match. The satisfaction of winning "ganks" is second to none, defeating multiple enemies at once is the greatest! It makes you feel like you earned your sit in Valhalla. Even the small parts such as performing a badass emote after a grusome battle is amazing, because it gives you the feeling that you are a warrior, that you are a legend, that you are a part of something of greatness! I am sure that after a successful 3v1 you will be screaming like a viking. When you parry the attacks of all 4 enemies at once, you will have that look of a samurai, and when you save your teamate from certain death, you will feel the glory of a knight!
Conclusion
For Honor is truly a great game, that has a huge variety of characters, loot, maps, and movesets!
I do recommend the game, despite the hate. If you can, I think the game is worth a shot.

Resident Evil 6 completely embraces the looney action genre that the series has been turning into since 4.  The whole game is rife with explosions, karate moves, and over-the-top action scenes. Despite all this, the story takes itself seriously, giving it a high budget B-movie feel. The game still has its horror moments but they're few and far between.
Gameplay is basically the same as RE4&5 with bit more mobility. Enemy variety is decent but the placement is horrible. Some characters can go through their entire campaigns without seeing certain zombies variants, while some chapters just consist of killing the same two zombie variants over and over.
The game does have a huge issue with the camera. It will steal camera control away from you just to point out a very obvious door at the end of a linear hallway or when your partner is critically injured leaving you confused and lost when control is given back. The camera has a tendency to lock on to cinematic setpieces, this is bad when you're trying to run away from said setpiece and you literally can't see what's in front of you.
Overall, I would recommend especially if you have someone to coop with.

I've been quite obsessed with this game. Pro and cons:
+ Matches are challenging; a lot of tactical considerations need to be made constantly. A replay function helps to review and learn from mistakes.
+ Six factions with many many possible styles and archetypes to play.
+ Little randomness.
+ Deck building is challenging and fun, can also be skipped by simply copying a deck from the internet.
+ Very fair free-to-play model (to be honest I actually invested money. 10$). You can get quite far without investing any money. By doing quests you can get about one card pack each day with good drop rates of rare cards.
+ Very helpful community, close to zero abusive behavior.
+ The match-making system works very well, matches are found quickly.
+ Well-done tutorial.
+ Gorgeous pixel art and sound/music.
+ The developers maintain the game actively and listen to community feedback.
+ For parents: can be played with only one hand (touchpad or mouse). Being away from keyboard for a minute if real-life calls is usually ok. Matches are usually fast (5-10min).
+ Good interface in-match.
- Very little single-player content.
- Quite demanding for a pixel art game (<30 FPS on my laptop with Intel HD Graphics first generation, but doing fine on later generations), however for most people that won't be an issue I guess.
- Awkward interface in deck building / card pool management.
- Very little statistics, but there are some community mods for that.
For veterans from Magic the Gathering:
+ Forget all problems involving mana. Here you get mana for free; each round your pool increases. One less random factor to care about, but definitely doesn't make the game trivial as there are ways to manipulate the mana curve.
+ Much less worrying about picking a good hand, because you get to mulligan two cards at the beginning (while seeing who your opponent will be, allowing strategic decisions already), and you can replace a card for free every turn (guaranteed not drawing the same card)!
+ There's a proper board which leads to more tactical depth.
+ A match is quickly found.
- Obviously not as many cards as MtG, but that's the same for most CCGs out there.

There is a lot to love about Hyper Light Drifter. The presentation is incredible - the art, music, and just overall style are some of the highest examples of what indie games can accomplish. Unfortunately, this game also present an excellent example of style over substance. As pretty and just plain cool as this game can be, it is frustrating beyond belief.
You often hear people praise good difficult games as "challenging, but fair." Hyper Light Drifter got through the first part of that phrase and decided that was enough. You have scant few abilities at your disposal, and none of them will keep you from dying, and you will die a lot. You have 5 hit points, many enemies can do 2 damage per hit, and there are no invincibility frames. This means that enemies can juggle you, and you can go from full health to dead in about a second and a half against some combinations of enemies. Too often your death is locked in the moment you get hit once, no matter how much health you have. You carry health packs to heal yourself, but even healing isn't guaranteed - there's a delay before the healing occurs, and it's far too easy to take that last hit after hitting the button to heal.
I did mention abilities, and there are a few, though most must be unlocked. You start the game with a dash, and after playing for 20 hours and completing my first playthrough, I still never felt like I was truly in control of it. Upgrade your dash so you can chain it and quickly teleport around the screen and - staying in control just gets harder. Considering combat is the core mechanic of the game, it's a problem that it never feels fully natural.
It also doesn't help that the story, abilities, and even the map are never fully explained. There is no text, no dialogue, just pictures and sounds. It took me getting through two of the four main areas to finally get a basic understanding of how the map works. And why does the dash ability that lets you absorb enemy bullets not always work? Does it only absorb bullets you graze, rather than impact directly? Or is it just broken? The game sure won't tell you. Encoded alphabets and vague, visual storytelling worked for Fez, because it's a puzzle game that's all about figuring things out. Hyper Light Drifter is primarily about combat, so throwing in all this mystery and ambiguity just alienates the player.
The most frustrating part of Hyper Light Drifter is that it has so much potential. If the combat wasn't so horribly unbalanced, this would be a masterpiece. As it is, I struggle to understand the near-universal praise this game gets. I have never felt so punished for giving a game my money.

Original Jan'14 Review: What's happened is this: They took a previously very successful game (Railroad Tycoon) and brought it into the modern age. At the same time, to make it more accessible, many complex features were removed and replaced with very basic ones, if any. Pathing is awful, hence the addition of a "pass through" feature, where a train blocked by another can slowly phase through it. Even on the more difficult levels, you can't really go wrong. A lot of the industry feels pointless, the maps are too small, and the AI is awful.
Revised Dec '17 review: SMR is a weird one. I've gotten a lot more into RTS games in the past few years and come to appreciate SMR for being an economic RTS, the most recent and successful exmaple being Offworld Trading Company. Taken in this light, this is an okay at best game. Disregard any sense of true rail efficiency and strive to play the game in the most effective way. Lots of direct routes, rather than sharing rail lines. I thoroughly enjoy OpenTTD, and for that reason, I find it very difficult to play SMR. Building multi track railways running dozens of services at once on OpenTTD is impossible on SMR. It has a lot of modernisation issues too, hence third party fixes, but it also generally doesn't hold up so well.
I'd now recommend going to play OpenTTD, for a very different rail management experience. Or, if you want an economic RTS, Offworld Trading Company is the only real choice.

Thomas Was Alone is a platforming puzzle game that utilizes various characters with different relations to gravity. It starts out quite simple and becomes extremely complicated by the end. The puzzles are very intuitive and interesting, and new concepts are introduced all the way to the end of the game.
Gameplay: There are many different characters that you meet along the way, and their powers become more interesting and complex as you go. It gets crazy when you combine all of the characters and have to solve huge puzzles with each of their powers. Besides these powers, it's a simple platforming game, getting from point A to point B. I thought the physics were well done and the controls were very responsive.
Story: This is where I had some trouble. There seems to be some underlying story that I'm missing, because I've seen loads of story and character analyses, but I never really felt that there was some deeper connection as I was playing. The characters are all given interesting personalities and relationships, but there was some sort of huge connection that I was missing. It seemed like the game was trying to be deep and intriuging, but I found it was just hard to follow and flat.
I enjoyed this game for the most part. I had some trouble with certain levels which got incredibly frustrating, especially those involving timing and switching between characters quickly. Most of the time, though, I was very pleased with it and thought the commentary of the characters was pretty cute. This is a well made indie game that lasts a fairly long time and gives a good amount of puzzles and challenges. 8/10

Thomas Was Alone is a minimalist puzzle game with an interesting narration throughout the levels. The puzzles are challenging without being overly frustrating, and the music was also great.
Throughout the gameplay, we are introduced to a series of quadrilaterals, each with their own name, special skill, and (within the narration) their own personality. For a game about shapes, many of the "characters" were described quite well, with their own little personality quirks.
I finished this game in about 5 1/2 hours' time, but it definitely has potential for replay.

There is an emerging category of games that are defined not by their game play style, but by the quality of the narrative, the overall experience that they deliver, and the memorable impression that they leave on gamers.
Thomas was Alone fits squarely into this class of game.
The gameplay here is a sort of rudimentary platforming with mild puzzle elements. There are over 100 levels in this game, but they are all brief. Maybe 1-2 minutes for most of them, and only a handful that require you to stop and plan.
These brief levels work, though, because they are triggers for narrative dialog of the story. Through narrative these blocks of color are given vivid personalities and character traits.
This works wonderfully. Voiceman David Wallace delivers a story in a manner that is, in turn, sarcastic, earnest, sad, wry, hopeful, and often very funny.
Thomas Was Alone is a smart and engaging must-play indie title. And just the right length at 4-5 hours. Enjoy.

The best iteration had to be the closed beta.  The connections felt the cleanest, the moves and counters were crisp and on time.. It was a fun game.

The release was an accumulation of all the terrible qualities that plagued this game from the betas and earlier.  Some flaws were okay to live with, but the P2P, terrible release, and continious degradation of the gamestate resulted in one of the most disappointing games I've ever played.
This game is the reason I no longer support Ubisoft.  It's a shame it took me this long.

This game is so weird, so unconventional I feel I have to recommend it for the novelty factor alone. There's really no other game on Steam like it!
Jazzpunk is built around a first person perspective in which you play a secret agent in a bizarre robotic alternate reality. There are a large number of optional mini-games all of which are silly in nature. For example one mini-game is "Wedding Cake" which is a parody of the first person shooter "Quake" but with a funny marriage theme. Another mini-game involves looking into a microscope and playing a "Space Invaders" parody in which you must destroy a swarm of bacteria.
Basically you will spend 90% of your time in the game exploring this weird robot world and waiting for something funny to happen (which won't take long). The other 10% of the time you'll spend on the main secret agent plot, but the difficulty level here is so low that your success is guaranteed (I'm not sure it's actually possible to fail). So this is a game geared towards casual gamers and it's well done.
There was one part where I briefly got stuck. While messing around during the mini-golf game I accidentally hit my ball far off the course and couldn't get it back on the course. But reloading my save put the golf ball back on the course so I could continue. So if that happens to you just save your game and reload!
Graphics and soundtrack are definitely not AAA quality, but I wouldn't expect that from an indie developer and as long as the humor is good that's all that matters. Completing the whole game will take 4-5 hours.
I do feel the $15 price is too high but it regularly goes on sale. If you're looking for a fun way to spend an afternoon without thinking too hard, check out Jazzpunk!

Steam desperately needs to add a "Maybe" option when recommending a game or not.
I was gifted this game along with the season pass.
BO3 is a mixed bag, as you can tell by the reviews being mixed, both in "Recent" and "Overall". The underlying game is actually rather solid, having been the base for Infinite Warfare with most of it's mechanics having been ripped from this one.  Specialists are RIGs, their abilities are the RIG's Payloads, the parkour and movement system is exactly the same (albeit polished and more fluid in IW, so maybe not EXACTLY), and many of the UI elements are heavily inspired by this game's UI. The controller target/aim assist in Infinite Warfare tracks your targets through walls before they've come into view, and is far too strong, negating recoil and flinch...just like this game's aim assist.
Yeah, Infinite Warfare is kind of the same game as Black Ops 3, just with a bit of polish in some areas, and steps back in others. It's almost uncanny, and it's more apt than ever to say that a CoD game is literally a clone of it's predecessor. I recommend buying this game over IW though, due to mod support and a bigger playerbase.
Black Ops 3 has more personality in it though, with every Specialist having unique match-end taunts if you're the top player on the winning team and various voice lines and one liners. Black Ops 3 knows it's cheesy, Treyarch knows it's cheesy, and the game itself just relishes in that fact. Even at launch, you weren't supposed to take this game too seriously, and that's fantastic for a franchise that's often done just that.
The campaign is easily the biggest departure from the norm that the series has ever seen, as it goes even deeper than it's predecessors (in name only, seeing as a grand total of ONE character from the previous games has a passing mention), quickly becoming a psychological drama, with a surprising amount of nuance and depth that you won't get the first time playing through. It's so strange, different and baffling for a CoD game that it has multiple different explanations as to what the hell just happened all across the internet.
You don't expect to be taken for a psychoanalytic, philosophical ride like this in a CoD game where usually all you expect is to shoot russians/robots/mercenaries/whatever while shouting "AMERICA ♥♥♥♥ YEAH". People complain a lot about the campaign for making no sense, but that's just the beauty of it; you need to think about it more than the average CoD campaign, and it doesn't lay out the entire plot for you on a platter. I won't spoil a thing, the only thing you need to know is that you need to pay a lot more attention than you would to, say, Modern Warfare 3, and you need to come up with your own conclusions, then read about what other people thought it all meant if you'd like to.
Zombies is...well, it's zombies. If you liked WaW or BO1/2's Zombies, you'll like this. It continues the quirky story from the previous games, which I haven't really played, so I can't really comment on that. I do enjoy it though.
Multiplayer is standard fare...at first, until you start learning to make use of your parkour abilities. Maps are often designed to encourage you to experiment, with shortcuts and wall-running spots to take advantage of. While it doesn't take advantage of your abilities as much as the parkour maps and Infinite Warfare's do, it's still a nice addition. Unfortunately, BO3 falters in map design at the same time, as Treyarch is obsessed with the 3-lane "semi-symmetrical" design philosophy. Many of the maps end up feeling the same because they were all designed with this in mind, compared to Infinite Warfare's more open-ended, non-linear design that caters to your abilities and speed better.
BO3 has too many wide-open lanes and straight edges that don't give you a whole lot of options for creative movement or escape routes aside from those aforementioned specific shortcuts and wall-running spots. I can't really say anything about the DLC maps either, because they completely split the playerbase, and the playerbase that has the DLC is so incredibly small compared to the one that doesn't. If you have the DLC installed, it's almost impossible to find a game. BO3's map design, as a result, feels a bit more campy and less creative than it should, compared to Infinite Warfare's which actively enourages you to always be on the run, always jumping wall-to-wall to gain more momentum, always taking advantage of the map to keep yourself from getting shot.
The maps aren't TERRIBLE, but outside of a few specific points, they aren't designed with your abilities in mind. So, for the most part, you'll be playing "boots on ground" outside of more intense 1v1 fights where you're trying to air boost and slide as much as possible to throw off your opponent's aim. This is where the next problems come into play; the flinch, the lag compensation/netcode, the supply drops, and the controller aim assist.
Treyarch decided to remove the crutch perk that removed the flinch you experience from being shot. Said flinch throws off your aim upwards while using the sights, potentially losing you a gunfight. This is a problem because it can reduce the skill ceiling significantly, both giving a player the opportunity to throw off your aim, or giving said player the opportunity to score a killing headshot on you because you flinched his/her aim high enough.
Worse though is the lag compensation or netcode; more often than not, you'll have a player with higher ping than everyone else. And more often than not, they may be host, but either way, they effect how the game plays for everyone else. You'll tend to experience what feels like you being a second or so "behind" everyone else, as if someone was using a wallhack against you and you got shot with inhuman reaction time after you came through a door. Yet when you watch the killcam, you come out of the door, then the player reacts accordingly and shoots you, in a much more realistic-looking scenario.
What unbalances the game even more are the supply drop weapons, including the Shadowclaw crossbow pistol, that can be dual wielded and equipped with a 3-way bolt, with every bolt being a one hit kill at all ranges. But what easily breaks the game the most, is the controller aim assist. Remember how I said earlier in the review that it can track you through walls, and often negates recoil and flinch? It also completely counters any evasive maneuvering you can do such as strafing or boosting, so 1 on 1 gunfights with a controller user usually end in your death unless you got the drop on them and killed them fast enough, or if they simply still aren't good enough in spite of their free aimbot.
When everything is balanced, when nobody's using broken aim assist or overpowered supply drop weapons, when there's no lag, the game is fun as CoD usually is when it's in that perfect situation. Weapon balance for the most part is pretty good, movement is perfectly smooth and feels fine, and the port is pretty damn good. But as per usual with a CoD game, it caters far, far too much to the more casual audience that wants instant gratification and little to no effort put into how they play, as well as catering to players with worse connection than others, intentionally or not. Worse, if your score-per-minute is too high, you'll often be put in teams that aren't nearly close to your skill level, and are basically expected to carry everyone else. The team balance is pretty bad because of this.
However, it offers such a complete package with so much content and things to do that it's easily worth your money. Not to mention mod support. Buy with caution considering it's issues, but if it goes on sale for low enough, I highly recommend it at that point.

Being a big fan of simulation games and a model railroader, games which combine the two interests are often quickly added to my collection. Soon after Sid Meier;s Railroads! came out, I purchased it on disk, and played it a pretty good bit. I enjoyed it, but found it rather cartoony and unrealistic, especially compared to earlier titles in the series (Railroad Tycoon 1, 2 & 3.) I also found that your railroad builds up way too quickly and you end up making more money than you could use after about an hour or so on a map. Also the maps are incredibly undersized, and in a matter of a couple hours, you can't build another line because there's nowhere to build it to, from, or across!
Railroads! is rather fun, but I completely lose interest in a map after a couple hours because there's nothing left to do. The scenerios are easy, quick and too few, steam locomotives never have tenders (which just looks wrong on most engines), and there are many features from older versions that are completely abandoned!
So a quick breakdown:
Pros:
-More approachable for beginners
-Good for quick games, unlike older versions
-Great opening cinematic
-More approachable for non-railroaders
-Very approachable stock market
Cons:
-Little content
-Unrealistic
-Over-simplified
-Maps are far too small
-No tenders on steam engines
-Poorly balanced
-Maps take less than a couple hours to lose their entertainment value
So my feeling is that if you want a casual Tycoon game, this is for you, but if you're a hardcore Tycoon, try Railroad Tycoon 2 or 3. (My favorite from the series is 2)

HANDS-DOWN, ONE OF THE MOST ABOMINABLE OPENINGS TO A VIDEO GAME...EVER.

I mean, I do appreciate that some Resident Evil fans actually prefer a zombie-kickboxing simulator to a more atmospheric gaming experience, but seriously, does ANYONE out there actually like all this mechanics-breaking, quick-time-in-lieu-of-a-cutscene ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥?!  Okay, so maybe The Walking Dead games get away with some degree of it...but if the Resident Evil games are now aspiring to the level of immersion and emotional depth that THOSE games achieve, they may want to start paying some attention to concepts like themes, storytelling, and characterisation, don'tcha think?
The opening sequence of this game is sooooo painful, they even give you an Achievement for getting through it, appropriately entitled "The Longest Night".  They even have the gall to call it a "tutorial", when it teaches you precious little other than how to die repeatedly because you don't understand the poorly-explained on-screen instructions of how to RUN...in a SINGLE DIRECTION...and then force you to watch the same ten-second snatch of cutscene OVER AND OVER AND OVER AGAIN to atone for your aforementioned sins.  Next time, Capcom, just hawk up a great big loogie and spit it straight in my face, eh?

Things then start to look a TINY bit more hopeful, as Leon and some chick we've never seen before make their slow, moody way through a super-darkened government building, which is seemingly full of spooky noises but no actual undead. It isn't long, however, before we're spin-kicking and pile-driving zombies, and trying to work out just how the hell you even switch from guns to grenades or use health items (all adventures in their own rights, believe me)!  On the whole, there's really nothing terribly intuitive here...not the controls, not trying to estimate how close you can get to a zombie with your flyin' feet before they can get at YOU...the early part of the game is a constant struggle, or at least it was for me, and I played this straight off the back of Resident Evils 4 and 5, and all the DLCS and "bonus episodes" attached to those (undeniably superior) games.

Overall, there's really not much respect given to long-term fans: this may as well be a big-budget rival company's rip-off of the RE franchise for all the continuity it serves up, both tonally and mechanically.  It's far from the worst game ever made...but it's definitely one of the weakest Resident Evil games, period.  (And I've even played obscure, long-forgotten♥♥♥♥♥♥like Dead Aim, the Outbreak series, and the Survivor series, for what it's worth.)

For much of its length, this is barely even a horror game.  It's an action game with unfeasibly dark lighting and horror undertones.  Hell, as zombie-action games go, it's a long way from bad - even slightly "thrilling" upon occasion - but it's hardly honest-to-God HORROR, at least seventy-five per cent of the time.  And for all its attempted surliness, its "grit" never surpasses that of a Michael Bay movie (nice stubble, Leon, but you still have pretty-boy hair); and when all is said and done, it's still every bit as corny as a field in Summer ("Mr President, please don't make me do this!" blubbers Leon, unwilling to shoot the prez, even though he's clearly turned into a FREAKING ZOMBIE)!

A message to the developers of Resident Evil 7: stop catering to the undiscerning fans of those awful Milla Jovavich movies, and stop pandering to whatever is de rigueur in video games right at this very micro-second in time.  Multiplayer and/or A.I. partners DO NOT MAKE GAMES SCARY.  Quick-time events DO NOT MAKE GAMES SCARY.  Endless kickboxing moves DO NOT MAKE GAMES SCARY.  And making parts of your games so visually dark that you can't even tell what the hell just wounded you, IS JUST FRUSTRATING, NOT SCARY.
Pretty pretty please, let's do a little better next time, eh? This series is still pretty good...but it used to be GREAT.  The Revelations games seem to be heading in the right direction...how about lifting the game of the MAIN series, whad'ya say?

Verdict: 7.5/10.

(Oh, and PS to the devs: there's this thing they invented a while back, called "save points", and you shouldn't feel obliged to limit yourselves to only one every half-hour or so of gameplay.  Just sayin'...)

Steam desperately needs to add a "Maybe" option when recommending a game or not.
I was gifted this game along with the season pass.
BO3 is a mixed bag, as you can tell by the reviews being mixed, both in "Recent" and "Overall". The underlying game is actually rather solid, having been the base for Infinite Warfare with most of it's mechanics having been ripped from this one.  Specialists are RIGs, their abilities are the RIG's Payloads, the parkour and movement system is exactly the same (albeit polished and more fluid in IW, so maybe not EXACTLY), and many of the UI elements are heavily inspired by this game's UI. The controller target/aim assist in Infinite Warfare tracks your targets through walls before they've come into view, and is far too strong, negating recoil and flinch...just like this game's aim assist.
Yeah, Infinite Warfare is kind of the same game as Black Ops 3, just with a bit of polish in some areas, and steps back in others. It's almost uncanny, and it's more apt than ever to say that a CoD game is literally a clone of it's predecessor. I recommend buying this game over IW though, due to mod support and a bigger playerbase.
Black Ops 3 has more personality in it though, with every Specialist having unique match-end taunts if you're the top player on the winning team and various voice lines and one liners. Black Ops 3 knows it's cheesy, Treyarch knows it's cheesy, and the game itself just relishes in that fact. Even at launch, you weren't supposed to take this game too seriously, and that's fantastic for a franchise that's often done just that.
The campaign is easily the biggest departure from the norm that the series has ever seen, as it goes even deeper than it's predecessors (in name only, seeing as a grand total of ONE character from the previous games has a passing mention), quickly becoming a psychological drama, with a surprising amount of nuance and depth that you won't get the first time playing through. It's so strange, different and baffling for a CoD game that it has multiple different explanations as to what the hell just happened all across the internet.
You don't expect to be taken for a psychoanalytic, philosophical ride like this in a CoD game where usually all you expect is to shoot russians/robots/mercenaries/whatever while shouting "AMERICA ♥♥♥♥ YEAH". People complain a lot about the campaign for making no sense, but that's just the beauty of it; you need to think about it more than the average CoD campaign, and it doesn't lay out the entire plot for you on a platter. I won't spoil a thing, the only thing you need to know is that you need to pay a lot more attention than you would to, say, Modern Warfare 3, and you need to come up with your own conclusions, then read about what other people thought it all meant if you'd like to.
Zombies is...well, it's zombies. If you liked WaW or BO1/2's Zombies, you'll like this. It continues the quirky story from the previous games, which I haven't really played, so I can't really comment on that. I do enjoy it though.
Multiplayer is standard fare...at first, until you start learning to make use of your parkour abilities. Maps are often designed to encourage you to experiment, with shortcuts and wall-running spots to take advantage of. While it doesn't take advantage of your abilities as much as the parkour maps and Infinite Warfare's do, it's still a nice addition. Unfortunately, BO3 falters in map design at the same time, as Treyarch is obsessed with the 3-lane "semi-symmetrical" design philosophy. Many of the maps end up feeling the same because they were all designed with this in mind, compared to Infinite Warfare's more open-ended, non-linear design that caters to your abilities and speed better.
BO3 has too many wide-open lanes and straight edges that don't give you a whole lot of options for creative movement or escape routes aside from those aforementioned specific shortcuts and wall-running spots. I can't really say anything about the DLC maps either, because they completely split the playerbase, and the playerbase that has the DLC is so incredibly small compared to the one that doesn't. If you have the DLC installed, it's almost impossible to find a game. BO3's map design, as a result, feels a bit more campy and less creative than it should, compared to Infinite Warfare's which actively enourages you to always be on the run, always jumping wall-to-wall to gain more momentum, always taking advantage of the map to keep yourself from getting shot.
The maps aren't TERRIBLE, but outside of a few specific points, they aren't designed with your abilities in mind. So, for the most part, you'll be playing "boots on ground" outside of more intense 1v1 fights where you're trying to air boost and slide as much as possible to throw off your opponent's aim. This is where the next problems come into play; the flinch, the lag compensation/netcode, the supply drops, and the controller aim assist.
Treyarch decided to remove the crutch perk that removed the flinch you experience from being shot. Said flinch throws off your aim upwards while using the sights, potentially losing you a gunfight. This is a problem because it can reduce the skill ceiling significantly, both giving a player the opportunity to throw off your aim, or giving said player the opportunity to score a killing headshot on you because you flinched his/her aim high enough.
Worse though is the lag compensation or netcode; more often than not, you'll have a player with higher ping than everyone else. And more often than not, they may be host, but either way, they effect how the game plays for everyone else. You'll tend to experience what feels like you being a second or so "behind" everyone else, as if someone was using a wallhack against you and you got shot with inhuman reaction time after you came through a door. Yet when you watch the killcam, you come out of the door, then the player reacts accordingly and shoots you, in a much more realistic-looking scenario.
What unbalances the game even more are the supply drop weapons, including the Shadowclaw crossbow pistol, that can be dual wielded and equipped with a 3-way bolt, with every bolt being a one hit kill at all ranges. But what easily breaks the game the most, is the controller aim assist. Remember how I said earlier in the review that it can track you through walls, and often negates recoil and flinch? It also completely counters any evasive maneuvering you can do such as strafing or boosting, so 1 on 1 gunfights with a controller user usually end in your death unless you got the drop on them and killed them fast enough, or if they simply still aren't good enough in spite of their free aimbot.
When everything is balanced, when nobody's using broken aim assist or overpowered supply drop weapons, when there's no lag, the game is fun as CoD usually is when it's in that perfect situation. Weapon balance for the most part is pretty good, movement is perfectly smooth and feels fine, and the port is pretty damn good. But as per usual with a CoD game, it caters far, far too much to the more casual audience that wants instant gratification and little to no effort put into how they play, as well as catering to players with worse connection than others, intentionally or not. Worse, if your score-per-minute is too high, you'll often be put in teams that aren't nearly close to your skill level, and are basically expected to carry everyone else. The team balance is pretty bad because of this.
However, it offers such a complete package with so much content and things to do that it's easily worth your money. Not to mention mod support. Buy with caution considering it's issues, but if it goes on sale for low enough, I highly recommend it at that point.

This is truly one of those games you should know as little as possible about the game before you play it. The only things you really need to know is that the game is a very cool and memorable experience easily worth the money.
Now for some mild spoilers: Pony Island is a game that plays with your expectations, a lot of the time it does this by breaking the 4th wall. The game seems to be segmented into several mini games that by themselves would be fairly simplistic and boring but together they provide to an overall satisfying narrative. Just when one part of the game stays out its welcome it throws something new at you to keep you going.
The game is about 2 hours long took me about 4 hours to complete it 100% and that seems to be the perfect length for this game.
In closing I just want to say that this game has provided a great start for the new year in gaming and if i continues like this then 2016 might even beat 2015 when it comes to great releases.

Only 4 days into 2016 and there is already a serious contender for Indie Game of the Year. Pony Island is, first and foremost, not a game about ponies. It is a game about fighting with the game itself--attempting to hack your way through its programming labyrinths and solve its coded mysteries while fighting for your soul. This is NOT a pure narrative experience; the gameplay is fun and the puzzles are tough. Saying any more would dampen the experience, so I must ask that you go in without another thought.

At the point Central Park is held aloft in huge earthly chunks settled atop writhing masses of metal tentacles, Crysis 2 turns to the player and shrugs in exhaustion: “That’s all I got, kid”.
A multiplatform follow-up to the PC-killing original, Crysis 2 makes significant trades in gameplay and environments in order to excel visually on consoles. However, even when using a walled garden approach where most maps are open expanses designed for multiple avenues of attack, Crysis 2 is a metric crap-ton more fun to play than any COD clone, including COD:BLOPS.
Unlike the original Crysis, where the player was dropped onto an island with a full suite of nano-suit abilities that allowed for increases in strength, speed, armor or cloaking and given leave to play in a giant sandbox, the sequel parcels out abilities over the first half of the game. Speed and strength are no longer selectable and are enabled by default. Using the energy remains of deceased enemy Ceph allows the player to upgrade the suit abilities throughout.
Like the first game, the story is an incomprehensible mess only set in Manhattan rather than a North Korean island. Flora and fauna are replaced by concrete and vehicles, creating impenetrable mazes of steel and glass, rather than flowing expanses of green. Playing as Alcatraz, a voiceless, personality free cipher of a marine, the player wakes from black (the first of a half-dozen overused transitions), embedded in the suit. Immediately mistaken for the suit’s original owner and apparently incapable of independent thought, Alcatraz begins a series of guided journeys, each lead by a different voice transmission.
The alien Ceph of the first game are succeeding in destroying New York City and only the nanosuit has the ability to stop them. Led through a series of switchbacks and double-crosses, Alcatraz blindly follows orders, leaving one to wonder if he had played too much Bioshock when not at work as a marine.
Epic and troubling imagery leverage the lingering memories of 9-11, as the city collapses during the journey beneath above and beyond, leaving the player slack-jawed. Unlike the seemingly endless vistas of the first game, Crysis 2 is also beautiful but limited. Particle effects and motion blur are used liberally to mask the limits placed on the engine and while the framerate does waver, it does so rarely.
Using the suit powers allows and even requires the player to use some strategy when engaging groups of enemies, especially early on as the enemies become more varied and more difficult, but never smarter. Unfortunately, common glitches manifest where a death-and-reload will cause scripted enemies to become frozen in place, robbing the game of challenge. Diligent hoarders of Ceph energy will also soon find themselves able to nearly max out the suit upgrades, leading to late game moments where a cloaked sprint can avoid engaging the enemy altogether.
Crysis 2 lacks the open world of its predecessor or Far Cry 2, causing it to fall into a nebulous middle where it is influenced heavily by Call of Duty but not yet as horribly linear, leaving it a refreshing change from claustrophobic corridor shooting.

If you've played Guitar Hero as a kid, this game is the grown-up version.
If you've played an instrument previously in life, this game is very easy to pick up and dive in to learning to play virtually any song you desire.
Be prepared to buy  things to support playing this game.
You're going to need a realtone cable, which can be bought on Amazon for around $28. Good headphones are a given.
I already owned a bass guitar and a pile of various guitar picks. Be prepared for calluses and blisters and aches.
The lessons are simple and forgiving when it's your turn to play. Playing through songs and picking trouble areas to practice are very easy in the interface. The section you select can be slowed to any percent speed and any difficulty level. This makes learning songs and memorizing riffs very easy. You can even set the difficulty or speed to increase after so many play throughs of the section. This makes it easy to practice and improve without having to take your hands off the instrument to click around.
Overall, this game is my new favorite. My finger tips disagree.

TL:DR edition
Basically Guitar Hero for guitarists, Rocksmith 2014 lets you play along with popular songs with either a 6-string electric guitar or a 4-string electric bass. You do need to buy a cable to plug your guitar into your computer, a special 6.5mm-USB cable specifically for Rocksmith which adds roughly $40 onto the cost of the game if you don't already own one so keep that in mind before buying it. Also DLC is expensive, just buy Cherub Rock and mod in songs instead.
+great tool for learning guitar (if paired with other things)

+solid selection of tracks in base game
+easy to mod
+supports both guitar and bass
+local 2p multiplayer
-only 2p multiplayer

-overpriced DLC
9/10
Full ver.
This game is pretty much perfect, and I would say it's an incredible tool both for people who want to learn guitar or bass and for those who already play and just want to jam some new songs. There's also a solid modding community who are constantly making "custom DLC"/CDLC/mods that import songs into the game unofficially.
I used to find the "dynamic difficulty" feature annoying and patronising in the first Rocksmith, you'd start off playing one note every 4 bars and the game would get harder as you improved. In the beginning it was annoying because it was too easy, once you got to a solid difficulty it was still annoying because it would drop you back down to baby mode if you ever made a mistake. This feature makes a return in Rocksmith 2014, but is vastly improved by the option to turn it off if you already know what you're doing.
I like that it has local multiplayer, a rarity in PC games, however it is a bit of a shame that you can only have two players at a time. Most songs on Rocksmith 2014 have 3 different parts for each song (rhythm, lead, bass). Unlike a console, you can have more than 2 USB ports and multiple displays on a PC and it would've been really cool for Ubisoft to include the option to have a third player on a second monitor. This way, a whole band (sans drummer) can practice and jam together.
There are really only a few minor issues I have with Rocksmith 2014, one of which is the tuner. It's pretty sensitive, which is good, but its idea of a guitar being in tune is a bit too lenient imo. A few times the game would tell me a string was tuned when I could clearly hear that it was out in relation to other strings.
Also, the game seems to have trouble detecting very low bass notes, low Cs are missed in songs that call for C standard or drop C tuning but maybe that's just my bass' volume being too low. I wouldn't know since I don't have a second one to test on multiple instruments.
Another problem is that many tracks teach the player ways to play the song that are harder than necessary. Gonna get a bit technical here. Keep in mind that in standard bass tuning, the 5th fret of every string plays the open note of the next string, meaning the 7th fret note of the E string (a B) plays the same note as the 2nd fret of the A string. Many songs will have you moving from, say, the 2nd fret to the 7th on the same string, when it would be much easier to stay on the 2nd fret but play the next string. R U Mine? by the Arctic Monkeys is a very good example of the game making a song harder than it has to be.
My final, and biggest, problem with this game is the pricing. Going by current conversion rates, the game costs $53.65 AUD. This would be a very reasonable price, however buying a separate Rocksmith "Real Tone" Cable is required to play and adds roughly $40 AUD onto the price (and a guitar, fairly obviously). The game offers a decent amount of songs without DLC but you'll want to make sure the song list is VERY much in line with your music taste if you want to get a decent experience from the base game. DLC songs cost $4 AUD EACH, which I think is a pretty unreasonable ask for one song, especially because this game has around 480 DLC songs at this point. Even if you don't care about most of the DLC songs it's still likely to run you a few hundred bucks for the ones you want. Thankfully the only DLC you need to buy is Cherub Rock so you can mod in CDLC. After that just torrent the other official DLC or wait until a sale if you REALLY want to buy it.

is a charming game with a nice aesthetic look, moderately challanging puzzles excellent narration. The way in which small cubes and rectangles are given substance or personality by simply projecting fears, envy and self-reflection on what is essentially a few pixals is applaudable in its own right.
However, I feel like the game is somewhat lacking as a 'game'. The puzzles aren't that difficult, and worse still, solving them isn't that fun. There is an increase in diffculty over time, but many of the more difficult puzzles are simply difficult because they require repetition, with the same act being repeated a few times. I'm also not entirely sold on the whole "AIs are devoloping, fighting clean-up code and accending to eventual freedom and citizenship"-subtext. The newpaper-quotes seemed to try to highten the stakes of the puzzles, making them into a re-telling of an historical event, rather than a fanciful self-contained story. Ultimately, this seemed like an unnecessery added element on top of the spot-on narration, filling in gaps which could have been left to the players imagination.

A truly amazing puzzle-platformer. It's complex in its simplicity. You play as a variety of blocks, each with different abilities and weaknesses. Add to it great dialogue and atmopsheric music, and you've got a really fun game. It's not terribly long, maybe a few hours, but it's worth it. The levels start off easier but get pretty crazy once you start combining double jumps, reversed gravity, a trampoline and switches to swap between various abilitites.
My only con: The music is great, but sometimes it seemed really dissonant, like there were two different tracks playing on top of each other in different keys. I don't know if this was intentional to set a mood or just some glitch that makes the music hang over from level to level.
I've never cared so much about a bunch of quadrilaterals before in my life.

Intralism is a face-paced, arcade fashioned rhythm game that may remind some of us of another game.
Your basic controls are AWSD, though for two-handed mode, it will include the arrow keys. I have not tried the latter, so my review will not include details on that feature. It’ll take some time to adjust to these keys when playing, and more coordination if you are playing harder maps that have you constantly clicking a streak or more than 1 key at once.
As a rhythm game, the player’s goal is to complete a song without fail. If you lean more towards the competitive side, you may even be facing the challenge of reaching the top of the leaderboard too. This is another part of Intralism that I also like, which is how the game appeals to a larger set of audience. Whether you’re a casual player, a competitive player, or even one who likes creating workshop items for the game, Intralism is one that fits the bill in many categories. I, myself, and a casual player and publish maps for the game regularly.
The overall design is neat and simple. There are options, setting and other features all available on the menu. When you play, you’ll notice how the environment can change from time to time, depending on the tempo and bpm of the song. This really heightens the players experience, and for me, really did made me
the music. Esepcially with the vibration effects of the centre notes. For workshop items, it could be even more appealing where there is a custom BG, text on screen and other effects to the map. I have yet to use these features on my own workshop maps.
Music almost all, if not 100% of the game’s value. The second you start up the game, you are hit with a tune of awesome EDM once you are at the menu. A lot of the default maps are sweet too, with one of my favourite from the set being Flaklypa. Needless to say, not all of the music available will be EDM. Have access to the workshop and you’ll see a whole range of different genres of music made by a small (but growing) community.
Surprise, surprise: The game also has Trading Cards, achievements and drops steam items too. What more could this game offer? I enjoyed this game and play it when possible. I strongly recommended to try Intralism, especially at the cheap price it’s at.

Well, here is a game where you are a fly jumping around on a person’s watch.
I’d have never thought that someday I will play something like this, but I like it!
You have to jump around a watch as you try to dodge its rapidly moving hour and minute hands. Tap the screen and your fly will jump from one quarter to the next in a counter-clockwise manner. If you get hit by the hands or jump on one of them, you die. Theoretically, this sounds more than easy but there is a problem. The hands move at different speeds and they get faster the farther you get. If you still think that this is easy peasy, just give it a try.
As for me, my record is 97 and I think only the devil himself can get the 400 jumps achievement.
You will also collect coins each round, unlocking new flies (there are more than 20 of them). In addition, each time you go for a new try you land on a different hand (or watch) and your little friend will have another hat on his head.
Fly O'clock is great fun, especially if you play it with your friends or with random opponents from the internet (you will also get a rating) and it is a good way to spend some spare time. But be careful, after jumping around for a time it could cause dizziness.
Positive:
+ great fun
+ very nice soundtrack
+ controller support
+ easy to play and hard to master
Negative:
- could cause dizziness
- you will loose 100%. It’s “just a matter of time”.
So all in all this game is definitely worth a try and it’s completely worth the price! Just give it a try!

This is one of those games that are fun to play when you're bored or just want something simple yet difficult to play.
You hop around on a wrist watch, avoiding both the minute and hour hand, and see how many jumps you can get before you get hit by the hands. Eventually you'll unlock new characters the more you play and how many points you get per game.
It's fun, addicting, and you might end up going "one more attempt!" five times in a row before you give up. Eventually you'll notice bit of a pattern with the hands based on where they start, and with enough time and patience you can score big.
There is local and online multiplayer, however I have zero experience to say anything about it.
It's worth a dollar, and might find the other games by the dev team fun that you might buy the bundle instead. It's also best to play this on a low resolution than you're used to, unless you're playing with friends locally and further away from the monitor.\

This is hands down one of my favorite games of all time. It's a god damn work of art. And quite literally, I suppose.

Interesting allegory about seeking asylum in another country. No save state, but the game takes no more than an hour to complete.

I got this because it was suggested by Extra Credits. But there's something wonky going on with the mouse control that makes it basically unplayable (the mouse cursor keeps flickering on the screen, the sensitivity is way too low, and the positioning keeps resetting, making it a difficult and iffy proposition to turn in any particular direction.

tl:dr
North is a short, abstract game about a refugee, seeking asylum.
The metaphors aren't really subtle but strong and bring home the point. Since it is really cheap and thought provoking i recommend it.
IMPORTANT:
The game doesn't really tell you what to do, but you will see a letter symbol in the corner from time to time. Go to a postbox, they are in the main areas of the city, there you will be able to read the letters and get hints on what to do.
Technical Stuff:
Besides the resolution options in the unity start up window, there aren't any menus and options inside the game. Occasionally the framerate drops, but since reaction speed isn't really needed, that's not really a problem. Only the WASD keys and the mouse buttons are used. No map, no inventory. The graphics are simplistic but suit the rather abstract symbolism of the game. The sound and music are eerie and fit the setting.
Conclusion:
It has its technical flaws and is pretty short, so it is not for everyone, but since it is cheap, I honestly don't think the game is overpriced. It puts you into the view of someone who isn't as fortunate as you, considering that a big part of the world's population doesn't have access to electricity, computers and an internet connection. It is a lesson in empathy, that i think is really needed in the context of the staggering amount of refugees in the world and the current refugee crysis and also shines a light on a lot of questionable things in western societies.
My recommendation for everyone is: Step out of your comfort zone and step into the shoes of someone less fortunate than you. Give this game a try!
Afterthoughts: !SPOILERS!
The big theme of this game is the strangeness of the seemingly wealthy and developed society to the eyes of someone from a poor, harsh and dangerous environment.

This is my opinion of the pros and cons of Intralism coming from an osu! player.
Pros:
1. Intuitive Controls - If you have ever used a keyboard in your life, the controls are easy to read, WASD or arrow keys, each part of the circle corresponds to one of the buttons.
2. Engagement - I felt pretty engaged with the music using the controls, which is probably the most important part of the whole rhythm game genre.
3. Community Accessibility - Easy to pull songs from the workshop, very good decision to implement custom maps.
All of these are great ingredients for a good rhythm game, but what I had issues with are some of the smaller things the were poorly implemented or missing (?).
Cons:
1. User Interface - Once you start a song, you are thrown into the game in its purest form. Except theres nothing to tell you how well you're actually doing. I will explain why this is a problem later.
2. Feedback - Something that osu does very well is making the player know when they have hit an object. In Intralism there is no such thing, sadly. When objects fall into place they take a little while and then just disappear after a delay (!). No sound to tell you if you hit it and no sound to tell you if you miss one that takes away your precious life points.
3. Visibility - It is sometimes difficult to see exactly how many objects should be played in succession, and is very frustrating for me, where I press the buttons somewhat quicker than what the map has, which leads me into my next point.
4. Settings - For any kind of rhythm game, the ability to adjust the audio offset so that all players can feel comfortable with the way that they hear the music. I am aware they are putting in some more settings in an update coming up, so I'm keeping this short.
The user interface is very important to have for those that want to be competitive when playing the game. On one hand, the game is fitted for the casual player with the checkpoints, and the score for competitive, but the lives are still important for both the casual and the competitive players. This coupled with the fact that there is no feedback when missing a object means that the player is left in the dark regarding their progress.

Consider my thumbs up generous for this title. Fly O'Clock is okay for what it is. But it lacks much of the charm of the hit Timberman.
When first breaking in the game, note that the early game (anything below 100 jumps) is dreadfully slow. I'm pretty sure that the velocity of the hands is tied directly to your jump count, not the number of revolutions they have made.
I got the game in a publisher bundle which was on significant enough sale that I spent maybe $.49 on average. I was more interested in Timberman and Surfingers, both of which in my opinion are superior titles in the hardcore-twitch casual-depth game genre.
Much of this game feels half finished and rushed in its design. For example, the achievements simple and boring—awarded at increments of 50 up to 400. The character unlock system is facile at best. And the lack of a volume slider is peculiar.
All that being said, as single button games go, this one does have the ability to hypnotize. Game induced altered states are not always enjoyable. But if played with the game volume down and Rachmaninoff in the background, you're sure to have a pleasant trip.
As I've said in other reviews, I find myself wishing for a neutral, mixed, or sideways rating. Depending upon my mood, I'd give this title between a 4/10 and 6/10. I wouldn't buy this title on its own or at full price. But if you got it as part of a bundle, as I did, maybe you might find it a worthwhile distraction for a few hours.

This is a short but immersive experiential game telling the story of a refugee in a strange land.  It's a stylised but realistic depiction of the realities of immigration, that might make people in the West think twice about the way they treat those who are 'welcomed' into their lands.  I think it represents normal immigration far more accurately than it does refugee crises, though elements of both are discussed here.
I must say, I absolutely loved it.  This isn't the type of game that exists to challenge your skills, but to offer you a different perspective on the world, and the way it does this through abstract and creative imagery along with the letters your character writes (a stroke of genius, the way these lead you through the game) is effective and deeply emotional.
The atmosphere created here is amazing; the landscape is oppressive and characterful, the music and characters eerie and alien.  The feeling of being frightened and lost in a strange land is spot on.  It's a must-play for anyone who enjoys experiences of this type, are politically minded and are open to games that are more about journeys than goals.
If any game I've played is perfect for VR, this is it; it could only serve to deepen the experience further.  Make it so, developers!
At this price it is seriously worth it.  You'll probably finish it just within an hour (not long enough to get the trading cards, which is a shame, but that's Steam's issue, not the game's), but you won't quickly forget it.

I give this game a solid 8 out of 10. It's a good game, don't get me wrong, but there are some aspects that i really don't like. First off, the game is just too short. If you don't seek out achievements and/or secrets, you could beat this game in at least 12 hours (with taking breaks).
Second, the New Game+ mode doesn't bring anything new to the table. You just have 2 health instead of 5, and have an outfit you can't change out of. The 2 health aspect of NG+ is just makes the game more frustrating.Which brings me to my next point.
When most bosses (and sometimes lesser foes aswell) can instanly kill you, your game is no longer fun, it is frustrating. which brings me to my next point, the game is just frustrating in some areas. The frustration factor is very apparent in NG+ mode, where all of your progress on a boss could be eliminated because you just couldn't avoid the damage, say, you couldn't dash away from a certain attack because you don't have the chain dash upgrade.
Also, you either have the upgrades you need to survive or you don't. The way to obtain these upgrades is through purchasing them with coins you can collect. But to obtain just ONE of these coins, you need to collect 4 "gearbits" as they're called.So in order to get the chain dash upgrade, which is ESSENTIAL to getting most of the game's secrets, you must first grind out 12 gearbits by finding them in crates, or having scripted enemies drop them. You can't just kill random enemies lke in most games like this, you have to find SCRIPTED enemies, and there is no indication as to which emeies carry them. No outline or demonstration of how to detect them, you just have to come across them on you streamlined travel.
Now for the stuff I thought was good about the game. The fact that heart Machine managed to explain the lore behind the world you are in without words (not counting the monliths that have to be translate outside the game) is pretty amazing. Using only pictures to explain the backstory of the zones you travel through or characters you meet is phenominal.
The combat system is fun to use, relying on timing and quick in-and-out attacks for your sword, and ammo conservation for your ranged weapons. Your weapon of choice is a sword. A lightsaber to be more precise. Your primary attack pattern is a quick, 3 slash combo. There are attacks you can earn using the upgrade system I talked about, charge strike as i will call it, where you hold your attack button and release when the time is right, note you are stationary while in the ready-to-strike stance for this attack, dealing massive damage (5 hit points) to anyting it comes into contact with. You also have two charge related attacks, which I will call "Slash Dash" and "Get the heck away Dash". Slash Dash it activated by dashing and clicking shortly after (dash before slash) you wil charge forward in a straight line, dealing massvie damage to anything caught in you path. Get the heck away Dash is activated by clicking , then dashing shortly after (slash before dash). You will dash forward a short distance and push your target back at a high velocity, deling 3 damage and possibly finshing them off by rocketing them into a wall if they collide with it short into their long flight. You can also get the ability to reflect projectiles which make a LOT of enemies and bosses that much easier.
You can can also get upgrades for your dash ability nothing special just chain dash and projectile destroy dash.
But what about GUNS? Do they have any upgrades? no. no they do not. just increased ammo capacity. that is all.
Along with upgrade that affect you character, there are upgrades that affect your gameplay. You can upgrade your character to unlock a new weapon, the grenade (which has no upgrades) and two more spaces for health packs, helping you last longer in harder fights.
But that's enough ranting, I could go on all day about the quirks of this game. like how the AI is just awful in navigating the map, often colliding into walls, or not even jumping over the simplest of gaps, or how the game needs to educate you on how to find secrets better. Once again, a solid 8 out of 10. Good job with this game Heart Machine.

If i felt more cynical about it i'd call it "wannabe Undertale, except for Satan," but some disjointed plot threads and forced writing here and there don't really make this game an experience I regret having.
This is like the fulfilled promise of two decades of bad Newgrounds games with cool concepts that suffered from being made by a 12 year old. I came in blind, didn't even see the trailer. Once I realized I was playing a horror game of sorts, I expected to get bad creepypasta, and I absolutely got better than that. It's tongue-in-cheek, and while that makes me roll my eyes from time to time, most of the time it works well. Puzzles aren't obtuse, there's an appropriate degree of silliness (ie not too much), and exploring the broken machine is satisfying.
It's definitely not without its flaws. The narrative shines when progressing, but all of the extra information you can get on the side (not just about the player character) feels meaningless to me at best, and complete nonsense at worst. And not that Undertale was the first game to keep track of things across multiple playthroughs, but it feels forced here and not nearly as elegant and meaningful as it was in that game. All the parallels to Undertale do this game a disservice, but they're being drawn for a reason; there are specific lines in Pony Island that made me cringe, they wanted so badly to be as good as Undertale's version of that line.
I wouldn't say it's a must-play, but it's much better than I expected. I'd like to think it says more that it drew me in and made me want to collect every ticket, reveal the whole backstory, etc. than that I was dissatisfied with what I got from doing it. Journey over destination.

I bought the "Pantera 3-Song Pack" from the first Rocksmith game and it worked in Rocksmith 2014 Remastered Edition without me owning the first Rocksmith game or the "Rocksmith 2014 Disc Import Tool" this originally was not possible do to the way in which steam handles DLC for one game seperate from DLC for another game but this has since been fixed (this info is hard to find online and old forum posts discuss how people were unable to even purchase the Rocksmith 1 dlc when they didn't own RS1 but instead owned RS2014)
If you purchase DLC from the Rocksmith 1 store page it wont show up in your steam library when you click on Rocksmith 2014 Remastered Edition, however it will show up in the game under "Learn A Song" and the realtones will show up under "Load Tone" where you can just mess around with that tone.
You can get Custom DLC (CDLC) that's not sold on steam for free at customsforge (google it)
you must buy "Cherub Rock" by "The Smashing Pumpkins" to play any of that free DLC
The reason for this is that most CDLC pretends to be that song and rocksmith will only play DLC that you have purchased
The song that your CDLC pretends to be (Cherub Rock) can be changed to another song DLC that you have purchased if you know how to do it (using a program from customsforge, once for every song you download... it's easier to just buy "Cherub Rock".)
Downloading from customsforge requires you to signup on their forum.
The reason they program CDLC to pretend to be "Cherub Rock" is because that was a pre-order bonus for the game when it was new so early adopters of the game typically had that DLC on day one.
