This is a fantastic strategy/card game

Positives:
I've had my backside handed to me by decks made using only common and rare (read: uncommon) cards. And it had nothing to do with luck either. They were just good. Very well balanced with the exception of a few odd cards, but the developers stay on top of everything and release nerfs and buffs quickly when needed. Grid based gameplay makes so much sense for the extremely Hearthstone-esque style. Every game feels like at least 80-90% skill as you think carefully about your positioning before each move, add up all the numbers, and try and deny your opponent the advantage.
Much like a certain other card game, you have several factions all with unique playstyles and a choice of two generals that changes the way the deck plays. Some brief examples: Abyssians flood the board with puny minions or produce shadow creep that damages enemies when they stand on it. Lyonar have loads of bulky minions and support spells to face threats head-on and bog the opponent down under massive bodies. Songhai are the assassins that specialize in aggro tactics, ranged minions, and high damage combos. Magmar are a bunch of huge lizards who specialize in becoming unreasonably powerful if left unchecked.
And here's the kicker: a lot of the paid stuff is really reasonable. If you can earn it with cash you can earn it in game and it never feels like you're climbing a mountain-sized progress bar for something that you could be forking out $2.99 for. If you do decide to spend some cash, you get pretty reasonable value too. I dropped $20 to support the publishers for a great game, and got (all up) 3 guranteed legendaries and 17 booster packs worth 5 cards each (one guranteed rare per pack). Better yet I did the math later and figured out that I could have got a better deal.
Negatives:
I love all the art personally, but almost everyone I've talked to seems to have a problem with either the hand-drawn stuff or the pixel art. Minor grievance but worth noting if you are bothered easily by art. The match announcer at the start is also a bit jarring and doesn't really mesh with the rest of the game. There are a few combos using mainly epic cards that can flatten newer decks, but that doesn't often happen in bronze and by the time you get to silver you should be armed to put up a good fight at the very least.
As far as microtransactions go, the loot boxes you are sometimes given are the only really irksome part. The first one comes with a key but after that there doesn't seem to be any way to get more for free, and the highest level chest required $10 for a key. The chests contain guranteed high value cards and cool cosmetics (which can all be earned free anyway), but in my opinion they don't contain enough items to warrant their current pricetag. I've been letting my loot crates form a dusty pile in the corner for now, as I heard somewhere that a free source of keys is on the developers to do list.
Overall:
Great developer support, tactical gameplay, fairly well balanced. Mostly good monetization (the bad bits are easy to ignore and nothing is locked off to free players).

Pretty much my favorite CCG of all time at this point.
I started out with MTG back in the 90's and moved onto other paper cards games in the early 2000's (including VS, WOW, UFS). I have been waiting for a company to translate CCG concepts to the digital realm since then. After stints with MTGO, Hearthstone, Scrolls, Solforge, and others, I feel like Duelyst is the first digital CCG that hits all the right notes for me.
First off, it's free. I choose to support the development of the game through purchases, but I think if you focus on a single faction or two, it's feasible to build competitive decks after a minimal investment of time. The cosmetics are expensive if you're into that type of thing, but the packs are reasonably priced when compared to paper or to other digital CCGs. There is zero friction in giving this game a shot to see if it's for you.
Second, the tactical element is excellent. Instead of just casting creatures and spells like most other CCGs, there is a 5x9 grid that you position your units onto and attack opposing units on. This spatial element adds another dimension to these games which makes it harder to master. To me, this adds to the appeal of game and has kept me coming back over the last year (I started before it was on Steam).
Third, matches are quick. The game I came from before this was Scrolls (screw you Microsoft). It also had a board and was a lot of fun. Unfortunately games were 30+ minutes each. Duelyst matches are usually around 10 minutes, which is perfect.
Fourth, good developer. Countplay games seems to unapologetically use what works in other digital CCGs as a foundation to build upon while not being afraid to push forward with new mechanics and designs. New cards are released each month and nerfs/buffs happen regularly, so the meta never gets stale. A game like this can never have perfect balance, but I think CP does as well as any developer can in this regard. Even when certain factions become more viable than others, the difference in win percentage isn't drastic, so you can play what you like and do fine if you're skilled. Also, they made bold decisions in the beta that were initially very unpopular with the player base. But over time those decisions have been justified. I have confidence in their vision for this game.
Other things worth mentioning: non-toxic player community, lots of space for deck building innovation, objectiively cool pixel art.
Still waiting for a Linux client, but at least it can be played in a browser.

If you are aware of my work - my reviews - then you'll already know that I don't dish out "not recommended" labels lightly. I try my best to like a game because I realise all the effort that developer's put into their creation. I can't, for the life of me, however, recommend this title in any way, shape, or form.
Let me start off by exploring the first half of the description of
: "...dealing with the issue of the contemporary refugee crisis..." Am I right in assuming that they're talking about the Syrian refugee crisis?
If "yes", then I've been following the refugee crisis for a very long time now. A lot of my friends happen to be Syrian, immigrants prior to the "modern mess" (term used lightly), so I try to do them the honour of keeping up with the news as much as possible. From the very first playthrough of the game, I couldn't understand where the "contemporary refugee crisis" label was being directed towards. Was it the graveyard in the work area? Perhaps depicting that the Syrians were working hard for "nothing" at this point? Or was it the broken down houses that were left in deplorable conditions? In that case, this game could've been described as a game "dealing with the issues of
and
".
In my opinion, this game does not portray the refugee crisis honestly, whichever one that may be. If anything, it is a slap in the face to those who face the real life hardships and realities of war, and I think it's a shame that the developer's - so it seems - just jumped on the bandwagon in order to get more sales by describing it as such.
Taking a step beyond that description, however, I can say that I did enjoy the graphics.
is set in a vibrant, colourful cyberpunk world, where odd alien like creatures "roam" the land. There are times when the colour just pops out, and there are also times where you will be unable to see things due to darkness.
The only other positive I can find in this game is the music and sound effects. When the aliens cry, you will
that they are crying. It is creepy, scary, and satisfying. If anythng, the developer's really paid attention to the detail of the sounds, but neglected other aspects of the game. That is never good.
While I praise the soundtrack, I do have to say that it was random sometimes. For example, the music was calm and soothing in one second of the game, and in the next, after I walked through a door, it went all synthwavey. Where's the transition?

was developed by Crytek Studios and released by Electronic Arts in March 2011. Four yours earlier, the same developers scored a huge success with the first game in the series, which was well-known at its time of release to be the most demanding pc game ever made. But apart from being a technical masterpiece, pushing graphics to a lever far beyond anything which had been yet achieved, the original
also offered good gunplay in a fairly big theater of operations. While not being without some problems, the game impressed me and so I started playing
with high expectations.
And that's probably exactly where the problems started: from the beginning, I compared this game to its predecessor. And so I expected a gorgeous looking, extremely demanding shooter within a rather open world, allowing for several routes to achieving one's objectives.
definitely managed to impress me on the visual and technical side: visually it offers anything one could wish for, taking into account the game was released over five years ago. The setting has completely shifted from the lush jungle of the first game to an impressive rendering of New York devastated by war. Although visually still impressive, with tons of details and lots of smoke and debris, the urban setting does diminish the large-scale feeling of the first game quite dramatically, and the different levels felt more constricted and definitely a lot smaller.
From a purely technical point of view, this game still stands firm, although it does show that it was a console port, rather than a game originally developed for pc. The controls are less fluid and intuitive, and seem geared towards playing with an xbox controller. This was actually the first first-person shooter I've ever played with my controller – normally, I definitely prefer keyboard and mouse in this type of games. But in this case, it simply offered better and more naturally laid out controls. As far as graphical settings go – often a problem with a game first developed for consoles: they were fine, offering enough possibilites to crank up the eye-candy to stunning levels and giving (just) enough options to scale the settings for those wanting to do so. It's not the most demanding game out there anymore, but it still can tax any medium-range system: don't expect it to run at full HD on the ultra preset with anything less than a recent, fast i3 and a good midrange gpu. Given the fact that the game has been used so often as a benchmark for computer systems and graphics cards, I was slightly disappointed not to find some sort if benchmarking tool included, but that's a very minor issue.
Much more problematic is the complete transformation as far as the actual gameplay goes. Gone are the open areas where there are several, often radically different, routes to one's objectives. Instead,
offers a series of set pieces: medium-scaled area's with primary and (sometimes) secondary objectives with one or two lines of approach. By using the "tactical mode" of your high-tech suit (more about this in a minute), you can scan the battlefield for enemies, supply stashes, but also for "tactical options", such as the ideal route if going for a stealth approach or the way to go if you want to flank the enemy. In other words: the game wants to hold you by the hand as much as possible! While this might be ok in a very linear first-person horror game, where scripted sequences are of the essence, it is in no way desired in a first-person shooter. I often tried to ignore the tactical suggestions, but mostly found out that there were no viable alternative routes, or that another approach than the one suggested almost inevitably resulted in a quick death. And with its horrendous system of saving only at set (and very irregular) waypoints, dying is something you definitely want to avoid in this game.
Fortunately, not all is bad: the story definitely kept my interest throughout the game and often made me persist through a difficult section. It's not a great story – there are a lot of unbelievable plot-twists and too often a mission ends rahter abruptly – but it's better than in most "super human rescues the world from bad guys and aliens"-games. The most interesting aspect of the game is actually the special combat suit (the nanosuit) which you use as the player throughout the game. Just like in the original
this suit offers several modes of operation: strength, armor & cloak – the last one of course ideal for a stealth-approach. Since I like being stealthy, the cloak-mode turned out to be my best friend, but it's also a tad overpowered if used correctly. The nanosuit can be upgraded during the game with energy provided by killing aliens, but those upgrades often felt tucked-on and didn't offer anything really new.
As far as the actual gunplay goes,
surely delivers big time. There are a lot of different, often high-tech weapons out there to try out, and after some playing around with them they proved to be very well balanced and offering more than enough firepower for any chosen playstyle. Especially the energy-based weapons, ideal for mowing down aliens, were great fun to use. In the end, I did enjoy this game, if taken on its own merits: I sneaked up on several guards from behind, killed them with my knife, dashed for cover when I ran out of energy for the cloak mode only to be discovered by an alien who then started to throw emp-grenades at me. Very often I could just hang on in a firefight, having to make split-second decisions in order to survive; at other points, I could move forward at leisure, popping in and out of cloak mode. It was great fun, but it wasn't a gaming experience which I'll remember for years to come.

I give this game a solid 8 out of 10. It's a good game, don't get me wrong, but there are some aspects that i really don't like. First off, the game is just too short. If you don't seek out achievements and/or secrets, you could beat this game in at least 12 hours (with taking breaks).
Second, the New Game+ mode doesn't bring anything new to the table. You just have 2 health instead of 5, and have an outfit you can't change out of. The 2 health aspect of NG+ is just makes the game more frustrating.Which brings me to my next point.
When most bosses (and sometimes lesser foes aswell) can instanly kill you, your game is no longer fun, it is frustrating. which brings me to my next point, the game is just frustrating in some areas. The frustration factor is very apparent in NG+ mode, where all of your progress on a boss could be eliminated because you just couldn't avoid the damage, say, you couldn't dash away from a certain attack because you don't have the chain dash upgrade.
Also, you either have the upgrades you need to survive or you don't. The way to obtain these upgrades is through purchasing them with coins you can collect. But to obtain just ONE of these coins, you need to collect 4 "gearbits" as they're called.So in order to get the chain dash upgrade, which is ESSENTIAL to getting most of the game's secrets, you must first grind out 12 gearbits by finding them in crates, or having scripted enemies drop them. You can't just kill random enemies lke in most games like this, you have to find SCRIPTED enemies, and there is no indication as to which emeies carry them. No outline or demonstration of how to detect them, you just have to come across them on you streamlined travel.
Now for the stuff I thought was good about the game. The fact that heart Machine managed to explain the lore behind the world you are in without words (not counting the monliths that have to be translate outside the game) is pretty amazing. Using only pictures to explain the backstory of the zones you travel through or characters you meet is phenominal.
The combat system is fun to use, relying on timing and quick in-and-out attacks for your sword, and ammo conservation for your ranged weapons. Your weapon of choice is a sword. A lightsaber to be more precise. Your primary attack pattern is a quick, 3 slash combo. There are attacks you can earn using the upgrade system I talked about, charge strike as i will call it, where you hold your attack button and release when the time is right, note you are stationary while in the ready-to-strike stance for this attack, dealing massive damage (5 hit points) to anyting it comes into contact with. You also have two charge related attacks, which I will call "Slash Dash" and "Get the heck away Dash". Slash Dash it activated by dashing and clicking shortly after (dash before slash) you wil charge forward in a straight line, dealing massvie damage to anything caught in you path. Get the heck away Dash is activated by clicking , then dashing shortly after (slash before dash). You will dash forward a short distance and push your target back at a high velocity, deling 3 damage and possibly finshing them off by rocketing them into a wall if they collide with it short into their long flight. You can also get the ability to reflect projectiles which make a LOT of enemies and bosses that much easier.
You can can also get upgrades for your dash ability nothing special just chain dash and projectile destroy dash.
But what about GUNS? Do they have any upgrades? no. no they do not. just increased ammo capacity. that is all.
Along with upgrade that affect you character, there are upgrades that affect your gameplay. You can upgrade your character to unlock a new weapon, the grenade (which has no upgrades) and two more spaces for health packs, helping you last longer in harder fights.
But that's enough ranting, I could go on all day about the quirks of this game. like how the AI is just awful in navigating the map, often colliding into walls, or not even jumping over the simplest of gaps, or how the game needs to educate you on how to find secrets better. Once again, a solid 8 out of 10. Good job with this game Heart Machine.

Let's start with the story.
I went into the game blind and came out of it as clueless as going in. There is some repeating scenes throughout and all dialogues are still frames. An original idea that couldn't translate what the story was trying to convey. Although a bit unengaging, it doesn't break a game for me. I say blind because after playing it for a while a found a mini-doc on youtube made by Vice explaining the motivation of the creator, which put the game in context.
Game type.
It's kinda like Zelda: A Link To The Past with its own style of combat. I say Zelda but it takes inspiration from a few games of the snes era in style and genre. On the surface it can seem like a difficult game but it is mainly because of mechanics. The 3 slash combo is something you should rarely do because it leaves you vulnerable, almost staggered for a second after the last offense. You're best bet is combining shooting and slashing. Slash twice, shoot twice and pirouette is the way to go. It is a timing dance. Hacking and slashing your way in combat will lead to an early grave. Another mechanic that can cause problems is the chain dash ability. It takes practice to master. These mechanics are by design so I don't think they can be seen as flawed. But if they don't irk you in story mode, in horde mode they might bring strained smiles of frustration.
I love the many secrets integrated in the game, but man is that map system awfull.
If you're missing Modules, Tablets, Keys, Outfits or Gearbits good luck. There is no way of knowing if the keys you are missing is hidden up north or out west.
The good.
the world is fun to walk around for the most part and the art is great. The hints that lead to secrets is a nice touch to keep the player alert and the diversity of monster type keeps encounters interesting. The 5 health cap is good to keep the game balanced throughout. I liked having the ability to upgrade the amount of health packs instead of the amount of health.
The Bad.
-Collecting 4 gearbits causes a short "animation" of them fusing into 1 currency. This is unskippable. (there are 186 gearbits)
-If you happen to die after this animation you will have to see it again. There was a particular spot I kept dying, and I kept having to pick up that gearbit.
-Auto-saves (checkpoints) happen every so often (certain areas), so if you die without attaining one you loose everything (secrets) you might have found.
-Camera movement sometimes slid across to a new area if I was close to the side of the screen while in combat.
-Outfits don't say what bonuses they give.
-Switching from keyboard to controller is doable only through the menu (very minor. I played with a controller. If I touched the keyboard it would switch, deactivating the controller.)
-music isn't something I particularly notice in games, which is good. But during some encounters I found it unbearable.
(other than those few encounters I liked the music)
I'll end by saying this is not a bad game. It has some great treasure hunter moments, some beautiful art and some fun battles if you know how to manage them. But the combat system under stress shows its flaws and the fact that overlooked secrets are meant to stay hidden.
I just can't recommend.

Between Pretentious Game and Thomas Was Alone (games that are similar in display, but not exactly in mechanical and narrative choices), I'd say the best bang for your buck would be TWA. I was immensely impressed with the idea of finding identification and empathy... in a bunch of pixels.
I don't want to give a lot away on Thomas Was Alone. That would sort of defeat it's "magic" and "charm", which it has bucketloads of (courtesy of Danny Wallace, a.k.a. Shaun from Assassin's Creed), where a simple but fun platformer requiring the use of multiple blocks to solve puzzles is made all the more touching, thanks to the character and storytelling the narrator provides.
I won't go into depth about EVERYTHING in this game, but I'll still remember Thomas, Claire, Laura, John, Chris, James, and Sarah and they're literally just blocks. But their abilities are so well in tune with their personalities, that you almost believe they're real characters, with real thoughts and relationships towards each other.
Does the story get a little convoluted by introducing a whole new cast of characters for the third act? Yeah. Is the "prequel" a little cheesey? It is. But the strength of Thomas Was Alone comes from it's minimalist graphics, heavy focus on story and character, as well as it's amazing music to convey obvious emotions and thoughts from a gamer. This is a high recommend to any big indie gamers out there.

If i felt more cynical about it i'd call it "wannabe Undertale, except for Satan," but some disjointed plot threads and forced writing here and there don't really make this game an experience I regret having.
This is like the fulfilled promise of two decades of bad Newgrounds games with cool concepts that suffered from being made by a 12 year old. I came in blind, didn't even see the trailer. Once I realized I was playing a horror game of sorts, I expected to get bad creepypasta, and I absolutely got better than that. It's tongue-in-cheek, and while that makes me roll my eyes from time to time, most of the time it works well. Puzzles aren't obtuse, there's an appropriate degree of silliness (ie not too much), and exploring the broken machine is satisfying.
It's definitely not without its flaws. The narrative shines when progressing, but all of the extra information you can get on the side (not just about the player character) feels meaningless to me at best, and complete nonsense at worst. And not that Undertale was the first game to keep track of things across multiple playthroughs, but it feels forced here and not nearly as elegant and meaningful as it was in that game. All the parallels to Undertale do this game a disservice, but they're being drawn for a reason; there are specific lines in Pony Island that made me cringe, they wanted so badly to be as good as Undertale's version of that line.
I wouldn't say it's a must-play, but it's much better than I expected. I'd like to think it says more that it drew me in and made me want to collect every ticket, reveal the whole backstory, etc. than that I was dissatisfied with what I got from doing it. Journey over destination.

Intralism is a fun, colorful, and fast-paced game. The premise is simple: arcs will come down from around the screen, and you use your arrow buttons (or WASD) to eliminate those arcs, making sure they don't reach the middle. Let too many reach the middle? You lose, and have to restart (from the latest checkpoint). The best part? They come down in tune with the music. I'll go over the main pros and cons of this game, and then comment on specific features.
Pros:
Very fun
Fast-paced
Good concept
Great map-making community
Really engaging
Difficult, but not too much so
Cool devs
Trading cards
In-game skins
Catchy music (it's EDM, so may put some people off the game)
Multiplayer support
Runs on potato computers
Easy map-making system
Cons:
Annoying checkpoint system
Community made maps aren't often synced up with music well
Basic settings menu
Hard to see arcs at times
This game is pretty solid, with some cons, but the pros definitely outweigh the cons. The game is really hard at times, and until you get the hang of the game, the first few “built-in” levels are table-slammingly difficult.
Gameplay
This game is *mostly* singleplayer, as there aren’t very many players who play this game to host any servers, and none of my friends own this game too. But that’s just theory as I actually don’t have any friends. The 6 included levels start mostly simple, but then get harder and harder as you unlock the next one. The learning curve for this game is quite steep, despite the simple concept. However, once you get the hang of the game, it gets pretty easy.  What’s really good about the singleplayer is the community workshop, which I’ll touch on in the next part.
However, despite the strangely difficult gameplay, it has some major flaws. Multiple arcs coming from the same direction at the same time can blend in with each other, causing you to lose lives. Colors from the background, the music visualizer, or the huge, pulsing orb in the middle can sometimes make the arcs hard to see. However, despite these design flaws, the gameplay is fine. Just keep your eyes sharp, and these problems shouldn’t be a big deal. Also, don’t worry about lag, I play on a horrible laptop with integrated graphics, and unless I’m in a custom levels with lots of colors and effects, I maintain a solid 60+ frame rate.
Community
This game has a very active (and very Russian) map-making community. There are plenty of maps to choose from in the community workshop, and they range from simple and easy levels for beginners (Gorillaz - On Melancholy Hill) to tougher levels for more experienced players (Caravan Palace - Lone Diggers). Most of the maps on the workshop are basic, with just a simple map, and nothing special. This is to be expected as the map-making system is really easy to use, even if you aren’t the best at the game. However, there are many maps (Galantis - No Money) that are simple in gameplay, but have breathtaking effects and colors that must’ve taken many hours to create; hats off to whoever created that level, it’s great.
Music
Most of the music in the game is EDM and dance music, with some pop songs. If you are a fan of this type of music, great. You’ll definitely enjoy the game. However, if you’re more of a fan of rock, metal, jazz, or even rap, it’s tough to find levels appealing to your music taste. There are only a few rock songs on there, and even less metal. However, this shouldn’t put you off the game, as even if you’re not the biggest fan of EDM and dance (like me!), you can still thoroughly enjoy the game.
Multiplayer
I don’t know much about the multiplayer, as I’ve only tried out hosting a server by myself. However, the core multiplayer system seems fun, and if you can get your friends to shell a couple bucks to get this game, you can have a competitive music duel to try to get the highest score (or work together for the Steam achievements). I won’t dwell too long as here, as in my opinion, this is a game that most people play alone.
Level editor
One of my favorite parts of the game, the level editor is simple, but still allows you to create awesome levels. Making a level is as simple as hitting “record”, playing a .ogg file (only ogg files are allowed), and pressing the arrow buttons as if you were actually playing. To test the level out, you can just go to “play” on the menu, and select the third category. There are other more complex methods to make your level more custom with effects and colors, but I have no clue how to even start doing something like that. It’s best to consult the “guides” section for that.
Overall, this game is really fun, a good time waster, and super engaging. It really gets your heart going, and is incredibly fast-paced. Despite some minor annoying problems that the game has, it’s really easy to see through them and have a great time with Intralism. And for that price tag? Get it. Those 2-3 dollars you spend on this game will translate to many hours of fun gameplay.

There are plenty of video lessons included, complete with "graded" practice tracks to help you with the techniques. Songs are learned through a system that auto-adjusts difficulty depending on how well you are doing, and the Riff Repeater allows the user to stop, slow down, and loop segments of the music (even the entire song) to help master difficult passages.

Ever since its release on Steam and the latest updates (balance patches & Denizens of Shim'zar) this game really packs a punch and the constantly growing community is there to prove it.
With an awesome blend of amazing pixel-art and high resolution backgrounds and effects , a huge cast of characters, spells and monsters and all of this with a highly fleshed out backstory,
this game doesn't only look good, it plays like a hyper-modern game of alien chess.
Games are turn-based, with each turn limited to 90 seconds.
Players start out with their faction's general on the game board, 5 cards each and 2 or 3 mana crystals (depends if your the starting player or not) which can be used to play cards.
Each turn a player gains an additional mana crystal with all of them being restored each turn.
When a player finishes a turn the game automatically draws a card for that player.
Generals have 25 attack points and 25 health points, which can be altered using spells and artifacts. The game is won by depleting the opposing general's health points.
The 'main' game mode is Ranked Ladder, where you can climb in rank by winning games or, after gaining a certain rank, falling down a rank by losing games.
At the end of the month you get rewards based on the highest rank you reached.
Players can buy new cards to gain extra spells, monsters (called minions in-game) and the newly added Shim'zar battle pets with spirit orbs.
These orbs can be bought with money or with the in-game earned gold, that can be gained by completing quests and winning games.
Alongside that gold you can also earn spirit, with which players can craft new cards to add to their collection.
Decks are composed of 40 cards, no more, no less. This often proves to be a difficult exercise because a player needs to find the right balance between spells, artifacts and minions.
Although new players start with the same base cards as anyone else, by collecting new cards two decks from the same faction will rarely be the same.
There are 6 factions, each with their own spells, minions, strenghts and weaknesses. It's up to the player to find out which ones become a favourite. the best way to find out is through playing.
Aside from faction-exclusive cards there are additional 'neutral' cards that can be used in any deck. Of course you can create as many decks for a faction as you want.
Players can change faction for each game as many times as they like, except when playing in The Gauntlet.
The Gauntlet is a game mode that lets players choose a faction out of 3 options and then pick 30 cards + a general. The objective of this mode is quite simple: win as many games with your newly picked deck. The more games you win, the better your rewards at the end (a Gauntlet run is over when you lose 3 games).
Because turns are timed, a game can become quite difficult to manage the longer you have been playing. When a game has been going on for several turns, players often have lots of minions on the battlefield, and thus, lots of options to consider.
Like timed a game of chess, fast thinking is necessary, but sometimes your turn is over before you could make all the moves you wanted. Which, in some cases, can be a gamebreaker.
In my opinion drawing cards isn't very well balanced, after about 7/8 turns a player often has only one or no cards at all to play.
Although there are many cards that have effects to allow a player to draw additional cards, to me this feels like something that has to be cranked up a bit.
The game's outcome heavily depends on the player's knowledge of the card lore. The better you know your own cards and the cards that the other player might have, the better you can work out a strategy.
But then again, nothing is certain because sometimes a game can easily change from a player having the upperhand to that same player being defeated in the next turn.
Even though I don't have that much time to play, I often find myself returning quite often to complete the daily quest and play 1 or 2 online matches.
Factions are well-balanced, and my favourites are Vanar & Abyssian.
The game looks nice, is fun (although sometimes very frustrating) and highly addictive.
Be warned :)

NORTH is a interesting story exploration game where you have to figure things out for yourself. The game tries to relate to current issues of the contemporary refugee crisis. I am unsure if the game really sticks to this issue well throughout the game though
This game seems to be according to the story as you play throughout the game. But as I got nearer the end of the game I felt like the whole game sort of forgot about the main issue the game was tryign to promote. Being a refugee in the city and having to deal with these new and weird experiences that you may come across.
The story of the game is rather interesting, but doesn't really tell the story in way that other games do. Throughout the game you will find letters that will tell the story and the story as the character you are playing as. This is a rather interesting way of portraying your game, that is if you are able to re-read these letters that you have collected. This wouldn't be a issue if the letters you find give you a background to the things that you must perform in order to progress. I mean I have found the letter, you would of thought that this person would keep these letter. Apparently not.
This issue with the letters also leads to another point that the game suffers from a lot more than it needs to be. This is the way that the game doesn't really help you at all, making it very unclear on what you have to do. I guess this can increase your game time in the game but walking around aimlessly not knowing what to do is a major flaw in this game. Possibly giving hints would be nice if the player is stuck at a certain point in the game.
The graphics of this game are rather bright and really do work well, although it doesn't seem to be as fancy as some of the other games on steam nowadays, and sometimes feel a bit flat. The game can be really dark at some points though, this does mean that there are some things that you can't see that you are suppose to walk upon such as doors and stairs that you are required to walk through in order to progress. The animation of the characters you play as is rather odd, it does seem like your character sort of floats from place to place instead of actually walking like normal people do nowadays.

The dodge/ Reaction attack mechanics- Truly adds a sense of control for the character while  being attacked and moving to evade oncoming fire, and its satisfying as hell to stop an enemies attack and return one in kind in one move.

The Bad:
AI- The AI of your partner in this game is like an eternal punishment consisting of stepping on legos every 30 seconds for the rest of your life, as well as getting a cheese grater forced into your anal cavity everytime you blink or breathe by a demented midget clown in a pink tutu, whos simultaneously tea bagging you.

What can I say about For Honor that is fair and yet informative?
I'll start off by saying the concept for the combat in online multiplayer matches is refreshing and a needed relief from games like League and PUBG. The combat is also intuitive *NOT EASY* but, once you get the concept it becomes a matter of skill most of the time. It is fun, in a basic sense, and at times rewarding when you're fighting 1vX and triumph. The gear progress is a very steep pay to win but its locked behind level grinding (albeit a short grind), but you don't need the gear to win at all. And the advantage is only noticeable when your entire team has literally no gear and the opposite team has max gear.
That all being said, it's UBISH*t and if anything has been proven lately from this developer it is that they literally do not care about the game and polishing the painfully noticeable problems with the game in many areas seems like a pipe dream at this point. It has been nine months or so since the release of the game and there still exist day one glitches, imbalances, and oversights that would have otherwise closed a game down by now. For example, the centurion (prior to the shaman) was unbearable to fight against. With nearly an infinite combo that no class can beat, your left hoping the other player misses the staggers, now the shaman is the reigning champ of bs. Wall clipping, very poor server hosting, and terrible AI team mates which are put into the game to compensate for dropped players due to the utterly game breaking server issues suffered EVERDAY day of game play, not counting the easycheat issues all make up a very frustrating experience.
The story is mediocre, and feels like it was haphazardly put together. If none of the things I assume about the game are due to negligence then it is because of the corporate bs that went into the game.
There is hope for the game though and it'll be pretty cool if they fix a lot of the issues players will discover with little effort. For everything I said is wrong with the game I'll probably be online tonight and playing multiplayer with my brothers, mainly because this the only game we have together but also because it can be fun to win with your friends on this game.

Duelyst is a free-to-play collectible card game and turn-based strategy hybrid developed by Counterplay games.
Pros:
1) Nicely done pixel art, animations are fluid
2) Tactical gameplay makes minion positioning just as important as what card to play.
3) Generous giving of Epics and Legendaries. You can open 1 legendary in 2 packs in a row even if you just open 1 pack per day. Allows for lots of Spirit for crafting the better cards.
4) Quest allow even beginning players to get gold just by playing and not requiring you to always win. Gold is gained faster if you win of course.
5) Has decent Basic removal, dispel and displacement cards for the neutral and Faction set meaning even if your opponent has a better card you can still have some chance to save yourself.
6) 6 Factions each with a unique playstyle and mechanics. Each faction has a General with an ability called a bloodborn spell that that has a 2 turn cooldown after use until the late game where its reduced to every turn. Each faction has 2 general each with their own bloodborn spell allowing for a preferred playstyle.
7) All consmetics can be crafted from spirit.
Cons:
1) Lack of a casual mode means that you can only play ladder which can be bad after a certain point for new players as you can get matched up with more experianced players who have more effective and synergistic cards.
2) Keys for Crates can only be bought with real money luckily these contain mostly cosmetics that you can craft with Spirit.
Conclusion: Duelyst is a free to play tactical turn based collecting card game with lots of depth and strategy. A decent chance to get higher rarity cards such as legendaries (around every 4 packs or so from the core set and every 6 packs from the expansion) allow even one pack opening per day to yield a decent collection after about 2 wks to a month. I recommend this game to anyone looking for a different take in the CCG genre.

The Basics: Very pretty disaster porny first person shooter with a cyborg suit
Previous Time Spent: 27 minutes
Expectation of learning Curve: low
Why I bought this: Extremely cheap steam sale (long enough ago that I don't remember it)
First Impressions: This is a good looking game, but my first impressions were marred by expecting it to be fairly boring/boilerplate. I found myself frustrated by the long, live-action CNN/Fox News intro, and the standard tutorial which slowly unlocks controls. I did find the submarine escape in the beginning kind of thrilling, but I ultimately found it to be more annoying due to loss of control than anything else. For a game that seems to be really about a cool cyborg killing small squads of soldiers, it spends a lot of time pretending that the audience is interested in it's story.
My 3 hours: I spent the entire 3 hour playthrough in the singleplayer campaign, figuring that a game this old would probably end up not well-supported on the multiplayer front. The game takes place in 2023 in NYC, with the main character as a marine who takes on the mantle of a crazy cyborg (nanosuit) suit of power armor. This power armor confers a bunch of special abilities to the player, including cloaking, resistance to damage, and seemingly extreme strength. In a lot of ways, it plays like a more violent, sprawling version of Deus Ex: Human Revolution.
Much of the gameplay is focused on advancing from checkpoint to checkpoint while dealing with environmental hazards and squads of soldiers. These challenges escalated in a pretty satisfying way during my 3 hours with the game, and did a fairly good job of introducing the player to new tactics/ideas in order to surpass them. The bread and butter of it is often finding cool places to hide/shoot soldiers from, while taking cover when appropriate, and sometimes turning invisible to feel like the Predator. The main character feels extremely powerful in the suit, bringing me back to old-school shooter games and the feeling of being a one man army.
The story that's told in the game is one of an alien virus and a harsh crackdown, and much of it feels pretty standard issue, but some of the environmental storytelling great. The scene that immediately follows the opening, allows the player to slowly acclimate themselves to a New York city that appears to be under martial law, between audio records on laptops, and the horrible remains of living people. It then allows the player to slowly make their way from Battery Park and head north. The game is at it's best when it's providing interesting combat challenges, or allowing one to feel like a tourist in a believable near future New York.
My Highlight: For me, the greatest joy I had with the game came fairly early, and is pictured above, a mix of combat and infiltration set in Castle Clinton, bringing me back to one of the early missions of my beloved Deus Ex. As you can see above, the historical marker is even legible, and the attention to detail shown in the environment conveys a clear sense of place. The game introduces the stealth mechanic there, which is pretty fun, and allowed me to feel like The Predator.
My Verdict:I generally kinda liked this game, but much of the joy I got out of it, I think I got because it reminded me of things I liked better. It made me think of Deus Ex and Half Life 2 the most, between the sprawling levels, the near-superpowers given by nanites, and the environmental storytelling. I can't strongly recommend it, but I think it's a game that is good at what it intends to do .

Hi there! I might not have a lot of hours at the time of writing this, but I've both watched and played the game by now. And I definitely recommend this game, particularly so with a friend! Warning, a bit long below I'm sorry.
First, I'll name off all the bad points, so we can get those pesky buggers out of the way!
The Camera hates you. You have to play with the options a bit - I definitely recomend cranking that field and aiming point of view as high as you can go - and sometimes it's just outright dumb. I think I died around 16 times on Amateur, the easy mode, in Chris' route. It was basically a run away from thing and they kept changing the friggin' camera angle twenty times, inverting the controls each friggin' time. JEEZ. It's my #1 beef of the game.
What's Inventory space? Your inventory space is well... very small. Unless you're like me, constantly needing herbs because you keep getting hurt, or you use up all your ammo because you're dumb at shooters and you miss all the time, you're probably going to be fighting for space in your inventory. One solution is to just not pick up any gun you don't really like to use - like say you're running melee, you don't need the sniper rifle dude - but honestly what kind of solution is that? So prepare to try to figure out what guns you're going to keep ammo for.
Stagger times are real. So if you get hit by a zombie, it takes eight years to get back up, and that's really frustrating when you have like five of them that manage to get right in front of you and eat your face. Or when some stupid little robot explodes, and it takes your forever to get back up and you're on limited time. I mean, it could be worse, but sometimes it's very sluggish to react, and that makes it difficult to enjoy the combat often enough.
So we're done with the bad! Onwards with the good!
I love, love, love the storyline. Playing one campaign will give you a general idea of the story, but so much is left in the air. As you play more campaigns, you start to understand the story more and more. And if you manage to complete all four? Well the story comes together in it's full, glorious picture. The characters are fun, for the most part - looking at you Chris - and it's actually fun to listen to them in other languages. The story has a lot of depth surprisingly enough, requiring at least a large amount of attention to catch every nuance. In fact, you'll see hints of the other campaigns in the one you're in, even in the background! Can you find where it all intersects?
Co-op. This game is CO-OP. Every campaign, you can play with a friend! And that's twice the fun! Honestly, the fact that you can co-op is really amazing with this game - in fact I even recomend to play this with someone else more then by yourself! You get to totally have fun with your friends, well most of the time, and each character has differences. For example, you'll see and do different things as Helena then you do as Leon. Sure you might be in the same campaign, but there still is individual flavours for co-op players and that's fantastic. And it actually doesn't take three years to connect to play together.
Action, Horror and Zombies. You heard me. Most people would look at me and go 'this game isn't horror' and I want to shot them down. So an undead corpse losing all their skin, transforming into a meaty beast that will lynch you and tear your body to pieces isn't horrifying? Or how about a being that regenerates and comes out of the grates and if it catches you, shoves it's tongue in your face, carving it out for it's babies? Yeah. That is bloody horrifying. It has some jumpscares, but the game isn't filled with them. And sometimes, they'll just straight up fake you out, making you think there's a jumpscare but there isn't. It's very action-oriented, I won't deny that, but to me, that's what makes it even more fun. Like each time there's a split path in the campaign? I'm scared. I'm honestly scared because sure I have guns, sure I can defend myself, but what will I encounter? What new thing will try to kill me next? I don't even have my friend with me to save me if I screw up... and that is truly, what's so horrorfying.
MELEE. The executions are top notch, and melee is actually viable. You don't have to sit there, and gun everything down - you can walk right in and spin kick them and watch them explode when you elbow drop them. It's so much fun to melee, and they even have a stamina system in place to make sure you don't abuse it - and if you go over it? you pay the consenquences. It gives you options to play the game, and that is what is very fun about the melee system. Oh, and the kickass execution cutscenes.
All the pretties. The art looks fantastic. The music is great and thematic and not super intrusive. You get wet when you enter the water. You can't run when you're in water. Water looks like water. I could go on forever, but honestly I've gone on long enough don't you think?
So basically, I love this game. It's not everyone's cup of tea, but I would definitely say at least go watch a video or two of it before buying it for yourself, make sure it's a game you want to touch. I definitely don't regret it!

If you love an almost cinematic art house feel in a game, this is great. If you don't, you will hate it, just like all the reviews of people complaining about a lack of direction, objectives and explanation. I'm not passing judgement on them, but they didn't like the game, so if you are looking for something a little more structured in that sense, you will not like it either.
That being said, it is very linear, and while you can choose the order of how you tackle the main objective, there really is only that objective and one way that it can be achieved.
The worst thing about the game was the controls. I am on a Mac, and the Mac version had frequent problems with the mouse - there were several points it became broken and unresponsive (playable, but only just) and also the mouse speed was not what I was used to. There were also parts that, seeing other people's screenshots and playthroughs, were not rendering right, like the Doctors area.
But all these things were not going to stop me from finishing it and I must say it was enjoyable. This game is what you would define in music as a "concept album", and if you like that idea, then this might be a fun one for you. If not, don't get it.

When your game has a message, a valid one, that you want to put across, whether you're telling it literally or in an abstracted fashion, the message should not be distracted by confusing, unclear gameplay objectives. If frustration and confusion are emotions you want the player to experience as part of that message, find another way to convey it that doesn't negatively impact the gameplay. If you don't, your message may not be heard at all.
Such is the case with North.

+ Interesting surreal world to explore
+ Very unique thematic ideas explored through the story. Essentially you are an immigrant from some far away horrible place, and you are to gain asylum in this foreign city while writing messages home to your family about your experience. You end up finding out that this strange utopian society is not as great as you imagined,
+ The game environments are so strange and alien that it drives you forward with intrigue of what may come next, and the letters you write do a great job of slowly unraveling the story and helping you understand what is happening.
+ Great music and use of ambient sounds throughout the game
- Fairly short, the game takes around 30mins to an hour to complete.
- You are unable to re-read the the messages that have important clues as to how to progress or solve some of the challenges.

In this game, for the measly sum of 79p, you can play as a Popefly. A POPEFLY.
What, you want to know about the gameplay? Well, fine. But… Popefly. Come on.
From the makers of the absurdly popular ‘Timberman’, Fly O’Clock is an incredibly addictive game. Your job (and you only have one) is to jump over the hands as they speed around the watch. The more you jump, the faster the hands go, and the higher the chance that you get sliced into tiny fly chunks.
I should probably add that I’m terrible at this game. My best score is 85, and the achievements go up to 400 (please present yourself in the comments below so that I can personally congratulate you if you achieved this).
The graphics aren’t much to look at but you do unlock various different vaguely adorable flying creatures as you level up, including a bee, and some - well, whatever-they-ares.
For the most part, it’s a fun distraction, with two elements; beating your own score in singleplayer mode, and upping your rank by beating people in multiplayer mode (either via online multiplayer or local co-op). Plus hats.
The singleplayer mode invokes that *just one more* feeling, because next time, for sure, you feel you’ll jump that little bit better, that little bit quicker, and hit another high score.
Multiplayer on the other hand, feels like it needs some work. For a start you might not find a game (it took me an hour or so of checking on and off before I could); occasionally you’ll get smushed when no smushing should have occurred, and sometimes you’ll click and you might not jump. The easiest way to win is to take your time, because the more you jump, the faster the hands go, and the more likely those evil watch hands are to bring their slicey wrath upon you.
All in all, for the price, why not. What have you got to lose apart from the rest of your evening and your dignity in front of random internet strangers?

Black ops 3 is overall a good game, albeit a bit complicated. It is definetly not for everyone, but if you liked the previous black ops games, you will likely enjoy this one as it has the same soul
The story in this installment of the Black ops story ultimately does not really connect to the two previous installment except for a few refrences here and there that most won't notice. The story in this game does however follow the theme of messing with the human mind that the last two games featured. This campaign centers around the struggles of future military combat where soldiers have been augmented with robotic body parts and brain implants. Into the later parts of the story, your character uses there brain upgrade to probe the mind and/or memories of those that have information they need, and gets infected with a "virus" artificial intelligence. This is a very interesting and mind boggling story thats worth investing extra thought into what it all means, and has theory worth twist ending.
Black ops 3 adds to the ever changing multiplayer experience that call of duty is becoming by making the addition of specialist characters and a fluid movement system. The specialist characters just enough to the game to be noticeable while not being too overbearing change to the formula. As for the fluid movement system, they have added thrust jumping, slinding, and wall running. The additon of these extra movement options changes the way game is played for those who like the run and gun way of playing while at the same time discourages camping.
Overall, the way that zombies is played in this game has not been changed much. You are able to unlock and add attachments to most guns in zombies which is helpful, but not required to play well. Also, instead of adding multiple different perks to this game, they added only one new one and supplimented the change with gobblegums. Gobblegums act as a kind temporary perk or one time use perk that was a welcome addition in my opinion.
The zombies experience of black ops 3 picks up right where black ops 2 left off with the alernate timeline of Origins, albeit with a seemingly unrelated story. Starting with Shadows of Evil where are group of murderers are manipulated by the Shadow man into freeing a long forgotten evil from what binds them. After righting the wrongs that they were responsible for and sealing the shadow man away inside the summoning key, they are intrusted with the safe keeping of the summoning key
The giant starts out with Richtofen just meeting up with the rest of the Origins crew at the Der Riese facility right after the original timelines Richtofen teleported Dr.Maxis and Samantha Maxis. Origins Richtofen kills the original timeline richtofen and in doing so changes the course of this dimensions timeline. After activating the flytrap, followed by lighting the Beacon, the Origins crew "borrows" a giant robot from the facility and heads for Austria.
There is a lot more explored with the purchase of the DLC.

Before starting my review I want to mention that I have been a fan of Fly O'Clock for 5 years now, been to FOREVER ENTERTAINMENT S.A. at Comiket 3 times (C81 / C85 / C87) for Fly O'Clock (nothing Fly O'Clock related at C83), I own the doujins including Fly O'Clockdise EX (not sold) etc. So I am quite an engaged fan.
I'll just jump straight to usual criteria when reviewing a Visual Novel. Minor spoilers below.
Graphics & Chara Design: 10/10.
If you liked the doujins, you will love the game. FOREVER ENTERTAINMENT S.A.'s work is great as always. There isn't much to write about this really, just look at couple screenshots and you'll make your own opinion in seconds.
Animations: 10/10
The e-mote engine makes characters really lively and provides a huge added value compared to a classic 2D visual novel. Scenes are never static; there is always movement which is great. And... the game has a chest bounciness slider.
H-Scenes: 9/10
There are 3 H-Scenes in Fly O'Clock. All three are really well animated and fully voiced. These 3 scenes are really long too and accounts for a solid 25% of your total playtime. The way the fly and the bee behave is in-line with the doujins.
If you get the game on Steam (all-age version); you'll miss them and frankly the game lose almost all its value without H-Scenes... which brings me to my next point.
Plot/Story/Character Development: 3/10
The weakest point of FLY O'CLOCK. There is barely any plot (didn't really expect any, still), everything is introduced way too quickly. You barely know anything about the background of the characters, the reader doesn't have the time to feel immersed and love characters... and the MC is really dull.
The first H-Scene is introduced poorly. You jump from a "We are like a family!" to "I'm in heat let's have s*x now" in... 15 minutes of gameplay. The whole game is rather short (about 6~7 hours). In time equivalent inside the story, that's about one week. The game has 8 chapters and one chapter is roughly one day. And in a single week characters evolve way too quickly which kinda ruins everything. The pace overall is just really bad.
Voices: 9/10
Voice acting is great and each seiyuu really matches well the personality of the fly and the bee (can't really comment for others since they don't speak much). H-scenes are voiced too which is great.
Music: 7/10
The music works well with the game but isn't anything special or memorable. There aren't many BGMs but since the game is short that's kind of normal.
Translation: 7/10
The English itself is decent (albeit a bit rough sometimes). The localization itself (when compared to original Korean text) could use some polish. If you don't understand Korean you will not notice that part however. Note that the game is also localized in Chinese (but I don't speak Chinese, so not reviewing that part).
Software/Polish: 10/10
The game is amazingly well presented, the software offers all the usual features you'd expect for a VN (Quick Save/Load, Autoplay, Autoread speed etc.); can adjust the volume of the voice of each character separatly, can save & comment when saving, 80 save slots (not really necessary but w/e). UI and Text language can be changed on the Fly O'Clock.  Heh, get it? It is also possible to display the text in two languages at once (i.e. English and Korean) which is really great if you are learning. Didn't experience any crash or any issue. Flawless.
OVERALL: 8/10
FLY O'CLOCK isn't a "game" or even Visual Novel for everyone. If you are looking for a long VN with an actual plot, this isn't for you. If you like cute flies and bees and want to play something short, enjoy couple nice H-scenes, then this is it. If you are a fan of FOREVER ENTERTAINMENT S.A.'s work you'll want to get the game no matter what.
While the game is short, its price is small too. The game doesn't have any replay value beside H-scenes3 (No different route, no choices to pick).
Eagerly waiting for Fly O'Clock 2

Black ops 3 is overall a good game, albeit a bit complicated. It is definetly not for everyone, but if you liked the previous black ops games, you will likely enjoy this one as it has the same soul
The story in this installment of the Black ops story ultimately does not really connect to the two previous installment except for a few refrences here and there that most won't notice. The story in this game does however follow the theme of messing with the human mind that the last two games featured. This campaign centers around the struggles of future military combat where soldiers have been augmented with robotic body parts and brain implants. Into the later parts of the story, your character uses there brain upgrade to probe the mind and/or memories of those that have information they need, and gets infected with a "virus" artificial intelligence. This is a very interesting and mind boggling story thats worth investing extra thought into what it all means, and has theory worth twist ending.
Black ops 3 adds to the ever changing multiplayer experience that call of duty is becoming by making the addition of specialist characters and a fluid movement system. The specialist characters just enough to the game to be noticeable while not being too overbearing change to the formula. As for the fluid movement system, they have added thrust jumping, slinding, and wall running. The additon of these extra movement options changes the way game is played for those who like the run and gun way of playing while at the same time discourages camping.
Overall, the way that zombies is played in this game has not been changed much. You are able to unlock and add attachments to most guns in zombies which is helpful, but not required to play well. Also, instead of adding multiple different perks to this game, they added only one new one and supplimented the change with gobblegums. Gobblegums act as a kind temporary perk or one time use perk that was a welcome addition in my opinion.
The zombies experience of black ops 3 picks up right where black ops 2 left off with the alernate timeline of Origins, albeit with a seemingly unrelated story. Starting with Shadows of Evil where are group of murderers are manipulated by the Shadow man into freeing a long forgotten evil from what binds them. After righting the wrongs that they were responsible for and sealing the shadow man away inside the summoning key, they are intrusted with the safe keeping of the summoning key
The giant starts out with Richtofen just meeting up with the rest of the Origins crew at the Der Riese facility right after the original timelines Richtofen teleported Dr.Maxis and Samantha Maxis. Origins Richtofen kills the original timeline richtofen and in doing so changes the course of this dimensions timeline. After activating the flytrap, followed by lighting the Beacon, the Origins crew "borrows" a giant robot from the facility and heads for Austria.
There is a lot more explored with the purchase of the DLC.

Seeing lots of negative reviews; I have to say, I'm enjoying this game.  It doesn't hold your hand, which the current generation of FPS fans seem to want anymore.  It took me about 8 hours of gameplay before I could actually perform well enough in multiplayer to not be a liability to my team...but damn, does it ever feel good to kick äss now.
What to expect if you start now:
You're going to die alot.
You'll be matched against players who have been doing this for a long time.
You WILL get your äss handed to you, over and over; there's no magical way to git gud early.
The things you learn while getting your äss handed to you repeatedly by better players will help you learn, if you stick with it and be observant.
You're going to have a blast whacking people with the battlefield implement of your choice, shoulder-checking them off bridges and cliffs, and generally stomping nuts.
To clarify some things I wish I'd known a long time ago:
There is a PVE storyline, but it seems designed to give you a brief intro to the three factions and the playstyles of some of their units.  If you really don't want to start your online play against human players, with their propensity for cheesing the most broken $hit in the game non-stop, you can play the same modes against bots, with your results helping the battle map between the factions as well.  This will give you a better chance to get the feel of the game's mechanics before going up against humans.
Customization in this game both is, and isn't, as meaningful as one might expect, if you look at this from an RPG perspective; some of the tweaks you can make via gear are very small, and some are more meaningful, depending on the stat/s you want to buff.  There's some trade-off required here, though, as you aren't going to buff one stat to crazy values without having another nerfed at least a little.
Visual customization, however, is pretty impressive.  If you like the idea of making your knight look unique, you'll find a lot of options for this, and those options only expand the longer you play said character.  Gear can be transmogged as well, so you're not stuck deciding between good stats or good looks.
The F2P model is great, IMHO; the in-game currency is earned in-game, as is the gear.  You can spend your currency (of which you can purchase more with real cash) on armor/weapon upgrades, transmog, or to purchase other visual tweaks for your knight.  It can also be spent on unlocking other characters, although this is really inexpensive, IMHO, and I only actually enjoy one of the characters I unlocked as much as the starter knight.
You'll notice I keep saying 'knight'.  Yes, there are barbarians and ninja-types as well, but I'm here to kill saracens and chew bubblegum, and while there (unfortunately) aren't any saracens in the game, the red team will do nicely.
TL;DR: You're gonna die a lot early on, but if you grow a spine and learn from your deaths instead of crying about matchmaker, you'll git gud and have a lot of fun!

Black ops 3 is overall a good game, albeit a bit complicated. It is definetly not for everyone, but if you liked the previous black ops games, you will likely enjoy this one as it has the same soul
The story in this installment of the Black ops story ultimately does not really connect to the two previous installment except for a few refrences here and there that most won't notice. The story in this game does however follow the theme of messing with the human mind that the last two games featured. This campaign centers around the struggles of future military combat where soldiers have been augmented with robotic body parts and brain implants. Into the later parts of the story, your character uses there brain upgrade to probe the mind and/or memories of those that have information they need, and gets infected with a "virus" artificial intelligence. This is a very interesting and mind boggling story thats worth investing extra thought into what it all means, and has theory worth twist ending.
Black ops 3 adds to the ever changing multiplayer experience that call of duty is becoming by making the addition of specialist characters and a fluid movement system. The specialist characters just enough to the game to be noticeable while not being too overbearing change to the formula. As for the fluid movement system, they have added thrust jumping, slinding, and wall running. The additon of these extra movement options changes the way game is played for those who like the run and gun way of playing while at the same time discourages camping.
Overall, the way that zombies is played in this game has not been changed much. You are able to unlock and add attachments to most guns in zombies which is helpful, but not required to play well. Also, instead of adding multiple different perks to this game, they added only one new one and supplimented the change with gobblegums. Gobblegums act as a kind temporary perk or one time use perk that was a welcome addition in my opinion.
The zombies experience of black ops 3 picks up right where black ops 2 left off with the alernate timeline of Origins, albeit with a seemingly unrelated story. Starting with Shadows of Evil where are group of murderers are manipulated by the Shadow man into freeing a long forgotten evil from what binds them. After righting the wrongs that they were responsible for and sealing the shadow man away inside the summoning key, they are intrusted with the safe keeping of the summoning key
The giant starts out with Richtofen just meeting up with the rest of the Origins crew at the Der Riese facility right after the original timelines Richtofen teleported Dr.Maxis and Samantha Maxis. Origins Richtofen kills the original timeline richtofen and in doing so changes the course of this dimensions timeline. After activating the flytrap, followed by lighting the Beacon, the Origins crew "borrows" a giant robot from the facility and heads for Austria.
There is a lot more explored with the purchase of the DLC.

Lara Croft, the protagonist in Tomb Raider, has become a sort of unwitting spokesperson for Eidos' new computer adventure. As the cover girl for just about every hard copy gaming magazine this year, this globe-trotting, gun-happy lass had become the matron saint of a new revolution in 3D gaming before the title even hit the shelves. But does the game really live up to all the buildup? Well, seeing is believing when it comes to Tomb Raider, and playing the game with the Rendition or 3Dfx chip, which are sure to find a home soon in every serious gamer's computer tower (a supportive patch will be available online for these), should almost be a prerequisite. Featuring several stunningly rendered 3D worlds and many a cliff-hanging moment, Tomb Raider makes gamers pay for the whole seat, even though they only need the edge.
As mentioned above, in Tomb Raider you play Lara Croft, a female Doc Savage who, tired of her wealthy English upbringing, has decided that dangerous adventuring is more her cup of tea. So she abandons a life of crustless cucumber sandwiches and piano lessons, eventually meeting a wealthy tycoon who hires her to retrieve a single artifact from a ruined temple in South America. After getting the artifact, you find out that the tycoon has sicked a bunch of her henchmen on you, and that the original piece you were sent in to retrieve is one of three hidden in various unplundered tombs around the world.
Your adventures take place in several "seven wonders" scenarios, from Egyptian sphinxes, to Greek temples, to Atlantis (what game would be complete without it?), each with distinct puzzles and traps to negotiate. Also Lara = H O T A F <3

Pros:
Split Screen Multiplayer
Tight, satisfying gameplay
Gorgeous Art (Perhaps not something for everyone, but the screenshots will tell you the art style and if you like it, that's the kind of amazing environments you'll find) and Soundtrack that fits the ambience
Very hard, but not so hard as to be just frustrating
Save system, when taken advantage of, that is useful and fair (and once you understand how it works it is reliable)
Large list of upgrades that are all reasonably achievable (I doubt you can get all the gun upgrades on one playthrough without getting all the currency bits, but most people will only use 2-3 guns, which is manageable)
Hard to 100% but definitely something you can do (not achievements, I mean in-game collectibles)
Established background lore to back up the environment and characters, albeit hard to gather
Non-linear, you can start at any of the cardinal directions (except for the South, which is blocked until you finish the other three for both story and gameplay reasons, it's harder than the other directions by a bit), it is recommended to start in the East by many but it's up to you
Cons:
Local multiplayer has a few issues, several bugs when moving etc that would require significant work to find all of them. It's a tad annoying, but overall it isn't enough to dent your enjoyment, but they are there (mostly in the form of occasionally getting stuck as the second player or randomly falling off passages to another area for no reason).

Just wanted to add a review for this game to say that it's probably my favorite game released in the last 5 or so years. I don't like the way most modern games' systems feel, especially concerning combat, and I've played many of the most hyped-up games of recent times (Bloodbourne, Doom, ..), and this is the first one in a long time that I *really* enjoyed. The oldschool style combat mechanics centered around movement and dodging instead of knowledge of animation frames and invincibility frames is super refreshing (I'm a little disappointed they actually added i-frames to the dodge move later on). This is a game that's easy to learn but hard to master; you will know immediately how to use all the abilities and what you need to do, but to learn to actually be able to do it - that is, to execute on it - may take you quite some time, instead of cryptically learning the arbitrary rules of which animation frames do what and "levelling up" i.e. increasing in-game numbers to make the game easier - i.e. in every respect exactly how it's supposed to be. It also has an absolutely fantastic art style and visual design with some amazing visual story telling (that never gets in the way of the gameplay) and extremely atmospheric music.

The game attempts to be vague by forgoing voiced or written dialogue by exposing story elements via slideshows in speech bubbles. The beautiful pixel art tinged in varying hues helps separate different regions. Cutscenes, though beautifully rendered in the same art, continues its trend of vagueness by displaying imagery of the Drifter's dark past, shadowy figures (that may or may not be caused by the Drifter's ailing condition), and destruction. It fails to grab the player's attention
but the plot was never its strongest suit. Combat, however, requires a methodical approach consisting of quick strikes from the Drifter's sword, careful ammo management of his different arsenal of firearms and bombs, precise dodges, and careful prioritizitaion between enemies. Ammo is replenished by melee attacks, thus balancing combat by forcing you to switch between fighting styles. Abilities can be learned or upgraded by collecting gearbits hidden around the world. Encounters get tense when confronted by multiple enemies to the point that it's overwhelming, but deaths are mostly fair and are usually your fault. Controls are responsive but the game's dash mechanic needs precise button presses to execute perfectly. With enough practice, infinite dashing can be achieved. This game provides a good challenge for casuals, but a true challenge can be had by unlocking Hard Mode and striving to achieve the "No-Death playthrough"

Overall, this game is good. The mysterious story, upgrade system, and difficult bosses make the game pretty fun to play, but only once or twice. After that, the game quickly loses value. Allow me to explain - doing anything fun outside of the main game - besides the boss rush mode - requires getting up to SIXTEEN hidden collectible items, which in itself requires you to beat every dungeon in every section of the map. It's a lot of work to go through for a wave-based arena mode and some outfits.
Additionally, the controls just feel off. Maybe it's because I'm using a PS4 controller through DS4Windows, but the game just feels unresponsive at times. Turning quickly to throw a grenade is difficult and usually never works, for example. Again, that may be just me.
There's also the upgrades. I like a game with an upgrade system, but this one irks me. A single upgrade requires finding twelve glowing yellow Bits, which can be a grind for your first playthrough. Plus, some of the upgrades are really not worth their price or even just don't work - there's an upgrade where your dash will shield you from projectiles if you dash towards them, but it NEVER WORKS. It's not worth buying at all, and yet it still costs the three gear bits. There's also the chain dash upgrade - it seems great before you get it, but it's a minor improvement at best since any dash chain of over three dashes causes you to slide on the ground, possibly to your death.
Next, replayability. This game has some, not as much as it strives for, though. Playing through once or twice is fun, but any more is really just a grind. And then you take into account the Alt character, which is even worse. Normally, a new character to play the game through with is AWESOME. With Alt, though, she offers very little to the game's experience - in fact, she takes away from it. Her primary attack is not upgradeable, and as far as I know the outfits cannot be used on her, save maybe for the companions. Using her takes away from the exploration of the game, and the want to find new, better gear.
Finally, quality. This game lacks it, that's clear. The bed at the beginning of the game isn't even fully real - the top half just doesn't have collision, so standing in it makes it look like you're in it without the effort of having to make a single animation for actually getting into bed. There's also a mirror in the starting room that, for whatever reason, shows your character two pixels too far to the left. That's just inexcusable for me. Not to mention the endless unskippable cutscenes for every time you get four gear Bits or start a boss fight. There's also the matter of getting hit around corners, which appears sometimes.
Here's my opinion - if you want to play this game casually once or twice, go right ahead, you'll enjoy it. Anything more than that is just an unfun grind for gear.
