So... What is "Intralism"?
That's actually not as easy to say as you might think. I'd personally use the words "Reaction-based rythm quick-time-event casual game". Sounds difficult? So then you got that right. Yea, that's the point... Let me explain with some sort of a list:
Pros:
+Awesome OST (in case you like electro)
+Pretty simplistic, yet epic visuals
+Easy to learn
+A lot of levels
+Pretty high difficulty
+Community levels
+Level editor (a really good one)
+Tutorial videos
+Fair price
+Items allowing tons of customisation
+Comes in bundle with "Linea, the game" and an exclusive item if you own both games
+No high requirements, this game will run everywhere
+Some hard or secret achievements
Cons:
-Unclear gameplay
-In-game-purchases
-Item-drops each require 60 minutes of playtime and cannot be achieved any other way than purchase
-So called "Mistery Item" which is currently beeing sold for around 105$ on Steam market (is this CS:GO or what?!?)
-Level editor uses ".ogg"- format; mp3 is NOT compatible
-Hard to master
-No display of lives, score or powerups during level
-Partially unprecise controls
-Unable to listen to the soundtrack while not in game
-Some stupid or auto-achievements
-Partially bad checkpoint setting
Summary:
Intralism is a fast, colorful game that requires precise timing and reaction skills to be mastered. The mechanic consists of pressing "W", "A", "S" or "D" keys or Arrow-keys at the right moment. All actions that are to take are represented by different colored (for standart it's red) "Archs", that means quarter a ring. They show up on one of the sides and you'll have to press the key according to that spot at the moment the obstacle hits the visualizer's layer. By mentioning the visualizer, it's simply a line pulsing in a circle, as seen on the screenshots. All the game looks pretty neat, the best I probably like the menu. As clear as the controls are, this game is an intense challenge to master. The patterns are irregulary, the checkpoints aren't always good and aditionally there is no spot to display your lifes remaining, so you will only notice having lost them once you're dead. That's what disturbed me a little. To name some good arguments, I have to admit that this game is pretty much the best if it's about the OST. Despites beeing unable to listen to it out of your game sessions, it's an insanely sick electro experience. In case you are into Dubstep, EDM or DnB this game is a must have for you. Awesome fact aswell is that you can buy new menu loops on the community market, so you can do with angles and effects. Instead of buying you can hope that you get some epic stuff dropped as a reward for spending 60 minutes within 24 hours at intralism, but "epic", a.k.a. rare items are, well, rare and way to overpriced. But the definitive reason I like this game for is: The level editor. Once you have figured out how it works or after you watched the tutorial-clip, there's nothing else to stop you from making awesome levels easily. Ignoring the copyright-disclaimer there are hundrets of levels created all over by the steam community, providing the game an entire new experience.
Should you play Intralism?
Yes, if you want to spend 2.99$ on a small challenge game with O.K. controls but with epic, minimalistic visuals, SUPER awesome electronic soundtrack and interesting level editor, play it, just now.
I won't recommend this in case you want to get this for items or achievements or if you came here for a fun game, which is highly entertaining for both, casual and long-time usage.
Otherwise, I see no reason to complain about this game.
Final score:
3/5

68/100

Of course the graphics can look too old for some, but as for me it didn't annoy me at all, because the universe is so well done that you immediately get into it. The gameplay is simple and nice, the various worlds quite fascinating, there's a good balance between puzzles/enigmas and beasts/monsters. I found the game rather easy as a whole, so it's a good think the secrets are here to bring some challenge.

Pendant des années, on m'a dit de part et d'autre que le premier opus était le seul de la série à avoir l'âme d'un vrai Tomb Raider, concentré sur l'exploration et les énigmes dans des mondes anciens plutôt que sur l'action et les ennemis humains, contrairement aux opus suivants. Et bien après avoir joué à ce fameux Tomb Raider, je ne peux que confirmer et dire que je n'ai pas du tout été déçue.
Bien sûr le graphisme peut paraître archaïque pour certains, mais personnellement cela ne me dérange pas du tout, car on arrive aussitôt à s'immerger dans l'univers du jeu. Le gameplay est très simple et agréable, les différents mondes sont fascinants, l'équilibre entre énigmes et bêtes sauvages (ou monstres) est parfait. J'ai trouvé le jeu plutôt simple et accessible dans l'ensemble, heureusement que les secrets bonus sont là pour apporter un peu de challenges.

Duelyst is a F2P strategy card game. It is one that is easy to learn, but hard to master. Imagine Hearthstone but the "board" is instead a large grid. Each players general starts with 2 attack and 25 health. First player to get the enemy general down to 0 health wins.
Things get interesting however when players can summon minions to fight alongside them and each general can use spells. Duelyst covers nearly every playstyle including aggressive players who like running up and smashing their enemies (Magmar), players who want to zerg rush their enemy (Abyssian), players who excel at playing tactically and focusing on positioning (Songhai) and much more.
It's not very p2w, as powerful legendary cards often are not a requirement until you get into the very top of the playerbase and many players have gotten to the top ranks using only basic cards/decks.
It's a great game any card game/strategy fan should give a try.

Just wanted to add a review for this game to say that it's probably my favorite game released in the last 5 or so years. I don't like the way most modern games' systems feel, especially concerning combat, and I've played many of the most hyped-up games of recent times (Bloodbourne, Doom, ..), and this is the first one in a long time that I *really* enjoyed. The oldschool style combat mechanics centered around movement and dodging instead of knowledge of animation frames and invincibility frames is super refreshing (I'm a little disappointed they actually added i-frames to the dodge move later on). This is a game that's easy to learn but hard to master; you will know immediately how to use all the abilities and what you need to do, but to learn to actually be able to do it - that is, to execute on it - may take you quite some time, instead of cryptically learning the arbitrary rules of which animation frames do what and "levelling up" i.e. increasing in-game numbers to make the game easier - i.e. in every respect exactly how it's supposed to be. It also has an absolutely fantastic art style and visual design with some amazing visual story telling (that never gets in the way of the gameplay) and extremely atmospheric music.
Easily one of my favorite games of 2017, if not this decade. Highly recommended.

The game attempts to be vague by forgoing voiced or written dialogue by exposing story elements via slideshows in speech bubbles. The beautiful pixel art tinged in varying hues helps separate different regions. Cutscenes, though beautifully rendered in the same art, continues its trend of vagueness by displaying imagery of the Drifter's dark past, shadowy figures (that may or may not be caused by the Drifter's ailing condition), and destruction. It fails to grab the player's attention
but the plot was never its strongest suit. Combat, however, requires a methodical approach consisting of quick strikes from the Drifter's sword, careful ammo management of his different arsenal of firearms and bombs, precise dodges, and careful prioritizitaion between enemies. Ammo is replenished by melee attacks, thus balancing combat by forcing you to switch between fighting styles. Abilities can be learned or upgraded by collecting gearbits hidden around the world. Encounters get tense when confronted by multiple enemies to the point that it's overwhelming, but deaths are mostly fair and are usually your fault. Controls are responsive but the game's dash mechanic needs precise button presses to execute perfectly. With enough practice, infinite dashing can be achieved. This game provides a good challenge for casuals, but a true challenge can be had by unlocking Hard Mode and striving to achieve the "No-Death playthrough"

Overall, this game is good. The mysterious story, upgrade system, and difficult bosses make the game pretty fun to play, but only once or twice. After that, the game quickly loses value. Allow me to explain - doing anything fun outside of the main game - besides the boss rush mode - requires getting up to SIXTEEN hidden collectible items, which in itself requires you to beat every dungeon in every section of the map. It's a lot of work to go through for a wave-based arena mode and some outfits.
Additionally, the controls just feel off. Maybe it's because I'm using a PS4 controller through DS4Windows, but the game just feels unresponsive at times. Turning quickly to throw a grenade is difficult and usually never works, for example. Again, that may be just me.
There's also the upgrades. I like a game with an upgrade system, but this one irks me. A single upgrade requires finding twelve glowing yellow Bits, which can be a grind for your first playthrough. Plus, some of the upgrades are really not worth their price or even just don't work - there's an upgrade where your dash will shield you from projectiles if you dash towards them, but it NEVER WORKS. It's not worth buying at all, and yet it still costs the three gear bits. There's also the chain dash upgrade - it seems great before you get it, but it's a minor improvement at best since any dash chain of over three dashes causes you to slide on the ground, possibly to your death.
Next, replayability. This game has some, not as much as it strives for, though. Playing through once or twice is fun, but any more is really just a grind. And then you take into account the Alt character, which is even worse. Normally, a new character to play the game through with is AWESOME. With Alt, though, she offers very little to the game's experience - in fact, she takes away from it. Her primary attack is not upgradeable, and as far as I know the outfits cannot be used on her, save maybe for the companions. Using her takes away from the exploration of the game, and the want to find new, better gear.
Finally, quality. This game lacks it, that's clear. The bed at the beginning of the game isn't even fully real - the top half just doesn't have collision, so standing in it makes it look like you're in it without the effort of having to make a single animation for actually getting into bed. There's also a mirror in the starting room that, for whatever reason, shows your character two pixels too far to the left. That's just inexcusable for me. Not to mention the endless unskippable cutscenes for every time you get four gear Bits or start a boss fight. There's also the matter of getting hit around corners, which appears sometimes.
Here's my opinion - if you want to play this game casually once or twice, go right ahead, you'll enjoy it. Anything more than that is just an unfun grind for gear.

Developed in 2013 by Mike Bithell, Thomas Was Alone is a simple indie puzzle platformer. A slowly stagnating genre, indie puzzle platformers are finding themselves in a place where the entire genre itself is suffering from consumers being tired of the same genre being overused by indie developers. However among the flood of low budget indie puzzle platformers on the market, Thomas Was Alone stands out as a superb example of the genre done right.
The premise of the game is simple enough. You guide the character/s from platform to platform on a 2D space to get to the next area. How the game does this is what makes Thomas Was Alone standout. The characters you play as are no more than a group of differently coloured rectangles. The titular character, Thomas, is a simple red rectangle. Along the way he meets several other differently shaped and coloured rectangles, Chris, a cynical little orange square, John, a tall happy rectangle, Claire, a large blue square who can swim, Laura, a long bouncy pink rectangle and many others.
None of the characters in Thomas Was Alone "talk" in a sense. The entire games story is narrated by Danny Wallace, whose voice acting is used to tell the story, describe the characters personalities, their relationships with the other rectangles, etc. Wallace delivers a terrific performance throughout the game, British narrators are go hand in hand with game narration it would seem. Bithell's writing deserves credit as well, not just for the development of the rectangular characters, but for the scripts itself. The dialogue is smartly written for its simple premise, going far beyong the expectations of an ordinary indie game. There are many funny and hilarious moments throughout, some sad emotional moments too. The game will make you will care about coloured rectangles simply because a British man talks about them.
The terrific storytelling by Bithell along with the narration by Wallace makes Thomas Was Alone something very special. Despite being simple coloured rectangles who don't even have any lines of dialogue, the characters have a lot of personality and character development. With just lines of narration that talk about the rectangles personalities and feelings, the game makes you care about different coloured rectangles, all because they have names attached to them. The story remains fairly simple, and it could be an easy aspect of the game to criticize, but to me, it feels like the story IS the characters themselves. The story is about coloured rectangles, their character development, their relationships and conflicts with the other characters. It wouldn't have been an easy job giving coloured rectangles life and personality, but Thomas Was Alone pulls it off.
All the gameplay involves is moving the rectangles from point A to point B, and yet the fact that it does so much more than just that and can tell a story at the same time is an achievement in itself. The game is a fairly short experience, only about 3-4 hours long, but it is the perfect length for the game. The stories pacing is just right, any shorter and it would have felt like a novel experience, any longer it would have outstayed its welcome.
The games soundtrack is also a treat to listen to. Composed by David Housden, songs are procedurally-generated throughout the game, matching the moments in the story. The songs are simple, yet effective at matching up with the mood in every level. It's a charming soundtrack and suits the atmosphere of the game. Highly recommend buying along with the game.
If Pixar were to make a game, I think that Thomas Was Alone would be the result. It's simple, funny, sad, and an emotional experience, all done with such a simple premise. You care about different coloured rectangles because a British guy talks about them a lot. The script is extremely well written, balancing those humorous and sad moments perfectly together. The soundtrack is great. In a genre that has become filled with every game playing the same way, and no innovation, Thomas Was Alone stands out as an example of how indie puzzle platformers can be so much more than characters moving from point A to B. A must have experience.

Pros:
*Unique concept pitting factions against eachother
*Unique combat system proving for fun gameplay
*Interesting map design (especially the newer ones)
*A level up system to make your character look godly
*Active devs and community
*A singleplayer to enjoy
*A wide variety of warriors to fight as, with more on the way

*A faction war to get rewards off of.
*Enjoyable gameplay
*Orders every day to help level up warriors and gain steel
*Only thing you have to pay for is the game and season pass, everything else can be bought with steel
Cons
*Absolutely terrible P2P connection.
*Combo spamming leading into stunlocking.
*Singleplayer is short and bears no meaning what-so-ever.
*Bots are genuinely annoying
*Optimized poorly
*9/10 chances you're gonna be thrown off a cliff
*FPS limit from letting you play online pvp matches
*Teammates can hurt you and knock you out of an attack
So would I recommend this game? I would. For PVE players it's a nice, calming killing situation with genuinely fun and easy killing with getting slightly less steel than playing PVP. For PVP players, it's an intense battlefield where anyone and everyone can kill you (Including teammates). The main issue is P2P but I think I remember seeing that Ubi said that they could switch to Dedicated Servers and have been trying to switch to them.
The server connection has issues sometimes, but the game is really fun and the single player game is great.

If you enjoy SRPGs or other Tactical turn-based games like X-Com and used to play Magic: the Gathering or enjoy Hearthstone you should really give Duelyst a shot.  Factions play out somewhat uniquely like the colors of Magic and your creature cards are actually played on a grid and can move and be deployed defensively.  Ranged creatures can actually try to stay physically distant from melee creatures. Good deck-building is rewarded but the game can be played rather casually as well.

I put up with the clashing artstyle for a long while for the sake of the gameplay, but many of the most recent additions added towards making the game a case of Rock-Paper-Scissors between the decks instead of duels of wit and outmanouvering your opponent. If you are playing a Magmar deck with rebirth minions and go up against an Abyssian with all the new cheap Shadow Creep you might as well concede. A Magmar that casts the four mana RNG fiesta that gives you four random eggs in random spots of the map either demands an immediate cheap AOE that few decks run in your deck or spells an immediate concede. The limited hand size initially encouraged players to play to their deck's strengths while also allowing some choice tech cards thanks to the 2-draw mechanic but it has since been replaced with single draw, removing much of the consistency and what made the game fun - you are no longer rewarded for adding a few tech cards to rapidly cycle into and rather punished for not having three of every important card in your deck. What was initially a game of limited RNG reached the point where the newest expansion Denizens of Shim'zar is full of pets that will choose randomly who to attack between two adjacent foes - which can be either game-winning or crippling. It hit me that this is just no longer the game I was having fun with when I downloaded it off steam one full year ago.

Here's a recipe for a thai green chicken curry
INGREDIENTS
2 tablespoons sunflower oil
2 baby eggplants, halved lengthways, cut into 2cm pieces
2-3 tablespoons green curry paste (see related recipe), to taste
500g skinless chicken thigh fillets, cut into 3cm pieces
2 cups (500ml) coconut cream
2 cups (500ml) Massel chicken style liquid stock
4 kaffir lime leaves (see note), roughly torn, plus 2 finely shredded leaves to garnish
125g fresh baby corn, halved lengthways
2 tablespoons fish sauce
1 tablespoon lime juice
2 teaspoons grated palm sugar (see note)
Sliced red chilli & Thai basil (see note), to garnish
Steamed jasmine rice, to serve
METHOD
Step 1
Heat oil in a wok or deep frypan over high heat. Add eggplant and stir-fry for 3-4 minutes until golden. Set eggplant aside.
Step 2
Add paste to wok and stir briefly. Add chicken and stir-fry, tossing to ensure paste doesn't burn, for 2-3 minutes until seared. Add coconut cream, stock, lime leaves and corn and bring to the boil. Return eggplant to pan, then reduce heat to low and simmer for a further 5 minutes until chicken is cooked and corn is just tender. Rocksmith 2014 is a great way to get into playing guitar.   I picked it up a couple years ago and have been playing regularly ever since.
Pros:
- Lessons: It has a good selection of videos that teach you basic things from picking up a guitar and restringing it to more complex techniques like pinch harmonics and double taps.
- It helps you feel like a rock star: Even as a beginner, the game only has you play a few notes of the melody, but you still feel like you're playing along with the backing band.   As you become more skilled, they progressively add more notes until one day, you are playing the lead guitar track on one of your favorite songs!
Guitarcade: A great selection of minigames that isolate and help you develop specific skills.   When I got frustrated playing a song, playing minigames for a few days still kept me motivated to learn, and when I returned to the song I found the song a little easier to play.
Session Mode: Silly band-in-a-box mode where you can create your own four-piece band that plays along with whatever you are playing.   Teaches you the basics of playing in a group, although I found the lessons somewhat brief/confusing.
- DLC: New DLC is released every week.   This keeps the game always fresh and introduces you to artists who you might not have considered learning.
Cons:
- It doesn't catch you if you start to develop bad technique.   I started mashing the strings with the wrong part of my finger and I still catch myself doing it today.
- No music theory.   I did not find a lot of what I had learned translated when I tried to learn the fretboard, how to read tabs and staff notation, or how to play with others.

Rating: 8/10
Genre: Isometric Action
The Good:
+ Exploration is a key component of the game. There is one large overworld split between 4 areas; north, east, west and south. Each area is filled with hidden pathways, caves, switches, hidden areas etc.
+ Collecting gear bits allows you to upgrade skills and weapons.
+ Combat is fantastic, providing  fun, fast and well controlled mechanics. Knowing enemy patterns and movements while dashing plays a big part of combat and survival. Different types of enemies will also force you to try new strategies and techniques.
+ Boss battles are varied and satisfying to beat.
+ If you find enough keys you can unlock horde mode and test your skills in combat.
+ Fantastic soundtrack that fits with the atmosphere of the game.
The Average:
+/- Though many people seem to really like the pixelated graphics I found it often disorienting especially during combat when things start getting hectic and there is a lot of visual information on screen at one time.
+/ - There is no dialogue or text, the entire story is told through pictures. On the one hand, given the nature of the game, the story does not get in the way, allowing you to focus on the amazing combat and exploration. On the other hand, it makes it very hard to care about what is happening. Surprisingly the story is pretty good but you must go online to make sense of it all.
The Bad:
-  You will collect many different types of equipment that change certain stats yet the game provides no description of what each one does. You must go online to figure it out.
- Lots of collectables and no in-game tracker.
Conclusion:
A brilliant game that was a joy to play from start to finish yet little design issues hamper the over all experience.  This is one of my favorite indie games of the year.

Just like its predecessor, Crysis provides both a unique and engaging premise for its campaign and top-notch graphics that once again raises the graphical benchmark for gaming. Well, kind of. It may not appear as instantly striking in terms of awesomness the original did with its lush, tropical setting but it's in the finer details and when things really escalate in the single player that will blow your mind. The sheer 'destructional' splendour of New York under alien siege has to be seen and played to behold. Seeing screenshots and a few gameplay trailers does not do it justice unless you're sitting there, at your desktop, plugged into your HDTV or whatever, with full surround-sound and maybe even 3D, escaping a sinking sub yourself. This being said, graphics don't make a game. And with such refined gameplay, it sure as hell doesn't make Crysis 2.
For the core gameplay of Crysis 2, I was initially disappointed about the nanosuit's powers being reduced to stealth and armour. That quickly changed, however. Having a button for each made switching between the two far more fluid than Crysis 1. On top of this, it adds a lovely twist and breath of fresh air to what is essentially your typical combat multiplayer affair. That being said, it is a step down from the large scale frantic antics of the original. But it's this added layer of depth to the tried and tested 'CoD-style' multiplayer offering that lends it an advantage.
But it was the single-player, like its predecessor, I bought it for. The original garnered some criticism to its rather basic plot, but having never seen it done so well, or in a videogame for that matter, it didn't hinder the experience one bit. Crysis 2, however, propels the Crysis universe onto a whole new level. It's obvious a hell of a lot more thought has been put into it. It's more complex, deeper and smart and makes for infinitely more compelling game. Couple this with the unique and shockingly-real depiction of an apocalyptic New York and well... I can't even begin to explain how awesome it is... 10/10

Damn I love this game.
Some will argue that this game is a shadow to what Crysis originally was, however this game was a different approach to the franchise and was not meant to be like Crysis 1. Instead of having that semi-linear "open world" gameplay C1 and CW had, it's a linear campaign. But it's not like Call of Duty in the sense that you're just in a small corridor for the entire game, in Crysis 2 you're in one of the world's largest cities- NYC. You can go into many shops, houses, hotels, and like Crysis 1 you can hide in bushes and shadows. Using that Crysis style of gameplay, you can get through enemies however you want- You can cloak through them, run and gun with armor, or just spam grenades or run away entirely. The main villains of the game, the CELL corporation and the Ceph are a bit less intimidating than the enemies you faced last time around, but they aren't stupid either. CELL will have enemies that rush you in numbers while the Ceph has giant robots, sumo wrestler aliens, and extremely powerful gunships. The story is so much more in depth and detailed than it was in the first game. Not to bash the first game, but all it was is "the KPA is hiding something Annnnd it's aliens" but this time around the characters are much more memorable (I really only enjoyed Psycho in the first game). It is ridiculous that Alcatraz, the guy you play as NEVER TALKS and if he could talk CELL would have never been hostile to him. You'd have to play the game to understand what I'm saying, but trust me you'll be thinking the same thing. But other than that, I found the story to be pretty good. The campaign itself is around 7-10 hours depending on difficulty, and it's 17 missions long (18 counting that the first mission is just a long cutscene).

Reviewing some old titles on Steam comes in handy since many of us are over 30 and we played some of the classics back then; classics that are either remade or still have sequels nowadays. It's been a while since several studios started releasing their classic games in digital format - the question is whether or not they can be run on modern day platforms.
I would like to criticise the store page a bit: first of all, the game was released on Steam back in 2012, however, the 1st Tomb Raider game that started it all dates back to 1996. It is, in fact, a game that is over 20 years old - I would rather use the original release date on the front page. Second, the number of added pictures is annoyingly low - a gameplay video or the original trailer from back then could, too, do some good here.
The game is very dated so don't expect beautiful graphics here. Throughout the story there's several cutscenes with a roughly 15-minute playtime. The rendered ones use a very low resolution. Also, controls were rather different back then - Lara is controlled by the arrow keys; we action by pressing ctrl and run by holding down alt. Our mouse is not configured, at all. This, and how precisely you need to land a long jump require some getting used to. I personally only had an issue with jumping as the game required a sec at least to register the press of the button.
Apart from the above this is a great classic game! I remember the installation only used up around 10 megabytes as pretty much the entire game was run on CD. And perhaps the most memorable moment was fighting the dinosaur in the jungle, though Lara's journey reaches Greece as well as Egypt when searching for a lost artefact called Scion. In this first episode most enemies were animals or mutants; henchmen sent by a corporation are mainly encountered as bosses.
In a bundle this is a great purchase with the rest of the classic TR titles. The game runs under DosBox (remember: back then it was released for MS-DOS) without any particular problems.

I have tried many, but this is likely the best collectible card game around. If you want a CCG which requires skill and with a limited luck factor, this is your best choice. Despite the high skill cap, the game is also very easy to catch up, since the rules and the interactions are ultimately very simple. If you ever played Hearthstone, you should understand immediately how Duelyst works, but you will be surprised by its depth.

Not sure why this game is getting so many bad reviews. At low levels, you can easily progress using basic (free) cards, and you can get a decent way into the higher ranks having crafted a few staple common (cheap) cards. The grinding in this game is considerably less than in literally any other F2P game I've played in the last two years.
Regular updates. Complex, satisfying gameplay. True, some factions are currently more prevalent than others, but CPG actively balances the most powerful cards to make sure that the meta doesn't stay fixed from month to month. Crazy weird synergies can be found anywhere.
Example: let's take the powerful dinosaur man faction, throw in spell cards which deal damage to summon minions at lower cost, then include minions which spawn other minions/deal AOE damage/deal damage directly to their General/etc, and we have one crazily powerful deck with 100% more green lizard men.
is a great place to go for links to all the guides, starting out tips, FAQs and miscellaneous chat about the game. Give the game a try and have fun!

The long and short of it - I've tried this game on two different occasions and it's not balanced at high level play. Or maybe it is, but everyone has to either play the same amount of time or buy in the same amount. When everyone is using the starter decks, it's fine. On several occasions, people pull these low cost cards that are absolutely devastating (one was a summon 4 random faction minions - they each were 4-5 cost cards for the price of one 4 cost card. The other is a 3 cost card that gives a general +2 attack whenever anyone on their side takes damage. That should be like a 6-7 cost card, as it is game ending.) I never got into crafting, as to do it efficiently, you would need to dump money into the game.
I feel like the deck drawing phases have some awful RNG to them, as well. You can have 25 unique cards in your deck and fairly consistenly draw the same cards without ever seeing some of what you put in your deck. How hard is it to randomly assign all deck cards a number and order them for true randomness? Or would that break the faulty design of the game?
All in all, I like the effort, but balance is poor which really impinges on the fun factor. It's free, though, so you'll probably get around 10-15 hours of enjoyment out of it at no cost.

Early impression: I wish that +2/2 or +4/4 grow cards didn't exist when they are very hard for new players to deal with after turn 1 as each turn usually has new players closely trying to outvalue each other with rather low hp minions on board and no dispel or destroy cards to get rid of them. sometimes you also get those 5 turn victories because of poor draws of the enemy and more than often your losses in constructed come from simply not having enough dispel or value to counter the enemy (as high value/dispel/removal cards rarely come up for you to pick).
otherwise the game is fun and while there are a lot of cards that feel unbalanced, there is more strategizing involved compared to many other f2p card games - and that makes the game worth playing for some time.
Edit: Played for longer and now I'm facing veteran players with custom decks when playing with starting decks, where people have cards with 2x more value than mine. I could summon 2 or 3 mana 2/3s with an effect, but the enemy has 0/6 2 mana totems that summon a 2/2 monster every turn or 2 mana 2/2 Pax that on death summon 2 2/2 dervishes for a total of 6/6 value as THREE monsters  against my (typically) low hp monsters (best probably fenrir warmaster for 6/4 value. Dispels do not have enough value to counter these kind of rush type minions especially when combined with buffed ranged minions because they use all the starting mana, a card from your action bar AND still leave the enemy minions with their original attack/hp values - giving no draw to keep up (and then you have to deal with distance of the ranged enemies or find a dispel for them as well). These are just some examples.
The game snowballs too easily and constructed requires heavy RNG in getting to choose cards that synergize and fit the meta. because of requiring a lot of grind to be able to fight against custom high value decks and a lot of rng to do well in constructed, I don't recommend playing more than up to level 11 casually on each class.

This game is something you really need to play to get the full experiene, much like the Stanley Parable and Undertale. Of course, you could get all the spoilers and then play, or not, as you like, but it's so much more satisfying to play it yourself. It was straightforward-- but it's not at all, with a deep backstory that we only have glimpses of.
The gameplay was smooth, using almost exclusively the mouse, and the puzzle introductions were incredibly clever. I only noticed during my second playthrough that the hacking sections had instructions in "code." Instructions! And commentary! It was frustrating at times, but never because it felt unfair, just because you didn't do well enough, but just one more try and you'll get it.
The achievements are a little... well, the last one you get is frustrating due to some RNG based things, but apart from that, most of them are the kind of thing you get as you play through the game. The boss battle formats were varied, but all were smooth and understandable. So far, this has been the only game I made a goal out of getting every achievement, and the satisfaction afterwards was so, so good.
Not perfect, and some things were implied to be more than they were (but told by word of God that it was a scrapped feature), but overall, a really good game to dig ito and focus on for some time.

This is a great game. Period. Hands down.
PROS:
- Great music
- Not EA
- Not Origin
- Great mods that add to the immersion of the game (assets, mechanics, etc)
Essentially, it's like the Simcity we wanted, but never got.
CONS:
- Later into your city, when you have 10k+ citizens, your performance starts to bog down. Naturally, this is due to the amount of AI, assets, etc etc all running at the same time, but if you have a potato playing this game, you have a limit of about 50k citizens before your potato decides to say "♥♥♥♥ you", and run your 50k city at abysmal frames.
- The DLC. Although they're great additions, I personally think these updates should be free, and not sold seperately. Natural Distasters came with the game in SimCity 5, but in this game, you have to pay $15 for some good fun. The others, I find, are solely revolved around a few extra mechanics. Not a big fan of that, but they can't make everything free.
All around, this is a GREAT city-builder, much better than that garbage SC5, so if you're looking for that type of experience, I totally recommend getting this game.
As for the DLC, the Natural Disasters is probably the most worthwhile to get. It comes with some very cool scenarios, and a whole lot of fun destruction.

This is one of the most important PC games ever made. It was an early example of 3D adventure, and it served as the debut of the iconic heroine Lara Croft! It went on to become one of the biggest franchises in video games. The first four sequels even share iterations of the underlying game engine.
The swinging, climbing, and jumping challenges are great. Controls are fairly simple and relatively accurate though the game shows its age in this respect. By about the midpoint of the game, players will have mastered the acrobatics, but the game compensates for this by increasing the frequency of combat challenges, which are relatively rare early on. The plot is straightforward with just a few twists along the way. The levels are not directly engaging in the plot for the most part, except during boss fights. Environments are varied enough though sparsely detailed.
The graphics are dated -- an unescapable fact for anyone playing the original 1996 release. The environment is built around a regular square polygon, which makes the jumps very repetitive. Walk to the edge, leap back, run forward and jump after she takes the second step, and she makes the jump every time. There are almost no jumps where the player can run forward and make multiple jumps in a natural fashion, instead repeating the aforementioned formula.
In all, the game is a classic and can still be appreciated as such. To see where 3D games grew out of and to get a flavor of the mid-90s, Tomb Raider is an excellent choice. It promises a great experience as long as players keep its age in context.

Duelyst is a nice game, except that the near s-rank ladder is a bit too grindy.
Duelyst is a Collectible Card Game on a 5x9 chessboard. It's similar to Hearthstone, but without the over-emphasis of RNG. Since it's on a chessboard, there are a lot of unique position-based mechanics, and that is the speciality of Duelyst. There are 6 factions/classes, and each faction has 2 generals, each with a unique Bloodborne Spell (Hero Power) which synergizes well with certain faction cards. Hence, there are at least 12 (in reality much more) playstyles and gameplans.
New-player experience is okay. They are definitely more generous that Hearthstone. There are a lot of hidden "achievement quests" that gives you a decent amount of gold, so that you could expand your card collections quickly in the early phases.
Most cards are well-designed and I seldom see cards that are outright bad (as opposed to the situation in Hearthstone). However, only a small pool of cards are used in high-ladder because those cards are simply too powerful. This case is more severe as the first expansion has rolled out - just like how Hearthstone was when Naxx and GvG came out. Quite an amount of potential deck archetypes are unviable because of the strength of some new cards. Ultimately, the game at a competitive level is grindy and somewhat stale - but I guess that happens in every CCG.
The publicity department of this game is also not so good. Their outreach is bad - if you don't play the game yourself, you have nearly no channels to know that this game is holding up a promotion. If it wasn't that a friend referred you to this game, it would take a miracle for youto discover this game. It doesn't matter that they have released an expansion 2 months ago, it doesn't matter that they gave away packs to newcomers a month ago, it doesn't matter if they're planning to release another expansion in 2017 Q1 when they do nearly nothing to increase the publicity of the game and reach out to potential new players. A comparison would be Shadowverse. It's another Collectible Card Game. they paid Reynad and Kripparian to promote their new expansion.
I reckon that this game's community is slowly dying as in this moment, even if the game is fun. There is nearly no one streaming this game. The relatively popular regular streamers of this game (none of them has more than 200 viewers) have recently stopped streaming as much. Forums are much quieter than anytime before (good thing is that ranting threads die as the forum is becoming less active).
TL;DR: All in all, Duelyst is good and has a lot of potential. The game is fun and rewarding, and there is a lot for you to explore in this game. However, the community of Duelyst is too small and they have little, if not none, publicity and outreach, that they may not survive the other competitors, such as Hearthstone, GWENT, The Elder Scrolls: Legends, and Shadowverse. Go pay a visit if you have free time, and see you like it - they've added a lot of supports to "casual" players so you could expand your card collection in a good pace, even if you don't invest much time into it.

Duelyst is a card game and tactics hybrid where you create a deck of units and spells and then play them out against your opponent on a tile based board. What I especially liked about this game was the movement and positioning that are required for the tactics portion of the game. Due to this a number of my really good matches were won through careful choices, calculated risks and proper strategic positioning of units rather than luck of the draw. That isn't to say luck of the draw doesn't happen given the card game nature of the game, but I've felt less of my matches came down to this than it did my opponent or myself playing well. I really enjoyed my time with Duelyst and am quite glad I gave it a shot despite it being F2P.

Skirmish Line is a WWII Rogue-Lite, RTS wave defense simulator on a tactical level, Specifically in the pacific theater. You command the United States army while the enemy commands the Imperial Japanese forces. Each with its own arsenal at its disposal.
The game has 3 types of game modes: Sector Defense, In Depth Defense and Campaign.
Sector Defense: The classic way of playing the game where your troops will spawn from the left and enemy will spawn to the right. Your goal is defend the left part of map with everything you got as waves of enemies come at you with increasing diffuculty. How to defend is all up to you, you can lay down some barbwires while your sniper picks them off, call for artillery support to spread chaos amongst the enemies ranks, fill your enemies with machinegun rounds while they tread your minefields or for the pyromaniacs, cook them up with some good old flamethrowers. The enemy, however, will send everything they have to push through whether its by using their own flamethrowers and snipers, sending in mass suicide charges to melee youre people to death or by simply sending in tanks to roll over your forces. Once 12 bad guys manages to push through whether its a lowly grunt or high ranking officer, your position will be overrun and you lose. And i tell you, the enemy will never surrender and they will come in endless numbers.
In-Depth Defense: Similar to Sector Defense but this time you defend 3 sectors divided into Areas A,B and C where each will be overrun if 5 bad guys get past. You start at Area C which if you lose it you will then fallback to Area B and finally if you lose again you fallback to Area A. Losing Area A will result in game over.
Campaign: This game mode will let you fully customize your squad with using points as you send them to missions whether its defending or assaulting enemy lines. If they comeback alive, they will retain all of the combat experience which will help them in future missions to come. As of now, this is the only game mode where you can be the attacking side.

I got this game as a gift from a friend for Christmas and I'm honestly not sure why it has such bad ratings. I played the physical board game of LIFE as a kid, I'm a massive fan of this game, which is why my friend got the computer version for me. This game is actually a really nice, relaxing way to spend an evening. It stays true to the original spirit of the board game and has added some creative minigames and a few extra features that weren't present in the original physical board game, which was a welcomed surprise for a seasoned player like myself. Oh, and major props for being able to choose your spouse's gender, regardless of your own gender. LGBT visibility is always a major selling point for me and I wasn't expecting that kind of progressiveness in a board game that was originally made in 1860, with the modern version we know today being released in 1960. Big thumbs up for that!
On top of the extra minigames and neat features, including being able to play online with your friends, it's just a really nice-looking game with a good soundtrack and cute cutscenes and animations for big events in the game, like getting married, graduating from university and having children. I found the entire thing really enjoyable and I was a bit sceptical going into it just because I am such a huge lifelong fan of The Game of LIFE and I didn't want to be disappointed. Not only was I not disappointed, I was actually pretty impressed. For the $5 it costs, it's a fantastic steal to add to your library if you're a fan of board games.
The only criticisms I can think of for it are when you're playing against computers, they can take their turns a bit too fast sometimes and I can't always follow exactly what they did on their turn. It would be nice if that was slowed down by just a couple seconds. Also, buying a house seems to be optional rather than mandatory in this version of the game. Not 100% sure if there was a rule change in 2016, my tabletop version of the game is a few years old by now.
Anyway, this game's bad ratings are completly unfair and silly. I don't understand it at all. If you like board games, definitely add this to your collection.

Crysis 2 is the linear sequel to an 'open world' Crysis, that became a more straightforward title. It was a promising title that fell short compared to its predecessor, ultimately failing to deliver an above-average experience beyond its next-gen appeal for its time.
It's only recommendable buying when on discount, when all you want is an 8hr experience of cinematic action.
Pros:
+Great graphics.
++Superb sound effects.
++Well detailed environments.
++Engaging gunplay.
+Slightly interesting although predictable story.
Cons:
-Short Single Player.
-Very much linear single player mode, go to point A to point B in a nutshell.
--Poorly optimized engine, framerate drops.
--Very glitchy and buggy. (Some alien stealth kills pop artifacts out of nowhere)
--No multiplayer (it wasn't too bright anyway -- very little people played it after its first year of release).
--Poorly implemented mechanics, ie. The Stealth detector upgrade (which is expensive) can be bought early enough in the game if you save enough to get it,
it is only useful in the near end of the campaign.
-Very few enemy types and weapons.
Overall it's not a bad game. Just lacking.

When one refers to Jazzpunk, they are referring to the all of the stupendous events in the history of the human race conglomerated into one quintessential magnum opus. The developers behind the game are nothing short of giraffes (so they have long necks, which they use to reach for the stars) bringing their dreams into reality with vigor. The trailer for this game says it all, perfectly displaying the succulent confusion and disarray found while playing “Jazzpunk.”
Brilliant 4k graphics power the thousand upon thousands of artists’ careful drawings and 3D models to create a gorgeous mosaic of infinite, cell-shaded beauty. The color scheme forms a delicious kaleidoscope of iconic tones and shades, each with its own scrumptious flavor. Despite this, the game runs as smoothly as a buttered Usain Bolt across an ice-skating rink (which is to say, it does, unless the ice skating rink is actually a blender). Jazzpunk has an art style that doesn’t require Prozac to be enjoyed, but also isn’t so erratic and screwball that you feel like you pumped six graves of lysergic acid diethylamide into your forearm. Its simplistic touch leaves the connoisseurs of gaming in awe.
Upon further inspection of the penultimate[1] gameplay, one can determine the true quality of the masterful plotting of its characters. As a wise man once said, "Procrastinator [Pro-Krazt-Ih-Nay-Tor] derived from the Spanish word 'procratelémathíon' meaning 'midnight snack' and the Viking word 'Astenetorr' meaning 'puckered cheeks'... it basically describes someone who sits on a sandwich in the dark.", which is what one will be doing when experiencing the masterpiece that is this, not a game, but rather an alternate existance of profound truth and mythicality.

Resident Evil 6 has a really big change as compared to Resident Evil 5 in terms of gameplay and control performance. The most noticable features is the multiple character selection and different campaign routes. Below will be a list of pro's and con's that I've summarized from my experience with this game.
Proz:
1. Chargin' strike! Melee isn't just standing on the spot and doing a slash that is literally face to face.
2. Execution from melee combo! This was from RE4 but was somehow removed from RE5 so I'm really glad it's here!
3. Characters. Each character has their style of attacking so have fun exploring them all!
4. Serpent emblems are bigger, and more easily spotted throughout the campaign.
5. Vehicles isn't just limited to cars anymore.
6. Dodging buttons. Many others say this feature is useless but I think it's kinda useful for doing side rolls through vents.
Cons:
1. No more weapon upgrade feature or portable gatling guns :(
2. Herbs are incredibly rare after Chapter 1 of any campaign.
3. Camera angle in certain zones. Experienced RE players will know the struggle.
4. Online community is pretty much dead. Either that or there'll be some rushing jokers with a lifespan of 6 seconds speeding through the game.
5. Inventory is a joke. I understand that for story's sake, each character will not have a shared bank system like RE5 but this is the main contributing reason why I'm stopping every now and then because I have to choose between herbs or ammunition. If Christ can stuff an entire grenade launcher AND a sniper rifle in his pocket, why can't he do the same for the rest??!?
6. 8 skill slots and only 3 skills for each. You can only select one slot at a time. I strongly don't see why anyone would need up to 8 slots.
Overall rating from me would be 7/10. It's a good game that you won't regret. Long hours of gameplay and the unexpected QTE's are the "fun" features of the game.

Tried this game because I'm a longtime fan of both tactics and card games. The tactics portion adds a lot to the standard card game lineup, and feels like an experience not to be missed.
I've started playing this a little more regularly than Hearthstone lately because the tactics portion adds a good amount of depth without things getting too crazy: Hearthstone feels like it gets solved every month or two, to the point that you can't play a fun deck, because you'll just hang out in the high-teens.  People netdeck something and it plays itself.  The positioning in this game adds a whole new way for you and your oponent to screw up, and so your fun deck is going to throw you higher.
My biggest complaint here is the art. I think its fantastic pixel art, but the grid-based system causes the fantastic pixel art to not-integrate with the environment very well.  Kinda just a problem with tactics games in general - with this one stressing the point more without clever environmental interactables.
Overall, grand game. Hope it keeps up. Haven't dropped a dollar on any other digital CCG besides Hearthstone, but this one caused me to open my wallet.  Haven't yet bought in too deep, but it seems pretty inevitable.

3D Factorio, how  can you not like that? Plus you get to build / customize a ship to accomodate your needs. Granted the ship is more useful as a stationary platform that beams from planet to planet, but for this game, it works fine.
Also, the game is more of two games in one. You set out to build a stargate and research via factorio style. Once that is built, it is a colony management game with money as a new resource to manage.

I’m getting a return on this game, like constructing a well-put-together production line gives out the success buzz of achievement. I’ve never play a factorio style game before and I was pleasantly surprise how quickly I got into building bigger, more efficient, more complex and multilevel production lines.
You start off building and setting up an oxygen and food generator, connecting power and plumping and really that’s all the survival element there is. From there you build into oar extraction and your first production lines and then you start to build up your infrastructure to include tech point’s production lines, spaceport, ship and producing materials for the galaxy gateway, a little pre-planning is wise. The last degree is to build your own colony with colonists, so I believe there’s an adequate amount of content.
Some cons, I think mostly on the to-do-list, like the need for more game saves but just minor stuff really. I don’t mind EA since the game is playable and to me it means that the developer is still developing and there is a whole lot of room and potential for the developer to explore and expand on.
In classic mode there’s some figuring out of what to do next stuff, like working backwards from the options to find out what you can or should build next.
The game first person and third person aesthetic makes it easy to mine, construct and produce materials for building capital of your own design. Infrastructure over infrastructure won’t suit full on action craving players but maybe a strategist style candidate, if that’s you.
This game differs from usual piece placement type in that there’s no auto utilities connection, so you have to build the infrastructure as you go along, thus inspiring your intellect.
The developers have fostered a contemporary genre and all in all a spiffing “playable” game for this genre type.

I played it with my parents and only finished it because I felt obliged to. This 2016 edition finds a way to make the players feel like spectators and generally disjointed from the experience. I've owned several other PC versions of this board game that were way more interactive than this. I believe that Atari's 1999 version seriously blows this one out of the water which is sad considering technology has advanced SO much since then.
There is very little that the user actually does then just click through dialogs. Some of the other editions find an interesting way to make you feel more attached to your choices. That is not the case with this 2016 edition- you choose a faceless peg and watch it drive around the board. To say there is no personality to this game is a gross understatement.
The most cringey addition are the odd prompts they've added to LIFE cards. I awkwardly laughed through forced interactions like "choose an opponent and compare your best karate chop". We also had incredible difficulty with the spinner which probably accounted for an additional 15 minutes of gameplay. I was happy when the game was over and promptly returned it.
I LOVE board games but I do not recommend this version at all. It seems like a shell of a game and even a bit transactional...which is not a feeling I attribute to fun.

It is rarely that I have played an FPS that managed to impress me and keep me on the edge of my seat with its action and at the same time completely impress me with its storyline. Mind you Crysis storyline might seem generic and cliche as they come and there's a definitely an element of truth to that.
Having played this game in 2016, almost 5 years after its release, I can certainly say that if you told me this was a 2016 game I've would have believed you. Sure the player models might seem a little stiff and dated, especially in a gaming era where facial animations are scrutinized constantly and Crysis 2 is worthy of complaints in that matter, the textures and the environment however still look as beautiful as ever. The times of old memes (WILL IT RUN CRYSIS) are perhaps gone, but this game is certainly worthy. Still looks good, especially in the maximum edition where it features the High Res textures.
Crysis 2 gameplay is also pretty damn good. There's smooth movement, decent aiming, the action flows greatly and constantly at your own pace; you can take a stealth route to eliminating your enemies or you can go guns blazing. Naturally in higher difficulites a proper combination of both strategies will net you a quite satisfying and intense experience. The gunplay is great, there's a variety of different weapons to use, each one with their own stats and modifications. Don't worry, it's super simple to customize your weapon and you can do it on the spot too! No need to go back to a bench/whatever to modify your gun.
You want to stealth this part of the mission? Add a silencer and a scope. You want to fire more bullets? Add extended clip. You want a secondary function to your primary weapon? Add a grenade launcher! It is important to note that not all weapons have the same modifications and some unique and powerful weapons might not have any at all, but still this is a great feature which has unfortunately been completely ignored in the modern FPS.
Last but not least, your nanosuit is essentially what makes you an unstoppable soldier. There's armor mode to reduce damage taken and stealth mode which makes you invisible and allows for a more stealthy approach. The modes are mutually exclusive which makes sense and use energy. Furthermore you can upgrade your suit as well with different enhancements which can also be done on the spot as well! Improve your armor absorb, make you stealthier, decrease the energy drain etc. Admittedly there around 15 to choose from but they are there and they can define the way you play through missions.
For completionists, there are several collectibles scattered around the different levels which include: emails to expand on the lore, collectible dog tags, collectible car keys and souvenirs from New York.
The level design is magnificent. The city of New York looks wonderful,
, the map progress allows for a semi-linear if you will completion of objectives. Don't think that this is not a linear game. It totally is, however there's a degree of freedom in which you can complete some of these objectives. You can avoid enemies if you will, flank them, use vehicles, detach turrets from barricades etc. The gameplay is absolutely great, never a dull moment and it keeps you on your toes constantly.
Now for me of course, since I'm a sucker for 90s/early2000s blockbusters (The Rock, Independence Day, Armaggedon, Crimson Tide, Black Hawk Down) the story is pop-corn entertaining fun. The dialogue is as good as it gets, you get your epic speeches, your betrayals, your arrogant villains, basically all the tropes you'd expect in a movie. And you know what? It ♥♥♥♥ing works. It works so well in the concept of the game and it fits perfectly. And I cannot stress enough that all of this would otherwise seem silly
Hanz Zimmer is one of my favourite music composers and he's also the primary reason why I fell in love with the Single Player campaign of Modern Warfare 2. The soundtrack is epic and it intertwines with the gameplay, superb dialogue and the game itself in such a way that I think that any other soundtrack would have seriously affected the way I felt after I finished Crysis 2.
Now the negatives which definitely exist but by no means take away the joy of the game. The enemy is AI is a little bit weird, don't expect smart enemies who will try to do everything in their power to kill you. Even at max difficulty, they behave is a rudimentary way. They hide behind cover, they fire, sometimes they might throw a grenade or two and they will try and move towards you. Nothing fancy and a bit on the silly side at occasions especially whenever stealth is involved. The models look a bit dated as I mentioned above and lip-syncing might be non-existant at moments. Notable example is the soldier talking to you while wearing a surgical mask, really shows that the developers didn't want to bother with lip-syncing and facial animations with the exception of some key characters. Most of the dialogue is transmitted to you via voiceover in the suitcomms however said dialogue I believe is vey well written
.
I'm not saying that this is the best dialogue in the history of gaming, but for the cheesy action packed game Crysis 2 is, the voice acting and the dialogue is brilliant.
Lastly the game is a bit short, not as short as such of the 4-6 hours of modern FPS single player campaigns (I estimate around 8-10 hours if you also want to get all collectibles), there's very few Quick Time Events but there are there, cutscenes while great tend to border on the unnessecary at times but overall Crysis 2 is a one of the greater games of genre and you should have the pleasure of playing it. I got this at less than 5 euros during a sale and I think it was a steal compared with the entertainment I got out of it.

Crysis 2 is a first-person post-apocalyptic shooter developed by Crytek Studios and published by Electronic Arts. The game was released in March 2011. The story continues from Crysis 1 where the Ceph invaded the Lingshan Islands into them invading New York, USA. The player plays as Alcatraz, a member of Force Recon One, whose mission to infiltrate and capture Dr. Nathan Gould goes terribly wrong. This review will discuss the campaign and the dialogue, the gameplay and the features, performance and graphics, and the issues with the game. I did not test the multiplayer component as the online portion went offline in 2015. In addition, the Maximum Edition aspect of the game is irrelevant as all of the contents were related to multiplayer.
Crysis 2 encompassed a good and logical storytelling campaign. The story expands on the Ceph invasion into America from the Lingshan Islands and the inevitable counter-attack by the Americans. Furthermore, the game provides great insight into the background of characters that carried before and through both games, notably Prophet and Jacob Hargreave. For instance, Prophet reveals that following Crysis 1, he found out it was not the last of the Ceph, rather the beginning of a new war. The story in the game made sense by the end of the campaign so I commend Crytek for elegantly telling the story. However, I do not like the massive logic gap from Crysis 1 to 2 because the sequel does not mention the aftermath of the cliff-hanger in Crysis 1 as the aftermath is explained through the Crysis comics series, which irritated me and I feel is an unwise business move. But, the dialogue in the campaign was excellent in telling the story. I completed the campaign in 10 hours and my favourite component was the team-based missions alongside the US Marines because many post-apocalyptic games result in a lonely protagonist. My second issue within the campaign was the lack of real excitement in cut scenes that clarified a major part of the overall story. For instance, when Jacob Hargreave reveals his knowledge about the Ceph, which I will not spoil, it comes across as another cut scene, not as a great storytelling moment, even if it was. Lastly, this game features some collecting aspects such as collecting dog tags on missions, collecting flashbacks, and so forth. It's not overly filler but it's not overly interesting to invest the extra time into finding the extras. Overall, the campaign is good because the story within the game, not the overall story is told with depth and precision and has minimal loopholes. The main issue of having to follow the comic series to determine what happened in the cliff-hanger from Crysis 1 does hurt my overall experience of the campaign.
Crysis 2 possesses a variety of gameplay features to mostly improve the game. First, the game features a levelling system in which Alcatraz can kill the Ceph and garner Nano Catalyst points to upgrade his nanosuit. There are four different tiers with three upgrades in each, which is separated into tactical, armour, power, and stealth module tiers. This is a decent system because it allows you to improve Alcatraz's overall combat effectiveness and it has a nice balance to not overpower him but improve him because as the campaign progresses so does the difficulty of the Ceph. My major annoyance with this system was the lack of clarification if an ability is active or not once you purchase it. For instance, if I buy threat tracker, the game does not mention whether its active. The second gameplay feature is the layout of missions in the campaign. I really like the layout of the missions because despite the game being linear, you can approach a mission in a variety of ways. For instance, when Alcatraz opens his visor, he can see his tactical options for the mission, which may be going 100 metres to the right through stealth to complete the mission or going forward 30 metres and grenade the enemy. Furthermore, the weapon customisation system expands on the variety of approaches in a mission because Alcatraz can alter his gun depending on what approach he wants to take, ie. Stealth approach and a silencer. This freshens the gameplay and missions because Alcatraz has various options in completing a mission and can suit his equipment towards that approach. Lastly, the weapon combat, melee system, and vehicle movement and combat are all smooth, fluid and enjoyable. Vehicular combat does spice up the game, particularly on long distance missions. Overall, I commend the gameplay and the variety of features because it all does enhance the game experience.
Crysis 2 has very consistent performance and beautiful graphics. This game reinforces why Crytek were the leaders in gorgeous games because this 2011 game is truly a stunning game. The graphics are superb, from the destruction that affects the landscape to the realism of characters to the overall tone of the post-apocalyptic atmosphere. Furthermore, I like the simplicity of the UI, which is the main menu. The performance as mentioned, is very consistent. On my mid-tier system, which specs are highlighted on my profile page, I played on very high settings and drew a constant 35-50 fps. When there were FPS drops throughout a mission, there was no stuttering, making performance steady throughout a mission. However, at the beginning of the majority of missions there would be a major freeze probably due to a massive fps drop for some unknown reason. Loading times varied in the game. Some missions took longer to load than others, which was annoying on some levels but not a major nuisance. Overall, the only hitch in performance was the start of the mission stuttering, but for the most part this was a smooth game. Likewise, the graphics was top-notch.
Despite most of the review containing positives and some containing negatives, this game had a ton of bugs and glitches. I encountered six bugs and/or glitches that occurred frequently throughout the campaign. For instance, the worst was the sound engine dying, resulting in me restarting my computer. The second worst annoying bug was dialogue showing up on the screen as I had subtitles enabled and the characters that were meant to say those lines went silent, pointing to more issues likely with the sound engine. And the other bugs and glitches was mainly relating to dialogue, event sequences and gameplay. All in all, the issues did hurt the game for me.
Overall, Crysis 2 is a good game that features a logical and competent campaign, great gameplay and features, a beautiful atmosphere and environment and consistent performance for the most part. This game had a deep and logical story that explained the specifics and the broader picture. It provided fluid combat and various approaches to tackling missions, freshening the linear aspect of the game. The main issues was the logic gap from Crysis 1 to Crysis 2 due to the business idea that the story should be advanced through Crysis Comic series and the amount of bugs and glitches infested into it. This game is $29.99 and you can get up to 18 hours in my opinion on the game fitting in the campaign and the extras. At $29.99, I recommend getting this on sale. However, if you are completely new to the series, I recommend getting the Crysis Collection at full price of $44.99 because there is three different games that tell a massive story and all of which have been well received.
Ratings:
I calculate the point system by rating each component I discuss and then averaging the total and deducting marks depending on the amount and severity of issues within the game.

Gameplay: 9/10
Graphics and Performance: 9.5/10
Overall: 7.75/10

Yes, this game has a foolish name. But it cloaks a really engaging game that, while short, will keep you playing for the few good hours it has. In essence, you're fighting against Satan the game developer in order to free yourself and others from his purgatory. And I was not expecting to use the phrase "Satan the game developer" before I played this game. He's really good at it, and I'd commend him if he wasn't trying to get my soul all the time.
The end goal might be obvious, but its the journey that matters. The hacking-based puzzle game that forms the meat of it kept me engaged and thinking, especially with the twists and new additions to that formula that you instinctivly pick up on. And the ways it clevery uses and twists the interface, making it part of the puzzle too, adds so much to the overall experience.
It's worth the $5 entry price. And it offers more content than some other games that are double the price. Pick this one up without hesitation if you are at all interested.

RE6 is an uneven experience, lacking the input of either its masterminds (Mikami and Inafune) and relying on a "let's do it all" mentality backed by unrelenting budget, resulting a decent game buried somewhere beneath layers of sloppy execution and odd design decisions.
Pros:
- Nice graphics, varied scenery and competent art direction.
- Unobtrusive music, great sound effects and terrific voice acting.
- Workmanlike story and writing with pleasant storyline intersections.
- When it sticks to the basics, the game plays great.
- Lengthy campaign featuring four large "acts" with multiple playable characters.
- The Mercenaries minigame can be great fun, even solo.
Cons:
- A metric ton of QTEs, some are easy, some are demanding, some are pointless and some are inhumane with insta-kill on failure.
- A metric ton of "sequences", those either rely on QTEs or on contextual actions. (tap button infinitly to do this, tap buttons in rhythm to do that, etc)
- The game often messes with the camera or strips you of control either to focus your attention on something or to show you a small, pointless cutscene.
- Game mechanics aren't well realized: cover is useless, sliding is useless (good for breaking boxes though), dodging is almost useless, skill system is limiting at best, Combat Gauge bar needs deeper integration.
- Atrocious inventory and inventory managment: you have to fumble through weapons/items with the wheel or with prev/next hotkeys like it's 1999. Also no hotkeys for weapon slots, which is a big blemish on the otherwise thorough KB/mouse support.
- Online community is near non-existent.
All zigzag, nothing else!
Buy if you have to and at the cheapest price possible...!

I fully reccommend this game.
It is a tactical, turn-based game and a card game. You use the cards to place units to the board, cast spells and equip your general with artifacts.
Mechanics -
The objective of the game is to kill the enemy general. Each round you have an increasing amount of mana to play your cards.
There are 3 game modes: Practice against a basic AI, Season Ladder which is the ranked PVP and the Gauntlet, where you build a deck from scratch.
There are endless possibilities of combinations with the cards and the board positioning. You can choose among 6 factions, each one having 2 generals with different playstyles.
Matches last around 10 minutes.
Aesthetics -
The quality of the artwork is AAA. Unit design and animation are superbly well done in a pixel art style, backgrounds are beautiful paintings. The soundtrack is great and the interface is beautiful, functional and responsive.
Dynamics -
I found the game very noob-friendly (even having zero experience on card games), the tutorial covers the basics and gets you up and running very fast. There are dozens of challenges that show combos and the basic mechanics from every faction.
You have so many cards to unlock and so much to rise on ladder that it guarantees endless, high quality entertainment for free.
Community -
So far, incredibly good. People tend to be nice and helpful. There are several great streamers that help with insights and tips, also, lots of content across different platforms - wiki, reddit, twitter.
Conclusion -
Definitely worth a try if you are into tactical, cards or both. A very well crafted game, with constant challenges, endless room to grow, healthy playerbase and friendly community.

ORIGINAL REVIEW:
Duelyst is a turn-based strategy game that you can play against the AI or other players, in one-on-one games. There are six factions and each have a pool of cards that you use to build your 40 card deck. The major difference between this and other CCGs is that cards are played onto a combat surface. Their proximity and other factors impact gameplay.
So far, so good. I am easily addicted to such games and so have spent a goodly amount of time already on Duelyst, enough to get all the factions to Rank 11 and do all the Quests.
You can play for free and accumulate gold to spend on packs of cards, I mean "orbs". You can compete in the guantlet (draft) for further prizes. Quests refresh every day as a way of earning more gold. You could certainly play this with zero real cash investment, which is certainly generous.
However, like all such games the rarer the card, the better (on average). So you might need to open quite a few packs to put together the deck you want. One cool feature is that you can tear down cards you don't want to gain Spirit, which you then use to "craft" cards you do want.
However, there is no trading with other players.
The basic interface and usability is very good. I encountered no crashes or glitches. Unfortunately a network time-out is handled very badly. Your opponent gets to keep playing while you are unresponsive!
There is also no chat system, only a limited series of emoticon things you can send.
The units themselves are rendered in 8-bit style. Not only does this clash with the rest of the aesthetics, it is difficult to see what the units really are supposed to be. It simply looks like the developers couldn't afford anything better.
Besides these points, there are a number of limitations to the gameplay itself.
The six factions have their own feeling, but the game is dominated by any number of excellent neutral units. Many games go by without me really knowing who my enemy is. There is little sense of personality. This is reinforced by the fact that cards don't obviously indicate their faction.
The board is a series of squares. All units move the same way, either two horizontal or vertical units, OR one diagonal unit. This clunky system indicates the designers have nevver heard of that magical six-sided figure, the hexagon.
Certain units cannot move at all. There is scope for different movement speeds but this was not incorporated.
Most units need to be in proximity to fight, except for ranged units that all have infinite range. Again, a lost opportunity.
Your main card is your General, but they all have the same hit points. Their only distinguishing characteristic is a single ability they can reactivate a certain number of times a game.
The card pool is also rather small. This might change over time.
All of this makes for a very limited game. There must be better examples of this archetype out there. However it cost nothing to try and so gets a thumb's up.
Note: I have played well over 50 CCG/TCG starting with Magic a few sets after release.

LET'S TALK ABOUT PRICING. Duelyst has a lot of nice stuff to like about it. I know a lot of people are used to F2P games; I am not. These prices are silly. Let's look at them.
Duelyst Micro-transaction Prices:
40 card packs - $50
Emote Packs - $13 each
General Skins - $8 each
Card Backs - $4 each
Profile Pictures - $3 each
Let's compare those prices to some full games. Steam is full of B2P (buy to play) games that are reasonably priced, get cheaper over time, and don't have hidden costs down the line. There are competitive multiplayer games in B2P that are very replayable too, not just short single player games.
Entire Full Games (sale prices):
AAA games 1-2 yrs old ~ $30
Chaos Reborn - $7
XCom EU Complete - $10
XCom 2 Digital Deluxe - $40. Also has an often overlooked VS MP mode.
Disgaea 1 PC - $15
Civ V Complete ~ $15
100% Orange Juice with all DLC ~ $11
Minecraft - $27 (Doesn't go on sale?)
Misc Indie Stuff Everywhere - $3-$7

Duelyst has huge "microtransactions" that are each larger than many B2P games. If Duelyst was B2P, it would probably be $15, and maybe get one or two $10 optional DLC expansions. Both the base game and DLC would go on sale too. Because Duelyst is F2P, it costs $$$$$ to get everything.
Please compare F2P games to B2P games you already own (free!) and B2P games you could buy instead.
