[TL;DR]
Duelyst is a great game. It has a charming community, a challenging and fast paced gameplay, nice soundtracks and gorgeous visuals. It is the perfect blend of Turn Based Strategy and CCGs like Hearthstone, fair and rewarding but still cheaper than the likes of MTG or HS.
Duelyst is a CCG at heart. You will collect cards, craft cards and assemble them in decks. Every card has unique properties that can change the course of a game. If at first it sounds very Hearthstone-ish, and not without reasons, in practice, the game is very different because of the board element.
In Duelyst, you will play on a board similar to a chess board. The gameplay actually is very reminescent of chess. You have a General ( a King ) and minions ( Pawns, Rooks etc ). In addition to this, you've also got spells. All of those elements come in various sorts, buffs, debuffs, miscellaneous effects and such and their use is balanced with a cost in mana. The goal of the game is simple and straightforward : kill the enemy General.
Absolutely not. Everything, including cosmetics, can be obtained through playing and each and every expansion is free. There are some lootcrates though you can not open without paying, but I can assure you that this game is the cheapest CCG you've ever seen. Drop rates are quite generous when opening orbs and not as hard to obtain as in HS. I like to call this game the Path of Exile of CCGs. Of course, you can still buy card packs by purchasing them if you want to.
If pixel art is your thing, welcome to heaven. The art in this game is beautiful. Easily the best looking pixel art around.
The lore in this game is incredibly deeper than you'd think. More is coming soon. If you like to speculate and go treasure hunting for every tiny piece of lore you can find, this game fits the bill. You actually can see me and others speculate about it on the forums. Speaking of which.
Easily one of the best communities you will ever be given to see. Rarely have I seen such a friendly and open community, especially in a competitive game. EVERYONE is here to help you.

Honestly, Rebuild 3 is easily one of my favorite games centered around re-killing the undead. Something is just so addictive about taking your humble little fort and slowly, but surely reclaiming a city. The first two games offered an experience similar, but in the end, Rebuild 3 is the best of all of them.
I liked all the dialouge, interactions, and the often funny and/or sad moments within them. I chuckled when I heard about the survivor who blew up his zombie-infested waterpark with a simple reroute of water pressure, I felt horrible when my decsions inadvertenly killed off a member of the fort or a friendly/likeable fraction, and so on.
But the main issue with it is, it just needs more. By that, character customization, generation, backstories, and perks feel quite a bit lean. Not to mention, quite a few perks are definitely better than others; with the Redecorater Perk being my least favorite of the bunch, because it will randomly replace buildings that are listed as "useless" but are rarely anything but, like Parks (endless materials) Police stations/Banks (improved defense) and Warehouses (more food storage.) Oh, and once those buildings are gone, they can't be replaced either.
Pros
-Fun, "easy to learn, tough to master" gameplay
-High replayability thanks to procedural generation of cities and the people who reside in them
-Nearly a dozen fractions you can ally or war with, each with their own events
-Easily the best looking game of the series with a much more detailed version of the first game and a less uncanny take on the second.
-Combines the specialties of the first game with the skill leveling and equipment of the second exceptionally well.
-It's just damn satisfying to build a completely self-succificent fort with zombie traps doing most of the work for you by the late game of various cities. ;P
Cons
-The character customization/generation feel lacking at times, as do the equipment, and some dialouge choices.
- Redecorator. Need I say more?

The factions can be incredibly annoying and tedious at times- but not enough that it has ever made me hate the game.
The levels can be repetitive, but Rebuild 3 is a game I will keep revisiting. It's a great casual game to relax to.

The first game in a four part Saga.
Alpha Centauri has you take control of the Quicksilver, a Passport/Cargo ship run by a Captain named Gail Pilgrim, whose last name is synonymous with the saga's title. Once you find your passengers, you head out on a journey accross space. This series has been enjoyable for me, partly because as far as RPG's go, this one has zero combat. At first I was opposed to the idea, but I quickly grew attached to the characters, adventure, twists and puzzle solving. Not to mention that I just love space in general.
The only downside to the first two games is that they're much shorter in length compared to the latter episodes. If you're good at puzzles and such, expect the first two games in the series to last about a few hours each. Also, the style of game might not be up everyone's alley.
All in all, I'd have to give the first rendition of the series 8/10. Two points were counted off due to the short length, but as far as RPG Maker games go, this one, as well as the others, are pretty fun and solid.

happens to be one indie platformer that is endearing and fun to play without coming off as pretentious.
The game is about a block named Thomas. You move and you jump. It starts from getting point A to point B, then gradually introduces more mechanics and more characters. That's where the game's personality starts to show, and it shows itself very well.
You'll meet new blocks, all of whom have their own names, shapes, and colors. Even though they're all four-cornered shapes, they all come with their own life stories. It sounds strange, but thanks to a witty and charming narrator, you grow with these shapes through their adventures.
This isn't just for good 'ol indie flavor. Their personalities speak to their capabilities. You'll have to control multiple blocks in some stages and use their unique physical properties to reach the end. You'll need to make use of each block's different widths, heights, and even bouncyness. You can't succeed without synergizing everyone's strengths and sensibilities. It's almost as if this game... is about friendship.

A beautiful pixel-art game with muted environments and flashes of magic and energy that scream aesthetic in the most glorious fashion. This game was a favorite of a friend of mine who chose this above all other games to be his introduction to speed running. He swore by this game, and I see why.
HLD can be, at times, clunky and un-weildy. The dashing feels like its fighting you at every execution, with every button press (on either gamepad or keyboard) chugging and giving the hint of fluidity. The combat, while crisp half of the time, also makes you feel like you are movnig through molasses, with your limited 3 swing combo leaving you open and requiring you to dash away and back in in order to keep up the punishment. And while this all would turn me off from a game normally, it left me thinking: maybe HLD chugs on purpose, furthering the narrative being told of the main character fighting off some unknown disease or affliction, which keeps him on the edge of being capable, a masterful balace of showing someone who is both a force to be reckoned with and someone who struggles to take every breath, every step, not knowing if what lies beyond the next corner will be the end or not.
That is, however, me projecting my experience and empathizing with the main character and the creator of the game. It remains that the game is sometimes very unforgiving, and not in a Dark Souls-y "this game is hard and requires mastery and patience" sort of way, but in a way that will have you slamming your fist down on your desk/chair and yelling at the screen because the game's movement is not condusive to a fun puzzle/platformer environment. Proper platforming means knowing that the only reason you missed an action was because you messed up the timing, not because the game has some invisible barrier that you happened to clip that left you in range of the giant crushing block.
There are truly some furstrating moments that makes the disconnect between palyer and player-character widen to the point of furstration: just because I can't dash and swing a sword doesn't mean my character, who by all means the game tells me they can, should feel clunky in a game that demands reaction and speed.
But I wouldn't be here recommedning the game if I didn't enjoy it. I do think that the warp points are a little few and far between, and having to slog through the environment over and over again was, at times, unbearable. Still, the game is a gem and deserves a play through.
9/10 numerical score for this game: the only thing that keeps this from being a must play is the struggle that the game seems to want me to have to move in a meaninful way. Flow is important to me, and sometimes the narrative does not come before the execution of the controlls. Still, definitely a must buy/play if you like LoZ-style games.

Get ready for the fourth wall to break over and over again.  A mix of retro graphics and classic/casual gameplay with off-beat humor.
This is a game designed to be played in a single sitting (between 2 and 3 hours), then considered.  Even the final act of the game encrourages this.

So the first major Undertale-influenced game is already here: primitive looking game with surprisingly deep and original mechanics such as 4th wall breaks that occur in para-game territory (menus/save states/coding become part of the gameplay and narrative) and cheeky infantile aesthetics transgressed by semi-psychological horror elements, AND the illusion of linearity that is actually subverted by non-linear actions in a rhizome-like fashion as you dig deeper and deeper.
So it's KINDA subversive like Undertale, you know, that game you probably have played, except Undertale at least had you *literally* dicking around with the code in order to explore more game and story (I mean, if you really wanted to; trust me). Then again, all of this meta-game horror was being done 5 years ago by 9 Hours 9 Persons 9 Doors which you probably didn't play, AND 14 years ago by that masterpiece psychological horror game you definitely never played called Sanity's Requiem.
Don't get me wrong; this game is rad and you should buy it. Just, you know, play Sanity's Requiem and 999 and Undertale first.

Resident Evil 6 (or Camera Madness as it is called in Japan) is a camera hijacking simulator with some shaky zombie shooting mechanics.  Literally, you shake and vibrate like the guns are red bull incarnate, and every time you fire, your weapon forgets what you were shooting at.  There are in-game skills to mitigate but not cure this, and they take up 2 of the 3 skill slots if you choose to buy and equip them.  Basically, if you use them, you're STILL shooting worse than in RE4+5.
The objective of RE6 is to survive all of the camera hijinks that are thrown at you.  The camera, which is also severely infected by the shaking virus (the main villain), will wobble around wildly before, after and during most gameplay segments, and will shake into oblivion during cutscenes, which may or may not have QTEs (why?).  The camera's hatred for you is so strong that it sometimes disables you mid-fight, causing you to take damage or die.
I would much rather be able to skip cutscenes instead of having a hundred QTEs shoved into the game, which damages replay value... and this game is designed to accommodate multiple playthroughs.  It's amazing that they didn't learn their lesson:  The worst mistake in RE4 and RE5 were the QTEs.
Waiting for AI partners to complete objectives that you can't help with is occasionally pretty cumbersome.  Blow up that goddamn helicopter already, Chris.
If someone would take out the cutscenes, QTEs, slow-walking segments, sneaking segments, vehicle segments, and plot, that would be great.  I wish they had focused on more satisfying gunplay considering they had basically gotten this correct already in 2005 and have since forgotten how to do it.
Stop interrupting gameplay to show me that there are zombies.  Believe me, I know about the zombies.
I would recommend this game if the final boss was the player's camera, and you could murder it.

The whole point of BattleBlock Theater is to be absurd and hilarious, and it does it very well. It's a great party game, but the single-player campaign is equally entertaining.
From the first cutscene in the campaign, you'll be laughing your head off. After every set of levels, another cutscene will bring to light the unfortunate story of the island you're trapped on and the cat overlords that inhabit it. The cutscenes are filled with absurd gags. Sometimes the humor is very childish and immature, but handled in a way so that they're funnier for being childish than for the actual joke itself. All the while, the story gets more absurd with each cutscene.
Then, level by level, you'll be slowly making your way through a gauntlet of deadly platforming challenges to amuse your cat captors. After every death, the announcer will make light of your unfortunate demise. The levels are well-designed and challenging, and are only frustrating in a couple tricky spots. On rare occasion you will find "secret" rooms, where the announcer sings an absurd song constantly. Luckily it only takes a minute or to get everything in a secret room (even if you take your time), so you're out before it gets annoying.
The multiplayer is very well-designed. There is couch co-op if you manage to get a few Xbox controllers, and maybe have one unfortunate player use the keyboard, but there's also online multiplayer. The lag can be noticeable at times, but is less of an issue for a party game. There are a variety of multiplayer modes, but I've found Muckle (team deathmatch) to be the most fun. The game is a few years old though, so finding an online game without coordinating with friends can be difficult. As for co-op, every level is redesigned to require cooperation with your partner. Ironically, the game gives you plenty of opportunities to sabotage them, even encouraging you sometimes. Good luck trusting your friends.
This game is not a serious platformer, and doesn't try to be. It's a unique, entertaining experience that will stick in your mind for years.

The Rebuild series has known long and drawn out games. Where this title differentiates from its predecessor is in creating a narrative with a restart-and-repeat progression between cities (with the exception of a few of your best and brightest). Rebuild 3 has used this to expand its formula while maintaining a consistency familiar with its origin. The coupling of expanded narrative structure, with additional micro-tactics begs the question, "How much is too much?". Too readily the game buckles into a grind where each city feels mindlessly insignificant, yet progressing between cities takes an overwhelming effort. It succeeds neither in expanding into a “full retail” game, nor as game focused as an elegant economics-centered scenario management title, from which it evolved from. Rebuild 3 is not a great game, but it’s not a bad game either. For those into the genre, you will find at least a few hours of entertainment, but a lack of fulfilment with the title. For newcomers, it may break down as incessantly complicating what would otherwise be basic mechanics building on accessible principles—this game may be too overwhelming to get started with. I give this a pass, with reservation, and ultimately recommend the original for newcomers.

A survival/strategy game that reminds me of a cartoony, less serious, less survivor hate/drama Zafehouse Diaries. There is a 13-level single-player campaign (although two are skippable) which has a decent story and a special ending if you do certain things (that you can do when you replay levels).
You start with several plots of land as a base and you expand from there. You beat levels by allying (doing missions/trading to gain 100 respect) or eliminating all other factions (or on rare occasions by finding and repairing a plane to leave).
Survivors can spend turns guarding (better odds against incoming zombie mobs), attacking (necessary to clear adjacent plots to claim them), claiming land, scouting (to reveal fog of war), scavenging/farming (get equipment/food/building materials), recruiting survivors, doing diplomacy/trade with another faction, missions, or skill training at schools.
There are four skills: Soldier (Combat), Scavenger, Engineer (Research/Crafting), Builder, Leader (Recruitment/Trading/Happiness). Your avatar is the only one who can easily learn/use all skills at once. Everyone else is a specialist who can only gain skill levels in their one active skill (although you can make them do activities that use their off-skills and use schools to switch their active skill).
There are a few resources to manage: Food (used daily, gained mostly by owning farm plots/scavenging), Building Materials (used to expand/build, gained by scavenging/demolition), Happiness (lowers naturally/by events, gained by survivor management/bars/churches), Ammunition (used for firearms, gained by scavenging) and Crafting Supplies (Fuel/Medicine, used in events/crafting, gained by scavenging).
There is also a simple branching tech tree that gives bonuses/unlocks buildings if you send engineers to laboratories.
Worth a look if you like turn-based strategy games (this is kind of like a simple 4X game) and are fine with the zombie apocalypse/survival theme.

Wall of text incoming.
The gun fight mechanics in this game are absolutely amazing, when before in 4 and 5 you can only do certain actions like dodge only when an enemy is about to hit you by using a combination of keys, now its free, you can roll anywhere, slide and you can use those mechanics together, for instance rolling and holding aim will keep you on the ground aiming instead of instantly standing up after finishing the maneuver, you can also use melee freely whenever you want, where before you could only melee someone if you stunned them by a shot to the head or the leg, and you REALLY need to use melee because if you don't you're not going to have enough ammo and you'll end up meleeing a boss and good luck with that. those great mechanics are the game's best and worst part depending on who you are, yes i prefer the old Resident Evil formula and i don't particularily like how Resident evil became more focused on action and explosions but give credit when credit is due, the mechanics in this game are amazing.
This game bit a lot more than it could chew for me, it tried to combine everything in one game by making seperate character paths that are all part of one big story and those characters collide occasionally, the concept is really clever but sadly instead of making the game unparallelled, it makes it an average experience for each character, the game needs more time and you can feel how rushed some of the things are.
Ammo is more scarce which is again, a good thing or a bad thing depending on you, Resident evil games prior to 4 were all about thinking ahead and saving ammo whenever possible, back to the matter at hand, you can remedy the lack of ammo drops with a perk that increases the drop rate for different types of ammo.
But what about the core concept of a Resident evil game, Horror? well the game doesn't deliver at all in this aspect, leon's campaign path is supposed to return to the roots with the classic flesh eating zombies instead of "las plagas" or "uroboros"etc, granted in some parts of the game it gets really classic but all in all with the exception of a few jump scares there isn't anything to be scared of.
In terms of Storyline, it's... well there, that's what it is at best, you're going to have a few emotional moments and a few really badass ones but it's cliche and you can see what's going to happen miles away, very predictable, but playing through all 4 storylines will reveal a lot of the things you didn't understand or just took for granted which is really good.
However the game can get challenging sometimes which is always good, you'll die and some enemies are really tough, and the lack of ammunition (if you don't use melee efficiently) doesn't help either.
I have a few minor gripes, for instance the graphics are great but the textures really kill it sometimes, you're walking in this amazingly lighted and detailed enviroment and you look at the floor and it looks straight out of resident evil 4 (non-hd), really needed more time here.
Playing it with a mouse has this bug, a HUGE mouse lag that makes the game unplayable, there is a fix but it hinders you a bit, you're better off with a controller for this one.
Lastly i can recommend this game if you have a friend that can play it with you, having a friend will make this game extremely fun and will use the coop nature of it to the max, if not then if you can deal with the AI (which isn't that bad) then by all means go ahead.

The whole point of BattleBlock Theater is to be absurd and hilarious, and it does it very well. It's a great party game, but the single-player campaign is equally entertaining.
From the first cutscene in the campaign, you'll be laughing your head off. After every set of levels, another cutscene will bring to light the unfortunate story of the island you're trapped on and the cat overlords that inhabit it. The cutscenes are filled with absurd gags. Sometimes the humor is very childish and immature, but handled in a way so that they're funnier for being childish than for the actual joke itself. All the while, the story gets more absurd with each cutscene.
Then, level by level, you'll be slowly making your way through a gauntlet of deadly platforming challenges to amuse your cat captors. After every death, the announcer will make light of your unfortunate demise. The levels are well-designed and challenging, and are only frustrating in a couple tricky spots. On rare occasion you will find "secret" rooms, where the announcer sings an absurd song constantly. Luckily it only takes a minute or to get everything in a secret room (even if you take your time), so you're out before it gets annoying.
The multiplayer is very well-designed. There is couch co-op if you manage to get a few Xbox controllers, and maybe have one unfortunate player use the keyboard, but there's also online multiplayer. The lag can be noticeable at times, but is less of an issue for a party game. There are a variety of multiplayer modes, but I've found Muckle (team deathmatch) to be the most fun. The game is a few years old though, so finding an online game without coordinating with friends can be difficult. As for co-op, every level is redesigned to require cooperation with your partner. Ironically, the game gives you plenty of opportunities to sabotage them, even encouraging you sometimes. Good luck trusting your friends.
This game is not a serious platformer, and doesn't try to be. It's a unique, entertaining experience that will stick in your mind for years.

For Honor is tough to describe. It's one of those games you hate to love. One minute you're beating a dude's head in, the next he's playing an overpowered character that won't get nerfed for a whole season.
Then you find a new opponent , which takes a pretty long time, and they're brand new to the game. So you teach them a thing or two and you fight them three weeks later and they're just as good as you now, and it's great and you're crying tears of joy as they rip your character's head off.
Then you find another opponent who's 40 levels higher than you and knows their character too well. You try and find a new person to play against, and you get them again. And again. And again.
Then you do it again, and whoever you're fighting leaves after you perfect them once, and you end up fighting bots that are tough as nails  (as of Season 4).
For Honor is a game that has all of the negatives of a fighting game (balancing, toxicity, unfair matchups, turtle tactics) and all of the negatives of an online game (no dedicated servers, penalties for players kicked out due to a bug that's been in the game since beta, laggy players, and weird errors), but has enough ingenuity that makes you want to love this game.
If you like Dark Souls PVP, Chivalry, 3-D fighting games, then give For Honor a try. It isn't for anyone. And you need to be extremely patient (both in fights, and with the game), but the second you land your first max damage combo as Raider, you'll know why this game is great.
Definetly flawed, but has great potential. Watch out for salt, though.

This is a promising game.  At the moment (Alpha 0.9, as I write this), the controls are clunky and there are a couple of odd bugs but it is playable and you can see the potential for a fun game.  It's kind of like a cross between Space Engineers and Factorio.
Pros:
- Systems (electricity, water, oxygen etc) are fun to assemble and pretty flexible.
- Gameplay concepts are pretty intuitive.
- Well designed machine models.
Cons:
- UI/UX is unpolished (your mouse does double duty as a pointer and view control, forcing you to change between states)
- Controls are clumsy (it'd be great to have a single 'use' button that recognises context)
- Player models are rudimentary and animations are very basic
- The world isn't really 'open' (if you run far enough it boots you back to the galaxy map)
- The written instructions (in the English localization) need a native English speaker to correct them.
Most of the cons should be ironed out as development proceeds. Of course, that all depends on the developer.  I'll give them the benefit of the doubt for now and recommend this game.  Make note: my recommendation is only for people who enjoy playing early access titles. This is NOT a polished final game at this stage.

1) English:
This is an early review that i would update with a few more hours of play and a few more patches.
Farlight Explorers is about surviving and building an automated base to cover all your needs for food and oxygen in a procedurally generated planet that you previously chose from a galaxy map. As far as i know, there are 5 types of planets you can choose or visit someday with the appropriate technology: desert, ice, gas, pure iron and asteroid.
Once you choose a planet, you crash into it and start the game with a few ship modules randomly dispersed through all the map that you can loot for resources. Apart from that, you need to create a base from the scratch, mining minerals to start crafting the machines you will need: solar generators, water pumps, oxygen and food generators, batteries to store the solar energy, ore extractors, furnaces, research machinery and a lot more.
The game is very stable with no crashes at all and character movement, although sometimes feels a little strange, is very fluid and precise.
The machines are just awesome, beautifully designed and the sky at night with all the stars you can see is also amazing.
The placement system, in my opinion, is a little confusing. You need to wire all machines to the power generators once placed and sometimes you don't know how and where to connect those wires.
This is one of the EA games more stables i played at release date and can have a brilliant future. As for now, you can play a lot of hours only to just create your base, test all machines and make automation.
2) Versión Español:
Este es un análisis que actualizaré con algunas horas más de juego y tras algunos parches.
Farlight Explorers es un juego de supervivencia y construcción de una base automatizada para cubrir todas tus necesidades de comida y oxígeno en un planeta generado proceduralmente y que previamente has elegido desde el mapa de la galaxia. Por ahora, que yo haya visto, hay 5 tipos de planetas que puedes elegir o visitar algún día con la tecnología apropiada: desierto, hielo, gas, todo hierro y asteroide.
Una vez has seleccionado un planeta, te estrellas en él y empieza el juego propiamente dicho con algunos módulos de tu nave caída dispersos aleatoriamente a través del mapa y en los que podrás encontrar recursos. Aparte de esto, necesitas crear una base desde cero, minando minerales para comenzar a crear las máquinas que necesitas: generadores solares (seguidores solares muy realistas pero más bonitos que los que existen ahora, claro), bombas de agua, generadores de comida y oxígeno, baterías para almacenar la energía solar, extractores de mineral, hornos de fundición, maquinaria de investigación y muchas más.
El juego es muy estable sin una sola petada y el movimiento del personaje, aunque algunas veces parece algo extraño, es muy fluído y preciso.
Las máquinas son, simplemente, impresionantes con un diseño muy bonito y el cielo por la noche con todas las estrellas que se ven es también asombroso.
El sistema de colocación de los bloques, en mi opinión, es algo confuso. Tienes que conectar todas las máquinas a los generadores de electricidad una vez colocadas y a veces no sabes ni cómo ni dónde conectar el cableado.
En definitiva, este es uno de los juegos "EA" más estables que he jugado el mismo día del lanzamiento y puede tener un futuro brillante. Por ahora, se le pueden sacar muchas horas para construir la base, probar todas las máquinas y automatizar todos los procesos.

I don't review games often.  Or much at all.  But for some reason I felt the need to write one for this game.
I also wrote this review day 1 of release, so don't judge this review too accurate a few updates down the line.
To start off, the controls are a bit wonky (mostly just the space bar switching between cursor and viewing mode).  That's probably my biggest pet peave of this game.  Otherwise the controls seem fine.
You choose the solar system and planet you want to start on, which is kinda cool.  I like that.  The mining is a bit wonky in visuals, a laser just pops from your nipples like rays of victory, but in reality you're shooting from a gun you can't see.
The planet has nice atmosphere (no pun intended) and desert planets feel like desert planets.  So far I haven't seen any other, although I'm not sure you're able to yet.  Haven't checked.
The wiring system and water piping is a bit wonky as well, there should be a 4-way connecter to help this sort of thing out, but instead you just place them on on top of the other facing different ways, which sometimes works, and sometimes just looks rather silly.
The Ore Extractor seems a bit glitchy and wont always extract ore, although it's day 1 so I'm not too picky.  The robotic arms will fling rocks or whatever it is they are moving, not just directly behind them, but if they are elavated, behind and to the side, a ways.  While this would be ideal for practicing some baseball, not so helpful when the furnace is not gettin any dlicious iron to feast on.
The good parts, however, outweigh the bad ones.
It's challenging (slightly, mostly just to figure out how everything works together) to get your base all set up and automated, which is a good thing I think, makes your finished base give you a good sense of accompishment.
The artwork is pretty sweet.
The sound affects of the machines are delightful.
The game isn't broken as far as I can tell.  The few bugs I've noticed are rare and not game breaking.
Runs pretty smoothly.

Farlight Explorers starts off in a procedurally generated galaxy. Selecting which planet you which to colonize and proceeding to land you then get to work scanning the unknown surface for raw materials to forge into base components. Thankfully your ship contained enough food and oxygen for several days so you stand some chance of survival.
The initial aim of the game as mentioned is to survive. While I have not run into hostile creatures yet I assume they exist as you are able to craft weapons, turrets and body armour. There seemed no dire need to focus on these and your time and resources were better spent on setting up a self-sustained base. Main structures all needed to be placed on platforms but there were elevators and other craftables for multistory designs. Most of these required power or water, which all had to be connected with pipes or wires like lego pieces before they would function correctly.
Advanced construction seemed to be focused on automating processes. Combining conveyer belts, robot arms and furnaces you're able to setup supply lines for harvesting resources much faster. Characters are able to research tech trees which seemed mostly focused on making things more efficient, quicker mining speed, lower power draw etc. Another aspect of the game I've not touched yet was the spacecraft building. Traveling around the surface you will discover space junk (which you see fall from the skies), searching these piles results in finding harder to make items and many parts for your ship. Once you construct the ship apparently you're able to travel between planets and setup trade routes, which should be a bunch of fun. :)
One of the other items your character started with was a jetpack, with unlimited fuel no less. You're able to fly up, rotate on axis and fall from great heights, all planets I visited seemed to have moon-like gravity. Overall the controls and user interface were quite good, placement of objects and player movement seemed intuitive though I'm sure the animations, graphics and layouts will be refined with time.
For initial release Farlight Explorers is a solid game and I found myself wanting to play more. After several hours play I ran into no major problems at all, so if you enjoy these kind of games it's well worth shortlisting. Cheers.

An extremely predictable LP/stream bait game. The plot is akin to a generic creepy pasta, so it doesn't scratch pretty deep to begin with. Thematically, it just jumps straight into being unsettling, leaving no real surprise when it becomes more and more satanic as the game progresses. The attempts to include biblical references are also pretty sloppy. This may come from the game being unsure if it's supposed to be funny or spooky. The music is pretty good, but equally as repetitive.
As you can probably assume from the screenshots, the gameplay is rubbish. You jump over hurdles and shoot your lazer. It never really gets difficult in any way, in that you have infinite tries in every single situation, including the final and secret final bosses.
The puzzle sections of the game are somewhat interesting in concept, being a sort of sequence puzzle, but it expects the player to be dumb as a stump and never pushes the complexity past a few minutes of trial and error.
In a game about breaking the 4th wall, it doesn't do enough with that concept. I expected a lot more player interaction but in the end I found the game was just funneling my choices by barring me from siding with the satanic voice comming from inside the game. For example, at one point in the game you are forced to cheat in order to get a lazer beam, but soon after the satan voice tells you to turn off the cheat. I tried to, to see if I could for some extra dialogue and the game had disabled the option to. It's things like this which turn a 4th wall breaking experience into an on the rails no fun allowed snorefest.
The only part that actually caught me by surprise was
I would love to see more things like that, where the fail state is a little more obscure and open ended than just dieing in a minigame and having to restart.
Basically, don't buy it unless you're a markiplier clone.

“Guide a group of rectangles through a series of obstacles, using their different skills together to get to the end of each environment.”
What made this game truly stand out was the characterisation.
This could have easily had no story to it and just focused on the blocks reaching the end of the level. But instead, each level has a voiceover and dialogue which progresses a story, and shows the personalities of each of the blocks that appear in the game.
The dialogue is witty and well done, and you really do find yourself caring about that motely bunch of rectangles that you're controlling, which is unexpected. You wouldn't think you could get attached to something that was just a colourful block, but this game does it. The dialogue can make you laugh and it goes in with the levels and the tasks the blocks have to go through.
It just goes to show that a good story and good characterisation can make even the most minimalistic of games an emotional experience where you care about the things you are controlling, to the point where failing puzzles isn't so bad.
The controls are smooth, they work fine with keyboard and gamepad and were responsive, I didn't make many awkward jumps or struggle with obstacles due to this. The loading screen sometimes took a while and made it feel not so smooth.
The graphics are very simple, the colour scheme is good so you can identify everything well between the rectangles and obstacles offered. One interesting effect about the graphics was how the light on a block followed you as you moved, making it seem more advanced and visually easier to follow what was going on. It probably isn't so noticeable unless you were really concentrating.
For a puzzle game, this has really relaxing music, which is nice considering puzzle games can at times get your brain really crunching in how to solve something, or stress you out. The music helps make it a more enjoyable process. The sounds itself help give character for the whole experience. The different sounds the boxes make give each one insight to their personalities, and the voiceover with an english accent is soothing and fits right in with the background music and the individual noises the rectangles make. This all combines together to make the game even more compelling beyond its simple visuals, and not many games can do something like that

This is one of those games where "playing it" doesn't improve upon  the overall experience. There is an interesting little story here and absolutely superb narration by Danny Wallace, but that is really all the game has going for it.
Thomas Was Alone is a puzzle platformer that doesn't get either the puzzles or the platforming right. You control a series of blocks and must guide each of them to their specific exit on any given level. Each block has their own unique ability, some allowing for double jumps and others allowing other blocks to bounce off them, but the game never comes up with anything interesting for them to do along the way. The jumps are basic, and the puzzles never amount to much more than "stack a block on top of the other blocks, now jump on that block" and that's basically it. One level had me build six of the same staircases in a row because apparently solving the "puzzle" once wasn't enough. There just aren't any interesting ideas here, not one single clever puzzle in the entire game. It gets so bad whenever narration would start up I'd just stop playing to listen to it, because it was literally the only thing interesting about the entire game.
Thomas Was Alone tells a good story and tells it well, but as a game this fails on just about every level. You could watch a friend play it or see someone else play it on YouTube and have exactly the same experience. It isn't worth buying as a "game" because it never really gives you a reason to want to play it. Watch someone else do it instead if you're interested in the story and save your money for something else.

Despite recommending this game, my feedback is qualified: I cannot really put in words the disappointment I felt when, with the game's settings universally set to Ultra, the first reveal of the game (when you emerge from the warhouse that Prohphet shot himself in the head in) showed that I was playing a sequel that looked quite some distance worse than the groundbreaking original.
I say this not because I'm a shallow graphics-♥♥♥♥♥, though of course I am to a certain extent, but because the immersion breaking consequences of a massive dropoff in technical achievement thoroughly robbed this experience of anything approaching the uber-ambitious gameplay - and the CURCIAL sense of wonder - of the original. Frankly, the buildings of NYC in this game look like they've been transplanted from a rushed-out-the-door licensed Spiderman game from the mid-00s, and how am I supposed to feel like a badass when the - let's admit it - utterly cheesball design of my character is the best looking part of a game that was spawned from a ground breakingly, heart achingly beautiful game?
It goes beyond the graphical achievements of the game, though. I understand that all of this downscaling was done as a result of the move to consoles, and I understand that by now I'm looking at a game that was scaled for the xbox 360 - there's no way it'll look anything like Metro 2033 Redux, for example - but I just cannot deny that the game is just less fun than the original was. In this game you basically move down linear coridoors - albiet city-street-sized coridoors - with the megerest of alternate routes threaded around them, whereas in the original (If you haven't guessed it now then I am indeed saying that Crysis should be bought immediately without delay if you haven't played it yet, certainly in preference to this game) one had what truly felt like a wide open island environment to cloak, drive, or blast your way around.
Okay, so the game is uglier and more constricted than the game it was supposed to be a sequel to. So why have I recommended that you get it? Because it's a good shooter on it's own, and when sales time comes around it is going to be worth picking up. Put it on your wishlist and bide your time, you
get a good looking, tight shooter with tactical combat and a lot of fun additional gameplay tweaks, with a bit more character building (not story development, character building) than the original thrown in. Get it. If it's on sale.
If you haven't played Crysis, do so immediately.

I find chess complicated - and I kid you not. I never was a fan and I don't think I will ever get a hang of playing it. Ever.
And yet here I am giving a thumbs-up to a game that's basically an evolution of that game. Or maybe it's chess on steroids. I don't know why I am hooked on it.
Maybe it's because you play out of a hand - which is more liberating and more variable than chess. It takes inspiration from a lot of games both old and even new, and makes it better.
I am not limited to diagonal, straight-line, or L-shape movements - I have six factions to build my army from, offering a load of uniquely designed minions and spells in colorful 8-bit artworks. A pawn can victoriously become your knight or queen with the right combination of cards. (and a little bit of luck on the draw)
Or maybe it's the fact that matches are short and sweet (and brutally satisfying) yet always different in every way due to the multitude of options the game throws at you.
Or perhaps it's the fact that it made me think of chess out of the blue - maybe getting a grip of "two steps ahead" will help me ladder. How it makes me wish that I knew the age old game better.
It's colorful. It's complex. It's addicting. It's Duelyst.

The War of 1812 was a military conflict that lasted from June 18, 1812 to February 18, 1815, fought by the United States of America against Great Britain, its North American colonies, and its North American Indian allies. Historians in the United States and Canada see it as a war in its own right, but Europeans sometimes see it as a minor theatre of the Napoleonic Wars, as it was caused by issues related to that war (especially the Continental System). By the war's end in early 1815 the key issues had been resolved and peace came with no boundary changes.
The United States declared war for several reasons, including trade restrictions brought about by the British war with France, the impressment of as many as 10,000 American merchant sailors into the Royal Navy,[5] British support for Native American tribes fighting American settlers on the frontier, outrage over insults to national honor during the Chesapeake–Leopard Affair, and possible American interest in annexing British territory.[6] The primary British war goal was to defend their North American colonies, although they also hoped to set up a neutral Indian buffer state in the Midwest.
The war was fought in three theatres. First, at sea, warships and privateers of each side attacked the other's merchant ships, while the British blockaded the Atlantic coast of the United States and mounted large raids in the later stages of the war. Second, land and naval battles were fought on the U.S.–Canadian frontier. Third, large-scale battles were fought in the Southern United States and Gulf Coast. At the end of the war, both sides signed and ratified the Treaty of Ghent and, in accordance with the treaty, returned occupied land, prisoners of war and captured ships (though neither side returned the other's warships due to frequent re-commissioning upon capture) to its pre-war owner and resumed friendly trade relations without restriction.
With the majority of its land and naval forces tied down in Europe fighting the Napoleonic Wars, the British used a predominantly defensive strategy in the Provinces of Upper and Lower Canada. Early victories over poorly-led U.S. armies, such as in the Battle of Queenston Heights, demonstrated that the conquest of the Canadas would prove more difficult than anticipated. Despite this, the U.S. was able to inflict serious defeats on Britain's Native American allies, ending the prospect of an Indian confederacy and an independent Native American state in the Midwest under British sponsorship. U.S. forces were also able to make several gains and score victories on the Canadian frontier; taking control of Lake Erie in 1813, seizing western parts of Upper Canada. However, a large-scale U.S. attempt to capture Montreal was repulsed in November 1813. Despite the major U.S. victory at Chippawa on July 5, 1814, serious U.S. attempts to fully conquer Upper Canada were ultimately abandoned following the bloody Battle of Lundy's Lane on July 25, 1814. The U.S. then fell back roughly 30 km (19 mi) from Lundy's Lane to Fort Erie, where they withstood a siege for several months. The British eventually withdrew, but as winter set in, the Americans demolished the fort and fell back across the Niagara.
In April 1814, with the defeat of Napoleon, the British adopted a more aggressive strategy, sending larger invasion armies and tightening their naval blockade. However, with the end of the Napoleonic Wars in Europe, both governments were eager for a return to normality and peace negotiations began in Ghent in August 1814. In the Deep South, General Andrew Jackson destroyed the military strength of the Muscogee (Creek) Nation at the Battle of Horseshoe Bend. In September 1814, the British won the Battle of Hampden, allowing them to occupy eastern Maine, and the British victory at the Battle of Bladensburg in August 1814 allowed them to capture and burn Washington, D.C. They were repulsed, however, in an attempt to take Baltimore and Fort Bowyer, and during their assault at Fayal. An American victory in September 1814 at the Battle of Plattsburgh repulsed the British invasions of New York, which, along with pressure from merchants on the British government, prompted British diplomats to drop their demands at Ghent for an independent native buffer state and territorial claims that London previously sought. Given that it took six weeks for ships to cross the Atlantic, news of the peace treaty did not arrive before the British suffered a major defeat at New Orleans in January 1815.[7]
In the United States, late victories over invading British armies at the battles of Plattsburg, Baltimore (inspiring the United States national anthem, "The Star-Spangled Banner") and New Orleans produced a sense of euphoria over a "second war of independence" against Britain.[8][9] The war ended on a high note for Americans, winning the final engagements of the war and bringing an "Era of Good Feelings" in which partisan animosity nearly vanished in the face of strengthened American nationalism. The war was also a major turning point in the development of the U.S. military. The poor performance of several U.S. militia units, particularly during the 1812–13 invasions of Canada and the 1814 defence of Washington, convinced the U.S. government of the need to move away from its Revolutionary-era reliance on militia and focus on creating a more professional regular force. Spain was involved in fighting in Florida but was not an official belligerent; some Spanish forces fought alongside the British during the Occupation of Pensacola. The U.S. took permanent ownership of Spain's Mobile District.
In Upper and Lower Canada, British and local Canadian militia victories over invading U.S. armies became iconic and promoted the development of a distinct Canadian identity, which included strong loyalty to Britain. Today, particularly in Ontario, memory of the war retains its significance, because the defeat of the invasions ensured that the Canadas would remain part of the British Empire, rather than be annexed by the United States. In Canada, numerous ceremonies took place in 2012 to commemorate the war, offer historical lessons and celebrate 200 years of peace across the border.[10] The conflict has not been commemorated on nearly the same level in the modern-day United States, though it is still taught as an important part of early American history,[11] and Dolley Madison's and Andrew Jackson's respective roles in the war are especially emphasized.[12][13] The war is scarcely remembered in Britain, being heavily overshadowed by the much larger Napoleonic Wars occurring in Europe.

While Rebuild 3 has a lot of deeply admirable traits going for it, it can't escape the fact that its core gameplay is slow, repetitive, and lacking in meaningful choice.
Leading a band of survivors in a post-zombie apocalypse, it's your duty to expand your borders while protecting from zombie hoards, forage for food and items, grow food, manage your people's happiness, and rebuild a proper and diverse city infrastructure. You do this through 5 skills/classes.
Unfortunately, all of this happens in very simple ways: You assign a task, preferrably to a unit who is currently training in that skill, and let them complete it. Soldiers sit there clearing zombie hoards, farmers stay in place growing food, leaders sit in place preaching or tending bar. While you will have to re-assign people to new locations frequently, it's rare to face an interesting choice. With a little bit of a thought, it becomes an easy task of rinse and repeat. Once assigned, your troops carry out their task until completed.
The UI has ups and downs. In some areas it's easy to click through and get what you need menu-wise, and nothing was awful, but sometimes I found myself clicking way more than I wanted, or getting confused which menu lead to which similar screen, or not being able to easily compare information. The click-and-drag map scrolling sometimes gets caught on placed-worker tokens, resulting in moving the workers instead of the map; this happens even when you click near, but not on, the worker token.
I think the game shines with the loving details put into flavor and story. I don't know if I'd say anything blew my socks off with awesomeness, but it touched me with how much heart was put into it. It was neat that in different levels the movie theater quipped about waiting for a movie, but a different movie each level. In quest dialogue, something similar- someone might lament about missing their favorite [blank], but the item would be different each time the quest came up. The factions, while cartoonishly overdone on the outside, had interesting text and flavor and choices that they presented you with. Within a quest, text and dialogue tended to make a lot of sense. A scene was painted with words, not just "bring me x widgets". Your survivors each had their own personal survival tale, which they would reveal to you in 3 parts as they hit level-up milestones. Each character also was given 3 skill choices per levelup, and at least one tended to match the character's backstory, and not their class. Random quests popped up, enriching the play-through with both strategic pluses/minuses, and more story and flare.
There may be a lot more content that I didn't yet get to- and maybe that would spice up the game. The achievement descriptions lead me to believe that there are at least a few more things that I hadn't yet seen. But the problem was- after dozens of hours- I didn't care to play more to see anything further. The core gameplay, even on harder difficulties, felt simple, repetitive, and predictable to me. There were too few things for each class to do, and too many *obviously* correct/incorrect choices to make. The most fun probably came on a level where my random-results recruitment lead to me only having members of the scavenger class. Which my options and resources extremely limited, for a short while every decision felt tense and interesting. As soon as I regained a normal spread of classes, all of this died away as characters efficiently, boringly sat on their normal tiles and waited for their timer to complete.
I would deeply root for this game's creator in a future sequel. There's a lot to like here, especially in the very loving details and more-than-expected text descriptions and stories. The core gameplay is almost fun, but needs a few more choices and sources of tension to make the game more than just an exercise in repetition.

For Honor is a Medieval melee competitve fighting game based around the factions of Knights, Vikings and Samurai fighting for control of the world.  It is primarily multiplayer based, but does have a decent single player campaign to provide backstory and act as a extended tutorial.
The Good:
+Everything about the visuals are amazing, from the graphics to the animation of the fighters
+Runs very well on my set-up with only one hard crash over 550+ hours (Intel i5 3570K 3.4GHz. Radoen RX 480 8GB, 16GB RAM)
+Decent single player campaign that takes around 5-6 hours the first time with replay value on higher difficulties and collectables
+Fantastic and brutal combat based on mind games and reactions with each character having their own specials moves and playstyles
+Variety of game modes with 4v4 objective based modes like Domination and Tribute as well as 1v1 and 2v2 fights
+Good customization of each individual characters with armor pieces, colors and effects.
+Great sound design with the clanking of armor, metal striking metal and charcters speaking thier "native" language (Knights=Latin, Vikings=Icelandic, Samurai=Japanese)
The Bad
-Connection Issues.  I personally haven't been a massive victim of this, but many people experience disconnections constantly due to the P2P system Ubisoft uses for the 4v4 modes.  They do plan on adding Dedicated servers to the game soon as of this review.
-Character and gameplay balance.  The biggest problem this game is it's gameplay and character balance.  Now, as of this review, all of the DLC characters have been released for the game.  The problem is that playing the vanilla characters againist many of the DLC characters is like you are playing Divekick while your opponent is playing Tekken 7.  Many of the vanilla characters are getting reworks but that is far into the future.
-Toxicity.  Like almost all online competive game, there is bound to be ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s being ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s.  For Honor is no expection.  There are still good or decent people playing, but they don't use chat to avoid these toxic pieces of♥♥♥♥♥♥
I really love this game, despite it's flaws.  I would recommed picking it up if you are looking for different competive fighting game from the norm or like brutal sword-based combat.

An extremely predictable LP/stream bait game. The plot is akin to a generic creepy pasta, so it doesn't scratch pretty deep to begin with. Thematically, it just jumps straight into being unsettling, leaving no real surprise when it becomes more and more satanic as the game progresses. The attempts to include biblical references are also pretty sloppy. This may come from the game being unsure if it's supposed to be funny or spooky. The music is pretty good, but equally as repetitive.
As you can probably assume from the screenshots, the gameplay is rubbish. You jump over hurdles and shoot your lazer. It never really gets difficult in any way, in that you have infinite tries in every single situation, including the final and secret final bosses.
The puzzle sections of the game are somewhat interesting in concept, being a sort of sequence puzzle, but it expects the player to be dumb as a stump and never pushes the complexity past a few minutes of trial and error.
In a game about breaking the 4th wall, it doesn't do enough with that concept. I expected a lot more player interaction but in the end I found the game was just funneling my choices by barring me from siding with the satanic voice comming from inside the game. For example, at one point in the game you are forced to cheat in order to get a lazer beam, but soon after the satan voice tells you to turn off the cheat. I tried to, to see if I could for some extra dialogue and the game had disabled the option to. It's things like this which turn a 4th wall breaking experience into an on the rails no fun allowed snorefest.
The only part that actually caught me by surprise was
I would love to see more things like that, where the fail state is a little more obscure and open ended than just dieing in a minigame and having to restart.
Basically, don't buy it unless you're a markiplier clone.

Thomas Was Alone could have been a pretty good game, if only the creators had not thought it a good idea to "enhance" gameplay by including really bad controls. First of all, do not try to play this game with a keyboard, because the keys do not respond quickly enough. Secondly, even with a controller the controls suck. When you jump, you have to keep pushing the movement key in the direction of where you want to jump, because when you let go of it, you immediately start falling straight down. This is awkward and completely different from regular controls of platform games. The problem is that as soon as you land, you have to let go of the controls in that instant, otherwise you slide further, and usually drop down into a pit or in a killing liquid, meaning that you have to start the level all over again. This game was obviously designed to make players empathize with the blocks and tell a story that way, which does not mesh with the hamfisted and frustrating control scheme selected by the designers.
Beyond that, the music is really awful and annoying. But you can turn that off. The color choices are also pretty bad, as on a tablet this game is almost impossible to play because of brightness issues -- which you cannot control in-game. Voice acting is brilliant, though.
Maybe I am just not mentally equipped to enjoy frustration in games. Or maybe I am just someone who prefers to get things done rather than starting over and over and over again. Or maybe I am just not good enough at juggling controls. Probably all three. Still, I cannot recommend this game -- at least not to people like me.
It is leagues better than "I Am Bread" in this respect, though. "I Am Bread" just had a disgusting control scheme chosen by the designers because they thought it would be "fun" to frustrate players. The control scheme of "Thomas Was Alone" simply was an honest but poor choice on the part of designers.

Note: My time played in this is off by 45 hours as I played it a lot while my internet was down for 2 weeks. Other reviews complain about timing issues. It isn't a bug. It's a design decision that some people just won't be a fan of. It takes some practice to get good at.
This is my favourite game of 2016. To start off, it's absolutely beautiful. The camera moves with such purpose that you feel like you're being pushed from one carefully composed artwork to the next. The world is lovely. It feels like it has history and atmoshpere. One thing that I noticed after a while is how little text is in the game. Besides a few tutorial pointers the whole story and all the gameplay that's introduced is done visually. It does an incredible amount with the medium and no exposition.
The combat is very, very challenging but oh so satisfying when you get it right. There are a lot of Dark Souls-esque elements such as when you die the monsters respawn in the same place so after a while you know where they all are. The combat has an incredible blend of ranged and melee that blends so seemlessly together that when you get it right you feel like a gun-fu master. The bosses are great too. Challenging but never frustrating. In the entire game I never felt like my dying was the fault of the game. I made a mistake and I died.
I played with a controller, but I've also played a bit with a mouse and keyboard and both are totally fine. I see a few reviews complaining about the timing when multi-dashing. The timing is a kind of ramp up in that time between the first dash and the second is slower than the time between the second and third dash etc. But after a few dashes the timing flattens out and becomes consistent. It just takes some practice to get used to and I really doubt that it's a "bug". It's just a design decision that some people aren't a fan of.
I could write 5000 words about why this game is great. It reminds me of so many things that make me love games the way I do. All you should know is that I love it and it's been absolutely worth the $20 I paid for it. A beautiful and tough but fair game that's absolutely worth your time. It's very difficult for me to fully explain why I love it so much. Every time I play it just makes me really happy.

An arena mode which can be played in local or online don't kill each other or do kill each other modes (also online or        local OR with AI)
Furbottom's features, which lets you play community generated levels or level playlists
A level editor which lets you free with every block in the game (you can also make your own playlist)
Gift shop where you can buy new heads for your character, or weapons, with the gems and wool you get in levels
PLENTY of other multiplayer modes which you can, of course create in the level editor

One of the best Card games out there in my opinion. You have almost infinite possibilities with the deck creation. You can build a deck that satisfies your needs and you won't be disappointed.

If you want a really good card game, with great strategy and community, where you can play the best decks, go play Android: Netrunner on
(seriously, fantastic game and using jinteki you get access to every card in the game). If you want rankings, join an online league. (A:NR is a Live Card Game, a LCG. So no randomisation of card packs)
However, if you want a really good card game that's also a grind, this is is better. Playing a reasonable amount - a few hours a day after work, a few more than that on the weekends - you get to open about 1 booster a day of play. It's fun to slowly (very slowly, to be fair) build up your collection. Dismantling a few cards to craft new ones you need to improve your decks to make it easily to win games and get the gold you need to buy more boosters and get more packs.
I focus on this last point becuase I thinks it's the only thing that makes me play it over A:NR, the working towards a collection.
However, I play it over other CCGs such as Magic and HS because it is a superior game. The mechanics are more fun, it's less pay to win, a budget deck can perform well against decks with legendary cards. It's a mix between card game and board game. It reminds me of the board game Summoner Wars, but you can't play that online with the same sort of development support.
Overall, I think this game is good fun, I really enjoy it! But it's a huge time sink - beware before you play. I also believe the cost to buy 'orbs', the game's booster packs are too expensive for what you get. If you want to play everything, and not drop loads of money/time before you can, please go check out Netrunner on
first.

- The levels, follower perk system, and equipment management are painfully tedious and repetitive. I had enough after the 7th city.

-Fast pacing with action packed set pieces
-Encourages multiple playthroughs by giving different perspectives of each character
-Arcade style bonus modes which allow you to get skill points for power upgrades
-Fantastic voice overs (even though some of the dialogue is cheesy)
-Unlike Resident Evil 5, AI partner cannot die and has unlimited ammo/health.
Cons:
-Graphics show a bit of age. Some textures look ugly/low res up close. Contrast issues (some super dark locations and some super bright areas)
-Fighting the same boss that mutates/regenerates multiple times throughout the story.
-AI partner can be dumb and cause you to die in some sequences.
Overall, fantastic game. If you like action games with Resident Evil characters you'll enjoy this title. If you like living in the past and get off by trying to unlock doors with helmet or shield emblems you might not.

A solid platformer with an even better soundtrack wrapped up in a brilliant story laced with wit and told with a childlike innocence while dealing with heavy themes.
This is a game about humanity's base desire for companionship, about finding our purpose and individuality and how others can help us find it.  The characters (all AI) are fully formed, all sympathetic and multifaceted; they just happen to all be quadrilaterals.  To some extent, this game is about watching them grow, almost like children.  They begin finding out more about the world around them, later meeting others who are like them, discovering their unique nature and the fact that they all want to change the world for the better.  Yet, before all this comes one thing: the aching need for someone else, as demonstrated by the game's titular first words from the narrator: "Thomas was alone."
The fact that all this is accomplished with nothing but shapes on a screen and the words of a narrator is the real joy of this game.  Thomas Was Alone is a perfect example of how interactive experiences (otherwise known as video games) can connect with people when using so little.

This was an excellent simplistic puzzle game that managed to draw me into the story of the little blocks I was controlling. When I first started playing, I was skeptical that it would interest me overmuch, but Thomas and friends managed to grab me and hold my attention until I had wrung every last bit of fun out of it. Very highly recommended.

Having this gifted to me from a friend who got the humble bundle I decided to try it out. Of course this is coming off of just this game not the series as a whole.
I am fully aware that the first game one makes on RPG Maker isn't really the best one or the one where the creator puts most of their dedication to perfect. This could have been a game that was probably used to flesh out the skills the creator needed for the rest of the series. If that was the case then I don't see why the game wasn't just one giant game rather than 4 different episodes. This would have allowed for seeing what lacked in certain parts and add a bit of more repolishing to it. The reason I bring this up is cause while the gameplay wasn't bad, as someone who uses RPG Maker to design his own games, I felt it lacking.
This first episode suffers something that a game like this should not have, it is too short for it's own good. There isn't much time to get to know the characters as the game instantly sets you up into a dire situation you have to get out of. There is no time to learn the characters and grow attached to them which is what a first episode is usually meant for. This in my own opinion is heavily detremental to a game as a whole.
Another thing that felt off to me is that the characters didn't have different face portraits for different pieces of diolouge. While not necessarily a major issue it does somewhat take away the experience of emmersing your player into the world by making your characters feel a bit more alive. It doesn't make sense for someone who is worried about your character to be smirking or for a character to be smiling while things are going sour. A few other facial expressions for the characters other than the standard ones would have been a way to resolve this. A few minutes off your time to make various portaits of the same character with different expressions doesn't take much time especially if you are using VX Ace's character creator.
The story itself felt like it went barely anywhere. It kinda felt like everything that happened in this game just happened to have it happen. Again going back to the fact that it seemed to be too short for it's own good. None of the scenarios you go through felt very fleshed out in this episode.
I do not know if these issues are fixed in the future episodes for I have yet to try them. However, this episode was not a very good start. It was ok but it wasn't up to my expictations of what the start of a series should be like. I cannot recommend this episode in particular. I'll eventually see what the others have to offer but if anything I can almost garuntee you can skip this episode and you will not have much of an issue understanding the rest of the game.
This is a fun short rpg with a interesting story. I got it from a bundle and was suprised by how enjoyable I found it. Hope the next episodes are also good.

I bought this as part of the Humble micro Bundle, it’s not something I would normally choose and it’s the first RPG Maker game I have played. It’s a 2.5D, pixel art, point and click adventure set in space and would normally cost £0.90 on Steam. I completed in the game in just under 2 hours with 7/7 achievements.
Things didn’t get off to a good start; episode one launched in teeny tiny windowed mode with no options available on the start menu or in game to change this. I used Alt + Return to get the game to full screen but it was stuck in 800 x 600 resolution. About 20 minutes into the game I pressed F12 in a vain attempt to take a screen shot and received the message “script ‘mouse support’ line 131: RGSSerror occurred. Dispose sprite” and the game closed without saving. There are actually no auto-save points, this needs to be done manually.
The story and characters (in episode one at least) are largely as two dimensional as the visuals, and the dialogue can be a bit stale. Everything felt a bit generic and the plot was a tad on the simple side, with events/puzzles playing out a bit too conveniently. There was nothing challenging about this episode and it offered nothing new. The best part was actually a side plot involving two robots in Act 3. This proved far more emotive than anything happening in the main story arch and the robots themselves were well written characters given their screen time.
The ending was somewhat anti-climactic. I won’t spoil anything but will suffice to say it was all too neat. There was no cliff-hanger or suspense to motivate me to play the next episode, everything wraps up in a way a bit too close to ‘happily ever after’ and left me feeling unsatisfied.
There are some positives, once you get past the above foibles. It’s nicely made for what is, and it was a fairly relaxing experience. If you particularly like this sort of game it is most likely worth the low price but it’s not for everyone and I probably wouldn’t recommend it.

So I think the general gaming community admits that the original Crysis was not exactly earth shattering in anything but visuals- though the story was a lot of fun, the combat/mechanics acceptably challenging/enjoyable, and of course the visuals jaw-dropping, the original Crysis was not a /spectacular/ game.
But, it had coherency- you could follow the story pretty well, the characters though simple were likable, and the AI wasn't totally bonkers.
Enter Crysis 2.
Crysis 2 certainly lives up to its predecessor in terms of visuals; if you want to see post-apocalyptic New York City at its finest, look no further. But the storyline is, at best, confusing and at worst rubbish. I played through the game and then had to look up the Wiki to understand what on Earth I had just accomplished/done. You have a silent protagonist that everyone addresses by name, sort of like Half Life 2's Gordon Freeman but without the self-awareness. It's like they couldn't afford the voice actor they wanted and the studio said "screw it, we'll make him silent."
I recall in the original Crysis getting to use all of the powers of the Nanosuit with fair regularity; speed was great for escaping, armor allowed me to tackle a slew of guys at once, and invisibility was great for getting the drop on folks. Something happened with 2, however, as Invisibility and armor are basically all that you use, generally flip-flopping between them in an attempt to bewilder the already chilish AI.
The AI, I think, is perhaps the most disappointing part. There were times where I misjudged my energy levels and decloaked not six feet from an enemy... who simply shrugs and walks away. Characters running up and down stairs endlessly is a frequent occurrence, and in general I found myself bewildered at what my enemies would do next.
Summary:
Crysis 2 basically only has its visuals going for it. A sloppy, incoherent storyline, unlikable characters, poor mechanics, and laughable AI serve to make the sequel to Crysis simply a crisis.

Years ago, I picked up a bass guitar and learned the basics of keeping rhythm and finger walking.  Rocksmith 2014 built on that, taught me new techniques and opened my eyes to just how talented some musicians really are.  It also convinced me to go out and buy an electric guitar and start learning how to play that.  If you have any desire to learn to play, this game does an excellent job of bringing you up to speed and allowing you to rock out to your favorite songs at the same time.

This is a pretty handy tool for learning to play the guitar.  It has a lot of mini-games, some are fun, others are kind of tough or tedious but helpful for improving your finger dexterity, knowledge of the fretboard, etc.  Learning songs is nice with the slow-down feature, but it can be difficult to get used to watching the notes come towards you and deciphering which ones they are.  I still haven't gotten used to associating the color of the note with which string that means I'm supposed to play.  I keep trying, and I keep forgetting.  I kind of have to go really slowly through each song and ultimately memorize how to play it in order to really make progress, because my brain just can't keep up with deciphering which notes to play on the fly.
It's an extremely challenging game.  I don't know if it's the easiest way to learn guitar, it probably isn't, but then again, maybe it is?  I came into it with about 10 years of guitar playing experience (off and on, nothing serious, I wasn't very good).  So I already knew all the chords and a lot of the scales and so forth, and I already had the finger dexterity and flexibility to play all of the songs in the beginning parts of the game, it was just a matter of getting used to the interface and deciphering the game screen, and practicing to learn the songs in the game.
I thought it was a very good and useful tool for improving my playing, though I don't know if I would have liked it if I had no experience with a guitar before.
Also, a word of warning, you must have a guitar that keeps its tune well and is properly set up (see a guitar technician at a professional shop, please!) with the intonation set correctly.  Not to get too complicated in my explanation of this, but intonation basically involves whether or not each fret as you move up the neck of the guitar is still in tune.  If your intonation is off, then as you move further up the neck of the guitar each note will be further and further off from where it's supposed to be, and the game (unfortunately) will not register it correctly.  So if your guitar is not set up properly, then you might see the game telling you that you're playing the wrong note when you ARE indeed playing at the correct fret.  If you experience any issues with the game telling you that you're not playing the right note, even though you are, you will need to get your guitar set up properly.  If you have a cheap beginner's guitar, it may be tough for you to play this game, and that's a shame, because this game is probably best for those starting out and who wouldn't have a quality (expensive) guitar to play on.
Keep all this in mind, and keen an open mind and *put the work in* and this game will make you more than capable of playing your favorite songs!

I want to recommend this game SO bad. The mechanics are amazing, and their is an actual adrenaline rush you are running through the map and come face to face with an opponent. Sadly, I cannot recommend.

The thing that bothers me about the game is the community. In every match, the opponents will very, very likely just stand next to a cliff and wait to spam guard break or another throw of some sort. I do appreciate adding environmental kills in the game, when it is used in moderation, but the gameplay seems to be basically countering guard breaks over and over rather than using the great combat mechanisms featured in the game to its potential. This problem could be easily solved by the devs by making maps with less environmental kills and/or nerfing the guard breaks or throws, but, instead, they encouraged this playstyle by making more cheesier maps and heroes that thrive on this way of gameplay.  I'm sure others will disagree, but, as good as I get with the combat in the game, I'd rather not spend my time trying to stay on a ledge rather than trying to win a fight.
TL/DR Great combat mechanics that has its potential squandered by maps and heroes that encourage cheesy tactics.
