Another transformation in the Resident Evil Franchise, RE6 continues the trend of taking what used to be a "survival horror" game and turns it into a full-on action game. If  you thought Resident Evil 5 was basically Resident Evil 4 on steroids with multiplayer mayhem, RE6 is more of the same, only even more extreme. Hollywood blockbuster movies would be shamed, as there is probably no movie that has the number or explosions, heroic sacrifices, and innocent civilian casualties that Resident Evil 6 has.
The story, while intense, is actually very stupid if realism and where the main story can go from here is something you are concerned about. However, if that doesn't matter to you, RE6 is one of the most over-the-top action experiences you will ever play. Add in co-op with a friend to go through the craziness together, and you will have a great time with lots bad guys (and monsters) to shoot up, while leaving a path of destruction in your wake.
Anything that can be said as a detriment about this game is also it's greatest strength. While this title may be a long departure from what this series has traditionally been about, there is something immensely satisfying about taking down an armored helicopter, while giving spinning DDT's to splatter zombie heads into the pavement, and then running from a crazy chainsaw monster while maneuvering a raft to avoid flaming debris all in a 5-10 minute time-frame. If you were looking for a traditional Resident Evil game, this game may disappoint you. But if the previous sentence about the kinds of things you do in this game interest you at all, it is immensely satisfying to play through.

I'm not at all a fan of "the chase" portion of card games, where you spend time acquiring cards to improve your decks. This leaves the draft or other game modes in terms of holding my intersest. Having a board on which to move and place your units allows Duelyst to have a cool puzzle mode where the player is given a board and they need to find out how to win in 1 turn, however most cards are designed with a very narrow set of situations in which they are powerful making these puzzles mostly about reading the cards and sequencing plays optimally as opposed to thinking about different ways to use the cards. The draft mode isn't amazing either because this same situationalness makes it so that it's very rare to see much broad synergy between cards making it feel mostly like an exercise in picking the most valuable card weighted for the curve you've already picked. Even in constructed, the situationalness means that punishes and advantage swings are extreme making the overall game more about tempo than anything else.
However, for those who like that extreme feel to a game, it's pretty successful at being a game of skill expression. The reason I have decided not to recommend this game is because I perceive that cohort that would enjoy this game to be a fairly small niche of players.

Duelyst is a pretty interesting game. It plays very similarly to Magic The Gathering and Hearthstone in that it uses the Cost/Health/Damage formula for it's units, but adds a neat little twist. Units placed on the board can be moved around like chess pieces (and in most cases must be next to an opponent's unit to attack it). It's a nice change of pace for a card game that holds your interest very early on, but one problem I find is that it gradually loses the hold on your attention span, especially if you're a long term player of Magic or Hearthstone.

Rebuild 3 is a pretty addictive turn-based zombie-killing simulation game. You take a small group of characters from a starting point and slowly, tile-by-tile, take over the surrounding areas that have been overrun by zombies or by other factions. Characters can be one of five different classes, each with different weapons and items to affect their skills. The learning curve isn't bad at all--you should be able to discern the different classes and what they are best at within an hour or so of playing. So, it's pretty easy to pick up and fun (but not difficult) to master.
The gameplay reminds me of a game like Civilization V, which is also a tile-based simulation game. They both can help pass the time very quickly and they are both in the same vein as the classic Risk board game, in that they are a "conquer the map"-type game. If you like conquest games, I would recommend Rebuild 3.

This review is seriously overdue, since I finished this game months ago. This is, of course, having the game sitting around in my inbox for several months before playing it...which just goes to show how much the story of these games, engaged me.
First, the plot is decent and decently written, but it never surprised me. Even with this supposedly big cliffhanger at the end of the game, I can pretty much make up my own ending and not be too far off what’s going to happen. The only thing that did surprise me was all the pointless meandering the main quest had. At best, the writing is cute, but needs some serious editing if it wants to be in the big grand epic it’s trying so hard to be.
The commentary from the previous game is back again, with the varying degrees of success from before. There were moments I found myself laughing, while others I found myself rolling my eyes. There is no better example of the latter than this weird Princess Bride homage that brings the story screeching to a halt. I wouldn’t have minded it so much if the plot didn’t say that the protagonists were on a time limit, and if the homage was, for lack of a better word, good. It completely misunderstood what made the scenes in the Princess Bride so good to begin with. Fox—the character you play as during all of this—acted completely confident and cocky the entire time, meaning there was absolutely no tension over whether or not he was going to succeed. And the scenes of the Princess Bride that were all but ripped off, were so poorly done I could go on for another couple of paragraphs picking this one quest apart. Seriously, I could. But I’ll cut to the chase: this quest probably wouldn’t have bothered me if it were a Side Quest. However, its inclusion in the main story line feels like pointless filler.
Actually, a lot of the meandering would be fixed if these irrelevant “key quests” were made into side quests. They could still be available at different points in the story, but making them optional would change how I felt about them. The game DOES have optional side quests, but a lot more of the key quests should have been made into side quests to get rid of the monotony and change my mindset about a lot of them. Example: THE STUPID MURAL PAINTING PUZZLES WITH THE DWARVES AND FAIRIES! (Yes, this is an actual quest.)
After being so negative, I just want to take a quick moment to say that I love the little details in this game. I mean, the level of polish is admirable. The bed animation was pretty cute. And the fact that whenever Lilly has an item equipped, you can actually see her holding it…little touches like that are great. I also appreciate the new banking system. Now I can horde money! :D
Okay, I wanna take a second to talk about Viper again. Thankfully, she’s absent for most of the game, which works in this game’s favour, but I’d like to add some new insights that I didn’t have when I wrote my review for Curse of the Immortals. Now, before I begin, I’d like to say that my definition of a Mary-Sue isn’t based on any concrete definition, but rather on a gut feeling. If a character trigger’s my internal “Mary-Sue Alarm” (for lack of a better way to put it) then I consider that character a Mary-Sue. If they don’t, I don’t consider them one. With that said, one of the weirdest things about Viper was that she never set off my Mary-Sue Alarm. No matter how much I disliked her as a character, no matter how well she played the part, I just couldn’t bring myself to call her a Mary-Sue. Naturally, this confused me, especially since there were no other Mary-Sues in sight, but after playing this game, I finally understand why Viper never set me off. That’s because Viper wasn’t the Mary-Sue; her mentor, Fox, was. (Well, technically, he’s a Gary-Stu, but same thing). The reason I didn’t pick up on this sooner was because he barely appeared in the last game. Here? There’s a specific part of the main quest where you cannot progress unless you fall down a hole and have Fox swoop in and save you. Egads, that was obnoxious! I mean, at least Viper was allowed to be disempowered and made mistakes. Fox, on the other hand, is always portrayed as “cool”, smart, strong, is always one step ahead of the villains, and saves our heroes on two separate occasions.
Also, quick side note, there is some blatant favoritism for the Thieves Guild in these games. The Fighters Guild is full of militaristic elitists, the Magicians/Mages Guild (can’t remember which) is downright corrupt, yet the THIEVES Guild takes in orphans and always comes to the rescue. Um…what? I would be fine with this if it was some sort of commentary, but the Thieves Guild members never actually steal anything on screen—for the orphans or otherwise. I mean, Viper’s an aspiring playwright (for some reason) and Fox is an alchemist extraordinaire/ninja/2-cool-4-u guy. Why is it even called the Thieves Guild if they never do any thieving?
As for the other main characters…well…they’re good ideas for characters, but none of them are ACTUAL characters. They are all very one dimensional and flat. Lilly wants to save her sister,
Griffin doesn’t like the ideologies of the Fighters Guild, Enoch is one with nature, Dak-Ho is a monk who wants to beat people up despite being from a pacifist society, etc. The only real exception to this rule is Viper, and she’s annoying because she’s two character traits mixed together that don’t mesh well. These aren’t characters—these are motives, and, at best, starting points for real characters. But, I will say that I liked Skye, even though she also suffered from lack of development. She replaced Viper as a Party Member, and while she wasn’t anything to write home about, she felt the most like a real person out of all of our protagonists.
Next, I want to touch on something that really annoyed me in this game specifically. See, throughout the game, you’re going through dungeons, trying to get things before the big bad
does. Not only do we cut to exactly what the big bad is doing throughout our quest (and thus killing the potential suspense), but after traversing through a dungeon for hours, nothing is more frustrating than sitting through a cutscene where the big bad breaks through the wall of the last room, and steals the treasure right in front of you while the Player is powerless to stop him
.
That’s not to say that the dungeons were all bad. I mean, there were a couple of dungeons that had really fun gameplay mechanics (snake flutes, snake whips, wheeee~), and quite a few of the puzzles that weren’t nearly as hard as the last game. While there were some puzzles that were really annoying (see dwarves’ mural paintings), others were quite creative and pleasant. Nicely done. Credit where credit is due.
I guess one of the most frustrating things about these two games is that I can SEE the potential they have for being great stories/fantasy-epic-games. But they feel more like a programmer trying to tell a story rather than a writer trying to make a game. I know that having an awesome programmer and an amazing writer isn’t always an option, but finding a story editor really wouldn’t hurt.
Despite all the negatives, it's a good game that I sort of recommend. It's just a shame that it isn't better. Again, these games feel like they should be one long game, not three separate games. (I would tell you to get third game if you want to find out what happens, but if you're anywhere as story saavy as me, you won't need to.) If you enjoyed Curse of the Immortals, then you're going to enjoy this one too, since they both share the same strengths and weaknesses as each other. But, if you're anything like me, you might wanna give it a pass.

There are a lot of games that I wouldn't recommend playing on their own, but would recommend playing with friends. Left 4 Dead is one of these games. Resident Evil 5 is one of these games. Dead Space 3 is one of these games. Even Daikatana, despite what many believe, is one of these games. You'll notice that there's a trend in these games, in that each one is worse than the last.
You'll also notice that Resident Evil 6 is not on the list at all.
Resident Evil 6 is a game that includes 4 campaigns, starring Leon, Chris, newcomer Jake, and the formerly secret Ada campaign. These campaigns total to around 30 hours in gameplay, with each of the first 3 campaigns being nearly as long as Resident Evil 5. You may think "Wow, what a bargain!", but you're missing one key component: almost none of it is worth playing. The game takes a severe quantity over quality stance, and even when the campaigns aren't directly overlapping (which is a feature, in which you might've been able to play with other people playing different campaigns in 4-player co-op at certain points if anybody was still around to actually play this game) you'll probably feel like you're just playing the same campaign over and over. Resident Evil 6 isn't a survival horror game, but it's not an action shooter either; it's just a third person shooter with really awful, gimped controls that are only worse when brought over to the PC. The only parts of the game that are even slightly redeemable are Leon's first chapter, which is about an hour long (some people will tell you that all of Leon's campaign is good, but those people are liars - all of Leon's personality and charm has been drained and given to Jake, instead) Jake's campaign, which is the only portion of the game that I would consider actually slightly worth playing at all, and the Mercenaries mode, which is as fun as ever. The story is a convoluted mess that puts literally anything in a series full of convoluted twists to shame, to the point that it makes Wesker suddenly returning with superpowers seem like a natural character development that was planned from the start.
Resident Evil 6 is, as a whole, just an absolute mess. A disaster. A waste of time, effort, and money. It feels like Capcom just got together 1,000 people and said "hey, make a video game" and let them each try to decide what horror is, and while Jake's campaign has an extremely noticeable increase in interesting locations and mechanics, the game as a whole just feels like a mess of ideas that don't go together at all and overall leaves the game feeling bland and mass-produced, and it's just not worth it. Even if you do play with a friend it's barely worth it, since it's not even good enough to play for the sake of laughing at since after more than an hour or two of 3 of the 4 campaigns your soul will have been stripped of the concept of laughter. Ada's campaign is bafflingly not even built for co-op in a game that spends 25 hours reminding you that co-op exists, and if you do happen to drag some poor soul into the game with you they get stuck playing as "Agent", a character with no dialogue, no background, no cutscene presence, and no physical prescence - he can shoot enemies, and that's about the extent, since he can't open doors, solve puzzles, pull levers, or generally do anything except get carted through the levels by teleportation whenever Ada uses her grappling hook.
I can't even begin to recommend this game to anyone. There are some games that I hate that I can understand other people liking, but I have yet to see any sort of defense of Resident Evil 6 that didn't absolutely baffle me. For $30, you could buy Resident Evil 6, but $30 also buys you a ton of bleach that you could drink and have a way better time.

I was once again about 5 years late in getting to this game. I enjoyed the gameplay of Crysis, and the powers and tactics afforded by the Nanosuit are fun. As far as the Nanosuit goes, it all seems the same from Crysis. At the cost of limited (but regenerative) Energy, you can have Super Speed, Super Strength, Super Armor, or a Stealth Cloak. Fun stuff. What's really obviously changed is an attempt at a slightly more linear experience in the vein of the Call of Duty's and Battlefield's and so on. The first Crysis took place on a massive, open tropical island where you had objective locations but you had a lot of freedom in how to approach them.
The areas in Crysis 2 are much more traditional, though they're by no means over restricted. Each major encounter area gives you the option of full frontal assaults, stealth, or some kind of special item/flank (a sniper rifle, turret, rocket, sniper nest, vehicle, etc).
Back when I bought it, I paid $20 for it, and it took me around 10 hours to beat the Campaign. So while the value could have been a little better for me, I have to admit I enjoyed those 10 hours. Even at 5 years old, Crysis 2 is a graphical powerhouse, and I didn't get any grief for using modern resolutions (2560x1440). There's nothing here that really sets Crysis 2 apart from a multitude of other first person shooters out there, but if you want to feel like a powerful super soldier and you've exhausted your Halo games, I recommend picking this game up on the next sale. I'm sure it would only be $5 or less.

This LeetCrew is skilled in the use of technology like us but are unskilled in the arts of war. They will make a fine proxy. Labs and Workshops work day and night rediscovering technology and making ammunition. Just in time for we have met our first threat.
The Last Judgement Gang is swiftfully proclaimed a raider group after one too many raids on our compound. The war is long & hard and left many brothers and sisters injured. We emerge victorius in the end and as a reward for their tenacity the survivors were all executed on the spot. We were unable to revel in our victory for our scouts reported the presence of heavily armed soldiers wearing emblems of the old world government! A settlement of sentient undead was discovered in the subway. While they were friendly and their leader Jesse an okay sort the laws of the Brotherhood is quite clear on the undead no matter what they act like. The 'Rotten' were exterminated in a blitz attack as to not prolong their suffering.
A group called the Granville Riffs were discovered. They too were well versed in warfare though their skills were more of a melee stance than our brotherhood's dogged use of firearms. We helped them until they got word of thier distant settlements experiencing problems. As they headed east they left us their entire fort. What honorable fellows.
Four new factions were met. The children of St. Michaels were of no threat. They were left alone like the Luddies. The Pig Farmers and Anachists were proclaimed Raider groups and wiped out. The Dalihas possessed a large amount of guns and ammo. That much weaponry didn't belong outside the brotherhood's more resposible hands so the dalihas were invaded and absorbed. We now have the strenght to take on the Enclave.
The War was long. The War was hard. Many brothers and sisters died. In a daring attack the Enclave's main HQ was assaulted by the Elder and his personal squad. The remnants of the Enclave were absorbed into the Brotherhood. With them on our side the undead on this city were of no threat. Civilization had returned to the world no matter how small...

God this one is so hard to review... It's long but it's too long, it's memorable but it's frustrating, it's good but it's bad but the good parts stay with you and you somehow forget the bad parts. The controls are piano-level complicated, and yet that's sort of refreshing in the age of dumbing everything down control-wise (see the Mass Effect games, where one button seemingly does everything). The enemies are repetitive, and yet the atmosphere created by things like the creepy soldiers that mutate into horrifying abominations when attacked is just brilliant and really stays in the mind. It's not scary 90% of the time but then stuff like the final boss of Ada's story is eerie as can be.  It's the bestworst game in the franchise!
It's a hoary analogy at this point, but it really is like a double album with a single album's worth of good songs on it, and those songs are good enough to justify buying it i think. It's a hot mess and some parts will make you want to burn down your own house with rage, but if you're a fan of the franchise and creepy bio-horror aesthetics then there's a whole lot of content here, and what's here is distinctive enough that it'll be someone's favorite game in the franchise and that someone could be you. As for me, i love the Revelations games above all, but i really don't regret playing 6-- the good parts make it worth it. When i finished it i swore to never play thought it again, and yet i still get cravings to play it-- it's damned confounding, but hell, it's unique.

I've wanted to learn bass for what seems like forever; yet, like many others, I've made one excuse after another why I should not get one. Well, I finally got my bass (Fender Squier Precision Bass starter kit, btw) and was checking prices in my area for private lessons. Would you believe I was quoted as much as $300 per month?! That's outrageous! Then, my friend told me about Rocksmith(R), so I checked it out.

Hyper Light Drifter is beautiful visual-wise and has extremely fun and satisfying core combat mechanics. Slicing enemies and charging your gun to blast others made me want to play this game for hours, However there are some things that I feel are wrong. Having to get eight coins by either finding them in very well hidden spots in levels or getting them as a very rare drop from enemies is extremely slow and makes getting upgrades dull. Instead of a feeling of rapid progression, constantly changing up my fighting style and getting new weapons/abilities, I get bored and angry. The game is also extremely hard, even on newcomer mode, and suffers from severe difficulty spikes. One of the best examples of this is the boss fights. The first two boss rooms give you tons of free health packs before fighting the bosses (who themselves are not too hard to defeat) but the third level boss gives you less/none. The third boss is also able much harder than the other bosses. While the first two took two or three deaths to beat the third for me has taken around forty with still no progress. Dashing around with a powerful attack and summoning minions (which you can make him kill while they are still  encased in crystal, but unless you get his patterns down he will waste any health you have in seconds when trying to do this) while hitting you with an attack that takes away two health with each hit(Max health at this stage was five for me) and a projectile attack you can do nothing about unless you got a sword upgrade previously. The game mechanics seem fun and everything looks and feels amazing but the difficulty and the lack of any kind of progression with upgrades makes the game significantly less playable for me. Unless you can handle a considerable amount of rage and difficulty I would not recommend this game for others

This puzzle platformer is excellently paced, giving enough time for you to build upon existing experience, while moving onto new concepts quickly enough for you not to get bored.
The 100 levels seem to fly by as you are eager to seek the next experience.
Although generally not TOO difficult, these levels vary in difficulty a little, with the easier ones being little more than an intresting environments/concepts, while the most challenging ones involving some tricky platforming.
The latter can feel a little frustrating at times (I don't really rate it as a 'Good' platformer as I don't get along with the jumping style particularly* , although I'm not particularly 'Good' at platformers either, so that's probably just me), but as it's mostly clear what you need to acomplish to complete a level, a little patience will get you through these.
While certainly very charming, most of the character's charm comes from the storyline/narration as the characters themselves don't exhibit a lot of character beyond their abilities.
That said, the storyline is wonderful and touches on quite a few subjects (understanding and co-operation, teamwork, self-sacrifice, love etc)  along the way that leave Thomas was Alone as a surpisingly thoughtful and touching experience considering it's a puzzle-platformer about coloured quadrilaterals.

I’d heard this game was bad, and having played the demo I decided to skip this. But then the years went on, and both critics and game developers popped their head out to say “Resident Evil 6 wasn’t that bad!”. Could there be something interesting here after all? No. No there isn’t.
Maybe it’s a matter of preference? The way games like Resident Evil Revelations 2 or The Evil Within are paced is like a rollercoaster. You have long stretches of buildup and tension before all hell breaks loose. They both do a great job at it. Neither are particularly effective as horror games, but as action games I love them. Resident Evil 6 on the other hand is more like being strapped to a rocket. There’s some anticipation at the start, but then it’s non-stop action with set pieces upon set pieces with maybe 5 seconds of breathing room between them. I only played the first chapter of Leon’s story, and I apparently killed 228 enemies during that time. That’s the kinds of numbers you’d expect out of late game Doom 2 or Serious Sam.
So all pretense of it being horror is out the window, and there’s minimal exploration and the pacing is nonexistent. This puts more strain on the combat mechanics. They better be good if it’s the only thing you’ll be doing. Unfortunately they tossed out the mechanics used in Resident Evil 4 and 5 and tried to come up with new ones. I can appreciate the thought. But what they have here is simply worse. Your guns and enemies somehow both feel weak and flimsy, yet they take more hits to kill than I’d like. When you shoot enemies with a shotgun, there’s no difference in reaction from when you shoot them with a gun. It feels like an underdeveloped system that was rushed out the door. This is especially true of tougher enemies. In the parts of the game I played there were higher evolved zombies that took loads of bullets to take down, and there were big fat ones that took the rest of my inventory to kill. None of them were intimidating or exciting to fight. All they did was add tedium because their health meant the action set piece would go on for longer than it already was.
I didn’t enjoy playing Resident Evil 6 at all. The story starts in a laughable manner, and it doesn’t get much better after that. In fact, almost nothing happened in the 2 hours I played, as characters insisted the story would start once I reached a cathedral. But on the way there I had to go through 9 action set pieces, one more tedious than the other. On every level from characterization, pacing, tension, the feel of the weapons, the enemy designs, and the way environments were designed and lit was worse than it has ever been in the series. I’m actually glad I decided to play it properly, because now I can finally write it off completely as garbage. If you like this for some reason, fine, I have nothing against that. But I can’t understand at all what the appeal is. This isn’t mediocre, it’s absolutely horrible.

Tomb Raider 1996 - Review
It’s hard to know how to review this game, if you hold it up to modern standards then of course it’s got more than its fair share of issues. But if you take it for what it is and compare it to games at the time it is one of the best games ever made.
At the time of its release we has seen nothing like this, the graphics on both pc and console where fantastic and the game play and level design where fluid and expansive. It really did blow allot of people away. I won’t go into too much detail regarding Lara's history or legacy as we all know the impact she had on the video game industry as well as pop culture its self. So let’s begin.
Tomb Raider puts you in the boots of arceologist Lara Croft who is approached by a rich and powerful business woman known as Natla to recover an artefact in Peru, and that is all that is know when Lara sets off on this adventure. The story on the whole is decent but It can be hard at times to piece together exactly what’s going on, I guess in modern gaming we are so used to incredible cinematic experiences that a handful of short FMV's and in game cut sense don’t quite cut it. The clues are there however and its a decent story that keeps the game moving on nicely. The game itself see's Lara tackle 4 areas that are broken up into 3 to 4 levels each, these are Peru, Greece, Egypt and finally Atlantis. The level design for the time is incredible and really second to none, its the classic Tomb Raider design of platforming, key/switch finding and occasional animal or boss battles but for the time is was fresh and exciting. My Only gripe with the levels is that each areas levels can feel repetitive from a graphical point of view, even though the layout of these levels are vastly different they use allot of the same styles and textures.
From a graphics and sound stand point, for a 1996 game it looks and sounds great. 3D environments bring the world together and Lara’s character model looks good if not a little.....pointy. Only issues are a poor draw distance which can be quite jarring in 2016 and sounds sometimes don’t play when they are supposed too however this is an issue in both PC and console versions of the game. The levels don’t have a soundtrack as such, but more occasional sound bites as you adventure, or sounds play to symbolise and secret being discovered or door opening. Sounds of Lara's movements, gun fire and other NPC's are all good for 1996. Some character models of other humans could be improved however as the difference between them and Lara in quality is quite obvious.
The game play is what we have all come to know, love and find frustrating. It’s the usual fair of run, jump, roll, dodge and shoot. There is allot more emphasis on platforming in Tomb Raider as opposed to the other games in the series and only a few enemies appear in levels. To be honest in 2016 Lara did not feel as "tank" like as I thought she might but it can be a challenge to move her around. More often than not I died because she did not jump when I wanted her too or due to the dated graphics a ledge was not as close as I thought. This was frustraiting in 1996 and is frustraiting in 2016 so be warned before you play. It did however not stop my overall enjoyment of the game and replaying it 20 years after it first came out was a complete joy. The PC version also bennifits from its ability to save wherever you like mid level, PlayStation and Saturn versions of the game had to make use of save cristals scattared thoughout the levels and this became more than a slight annoyance on the consoles.
Over all Tomb Raider is a fantastic game, it blew us away in 1996 and in 2016 it’s not as hard to play as I thought it would be. The story is solid and helps move things forward nicely and the overall presentation for the time of release is top notch. This is all complemented with fantastic level design if not slightly aesthetically repetitive. On a modern PC with windows 10 the games runs well, only issues I had is FMV's stretch to fit the screen which can make them harder to watch and there is also a slight delay between them starting and playing on screen only a second or two but this really does not detract too much.
Overall Tomb Raider is an all time great that will go down as a classic. - 9.2/10 - PC     9.0/10 - PS1/Saturn

Intro
I know what you're thinking.  Damn, man, this thing is ugly.  Yeah, the low-poly models and low-res textures are a bit hard on the eyes.  I admit it.  But everything else is in such good order that you will very quickly be fully immersed.  The visuals will melt away and what you'll be left with is one of the most fantastic adventures in gaming history.  Bar none.
Pros
The Tomb Raider franchise almost certainly requires no introduction and this first game in the series is, in my opinion, its best.  When gaming made its transition from 2D to 3D and from cartridges to optical media, Tomb Raider took astounding advantage of both.  The adventure is a sprawling epic that gifts players with a good many hours of challenging gameplay.  The environments are interesting and varied.  The puzzles and object hunts meld well with their contexts and level objectives.  The plot is fairly well developed and the dialogue is appropriately cheeseball.  The music and ambient sound, however, are extraordinary, even by today's standards.  Among the very best I have ever heard, period.
Cons
The only criticism I would make of Tomb Raider - and it is very rarely a hinderance to enjoyable gameplay - is that the camera is a little wonky when Lara is in tight quarters.  This can make pathfinding a little rough on occasion.  Other than that and the understandably dated 3D graphics, however, the game is, to me, practically flawless.
Setup
Like a good many old school games here on Steam, Tomb Raider is delivered as a DosBox configuration, fully packaged and ready to go.  The team even went through the trouble of including a Glide emulator with the game, allowing the enhanced 3DFX graphics engine to provide a 640x480 resolution and mipmapping.  I strenuously recommend upgrading this to the very accessible nGlide by a fellow called Zeus.  It has me running the game at 4K resolution with tweaked gamma and I have to say, the result is stunning.  Yeah, I said it.  Xazuki offers an easy to follow guide here:
One thing the team didn't do such a fantastic job of is providing gamepad support in the configuration.  Fortunately community member Darth Sidious [PT] came through with a super-simple fix.  You'll edit one line in a text file and copy another file into the game's working directory.  Boom!  Perfect gamepad support.  Head on over to the link below and treat yourself.
Conclusion
If you like a good adventure and you have enough of an imagination to be swept up into a great game, despite some aging visuals, then you should pick up Tomb Raider without hesitation or reserve.

AN INCREDIBLY FUN GAME.
Having said that, the learning curve involved in developing crucial piloting skills in this game is a challenging one - three or four solid hours of play are required at a minimum before most users feel comfortable at the controls. I highly recommend you take the time; those who do seldom regret the investment.
Would you like to know more? Read below. My recommended control input mapping scheme follows:
Fair warning - effective use of the controls takes time to master. Use of the "advanced" control mode and some remapping of keys and mouse axis will probably lead to greatest success, but this does require some experimentation and several hours of practice.
Stick with it, however, and you will discover and incredibly fun and rewarding game. Worth the (relatively) bargain price and highly addictive. Future updates seem to be on track to polish the rough edges and increase fun factor.
Tips: use pitch attitude (cyclic) for airspeed and power setting (collective) for altitude control. Seems slightly counterintuitive, but results in much greater control of the helicopter (and happens to be how real-world aircraft are flown).
USE "ADVANCED" CONTROLS from the Settings menu and map the following:
Cyclic pitch (foreward / aft aircraft pitch input): Mouse Vertical.
Cyclic tilt (lateral / roll input): Mouse Horizontal
Yaw (left / right pivot input): A/D keys
Collective pitch (power setting): W/S keys
Fire weapon 1: Mouse 1 (left click)
FIre weapon 2: Mouse 2 (right click)
Fire weapon 3 / Gun pod: Mouse 3 (thumb button, mouse wheel, etc.)
Next / Previous weapon: Mouse wheel up/down scroll
Binoculars (Scout helicopter "enemy spot" feature): Any free mouse button or keyboard key that you can reach without losing your hand contact on the WASD keys. For me, this is a middle mouse button just below the wheel.
USING TURRETED WEAPONS:
Many Scout and Attack helicopters feature turret-mounted weaponry to allow for off-axis engagements. In the real world, best use of these weapons systems requires multiple crewmembers and / or head tracking technology, but there are a few control tweaks that will allow you to use gunship turrets with greater effect in Heliborne. The following changes will essentially turn your Left Shift key into a toggle that swaps you into the CoPilot-Gunner's seat when held down, allowing you to fire certain weapons off-axis.
SET FREE LOOK TO MAKE USE OF TURRETS:
Step 1: I recommend remapping the Left Shift keyboard key to "Look Around" in advanced control settings.
Step 2 (IMPORTANT!): Now choose the General Settings tab and make the following change: ensure that the field labeled "Advanced controls: looking around" has a CHECK MARK next to "Block controls".
Step 3: Map "Look Horizontal Full Axis" to your Mouse Horizontal input and "Look Vertical Full Axis" to your Mouse Vertical input.
By making these three changes, holding down the left shift key will decouple your mouse inputs from the flight controls and allow you to slew your viewpoint around the aircraft. Any turreted weapons onboard will continue to follow your mouse (to the limits of their mechanical ability), and their current aim point will be reflected by the gun crosshair symbology (if your turreted weapon is the currently selected system). You can now engage enemies off-axis without having to make dramatic pitch and roll changes to the helicopter, which is the primary advantage of such systems to begin with.
One last friendly reminder: POWER (W/S keys) FOR ALTITUDE, and PITCH (mouse vertical axes) FOR AIRSPEED. Keep in mind that adjusting pitch of the nose to aim fixed weapons may have a fairly dramatic effect on your airspeed and altitude. Real aircraft react in the same fashion and successful gun runs will require practice, patience, and skill. Now get in there, mix it up, and enjoy.

TL;DR
Rebuild 3 feels like a board game adaptation.  It’s mechanics are simple enough to grasp, and survivors have a decent degree of customization, but the systems are, never-the-less, a bit too simple to inspire very much subtle strategy.  The different map types change the map enough to notice the difference, but not enough to make them seem different.  Overall, Rebuild 3 was fun, but I had nearly lost all interest by the time I finished the story campaign.  I did enjoy a good deal of my time with the game, however, so I’m still going to give it a tentative thumbs up,  just not an emphatic one.
What is it?
Rebuild 3 is RTS/TBS strategy game where you take the role of a survivor of the zombie holocaust who makes his/her way across the pacific Northwest carving walled towns out of the ruins of formerly great and small cities.  You recruit randomly generated survivors along the way, level them up, equip them, and negotiate trade and alliances with Ai controlled factions, and, of course, fight zombie hordes.

Rebuild feels much more like a board game adaptation than a native computer game.  The map is procedurally generated on a grid pattern using 1x1, 1x2, and 2x2 tiles for the buildings, ruins, and farms of the cities as well as rivers and other impassible terrain.  The goal of the story campaign is to clear story objectives on some maps and eliminate/ally with each other faction on others.  Once the listed objectives are met or the town is yours, you move on to another semi-random map.
The basic process for conquering a map involves clearing a zone of zombies by positioning one or more of your survivors there and letting them lowly clear it out off-screen.  Depending on how many zombies there are and how effective the survivors tasked with clearing it are in combat, there is also a percentage chance one or more may be injured or infected.  Battles with survivor gangs work very similarly as their wandering units will occasionally raid or invade if your attitude with them is too low.  Once a location is safe, you can send in your specialized builders to add the location to your territory making it impossible for zombies to spawn there any longer.
There are 5 basic resources to manage, Building materials, food, and ammo, medicine, and fuel.  Each survivor in your band costs food to upkeep and food is produced by your farms, scavenged from ruins, or traded for.  Building materials can be obtained from parks and forests as well as scavenged or traded for and are used to “Fortify” a location, ie add it to your territory, as well as create certain single use items.  Ammo can only be obtained from scavenging or trading and is required to make use of the combat bonuses associated with gun items.  Medicine and fuel are obtained the same way as ammo, and are used to create items or traded as a commodity.
Survivors come in one of 4 types, although they can be switched between types as need once you have secured a certain type of location.  Soldiers fight, Builders build, Engineers unlock the tech tree, and Leaders help ease the political tests and recruit randomly spawning survivors.  Each survivor has a weapon slot and a tool slot that can be used to equip gear to boost their attributes or give them special abilities.
Pros
- The mechanics fighting zombies, conquering territories, and politicking are simple and fairly intuitive.
-The difference between rural and urban maps feels significant enough to be noticeable.
- While the writing won’t win any Hugos, it was decent enough that I read a lot of survivor backstories
-Carrying over your protagonist and three favorite survivors incentives you to become attached to your core gang members.
Cons
-The mechanics don’t have a lot of depth and repetition sets in be the end of the first tutorial map.  Later maps don’t feel more complex, only larger and grindier.
-There aren’t enough random scenarios or survivor backstories to avoid repeats during the bigger maps.
-A strong core group can trivialize the early game of subsequent maps, especially on easy.
-The main quest line can be devilishly random and some of the events required to reach the “good end” are virtually impossible to stumble upon without a walkthrough.

Absurdist Adventure.
The best way to describe Jazzpunk. If you don't know what absurdist means, simply Google it and the definition will appear in large writing, perfectly describing the comedy angle of this escapade.
Humor is subjective, so to say Jazzpunk is funny is purely true or false on a person to person basis. However, Jazzpunk made me chuckle many times. The comedy feels a bit random, but I also feel it would be unfair to simply call this "LOL SO RANDOM" humor that I've experienced out of bad, modern TV cartoons or Youtube videos watched primarily by kids in their adolescense or early teen years by the time this game was released. There's enough "reasonable reaction" from each humorous moment in Jazzpunk, even if many of it will make you say "What the F***?" or "Ok, that's a thing."
Jazzpunk plays as a first person adventure game, where apparently you're some sort of spy infiltrating places and taking things. If you're concerned about getting stuck because of stealh portions, or non-sensical developer puzzle logic, you don't generally have that problem here. The majority of the game is simply walking around the areas and talking to NPCs and intereacting with objects and pickup that are generally obvious to what you need to do with them, if an NPC doesn't already explain it to you already (such as shooting pigeons, or needing to knock on a door). You're less likely to need a walkthrough or guide with this game, unless you forget what you "need to do" after coming back to the game (if you didn't finish the game in one session, like I did). The level objectives are available in the pause menu, so, except for the third "level", the game explains essentially what you need to do. Jazzpunk is a good adventure game for people who don't like adventure games because they are too difficult or obtuse for them.
One potential criticism of Jazzpunk is the somewhat heavy use of references near the latter portion of the game. This isn't a problem in the first two levels, but the third level seems to contain more references to other pop culture media, instead of relying on its own humor that was well established in the earlier game. This didn't bother me, and won't bother alot of people, especially since I understood and appreciated some of the references, but this also means there is less "that was a good joke " moments and more "don't you remember this thing from this show/movie/game" moments.
I completed Jazzpunk in 4 hours, and I think others have done so in 3 - making it a perfect game to knock off your backlog. $15 may feel a bit expensive for the amount of gameplay you get here. Otherwise, the biggest hump for anyone looking to play this game will be it's sense of humor. Jazzpunk is the sort of game where you would spoil yourself for watching it instead of playing it, but if you find yourself amused by the first few minutes of gameplay from a video, you should stop watching any further and give it a play instead.

-Difficult yet rewarding fights
-Neat upgrades (including different gear)
-Beautiful graphics and music

-Different characters (Alternate Drifter or NG+) for more challenge once you've completed the game

-There is no dialogue which makes for an interesting experience, but at the same time the objectives are a little difficult to grasp
-Although the map looks neat visually, it wasn't very helpful
-Doesn't play well with a mouse and keyboard

Indie, ARPG, things to find, easy to play, hard to master. Apparently I was playing on easy mode, though. You could play to the end in 10 hours if you wanted, or you could try to perfect everything, which might take you 50 or more.
This reminded me a lot of FEZ in terms of art style and music. Some puzzles, but once you understand how they're signaled, there's not much to do other than look for that mark on the ground.
Compared to, say, Link to the Past, or Super Metroid, I have a harder time keeping track of where I am. The mapping system is unintuitive, mostly because the "real" map is so faded that you don't even realize the second "detailed" map is actually an overlay, not an alternate.
For combat, things are fair, balanced, satisfying. I think the game could stand a little more variety -- but not much.
My main gripe is NG+. The designers chose to let you keep the bigger upgrades, but force you to chase after the tedious ones that make very little difference. I would have done the opposite, so that you can once again feel yourself become more powerful as you progress.

This is a good space adventure game that is done through an RPG Maker program.
Despite the lack of RPG elements like battles and side quests, the games story telling and suspense is what makes this game enjoyable to play.
There are several downsides to this game that is understandable, the downsides being short and linear.  This game (or episode one) is short because it's an indie game.  Many indie games are normally this short.  The price tag of $1 makes up for the length.  Also, since this game is more of a point and click adventure game, it's okay that it remains linear as most point and click adventure games are.  This is not an RPG.
What makes this game interesting is that it's a point and click adventure game with the look and feel of an old school RPG.
For the full experience, with a great start for episode one, I recommend continuing the series especially with a low price tag.

-Fun little point and click game
-Amusing lovable characters
-Lighthearted, casual experience
-Simple control scheme
-Short
-No replayability
-No real challenge; it's really more of an interactive visual novel
This is one of those games that takes less than 2 hours to finish completely.  It's short, and fun.  There's no staggering plot twist, and the characters are likewise light on the plot.  The game feels like a one-off episode in a series... which it is.  There are three more episodes after this one.
Personally, I enjoyed myself.  This was a good way to kill time when I didn't have time to sit and play longer, more involved games.  Be aware that you won't get more than a couple of hours of entertainment from this.  Once you beat it, there's no real reason to go back and replay it.
As a final note, you shouldn't be paying more than about $0.50 for this game, as it goes on frequent heavy sales.  I suspect that the maker simply cycles through a sale on each episode, but either way, don't pay full price when you don't have to.  I got all four episodes for $2.00 total.

Reviewing a 20 year old game (seriously, 20 years old) is pretty hard. Compared to today's standard of controls, graphics and music - yeah the PC version shipped without in game music - Tomb Raider is obviously lacking.
I can only recommend this game to those who have already played it or those who know they can cope with the limitations that come with a 2 decade old game.
Gameplay - The level design in Tomb Raider is fantastic with some truly memorable set pieces and enemies. Secret areas are hidden well and the game offers a decent degree of challenge. Flipping through the air with dual pistols auto locked onto the wolves running at you is rather satisfying. The only thing letting the game down at the moment is...
Controls - Not the worst I've ever used but I certainly remember it being easier on a PS1 controller a very long time ago. On PC and in comparison to today's standards, the controls in Tomb Raider are clunky, difficult to use and incredibly good at♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥you off. When you're getting through a timed jumping puzzle and fall to your death only because of the painful control scheme, you can only feel betrayed. Oh, and the swimming controls are about as useful as pedals on a wheelchair.
Graphics/sound design - I really like old school graphics and Tomb Raider looks very old school. It might be offputting to some, but I personally think it doesn't look that bad. In terms of sound, well there's no music. And the sound assets that do exist get rather repetitive.
I stopped playing after about 4 levels just due to the controls. I'll finish it if I ever get around to picking up a Dualshock 4 (assuming I can use one for this game, I haven't found out)
Overall, Tomb Raider truly is a classic. Looking past its new-age issues it still stands up on its own and it's still really fun. It's not for everyone, but I do think everyone should try it first. It might surprise you.

Jazzpunk is one of those diamonds in the rough that you find once in a while, although it isn't the longest game out there, it still has a lot of fun and hilarious content packed into it. i found myself wanting so much more from the game after i got to the end.
You start the game as Polyblank and from the intro credits video it shows you are being shipped somewhere in a human shaped suitcase. Another example of the different style of comedy this game portrays.
I wasn't invested with the story as i was too taken by what was happening at that moment in time. One second it's sitting in a room reading comedic hospital booklets, next it's swatting flies in a vase shop. The game always has you knowing that something funny can and will happen. So i never really payed attention to the story as much as i should, but i did gather that You're an agent for some agency that has their headquarters in a seemingly abandoned subway station, from the way the game is and its style it feels like its 1950's to 1960's era. but you talk to "The Director" in the organisation and he assigns you to do these James Bond style of missions. The missions start after you take "Missionoyl" pills which i found quite humorous.You need to save the director who gets kidnapped near the end which came with some funny yet new ways of comedy.
The game has an mix of looking both cartoon and drawn, it really sets it apart from a lot of other games. the game-play makes it much more exciting to explore instead of going straight to the objective, the game will be quite short if the player just went for the objective, but as do any games the side quests tend to bulk it up. But as much exploring i did, and i tried to see everything, it still felt rather short as i completed the game in just 3 hours. It left me wanting a lot more of whatever charm that Jazzpunk had.
I really enjoyed Jazzpunk, i hope that whenever Jazzpunk 2 or similar comes out that it keeps me as humoured as Jazzpunk

Seems like the best city-builder since SimCity 4, not many problems aside from the one that renders it unplayable: the text is slightly blurry.
I know, sounds like a lame and minor thing you can totally ignore and play the game, maybe without ever noticing, but you can't.  It physically strains your eyes until you take a closer look and go hey, why does it look like I'm wearing off-prescription glasses?  An hour or so later and you get a nice eye-induced migraine.
There are mods that attempt to fix this with different fonts or increased size but this is somehow a problem with the unity engine with no solution.  Protip: don't make a game engine that can't render text correctly in the year of our lord 2-thousand-anything.  We aced this process back in the 70s, really shouldn't be a deal-breaker in literally any software with a publication date post-Y2K.
Other than that, solid game, pretty decent mod support and the gameplay is both engaging and relaxing.  I'd probably have lost a few hundred hours to this if not for the aforementioned eye-murder.

Fast, ominous and vague, Hyper Light Drifter is a chilling adventure.  Recommended for anyone who likes top-down view adventures like Legend of Zelda, mixed with the brutality of Dark Souls (though not quite so difficult).  Throw in some great movesets and the ability to jump around the battlefield, and you got a recipe for a game to hook it's claws into you.

I recommend this game for it's unique combat and graphically stunning visuals. It's very fun and even if you're playing alone, you can enjoy the fights and kills you get. Executions feel awesome and rewarding for a victory against your opponent! If you're new you will lose.. a lot, but, when you finally get experience and understand the mechanics you can improve and understand the higher level mind games each class brings (some classes have more mind games then others.. for now). The mechcanics are easy to learn and hard to master. Balance is not perfect but, acceptable and by no means game breaking. All of the older classes will be getting 'reworks' to be on par with the classes that are considered 'overtuned' at the moment. I enjoy the challenge of random encounters with all different types of classes, opponents, and players. Since each class has different movesets, there's a style for everyone, and from general experience no one plays each class exactly the same.. sometimes you'll get destoryed in the first fight.. respawn and come back for round 2, when you've figured out your opponents 'mind game' and destroy them back. Again, easy to learn and hard to master. Win some lose some.
The only 'con' I can comment on but, has not effected me very much, is the lack of dedicated servers. However, this is also being addressed in the near future and the game will have full dedicated servers!
You'll read several reviews about players getting stomped by higher rep. players via match making.. coming from people with less than 2 hours of play; etc.. Take this with a grain of salt. These reviews come from people who are 'mad cause bad'. You need to learn the game to be as good as people with hundreds/thousands of hours. Like in any game.. practice makes perfect. Level in this game is directly related to how much you play it, not skill. Lot's of high rep. players really aren't high in skill (not everyone of course). There's several ways to practice in the game and you can even compete against bots for fun, with friends or randoms. First and formost have fun.
No game is perfect but, the dev's are aware of issues and are always keeping the community up to date with what the plans are moving forward with the game, which is more then most AAA gaming companies do now-a-days.
If you're looking for something fun, unqiue, and a challenge, I recommend giving this game a shot.

First off, buy the first two to understand what the hell is going on.
Secondly, it's Crytek so unless you're on NASA's supercomputer, don't even try and put the high settings on, this thing is a tech-wank.
Thirdly, the review:
Crysis 2 is set a few weeks after the events of Crysis 1/Warhead in an infected, destroyed Manhatten.
You are [insert name here]. That's right; unlike the first two games where you knew who you were playing as this is the kind where your code-name (Alcatraz) is all you get. No voice lines, no backstory, nothing. Alcatraz coulds be called Daisy Chain McFluffy and have a penchant for modelling for all you know.
Anyway, you wash up on the shores of Manhatten and wake up find your broken body encased in the much-loved Nanosuit with the body of dear
at your feet.
You must arise into the city for a campaign set on the survival of the Human Race etc. etc.
The campaign is well thought out but depending on the calibre of gamer you are the plot twists can be somewhat obvious. The storyline is a fun one to play though, and not to short at that.
The gameplay is brilliantly responsive and unbelieveably dynamic. The game encourages you to not just tank every level - seriously, if you can do that on Delta difficulty, you are some sort of gaming deity.
And an idiot, because the fun is in the sneaky stuff, figuring out a way to pick them off, 1 by 1. Sure, you get some help from your goggles sometimes but it's your battlefield, a sort of mix between open world and linear that works.
Crysis 1 gave the most freedom but this is still a contender.
There are collectibles. SO MANY COLLECTIBLES! From car keys, to email, to voicemails to *HA!* speeding tickets.
This can get irritating though,
.
The enemy AI isn't stupid and can pose a challenge, but - like Crysis 1 - still suffers from things like enemies looking but not shooting at you whilst cloaked. The AI knows you're there but knows it can't shoot. It's odd but workable. They will only blind fire if you cloak in front of them like an dummy.
Unfortunately there is one paramount technical issue (for me at least): the inter-mission videos. The frame rate and sound accompaniment would suddenly drop. I had to go back to the main menu to view the videos from the unlocks screen each time. This got tiring quickly.
Other than that this game is fantastic. However I can only recommend it to you if you have played it's predecessors. Enjoy!

I generally don't like games which look like mobile/flash conversions and have a sequel number in their name. They tend to be rubbish. But Gangs of Deadsville turns out to be a decent strategic management game that is worth more than a few hours of your time. Building up skilled characters that you can take along to the next level can be quite rewarding and the learning curve is spot on in the first few campaign levels. There are also scenarios that can be played without the main campaign and widely available mods along with the ability to create your own.
So it's a fairly good game for which the metacritic score of 75% is pretty accurate. It plays like a 4x game crossed with an RPG without too much micromanagement and a text based diplomacy layer that does its job sufficiently well. It's no world beater but you could do far worse than sink some time into this surprisingly solid and enjoyable offering.

While the micromanagement is fairly substantial, this game is fantastic for generating 'flow' - the 'one more turn' phenomenon.
It's well-scaled (about the right amount of units to control in a level) and unlike many 4X games is interesting both before and after the map is explored. Very few titles get this transition right. The difficulty settings provide a challenge at the top, too, as well as a sandbox at the bottom.
If you want to see if you like it, Rebuild 2 is free on places like Kongregate. Rebuild 3 is atmospheric, compelling, and generates incredible flow to rival games like Civilization.
Such an amazing game, I couldn't recommend it more.  This is something everyone needs to play.

An enjoyable mix of the Legend of Zelda and the Souls series.
A top down exploration and combat heavy action adventure game with some minor RPG elements.
First, yes, the game looks bloody brilliant. It's visually and audibly one hell of a trip that will leave neon stains burned into your retinas and the hum of analog synth forever playing in the back of your head. Also, it's fairly brutal if you don't properly time your actions. Dodging isn't an instant cancel and believing it is will get you killed.
Second, starting with the adventure... well... I barely understood what was going on with the larger picture, but it looked great. The locatiions are all very well designed with lots of visual clues to lead you on to the secret paths. If you're looking out for mishapened walls, small rectangles on the ground, or ledges that seem like they should lead somehwere you're bound to find the majority of secrets on your first run. If you're just rushing expect to miss quite a bit. The adventure itself will pit you against a number of bosses each unlocking a new zone before finally being able to face the final boss. Along the way you'll pick up chips that act as XP which you trade for new moves or items along with cores that are required to progress through levels.
Third, the mechanics. The gameplay requires fervent use of dodging, poking, displacing, and repeating. If you stay in one place for more than a few seconds you WILL get hit. End of story. This doesn't mean there's only one style of play though, the game has various upgrades that can change how you handle encounters. You can focus on a range heavy style using rifles and pistols along with mixing in dodge combos that push enemies away and grenades, you can focus on close and brutal encounters using charged sword swings and shotguns, or you can mix and match creating a jack of all trades character that builds well into the late game once you have a lot of XP chips. That is to say, early on your choices in upgrades matter, but as time progresses you will eventually aquire most gear.
Finally, the difficulty. Is it hard? Yes and no. You may die a lot, but the game saves on a majority of the room changes and in most cases enemies will not respawn (unless you teleport) which means you can slowly work your way through packs of enemies and leave the room for a reset. If you do die then you lose a room or two of progress which you can save at many points simply by walking out then back in. Quick respawn times and forgiving checkpoints releaves a lot of the stress and time consumption that many tie with difficulty. The bosses and enemies all have fairly easy patterns to learn and can be aggroed or cheesed quickly after a fight or two. The game may seem hard, even brutal, at the start, but once you push past the first zone everything should click and fights should get a lot smoother.
Overall:
Is the game good? Yes. Definitely. Is the game great? While I won't go as far as some of the other reviews are saying, I will say it is very good. If the visuals interest you at all those alone should pull you through to the end.

I have now finished with my first town in Rebuild 3: Gangs of Deadsville and begun rebuilding the second. My opinion of the game, in short: it's good, and it's made some big improvements over Rebuild 2. But it's introduced some problems too, and it's not nearly as good as I was hoping.
I first played the original Rebuild (R1, R2, and R3 from now on) on Kongregate in 2010 I think.  It was quite a cool game even in that early state, and quickly became a favorite. I think R2 came out about a year later, and it was wonderful to see. R1 was already a great game, and seeing the creator of a great game go on to improve that game even more was--well, even greater. I can't remember all the changes from R1 to R2--the two games blended together in my mind, even more so since I didn't much like R2's music, and so while playing it I would mute its music and play the R1 music instead.
Later still I heard that Sarah Northway was working on R3, which got me very excited. And she was actually going to sell the game herself, rather than putting it on Kongregate. Good for her! It was already such a fun game she'd cooked up--she'd probably need to add a fair amount of new content and improve some of the gameplay--if she didn't make enough changes from R2 to R3, then players would just stick to R2, since, you know, it was completely free to play on Kongregate.
For me life took some twists and turns, and when R3 came out I was in no position to be spending money on it or anything.  But I've kept my eye on it, and now with the Halloween sale, I finally decided to buy.
More than R1/2, R3 has a big emphasis on storytelling, I can see. The game now has a completely separate "Story" mode, distinct from "Quick Play." Some improvements include cool stuff like:
+More with factions of the game, such as Gustav the trader and the Last Judgement Gang, as well as several that weren't in R1/2.
+Interactions with the survivors in your town. You can talk to people a bit, learn backstories, and choose perks when they reach high enough skill levels. I haven't gone incredibly far with this--I've leveled up and talked to maybe 10-15 survivors--but so far I don't think I've seen two survivors that both had the same story. But sadly, with so many survivors to talk to it becomes repetitive and unmemorable.
+A more fleshed out trading system. Instead of being railroaded into pretty much choosing yes or no when Gustav offers me a trade, R3 assigns values for the different items Gustav is selling, as well as for all the items I have, and then lets me make exchanges with Gustav according to those values. There's now even a "Haggle" feature, similar to that feature in The Elder Scrolls: Oblivion, allowing me to get a small discount on Gustav's prices.
+Graphics changes. The character icons are a nice touch. And the mouse wheel can be used to zoom in and out.
+Bigger, more cohesive story, shovels, pickaxes, more items than ever, lots of research, random events/sidestories, moral/policy dilemmas aplenty--BOOM! This is where I think most of Sarah's hard work went.
With all this said, unfortunately, I see quite a few problems in R3. Some are things that worked in R1/2 but are now broken, others were just never fixed from previous games, and some are all-new.
-Many underlying gameplay mechanics:
1. Housing. 2 people can live in an apartment building on normal, 3 on easy--but apartment buildings have dozens of rooms.  HUH?  Two-single-family homes can house 2 people. HUH? 20 people could live in 1 single-family home. They might have to cram in and sleep on the floor--but with a freaking zombie apocalypse, you SLEEP ON THE FLOOR!
2. Food rations, and other policy changes. You should be able to, at any time, require food rationing and other things. (R3 lets you do so randomly/when you build a City Hall.)
3. Multi-purpose missions. Why can't I send out a guy to pop off a couple zombies in a building, do a little scavenging, and maybe try to recruit a survivor while he's at it? R1 had the same silly gameplay, forcing 1 action per mission.
4. Other stuff, like having your people move faster but be less thorough on missions, or take their time and be meticulous--as well as loud and fast or slow and silent? (Zafehouse: Diaries, which has a lot in common with Rebuild, gives some of these options.) If there's ever an R4, I hope Northway takes Oregon Trail to heart, which gives you options for changing your speed and rations at any moment in the game.
5. Too many silly rules/features.
-In R2, each survivor could max out in all 5 skills--kind of unrealistic, since different people have different talents and potentials. R3's system is a bit confusing, and I don't think either is optimal--each character should have different maximum capacities/learn rates in each skill.
- The interface feels messy--worse than R2. I usually like to be efficient in killing zombies and keep my people from taking injuries or getting killed, while still killing as many zombies as possible. In R2, you select a building and see at a glance the % chance of risk--the chance of death or injury to a survivor you send. In R3 you select the building, then select a mission, then mouse over an icon and wait a second, all to see the % risk.  I ask: why did Northway see fit to require the player to take these extra steps that were never necessary in R2?  Five steps forward, three steps back.
And then, once I'm done looking at that info in R3, in order to select a new building to compare the 1st to, I now have to click to get out of the info screen on the 1st building, then click again to bring up info for another building.  That may not seem that bad, but consider that in just my 1st town I had to do all this hundreds of times, to select the right targets for my soldiers.  Multiply those extra 5 or 10 seconds each time by 500 or 1,000, and then by 5 or 10 or 20 towns I'm probably going to be taking over in the course of the game, and it quickly adds up to a BUNCH of time wasted just clicking, vs. R2. Now, why in the world Northway changed this--a feature that worked so well in the original, but now makes the game a lot more annoying--I have no idea.
A similar interface issue: R3 lets you click a survivor icon and drag it from one building to another, bringing up a small menu that lets you begin a mission--giving an order to scavenge, hunt, kill zombies, etc. I guess the idea of this system was to simplify the interface, but for the most part I ignored it. I did find that it was excellent for scouting, since it's quick and easy and there's no risk when scouting. But for any task where you're worried about risk--which is the case most of the time--you'll have to instead click the square, bring up the mission, and put the mouse over the icon to show you the risk. Why, Northway, didn't you incorporate the risk % into the order icons?  IE, drag a survivor to a square and the menu that comes up shows you, at a glance, the % risk, # of zombies, food/resources available there, and the time it will take? R3 micromanagement load=big.
In my view, R3 is about 5 steps forward and 3 steps back, plus some no-brainers that weren't fixed at all. Northway ought to have really upped her game--compared to its potential, I don't see R3 as that huge an improvement over R2. I can't rate as high as I'd like.

At the moment, anyone looking for a competitive card-based strategy game on PC is spoiled with options. Although Blizzard obviously didn't invent the genre, Hearthstone's runaway success has inspired other games aiming to tap into that player base and become just as successful. Duelyst might seem like just one more game on that ever growing list, but in spite of its similarities, it successfully distinguishes itself from the competition by adding a few new twists to the format.
A lot of the trappings around Duelyst will make longtime Hearthstone players feel perfectly at home. You can select from several factions--equivalent to classes--and enter practice matches against AI, online matches with other players, or a tournament mode where decks are built on-the-fly. Three losses in a single tournament (a mode which is still in development and is therefore not always available) equals elimination, while the number of victories dictates the value of the reward a player receives. There are orbs instead of card packs to purchase with in-game or real currency, but they function in much the same way. Once opened, they spit out cards of varying rarity for the game's different factions, as well as a neutral faction that you can freely utilize. Unwanted cards can be broken down, coveted cards crafted, and decks can be customized to your heart's content.
It all sounds so very familiar, but a match in Duelyst doesn't actually bear many similarities with Blizzard's blockbuster card game. Rather than playing cards as static objects on a 2D board, Duelyst's battles are set on a grid with opposing generals starting out on either side. Cards are then played to summon minions, but instead of being static actors on the board these minions (along with your general) can be moved around a set number of spaces in order to close-in on and attack the enemy. Ranged fighters and certain spells or abilities can accomplish that from a safe distance, but for the mostpart both minions and generals will need to get right up in a foe’s face to deal their damage.
There's much more to Duelyst than playing the right cards at the right time, or building the perfect deck. Positioning can be just as important as any other element of play, and for every deck built around a highly mobile play style there's another built around denial of movement and rigid board control.
The way minions can move and attack vary depending on the type of minion and the faction they belong to. Many Abyssian minions are low cost and low damage summons for example, but Abyssian spells are great for beefing them up to quickly overwhelm an opponent. Meanwhile, The Vetruvian faction favors flying minions who move unimpeded across the board. A Vetruvian player could build up their forces in an isolated corner out of harm’s way, then descend on the opposing general in a single turn. It’s a system that can feel a little intimidating if you’re not used to worrying about physical space when you lay your cards down, but the various faction specializations make it quite fun to experiment.
It’s also worthwhile to experiment with the character at the helm of your deck. There are multiple generals in each faction that a player can choose from, each with their own distinct abilities that play to their faction’s strengths. Generals can also be enhanced by playing artifact cards which give them weapons and abilities. The right general combined with the right artifacts can be absolutely devastating, but three hits and they’ll be disarmed.
The card system could potentially feel restrictive to someone coming to Duelyst from a strategy background, while a card gamer might find the board-based aspect an unnecessary complication. For those new to both, it may just feel overwhelming. There are a lot of very clever moves to be made when a solidly built deck, a lucky draw, and thoughtful board placement all converge, and thankfully Duelyst has a built-in way to show some of them off in the form of solo challenges.
Solo challenges are presented like a puzzle, where you enter what appears to be a match-in-progress and are charged to end it in one turn by using a specific ability or trait. As an introduction to advanced techniques, these challenges are incredibly helpful because they provide practical examples and let you learn through experience, rather than by following explicit, dry tutorials.
Unfortunately, practice mode is far less fruitful. The AI in practice matches is almost always predictable and easy to defeat. If I'm looking to develop and test strategies against a particular faction and their preferred techniques, playing against AI which hardly ever employs faction-specific capabilities isn't going to do me much good. Even if I want a more general form of practice, playing against AI that wastes turns on meaningless moves is not going to provide meaningful training. Solo Challenges make up for this in a way, but hoping for the perfect storm of cards in your hand and placement on the board so you can execute on that super hot trick you just learned isn't the most reliable strategy in an actual match.
Visually, this game captures a bright and wonderful retro aesthetic, but as much as I could appreciate its style, I still found myself pining for the glossy, gilded illustrations and animations found in similar games. Duelyst's art is absolutely well done, but it fails to leave a lasting impression.
Duelyst overlaps enough with similar games in the genre that stepping into it doesn't feel like starting from scratch, but it still manages to distinguish itself with some clever additions. While it still has its faults, those faults never overpowered the satisfying feeling of executing a perfect play. Even if you're still devoted to your competitive card game of choice, Duelyst is definitely worth a look.

This game was still in its early stages at the time of my review. But I like it. It is a very basic helo game. It doesn't live up to Desert Strike or Jungle Strike SEGA games from the 90's, no one seems to be able to capture that magic this many years later...shame. Anywyas THIS game is basically you fly around trying to complete the same objectives:
Kill a vehicle patrol
Kill random enemy soilders
Drop off infantry to reenforce
Capture Zones
Escort convoy
There is not any extract VIPS or POWs or anything like that unfortunatley, also no blow up target building objectives either. You win by your convoy reaching the last enemy base, which can be easy or hard depending on how you set up the game.  FI...You get more reasearch XP in multiplayer PvP games than you do in coop. You can play the USA side or the Russian side of helos and there is a decent amount to choose from after you research them. Most helos have machine guns and rockets, but some other weapons are ATGM, grenade lauchers, and AA missles. The scout class helos can call in mortar strikes if someone dropped off mortar infantry on the map.
You work together with team mates to achieve these objective against enemy AI or PVP over and over and over again. There is no AI helos though, you only battle other helos in PvP. When you verse AI its the AA, groudn vehicles, and infantry your fighting against. You can drop off RPG, Stinger, and Mortar infantry to assist you. The game also lets you research modfications to customize your helo's defenses/weapons.
The problem is this game doesn't advertise much. I randomly found it one day. I do recommend it, because its a cheap and a fun way to play helos. It is not by any means a helo sim, its is more an arcade helo game. The game has been updating well enough. I'd like to some more objectives in the game like extractions and destroyable buidling targets, but that is just because it was fun in the old SEGA games...
Some people won't buy games without Steam cards or achievements, so note that this game has no Steam achievements at this time. It does however have trading cards.

What can I say? For me as a military as well as a helicopter enthusiast and history buff this game is just perfect. It's not as boring as many hard core sims are yet it is not a crappy arcade game. The graphics are nice and the whole concept of the game keeps it exciting and interesting even after over 500 hours that I played it up until now.

I have never followed an early access game as intensely as HELIBORNE having personal contact to you guys and even contributing my tiny part (even though it hasn't made it into the game yet). So, I may not be completely objective when writing this review.
