Could the game get any better? Of course, and it will be. Expanding the content should be the most important post-release task. I personally would like to see more maps (more Vietnam, maybe a Korean scenario for tier I/night conversions). But since I know it's being worked on this is not a critic at all.
What can I say, I LOVE HELIBORNE and I wish you all the best!

I've been playing guitar for about 9, maybe 10 years now and the biggest problem I've had is finding motivation to practise and learning tricky songs. Rocksmith manages to get rid of both problems for me. I've not had this much fun playing guitar since I started, it's 'note progression' system makes learning difficult or tricky songs incredibly easy and it progresses at your level, and even if you can't keep up you can simply pull it back a few stages to a level you can keep up with.
It's helped me to learn songs I've loved for a very long time and failed to learn such as Electric Eye by Judas Priest (DLC song), Fear of the Dark by Iron Maiden (DLC song), Knights of Cydonia by Muse and Pour Some Sugar On Me by Def Leppard. It also gives you the option to learn the bass, lead or rhythm sections of each song allowing you to choose what you want to focus more on per song.
To sum up, whether you're new to playing guitar, or you've been playing for years or even if you're looking for your first lesson, Rocksmith can definitely help you out, and I'd reccomend this to anyone with an interest in playing guitar.

For this review, you must keep in mind that I recommend this game for what I got it for, not necessarily everything else.
My main interest in this game was custom zombies maps. That is quite literally the only reason I bought it. As a long time zombies fan, I have put hundreds of hours into solo and co-op zombies from WaW all the way through BL2. Each iteration brought new maps and that was always the most fun part (the new guns were cool too). However, I always came back to WaW on the PC because of the custom zombies maps. Play one map until you get bored, then download a new one. Rinse and repeat. There was no limit to creativity and depth in the custom mapping community. The only one thing more I wanted out of it was split screen multiplayer support.
When Treyarch announced Black Ops 3 would have mod tool support, I flipped out. Updated engine, split screen multiplayer, and potentially a revived mapping scene would arrive for custom zombies. It took a long time and was well worth the wait. I didn't even purchase the game until the tools were released to the public.
The mapping community started out pretty slow, as is to be expected. The biggest issue is that many players have moved on from this iteration of CoD already due to the late release of the tools, but at the workshop remains growing and better maps are being released all the time. Hopefully it continues to grow and content creators continue to be inspired to map for this game.
As for the singleplayer campaign, I did play through it. Took me very little time (maybe 10-15 hours max) and wasn't very challenging even on Veteran. I did want to go back and play Realistic with a friend but honestly the storyline is somewhat boring and is riddled with cutscenes and gameplay sequences that feel scripted. Not really my favorite campaign out of the CoD series and if I had bought this game for it I would have been extremely disappointed.
The only time I touched multiplayer was when they did a free weekend and it was riddled with cheaters. Honestly I don't know why you would play CoD multiplayer on the PC when there are way better alternatives. You want something competitive? Play CS:GO. You want something realistic? Play ARMA. The only thing it has going for it is decent visuals, but even then any of the Battlefield iterations look better than this.
All things considered I wouldn't pay 60 dollars for this game. It is older and two of the 3 gamemodes are pretty weak. If you can catch this for half off or more and are a fan of zombies then it is definitely worth it.

If one had to play only a single Indie game, Thomas Was Alone would be the one, hands down.
A player starts the game as Thomas, a plain, red rectangle that has just gained sentience after being part of an artificial intelligence experiment in the real world. However, in the digital world, Thomas learns to feel and express himself, attempting to learn more about the world and his inner-conflicts and importance. Along his journey, he meets up with other shapes each with a unique ability, such as being able to double jump (Thomas and all the others can only single jump), to be used as a springboard, or to swim (which the others cannot). These shapes are a few of many characters that exist in Thomas Was Alone. Each shape has a unique personality that is conveyed by the narration throughout the game. In addition, each shape Thomas encounters is also controllable by the person playing the game, which creates the need for teamwork and strategy.
At first, the shapes think too highly of themselves to feel the need to cooperate with the others. They soon figure out that they can escape to the real world, become architects, and change the virtual world they inhabit, for the betterment of all shapes. This creates a common goal that they work toward as a team instead of as individuals. To make progress, they need each other's unique abilities.
Thomas Was Alone is a game that teaches fundamental lessons about life. We all are a part of a bigger picture and we must coexist and cooperate to make any sort of advancement.  We all need to learn how to overcome obstacles to cooperation. We all need to learn the meaning of true friendship while discovering our true selves and our unique talents. These themes reverberate throughout the game, or should I say, work of art.

Well, after having had so many bad experiences with RPG Maker games, I am actually pleased to see one which is actually good. Maybe because it's nothing like the other RPG Maker games and tries to be original, which definitely came as a pleasant surprise.
To tell you the truth, I got tired of all the same stories and settings present in RPG Maker games. It's always high fantasy, always some legendary warrior on a quest to slay goblins, wolves and slimes. This game her,e however, takes place in a Sci-Fi setting with no fighting. Instead it tells a story by making you solve simple puzzles in a way a point and click game normally would.
I welcomed the change because I got tired of all the battles in which you would spam "attack" all the time anyway. There are no battles here, just a story to experience. And since RPG Maker games are always quite simplistic, that's the best use for them anyway. Coming up with good and fun gameplay mechanics for this kind of engine is hard, even more so getting the balance of combat right. Many RPG Maker games struggle because of this and fail because they have to do all that and create a immersive story on top of it.
So it makes sense that this game ditches battles and balancing altogether in favor of creating a fun story and compelling characters instead.
And it works.
The story, albeit short, is genuinely interesting enough to get you absorbed into the world, if you are willing to allow it. The characters have their unique traits and feel alive. There are a lot of things you can examine as the MC to get many interesting lines from both the MC and her companions, even very humorous ones at times. The game also looks rather good for a RPG maker game. Sprites fit the atmosphere and setting and every character has their own portrait, even irrelevant ones.
All in all, I can say that this is an RPG maker game that had some serious effort put into it and you can tell by playing it. This isn't the usual trash that gets put together in a hurry to put it on steam and make some cash. And even though it is quite short and cut into four parts, I would still wholeheartedly recommend this series for being one of the better games the RPG maker niche has to offer.

HANDLE THE TRAFFIC JAM!
Cities: Skyline comes with many very promising points. It's a VERY nice idea and really urgently needed to bring out an alternative to Sim City - I do love intelligent and complex building-up games, especially when they try to simulate the reality and its complexity as close as possible - what I  suppose paradox is trying exacty this in all their games I knew as far as possible - and Cities: Skylines really
earned some plus points.... BUT:
Besides some things I'am missing
- you have 4 kinds of areas to build: residence, industrial, commercial and offices, but three indicators only (where is the indicator for offices?)
- the mid game. where is the (mid) game?!
After you've managed to start a running town, everything seems to be targeting at tourism: Build special buildings - that all attract tourists - where are the hotels? where the yacht harbors? you cannot build a holiday paradise at the beach, becasue you cannot say:"this commercial area is for hotels, restaurants and bars only...)
-...many little things more...
after all it's
"Handle the traffic jam, that cannot really be handled well".
First you start to build a little town that earns money on which you can start to build up your real city.
You quickly learn that neither water nor power are your problems:
Like electricity any amount of fresh and wasted water can be passed through a single double line -  you simply have to remember to connect all parts to the water distribution net and check once in a while to ensure you have enough fresh water- and wasted water pumps (Use watertowers. They produce water out of nothing (realistic?) and are  cheaper than waterpumps and can be placed anywhere).
Also a quick calculation of Credits/MW shows you, the cheapest way to receive electrical power is by building wind and solar power plants only.
I never built neither a Water- nor a nuclear power plant; the power output per occupied space with renewable energy is unerealsitic way too optimistic and besides here you get the most cheapest power anyway (water- and nuclear produce the most expensive power).
After a while (at a population of app. 30...40k) the first thing you'll recognize is, that your city is drowning in garbage.
So you build more dumps or better waste incineration plants, even you info indicator tells you the capacity is more than sufficient.
Okay, no problem so far.
A little later you recognize there is a growing number of bodies lying around in the city everywhere - even, if you have more than enough capacity with cementaries (a bigger one would be useful) and/or crematories, and even less than half of all hearses are in use.
...what the...??
The reason:
Traffic jam.
All your garbage trucks and hearses stuck anywhere on the road.
So you build more and bigger roads, and avoid building buildings directly at the sides of mains streets that connect whole quarters to a round-about or highway, because vehicles that reach a destination slowing down their following traffic.
Short time later your town drowns in trash and bodies again, additionally you receive more and more burned down buildings although you have way too many of the (very expensive) fire departements.
The reason:
All your hearses, garbage trucks and also ambulances, police cars and fire engines stuck in traffic jam.
It doesn't much matter if you build small roads or big one way streets with 8 lanes.
No matter what 99% percent of all vehicles sort themselves in one long cade on a single lane - leaving the rest of the road unused. It's a bit like on german highways where many believe you could drive as fast as you want but in reality a long cade is running on the left lane with 1 km/h faster than the truck they are overtaking leaving 60% or more of the road's capacity unused...
Emergency vehicles do a lot of flashing and noise but they do not work themselves through the traffic quicker nor past it. They simply queue themselves in the line as all other vehicles - taking ages to reach their destination.
Besides the unefficient use of street's capacity  I figured out that traffic lights are second most important bottle neck and the cause of traffic jams.
Even at crossroads where high traffic crosses an empty road the duration of green and red light phases have always the same duration.
So you see a growing motor cade stop and going slowly to crossroads. 3..5 cars passing, then the whole cade stops again, waiting for several seconds for green light again, while at max. tumbleweed crosses the empty street...
It would be a great improvement, if there would be at least a simple traffic light control per each crossroads depending on the amount of traffic (A city wide flow of traffic control system would be an amzing feature that would be worth to be achieved - but that's really very complex to realize.) or at least could manually adjustable prioirty of traffic lights or priority of roads and right of way.
So you try solve the problem by using the tools you are given only such as building round abouts - figuring out, that they also have traffic lights at their junctions - building highway round-abouts with one way connections, because on highways there are no traffic lights and the traffic practises fluid zipper system, reconfigure your city street's with a complex system of one-ways...and back again ... only to figure out, that this relocate your traffic jams just to another place, move the traffic just to another bottle neck and sooner or later backflows back on your highways,  besides killing your bus lines or make them more uneffciently, causing more and more traffic jam...
...after wildest construction of highway shortcuts over and under round-abouts reminding me of road constructions I've seen in the outskirts of San Fransisco - ugly and all in all not solving the problem once and for all... I realized:
In a long term this simply cannot work, because you try to fight the problems you have with unused street capacity, unbalanced traffic lights and stupid emergency cars with way too insufficient and dull tools.

And shortly after you've beyond the very beginning of the start of a new city the very most of what you are doing in this game is trying to solve traffic jam by building new streets, tearing down streets or buildings, build more streets, reconfigure, tearing down, building new,... and so on, but never see a satisfactory solution, only moving the traffic jam from one corner of the city to another.
And street construction is not funny, because if you don't want to have rectangular ways only the tool that helps you editing the roads  is not really pretty to use. I need to build a road 4..6 times until it looks half way that I inteded but it's still wry, ugly an inelegant, but you think:"don't care! Just solve my traffic jam problem. Can build a nicer looking version later on..."
But you don't, because as in most games I know the computer citizens don't look for their quickest, most efficient way but for the shortest most direct only - and you cannot solve the traffic problems.
Even with a perverted net of buses, subways and trains and the feature of free public transport way too few people use them so the problem stays on the street.
Already early in the game you have no money problems no more (You'll quickly learn to keep an eye on your budget and set tax rates a little bit higher - what also slows down the population growth and thus the growth of your traffic problems.)  And it takes not long you'll have millions of credits in your city's treasury that cannot be spent.
Because you are in reconfiguring your traffic system, don't need more money and don't want to enhance the city, because that only causes more (unsolvable) traffic problems, and you badly want to avoid that.
And a game you avoid to play is not worth to be recommended.

I have now finished with my first town in Rebuild 3: Gangs of Deadsville and begun rebuilding the second. My opinion of the game, in short: it's good, and it's made some big improvements over Rebuild 2. But it's introduced some problems too, and it's not nearly as good as I was hoping.
I first played the original Rebuild (R1, R2, and R3 from now on) on Kongregate in 2010 I think.  It was quite a cool game even in that early state, and quickly became a favorite. I think R2 came out about a year later, and it was wonderful to see. R1 was already a great game, and seeing the creator of a great game go on to improve that game even more was--well, even greater. I can't remember all the changes from R1 to R2--the two games blended together in my mind, even more so since I didn't much like R2's music, and so while playing it I would mute its music and play the R1 music instead.
Later still I heard that Sarah Northway was working on R3, which got me very excited. And she was actually going to sell the game herself, rather than putting it on Kongregate. Good for her! It was already such a fun game she'd cooked up--she'd probably need to add a fair amount of new content and improve some of the gameplay--if she didn't make enough changes from R2 to R3, then players would just stick to R2, since, you know, it was completely free to play on Kongregate.
For me life took some twists and turns, and when R3 came out I was in no position to be spending money on it or anything.  But I've kept my eye on it, and now with the Halloween sale, I finally decided to buy.
More than R1/2, R3 has a big emphasis on storytelling, I can see. The game now has a completely separate "Story" mode, distinct from "Quick Play." Some improvements include cool stuff like:
+More with factions of the game, such as Gustav the trader and the Last Judgement Gang, as well as several that weren't in R1/2.
+Interactions with the survivors in your town. You can talk to people a bit, learn backstories, and choose perks when they reach high enough skill levels. I haven't gone incredibly far with this--I've leveled up and talked to maybe 10-15 survivors--but so far I don't think I've seen two survivors that both had the same story. But sadly, with so many survivors to talk to it becomes repetitive and unmemorable.
+A more fleshed out trading system. Instead of being railroaded into pretty much choosing yes or no when Gustav offers me a trade, R3 assigns values for the different items Gustav is selling, as well as for all the items I have, and then lets me make exchanges with Gustav according to those values. There's now even a "Haggle" feature, similar to that feature in The Elder Scrolls: Oblivion, allowing me to get a small discount on Gustav's prices.
+Graphics changes. The character icons are a nice touch. And the mouse wheel can be used to zoom in and out.
+Bigger, more cohesive story, shovels, pickaxes, more items than ever, lots of research, random events/sidestories, moral/policy dilemmas aplenty--BOOM! This is where I think most of Sarah's hard work went.
With all this said, unfortunately, I see quite a few problems in R3. Some are things that worked in R1/2 but are now broken, others were just never fixed from previous games, and some are all-new.
-Many underlying gameplay mechanics:
1. Housing. 2 people can live in an apartment building on normal, 3 on easy--but apartment buildings have dozens of rooms.  HUH?  Two-single-family homes can house 2 people. HUH? 20 people could live in 1 single-family home. They might have to cram in and sleep on the floor--but with a freaking zombie apocalypse, you SLEEP ON THE FLOOR!
2. Food rations, and other policy changes. You should be able to, at any time, require food rationing and other things. (R3 lets you do so randomly/when you build a City Hall.)
3. Multi-purpose missions. Why can't I send out a guy to pop off a couple zombies in a building, do a little scavenging, and maybe try to recruit a survivor while he's at it? R1 had the same silly gameplay, forcing 1 action per mission.
4. Other stuff, like having your people move faster but be less thorough on missions, or take their time and be meticulous--as well as loud and fast or slow and silent? (Zafehouse: Diaries, which has a lot in common with Rebuild, gives some of these options.) If there's ever an R4, I hope Northway takes Oregon Trail to heart, which gives you options for changing your speed and rations at any moment in the game.
5. Too many silly rules/features.
-In R2, each survivor could max out in all 5 skills--kind of unrealistic, since different people have different talents and potentials. R3's system is a bit confusing, and I don't think either is optimal--each character should have different maximum capacities/learn rates in each skill.
- The interface feels messy--worse than R2. I usually like to be efficient in killing zombies and keep my people from taking injuries or getting killed, while still killing as many zombies as possible. In R2, you select a building and see at a glance the % chance of risk--the chance of death or injury to a survivor you send. In R3 you select the building, then select a mission, then mouse over an icon and wait a second, all to see the % risk.  I ask: why did Northway see fit to require the player to take these extra steps that were never necessary in R2?  Five steps forward, three steps back.
And then, once I'm done looking at that info in R3, in order to select a new building to compare the 1st to, I now have to click to get out of the info screen on the 1st building, then click again to bring up info for another building.  That may not seem that bad, but consider that in just my 1st town I had to do all this hundreds of times, to select the right targets for my soldiers.  Multiply those extra 5 or 10 seconds each time by 500 or 1,000, and then by 5 or 10 or 20 towns I'm probably going to be taking over in the course of the game, and it quickly adds up to a BUNCH of time wasted just clicking, vs. R2. Now, why in the world Northway changed this--a feature that worked so well in the original, but now makes the game a lot more annoying--I have no idea.
A similar interface issue: R3 lets you click a survivor icon and drag it from one building to another, bringing up a small menu that lets you begin a mission--giving an order to scavenge, hunt, kill zombies, etc. I guess the idea of this system was to simplify the interface, but for the most part I ignored it. I did find that it was excellent for scouting, since it's quick and easy and there's no risk when scouting. But for any task where you're worried about risk--which is the case most of the time--you'll have to instead click the square, bring up the mission, and put the mouse over the icon to show you the risk. Why, Northway, didn't you incorporate the risk % into the order icons?  IE, drag a survivor to a square and the menu that comes up shows you, at a glance, the % risk, # of zombies, food/resources available there, and the time it will take? R3 micromanagement load=big.
In my view, R3 is about 5 steps forward and 3 steps back, plus some no-brainers that weren't fixed at all. Northway ought to have really upped her game--compared to its potential, I don't see R3 as that huge an improvement over R2. I can't rate as high as I'd like.
Is it worth buying? Probably, during a sale.

I used to enjoy the first two parts of the Rebuild series. So I was looking forward to one day play the third part aswell.
It's a good game with a - to my knowledge - pretty unique idea, yet it is less than I expected and came with flaws that annoyed me a little.
- The writing. Allthough I didn't really like the main story line, i have to admit that it's objectively good because the writing itself is very creative which not only accounts to the main story but for the uncountable little sidestories aswell.
- The game is written, programmed and shaped by a woman. You will notice that on a few occasions, in several flavor texts and it gives the game a special flavor which i liked a lot. I really don't want to sound sexist but maybe women have a different approach when it comes to the zombie-apocalypse? When compared with other titles of this genre, it stands out. So even if you're bored by these kind of games allready, chances are high, Rebuild 3 offers you something that you haven't had before.
- The overlay management is brillant. That's important in a game that depends on micromanagement a lot and it's performed comfortably.
- The game is very ressource-friendly on your computer and by that runs fluently on my system even when I play the maximum sized map with the maximum amount of survivors possible. In general: No lags, no crashes, technically very good.
- The graphics are allright. It's a simplistic yet unique style that you may or may not like but it suits the game. All in all the game isn't ugly nor boring.
Cons:
- Limitations! They are everywhere! Want to hear some? Maximum amount of...
Survivors: 250
Food/Materials: 999
Ammo/Fuel/Medicine: Most certainly 999, too.
Even the map size "Epic" is not big enough for my taste.
Why couldn't anything be a little larger? It's not like you would need more people to get the jobs done, but the game actually offers you to say that you want to repopulate the world and then you can't take new guys in because the game doesn't allow more than 250 persons in your huge city!? That's just arbitrary and counter-immersive.
- Game mechanic wise there is a blatent lack of depth in content. As in: There is a ton of things to interact with but doing so doesn't lead you anywhere once you claimed enough buildings of each type. Maybe it's a missed opportunity for not allowing players to find some special rare buildings to get boosts of some kind and fight for or certain questlines. Maybe it's a problem with balancing in general. I'm not sure, there are different ways of approaching that issue. Still I had a problem with it.
In my opinion the games tries so hard (and succeeds in it) to give you a good feeling about your survivors, their stories and needs, about how your every surivor is an individual with a unique story, that it forgot to put its focus where it was actually supposed to be: Rebuild your city. Reclaim the territory, fight for it, manage to do that your way and manage to keep your colony alive.
But I'd lie if I said I wouldn't have enjoyed it, the way it is. It is a pretty decent little game. Maybe I'm the one who is wrong with this review for simply having unmet expectations, that you can't blame the developers on.
Try it yourself. I'm pretty sure I tell you the truth that you will not think you've thrown your cash out of the window if you give this game a chance. If you were looking for a nice singleplayer game that runs on bad computers), focusses on having your survivors reclaiming a lost city, this game is for you.

Rebuild 3: Gangs of Deadsville sets up in a Zombie Apocolypse, where almost every huge city has been overrun by zombies. You, and a few groups of survivors, decide to liberate the cities from zombies and discover the cause and the cure for the virus.
PROS
~This game has okay graphics
~The random events are quite varied, some leading up to a bigger plot.
~The building mechanic is fun, but very exploitable, to the point where you have pretty much infinate ammo
~The gangs are actually quite varied and unique, each with different strategies. A few factions I can remember are the faction of kids, faction of gamers, the government, drug dealers, and martial artists
~This game takes some bold and brave moves, like Abortion, or depression, which I admire
CONS
~this game has very few animation, its more or less slide and story telling
~Although some missions are longer than others, this game feels extremely easy. It just tricks you into thinking its harder by making necessary resources farther away from base
~Like I said in the beginning, this game is highly exploitable, from making infinate ammo to having ways to overfarm
OVERALL
6.5/10

The game provides lots of lessons, starting from very basic stuff all the way to the "master" level lessons. The way things are taught is good and simple, even I understand them!
There are also different sorts arcade games in which you can practice different techniques and finger dexterity, altho I have to admit that the game design in these minigames is not that great. Many people might say that it's down right broken, but I'd say that at least you can improve a bit while playing, despite how merciless the minigame might feel like. For example the Harmonic Heist -game can be rage inducing when it comes to the guard you have to avoid. Sometimes you just can't avoid him despite how well you're performing.
Learning a song starts off simple enough. Once you've completed your first song the game gives you tips what to do and where to focus on improving. There's also a neat feature called Riff Repeater, which allows you to practice specific parts of the song. You're allowed to slow the song down and practice that part as long as you like. For me this tool has been a blessing.
You might wonder if your electronic acoustic guitar works with the game? At least for me it does, but keep in mind that the mics in a acoustic guitar might not be as good as in electronic guitar. For example while doing bends my acoustic's mics are giving me trouble, most of the time I get misses while bending the strings. The problem might be guitar specific but then again, I don't have hard evidence.
So far I've loved this game. I've improved a lot and the passion of playing guitar burns bright in me once again. I'd highly recommend the game if you're about to start practicing and have few extra bucks in your pockets. Some purists might say that you'd be better off practicing like they were before the wars, but that is just a preference in my opinion. Pick whatever style you find comfortable for you.

HLD was an interesting experience. The game takes a retro/neon pixellated art direction (similar in feel to the Neon Dragon far cry spinoff). Gameplay is top-down sword/gun combat, and for the most part it works well. Quick reaction time and strategic use of your abilities is important to survival, especially in some of the challenging boss fights. Not all was stellar though: Dash-chains can be extremely finicky, and the 800 dash challenge was ludicrous... I resorted to putting on my metronome, and even then the game wouldn't register some clicks.. either that or I lost focus for a small moment. That's one thing that I'll never be replaying in any future run of this game if I pick it up again (that was optional, but required if you want the "all outfits" achievement). What you start with, is kind of how you end the game. You will need to search the game for money to upgrade your character, but they aren't very essential... you could probably play the game without a single upgrade. Sword/gun is the game's bread and butter, and it doesn't need any fancy gadgets (by design).
The music matches the retro theme, and sets the atmosphere well... I like how the battle music just ramps up the basic peaceful theme a bit to sound a bit more aggressive/urgent... it never changes into "fight song" mode.
The thing that let me down though was the game sets up an interesting world, and tells a lot of it through your own exploration (rarely is anything actually written in English to explain to you what is happening, or what you need to do). You set out into the world, and kind of figure it out as you go along: "I guess now I need to unlock these triangle mechanisms", "This icon looks like a boss, I guess I need to fight it", etc. The few npcs that will talk to you, will only communicate through pictures (revealing some genocidal invasion, some cult takeover, some mysterious enemy) to give some backstory, but nothing is ever really explained. I didn't 100% the game yet, but the main part of the story is left unexplained, which is a real let-down.
The game starts by showing you a massive explosion, then some sort of strange dream/hallucination world mixed with an egyption/native american homer simpson pepper acid trip, then you're rescued. You have recurring nightmares of some strange enemy killing you, your character keeps strangely coughing up blood... none of this is answered or explained. The world has 4 zones and a main safe zone, with each world has its own "catastrophe" with an overarching theme of some giant terminator robot like war/extermination.. again, it's left unanswered.
While I do like using my imagination to fill in the blanks, the game already has a TON of that. If you're going to set up big overarching themes and ask some interesting questions, make sure you wrap them up in some sort of satisfying way. Not everything needs to be hamfisted and explained (cough, medichlorians), but you can't just flash a bunch of cryptic imagery and say "isn't this cool and mysterious" then never explain what/why. There's plenty to explore in the main world, plenty of secrets for you to find, etc, but I wish there was an actual pay-off to the story.
Spoilers about the ending follow:
Destroying the final boss, the nightmare monster that's been haunting you doesn't answer anything about the giant robot invasion, who you are, what the strange eye thing is you were reaching for... just a big light show in the sky, and game ends... very, very anti-climactic. I'm fine with mysterious characters... the guardian who saves you, the one who the jackal leads you to in each of the 4 worlds, he dies, and you feel bad. That was fine, we knew enough about it. But why was he also sick? What is the jackal? Why were we powering up these 4 beacons, to destroy the evil robot/alien thing? ok but what happens after we destroy the eye, why was the eye there...
Just poorly executed on the ending to the story. Kind of the opposite to owlboy. Owlboy had the starting and ending planned out, but didn't know what to do with the middle. This game had the puzzling start, built up the world enough throughout the middle, but there was absolutely no climax... Like walking through a haunted house with all these things happening, and at the end you open the final door and you're just back on the sidewalk outside and everything is over.
So would I recommend it? I think so, probably get it on sale though. Combat is challenging enough to be satisfying. Boss fights can be unforgiving, but you'll learn the patterns with enough retries. The world exploration is engaging, and there are plenty of secrets to locate. If that sounds like something you enjoy, pick it up. I guess I would compare this game to a top-down zelda game. You get a more combat oriented game, but with a major trade off to a satisfying overall story, which to me is very important.
I also didn't want to add this in, but it was a little surprising to see Sarkeesian and Quinn thanked in the credits (among a long list of people). Their regressive anti-gaming politics however didn't show itself in any capacity in this game, so if you saw any threads on reddit or whatever about them being thanked, you can rest assured there was nothing eye-rolling added into the game. Don't let that miniscule inclusion influence your decision on whether or not to purchase this title.

When I started playing this game, I was enthralled. The first several levels are on par with games like Half-Life 2 and Bioshock, evoking a real sense of wonder and exploration. As you begin to explore, you slowly learn about what's going on. The game does a really good job keeping the tension at the start--the pacing is great. The basic premise is very generic, but it seems like a pretty interesting version at first. The experience of wandering the beseiged NYC alone looking for answers as an unlikely hero forced into an inhuman monster was great. I had to keep playing just to see what would happen next.
Unfortunately, the plot quickly falls apart. After a few hours, all the mystery is lost, and it devolves into yet another "Heroic U.S. Military vs. Fictional Bad Guys" kind of game. You get shackled to some idiotic squadmates, and it's no longer about exploration and discovery, it's about following the orders that get shouted at you. Not a satisfying experience for me.
Also, as I got further into the game, it started crashing more and more. I think I'm about 3/4 of the way through it, but every time I play, it crashes within an hour. And when i say "crash," I mean it freezes, messes up my video card drivers, quits big picture, and I have to♥♥♥♥♥♥around with ctrl-alt-delete for several minutes just to get back to normal. At this point, it's not worth the effort.
Other Pros and Cons:
+Controls are perfect
+Graphics are quite impressive (mostly I was impressed that my computer could handle it)
+Immersive (at first)
+Good gun feel
+It's fun watching New York get more and more ♥♥♥♥ed up over the course of the game
+Gun customization is good
+Nanosuit powers are cool
+"Tactical options" are a nice addition
+You can see your own legs
+Some voice acting is pretty good
-Most voice acting is pretty bad
-Why even bother carrying bullets when you can kill anything with a couple of punches?
-AI sucks
-Stealth sucks (the enemies always know exactly where you are, and will start shooting immediately when you decloak)

All in all, I'd say that if you've got the money for it, and you're in the market for a minimal, narrated 2D platformer, go for it.

I can't think of one reason not to recommend this game to literally anyone.

As a person who has 400+ hours on PC, 300+ hours on Xbox One and 300+ hours on the PS4, I love the game. It is an incredible game, however, it have a lot of issues.
It was an innovative game which a unique gameplay and the graphics are amazing, The graphics are amazing, even at the lower quality, and well optimised. I rarely have frame drops, unless it is dominion or an older map.  With all my hours in this game, it shows how much I love playing this game, from learning the basics of blocking and attack to learning how to parry to different mix up ending with learning the near impossible, but now removed, parrying Warden's Crushing Counterstrike.
However, with all this, I got to admit the game has a lot of issues with the connection type being peer-to-peer to some classes being completely outclassed to the dreaded game mechanic exploits.As much as these are issues, the developers are heading to the right direction with implementing servers (although late, better than nothing) and removing/fixing a lot of bugs, exploits and things not intended (RIP parrying Warden's Crushing Counterstrike). The older maps are not optimised and causes a lot of frame drops, from my experience.
One thing is that I do not like is the match making system, for both casual and competitive. If I am playing casauls with my friends who doesn't play as much, we either get matched with people above my skill level, which is realitivly high, or his skill level who doesn't know how to block. If I play competitive I am placed in Platinuim III, if play with people around gold level (which I am rarely matched with) and lose, I lose approximately 60%+ of the division I am in, whereas, if I play against diamonds (which I am constantly matched against), it is realitively one sided, for the most part. I guess I do learn what I am doing wrong and what I can improve on, whether it is playing too aggressive at certain time or playing too defensive. This is because they are usually better than me, most of the time, so I am bound to lose, most of the time, however, I still lose around 50%+ of my division which I see is unjustified on why I lose that much against an opponent which I should lose against. Whenever I do win a game of competitive, it isn't as rewarding as I earn around 20-40%, even when I play against diamond players, most of the time. Sometime I earn less. When I play against lower rank players, I don't even earn 10%, which is justified.
The campaign has to be in it's own category. The campaign, although fun, is only a one time play. I had a great time playing the game the first time, especially in realistic where I have to learn each hero's fighting stance and attacks. The bosses are great to play against. However, it is a campaign that can not being played mutiple times. It gets extremely repetitive and stale, it uses old mechanics of the game, the storyline is dreadfully short and it is does not make sense. I do hope that they do add more to the story later on the games life, whether it is paid DLC or it is free, I will play it.
With all this, I have to admit it is a damn good game, in my opinion, and I love the gameplay and the unique gameplay, however, in my humble opinoin, I can not recommend it, as of now. There are still things to fix such as match making and connection type. Other than that, I would surely suggest buying the game. As I said, I love this game and I wish anyone who buys this game to have a amazing time,
I will say is that when the price reduce, purchase the game, whether it is from steam reducing the price or ubisoft reducing the cost. That or purchase the game when the main issues are fixed (connection type and exploits).
If you buy this game, I hope you have a blast playing the game, and if you read this review, I hope I gave you the information to help you decision on whether you should buy this game or not.

Awesome game, I rember playing this game back in the day, with my family when the only pc we had was running dear old Windows 95. Although the standard in videogame making has been raised exponentially since this game came out (not really a surprise) this is still extremely fun to play. I personally love the lack of hints and all those helps that you get nowadays; of course when you die and the last time you saved was 2 hours ago you get a bit mad, but this is part of what made this game (and others) so cool: it teaches you to care for Lara, unless you want to spend half the time you play saving.
It's also great when you want to take a little break from newer games, it just has a complete different vibe to it.

First of all, yes, this game does desperately need an update for new systems. I didn't finish it for just that reason. That is to say, the game runs alright on modern systems, but uses a downright bad DosBox emulator which crashes whenever the Windows key (or a few others) is pressed, which is especially annoying given the fact that particular key falls squarely in-between two of the most commonly used buttons in the game. One slightly wrong move and you've blown it. Also factor in the 1996-era computer graphics and controls (which are particularly notably bad here, as you not only have the all-too-common directional issues of the era that always make me wonder how we didn't pull our hair out, but also a character that sometimes downright refuses to jump and move in a given direction at the same time), and this game is particularly dated and as such is at times frustrating. These are definitely cons which, depending how you feel about playing classic games from the period, could be a deal-breaker.
Yet, I do still recommend it for those who want the original experience of playing one of the best games of the Lara Croft series, and have the patience and ability to do so. Unfortunately, the graphics of the period are particularly hard on the eyes, so if you have vision issues like I do, be prepared for the possibility of extra strain. But, while it is old, it is still very much the game that you might remember, frustrations and all. The game is immersive, the puzzles and encounters engaging, and it simply feels like a genuinely death-defying Lara Croft adventure (though, admittedly, some of the challenge of defying death comes strictly from the poor controls) where one truly is free and forced to jump, climb, shoot (though there is auto-targeting as long as you're facing the right direction, or it'd be downright impossible with these controls), and dangle with the unforgiving precision necessary to survive. If there's one thing games of the era tended to get right compared to today, it is definitely the lack of hand-holding despite the inferior controls. This is a true adventure game.
Overall, though highly dated, it is a truly great game, and one that would serve the series very well as a future remaster rather than the modern inferior sequels they keep releasing.

Ok so lets get the Elephant in the room out of the way...
Alot of reviews have said `Well its not Resldent Evil really is it...`. Well that is utter tripe. It is a logical continuation of the RE  franchise.Sure it isn't classic Survival Horror but that has been done countless times in the series and things need to move on.
I for one would not want another game stuck with the frankly horrid and awkward controls we have been saddled with since RE:1. People do not rotate on the spot, neither are they incabable of walking and shooting and it's about time that convention died a sad and lonely death.
This is a good game and has plenty of old and new characters meeting across intersecting story lines. So far I have played Ada's campaign and had a blast. There are plenty of secrets to find, icky things to shoot and the odd classic `makes zero sense` puzzle thrown in.
There is a ton of Co-op, Versus and Online action to be had across the various DLC packs and plenty of replay value.
That is the pros out of the way, sadly there are a few cons you should be aware of:
There are more Quicktime events than in the Tomb Raider reboot and that is really saying something. I personally HATE QTE's and just wish programmers would sod off putting them in games already. My percentage scores for Ada's campaign is tragically low due to the amount of times I died because I failed yet another QTE mini `game`. Games are fun, QTE mini games are not.
I can handle dying because I played like an eejit and ran out of Ammo or walked into an obvious Ambush but failing to waggle the joystick, press X at a specific time then hit RT in the right order at the right speed is annoying beyond beleif.
The Controls are way better than previous iterations and being able to run and shoot is a godsend. However  there are ALOT of contextual actions and sometimes things go a bit wonky and you end up running into an enemy rather than actually pulling off some awesome takedown.
Other than those negatives this is definitely worth your time and money if you have any love for the RE series in particular or action games in General.

Having played
on Newgrounds (or Kongregate?), I too picked this one up for nostalgic reasons.
is a sort of casual 4X with a bunch of interesting twists. For example, your units don't have move points—at all. You can at any moment move them to any available location, which definitely makes the game more dynamic and fun.
However, most 4X games share a bunch of downsides, like boring late-game and plentiful micromanagement... and oh boy, does Rebuild 3 show its browser/mobile roots by embracing those. It has no general notification system, so you can easily miss that one of your survivors is idle. It also has no sense of late-game, no new challenges to add, and to destroy a faction, you need to grab each piece of their land, so you end up having to click them to death long after they have become helpless. Land-locking your opponents becomes trivial from City 2, since the only thing you need for them not to be annoyed is a lvl 8 Leader, who makes the whole mechanic pointless.
The visual clutter doesn't help: for example, it's hard to tell at a glance how many livable buildings you have. The character variety is also annoyingly low—which is a functional downside, since faces are generally how you distinguish people on the map.
Still, there definitely is charm to the game. It's mechanically robust, but still simple compared to other 4Xs; it also plays relatively fast. A bunch of its quirks are very cool (for example, you can take care of a child/teenager, who is an 'item' giving negative modifiers, but after a while, when they grow up, you get a citizen for free). And, seeing how you can transfer your top three units from city to city, you do kind of get attached to them.
All in all, while I think
is far from perfect, I would cautiously recommend it to fellow lovers of management sims, strategies, and 4Xs. Just wait for a sale, perhaps.

I beta tested the old Rebuild 2 a ways back, though I doubt the Northways remember little ol' 12 year old me. I wasn't the best beta tester, didn't even get my name in the credits! I was too busy having fun to actually give feedback on the game. Same is true here. At first I was a bit put off by the move from a more photorealistic graphic styled characters to this more cartoony one. Then I realized this game is almost a direct upgrade in a lot of ways. You lose the ability to train a survivor in every skill like the last game, but this added more depth to the strategy that I eventually grew to appreciate. The story is good and classic-arcade era style where to get the best ending possible you will most likely find yourself restarting over and over again.
If a Rebuild 4 ever comes out, I hope that there is some sort of way to interact between reclaimed cities, like an overworld map of some sort. I would sure love to have more than a new-game plus, which sadly brings me to the part where I must not give into nostalgia and give some fair critisims.
The game gets dull once you've learned every nook and cranny. Once you know what each building does, and what the special ones can help you with you really have no reason to keep playing. You can only customize one character (your 'hero'), so you can't do a 'Me and my friends/family/celebrities against the world' sort of scenario which is always funs in games like this. After you reclaim a city, no matter how you do so, once you move on to the next city, nothing but stats carries over. It doesn't matter if you made a daring plane escape or set up some sort of government and moved on, the options have no weight in the new game plus. Speaking of endings, the game is lacking them. Rebuild 1 & 2 had multiple endings. This game, outside of storymode, which has about only three mind you, has two. The original Rebuild had multiple endings. Escaping to a secret cabin in the woods, curing the disease (which is now story mode exclusive), reclaiming the entire city was a little celebration, and an ending for cultists overunning your society, and that's only off the top of my head.
Now I hope you aren't intimidated by that, but for those who don't like paragraphs, heres the TL;DR!
Pros:
* Campaign mode!
* More strategic than the last instalments
* More building variety than the last instalments
* More items and weapons to equip survivors with
* Perks to make survivors unique are a great addition and are really fun to play around with
* Factions! Cities aren't so lifeless and now rival factions will try to reclaim the city for themselves now. Each one is unique and interesting!
* Micromanagement isn't necessary, but it is rewarded. Making sure every survivor is doing their role every day helps a lot. If they aren't they are just passivley guarding, which helps too.
Cons:
* Quickplay has two endings, leave the city after being nice to/killing all the factions or escape via airplan
* Can only customize your protagonist (No family/friend adventures unless you get lucky)
* Power plant building provides a lab tech you can research within the first 90-180 days, whilst it will take you far longer to set up the power plant, if you are lucky enough to have one nearby that is.
* Useless buildings remain useless, unlike Rebuild 2 where some of them could have blessings in disguise (Banks had a telegraph, which could be used to call Gustav the trader.
* Explosives are a waste of resources, they level a building, forcing you to waste resources to rebuild it into something useful once you reclaim it. Yes its an isntant horde clear, but it is not worth the 5 rare, precious fuel you spent to get it.
* Moving to a new city is just a fancy way of saying New Game+
All in all I do love the game a lot, and I hope I have given you the insight you need to decide on that final purchase!

HLD was an interesting experience. The game takes a retro/neon pixellated art direction (similar in feel to the Neon Dragon far cry spinoff). Gameplay is top-down sword/gun combat, and for the most part it works well. Quick reaction time and strategic use of your abilities is important to survival, especially in some of the challenging boss fights. Not all was stellar though: Dash-chains can be extremely finicky, and the 800 dash challenge was ludicrous... I resorted to putting on my metronome, and even then the game wouldn't register some clicks.. either that or I lost focus for a small moment. That's one thing that I'll never be replaying in any future run of this game if I pick it up again (that was optional, but required if you want the "all outfits" achievement). What you start with, is kind of how you end the game. You will need to search the game for money to upgrade your character, but they aren't very essential... you could probably play the game without a single upgrade. Sword/gun is the game's bread and butter, and it doesn't need any fancy gadgets (by design).
The music matches the retro theme, and sets the atmosphere well... I like how the battle music just ramps up the basic peaceful theme a bit to sound a bit more aggressive/urgent... it never changes into "fight song" mode.
The thing that let me down though was the game sets up an interesting world, and tells a lot of it through your own exploration (rarely is anything actually written in English to explain to you what is happening, or what you need to do). You set out into the world, and kind of figure it out as you go along: "I guess now I need to unlock these triangle mechanisms", "This icon looks like a boss, I guess I need to fight it", etc. The few npcs that will talk to you, will only communicate through pictures (revealing some genocidal invasion, some cult takeover, some mysterious enemy) to give some backstory, but nothing is ever really explained. I didn't 100% the game yet, but the main part of the story is left unexplained, which is a real let-down.
The game starts by showing you a massive explosion, then some sort of strange dream/hallucination world mixed with an egyption/native american homer simpson pepper acid trip, then you're rescued. You have recurring nightmares of some strange enemy killing you, your character keeps strangely coughing up blood... none of this is answered or explained. The world has 4 zones and a main safe zone, with each world has its own "catastrophe" with an overarching theme of some giant terminator robot like war/extermination.. again, it's left unanswered.
While I do like using my imagination to fill in the blanks, the game already has a TON of that. If you're going to set up big overarching themes and ask some interesting questions, make sure you wrap them up in some sort of satisfying way. Not everything needs to be hamfisted and explained (cough, medichlorians), but you can't just flash a bunch of cryptic imagery and say "isn't this cool and mysterious" then never explain what/why. There's plenty to explore in the main world, plenty of secrets for you to find, etc, but I wish there was an actual pay-off to the story.
Spoilers about the ending follow:
Destroying the final boss, the nightmare monster that's been haunting you doesn't answer anything about the giant robot invasion, who you are, what the strange eye thing is you were reaching for... just a big light show in the sky, and game ends... very, very anti-climactic. I'm fine with mysterious characters... the guardian who saves you, the one who the jackal leads you to in each of the 4 worlds, he dies, and you feel bad. That was fine, we knew enough about it. But why was he also sick? What is the jackal? Why were we powering up these 4 beacons, to destroy the evil robot/alien thing? ok but what happens after we destroy the eye, why was the eye there...
Just poorly executed on the ending to the story. Kind of the opposite to owlboy. Owlboy had the starting and ending planned out, but didn't know what to do with the middle. This game had the puzzling start, built up the world enough throughout the middle, but there was absolutely no climax... Like walking through a haunted house with all these things happening, and at the end you open the final door and you're just back on the sidewalk outside and everything is over.
So would I recommend it? I think so, probably get it on sale though. Combat is challenging enough to be satisfying. Boss fights can be unforgiving, but you'll learn the patterns with enough retries. The world exploration is engaging, and there are plenty of secrets to locate. If that sounds like something you enjoy, pick it up. I guess I would compare this game to a top-down zelda game. You get a more combat oriented game, but with a major trade off to a satisfying overall story, which to me is very important.
I also didn't want to add this in, but it was a little surprising to see Sarkeesian and Quinn thanked in the credits (among a long list of people). Their regressive anti-gaming politics however didn't show itself in any capacity in this game, so if you saw any threads on reddit or whatever about them being thanked, you can rest assured there was nothing eye-rolling added into the game. Don't let that miniscule inclusion influence your decision on whether or not to purchase this title.

What a huge disappointment.  It gives off a presentation of being crazy and wacky, with old-school roots in its humor - poking fun with the 1960's version of sci-fi tech and trying to throw you off with wild scenarios and pop-art.  What it actually comes across as is nonsensical bull♥♥♥♥♥♥with boring pop culture references.
Minor spoilers I guess.  I got to punch a car, and we both had yellow life bars, and when I destroyed it it said "You Win!  Perfect!".  I found a "public domain man in carbonite".  There was a James Bond intro sequence, what with him shooting the camera.  I clicked a thing and an orcish hand appeared, with a "Something need doing?" voice line being played among other things.  I had a resort receptionist recite the Konami code to me as something to try to fix my complaints.  I once played as a cat to tear around an apartment tearing things up because cats are evil xDDD.  There's more than one Wilhelm scream.  Leetspeak, conspiracy theorists, and a voice acted line saying something to the likes of "this is just background noise, the player won't even notice" all line up to pinpoint very naive humor with weak delivery.  It's not creatively introduced into the game, it just exists because pop culture.  Each new encounter with such things just made me sigh and consider stopping playing.
In the first level, there's a ton of things to interact with, except you have to go out of your way to poke them, and the result is just garbage.  Sometimes literally.  Characters and objects spout unfunny gibberish in no relation to the universe or game.  After doing "side quests" and poking around the whole level, I was so bored I actively avoided almost everything extra in the rest of the game.  I could slam even more content, but instead I'll try not to drool all over myself.
There's something promising underneath all of this, but I'm having a hard time figuring out what.  The few minutes in my under-two-hour completion time where I was doing actual "60's spy things" and not being bombarded by bird crap - again, sometimes literally - gave me a small hope it would expand into something more interesting.  Nope.  Just a series of art projects linked by 5 second music loops.
Edit:  Wanted to add that the art and aesthetics in the game are unique and inviting in and of themselves, and I do appreciate a good chunk of them, as much of it is well-presented.  Heck, the intro sequence could be a standalone animation.  Unfortunately I don't find that enough to carry the rest of the game's weight.

93 hours in and only a few things are stale.
Yeah folks, 93 hours and I am still having fun with a $20 game. At about 89 hours I unlocked all the helicopters and all the weapons. Truth be told, I'm guessing 80 hours will get you all the toys, but I like paint jobs as well. Nothing  quite like ripping up a mountainside with a Jetranger in Sheriff's markings.
This is a fun game. It can be as serious or mellow as you like. Now that I've played for over 90 hours, how do I feel?
I am still having a blast. I've trying to excel in some of the older helicopters, and I am still tearing up the world. I've leaned HEAVILY on the US side of the tree and I've done very little PVP.  I want to do more of the Russian side, but getting players to do that on the US server is a bit of a challenge. THe few games of PVP I've played were fun, but not my cup of tea either.
Bottom line, great game that you can be mellow with and have fun in. It is actually relaxing (except level 4, I've lost more helicopters to high-power lines than a bug zapper gets with mosquitos). I wholeheartedly support the game so much I bought all the skins (becuase looking cool is awesome right before the mid-air collision). Right now it is $20 for the game and well worth it. If you are reading this during a sale, just hit buy. Not sure still? Watch 'The Mighty Jingle' review of it. (it is how I heard about it.
Cons: (yeah I skipped PROS because I love the game so much).
-infantry needs more random locations. There are times were you can shoot blindly and make points becuase there is going to be a bad guy there. (solution is to make them not count if you can't see them or randomise their location)
-There are a FEW @$$hats that will screw up you game and there isn't  a way to boot them. luckily they are very rare and if you bail mid-game... you still get all your points.
-military convoys need some randomization as well.
- The game lobby needs work, but if I understand it right, this is 4 guys making this game so I will cut them some slack... 90+ hours on a $20 bill? I didn't get that with Asteroids in the 80s.
-More maps or options would help people like me that have played this way to much. Not the DEVs fault... well it kind of is... you made a great game and we are burning thorugh the content.... $20... oh yeah.
TLDR - if you like flying helicopters in a casual combat nature, buy this and have fun. I'm at less than $0.25 an hour and I have no near future plans to stop. There is nothing else like this on the market.
Watch 'The MIghty Jingles' review of this. It is spot on (great for the American audience).

All the addiction and strategy of YuGiOh or Magic, combined with a bit of chessboard.  Its fun and engrossing and you keep finding yourself wanting to play more to unlock more cards and develop a stronger army.  I'm reminded a tiny bit of Unholy War, one of my old time favorites, but it's not quite that.
Its a game that does well everything it sets out to do... and its free!  Hard to argue with!
I've clocked some 80 hours into the game in my first month of playing it.  Now, that's harder to judge time than most games, because that's not pure playing time, but also looking at all the cards available and editing your own decks... so its easy to sink a lot of casual reading time in.  Which is fine!
I've seen some negative reviews complaining that the game is pay to win, and that's just not true.  Maybe if you want to be absolute top of the pack S+ tier pro level and compete with people that have been playing for two years, sure, but even the raw base cards are pretty good and dependable regulars that can carry you through the starting ranks of the game without much trouble.  The game is pretty generous with in-game currency and starter quests... it'll just give you a few free packs for playing through all the tutorial challenges and early easily achievable things.
After that, if you just play regularly, there's bonuses like first win of the day, win two games, welcome back bonus, and easy challenges like "destroy five minions" and "do 40 damage" that will very easily net you 100+ coins every two days or so, enough to easily buy another pack or attempt the gauntlet challenge.  And if you can get your skills up enough to participate and win in gauntlet mode, you earn even more cards and coins.  If you can make it to even the second game rank, you'll get free cards at the start of the month.  Plus, whatever cards you dont like you can grind up to make other cards.
You can buy packs to speed things up, yes, but just playing will get you the same rewards in fairly short order.   After clocking in 40 hours on the game I tossed 10$ at it to get a few packs, but that was more to support the game I'd been enjoying  than anything else.... and the results of those packs were the same as what I'd been getting for free...  just a chunk of them all at once. I would have gotten the same rewards from just playing another two weeks.

I will have this in my "go to" list for years to come along side Minecraft and Terraria.
Now with a few of the problems with these types of games that is more player than developer in some cases. First I took issue with the progression system. In many cases people were exploiting the progression by auto queuing and idle timing out, or using lag code to prevent the client from establishing a connection during the initial connection phase. This exploit takes advantage of the "double win" scenario as well as help keep unskilled players higher in the ranks. Another exploit I was noticing is the play bots that we saw in Magic the Gathering Online. I do believe that in any competitive game the absence of these bots may never be possible with the way privacy and national policy provide. SO play as you wish but do not dig in and pretend you will never encounter issues, bots or bugs.
As always play on, report bots and do your best to keep the community sassy!

Don't let its title fool you: Resident Evil 6 is not a survival horror game, but action-shooter.
If you seek to enjoy titles similar to Resident Evil 1 and Resident Evil 4, then, this game is not for you. Resident Evil 6 is more like a World War II game, more, or less.
Cons/Pros of the title:
Pros:
+ Great character depth and realistic personalities (Piers Nivans, Helena Harper, etc).
+ Four major campaigns (Leon's, Chris's, Jake's, and Ada's) with 5 chapters each.
+ Multiple Protagonists (over 7) for you to play, across these 4 different campaigns.
+ Partner system, like in Resident Evil 5, with the only difference that the partner in Resident Evil 6 has infinite ammo and infinite health if controlled by the AI. (Thankfully! No more notorious AI Partner deaths!)
+ Huge variety of enemies and bosses - From the classic zombies to the J'avo. (J'avo are infected humans, similar to the Las Plagas from RE4 and can carry weapons and feature many mutations)
+ Each of the 4 major campaign offers different atmosphere / theme:
++ Leon's campaign has the dark classic theme - contains zombies, dark corridors and is closest to Resident Evil 1 and 2.
++ Chris's campaign has the World-War-style acton shooting theme - the most "american" of all 4 campaigns, and is close to Resident Evil 5 in terms of action and shooting.
++ Jake's campaign has the Tyrant theme. You are being chased by a Tyrant-type of monster like in Resident Evil 3.
++ Ada's campaign... well, for this one... I leave this to you to see what it is all about.
+ Character/Story crossovers - during the story you meet some of the other protagonists, controlled by others or the AI.
+ Skill system, that allows you to influence various aspects of the gameplay.
+ Different graphical UI styles for the inventory and menus. Each of the 4 campaigns will have different visual UI style, as if you are playing a completely different game.
+ Herbs and ammo boxes are here like usual! Lets refresh our memory. 1 Green Herb + 1 Red Herb, what does it do? :)
+ Melee combat moves / Extended combat system for certain characters.
+ Dashing and running system.
+ Excellent Dodge system. With proper timing, you can dodge almost any enemy/boss attack in the game, if done right. This allows you to leave the battleS unscratched!
+ Each of the 7 protagonists have their signature weapons and moves which others cannot obtain/learn. Ada for example has her trademark weapon, the famous crossbow, when Sherry has her unique Stun Rod and Jake is skilled in the Martial Arts and can deliver great blows with his bare hands, etc.
Cons:
- Your weapons and firearms cannot be customized, upgraded or improved. The ability of upgrading your gun stats, from Resident Evil 2, 4 and 5, has been removed completely from Resident Evil 6. This means, with simple words, that, whatever weapons you may have, will stay the same forever.
- Camera is your biggest enemy. Causes troubles at times, especially when you need it to stay on your character's back but it doesn't. Super annoying!
- During cutscenes, the player's character can die. When a cutscene plays, your character will stay frozen solid, but the enemies will not. This means, if it happens there to be enemies nearby when a cutscene triggers, they can (and will) attack your character and kill him! And, no, it is not possible to defend your character from these hostile attacks, as you will have to wait for the entire cutscene to finish playing (!) and then for the camera to return back to its position over the character's shoulder (!) before you can resume control of your character. And if you see the Game Over screen after the cutscene, it means your character got killed and that you will have to start all over again... How shameful of Capcom's part to let a such oversight in a modern-day videogame like Resident Evil 6 to happen. Trully shameful. The Game Over screens right after cutscenes shows how poor job Capcom has done with Resident Evil 6.
- Most cutscenes can be skipped, but there is a good amount of them that cannot be skipped at all when the appropriate button is pressed.
- Way too many Quick Time Events. At least x10 times more QTEs than in Resident Evil 4.
- The game is trying hard to impress the player by adopting a Hollywood-style gaming  experience, at the expense of the player's own joy and comfort. Too many explosions and destruction in the surroundings, (such as cars blowing off, etc), can get repetitive and boring... And the camera leaves your character's shoulder way too often...
- AI is very stupid and poorly written. Enemies could come for you, pass by you, and then forget about you,
- Your partner has "body mass" and thus, you cant walk through him. This often leads in him blocking your path, especially in narrow areas and corridors. The problem here is that, due to the stupidity of the AI, he wont realize that he is blocking you from passing through a door, and thus, he won't give a♥♥♥♥♥♥about that. For example If you want to pass through a narrow door (narrow = wide enough for just only 1 person to pass through it) and it happens that your partner is standing in the middle of that narrow door, you wont be able to pass, well, at least not right away... So, if you are in the middle of a gunfight and you want to get past a door for cover from hostile fire, your AI partner may prevent you from doing so, and thus, increasing the risk of you dying or getting hurt, especially on the higher difficulties...
- The Cover system (Cover = taking shelter behind obstacles such as fences, corners and walls to protect yourself from enemy fire) could have been better... You enter into Cover Mode even when you don't want it, all just because Capcom decided that it was very practical to have the button for the Take Cover to be merged with the button for Weapon Aiming! Yes, you read right: if you hold the Aim button to shoot at an enemy with your firearm, but your character position happens to be near a corner, a crate, a fence or an wall, you will, instead of aiming + shooting, go into Cover Mode even if this was not your intention... how frustating! Capcom, you screwed it...
- The game's story spans 3 continents (America, Europe, Asia), but it lacks any depth. It could have been better.
- Your partner, when he is controlled by the AI, will rarely use the dash ability unless it is scripted to do so. This can be a problem, especially if you are seeking to get good timing scores / planning to do a speedrun in  chapters that feature very long corridors and paths.
- Graphics could have been better. The game allows you to visit many different places, such as cities, mountains, ships, etc, but the graphics in some of these places feel really outdated...
- It is not a survival horror title, despite its name. It is an action shooter title. It seems that Capcom took Resident Evil 5 and added a tons more unecessary action to its successor, distancing Resident Evil 6 even further from the series's successful and memorable roots.
- No costumes or extra weapons unlocked once you beat the game.
Capcom has utterly failed all my expectations for this game. Story is poor, no gun upgrades besides using skills, etc... But, at least, it got some funny steam achievements. And as a true Resident Evil fan and an Achievement completionist, I cant help but play this game for at least 400 not-so-entertaining hours. But once all the 50 Single Player Mode achievements are unlocked, I am gonna uninstall the game. And I mean it. The game is having problems and it isnt really worth of taking disk space in your computer if what you seek is to enjoy and experience a true successor of Resident Evil 1 or Resident Evil 4... Lets pray that Capcom wont repeat the same mistakes with the upcoming Resident Evil 7 title. We can hope that the Resident Evil Revelations or the Resident Evil 4 will be used by Capcom as examples on how to make a true AAA Resident Evil game title... We can hope at least... After all, hope dies last.

Thomas Was Alone is an indie puzzle plateformer video game. In this game, we control IA, represented by coloured squares and rectangles, which all have a special skill. The objective is, at every level, to bring these forms to their respective exit. Thus, you will have to combine their competencies so that every character can reach its own exit.
Thomas, the red rectangle, is the main character, and can jump higher than the others. Claire, the blue square, can float on the water and thus transport her friends from a bank to an other one. Laura, the pink rectangle, allows the other IA to bounce on her, and so will help the small Chris, the orange-coloured square, to reach his objective. James, the green one, can walk on the ceiling and activate the inaccessible buttons to open doors for the others.
Thomas Was Alone is addictive. It's not globally complicated: the riddles are rather easy to solve, and the platform part is hardly more complicated, especially thanks to the numerous checkpoints. Graphics are minimalist, it is thus difficult to speak about beauty, but we are quickly immerse in the universe. The music, composed by David Houdsen, is pleasant and serene. A narrator, voiced by Danny Wallace, tells us over time the intrigue and the mind of every character.
Indeed, the funniest part is not the game itself, but the thoughts of each character and their evolution. Laura, who can float in the water, takes herself for a superhero. Chris is the cynic of the group, but he is going to become attached little by little to the others. John likes making sports performances, but needs an audience to achieve there and doesn't like to be alone.
In a word, Thomas Was Alone is a small cool game, but which will occupy you no more than 3 hours!

Now here's a clever little game that stands out from the rest. If it were a tripod then the three legs it stands on would be Design, Music and Storytelling.
Design
The game is really clean and stylish, they've pushed this poshy zen minimalism that Steve Jobs  used on Apple products. Thomas Was Alone could easily be considered a lifestyle game, a building block for identity and self determination.Does it work for the game's benefit? Indeed it does, the game feels attractive, smart and easy on the eye.
Music
The music is again something that's extremely classy for a computer game. They use minimalistic melodies combined from crisp clean piano and radically electronic soundscape which kind you'd expect to find from a Björk album. In-game it kinda helps to reflect the openness of the space. A soothing experience to the ear.
Storytelling
There's an amusing story to the game. The cubes, that the player controls are all different characters with their own ups and downs and their own agendas. The story is delivered by a British-sounding narrator who manages to make it humorous, personal and overall soulful.
Couple of things that bugged me:
- Too many too simplistic levels in the first part of the game. There were these levels where you figure out the solution in 5 seconds and then it takes 2-3 minutes to complete it, which didn't feel very rewarding.
- For some reason jumps are not registered upon gentle tapping of the space button. Instead you have to smash it down quite hard.
Verdict:
The trouble they've gone into making the whole thing such a complete experience shows the developers seriousness and makes it easy to appreciate the hard work they've done. The game is a piece of art and if aesthetics is important to you then this one might be a treat.
