Okay, I HAVE to brake up this rewiew into two different parts. First part is mechanically the game (completely spoiler free), devoid of any story, and then the story (major spoiler). Because the story....
1) The game starts out with a handful of survivors, four, to be exact, on each new map. Each survivor has Defense, Leadership, Engineering, Building and Scavenging skill, ranging from 0 (utter noob) to 10+ (peak of humanity). With traits (gained as you level up the survivors and research Survivor Management) and equipment you can raise it above ten, and it does increase efficiency and decrease mission time. The top I've managed to pull off was about 21 building skill on a survivor. Not all traits raise skills, some give different bonuses, like immunity to the disease, reduced danger during far away mission.
The map contains several different types of blocks, ranging from one, two and four blocks, on a sqare grid. Each different block gives you different bonuses. Farms produce food based on size, apartments and suburbs give living space also based on size, hospitals accelerate healing, laboratories allow research missions to be completed, workshops provide crafting of Ammo, Medicine, and other one-time used items, pastures allow hunting for food, forests also allow hunting AND woodcutting, which provides building materials. Forests are one of the most valuable tiles, since those provide a steady supply of building materials, and while some maps edge is also forest, not all of them, and sometimes the starting position is in the middle of the map, essentially cutting off that until late game.
The resources are Food, provided by farms and hunting on pastures or forests, Building Materials, provided by woodcutting, Ammunition used in rare events and in case the defenders/attackers of the player has firearms or similar ammo consuming item on them (like crossbows) gained from crafting in workshops, Medicine, used in rare event, gained also from crafting in the workshop (yes, autocraft for infinite number is in the game for it, and these does not seem to consume any materials), and finally, Fuel, used in powering a maps powerplant and crafting. There are craftable consumables also, Explosives made from Fuel, Medkits made from Medicine, Traps made from Building Materials.
The game can be played in an RTS style, or in turn based style, depending on your preferrence, it can be changed anytime during the game.
The zombies on the map indicated by four colouration of a tile (after scouting). No colour is no zombies, green is few, yellow are mediocre, red is swarming. A tile can be reclaimed once all zombies are destroyed on the tile through an eradication mission option. Periodically zombie mobs actively attack the player.
2)

Tomb Raider 1 aka Big Game Hunter: Spooky Aztec Tomb edition has almost reached it's twentieth birthday. The big question you should be asking yourself is: has it aged well? To put it shortly, no.
To put it longly however, the game is a DOS port of a console port. Two strikes which hinder the game's modern playability. Straight out of the box, you're launched into a 4:3 640x480 resolution cube with which you can gander upon the stuttering walls, warping models, & render distance fog. Control wise, Lara chugs across the landscape like a tracked vehicle that can jump & grip ledges. The camera is glued to a pole on the back of your head, so hazards hiding around corners is nigh impossible. Gameplay wise, you'll only encounter two enemies: timed stage hazards & animals. As you mercilessly gun down the local fauna & trudge through the platforms, the only sound you'll have to accompany you is the diagetic falling of rocks. Whenever music does appear, it's entirely scripted to appear. For the most part, the game is clunky & boring when compared to modern titles that have come about because of this game.
If you're looking to the reviews to ascertain wether you want to buy this or not, I cannot recommend it. Anyone who actually wants to buy this game would've done so already. Don't get me wrong, the game still has its perks. If you're an enthusiast who likes playing old games, or just someone who wants to relive the days when you only had a handful of games to play so you explored every nook and cranny in every game, definitely go for it. Otherwise, the game isn't really for you.

As noted by the description and various publications, Hyper Light Drifter is a top down action-adventure game made popular by early 80's video games like Legend of Zelda, Crystalis, and Hylide. You wander the map in search of goodies, weapons, currency, bosses, and challenge.
Like any action adventure game, combat is one of the main focuses of Hyper Light Drifter. The main character's primary weapon is a sword supplemented by a gun. Dashing is the main form of evasion and what makes the combat so enjoyable- there are no limits to the amount of dashes and players are encouraged to tag in and out of combat to ensure survival of their fragile “Drafter”. With only five health and mounds of enemies to fight, players can be overwhelmed quickly if baddies are not dispatched quickly enough. Though you can recharge your health, doing so is risky- you only have a few health kits and do so makes the drifter vulnerable while he heals.
Another facet of combat is how the encounters are designed. Like many action oriented games, there is loads of enemy types- small but numerous baddies, evasive close combat goons, enemies with ranged attacks, stomping brutes, and so on. As you progress, enemies don't get bigger, stronger, faster, and what have you. Instead the encounters are designed to have a mixture of troops. Swarms push you towards unfavorable terrain, sword wielding goons try and surround you, ranged enemies try and pin with suppressing fire, and all the while those big mofos trudge towards you. Its this great mixture that keeps players on their toes and invigorates combat with the diversity of enemies and tactics they practice.
Bosses round out the combat experience with intimidating designs,  large health pools, impressive attacks and exploitable patterns. All offer a good challenge, which sweetens the victory when players finish a dungeon.
But its not all action. Exploration and treasuring finding is woven directly into the experience. The world is fantastically illustrated in bold pixel art supplemented with an ethereal and soothing soundtrack filled with echoing synchs and meandering melodies. Indeed, there are very few “intense” tracks, and the somber music flows while teasing out secrets and combating foes.
The game's currency, an unnamed yellow block, can be found by searching high and low for secret tunnels, platforms just outside sight, and experimenting by interacting with the environment. This currency (which you need four of to make a “whole”) is used to upgrade the drifter. There are also other pick-ups like keys to enter doors, special weapons and armors, tucked away in the world. Some of these hidden places have challenges that make use of the various upgrades you buy, usually involving dashing and precise dodging.
One of the little things that makes me giddy is that the drifter has a “sit” option by pushing the down direction on the controller's pad. Its a great way to take a screen shot or just to relax and absorb the environment and music. In town, the drifter doesn't swing his sword and whip out his gun. Instead he nods and flicks open his poncho. Its a great touch and helps draw the player into who the drifter is. Its like saying, “I'm in town, there is no need to break the peace.” The drifter has the same interactions when around people in the wilds and dungeons. Its a nice touch and I wish more games would use such interactions.
This is all tied together with the game's narrative- which is left open in many respects. Outside the menus, there is no text. Some of the world's inhabitants tell stories through pictures and grunts, usually two to four pictures long. They tell of events that happen or the location of the area's head boss. Off the bat, players know there was some sort of disaster and the game takes place, what seems to be years, perhaps centuries after the event. Remnants of battles, bones, and weapons litter the land. But its up to the player to come up with what all that means. Why did it happen? Why exactly is the drifter is searching the land? What is his roll in all this? What are these collectables even called? What's up with that dog? The broad picture is easy to interpret, but the details are left to player. It reminds me a of getting a game back in the 1980's, but no instruction manual to tell you what the game's story is and name of the various items, enemies, areas and allies.
While this game enjoys to harken back to the 80's and 90's era of top-down action adventure games, it does bring a few archaic designs from reaching into the past. With no text, some of upgrade “descriptions” (which are short demo animations) are ambiguous. The most infamous of these is the “multi-dash”, which is represented by the drifter dashing in a triangle. This doesn't even convey remotely what it does, as it allows the drifter to dash before his current dash is finished- allow the player to move very quickly. There are also two “slash-dash” upgrades. One deals moderate damage while the other is used to push enemies around. Again, the short animations don't do a stellar job showing this difference and its tough to compare because the upgrades are in sold in different shops.
Another is creating a false scarcity when it comes to health packs. Once you get a health pack, its gone till you leave the area. The only way to get a health pack is by roaming the world and picking them up. However if you played poorly in a dungeon and you need to drum up some health, prepare to waste 5 to 10 minutes dashing around previously discovered areas to refill your consumables. The development team could have had a place to stock them, like in the central village. Instead the player is forced to perform choir. Its 2017 people.
Most glaring is the knock-down abuse some bosses are made to do. Some boss's attacks can knock the drifter on the floor, leaving him vulnerable when he gets up. Many bosses have attacks they use just as the drifter gets up, allowing the player no time to dodge, attack, or heal. Due to the low health the drifter has, many bosses are able to wipe to player up efficiently after a good knock down. It just has a dirty and cheap feeling to it, especially when a player first tries to work out the boss's patterns.
Though none of these hiccups damn the game, they are noticeable rough spots in an otherwise smoothly made product.
But its this combination of fighting and discovery that makes wonderful peaks and valleys of intensity that keep the game both varied and interesting to the player. The vast assortment of hidden goodies and secret passages peak interest and satisfy the collector/discoverer kind of player. (Though its not required to find these secrets as many are a challenge to find on your own) The sharp visuals and relaxing audio tie the whole game play experience together.
The game also features a new game+, though the drifter simply starts with two health and is locked out of wearing other ponchos. If you enjoy the challenge of simply not getting hit, its a nice addition. If your actually looking for a game that plays differently with new challenges and enemy behaviors, its a total pass.
If some of your favorite games include The Legend of Zelda: A Link to the Past, Secret of Mana, or Illusion of Gaia, then Hyper Light Drifter will satisfy the need to slash and explore, especially if you haven't played one in a while. If you never got into the action-adventure genre or wasn't around during the 80's and 90's, Hyper Light Drifter is a decent entry into the genre. However, you may find older titles more sluggish and “tanky” compared to zippy nature of Hyper Light Drifter.
Overall, Hyper Light Drifter is worth while addition to any action-adventure lover's library.

I will start with outlining a couple of characteristics first - this game consists of:
- RPG-style graphics with adventure point-&-click game mechanics (i.e. inventory, items, journal for game progression, clicking, interacting with environment, saving option)
- 3 acts
- 2 playable characters
- a handful of additional characters (some of these end up as allies, whereas others as antagonists)
- a duo of funny robots
- some funny lines
Now on to the game specifics:
The art style is cute and very much like JRPGs, though the game plays more like an adventure point-&-click.
It is simplistic & basic but fun & very straightforward (not difficult to figure what to do next).
Great for those times when you want to relax, have some fun and keep yourself busy.
There's an inventory, that contains whatever item that can be picked up in your environment and are expected to use for some kind of purpose.
Like any good adventure game, there's also a journal to keep track of the dialogues and objectives (thank god!). If it wasn't for this, I would've forgotten what I needed to do next.
As for game progression; at times you're prompted to combining items so as to create a more fitting object in order to proceed further.
The characters reveal in a very straightforward manner what their intentions are and what they need to execute their plans. It's a no-brainer really.
It looks fairly easy on the eye and there's no brain-busting puzzles (phew!).
I absolutely loved the portrets. They looked close enough to the character sprites.
I find cohesion and consistency very important (in any type of game).
This game definitely looks and feels cohesive & consistent (from character design, to environmental design to story progression).
The story is well written as well and it made sense.
It was definitely worth the investment (not that this game costs an arm and a leg - far from it).
I got it on sale (including 4 Space Pilgrim chapters) + an additional game by the same developer (for the curious people reading this, I'm referring to 'Crown Champion Legends of the Arena') - which cost me less than 5 bucks.
The developers are definitely not afraid of trying things and dabbling into different genres. I really like that and I appreciate it (and they use RPGmaker every single time).
I'm amazed at what they've squeezed out of this piece of software (which enables developers to focus on the artsy aspect without needing to break their heads too much in regard to any intricate technical stuff).
They really do seem like they care about what people have to say and try to implement feedback and improve their material.
There's definitely great potential here and if they continue like this, I do believe they could create something beautiful & rich (one step at a time!).
I absolutely love investing in people who care this much and are capable of delivering decent quality products, time after time.
It's very heartwarming and beautiful to see how they're progressing with every title that is released and I am so proud of them, because they serve as a great example of what it means to start small, and grow bigger.
I'm curious to see more! I give credit where credit is due and they deserve every bit of it.
PS I wouldn't mind investing in some of the artwork :).

Considering the game is in Alpha as of this review, and assuming you enjoy general tycoon games or management games this is really fun and I look forward to the finished game.
Pros-
-The art style is simple but cute. The texture on all the models really fit the game well.
-Unique rooms, unlike other tycoon games this being set in what I assume is more of a medieval time gives you some interesting guests and items to play with.
-Easy to get started.
-With all the bugs it is still fun and easy to see this game will go far once it is finished.
-Over all fun tycoon game.
Cons-
-The game does poorly to explain things to you. Example: I was making more and more money but my reputation was going down the drain. It took me about a half an hour to realize it was because my guests wanted rabbit stew and I had not made a huge effort in research. The game DOES tell you to research early but doesn't explain why or what benefits it would give you long game.
-The game doesn't clearly state what items do or how much they help you/make guests happy.
-The music is painful to listen to... over and over again.
-No general interface to show what guests are happy, whos waiting, and if an item can't be used (due to placing error)
-No actual pause button.... Not sure if the game freezes when I his the menu but I don't feel like it does.
Bugs-
-Guests kept getting stuck when I placed items down! Sometimes making the items unusable.
-Some bugs where items or rooms stop functioning. Fixed by replacing the bugged furniture.
-Some buttons do not work. The wait or leave option in policy menu does not work. Other buttons do not work as well.
-Every so often the game will minimize. Unsure as to why. Not a huge problem but can get annoying.
Final Notes-
Again, it is in Alpha stage so I forgive most bugs. the price for an early alpha is alot but hopefully the game will progress and I really can't wait for this game to be finished.

I want to start this by saying that I really love this game. And, for $20, it's practically a steal.
Heliborne is like what War Thunder should have been. The controls are very responsive and usable, even with only Mouse and Keyboard controls, the game handles well, the graphics are nice, and the gameplay is very active.
---Pros---
-Good graphics
-Responsive Controls, even M+K controls
-Decent physics combined with a game that's arcade enough to be enjoyable
-No "Premium Vehicles", so there's no Pay-To-Win
-You can have as many squads as you want, so feel free to unlock all the Helis and experiment
-The "grind," if you can call it that, is actually very enjoyable
-Deployment Points System prevents players from equipping the most combat-capable Helis with the top gear and seal-clubbing
-Night battles at Tier IV are awesome. Yes, I said Night Battles, and, yes, those are the same proper Night Battles that are currently unavailable in either War Thunder or WarGaming products.
-Balance is acceptable through most tiers, except maybe Tier III
---Cons---
-Damage System can seem bewildering sometimes
-ATGMs have too much range with their magnification settings currently. This tips Tier III balance towards the Soviets because they carry more ATGMs and their Wire-Guided Kokons are more accurate than the American Wire-Guided TOWs. This gives the Soviet Helis like the Hind the ability to sit outside of standard rendering range and punish targets with ATGMs. A simple reduction of ATGM magnification should fix this.
-Kill-assignment can be a little messy. Sometimes, if you shoot an enemy Heli down, it is counted as a "crash" instead of a kill, even if you hit them directly with an ATGM or Stinger. The Kill-assist system seems a little borked as well.
Overall, this game is very good, as it maintains a very solid balance of simulator and arcade. And, from what I've read of the Developers' plans for the future, like Sling-loading (transporting vehicles), commandable troops (other than Mortars), and Special Forces insertions, I think this game is only going to get better and better.

Okay, I HAVE to brake up this rewiew into two different parts. First part is mechanically the game (completely spoiler free), devoid of any story, and then the story (major spoiler). Because the story....
1) The game starts out with a handful of survivors, four, to be exact, on each new map. Each survivor has Defense, Leadership, Engineering, Building and Scavenging skill, ranging from 0 (utter noob) to 10+ (peak of humanity). With traits (gained as you level up the survivors and research Survivor Management) and equipment you can raise it above ten, and it does increase efficiency and decrease mission time. The top I've managed to pull off was about 21 building skill on a survivor. Not all traits raise skills, some give different bonuses, like immunity to the disease, reduced danger during far away mission.
The map contains several different types of blocks, ranging from one, two and four blocks, on a sqare grid. Each different block gives you different bonuses. Farms produce food based on size, apartments and suburbs give living space also based on size, hospitals accelerate healing, laboratories allow research missions to be completed, workshops provide crafting of Ammo, Medicine, and other one-time used items, pastures allow hunting for food, forests also allow hunting AND woodcutting, which provides building materials. Forests are one of the most valuable tiles, since those provide a steady supply of building materials, and while some maps edge is also forest, not all of them, and sometimes the starting position is in the middle of the map, essentially cutting off that until late game.
The resources are Food, provided by farms and hunting on pastures or forests, Building Materials, provided by woodcutting, Ammunition used in rare events and in case the defenders/attackers of the player has firearms or similar ammo consuming item on them (like crossbows) gained from crafting in workshops, Medicine, used in rare event, gained also from crafting in the workshop (yes, autocraft for infinite number is in the game for it, and these does not seem to consume any materials), and finally, Fuel, used in powering a maps powerplant and crafting. There are craftable consumables also, Explosives made from Fuel, Medkits made from Medicine, Traps made from Building Materials.
The game can be played in an RTS style, or in turn based style, depending on your preferrence, it can be changed anytime during the game.
The zombies on the map indicated by four colouration of a tile (after scouting). No colour is no zombies, green is few, yellow are mediocre, red is swarming. A tile can be reclaimed once all zombies are destroyed on the tile through an eradication mission option. Periodically zombie mobs actively attack the player.
2)
The story...
SPOILERS. Stop Reading if you want to experience the utter HERESY Ms Norway calls a story.

Get it on sale for the gameplay, if you can tolerate the atrocity of the story.

This has about the most basic gameplay mechanics you can design in a platformer, so when you actively find yourself loving the gameplay, it's surprising at first. Add a personalizing, caring and fun narrative and you turn shapes into characters, and gameplay into a fun packed, occasionally tense story. Wrap it all in well designed levels and cover it in a great simple UI and you have everything a well designed game should be.
The fun, character and world building narrative is the main thing that brings this game to life, but it wouldn't be for naught if the gameplay wasn't also so polished and solid. Great game design exists in every facet of this game.
* Great ambient music and sound artefacts that, when combined with other elements, create some genuinely tense moments
* Fantastic simple UI and controls that always feel light and reactive
* Light but intelligent humour
Not a single one. Everything is well made and comes together to make a great, fun experience. Anything I could point out that isn't perfect about this game is simply nitpicking, but for the sake of completeness it's worth mentioning that some may find the game stale, repetitive or unchallenging at times if they don't like the narration and tone. It's also fairly short and despite some good accomplishment based achievements for completionists, it doesn't have a strong amount of re-playability.
Thomas Was Alone is fairly short, and clocks in at about 4 hours of gameplay, but it's worth another play or two a few years down the line, and has some good achievements. It's priced at £5.99/7.99€/$9.99 which is fair for such a well put together product, but may feel overpriced for the game length. It regularly goes on sale for -75% and occasionally even less.

As noted by the description and various publications, Hyper Light Drifter is a top down action-adventure game made popular by early 80's video games like Legend of Zelda, Crystalis, and Hylide. You wander the map in search of goodies, weapons, currency, bosses, and challenge.
Like any action adventure game, combat is one of the main focuses of Hyper Light Drifter. The main character's primary weapon is a sword supplemented by a gun. Dashing is the main form of evasion and what makes the combat so enjoyable- there are no limits to the amount of dashes and players are encouraged to tag in and out of combat to ensure survival of their fragile “Drafter”. With only five health and mounds of enemies to fight, players can be overwhelmed quickly if baddies are not dispatched quickly enough. Though you can recharge your health, doing so is risky- you only have a few health kits and do so makes the drifter vulnerable while he heals.
Another facet of combat is how the encounters are designed. Like many action oriented games, there is loads of enemy types- small but numerous baddies, evasive close combat goons, enemies with ranged attacks, stomping brutes, and so on. As you progress, enemies don't get bigger, stronger, faster, and what have you. Instead the encounters are designed to have a mixture of troops. Swarms push you towards unfavorable terrain, sword wielding goons try and surround you, ranged enemies try and pin with suppressing fire, and all the while those big mofos trudge towards you. Its this great mixture that keeps players on their toes and invigorates combat with the diversity of enemies and tactics they practice.
Bosses round out the combat experience with intimidating designs,  large health pools, impressive attacks and exploitable patterns. All offer a good challenge, which sweetens the victory when players finish a dungeon.
But its not all action. Exploration and treasuring finding is woven directly into the experience. The world is fantastically illustrated in bold pixel art supplemented with an ethereal and soothing soundtrack filled with echoing synchs and meandering melodies. Indeed, there are very few “intense” tracks, and the somber music flows while teasing out secrets and combating foes.
The game's currency, an unnamed yellow block, can be found by searching high and low for secret tunnels, platforms just outside sight, and experimenting by interacting with the environment. This currency (which you need four of to make a “whole”) is used to upgrade the drifter. There are also other pick-ups like keys to enter doors, special weapons and armors, tucked away in the world. Some of these hidden places have challenges that make use of the various upgrades you buy, usually involving dashing and precise dodging.
One of the little things that makes me giddy is that the drifter has a “sit” option by pushing the down direction on the controller's pad. Its a great way to take a screen shot or just to relax and absorb the environment and music. In town, the drifter doesn't swing his sword and whip out his gun. Instead he nods and flicks open his poncho. Its a great touch and helps draw the player into who the drifter is. Its like saying, “I'm in town, there is no need to break the peace.” The drifter has the same interactions when around people in the wilds and dungeons. Its a nice touch and I wish more games would use such interactions.
This is all tied together with the game's narrative- which is left open in many respects. Outside the menus, there is no text. Some of the world's inhabitants tell stories through pictures and grunts, usually two to four pictures long. They tell of events that happen or the location of the area's head boss. Off the bat, players know there was some sort of disaster and the game takes place, what seems to be years, perhaps centuries after the event. Remnants of battles, bones, and weapons litter the land. But its up to the player to come up with what all that means. Why did it happen? Why exactly is the drifter is searching the land? What is his roll in all this? What are these collectables even called? What's up with that dog? The broad picture is easy to interpret, but the details are left to player. It reminds me a of getting a game back in the 1980's, but no instruction manual to tell you what the game's story is and name of the various items, enemies, areas and allies.
While this game enjoys to harken back to the 80's and 90's era of top-down action adventure games, it does bring a few archaic designs from reaching into the past. With no text, some of upgrade “descriptions” (which are short demo animations) are ambiguous. The most infamous of these is the “multi-dash”, which is represented by the drifter dashing in a triangle. This doesn't even convey remotely what it does, as it allows the drifter to dash before his current dash is finished- allow the player to move very quickly. There are also two “slash-dash” upgrades. One deals moderate damage while the other is used to push enemies around. Again, the short animations don't do a stellar job showing this difference and its tough to compare because the upgrades are in sold in different shops.
Another is creating a false scarcity when it comes to health packs. Once you get a health pack, its gone till you leave the area. The only way to get a health pack is by roaming the world and picking them up. However if you played poorly in a dungeon and you need to drum up some health, prepare to waste 5 to 10 minutes dashing around previously discovered areas to refill your consumables. The development team could have had a place to stock them, like in the central village. Instead the player is forced to perform choir. Its 2017 people.
Most glaring is the knock-down abuse some bosses are made to do. Some boss's attacks can knock the drifter on the floor, leaving him vulnerable when he gets up. Many bosses have attacks they use just as the drifter gets up, allowing the player no time to dodge, attack, or heal. Due to the low health the drifter has, many bosses are able to wipe to player up efficiently after a good knock down. It just has a dirty and cheap feeling to it, especially when a player first tries to work out the boss's patterns.
Though none of these hiccups damn the game, they are noticeable rough spots in an otherwise smoothly made product.
But its this combination of fighting and discovery that makes wonderful peaks and valleys of intensity that keep the game both varied and interesting to the player. The vast assortment of hidden goodies and secret passages peak interest and satisfy the collector/discoverer kind of player. (Though its not required to find these secrets as many are a challenge to find on your own) The sharp visuals and relaxing audio tie the whole game play experience together.
The game also features a new game+, though the drifter simply starts with two health and is locked out of wearing other ponchos. If you enjoy the challenge of simply not getting hit, its a nice addition. If your actually looking for a game that plays differently with new challenges and enemy behaviors, its a total pass.
If some of your favorite games include The Legend of Zelda: A Link to the Past, Secret of Mana, or Illusion of Gaia, then Hyper Light Drifter will satisfy the need to slash and explore, especially if you haven't played one in a while. If you never got into the action-adventure genre or wasn't around during the 80's and 90's, Hyper Light Drifter is a decent entry into the genre. However, you may find older titles more sluggish and “tanky” compared to zippy nature of Hyper Light Drifter.
Overall, Hyper Light Drifter is worth while addition to any action-adventure lover's library.

Quite simply, this game is the unholy mixture of Undertale retro vibes, Five Nights At Freddy's creepy lore, and .Exe puzzler mechanics and core story element. Many elements of the game are subtle and designed to mess with your head as you play- you're not hallucinating... well, at least not entirely.
Through a mixture of ingenius and cleverly disguised elements of code, the game plays almost like an interactive puzzle that constantly keeps you on your toes. Yes, the puzzles are not exactly my favorite (and it can be easy to get maddeningly stuck on a few, because the back of your head will KNOW the answer and your brain will just refuse to catch on), but the style and narrative are simply unparalleled except by its fellow classics such as Undertale.
Quite simply, the game is an instant classic. The story is devastatingly simple, yet deceptively deep and highly interpretive, and the fourth-wall breaking moments are truly unnerving. This game is a must-play for anyone who craves something fun to play with plenty of subtlety and engrossing plot devices. PLAY THIS GAME!

This game, despite its basic graphics, was a happy find! More of an interactive story than a point and click adventure, the storyline is engaging, witty, and satisfying. I completed the game in under 90 minutes (with all achievements), so it is not a long game, but you can pick up the bundle of all 5 episodes for a very reasonable price.
I'm writing this review before I play the other episodes so I can give an unbiased review to just this episode.
- Great storyline
- Interesting characters
- Straight forward game play
- No frustrating puzzles/random inventory combining
- Can be played as stand-alone story (do not need other episodes) if you want to try it out.
- Steam trading cards and realistic achievements (if you like that)
- Very small windowed gameplay
- Inventory menu not brilliant - can be frustrating trying to combine objects on the few occasions you need to
- Pixel graphics - can't say I'm a fan, lived through that in the 80s!
- Not much in way of soundtrack. Can turn on intercom music and a few effects.
- Short, sorry to see it end.
If you're happy with a point and click story, and like to check out every object in a classic adventure gamer obsession, then you will really like this game!

For $250 CAD and free shipping via Amazon, it was hella quick to arrive in just two days. Check it out if you're thinking of getting a good quality but affordable intermediate guitar above the crappy beginner Epiphones / Academy / Squire models that are about $100-150.

• Movement and thrust jumps are much better than the last game and feel very smooth and controllable.
• Many different gun customization options which are all very well balanced for the amount of content in the game.
• Tons of guns to choose from all with unique traits
• Almost all guns are usable with a decent amount of skill
• The original 'pick ten' loadout style works very well in this game and even allows for full six attachments on primaries
• Weapon sounds are very similar and aren't particularly diverse but is still very pleasing to the ear
• Very unique and plentiful gamemodes that are fair and enjoyable
• Specialist character system is very creative
• Guns have very fair recoil which is reasonable for a game like Call of Duty
• Verity of scorestreaks which compliment the rest of the experience and sets apart the good and poor players
• Huge amount of replay value in the form of progression
• Vast amounts of challenges to earn weapon camos and calling cards
• Dark Matter is a camo that takes a very long time to acquire by completing challenges and is very rewarding when completed
• Prestige's are nothing new to the series but now offer a level cap of 1000
• Game is updated frequently and new content is still being added after the it's appeal seems to be fading
• Graphics are standard for 2015 but still are enough to impress
• Supply drops allow you to unlock camos and new guns that overall are a nice addition
• Maps are very detailed and aesthetically pleasing
• Game is one .exe file so switching gamemodes doesn't require opening up the game again
• Workshop allows you to create custom camos for your guns which is very fun and easy enough for anyone to make something cool
• Almost no players online just less than a year after release
• Only available modes are team deathmatch and occasionally domination on weekends
• Brecci and the Haymaker shotguns were nerfed but still dominate with ease
• Mods took way too long to be released and doesn't offer enough to want to keep playing the game
• Most maps play very slow and aren't very fun to play on
• Spawn points are awful and in some gamemodes cause you to loose the game because you spawn so far away from the objective
• Toughness perk from earlier games was removed and now every player gets flinch but when taking one on one gun fights, getting hit will flinch your aim to their head being lethal with the high caliber attachment
• Developers added the ability to get supply drops with real money which doesn't make the game unfair but excludes players from getting new weapons
• No party games which was very fun in previous titles
• Although the game is very good, the series is better off without the switch to futuristic settings
• The game is completely different from the previous two games and shouldn't even be named what it is
• The sub-machine guns are very easy to use but still are the most powerful guns in the game which ultimately drags down the skill ceiling
I bought the multiplayer starter pack because it was on sale and I recently played the game for during the free weekend. I liked watching videos on it and gave it a try. Many people in the community are upset because of the futuristic setting and the fact that Call of Duty is not what it used to be anymore. I like that the series wasn't staying stagnant and thought it was a very good game dispite it not being a typical Call of Duty title. I loved the progression system and the lack of simplicity very much. Unfortunately, the developers did made some greedy decisions and focused on making money rather than improving the game as a whole. I played the beta version on PlayStation and was impressed, but I never purchased the game because I was frustrated from the disappointment of Advanced Warfare. My friends had a ton of fun with the game at its release but by the time I purchased it, the game had already faded so quickly that it wasn't as enjoyable as I anticipated. Since I only had the multiplayer starter pack, I was never able to finish the dark matter challenge without buying the full game. I did have a lot of fun completing the challenges which no other game has provided intense but fair challenges like this game has. I usually would just listen to some commentary while getting kill challenges done which I enjoyed spending my time doing and it felt very satisfying to get the final camos. This also shows how this game has little to no competitive aspects to it. Like earlier games in the series, Black Ops III does not offer a good competitive experience. It is a casual killing arena with some objectives, which would be fine if there was higher skill ceiling. The developers failed to give a competitive experience for players like me who love very competitive games, and have not changed the game formula in years. If they don't consider this, the developers will continue to see downward facing line graphs and faster fading games such as this one.

Nice game. A bit arcade, but flight model and terrain is really nice done.
Pros
- Good helicopters models
- Good collisions and destruction/explosions models
- Really good flying model, with not so hard realistic problems like in real chopter flight. A bit arcade, bit fun, and modeled engouh to feel it. It's not DCS if you know what I mean.
- Firing weapons and flying around is satisfying, chilling and nice.
- Weapons choice and progress of exp is nice.
- Flight with mouse/keyboard is perfect, as it should, steering a bit similar like planes in WT.
- Also, there is fair singleplayer with offline mode so it's big plus.
- This game rock on coop games, then this game is shining.
- There is zone gathering, recon of enemies, troops placement in any place, all those things in game and makes this a lot of fun.
- Helis divided to 3 groups: recon/attack/transport. It's quite enough to differentiate gameplay.
- Beside, they placed Huey heilcopters in game, so +1.
Middle
- PVP is hard and not so fun, most because AA missles can purge helis like hell. Quite imbalanced and hard, but it's ok.
Cons
- Not too many helis to choose.  Don't expect so huge technology tree like in WT or something.
- I wanted more camouflages, not all helis have all possible, even if you buy DLC's.
- Not too many maps so far. It's like 1 per one era, which means 4 maps.
Recommended for ppl with friends, to make coop games together.
But even if, coop is possible with random players so every time is someon to play with.
Overall: 9/10

I ran into so many issues within just 24 minutes of "playing" the game that I think I might just quit right away, sorry...
Without even playing the actual game appart from the 3 first tutorials, which was clunky and really not that informative at all, you know... getting 5 cards being told you can swap out 2 of them but the tutorial just lets you swap out only one exact card so it can continue the script and give you 2 artifact spells which say "0 mana to cast" but you can only cast 1 ... because the tutorial just wants you to use ONLY 1 right now and then insist on you doing some other stuff, making you think "oh so I can only use 1 artifact per turn ok" but thats not true because when you try doing 2 per turn later on it just works like a charm. and the tutorial displays a huge textbox above the head of a card telling you to play it but that exact same textblock just blocks your sight so you can't even see what the cards description below says. So you end up being forced to play a card that you can't even find out about what it does at all...
So In terms of "teaching" me stuff about the game the tutorial just failed alot. Just so so many very basic things going terribly wrong here, again before you even start playing at all
Next, the humble keys I got did have a space you had to delete after copy pasting them which took me like 2 minutes to find out by using google which included comments by the actual support/dev/publisher... I dunno (yellow name with an admin star, whatever that means in detail, like... is he a steam Admin, Dev Team Member, Support Admin, Publisher Staff?)
but what I'm trying to say: if it takes a user just a few moments to figure, then why doesn't it say so somewhere at humble bundle or as a side note at where you put in the keys?
2nd: after finaly getting the codes to work, well at least it told me they worked by showing some green marker and then... well just... where is it? Where can I see what I just unlocked? I browsed through all of the game menus multiple times and I cant find any display for these "cosmetic" contents that I assumably just unlocked. And for the second key which should have added some currency "spirit orbs" well... under the crafting menus I found some display saying I still have "0 spirit" dunno if that would refer to "spirit orbs" tho but ye... where is the stuff?
And pls dont get me wrong here, I'm not ranting about pretty much free stuff that I should just be thankful for if anything and keep my mouth shut. No I'm talking about a glimpse of experience into the premium content of a game that I might have wanted to play and get some $$$ shizzles for in the future, but when I cant see that stuff anywhere at all, then its simply not worth a single future penny!
Anyway, I thought maybe I'd have to restart the client to refresh all the displays (which would be sad enough for a released state game of 2016) but that brings us to:
3rd, just on my SECOND EVER attempt to start the game it just locked itself in that very first black screen with the white "Duelyst" logo and it didnt even allow me to simply go to my desktop and shut it down - so it kind of soft locked my entire system which I really dont like at all (which is also partial a Win10 issue but ye... lets say 50/50 on that one)
not to mention I still cant see any of the added items after being able to start the game in the end.
So all I really wanted to say is: I've seen some potential but before I got even started I'm not really feeling an urge to start the game a 4th time ... ever, because first impressions you know...
And I know the game is F2P but thats just the point, if you run a F2P you obviously rely on cosmetics, boosters and other premium microtransactions but when a player can't even get any visual feedback from purchases people just won't buy it...

ANY other game or account I ever tried to verify to within the last like... years would just provide me with a code within verification emails which you can then put into some form if provided links refuse to work but ... CHROME?!

Updated Review, changing to recommended after initial review of Sept 28th. Counterplay has made lots of positive changes since Sept. Such as nerfing a lot of overpowered cards and minimizing the "bring out big creature/dispel/another creature/dispel/oops you ran out of dispels/removals first you lose " gameplay. In addition to adding starting packages for purchase with guranteed rarity of cards(one time starters at reasonable price) and a fixed price expansion where you can get all the cards including maximum duplicates for $20.
So a beginner who after playing through the tutorials and decides they like the game, can get started for about $15 to $45 for semi competitive decks and be able to grind for cards with a decent number of wins. Which is a little necessary as there is only a ranked mode that counts toward free gold quests.
However the gameplay is not for everyone as it is fast paced hard hitting combo card gameplay.

The game is simple at the beginning but once you obtained the basics of the game you'll realize the huge amount of content the game could offer.
I love the pixelized graphics of the minions and spells and also the generals.
Though I would say something about the buying of card packs in the game. It makes me feel that the game is a pay-to-win game though not that strictly because sometimes you earn gold that you can use to buy card packs without spending any money.
I used to play League of Legends and because of it I had anxiety playing ranked games. I wish this game would put more content on players who prefer to play the game alone, just collecting stuffs and playing with bots and friends.
Overall the game is really really good and well thought of. It's one of those games that you wished you created because it's so good. So yeah I recommend it.

I have enjoyed this game very much so far. The pixel art is absolutley amazing and the animation is very fluid. The game is similar to hearthstone and magic this is actually a good point. Meaning the game is easy to pick up. There is also a mechanic which enables the player to replace a card in your hand with another random card in your deck, this helps combat the RNG mechanics of virtually every card game. Also the blend of cards and a board is very well done in this game. Finally card packs are easy to gather through minor play time. P2W aspects are still there but someone who hasent payed a dollar can easily compete with someone who has. For a free game it is amazing and gives you that satisfying feeling when you outsmart your opponent and snag the win. 9/10 would play again.

Thomas Was Alone is a simply beautiful game.
This game manages to have simple yet fun gameplay along with a fascinating story. The fact that the characters are just colored figures, yet still relatable enough to worry about them is proof of this.
However, we're not told everything about the story; the quotes at the start of each chapter point out to something more out there, and the ending is rather ambiguous. But this just gives the game a sense of being much greater, of that what we're doing has the possibility of affecting the world without actually pointing out we're doing so.
Plus we have a british guy narrating the story.
The only con, I would have to say, is that the game is a bit too short.
But at the end Thomas Was Alone is a small masterpiece that showcases a perfect mix between a deep story and fun gameplay.

Thomas Was Alone is a delightful, unassuming platformer that will make you care about quadrilaterals. The levels go from super basic to quite clever by the end of it, but ultimately the tone and play of the game is pretty lighthearted--certainly not meant to be some uber-challenge, anyway.
This game has been out for long enough that you don't need to read me explaining how the visual style of this game is not a cop-out and is essential to the game play(--but there, I said it). The music is hypnotizing, and the narrator's voice is engrossing--reminds me of the Stanley Parable.
Teaching life lessons since 2012

who would have thought so much emotion could be packed into such small geometric shapes?! i've never really felt connected to characters in any game like i have been to these, and they're /cubes/.
this story is phenomenal. i'm a huge fan of unique and inspiring narrative and this did not disappoint. like i said above, the narration (which is done very well by the way) gives so much life to a group of misfit squares and rectangles. they each have their own unique playing style and personality, & the way they all clash and simultaneously work together to solve puzzles is fun to play and fun to experience as well.
the soundtrack is absolutely beautiful and you should purchase it if you have the chance or the extra cash. makes for good ambient background music & adds a really enjoyable level of atmosphere to the overall game.
there are very few things i dislike about this game. the major gripe i have is the replayability factor. it's got little to none. i love the story so i've found myself revisiting it once or twice but once you know the puzzles and knock out all of the achievements, there's not much else to do. the only other complaint i have is certain aspects of the gameplay. it's very unique in most senses, but it also grows stale when you have to continuously go up flights and flights of stairs with characters that cannot jump that well. there are other aspects such as these that get very old, /very/ quickly, but this is a very minor complaint in the large scale of things.
all in all, i wholeheartedly recommend this to any and everyone. it's worth the price just for the story & if you're like me you might be in tears at the end of it. crying about shapes, how sad. honestly though, this is a game i think everyone should have because it's such a unique platformer and it's not just a game to me, it's an experience, and one i think everyone should have.

There are 4 campaigns to play through that intertwine with each other that can lead to a lot of similar fights and locations being revisited. This can makes the game campaigns feel slightly lazy in comparison to previous games. However, other than the final campaign mission that was offered as dlc, each campaign is approximately 4 hours long. You couple the repetitiveness of the main campaign with some very Bollywood action sequences and it really is a toss-up whether or not you will enjoy it. Personally, I had no problem with it because if you can accept monsters, mutants, and zombies then you might as well suspend disbelief on the rest as well.
Where the game really REALLY shines is the mobility of play style and improved combat system. There is sliding, rolling, jumping onto your back, running (like really running, not just the light jog from previous games), countering attacks, and a bit more.

Oh and it has
, the fact is, if you have one friend, just one friend that will visit you to play games, Resident Evil 6 is fun. Sure, the way the split screen works is a bit funky and very poorly implemented but I personally have zero problems with it. Therefore, if you have a single friend to play games with and an extra controller I promise you, your game play experience will generally be entertaining. However, if you play Resident Evil 6 alone, the game will be a bit of a slog at times.
Despite some obvious negatives you do get your money's worth when purchasing this game.

First to you Steam, this is my first time buying a game on steam, and the last time. But now to the fun part:
Hyperlight Drifter is a game about a postapocalyptic toxic world full of nature wonders, whose beautifully told story unveils itself only by the power of pictures. Theres no text, and the game doesnt need it at all. Its gameplay introductions are flawless so its even fun to dive in from the first minute.
Combat is hard but fair, if you die, its your own fault, i never had the feeling to be treated unfairly and the checkpoints dont punish you too hard for failing, so its the best thing about the old Snes/NES games, a real challenge, without repeating areas over and over again.
A buddy can come into the game any time, which reminded me on the coop fun we had with games like shovel knight or secret of mana.
Zeldalike there are dozens of secrets in every screen, theres a lot to explore, actually everything is to explore. There are new costumes wich give you small improvements, You can buy new combat abilities, theres a Boss Rush, a fighting arena,
minigames, and even a new character to play in a second playthrough.
Its a game about exploring and evolving in an impressive pixelartistic atmosphere which reminded me of 80s fantasy movies. The Soundtrack fits perfectly, Disasterpiece was the best choice for this one, even making fez jealous of this new relationship. The game has loveable characters and is also humourous from time to time, but that only makes it worse, cause this world is heart breaking cruel and violent. The graphical themes remind me of Neon Genesis Evangelion. But i guess there are a lot of references to other franchises. There are a lot of Developers referring their game to the Zelda formular, but this game NAILS IT. As someone who played all Zelda games since the original on the NES i tell you this game is truly about exploration in an open environment on the same classy level. This game understood to the core what all the reference material is about: Neon Genesis, Zelda, Supernintendo/NES difficulty, 80s Fantasy movies, secret of mana and the art to tell storys by pictures.
Hyperlight drifter is a game whose lead developer Alex Preston has some sort of heart disease, which he also made as an underlining theme, but theres more to it. This game feels like a final game: Its honest, complete, polished, expressive, concluded in itself and treated like its the last game youll ever made. A one time journey with a definite end. But lets hope its not really the last game that mr Preston will be part of as the indie community needs more talented guys like the team of heart machine.
I know im very late with this review playing it mid 2017, but its my new indie no.1 next to journey, fez, ori, child of light and shovel knight. I usually play through a game once and go to the next thing, but this will be a timeless favorite i will always return to.
Congratulations to Heart Machine, and Steam go $%&$ yourself

An enjoyable game and a great story.  I played all the episodes and they make for a positive and solid experience.  There's no combat or leveling up, only a great adventure with lots of storytelling, puzzle-solving challenges, and well-fleshed out characters.  The game world had a good sense of history and you really started to feel that there's an entire universe to explore even though most of the (first) adventure is set on your starship.
This is an example of how an RPG story should be made.

The Space Pilgrim series is a classic point-and-click adventure game that's well worth your time if you're a fan of the genre.  The story and dialogue is excellent and the characters are engaging and seeing them develop over the course of the series was fun.  The puzzles weren't terribly challenging though i did get stuck once or twice, but the solution always made sense.  Each episode takes an hour or so to play through, so it was an excellent game to use as a break from other work.
I picked the game up on a whim since it cost less than a latte, and was pleasantly suprised when it turned out to be so good.  Seriously, play this!

The point of playing a game is being entertained, and this one just hits the spot.
If anything can make a game enjoyable, it is the writing and excellent execution in using RPGMaker as a medium for storytelling art, reminiscent of the witty quips I found so enjoyable in classic retro games like Space Quest and SCUMM games like Zac McKracken and Maniac Mansion.
On top of that, the game is never a chore, unlike many other adventure games that features frustration as the combination of clues get exponentially harder and harder to connect together, Space Pilgrim ensures each chapter is playable in a reasonable amount of time to keep it fun.
The first episode is very short, but subsequent episodes gets longer and more complex, so even at full price for each of the 4 episodes, it doesn't cost you more than a burger for lunch, and the end product feels like a labor of love, it's pretty polished and complete, and leaves me quite satiated.

I'm not one for this style of game. It's never something I've particularly enjoyed. However, this game drew me in! I'm not finished it by any means, but as someone who isn't particularly fond of the RPGmaker style, I can safely say that this game is a fun timekiller and something I would definitely recommend even if you're not into RPGmaker games. This game will not hold your hand throughout, but will give you the pieces and clues you need - Playing this game makes me feel creative. I get to figure things out with the pieces the game provides, instead of being told to simply "Do X" or "Combine with Y".
If you like space/scifi-esque games, I would recommend this game. It may be my favourite game of this style!

This game will teach you how to play guitar. Should you also look up lessons online and watch videos on YouTube? Absolutely, but honestly this game is one of the most amazing purchases in regards to learning I've ever made, and I already sort of knew how to play in the first place. The game will adapt to how accurate you play, but if its still too hard or fast there is a built in system that will let you change the speed or difficulty. There are also tons of fun minigames to help you practice getting used to watching notes fly at you quickly, so don't be afraid of that. There is a reason this is my favorite steam game, learning music and playing a video game at the same time is one of the most amazing things I could think of. The only thing that I don't like about this game is that they took out a couple features from the original that I enjoyed, which was the ability to select different guitars and have their tones digitalized. However, they more than made up for it with the crazy in-depth amp customization and super cool session mode that can quickly teach you an entire scale and how to jam with it.
Overall I'd say this game deserves a 9.5/10, and I am seriously in need of a Rocksmith 2017 or whatever the next one will be called.

I started playing guitar when I was 19, in 2003. Recently, I hadn't played in about 3 years because I felt like I'd plateaued, being mostly self taught with no time or money in conjunction with each other to be able to take lessons. I played the original Rocksmith some on the PS3 but it was a hassle bringing the guitar down whenever I wanted to play and I just didn't feel like I was getting it.
Then back at the end of April (2016) I broke my leg. I was off of work for 6 weeks and decided to start playing again. I worked on a few things myself again, but then I picked up Rocksmith 2014, this time for PC which is in the same room I keep my guitars. I have been practicing an average of 1-2 hours every day since and can already tell I've been getting better and been able to tweak a few issues in my playing that I didn't even know I had. This is a great tool to help you master songs in your preferred genre, as well as step outside your comfort zone and test your chops on something new. I have been able to identify areas I know I need to work on and begin the work to get better in those areas as well. So many of the songs are fun to learn and it feels great when you finally master one and gain the confidence to be able to play it note for note at the intended speed and make it sound good. I really enjoy this game and see it being a helpful tool even as I plan to move into lessons at some point down the road.

Pro's:
1. Lots of fun, tonnes of depth.
2. Maps are super destructable in a useful way. You can break through floors and shoot the people on a lower floor, you can blast through walls to get hiding campers. The defending team can level walls so they have clearer lines of sight. Unlike battlefield, its "useful" destruction that you're expected to use.
3. Maps are intricate and well designed.
4. Sound design is the best in the business. You can hear explosives two floors below and they'll sound muted but they'll shake the foundation of the building. You can hear players walking around the house. It's a sound ♥♥♥♥♥'s wet dream.
5. Operators are well design and mostly balanced. The abilities are powerful but not gamebreaking.
6. It's a team game for sure.
7. Runs really well
Con's:
1. Ubisoft
2. DLC operators are very expensive (in game currency) relative to the vanilla operators to entice you to get the season pass. The season pass is worth it, but its kind of scummy.
3. Map knowledge is huge so the learning curve is really steep. Some operators are really tough to play because their abilities rely heavily on map knowledge. This is probabbly the hardest part of the game.
4. Community can be obnoxious.
5. People with no situational awareness will ruin the game for you

This game is excellent.
It is a worthy successor to the helicopter sims of the late 90s and early 2000s that formed my tastes. Smoothly combining realistic physics with simple controls, the game gives the feel of driving a helicopter without requiring hundreds of toggles or switches. It's not quite a sim, but it's a little deeper than a pure action game, too - knowledge of the tools you're using will benefit you as you engage armor, infantry, and other helicopters on the battlefield.
For a game like this, the core mechanic has to be fun, and it is; the feeling of maneuvering around various terrain, over meadows, through mountain passes, and across jungle rivers, is the first appeal. The combat and progression mechanics, both of which are excellent, are the second appeal, and between the two, I would heartily recommend this game to anyone with an interest in military history and/or a taste for combat flight.

My credentials:
-Made it into S-rank, the top tier on the ladder.
-12 win run in Gauntlet (the max).
-Been playing about 8 months
-Spent about $50 on the game.
So what is Duelyst? Duelyst is a free-to-play CCG that uses a 5x9 board top play cards on. Each player has a general with 25HP and 2 ATK. Each unit can move 2 squares, and then attack (this includes generals, as they are units too). Each general belongs to a faction and has a unique "Bloodborne Spell", which refreshes at set intervals and doesn't cost a card. Your deck will consist of cards that are exclusive to your faction and the "Neutral" cards, which everyone can run. To get cards, you buy "Orbs" (aka packs of cards) with gold, the ingame currency. The resource system consists of a mana pool that grows each turn, and tiles on the board that act as "get +1 mana this turn" if you have a friendly unit walk over them. You draw one card each turn, and have the option to replace one card you dont want from your hand each turn, and you are guaranteed to not get the same card back.
Why do I mention the replace mechanic specifically? Because the replace mechanic, along with the board, really set Duelyst apart from other CCGs. Since card games rely on Random Number Generators (or RNG) to create variance and make games play out differently, there will be times that you flat out lose due to simple chance. That is the nature of RNG. Duelyst's replace mechanic helps to minimize this as much as possible- if a card doesn't help you, throw it away and get a new one! Top-decking is less frustrating just because of that feature.
As for the gameplay, it's awesome.
-Games are relatively fast-paced
-Every faction is viable at the highest levels (some generals are not as much, but you get the choice of 2 generals per faction)
-Several different viable deck types
-New players can, with enough skill, make it surprisingly high on the ladder without any investment.
-Three copies of any given card, combined with a deck size of 40 and the replace mechanic, make decks consistent enough to feel like you can find the cards you need when you need them.
-Daily challenges force you to think about unit interactions, and reward you for completing them.
-Gauntlet allows you to draft a deck by choosing 1 of three randomly chosen cards of a given rarity, 30 times. You play until you either get 12 wins (the max) or 3 losses. You only need 7 wins to get a ticket for a free Gauntlet run, so going infinite is fairly easy once you have experience.
However, not every game is perfect.
-Devs have not been as transparent as they should have been. The past few updates have had changes that negatively impacted players gold income as well as nerfed rarity rates in the expansion orbs.
-Newly added cards are "raising the bar" and causing some power creep. When playing against optimized decks in higher ranks, you can find yourself in "Answer this or die" situations several turns in a row.
-Cosmetics are fairly expensive in real-world currency. Thankfully, they are ONLY cosmetic and do not affect the game. On top of that, you can craft the cosmetics you want by destroying cards you don't want for in-game currency.
-Game is laggy on old rigs. Even some newer rigs can struggle at times.
-Managing decklists is painful. There is no officially supported API, and no official way to import/export decklists. One player has created scripts to do this, but this should be officially supported and not require the community to fix.
Overall, there is too much to say in one post. The game is great and well worth giving a try. For a short time, Humble Bundle is giving out free codes to brand new players for 20 free orbs and a free legendary. So there's no better time than now to give it a shot. There are some things that need to be addressed, but few games are perfect. This one comes pretty close to it though.
Overall: 9/10

Tomb Raider is an action platformer made and released by Core Design in the year 1996. This game was originally released for the Playstation 1, and Sega Saturn. It was also released for PC through the usage of DOSBox. For those who are wanting to get into the Lara Croft : Tomb Raider series, this game is somewhat hard to recommend, despite being the first of the franchise.
Please not that I have played and beaten both, the PS1 and PC edition. This review, however, is based upon my experience with the Steam version of Lara Croft : Tomb Raider 1
The story is decent. The cutscenes just tell you enough to get you started, then leaves the rest to your imagination. It reveals itself the further  it goes in, followed by a lame plot twist at the end which left me dumb founded. Overall, its not bad.
For an old school game, it looks alright. The game was made back when polygonal 3D graphics started going big, so there was much work to be done before they could perfect making any round objects. Back in it's time, it was no doubt some of the top of the line graphics. Compared to today's technology in graphical development, it's hard to get into this type of game unless you're a fan of the classics. If you are are into the "shiny" and new games, then look away, this game is not for you.
I'm usually very picky when it comes to in- game music, sound effects, etc... but TR had nothing I could really complain about. The music and effects seemed pretty immersive, which left little to be desired in this specific type of game. The battle music is intense and frightening, giving the game more of the survival feel in intense situations. Also, the music for the theme, finding secrets, and walking into a mysterious place has always suited the moment well. As for the effects, they are alright for an old school DOS game. Every creature, environment, and protagonist has the appropriate sounds for the given situations, which yet again increases immersion. The only aspect I disliked was that of the main protagonist, Lara. Every time she climbs a ledge, runs into a wall, jumps... it sounds far  too artificial... like she's having an... errr.... nevermind. ( ͡° ͜ʖ ͡°)
The gameplay is my favorite part about this game. The puzzles are somewhat challenging, and the parkour is fun and feels dangerous. The gun fights feel stiff due to the controls, but is still enjoyable. And the thing that makes this so great is the dangerous traps that lurk in each tomb. Avoiding and trying to expect what trap is next is what TR is all about. Feeling that you know something is wrong down the hallway, there probably is. There could be a boulder coming from both directions, or some poison darts coming from the walls, or maybe even a dinosaur will break through the ceiling? That's what makes these kind of games so fun. You don't really know what to expect (At least on your first playthrough). Most of the traps are somewhat unpredictable, so this definitely deserves some big pointers.
The controls are a tad bit funky. Why? Because I said so (Kidding).
For reals, the controls aren't as bad as what people think. The controls are very stiff, so manueverability is somewhat an issue.  I personally used my number pad to link my actions to, then used my wasd as movement. It too some getting used to, but in the end you'll manage.
However....
If you are more of a console enthusiast, or just cant stand using the keyboard for this game... then check out this controller support guide by Darth Sidious ~
Since this is an old school game I'll give it some slack on the controls.
The cimematics for Tomb Raider were great in terms of quality. That is, I wish I could say that for the PC version. Compared to the Playstation version, the cutscenes are astrocious. Even with all the DosBox tweaking guides I dug up, nothing would seem to fix it. However, this game is not plagued with too many cinematics, so this can be forgiven easily.
This game has very little replayability to it. After my first playthrough, I never really felt the need to collect all the secrets collectibles since they never did anything special. For those of you who played it before purchasing the game on steam would most likely replay it due to nostalgic reasons. But besides that, I wouldn't really see much of a point.

This is the most highly conditional "Yes" I've ever given a game on Steam. This review also applies to Tomb Raiders II through IV, and probably V and VI as well though I haven't played them yet.
There isn't much to say about this game. The graphics are clearly something to sneeze at, and the audio is nearly nonexistant. There is no plot to speak of, and there isn't much variety in mechanics. The entire meat of this game is through the gameplay.
Tomb Raider I has some pretty solid gameplay, but this is only true when we recognize that the game was released in 1996.  The movements, while extremely clunky, give you a wide range of mobility options for each scenario. In terms of how this game is meant to be played, it is unlike any other game I've played before: instead of emphasizing reflexes, strategy, or problem solving, this game test the player's dedication and perception. You are tasked with exploring many different landscapes where all of the textures look very similar, and this game pushes this test of perception to an extreme. This game is not for the feint of heart, and I certainly did not enjoy it very much.
So why do I recommend it at all? Because I believe that it would be a very enjoyable experience
. If you have a team of people all soaking in your surroundings, you are much more likely to progress in the game, and find the crucial secrets that help you get extra medpacks. You can laugh at the corniness together, or maybe even try to progress through a level with everyone drunk. I believe that this would make a great game for a small friend group where everyone likes to experience new types of video games. The reason I did not enjoy the game when I played through it was because I was playing it alone, and heavily relied on a walkthrough so I wouldn't keep dying. But if you have some friends like on Game Grumps e.g., you can probably power through this game pretty quickly (and maybe have a walkthrough open just in case you guys get stuck as well).
If you haven't played a Tomb Raider game before, this might be worth picking up. Play it with friends.

Going back to the original Tomb Raider, I expected my experience to be brief and purely nostalgia driven. My only memories of playing the game when I was younger are ones of frustration at the controls and an infantile infatuation with Lara Croft which probably kept me playing a lot longer than I should have.
What I found however, was a pretty solid, 3D action-adventure game that holds up way better than I thought it would. The controls can feel counter-intuitive at first but once you get a basic understanding of how it all works, It starts to work pretty well, at least for a game that was designed before the advent of dual analogue sticks.
The game has you exploring various environments, encountering traps, enemies and platforming puzzles along the way. It's pretty simple. Levels will often show you a door requiring multiple keys and leave you to explore the surrounding area in search of them. The game doesn't offer much guidance for locating these keys and that's what really drew me in. Being left alone to explore an area with just a compass (which I'm pretty sure has no in game use) and two guns with no immediate direction provided a very liberating sense of exploration that I haven't felt in a video game for years.
It'll require a little patience and maybe looking at a walkthrough a handful of times but there is absolutley a good time to be had with Tomb Raider 1 in 2016.

Tomb Raider I: Lara "Don't sweat it kitten" Croft
It's been exactly 20 years since adventures of the second most famous tomb-digger have started. Lara Croft is hired by a wealthy woman to find 3 pieces of an ancient pendant. Along the way, she encounters strange discoveries, led-filled betrayals and terrifying enemies, leading her to unravel a great mystery that was supposed to remain in the past.
Even today this game is amazing: levels are interesting and challenging, Lara's movement is detail-rich and precise and puzzles are well-though and rewarding. the first TR plays more like an action version of chess, where every movement and jumping must be precise, and the player must progress slowly and with a plan ahead. PC version of the game, without patches or mods, has no in-game music, but that only strengthens the atmosphere of exploration and trepidation while you encounter the next challenge.
While the graphics are simple by today's standards, they do their job well in portraying the feel of Hollywood adventure movies. Lara's movement however is great, with an emphasis on small details as she moves and fights. The combat is on the other hand slow and clunky, and it has not aged that well as the other aspects of the game have.
The story has a great setup, but as it develops, it remains shallow and short. Design of the main antagonists is great though, still inspiring that same sense of dread, repulsion and other-worldliness. The pinnacles of artistic design are the last two levels that feel amazing and strange at the same time.
Tomb Raider is a great game despite its flaws and age and all would-be archaeologists with a lasso and a dusty fedora owe to themselves to play it. Two thumbs up!!
