is an addictive point and click strategy game that can be played in real time, turn based, or a combination of both, as you can control the speed and change to turn based by playing on pause. You are a survivor of the zombie apocalypse, rebuilding the city around you. This can be in standalone quick play, or in multiple cities as you progress through a storyline in campaign mode, attempting to find a cure and save the world (of course!) You do this by recruiting people and setting them on tasks. Each person has different skills and perks, and the tasks involve expanding your territory whilst ensuring that you are well defended, have food, building supplies and that your populace is happy (harder than it sounds especially with a larger group to manage). On Easy, there is very little you can do wrong, but you can set the difficulty level up and on hard, it's very difficult indeed. Every single move you make you'll need to look at all the angles. As your city expands, you have more people to manage, and more threats to come in, from zombie attacks, as well as multiple factions. You'll need to decide whether to go for diplomacy or fight; and you then need to manage your political manifest that will affect your populace city-wide.  There's also a skill tree that you research at, a workshop with some crafting items, and a variety of buildings you can choose to build with their own advantages.
You'll get random events that pop up, ranging from the predictable to the very odd, with some tongue-in-cheek silly humour, quirkiness, and also some quite touching backstories to the characters. Your citizens will periodically want to chat to you about their past, which unlocks perks for them, as well as random events with them, where the decisions you make will have permanent affects. On the surface it seems like a fairly shallow amount of moves you can make each turn, but at higher difficulty levels, as your city progresses, the amount of strategy is actually quite complex. It's shockingly easy to make a mistake on the hardest difficulty setting that will send you into a spiral of doom and gloom. Citizens rioting, Z hordes amassing and factions baying for your blood. Send help, please!
However; the one major downside it has is that it is reptitive. Playing through the campaign offers multiple cities, and gameplay in each city starts out the same, although there are different objectives. Because of this the first part of every city felt like I was simply doing stuff I'd done before to expand my base and set the city up. It only becomes more exciting once the random events start rolling in and since these are pooled from a set of scripted events you will eventually experience them all, and some of them seem to occur quite frequently. Once you've completed the campaign, you can always play it again on a harder difficulty, or play random maps through the quickplay function, but I can definitely see this getting a bit samey and monotonous.
Value is obviously entirely subjective and if you're not sure if this game is worth whatever the current asking price is - simpler javascript versions of Rebuild 1 and Rebuild 2 are available on
. Rebuild 3 has considerable more depth and a full length campaign, but if you just want to try the gameplay out and get a feel for the game, head over to Kongregate and try out the previous completely free iterations first so you can experience the style.

As a long-time fan of the Rebuild series, I was pretty excited to have contributed $20 to the kickstarter page back in late 2013. I felt like I was truly helping with fun developers make something new and improved in a series they've been using as a juggernaut.
However, perhaps I overestimated how in-depth the game would be. As a few other people have mentioned, the gameplay becomes extremely repetitive once you play through at least 3 or 4 cities. It's still fun to play, and at least a decent way to think about how you use resources, but outside of the plot, there's not much else to it.
Earlier, I mentioned I put $20 to the kickstarter. According to the kickstarter page, I would have access to the alpha (which I did) and later the Deluxe Edition when the game finally came out. I've received no notification to this day of such a thing, meaning I essentially paid $5 more for the final product than the average player. Doing some research, I found others experienced this problem and tried inquiring, only to get handwaved away. In short, I find that's a bit of a backhanded move on the devs' parts. Whether they deliberately held back on their end or simply bungled the situation, it really makes it difficult to want to put faith in any future titles they put out.
And speaking of the price, $15 is a bit steep for a game that has a total of maybe 20 hours outside of free-play mode. I get that you need to put food on the table and make sure to have enough for travelling, but the simple fact of the matter is at $15, it's not worth it.
Sorry, Ms. Northway, but I'm gonna have to give a Thumbs-Down for this. :\ The quality of the game and the price you're demanding for it could be overlooked if you had at least delivered for the kickstarters.

tl;dr: Surprisingly addictive, coming from a guy who prefers tanks to helos. Just don't expect to fly the iconic ones (Hind, Black Hawk, Huey, and Apache) on the PvE side because most seem too selfish/unaware of the class system to bother switching to anything else, leaving you to pick up the slack in a lightly armored tin can. On the upside, prepare to get decent at flying scouts and raking in that sweet, sweet assistance EXP! Just please hit that damn B key to paint spotted targets for your team! Seriously! Also, the grind is considerably more tolerable than those in World of Tanks, War Thunder, and (what remains of) Armored Warfare.
Full review:
This is a surprisingly addictive little gem of a game, especially if you're a fan of helicopters. Which I'm not. I prefer tanks. Hopefully that says something good about this product if it can get someone like me interested/excited/satisfied.
I know I haven't played all that much, but I already have to say there's one issue I have about this game, and that's the inclusion of such well known helos like the Hind, Black Hawk, Huey, and Apache, and how most matches (at least what I've seen on the PvE side) tend to play out as a result. Even as someone who isn't really a fan of helicopters, I know what the four I listed are, and I want to fly them. As does LITERALLY EVERYBODY ELSE. This, of course, wouldn't be an issue, were it not for the class-based system.
You see, without a scout on your side (specifically, one who actually knows to light up spotted targets with the B key, which is surprisingly rare thus far), your fancy gunships and transports can't see a thing unless they're borderline on top of what's shooting them, at which point they're most likely already full of holes. The thing is, NO ONE (again, thus far) is willing to switch roles to something that'll help the team in such a situation. As such, that role will (and does) fall to YOU. You, and you alone. While your team's having their power fantasy raining death from above with 128 S-5 57mm rockets (Hind- Mi-24A, Mi-24V), turning the ground into swiss cheese with a nice crimson circulatory system sauce using a M230 30mm gun (Apache- AH-64A, AH-64D), blasting Fortunate Son while taking care of Charlie with 38 Hydra 70mm rockets (Huey- UH-1B, UH-1D), or taking revenge for those lost during the Battle of Mogadishu (Black Hawk- MH-60L DAP), YOU get to fly a lightly armored tin can! Again, because no one else will bother to do so.
However, all that experience with scouts means you will undoubtedly get pretty decent at flying them and, above all, you may end up raking in MORE experience than those of your team who refuse to leave their current helo. IF. YOU. HIT. THE. B. KEY. You do that, you get assistance EXP. That's 2 XP per infantry kill from your team, while you'd only earn 1 per infantry kill if you did so on your own. I want to love this game, but it's turned into an IAP ♥♥♥♥♥how, plain and simple. As a Kickstarter backer, it's disappointing to see a promising pixel turn-based strategy game turn into an IAP saturated Trading Card Game (TCG). I summarily pulled my backing after the announcement was made.
It has since become a Free2Play TCG, so I decided to give it a try. The good news is that the core gameplay is enjoyable and well paced. All the cards seem to have their place in their respective strategies. The bad news is that in order to make it free, Counterplay Games has crammed every monetization scheme possible into one game.
From cosmetics to cards, if they can sell it to you, they will. Avatars, card packs, card backs, character skins, emotes and bundles can all be purchased. Cards are awarded through spirit orbs (read: card packs), which is par for the course if you consider Hearthstone the benchmark for TCGs. The final kicker though are the mysterious crates.
Mysterious crates are awarded for ranking up in online play (think leveling up a la Overwatch). The problem is, in order to open a mysterious crate, you have to purchase a key (like CS:GO).
Now, I don't necessarily have a problem with any of these pricing models separately, but when they're all combined into one game, it makes me cautious. And even if it can be considered forgivable on its own, Counterplay recently introduced promotional keys for 20 Orbs and Cosmetics (roughly $30 value, $20 card value), but made them only redeemable to new accounts. So if you started playing when Duelyst launched on Steam AND spent $10, you are now on par with new players that have spent nothing. Likewise, they have been "balancing" quests so that you earn less gold and therefore open less packs.
All in all, there is an enjoyable game here, but for myself and others who are sensitive to over-monetization, I'm of the opinion that Counterplay Games is leaning heavily towards greed. But I am just a short term player, here is longer (and admittedly better) assessment from a long time player:

Before reading this, just take into consideration that I suck at card games. Deck building is something I've never been able to get the grasp of. That being said, Duelyst is a fantastic card / tactics game. It has a beautiful pixel aesthetic (not dissimilar to Dungeon of the Endless) with a lot of style and great animations.
But how does it play? Well, it plays great. You choose one of 6 factions, all of which have 2 generals (one default and one alternate one that you have to unlock). The general is you. If the general dies, you lose. After you choose your faction, you can either choose a default deck or create your own. You can unlock individual cards from leveling up or you can buy booster packs with in game currency as well as real life currency if you want.
The cards are where the game gets quite interesting. Each faction has its own unique set of cards as well as a 7th neutral set of cards that all factions can use. The cards are divided into minions, spells, and artifacts. Minions are summons that you can place on the battlefield. The minions themselves have TONS of variation. There are the average tanks, melee damage dealers, and ranged minions, but there is so much more to it than that. Many minions have abilities. Some have abilities that proc when you play the card. Some have abilities that proc when the minion dies or when other minions die. Some have abilities that proc at the end of your turn. I think you get the point. There's a lot of abilities.
Spells are one time use cards that create some effect. Like minions, quite a lot of variation here. You have spells that heal or do damage, spells that buff, and a lot of other random stuff. Artifacts are similar to spells, except they usually just buff your general in some way. The artifacts are mostly unique to each faction with each faction basically serving as this game's version of a class. Each faction focuses on different styles of play.
When you have built your own deck of 40 cards or decide to use the default deck, you go into a 1v1 battle. The battlefield is a grid, with each general automatically placed at either end. The battlefield is big enough to allow evasive maneuvers, but small enough to prevent people from totally running away from battle.
Each player takes turns casting their cards and moving their generals and minions around. Each card has a mana cost which leads to deep strategy. You have to do your math or your turns may not end up as planned. The person who starts second has 1 extra mana point to make up for the fact that they move second.
This is the game. You take turns going back and forth, casting your cards until one of you kills the other's general. One thing I absolutely adore is how attacking works. Unless the minion or general is ranged or some other buff/debuff comes into play, your melee attacks are met with counter attacks. That's right, you cannot melee attack without the enemy hitting you right back! This creates tension that leads to high strategy.
The real fun in this game is learning the intricacies of each faction. The variation in playstyles is quite impressive considering there are only 6 factions to choose from. Each faction feels very unique. Test them all out and i guarantee you will fall in love with one of them. They're all very clever and have advantages and disadvantages. Although, you can sort of disregard the faction system altogether by using a lot of neutral cards instead.
This game is very strategic and A LOT of fun. It's free to play, but I would gladly pay to play this if it weren't. If you like card games or tactics games, you've got nothing to lose! Give it a try. I hope you'll enjoy it as much as I do.

The good:
Co-op campaign with progression and challenges. Spin-off of said campaign that replaces standard enemies with zombies (Nightmares mode). Best Zombies experience yet with progression, story, and improved gameplay. There's also an arcade-style Zombies mode called Dead Ops Arcade II. Multiplayer is basically Black Ops II with advanced movements and Specialists added. MP has a bonus Free Run mode for racing obstacle courses (time trials). This has the most content (even before DLC) out of any CoD to date.
PC-specifc features: FOV slider (65-120), render resolution (useful for weaker PCs to make the game more playable, or for stronger PCs to supersample), server browser, proper KBM support in UI, and of course the mod tools where users can submit ZM, MP, or standalone mods/maps (uses the Steam Workshop). There's also unranked dedicated server support. Definitely the most active and properly supported CoD on PC as of now.
The bad: Low population, yet unsurprisingly higher than Infinite Warfare. Limited gamemodes available: expect to be stuck playing TDM, S&D, or Dom. This is due to the low population on PC. To be fair though, on PS4 it's practically the same now that most people have moved onto IW & MWR, or even switched entirely to different franchises (BF1/TF2/OW). Optimization can use some work in specific situations, but it's much better than what people give it credit for.  An example budget build my friend has: A Pentium G4400, RX 460 4GB, & 8GB RAM can run the game at 1080p60fps on high settings/FXAA at 80FOV. He runs it just fine with his $400 build.
The ugly: DLC, microtransactions, and Activision's pricing. DLC splits up the already-small PC population. Activision yanked individual DLC packs from the store to reduce fragmentation (base game vs season pass holders, instead of the various DLC combinations you'll see in matchmaking for consoles). Supply Drops and CoD points: there are weapons (not just cosmetic ones either) that can only be obtained through lucky grinding or by spending money and gambling for them. This is horrible and downright greedy of Activision. A lot of the weapons only available in the Black Market aren't better than base weapons, but some are OP (like the Marshall 16), and most of them are unique to the game that provide an experience no base weapon can offer (the D13 Sector disc gun can richochet off walls and score you really fun, cheeky kills). There is no way to earn a specific gun or outright buy it. Contracts can potentially help you get what you wanted, but essentially you need to spend real money to have a good chance of getting what you want. The odds are against you so I would not recommend it. Finally, you will either need to wait for a Steam sale or buy a key from a third-party website if you want to buy the game for a reasonable price, as Activision seems to think their games never lose value over time.
If you love Call of Duty, this will arguably be the best experience you can currently have on PC. Of course, you could always go back to older games like CoD4 (OG), BO1/2, WaW, and MW2 and still find games, if you so prefer. I'm looking forward to Treyarch's next release in 2018 as it will probably be the only worthwhile CoD for PC. Keep in mind that if you don't care about mods and only want to play MP, there is a multiplayer-only version the game that limits the way you can level up, but it's there for only $15.

Whoever green-lit this game was a genius! Anyone who's ever played Rockband/Guitar Hero has had the thought of "man, I wish there was a game like this where you could plug in a guitar and get good for real". And this game indeed grants that wish.
While I wouldn't make it a primary teaching source, it is exemplary supplementary material that will familiarize you very quickly to the fretboard, the strings, and the feel of holding your guitar via a marvel of lessons (excellent introductions for novices, and decent review for the experienced), cute arcade-esque games (with LEADERBOARDS to give you some competitive motivation)…and of course, a♥♥♥♥♥♥ton of DLC songs to play along with (yes, the vast majority of songs are only available as DLC-- suck it up and support your favorite artists already!!).
I had purchased Rocksmith 2014 under the impression that it was going to ride hard on the gimmick of using a guitar as a controller, but nope! You can tell that all hands on the drawing board really goaled for a feasible, functional, addictive, QUALITY product and could be both instructively useful and still hella fun.
Much of this game is quite intuitive in what and how it allows players to control their practice. For instance, song difficultly gets automatically upped ever so slightly whenever the game detects you getting a steadier handle on certain song segments. And plus, there's RIFF REPEATER!: You can control the speed, select which part of the song you're struggling with, and even manually lower/raise the difficulty-- and it loops automatically.
^^ Those are such little things that really facilitate the learning process in how much it smooths over what could have potentially been extremely frustrating moments to a player. And in a world where more and more devs seem to delight in ripping off their consumers with crappy product and shrugging and spouting bs like "TRUE fans won't complain!", it's so gratifying knowing I gave my money to people who actually seem like they cared and put a lot of thought into the players' experience.
And as a result of their effort, I tend to plug in my guitar with the intention of only playing for a bit to kill time, and then only much much later realize I'd just spent hours simply dicking around on this game. It is that enjoyable. Definitely one of those things that earns the 'what a time to be alive' phrase.

More than a decade ago I was in love with the
. 1 was great, 2 was the best;
was too hard  for me but I tried to enjoy it anyway. Time passed, I discovered the
(which is like a casualised HoMM) and loved those too -
is my #1 singleplayer-only game in terms of hours spent at the time of writing. Time passed once again and the cycle continues. I discovered Braveland, which I consider a casualised King's Bounty. I want to believe this is the bottom and there is nowhere else to go, especially not downward.
The world is explored along predetermined paths. There is no castle management. Hero stats and upgrades are next to meaningless. The writing is very generic. The combats (on a hexagonal grid) feel satisfying but lack depth. The look of the  interface makes me think it was designed for mobile devices first and ported to PC later.
It might sound like there are many issues but those are relative, and visible mainly when compared to more complex representatives of the genre. Perceived alone, Braveland is decent and brought me quite a bit of fun. It's relaxing and I still enjoyed seeing the story to its conclusion, collecting gold for troops, figuring out efficient combat orders. The graphics are okay and the music fits the atmosphere. I also appreciated that it's possible to get all of the achievements in one playthrough, even when playing on Hard (which is barely hard). If you end up with a "fun but shallow" opinion of Braveland, check out the games I mentioned in the first paragraph.

You might be scared because this game is part of a series that you probably never heard of, and it looks and feels like a mobile game ported to pc. But that's not fair, because it's actually surprisingly a good pc game. The gamestyle is casual, but has just enough RPG elements to make it interesting while not overburdening with complexity.
Rebuild3 is centered around managing a gang of survivors within a city. You control their equipment and assign them to missions. Each has five skills (combat, building, scavenging, leadership and engineering). Each member has an specific skill they are good at and can improve with the corresponding related mission. For example, you send fighters to attack zombies or builders to claim an empty buildings. Adding additional crew to a mission improves the rate of success. Over time, crew assigned to missions together may become friends or enemies (influencing happiness).
Throughout the game, you are presented with decisions how to lead people (e.g. help strangers vs being cautious). Once you succeed in a city, you learn a little more of the story and move on to the next city, leaving behind most of your gang. There are different endings based on your decisions.
Cons:
Overall, I would recommend Rebuild 3 if you want to play something slightly casual or if you like management sims. If you prefer action, this game is probably not for you.

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

This is one of those older games along with the original Sonic the Hedgehog and Metroid that happens to be mediocre, and no one ever really says it is. For some reason, these games are considered "classics", "timeless", and called the best games of all time. And I heavily disagree on Tomb Raider (1996) being considered one of the best games ever.
I grew up on Anniversary, so as it usually is when I play a really good modern remake or sequel, and play its highly-praised  predecessor I end up very disappointed. Anniversary was alive with dynamic music, great characterization, and creative level design. And the original that it's based off of is... incredibly dull.
Now, you might say I have no appreciation for older games, and need to praised them more for their "historic impact" on the gaming industry. A game could have certainly done a lot for the cause of gaming, but the games that have built off the foundations laid by these games and made something really special. Think about it. Do you, personally, know the first film ever made? The first Oscar winner? If so, do you consider them the among the likes of The Godfather and Citizen Kane? Of course not! Then why should we give so much credit to the original Super Mario Bros. and Grand Theft Auto III? They are fun, but they aren't anything special, like other much better-made games like The Last of Us or The Unfinished Swan.
The only problem with this for Tomb RaideR 96 is.... it's not even fun! The game felt more like a chore than an escapist video game that I could have fun playing, because everything is the game is so slow- from Lara's tank-like controls, her awkward and unpredictable jumping, and massive wait-time on pushing crates around. The puzzles in the games are a little challenging, but the main platforming of the game completely falls flat, since it's so stilted and strange to control. Even more so is the "combat", which is basically jumping and holding the "shoot" button until everyone in the cave/room/corridor is dead.
The sound is nearly inexistent. Sure, the sounds can be ambient and this was the 90's so games like these weren't that technologically impressive. But any ambience the music could possibly muster is brought down by the very short draw-distance, which breaks the illusion that the game I'm playing is a game. Especially when the characters have no personality behind the one line they speak in cutscenes. I liked Anniversary's take on the original, because Lara Croft was a complete badass. She would kill when necessary, and faced her obstacles with daring in the expressions she made on her face in the cutscenes. Sure, you could say, "Lara in the original Tomb Raider could have been easily replaced by a man, which shows that they've handled her well." But the whole marketing for Lara Croft is her very obvious sex appeal, and it was nice that she showed a lot more unique talents for her gender that she used to her advantage in Anniversary.
I'm not saying I had Tomb Raider 96, either. It's just pretty average. But you have these die-hard fans that think it's superior to Underworld, Legend, and Anniversary- which had a better focus on character and story (again, they're not perfect either) which blew the simplistic, tomb-raiding 90's video game out of the water. Hyper light drifter is a fun little rpg-like game with intuitive action gameplay. The art and locations are gorgeous, and the music is atmospheric for each of the 4 main areas. The bosses are fun and challenging, which the dark souls side of me loves. The story and world are interesting, but there isn't quite enough there to actually understand whats going on without outside research. The combat evolves as you collect guns and skills from exploration, but starts to become repetitive after you have purchased all the meaningful upgrades. While the exploration is incentivised by money and healthpacks, a lot of the other collectibles seem useless except for achievement hunters that will have to comb through the areas extensively. While not perfect, this is a quite enjoyable 5-15 hour experience that I can solidly recommend to anyone, and highly recommend to those who like the bright pixel aesthetic, fast combat, and speculative story-telling. 7/10

This was a nice surprise, bought the game on a whim. This game plays more like a helicopter shootemup rather than a sim. The gameplay is capture and hold, you can jump in and join the action either in a PvP or 4-player coop. If you crash and burn there are no penalties and no losses, just go nuts trying your stunts.
For a successful game you'll have to cooperate with your team mates, whether it's PvP or coop. Some vehicles have special abilities, like the recon get highlighted enemies and can send those coordinates to team mates, something your allied gunships will appreciate. You've also got personel transport which is required to capture and hold. Some vehicles mix a little of this and that, making them recon+attack or personel+heavy assault. Pick what you think is required for the situation and try to make it a good team combo.
There is no pay to win, you grind your points to unlock and research vehicles. That said, it's not that grindy, things progress rather quickly. Matches are restricted by vehicle tier level so you can't wreck noobs simply by vehicle stats. However, some players are just really good at flying. While the mechanics are simple (compared to a sim) they still take a lot of skill to master.

Crytek decides to address the consoles for its next chapter of Crysis, enriching its history but with the consequences of being designed to run on limited hardware.
- Excellent artistic direction (although it was designed thinking on consoles, Crysis 2 boasts a spectacular design of the city of New York, enemies and characters).
- Wonderful attention to detail (from the photos on posters of missing people in the disaster to the inside of a newsstand, Crytek's hand into this title is pretty evident).
- Solid and immersive history (a new step forward in the narrative structure of the series, answering questions from the previous installments and paving the way towards the close of the trilogy).
- Weapons arsenal quite varied and original.
- Long Campaign (beyond collectibles scattered in the most remote corners of the maps and the relentless search for accessories for your equipment that may already increase your playtime).
- Improved IA over previous titles (although there is the possibility that enemies can "stuck" in specific places of the maps).
- Consolized (From the ridiculous FOV of the render of the weapon you hold, passing through the reduced level design and ending with the simplification of controls and gameplay elements).
- Multiplayer support is discontinued (with the shutdown of GameSpy servers there is no active multiplayer... but, there are ways...)
A solid game all around, especially in the artistic and narrative department. However, fans of the two previous installments probably be disappointed when they see how much the saga has been reduced, technologically speaking.
Note: Played it on Microsoft Windows 7 Ultimate - 64 bits

Definitely an awesome tool to help you play, practice, and just enjoy the guitar. I started playing guitar about the same time (almost a year ago as of writing this) that I bought this game, and it's helped me extensively.
The song selection is pretty good, there's lots of variety for no matter what you're into. I even discovered a few indie songs I've never heard that I actually enjoy very much. Some of the songs are more difficult, while others are a good match for even beginning players. The dynamic difficulty is a really great feature, as it really teaches you the song slowly so that you can get the hang of the structure of the song before the game unleashes all of it at you. Even if you're playing a really difficult song, you can still enjoy it and not get completely overwhelmed by it because of dynamic difficulty. Something that was useful for me when I bought the Megadeth song pack after only playing guitar for a month...
Whether you prefer chords and rhythm guitar, the bass, killer solos and lead guitar, there's for everyone.
The gear unlocks and progress meters on tracks really give you something to work towards. Picking up a guitar for the first time and learning the basic mechanics is a grueling process that many give up on, but the game has tutorials for everything, even things as simple as how to hold a pick, to help you through the learning curve.
There's even a website with custom songs you can add into the game. I've added over a hundred custom songs I've downloaded. The vast majority of songs I've added (even lesser known ones) include rhythm, bass, and lead as do most of the ones I've seen as well.
Ultimately, if you've ever wanted to learn to play the guitar or bass, I recommend this game extensively. Even if you already know how to play, whether exceptionally well, or pretty mediocre, there really is something for everyone here.
As a guitarist, this is easily the best game I own, and the most value for my money.

Rocksmith 2014 is essentially an improved version of the earlier installment in the series, and I have to say that Ubisoft really nailed it with this one.
The game provides a simple, good-looking and smooth experience for people to learn and play the guitar, regardless of skill level.
With this game you can learn to play along to your favourite songs, practice your slides, harmonics, chords, play minigames in the Guitarcade, test yourself to reach higher and higher scores in the Score Attack mode and much much more.
Being an intermediate guitar player that just picked up the electric, I have to admit that playing this game has been a blessing. Within the first five hours of playing I had already learnt more than I had after 3 years of lessons. The game is easy to use and gives you plenty of time learn the songs you love, allowing you to increase and decrease the difficulty and speed of specific segments with the Riff Repeater.
The game starts off with a generous amount of songs for you to play, and allows you to purchase hundreds of other songs for a relatively cheap price with new DLC being brought out weekly. If there's a song that you want to play that isn't in the main game or any of the DLC, there's also a great chance that you can find and download a Custom DLC from any of the many community websites.
The only bad things I can say is that the game might not recognize you playing some power chords if there's a lot of distortion going on, and that you have to go to a store and buy a Real Tone Cable before you can play.
Buying this game is probably one of the best decisions I've made recently, and  if you are a beginner and want to improve your guitar playing skills, or if you're a master and just want to have som fun challenging yourself to clear Fury of the Storm with 100% accuracy. I started playing this game back in 2010 when it was featured on Kotaku.  Of course since it was featured on that site, as well as a couple others,  the servers were packed and and the community was full of kids with homophobic slurs and bans for no/good reason (shamans were trolling or clueless).  One time I got banned since the room went trigger happy and I threw one or two cannonballs ;)  It was a weird summer as I played that game religiously, even made a few game friends in the process.  If Steam was tracking us at the time, I would've had at least 200 hours logged.  After so many rounds of anvil gods and breaking a map with large crates, I decided to call it quits sometime early next year.
I found out 6 months ago that this game showed up on Steam when I was looking at a friend's profile, and it picked up my interest.  Coming back was like Marty McFly travelling to 2015 from 1985, it was still the same game but so much has changed.  Hats were a thing back then, but now expanded tenfold.  Shamans had new powers plus new ranks.  There's music now, WTF?  Also events like the Christmas one where you got presents that could be exchanged for useless floating pets that disappeared when the event was over.
Of the stuff that stayed the same:
I believe that almost no one from back then still plays this game on a regular basis (I only play on and off again when I'm listening to music or need a distraction).  The 2016 community is much more mild from the 2010 one, but can still be bad at times.  On the plus side, I found out one of friends from back then still plays occasionally.
Even with new maps, some objects just poof out of existence.  They took out the worst offenders, but you can still recreate monstrosities that will annoy your fellow mice >:)  Also you can still moonwalk, which redeems everything.
After everything I've been through with this game, I still enjoy it.  Trying to collect cheese and take it back to your mouse hole brings a small amount of joy, even if the map is/"was made" difficult; bonus points if you made it first.  I completely forgot how a shaman works and their skill tree confuses me, but it's cool when you're helping/
mice that look up to you.  It's F2P, you won't really lose much except a couple minutes if it's not to your liking.
Now if you excuse me, I'll be moonwalking to that cheese over there.
It's just a huge clutter of garbage with a worse interface. Potential for a game here, but it's not here yet. Needs lots and lots of polish to carry the weak physics system

This game is amazing. It is like a free to play game like world of tanks but without the endless advertisements for gold payments. Once bought, you have immersing gameplay with various cool helicopters at your disposal. By playing three games with a certain helicopter you are able to move up a tree, making the grinding aspect negligible. Furthermore the game is not invested with premium ammunition and consumables! Yeah!
Apart from PvP battles, the game also features coop battles which are fun and engaging. The graphics are totally fine and reflect the graphical representation of free to play games like World of Tanks. However the fact that this game is made by only 4 developers puts other companies (I'm looking at you Wargaming) to shame.
The only slight con I have is the somewhat low fps I get every now and then, especially on the testmap where you can try out your helicopters. And by low I mean 30ish. In PvP and coop is stays above 60 with my i3 and GTX 750.
However the pros far outweigh the cons and I don't think you are wasting money if you pick up this game. If you like World of Tanks or Warthunder and you are fed up with matchmaking, premium ammo, premium tanks, grinding credits or grinding xp and you just want to get into a helicopter and shoot stuff, THIS is the game for you.

Crysis 2, like the original is a first person shooter. The game was released in early 2011. It also follows on from the plot of Crysis 1 as well. Although you don't really need to have played the original in order to follow the story. Crysis 2 was also the first game to use the CryEngine 3.
The game play has all of the regular FPS style features. You play the role of a Recon Marine, called Alcatraz. You are able to customize your weapons to match the situations you are in, as well as customizing your suite to the same too. Crysis 2 is set in New York City, which is often referred to by many as an urban jungle. This does however offer various different tactical options when it comes to planning attacks; allowing players to navigate between floors and buildings, and ruined buildings.
We also see a few changes in the Nanosuit used by our character too; this time you are able to use more than one suit power at a time, the strength and power modes have been combined into the same mode, and the stealth suit has been improved slightly.
Crysis 2 has AMAZING graphics; this could easily pass as a game being released recently. If you put all of your settings up to full, you are going to be in amazement at how good this game looks. You will need a beefy rig to keep a steady 60 fps, but my oh my it is worth it.
I sadly see no replay-ability in Crysis 2, there are the addition of a couple of difficulty modes, but to be honest; once you have played it the once, there is no reason to play it again. The single-player campaign is a decent length though - we are looking at a 18 hour long story mode which is very good for an FPS.
Thankfully I had no technical issues with Crysis 2 (unlike I did have with the original), I was able to play with every graphical setting on ultra and still had 60 frames the whole time. The only thing I will mention is there is no longer any multiplayer support since GameSpy shut it's servers down in May 2014.
If you enjoyed the first Crysis game, you will basically enjoy Crysis 2, it's the same just with even better graphics, more compelling story, and stellar FPS action and did I mention the amazing graphics? People may think £20 is a bit steep for a game of this age, however I am completely happy with this price as it almost fits into the £1/hour ratio.

Definitely an awesome tool to help you play, practice, and just enjoy the guitar. I started playing guitar about the same time (almost a year ago as of writing this) that I bought this game, and it's helped me extensively.
The song selection is pretty good, there's lots of variety for no matter what you're into. I even discovered a few indie songs I've never heard that I actually enjoy very much. Some of the songs are more difficult, while others are a good match for even beginning players. The dynamic difficulty is a really great feature, as it really teaches you the song slowly so that you can get the hang of the structure of the song before the game unleashes all of it at you. Even if you're playing a really difficult song, you can still enjoy it and not get completely overwhelmed by it because of dynamic difficulty. Something that was useful for me when I bought the Megadeth song pack after only playing guitar for a month...
Whether you prefer chords and rhythm guitar, the bass, killer solos and lead guitar, there's for everyone.
The gear unlocks and progress meters on tracks really give you something to work towards. Picking up a guitar for the first time and learning the basic mechanics is a grueling process that many give up on, but the game has tutorials for everything, even things as simple as how to hold a pick, to help you through the learning curve.
There's even a website with custom songs you can add into the game. I've added over a hundred custom songs I've downloaded. The vast majority of songs I've added (even lesser known ones) include rhythm, bass, and lead as do most of the ones I've seen as well.
Ultimately, if you've ever wanted to learn to play the guitar or bass, I recommend this game extensively. Even if you already know how to play, whether exceptionally well, or pretty mediocre, there really is something for everyone here.
As a guitarist, this is easily the best game I own, and the most value for my money.

Rocksmith 2014 is essentially an improved version of the earlier installment in the series, and I have to say that Ubisoft really nailed it with this one.
The game provides a simple, good-looking and smooth experience for people to learn and play the guitar, regardless of skill level.
With this game you can learn to play along to your favourite songs, practice your slides, harmonics, chords, play minigames in the Guitarcade, test yourself to reach higher and higher scores in the Score Attack mode and much much more.
Being an intermediate guitar player that just picked up the electric, I have to admit that playing this game has been a blessing. Within the first five hours of playing I had already learnt more than I had after 3 years of lessons. The game is easy to use and gives you plenty of time learn the songs you love, allowing you to increase and decrease the difficulty and speed of specific segments with the Riff Repeater.
The game starts off with a generous amount of songs for you to play, and allows you to purchase hundreds of other songs for a relatively cheap price with new DLC being brought out weekly. If there's a song that you want to play that isn't in the main game or any of the DLC, there's also a great chance that you can find and download a Custom DLC from any of the many community websites.
The only bad things I can say is that the game might not recognize you playing some power chords if there's a lot of distortion going on, and that you have to go to a store and buy a Real Tone Cable before you can play.
Buying this game is probably one of the best decisions I've made recently, and  if you are a beginner and want to improve your guitar playing skills, or if you're a master and just want to have som fun challenging yourself to clear Fury of the Storm with 100% accuracy. I suggest that you spend the around 50€ for the game and the cable, and go have some fun! ;)

If you are learning the guitar I think this would be a great tool, but I have been playing the guitar a long time and bought it as a practice tool, there is nothing more boring than practicing by yourself - so I was basically looking for glorified backing tracks and maybe to branch out and play some styles I wouldn't ordinarily play.
The first problem I hit is that you have to basically learn a new notation, also I am colour blind so the colour coded strings were not a great help to me. I've spent 20 years reading tab and standard notation sheet music and suddenly I have to learn another system, let's just say that motivation was low.
Also as other reviewers have mentioned it starts you out very slowly which is frustrating if you know the song, but I discovered if you just play the full part then it will quickly build it up. The problem I came to was when I was completely unfamiliar with the song I didn't get enough warning of what was going on to follow along. So a song I could have easily played along with if I had had the tab or music I was left with no idea what was going on.
Another issue I had was it not recognising when I had played the right notes, especially at the low end on my Les Paul - maybe it didn't like the signal from the humbuckers. I found it greatly frustrating to have played something note perfectly and it to tell me to repeat a passage because it hadn't registered the input correctly.
So - in conclusion: If you are an experienced guitarist this may provide more frustration than fun, but for a beginner I can see it being a fun way to learn.

Take heed -- Rebuild is TOUGH and you can easily screw yourself over if you get careless or overconfident. Hey there, Rebus Forever here with another 'One Minute-ish Review!' for a game called Heliborne.
This game got in the way of me playing total war so I kinda resent it.
Anyway, here goes.
A video version of this review is available here, it's only wafer thin.
Did a certain helicopter scene from Apokalypse Now leave an indelible mark on your subconsious?
Has your military hardware fetish checklist had a helicopter shaped hole in it not filled by
or War Thunder?
Have you  Always wanted to play a helicopter game but been put off by the majority being more simulation based?
Then Heliborne might be the game for you.
Heliborne is a multiplayer focused wargame played out on large maps with battles decided in versus mode by one teams ground forces making it to the opposing teams landing zone with various control points littered around the map.
In this game you are helicopeters so must influence the course of the battle by helicoptering as hard as you are able.
Helicoptery things you will be expected to do include, destroying ground troops at control points, escorting or flying transports to take command points or deploy anti air, anti tank and mortar teams where you please- or generally making a nuisence of yourself amongst the enemy helicopters.
When you begin you may be forced through the repeated destruction of your helicopters to ask yourself "are my methods unsound?".
Sticking with the game and getting used to the process of flying and aiming while maintaining speed you will in due course improve and get your tally of kills up.
As you play you earn points to unlock more helicopters and research more advanced equipments or skins for your individual warmachines.
The tiers are the main system by which the game controls matchmaking balance so expect some totally unwinnable battles where the opponents are all just a mile better than you and learn to enjoy the losses as much as the victories while learning as much as you can from both outcomes.
Making the right choice about which of your veichles to choose from be it a scout to call down mortars, a transport to take points or an attack helicopter to mess up anyone trying to do either of the previous options is as bigger part of the battle as flying well independantly.
In co-op or verses teamwork really makes a difference in this game so try to pay more attention to what your allies are up to than i tend to do.
I have racked up a bunch of hours with this game without even realising, I assumed I hadn't played it enough yet to warrant a review, turned out Ive played 30+ hours, its that sort of a game...
So, If you love the smell of napalm in the morning maybe you should buy this game.
Thanks for your time and check out some of my other reviews if you liked this one.

Slow-and-steady is the best approach to "winning" this sim (that is, not running out of money). Of course, you can always cheat by enabling infinite monies. :)
You fail at this sim when your population goes through boom and bust cycles (that is, dramatic growth and dramatic death). If you gradually grow your population by zoning (in small chunks) when there is demand for it, your city will grow and not crash horribly later on.
The only game where, if you set up your city right, you can let it run, ignore it for hours, come back, and watch the city sustain itself. Spent hours just watching different parts of my city grow. Felt like Superman flying over the city to see things looked like at ground-level then zoomed up high to see what the situation looked like from above and then back down again.
Was surprised this "game" simulates reality quite accurately.
Any problems I encountered in-game could be solved by just applying the layout of the city I live in. :) Learned much about city planning headaches and solutions.
For me, it was definitely more of a city simulator than a game. I appreciate the layout of my city a lot more because of this "game". I look at a neighbourhood layout or a road layout with a keener eye now. This game can be classified as more of an edutainment product.

About me:
I starting playing guitar in January of this year and bought the game two months later. I am playing on a Yamaha FSX700SC acoustic. Although music has been a part of my life for many years, this is the first time I have tried to learn a traditional instrtrument.
Rocksmith 2014 is a great tool for learning songs and techniques without requiring the use of teachers or traditional self help books and videos.
I do not recommend using this game as the only resource for learning the guitar but it is a great adjunct for players learning in a more traditional way. The learning curve has felt daunting and frustrating at times but patience and persistance has helped me learn some really cool stuff from this game.
With that said, there are some things that this game cannot teach you:
Strum patterens are covered in some detail in the Lesson mode but the game never indicates if you need to strum up or down. This makes playing 'rhythm' songs that are very chord heavy almost impossible unless you are already familiar and comfortable with this concept. Same with alternate picking; there is a lesson on it but beginners will inevitably have bad habits because the game has no way of knowing or correcting your technique. Learning outside of the game seems crucial for really getting better down the road.
Now here's what this game can teach you:
Self help books and videos are great when it comes to timing, strum patterns, and reading sheet music but one thing I love about this game is that you are playing real songs which means you are constantly playing up and down the neck. Books and sheet music for a beginner feel restricted because it is a very slow process. Learning scales and keys means that you are only working with a limited amount of frets at one time. This game has helped me learn which string/fret represent each key in a way that is fun and fast.
Chords are obviously essential and this game is worth it for the chord book alone. Learning all the different shapes and barre chords can seem daunting but this method of learning is a lot more intuitive and fun. I really like how it tells you the chord names as you are playing/learning a song.
My experience with playing the game on acoustic has been alright. Electric might be better for this game because a lot of the songs were originally played that way. Also, there can be some sound issues with acoustic because of how loud they are but the 'Mixer' option let's you tweak the sound to your liking.
If you are thinking of picking up a guitar for the first time this game is an essantial learning tool. Learning the guitar without real lessons or a teacher can be almost impossible in the long run but this game is the beginning of something exciting. I credit this game for the majority of my current skills with guitar, and who knows where I would be in terms of skill without it. Sure, I may have bad habits in some areas but the gratifying feeling of playing real songs and learning real concepts is unparalleled to other methods of learning.

I purchased this software 3 months before my 49th birthday.  I had always wanted to learn to play the guitar but I just never had the time or money to do it before so I had absolutely no experience when purchased.  I was a total novice.
The initial investment was expensive (I purchased a very cheap electric guitar online along with the realtone cable and some picks, a strap, etc.)
When I first started the lessons I was having some trouble with the software not picking up the notes as I played them but this was fixed by turning the gain on the realtone cable up to around 5.5 db or so (2/3 of way up bar.)  Once this was fixed I spent the next 3 weeks injuring my left wrist by playing as much as my  body could stand.
I had to take a week off of playing.  When I went back I quickly realized my fingers were too short and fat to effectively play a 6-string at the level required.  I was muting way too many strings.  My chords sounded awful and I couldn't get passed 60% mastery on any songs.
Before I totally accepted defeat I decided to bite the bullet and invest in a bass.  Probably a better bass than I should have.
The first song the program suggested to me was Def Leopard "Pour some sugar on me."  As I was playing it I noticed (with more than a little amusement) that the entire song only uses 2 strings.  Since the program slowly shows you more and more notes as you play (you start off only playing certain notes in a bass line and the program will slowly fill in more notes as you properly hit the ones they are displaying [it is genius]) it took me around 5 tries hit 102% mastery on it.  This truly boosted my confidence.  While this song is easy to play I do love it and have since I was a teenager *cough*
As I tried more difficult songs and moved through the bass lessons and mini-games I realized that the extra space the neck of the bass provides between the strings allowed my fingers to move a bit more easily up and down the fretboard.  The thicker strings also stood out more to my pudgy fingers.
I am sharing all of this with you, reader, essentially to say that now that it is 2 weeks before my 49th birthday I just tried to play "Everlong" by the Foo Fighters and nailed a 99% accuracy on my 2nd try.
I am bouncing up and down the fretboard like I have been playing the bass for a year.  The more difficult songs still give me trouble.  "Play that funky music" by Wild Cherry and "Satch Boogie" by the great Joe Satriani are examples of just hellish bass lines.
I have managed to impress all my friends and I play a version of "Hollow" by Alice in Chains that brings chills to them (they say.)
At this point I will only get better at the bass and I cannot believe how well this program has taught me (along with help from some youtube courses to nail techniques.)
If you are willing to put in the time, money, effort and maybe even some blood this program will teach you how to play a guitar or bass.
How well you do does depend a bit on talent of course.
I whole heartedly recommend this program.  It has been worth every penny.  But I usually wait for a good sale to get the expensive song packs.
Edit on August 18, 2017:
Well it is now 2 weeks before my 50th birthday and I just ripped my middle finger open mastering "Texas Flood" by Stevie Ray Vaugn and Double Trouble but that is okay because I just flippin' mastered "Texas Flood" by Stevie Ray Vaugn and Double Trouble!!!
I cannot sing this program's praises enough.  If you have any interest at all in playing a guitar or bass get this program.
Highly Recommended.

This is a game I've simply taken far too long to finish.
It is everything it has been praised for. Sleek, clean aesthetics. A moving and wonderful soundtrack. And a beautiful story that's excellently told: neither too much nor too little.
Thomas Was Alone is a simple puzzle platformer that is easy to approach--even for newbies to the platforming genre--and yet still very rewarding to finish in its elegant level design. The characters, despite being quadrilaterals, are all very endearing and amazingly human. The narrator portrays their personalities and their motives and their feelings very well.
The game isn't without its flaws, namely in that the controls feel a tad bit buggy. There are times where you are moving a character but the jump doesn't register, which can get frustrating when you're trying to hit certain pixel perfect jumps. I also ran into a few audio bugs, where different tracks started to overlay each other which is a bit disorienting to say the least...
Despite that, the game plays very smoothly. I'm not sure what more I can say about it. It's a game that truly values clean design and admirable minimalism. And yet despite the almost mathematicalness to its aesthetics, it's full of feelies. I highly recommend Thomas Was Alone to anyone who's looking for a light, touching story and a little bit of puzzliness.

Like others, I first played Rebuild and Rebuild 2. I completely missed the memo that there was a 3 on Steam until the Winter sell happened. Oh boy did I get my immediate moneys worth.
I'll start with the things I am not impressed with. The music. It's just not that fantastic in my opinion. I muted it and played my own music, which might have helped to increase the overall experience for me. I played this game in two four hour sittings already and I can say my own music helped immerse me far more than the games soundtrack.
Now for the good.
If you ever played Rebuild 1 or 2, you can say good bye to the 'normal' flash graphics and welcome the same style, but more refined. The controls are super simple, and the ease of use between the GUI and the map is fantastic. I can quickly and simply execute any command I want without to much hassle. The only hiccup would be with quickly checking my survivors happiness. This minor annoyance is saved due to the fact all the menus open and close instantly, so I don't feel like I am bogged down waiting for things to load or transition.
The gameplay for the uninvolved is easy. You have 5 trades. Builder, Scavanger, Guard, Engineer and Leader. They all can do each others jobs, but whatever role they specialize in will yield faster and better results. You want your builders to improve buildings, reclaim territory, hunt or chop wood. You want Scavengers to scout, collect goods and farm. Guards to protect your settlement from hoards or mobs, or to clear zombie nests faster. Engineers to do your research or fix key buildings on the map. Leaders for trade, recruitment and negotiations.
You start with 5 'squares'. Your goal is to reclaim more squares to build up your settlement. You'll find survivors, supplies, zombies, and other factions along the way. Each square has a property to it that helps you in some way, or at least has some flavor to (like a movie theater. It serves no purpose, but you can rebuild it to be a farm or church). The balancing act is deciding what to reclaim first. What to rebuild. Who to assign to what. What items during your hunts do you equip to who?
One of the main driving factors of the game (besides the zombies) is the random events. You'll get prompts. Ranging from 2 or more options. Depending on the action, or skill of your character affected. You may get only 1 due to unfortunate events, or 5 with a great chance of rewards. Do you give food to that random stranger who showed up at your gates and let them stay the night? Will the rob you? Give you a chainsaw? Join your struggling community? Let the zed in?
The game can be as fast or as slow as you want it. The default speed makes the time bo by 15 minutes. I play an hour a second for my speed and I enjoy how fast paced the game can be when your settlment grows large. Of course you can pause at any time during your micromanagment. You can play at any pace you desire and should find enjoyment all the same.
If I were to really get you to take a chance with this game, then I feel you would havve made the right choice. Even if you waste 3 hours of fun with it before you give it up, I believe your money would be well spent. The personal stories of your survivors (new to the series) helps give it more life. The story mode is fun, if not rather normal for this genre. Customization is not stellar, but satisfying.

I enjoyed the dialog so much it was a shame that there was no option to engage in dialog trees. Perhaps this is an RPG Maker limitation? I've only played one other RPG Maker game (To The Moon), so i was prepared to face pointless fetch quests, but Space Pilgrim manages to spice it up a bit by making the fetch quests meaningful and adding some simple inventory puzzles. For the price, this is one of the neatest sci-fi adventures i've played recently.

A leitmotiv among Space Pilgrim Ep. 1's numerous positive reviews are that "it is a good game for the price".
The price being
, this might in fact not be a very good game at all.
There is little point in being overly harsh about something that wasn't offensive in any way (except for the typo on Dvořák in the credits).
is a space-themed point-and-click adventure made in RPG Maker that will last you less than two hours. The game is linear and offers no challenge at all (it is impossible to die/fail), so don't expect any replay value. The visual and audio design, albeit not horrid, is exceptionally average and uses a lot of existing assets (which, fairly enough, are properly mentioned in the credits).
So what is left to enjoy? The story and the writing quality. Once again, nothing offensively atrocious there; it is just... painfully average. The story has as little depth as you'd expect from such a short adventure. The dialogue has its moments, with a few chuckles coming from the clash between the scientist's cynical demeanor and Captain Pilgrim's simple-minded antics... but that's pretty much it. Nothing really memorable stands out. Surely there was room for more character development and slightly deeper exchanges, even within the context of a two-hour adventure.
I will most certainly concede that
is fair for its price; but I wouldn't go so far as to recommend playing it, unless you're an absolute sucker for short sci-fi stories and you feel that actual books have too many complicated words.

A casual turn based strategy game with some RPG elements.  Even at its toughest level, the game is still perfect for casual gaming.  The graphics are flash like animations, the music is decent, but most importantly the game is fun.  You start with a small recruited army and as you move forward through the map you will encounter new enemies, new recruits, and new items to increase your stats.  Every fight will get you gold and experience.  Gold can be used to purchase more recruits and the experience can increase your stats.  What makes this game casual is not the fighting, you will definitely need to know how to fight in a turn based strategy game.  What truly makes it casual is that when you finish a fight, the gold received from winning the fight is automatically used to revive your dead troops from the previous fight.  This means that typically, unless you get your butt kicked, you will maintain a stronger and stronger army as you move through the map.
It is not a very long game, and there are two other games to continue the very forgettable storyline.  If you are looking for a simple, yet entertaining game of this genre, I definitely recommend it.

I've played a lot of For Honor, before it's release during open beta and pretty much every day since it's launch. I'm not usually one for writing reviews, but I have a vested interest here as I feel that most of the posts here are a tad too hyperbolic and I want people considering trying this game for the free weekend event to get a better perspective.
First, I want to examine the main problems that For Honor both has in excess, and those that people greatly exaggerate. The game is not very stable. This is undeniable, and it is certainly a problem, but the game is way more so now than at launch. People complaining about P2P are not really understanding how these systems work; P2P is often employed in FGs, and indeed it works very well in duels and brawls. The problem really lies with the 4v4 modes, where disconnects are more frequent. I'd say I disconnect from an in-session game once every 1.5-2 hours, and fail to join 3/10 games before I get the chance to load in. It's annoying, but it's not un-playable.
Balancing issues exist in every single game with multiplayer modes and that holds competitive aspirations. Every such game has a meta. The problem with For Honor is that the prevalent meta is frustrating since it favours defensive centric play, especially at higher matchmaking ratings. Characters are ranked according to their ability to break open turtles, which is why there is seemingly such a gulf between the S and C tiers; there are not many heroes that excel at getting through a stout defence. Personally, I am of the firm belief that you can make any hero work, especially in the 4v4 modes (where you don't often have the luxury of time and space to maintain a defensive mindset), and doubly especially at lower MMRs. S tier characters will simply have an easier time of things. The devs have been aware of this meta problem for a long time, and whilst the fixes have been frustrating few and far between, there is hope; after a significant meta patch in the future, most vanilla heroes (often the weakest, such as Berserker, Nobushi, Conqueror, Lawbringer, Orochi, Valkyrie) will be recieving significant reworks to make them more appealing and viable.
This game is most assuredly not pay-to-win. The micro-transactions are almost entirely cosmetic, and those that aren't are almost entirely pointless (such as paying steel to unlock all of a character's feats right away, when you unlock them through leveling after maybe 3 hours play time). The steel drop rate isn't too bad, if I do my daily orders and 3 main ones, I get about 1.2k steel a day. There is absolutely no incentive to buy steel, unless you truly cannot wait to own the new mythic outfit, or the new executions, etcetera.
The community, for the most part, is indefensible. Vitriol, main-shaming and rage-quits are very commonplace (the latter of which does not help game stability) and they do, unfortunately, detract from the experience. My advice; play with manners and ignore those with unhealthy levels of salt in their diet. It's a shame, but I suppose it is to be expected in a game like this.
A final point, one I don't like having to mention, but one I feel deserves to be brought to light to people who do not know; For Honor is currently running without a lag compensation system, since the devs removed their 'timesnap' system. This is, to mine and many other player's minds, the single biggest problem with For Honor right now. For the sake of brevity, not having a lag compensation system in place means that your experiences fighting heroes will drastically differ between different players. This is because the speed of attacks, and their subsequent block/parry timings, are now determined by the quality of the internet connections in question. Frustratingly, it appears that this benefit is skewed to favour the player(s) with the worst internet. In the most extreme cases, it can speed all attacks up by 100ms - messing with your defensive response timings, whilst making some select attacks nigh un-reactable. The devs have announced countless times that a new LC system is coming, but as of yet, there is nothing in place.
Now for what I love about the game.
Visually, For Honor is simply stunning. The textures are crisp and vibrant, yet still retain the grittiness of war. The animations are excellent, truly some of the best I have seen in a game. I still like watching in-situ executions, despite playing for almost 1,000 hours, whereas in The Fractured But Whole, I grew tired of the ultimate attacks after 5 hours. All in all, it's visceral, it's beautiful and even charming, despite the recent fantasy-esque cosmetic additions.
The combat system, The Art of Battle, is incredible. I've never enjoyed combat this much in any other game. That's not to say it is perfect (it isn't, aforementioned balance problems and parrying being just two areas that need work), it's to say that the game is compelling despite the imperfections. I found it a little overwhelming at first, probably owing to this being the first multiplayer game I'd played in a while, but quickly grew to love it; even whilst still learning to not be trash. Combat mechanics such as this are going to be popping up in more and more titles, mark my words. It is without a doubt For Honor's greatest appeal, and I'm happy to say that despite this game being incredibly frustrating at times, I'm still compelled to play it. The drive to improve is still strong, and my enjoyment of it, whilst somewhat oscilliatory, definitely trends postively.
For Honor is the type of game that if you play with friends, you will see your enjoyment increase exponentially. It's a lot easier to ignore the frustrating aspects when you are playing with someone you like. I have experienced very few more satisfying moments in my gaming career, than flawlessly executing a good stratergy with friends in, say, Dominion.
All in all, I'd recommend this game to anyone who asked; provided they have the patience necessary to bear the frustrating problems it still has.

I bought 3 RE games in a package (RE 4,5,6). I played a couple of hours on RE4...it felt a bit stale and slow. Decided to give RE6 a try. In terms of graphics and gameplay, I don't see much difference in quality between RE4 and RE6.
A few things that get annoying really quick:
1. Cut scenes and worthless narratives:  I love a good story. Unfortunately, there's not much of a story happening here.  Shoot zombies. Go somewhere else. Shoot zombies. The pace is interupted by cut-scenes which serve no apparent purpose. Two hours into the game, I'm still unsure why I'm here and what I'm after.
2.  Linear, stale, canned environment: It's the zombie apocalypse, so every building and street is in disarray. The game creators have used piles of junk to seal off areas and make the map appear bigger than it is. But there's no consistency to the barriers. In one rooom, you might be able to jump over a bench or a table. In the next room, you can't. Or you might find that a small board blocks a hallway that, somehow, you can't smash or crawl under.  It's just a very poorly constructed environment. RE needs to go open-world!
3.  No tips/tutorials for crafting:  Herbs are a mainstay. I mixed them, I eat them, I'm healed - but there's no way to tell if I'm "doing it right".  Anyone new to the franchise would probably be confused. Find a plant. Combine the plant. Be sure to put the mixture in a vial. Then use it to heal. Not tremendously complex, but crafting in any game deserves a small tutorial or entry on the "Help" menu. What's the diffrence between red, green, etc...? It's a guessing game. So I had to take 5 minutes to restart from a save point and play around with herb combos. Worthless waste of my time. Just provide the information up front. (FC3 does FPS crafting right, CapCom should take a page from Ubi's playbook.)
4. Cheap, underhanded AI tactics: For example, I see a zombie laying on the ground. I shoot it in the head. Bullet goes right through, no damage. Just a dead body, right? I walk up and try to kick it. Still no reaction. I walk past it. The zombie comes to life and attacks me from behind. I don't mind a genuine surprise attack from the AI, but tactics like this are off-putting to the player.
After playing RE 4 and 6 for a total of about four hours, I'm calling the Resident Evil franchise broken. The linear style can't compete  with open world FPS.  The narrative is old and tired.  Even at half-price, it's still too much money.

Crysis 2 exceeds in graphics, gameplay, optimization, audio design, music, etc. Even the story is pretty good, written by Richard K. Morgan, who wrote one of my favorites, Altered Carbon.
Set five years after the first game where you first witness the Ceph in all their terror on Langshan, the Ceph have made their way to NYC, an urban jungle (as described by Crytek devs). I think the most remarkable thing about Crysis 2 might be the attention to detail with the recognizable buildings and showing their true height, just looking up at them in a video game shows how massive NYC can really feel from a virtual perspective. Obviously, it helps that the CryEngine is perhaps the best engine out there in terms of graphical prowess.
I really liked the story, mainly because I'm a sucker for sci-fi games. So the various twists and military factions you encounter while trying to survive from the Ceph was nice. Well, sort of.  Maybe it aspires to be Theme Hospital.  It is an early release, and I love the premise of it.  Run a bar full of drunks, fighters, mages, noblemen.  The room ideas are good.  You could ride ThemeHospital's additions to a full game of interesting strategic elements: where can I fit this room, you need a spa to make champions happy, research that turkey leg!
Unfortunately its not quite there yet.  There's a lot of gameplay issues that should get reviewed before I would feel like this game is ready.
-Moving handymen onto spills or barf doesn't prompt them to clean it, they just wander away.
-Editing rooms or even just moving a table takes a menu action, then a highlight, then another menu action, then you can reposition.  Right click to move objects.  Single click room edits.  Please. Please. Please.
-ECONOMY NEEDS FIXED.  Why does a bar cost 1200 gold but you get 30 gold per drink. You break even after 40 drinks.  Not including the bartender staff costs.  You will never recover this gold.  You will almost never recover gold spent on improvements.  Revenue from the tavern covers staff costs, that's it.  A potted plant costs 580 gold.  Beer costs 30 gold.  To recover the gold spent on a plant takes serving 20 people at the bar.
-No feedback on how you're doing.  There's nothing to say why people are leaving unless you hover over them, I don't know if liquor is popular, or if I'm making back gold on the guest room I built (also stupid expensive and never recovering gold).
-Special events, Lord Peter wants a reservation of X people.  Every month.  Switch this up, make barbarians just show up, have a legendary hero come in and if he's happy he boosts booze sales or reputation.
I don't have any issues on the graphics of it, it looks like it belongs in the 2000's but grahics are not why you're playing a tavern management game.  Hoping that over time we get some extra polish on this game because conceptually it's great.
It's ten bucks, if it fixes some of the issues it's totally worth it.

There is a lot to be said about Thomas Was Alone. It is a cute 2D platformer with simplistic graphics and a stunning use of narration and lighting. Now, the main draw for myself was the narration, and at the end of the experience, the narration was the highlight. It is difficult to describe the connections you end up making with each little character as you progress, all due to the clever use of narration. All the characters have distinct personalities, and all of them end up sticking with the player. I eventually even had a favorite character, and all the while I realized how ridiculous it was that this character happened to be a rectangle with a color assigned to it. Each character has its own gimmick. Whether it is jumping high, being able to swim, fit in tight spaces, etc. These gimmicks create the puzzles that make up the entire game. Without them it would be quite bland. They are always exciting, and easy to understand as they are introduced cleverly. Do I recommend it? Yes I do. For those who want a slow-paced, narrative driven puzzler, this game is the best out there. I loved it. An experience I will remember for years to come.

Another game that shows why Steam needs a mixed rating. I enjoy playing for free with the daily challenges and single player, which act as standalone puzzles that don't require any grinding or payment. On the monetization side, I'm echoing the voices about how shady the promotional tactics are.
The Humble Bundle new account creation promo for 3 free $10 card packs isn't actually that big of a deal, but what shakes my confidence is how they marketed discounted booster packs beforehand.
It actually doesn't take that much time to get to that point, though maybe that's a red flag in its own way. There's perhaps an understandable catch-22 with that situation. If the 3 card packs were easy to grind for, why the hell are they $30? If the 3 card packs were hard to get on the other hand, existing players just got burned.  As is, the issue is less about new accounts having an advantage, and more of the store having questionably expensive items.
But again, as long as you have realistic expectations for the F2P nature of multiplayer, the single player challenges are quite fun. Matchmaking for completely new accounts is also not a bad experience since you'll be matched with other newbies, but I hear that higher tiers begin to reveal the typical pains of any collectible games that allow grinding with time or paying for boosts.
