TL;DR: Pony Island is an unusual puzzle and gallery shooter game that's fairly meta, but not nearly as intelligent as it wants you to believe it is.
My experience with Pony Island was not very thrilling.  I was bored throughout most of it.  I spent the first hour or two trudging onwards, telling myself that all the cool stuff was going to start happening eventually, and I just had to wait it out.  Before long, though, I realized that that wasn't the case—that the repetitive pony shooter really was all there was to see here.  There's some ticket-collecting gimmick here for all of the virtual crack addicts, but not much of substance—nothing that really makes you laugh, or feel things, or stop and reflect, like a good indie game would, nor is there much of a challenge.  It's just kind of... a thing that you experience.
With that, I'm left wondering what the game's appeal was supposed to be.  It's not really funny—I think I laughed a sum total of once—it's not really witty, and the music doesn't do much for me.  The game is embellished with a few meta-heavy gimmicks and a narrative of "the game is possessed by an evil force that is being a jerk to you", but the bulk of the "gameplay" is split between a gallery shooter with a laser-shooting pony, and some "put the right item in the right place at the right time" puzzles.  With slight variations, you'll go through the same kinds of puzzles and shooter stages over and over, for bulk of the 3 hours of the game.  With regards to this, I think it fair for me to summarize the game as being a one-trick pony.  (Hah!  Get it?  My joke is almost as clever as the game itself.)
On the positive side of things, the game is competent.  Stylistically, in terms of graphics and sound, it nails the atmosphere that it's going for.  However, style doesn't cut it for me; I'm looking for subtance, and I found Pony Island lacking in that category.
Another positive: There
one boss "fight" that I thought was kind of neat, and some of the meta stuff happening there really took me off-guard.  But that's just 10-15 minutes of the game.  I spent the rest in boredom.
Lastly, the game is only $5.  This is a plus, because if it looks like the sort of thing that would appeal to you, despite my negative view of it, you're not putting a whole lot on the line to buy it and see for yourself.
In closing, there's a lot of hype surrounding this game right now, but I don't think that it's warranted.  Pony Island is simply a repetitive game with very little to say.  I think people lauding this game as an early contender for GotY 2016 are gravely mistaken, as I doubt that anyone will remember this game come the end of the year, much less 5 or 10 years from now, when an actual great game's legacy would still be vibrantly alive in its fans' minds.  There's just not anything really memorable or insightful here.
In short, I don't recommend spending your time on Pony Island.

I like to take little games and spend about one hour with them and then write a short review.  This is my first one!
Braveland is a cartoony little game where you (mostly) travel a linear path of battles with the option to make a few adjustments and changes to your playthrough depending on choices you make for your "squad" and "items".  You have a few basic stats, (Attack, Physical Defense, Magic Defense, maybe one more?) and there are a half dozen different types of little "squad" members you have  that act as units for your battles which take place on a hex-grid in a turn based format.
Braveland is an adorable little game, best suited for a quick few hours waiting at an airport or to let your son/daughter enjoy.  I would argue it's a good introduction to gaming for children, because it lacks the depth or complexity that can make most games like this frustrating.  Some see this as a reason not to recommend the game, and it could be, but it's also sometimes relaxing to do something completely mindless.
I wouldn't recommend buying the game at full price, you should be able to catch it on sale for $1-$2, or in some kind of indie bundle.

So, short review. I like this guitar learning tool. It's easily the best way to learn guitar because it gives the player incentives and puts the notes right there, on the screen and you play that note like it's Guitar Hero, only real. This game has several different modes too, it has a session mode where you can jam with a virtual band equip with any musical style you wish to jam with as well as having several minigames that help you hone different techniques. There's a game where you have to bend the string at a precise point, there's a game where it's like Space Invaders and you hit the notes on your guitar to shoot at the aliens coming down. Rocksmith's main feature is the song list it has and by itself. this song list does appeal to everyone, even the old rock fans, like myself. I got to play Don't Look Back by Boston or My Generation by The Who. It's got other songs that tackle different genres but I haven't really paid any attention to those. The game will adjust to your skill level and you can, now, manually adjust to the skill level you think you're ready for and the game will work with it. I highly recommend this to beginners and advanced players alike because Rocksmith 2014 is just plain fun and you can even get the DLC from the previous game so it's a win win. Don't get the previous game but this one because it improves everything from the old one. The old one felt clunky and didn't let you play at a skill level at your choosing. This one does. You can also play Bass on here so if you're a bass player, they got you covered.

Overall it's a great way to have some fun playing with a guitar, even if you have no prior experiences.  You will want to look into CDLC or else you might get bored with the limited selection.
Also, they don't really update these games aside from releasing more songs you can buy, so when you run into something that annoys you you're stuck with it until they make the next version of Rocksmith. Feels more like a console game than a PC game in that way.
EDIT: see comments for a link about RockSmith2014 Remastered edition. Sounds like they are giving us a 'core game' update.
But with that said there isnt really any competition making this the best of its kind. My only complaints are things like not enough minigames, not enough options for sorting songs and making playlists, and just some general interfacing issues.  The core gameplay itself is still really solid.

-Good Traffic (data) simulation
-Zone building (low/high resid, low/high com, ind and office)
-Scenario/Map Terraforming tools
-Regions (to manage individual parts of the city and apply different specializations, laws and economics into them)!

-

All in all, a true masterpiece, in it's current form i would give it a 9/10. Recomended!!!

My first week I was very into Cities:Skylines. But then I quickly realized this game is not a city sim or even city builder/designer game. No, its pure traffic sim. You will lose yourself for hours trying to fix the idiotic AI that is Cities:Skylines traffic.
Drivers will only drive in the center lane near an exit ramp. This creates chaos. They will come to a dead stop with two other clear lanes but no one will drive in the other lanes. I'm convinced this is not by design, but a bug due to poor AI. Why have six lanes or a three lane highway if the sims are not going to utilize the lanes during heavy traffic. Also, a town of 50,000 is not going to have enough population or demand to clog up a 3 lane one way highway(total of six lanes), let alone the 2 connecting highways on my map, and then a third highway I built.
To add to this chaos, garbage collectors, cops, firemen, hearst drivers, etc, do not stay in their own area. They will abandon their area and go clog your highways while your citizens near the service home suffer. There is no AI to make them only stay in their area. Even if you have every area covered they will still go across your map.
The only challenge to this game is making an entire city with no traffic stops - nothing else is a challenge. Even with well executed roundabouts you're still going to have extreme highway challenges that all orginate from 1) too much traffic being spawned despite a low population, 2) poor AI because sims do not utilize highways correctly. At first, I found it fun to try and beat the traffic, until I realize I've spent hours on it, and have noticed the sims erratic, pointless driving. Its just poor AI. I'm sure there are other traffic sims that have proper AI, not that I even wanted a traffic sim, I was hoping for a city builder/designer. So, unless you want a frustrating traffic sim game, with a bity of city builder thrown in I would say only get this if its on sale. And do not bother with the overpriced DLC. If they fix the traffic AI, then it'd be a fun little game.
Also, another unrealistic aspect is you can follow a car, and in good traffic it will take this car days to reach its destination. In bad traffic it will take weeks... C'mon. Regardless, just a poor traffic sim game.

Been playing since November '15 so ignore the lack of hours on my record, it's closer to the 1000-1500 hour mark!
The game is very very good. While it starts off slowly, and you will be losing a lot of games to begin with especially if it's your first ever card game you will grow and grow as a player and start to unlock spirit orbs (pack of 5 cards) and start winning games very quickly all while being FREE TO PLAY, and it doesnt require you to buy orbs to be good, although there is the option of that too.
Not all of the great cards are Legendary or Epic; one of the best cards in the game is a common, there are plenty of Starter, Common or Rare cards which are very highly rated and can get you to the very top. Granted Legendaries are very good, but they tend to be more of a situational card than something which is insanely overpowered.
What sets this aside from other card games is that there is a chess board of such, you move around the board and the cards have a life, positioning is the most important part of the game. You can have a card which can destroy your opponents General in one hit, but if you can't reach them then its useless.
RNG is often a big part of card games, while there is some on here, it's limited. You start off with 5 cards in a hand and you get the chance to replace two straight away and then one from each turn onwards. If you know what you're looking for and which cards you need, it's likely you will encounter it for when you need it.
+ FREE TO PLAY
+ Most essential cards are lower rarity
+ Limited RNG
+ Legendary drop rate is ~1/4
+ More than just cards with a board to play on
+ Very easy to get gold
+ Six different factions to choose from, each with two generals which play as a different archtype
- Very Bad S-Rank system (a new one is in the works)
- Not as popular as other card games for now

Is this game fun? Well, that depends. Does your definition of ‘fun’ include dying 20 times in a row while you try to get past a room full of respawned mobs you’ve already cleared twice because the lack of instructions and unreadable map mean that you have to stumble around trying to retrace your steps by memory so you can get to the next zone? Are you a fan of games where the margin for error is 2 points, maybe, if you’re lucky and you remembered to check for a health pack hidden in the bushes, and if you didn't then there IS no margin for error? Do you ever wish that video games included more repetition, frustration, and staring at the screen while your avatar takes an extra 5 seconds to go through the unskippable ‘standing up’ animation after every single time you die? Do you love pain? If these experiences sound like something you would enjoy, then run - don’t walk - to your nearest Steam Card retailer, and buy Hyper Light Drifter before the summer sale ends.
All jokes aside, this is a beautiful game with a lovely soundtrack and a very unique way of telling its story. Outside of the main menu, there is no text in this game - just pictures, slideshows, animations, and of course the pixel-art world itself. Someone clearly put a lot of love into Hyper Light Drifter, and I would adore it if the combat wasn’t so bloody hard. If you’re the kind of person who likes challenging games, give this a try. If you’re just looking for a casual RPG with pretty graphics and and interesting plot, go buy something from Supergiant Games instead.

Having played the original "Rebuild" games extensively back in the golden days of flash gaming, I was pleasantly surprised to hear that a new one was coming out. I didn't expect too much, but Rebuild 3 improved upon all the aspects that made the originals what they were: addicting strategy games that you can really soak some time into.
I have genuinely enjoyed my time with Rebuild 3, and I do believe it was a worthwhile investment.

Rebuild 3: Gangs of Deadsville is a light-hearted zombie apocalypse game in which you find yourself starting off in a humble encampment. Your goal at first is quite simple - rebuild - but there are also other matters that require your attention. You'll find out soon enough that your beginning supplies are only going to last you a short time and that, in order to survive, you will need to send scavengers out into the city to bring back precious resources such as medicine, food, ammunition, and building materials. However, time does not idly wait (unless you play turn-based mode) and there are still more things to be done during the day. You will need to research various technologies to improve your people's lives as well as constructing new homes for them to live in. Of course, you will also need to provide buildings to boost their happiness such as bars and churches but this extends to things such as pets too. Eventually, you will find that your survivors begin anew and form relationships with one another ranging from enemy all the way to husband/wife.
So what are the qualities of the game that make it something everyone should try?
The campaign itself can be either fairly short or long depending on the difficulty, as well as how many of the side objectives you decide to pursue. The story itself is, for the most part, your standard zombie apocalypse drama. However, humour has been sprinkled generously throughout the writing in order to cast a slightly happier light on the situation. Many of the survivors also have their own stories which they reveal in bite-sized portions throughout the game after you've researched survivor management. These also come with the opportunity to select a new perk for your survivor which can include things such as Firearms Training, or being Stinky.
The graphics are a massive improvement over the previous two games, and quite interesting to look at although there is a little inconsistency between the faction leaders in terms of their graphical style. An example would be comparing Senator Davis to Farmer Bucket, although it should be noted that such a thing is negligible.
The sound effects are probably the weakest point of the game as there aren't very many of them at all. It doesn't detract too much from the experience, but it definitely would have been a boost to the atmosphere to have more sounds going on throughout the day.
The music of the game is fairly good and some of the tracks add to the atmosphere of the game quite nicely. It should be noted that there are several 'ambience' tracks which play in addition to the main ones which is an interesting design choice. However, it does pad out the time between each of the tracks playing so that the music doesn't become annoying too quickly. Overall, the music fits very well with the light-hearted atmosphere of the game.
Overall, Rebuild 3 is a great game and one that I would recommend to anyone looking for a light-hearted strategy game snack. The game is interesting enough that you will get a fair amount of playtime out of it, and it is one that you will find yourself coming back to every so often.

A surprisingly decent zombie game despite being ported from a phone app.
The game has all all the ingredients of a typical zombie game, survival, scavenging for items, research, crafting, building, survival, other factions of survivors, and obviously lots of zombies.
However unlike most zombie games where bands of people are struggling to even live, this game has one outlandish concept. You can actually reclaim an entire city, and form your own government with its own constitution on what your civilization represents. Despite this outlandish feature the game plays well with all the ingredients of a zombie game.
The game also has a decent story campaign for you to progress.
It isn't game of the year material, but it is a good game to buy if it is on discount and when you have nothing better to play.

Braveland is a fun little strategy RPG where you play a guy who's village was destroyed and he's out for revenge. You have a overhead map you move around on going from point to point. Each point either has an enemy, friendly, store, or treasure.
You can buy and find or buy gear to increase your attacks, and defenses. You will also earn specials that can be released after being hit so many times. Each special costs a different amount and can be pretty helpful at times. As you progress through the map you will come across friendlies who will join up with you. You'll get help from knights, archers, and healers for example.
When building a team for battles they give you a point system. Each unit stack costs a certain amount and your max points to use is 15. So for example farmers costs 2 points per stack and archers are 3. Then after leveling up your main character you will be allowed to recruit more people per unit stack. This way when you go into battle you would have like 15 farmers per stack, 10 archers per stack, and so on. Enemies may only take some damage or may wipe out a few people from the stack. After each battle you are given exp points and gold. Then if you lost people you get charged a certain amount to revive them.
I played the game on easy considering I have a ton of games to play and really want to clear out some backllog. It has a cool little story and was fun to play. I finished it in about 5 hours. Braveland is definitely worth playing.

My first week I was very into Cities:Skylines. But then I quickly realized this game is not a city sim or even city builder/designer game. No, its pure traffic sim. You will lose yourself for hours trying to fix the idiotic AI that is Cities:Skylines traffic.
Drivers will only drive in the center lane near an exit ramp. This creates chaos. They will come to a dead stop with two other clear lanes but no one will drive in the other lanes. I'm convinced this is not by design, but a bug due to poor AI. Why have six lanes or a three lane highway if the sims are not going to utilize the lanes during heavy traffic. Also, a town of 50,000 is not going to have enough population or demand to clog up a 3 lane one way highway(total of six lanes), let alone the 2 connecting highways on my map, and then a third highway I built.
To add to this chaos, garbage collectors, cops, firemen, hearst drivers, etc, do not stay in their own area. They will abandon their area and go clog your highways while your citizens near the service home suffer. There is no AI to make them only stay in their area. Even if you have every area covered they will still go across your map.
The only challenge to this game is making an entire city with no traffic stops - nothing else is a challenge. Even with well executed roundabouts you're still going to have extreme highway challenges that all orginate from 1) too much traffic being spawned despite a low population, 2) poor AI because sims do not utilize highways correctly. At first, I found it fun to try and beat the traffic, until I realize I've spent hours on it, and have noticed the sims erratic, pointless driving. Its just poor AI. I'm sure there are other traffic sims that have proper AI, not that I even wanted a traffic sim, I was hoping for a city builder/designer. So, unless you want a frustrating traffic sim game, with a bity of city builder thrown in I would say only get this if its on sale. And do not bother with the overpriced DLC. If they fix the traffic AI, then it'd be a fun little game.
Also, another unrealistic aspect is you can follow a car, and in good traffic it will take this car days to reach its destination. In bad traffic it will take weeks... C'mon. Regardless, just a poor traffic sim game.

This game is absolutely great. It has an active community, an engaged dev team that talks to the playerbase, fun gameplay and a reasonable level of graphics. Jetcat Games have made me reminisce about playing Army Men: Air Attack, which I never thought would happen again.
The game plays fairly similarly to the likes of War Thunder and the Wargaming series of titles (World of Tanks, World of Warships), in which you have to earn XP to unlock new helicopters and different weapon loadouts, but unlike F2P titles, the progression is much faster. As of 8 hours playtime, I have done about 1/2-2/3 of the US tech tree and 1/4-1/3 of the Soviet tech tree.
While the game is more arcade than sim, it doesn't detract from the experience. It more allows you to jump in, play a few rounds and have fun, then jump off. Which is great for people who are time limited. It allows for new players to get to grips with how the game mechanics work, such as flying, shooting, and the objective system.
The only downside is the lack of a proper tutorial, which can lead people to feeling like the game isn't accessible enough. But if you look around on Youtube or Twitch, there is plenty of good information to help guide your experience in learning how to play the game.
Overall, the game is worth it, if you want a fun, action packed game of flying helicopters. Bonus style points if you have appropriate music playing in the background.

For Honor is the opposite of what it name suggests. The more you level up and the more competetive the game becomes, the worse the fights get. I've seen low levels do logical, expected combos to strike resulting in a duel filled with epic action and eye candy. Then you meet a Prestige 10 guy and all he does is Guard Break the entire game. For Honor had a huge potential to be an original, popular game of medieval combat. But its lack of balance and its corrupted community has ruined the beautifully planned IP.

The amount of negativity and blatant untruths surrounding this game baffles me. I see reviews ragging on the balancing, complaining about server issue being WORSE than launch, and general frustration regarding the combat aspects of the game and Ubisoft's practices. It seems to me that people are still caught up in and frustrated by this games admittantly shaky launch, and are now taking all forms of negative cirticism, regardless of its factual basis, as gospel.
So, instead of just telling you "ignore all the hate, the game is great (which it is)", I'm going to go through every bit of criticism I've seen and can think of, and categorize them based on whether they're true or not, in hopes of giving the potential consumer an HONEST briefing on the state of the game.  So, without further ado:
-

This is unfortunately true. You get precious little for each match you complete in most modes, and emotes and executions are on the pricier side steel-wise. However, there are orders which give you a fair amount of currency on completion, and they tend to be very simple tasks you can knock out in half an hour to an hour of play, though it will still take a solid week of doing these orders to save up to get most of what you want.
-

Competitive games are a growing vat for toxic players, and For Honor is not free of negative behavior. For the most part, For Honor has an O.K community. However, don't be surprised when you come across a very salty or arrogant individual in your time playing. Even still, it's nowhere near as toxic as Overwatch or CS:GO's "communities". It's tolerable, but not even close to pristine, and you'll typically find that most forms of toxicity are minor, like "Wow!" spamming.
-
Yes, the matchmaking leans strongly to the bad side of this game, and is one of For Honor's greatest downfalls in my honest opinion. Low level players will be paired with people far higher in rep and game time than them, and higher level players will in turn be put into games where they easily stomp because of that. You'll often be put in the same match with the same people, too, which can be very frustrating when you left due to laggy-players or salt-lords.
-

This is true in some respects. There's still a bit of wonk to the connections and P2P systems, but it has VASTLY improved since the open-beta/launch. Tele-hits and other gameplay issues caused by the lack of stability have become far scarcer these days. Matches drop a lot less frequently in most modes, and the connection is generally better. This next season, dedicated servers are being added as well, so the P2P issues will become non-existent this coming month.
-
This is true in part. Certain bits of terrain can make hitboxes a little bit off, and certain characters have hitboxes that aren't large enough. Kensei, for example, will consistantly miss his left hyper-armored swing when trying to OOS punish most characters. You CAN hit with this when your opponant is falling, but swinging while their falling makes him miss for whatever reason. There are other instances similar to this, but most have been patched or are too minor/specific, to be an issue.
-
Not by any stretch of the mile. No character in my eyes is truly insurmountable due to being blatantly overpowered. You will see a lot of people who will adamantly complain about characters like Peace Keaper and Centurion (who has been nerfed severely), even though investing enough time into learning the combos and patterns a player tends to use and getting better at parry their attacks can make fighting them generally simple. The only form of unbalance in this game is slight underpowering. I feel that certain characters, like Raider and Valkyrie, are in need of better mix-ups and tighter recovery times. But other than that, balancing is sound.
-
This, out of all of the other false information I've seen, is the one that frustrates me the most. It pushes people away from this game more than anything else, and I see it being said everywhere. For Honor is not dead. Not by any stretch. Playing the modes I frequent, 1v1 and 2v2, I have no issue finding a match. In fact, I've found this game to be incredibly quick in pace for finding games. Some modes, Skirmish in particular, you'll have to wait a bit longer. But the game itself is not dead. The playerbase is strong enough in my eyes, considering it's able to knock out PC community events in a day and half. The steam community is small, yes, but that is only a small chunk of the whole, and I implore you to NOT factor in the criticism of this game being "dead" when you try to decide whether or not to purchase this game, because it easily one of the most untruthful statements I've seen about this title.
-
One of the top reviews on Steam says something along these lines, and frankly it isn't true. The developers are actively balancing, fixing, and adding content to this game at a fairly solid pace. Yes, seasons can be a little bit lengthy, and  big content patches that include heroes and maps may be a little sparse, but the devs don't disappoint in what they bring to the table when the time comes. They are working on this game steadily, and a LOT of the bugs that plagued this game are fixed. Flickering is incredibly rare now, GB feints I haven't seen, light feints are gone, and a ton of other issues have been patched since launch. Invevitably, there are things that are still awry, tracking being one of them, but it's being fixed, and people should keep that in mind.
-
Though this critique is far less frequent, many stray away from Ubisoft games just because they're Ubisoft games. Ubi hasn't made this game terrible. Their business practices haven't been too intrusive, nor has their application. Though I don't particularly like Uplay, it doesn't ruin this game, and you shouldn't worry about it being here. It's really only there for a second at boot, and then as the overlay/friends playing. Nothing else. You don't have to weave your way through menus and cry out to tech-support or the forums just enjoy the game.
-
Ick. I don't even know where this stems from, if I'm being honest, because the game isn't even remotely pay to win. For the sake of the review, I'll assume that it's the Gear Stats/armor/feats. Gear stats aren't an issue. They affect only dominion and skirmishes. They're irrelevent in the other modes, and their effect on the modes they to take part in are unremarkable at most. The amount of stats they increase compared to what they decrease make them balanced enough, though at one point you could become a little OP (talking about revenge builds, which now cease to exist for the most part). If you're good enough at parrying, dodging, and predicting your enemies attacks, you'll still win your fight, gear stats or no.
Feats are either granted organically through levelling, or bought for steel, and only affect dominion/skirmish modes. The buying them with steel part is erksome to many, and I understand. It's a little bit shady, and I'm not going to rocket to Ubi's side and insist it's a great decision, but you should keep in mind that you earn your feats swiftly, and you get feats to start with anyways. You're not left with nothing if you haven't leveled to get them or purchased them.
I hope my thoughts and information has helped guide you in the right path when considering this game. There are things I might add or tweak, and I'm sure there are many typoes, but I still believe I've conveyed what I needed. Thanks for enduring my ramblings.

The game is very very good. While it starts off slowly, and you will be losing a lot of games to begin with especially if it's your first ever card game you will grow and grow as a player and start to unlock spirit orbs (pack of 5 cards) and start winning games very quickly all while being FREE TO PLAY, and it doesnt require you to buy orbs to be good, although there is the option of that too.
Not all of the great cards are Legendary or Epic; one of the best cards in the game is a common, there are plenty of Starter, Common or Rare cards which are very highly rated and can get you to the very top. Granted Legendaries are very good, but they tend to be more of a situational card than something which is insanely overpowered.
What sets this aside from other card games is that there is a chess board of such, you move around the board and the cards have a life, positioning is the most important part of the game. You can have a card which can destroy your opponents General in one hit, but if you can't reach them then its useless.
RNG is often a big part of card games, while there is some on here, it's limited. You start off with 5 cards in a hand and you get the chance to replace two straight away and then one from each turn onwards. If you know what you're looking for and which cards you need, it's likely you will encounter it for when you need it.
+ FREE TO PLAY
+ Most essential cards are lower rarity
+ Limited RNG
+ Legendary drop rate is ~1/4
+ More than just cards with a board to play on
+ Very easy to get gold
+ Six different factions to choose from, each with two generals which play as a different archtype

I've been playing this game pretty steadily since mid-February of this year, and there are things I really like, and things I really don't like about it. Rocksmith gets you playing, and it has a lot of good technique games to make learning fun. And the Riff Repeater is basically ♥♥♥♥ing magic. But ultimately, its strength is also its weakness; the game format encourages rapid improvement at the expense of proper technique. This isn't an explicit thing, but rather a side effect of the edutainment approach. Naturally, one would want to improve their mastery score, or go for high scores in the Guitarcade games. But since the game is very forgiving about note inputs and only cares about the input frequency, it's easy for a player to develop bad habits and techniques that become obstacles as they become more advanced players. You can nail a song at 110% mastery, but if you play with the backing track off, you may notice that your technique may not sound as good as you thought. The game has some basic technique videos, but again, they don't actually go into any sort of detail or explain any kind of nuance. As a result, one can easily fill in the blanks with improper technique and develop bad habits that they would need to unlearn.
Another thing I don't like is that it doesn't go far enough into the theory concepts. I like that it focuses on scales and modes so strongly, but it doesn't go far enough in my opinion. It doesn't explain anything about intervals, how the scales are created from them, how the modes are formed from the different keys, or any of that fun theory stuff. And it completely falls flat (har har) when it comes to chords. I appreciate that it shows the chord names in-game, but it doesn't even go into how the chords are constructed? Seems like a pretty glaring omission to me. Like, why is this set of notes called G#Maj7(add9)? Ultimately, I have to echo a statement I read about the game elsewhere: it gets you playing guitar, but it doesn't really make you a better musician (although I will say that session mode and practicing scales is a great start).
Don't get me wrong--I love the game to death. Got me playing my bass again after all these years. But Rocksmith shouldn't be your only learning tool; you need to go beyond the game and seek out technique videos or one-on-one instruction if you really want to get your playing to the next level.

While it breaks no ground, and this is nowhere near a commercial quality release, with a bit more polish (16-bit sprites, better overall resolution, better character portrait that matches trading cards instead of the 8-bit sprite-look, better interface)  this can be a proper shareware style title with a free or deeply discounted first episode and paid multiple episodes or subscription.

I honestly can't understand the praise this game has.
I loved Crysis because it was unique. You had to plan out your situation with binoculars from a safe distance, make sure you tagged EVERYONE, and use a combination of stealth and skill to either quitely move through, or silently kill the enemies in a given area.
Let me start with the gameplay.
The visor doesn't really serve its' purpose anymore, since enemies now spawn in during gameplay, so even if you've tagged all the enemies, some might spawn in later that you would have had no way to account for (with the few exceptions of dropship reinforcements).
For those of you familiar with the orginial Crysis, the suit modes have totally changed:
Maximum armor is now its' own mode, and is no longer the default mode. This is one of the few things I liked about this game, as armor mode actually feels like it's own mode now.
Cloaking in-front of an enemy actually causes them to lose track of you, however your window of opportunity when an enemy is looking at you while cloaked has decreased to the point of being near-negligable.
Maximum strength doesn't exist: It's a passive ability, as you jump high by default.
I found the stealth kills to be a nice addition, but since you can't stealth kill someone while they are facing you, using the stealth kill abillity is inherintely risky, as the enemy could just turn around at any moment, and with the aforementioned nerf in the cloak, that enemy will IMMEDIATELY see you.
Power kicks are also fun. While I find it's usage very limited, kicking a car into a group of enemies is one of the more satisfying things that I've done in a game in a while.
In a nutshell, the gameplay has totally converted from planning your moves step-by-step, making sure you tag everyone, and making sure that you keep track of everyone to not get overwhelmed by enemies, to a far more AAA FPS style of combat-oriented shooting.
Also, before I move on, it would probably be worth mentioning that the nanovision seems pretty worthless, and I haven't touched the nano-upgrades yet, since I'd like to see what they all do before spending my nanocatalyst, as you aren't given a description when you have insufficient funds.
Now, for the story (SPOILERS).
The story is basically, plot holes the video game. It's never explained how Prophet managed to get your suit on, given it's a piece of technology that you can't take off all that easily, and is kind of engineered to bind with your tissue, as we see in the intro cutscene to the original Crysis game. It's never explained what happened to your character from the original Crysis, it's never explained why the suits capabilities (i.e. gameplay mechanics) changed. I mean, there are so many questions, I'm more confused by how anything got anywhere than I am on some of the missions.
Conclusion
If Crytek just kept with the original gameplay, and added the little abilities that they added in this game, it would be a perfect continuation of the series. That being said, between the shift from a stealth FPS game to a AAA FPS, to the story that has more plot holes than a bad Hollywood movie, it's just a really bad game that isn't worth the money, and Crytek should really be ashamed of themselves for taking what could have been a great series, with a great launch title, and just throwing all the good stuff away to jump on the AAA bandwagon.

Thomas Was Alone is a relaxing little puzzle game. The main story will probably take no more than two hours, if that. Of course, bonus challenges could last one a lot longer, if one finds enjoyment in the gameplay.

One thing, Combat fluidity.   RE games are supposed to make you feel restricted in movement. It is what makes them hard. Player satisfaction is high when achieving that awesome melee attack after stunning your enemy or counterattacking(bloodshots am I right??? :)  I hope they continue to improve on responsiveness when executing certain actions.
RE6 is not really big on the horror. There are points when you may feel some urgency to get things perfectly executed but no beads of sweat should be dripping.  Not too many jumpscares.  Jumpscares are really only good the first time around then you can anticipate them,   If you want some RE style jumpscares I recommend RE4(for similar mechanics) , or RE2.
One thing I didnt like was the QTEs.   CAPCOM decided to go nuts on Leon's campaign with it,  Im glad the other campaigns had very little.   Sometimes you just want to sit back and enjoy some story but not be immersed into a sudden button press that you will miss and die from.
2013 graphics compared to 2015 graphics....  They are okay, but what if they waited to release it for the XBOX 1 and PS4?  It would have been beautiful.   Witcher 3 has set the bar high for my tastes.

This game is a strange mix of runner-style platforming and puzzles, with elements of glitch horror, satanic themes, and some undertones of the difficulties of game development, including self-doubt and criticism from the public.
You're trapped in the Devil's own game, "Pony Island", and find that it's a barely-functioning purgatory that you have to fix, and further break, in order to escape with your soul intact. Plenty of twists and turns in a fun, compact, game that's easy on the wallet.
Absolutely recommended, play it before watching any LP's or extensive reviews.
Pros:
+ Really cool concept and great execution.
+ Genuinely creepy moments, a very fresh take on horror.
+ Puzzles get progressively more challenging, and feel great when you complete the trickier ones.
+ Only $5.
Debatables:
+/- Short, at about 2 hours long.
+/- Ponies may be offputting to some, but as the trailer says, it's not really about the pony.
+/- Offensive to religious people? Maybe? I dunno.
Cons:
- You'll probably only play through it once or twice.
- Some sound effects are a little irritating.

game is a converted and updated flashgame.  DOES NOT PLAY LIKE ONE!
there's a lot of stigma around mobile games, flash games, console games... and sometimes, SOMETIMES, there's games that surpass and challenge those stigmas.  this is one of them, so don't let the game's development history alter your opinion.
first off, the game offers a robust campaign mode, with solid gameplay if you like strategy games.  music is decent and art is quite good.  upgrading and equipping your town's members is rewarding as is expanding the town and researching new tech.  game's canpaign storyline is quite good too, and gets pretty fun at more than a few points which makes for a strong incentive to keep playing through.
couple negatives:
campaign missions can be repetitive.  some repeatedly require you to "ally or eliminate Xnumber of factions," and often there is no way to do so other than to take their land piece by piece or grind up their reputation.  some missions offer you ways to ally/eliminate factions through mission choices, and i only wish that this was more prevalent through the scenarios.
it can be hard to determine your city's border at times due to the art of the wall of your city.  this is "fixed" later on though as you unlock better wall types.  i just wish there was some sort of color overlay that showed boundaries better.
overall the negatives are small compared to the gameplay value inside.  recommend picking it up for any strategy/sim/management game lovers, and picking it up on sale for other genre lovers.

So, after alot of time and hours sunked into the game, i feel like i can finally make a review.
Let's get the big one out of the way first, p2p connection.
yes, it's♥♥♥♥♥♥ and horrible ad what not, but it's mainly in dominon. in duel and brawl you will have the occasional disconnect, but that's mainly because the other player, or yourself had very poor internet. in duels, i never get any disconnects, and it's alot of fun.
Gameplay
the fighting mechanics of the game is amazing, played it first in the open beta and fell absoloutely in love. the many moves you can do, the counters, the mind games that can be played are awesome. granted there are a few moves that can be considered "bs" but, it's a much greater achievement if you overcome it.
Bugs/Glitches
i've had a few glitches and bugs, none gamebreaking or anything. some of them are fun, such as conqs body flying off into the heavens if you don't execute him. i've had a few black screens and one or two crashes. overall i have a great time playing.
Story mode
Story mode is a glorified toturial, tho i'm glad they put in some effort in order to make some sense of the world. the story is short, yet it's a good training tool. i'd reccoment playing on hard first and then realistic later to learn the mechanics, based on indicators and animations.
The skill.
Now some people might disagree with me here, but i feel like the game is heavily skill based. as i said there are some moves that are annoying, or quite fast, but everything is dodgeable, and what not, so everything has a counter. personally i don't feel cheated out of a match or anything, they're always intense and thrilling and almost every one of them is a hardfought victory.
The community
Yes, the community is very toxic. Combine overwatch and LOLs salt and toxicity and you have for honors. now while a lot of bad apples are out there, mainly in dominion, in duel most people are helpful, and nice.
Turtle meta/OP characters
The turtle meta is a proplem, and it is reflected in the game, however most turtles can be feinted out of their shell, or if your character has a sort of opener which is lovely. now getting into the op characters, which many consider to be pk, orochi and cent. pks lights are fast, sure, and her zone is ridiculous. however as you play you gain the skill enough to parry the lights and you know to block to the right. there will always be balance issues, since it's an issue in every competetive online game. once one proplem is fixed, another arises.
Summary
all in all, for honor is a good game, with some flaws, mainly being in 4v4 modes. if you play duel or brawl you'll have a great time.

-Really Big maps for one city
-No grid-based construction of roads, trains, etc.
-Good Traffic (data) simulation
-Zone building (low/high resid, low/high com, ind and office)
-Scenario/Map Terraforming tools
-Regions (to manage individual parts of the city and apply different specializations, laws and economics into them)!
-Rich map/city data of diverse type (traffic, polution, crime, fire stations, water and air info, etc.)

-

My first week I was very into Cities:Skylines. But then I quickly realized this game is not a city sim or even city builder/designer game. No, its pure traffic sim. You will lose yourself for hours trying to fix the idiotic AI that is Cities:Skylines traffic.
Drivers will only drive in the center lane near an exit ramp. This creates chaos. They will come to a dead stop with two other clear lanes but no one will drive in the other lanes. I'm convinced this is not by design, but a bug due to poor AI. Why have six lanes or a three lane highway if the sims are not going to utilize the lanes during heavy traffic. Also, a town of 50,000 is not going to have enough population or demand to clog up a 3 lane one way highway(total of six lanes), let alone the 2 connecting highways on my map, and then a third highway I built.
To add to this chaos, garbage collectors, cops, firemen, hearst drivers, etc, do not stay in their own area. They will abandon their area and go clog your highways while your citizens near the service home suffer. There is no AI to make them only stay in their area. Even if you have every area covered they will still go across your map.
The only challenge to this game is making an entire city with no traffic stops - nothing else is a challenge. Even with well executed roundabouts you're still going to have extreme highway challenges that all orginate from 1) too much traffic being spawned despite a low population, 2) poor AI because sims do not utilize highways correctly. At first, I found it fun to try and beat the traffic, until I realize I've spent hours on it, and have noticed the sims erratic, pointless driving. Its just poor AI. I'm sure there are other traffic sims that have proper AI, not that I even wanted a traffic sim, I was hoping for a city builder/designer. So, unless you want a frustrating traffic sim game, with a bity of city builder thrown in I would say only get this if its on sale. And do not bother with the overpriced DLC. If they fix the traffic AI, then it'd be a fun little game.
Also, another unrealistic aspect is you can follow a car, and in good traffic it will take this car days to reach its destination. In bad traffic it will take weeks... C'mon. Regardless, just a poor traffic sim game.

Another "too deep 4 u" game where nobody talks. They communicate instead with vague pictures. So in other words, you'll be completely lost at what you're doing until you look up a walkthrough online. Story, objectives, and buying items from the shops are all impossible to discern. Why can't they just use words to tell you how to play the game? Because that's just par for the course for pixel sh*t. They have to complicate it and make sure you know how pretentious their game is, at the expense of YOU, the customer.
They could have still had a decent story and dialogue and retained the atmosphere of the game without resorting to this style of conveying information. It's confusing from the very beginning: in the game there's four pathways out of the main city; which one you should tackle first is never explained so you just have to wander.
The controls are godawful. Shooting and dashing are controlled with the mouse instead of the keyboard. So point your mouse in the direction you want to shoot/dash, instead of just using the direction you're facing (I imagine if you're using a controller it would be the right analog stick instead of a mouse). Why? Who knows. Also the game has a really nasty habit of making you progress through obstacle courses with large moving blocks that kill you in 1 hit. It's so annoying make it through multiple rooms, only to get smashed by a block and lose over 10 minutes of progress. If the developers were going for a Zelda sort of style of play here, they've failed because there's nothing Zelda-esque about needing pixel-perfect skills to dash through the blocks. Exploring shouldn't be a chore.
This is honestly my biggest gripe with the game are those godforesaken f*cking blocks. Who thought dodging blocks and memorizing their patterns--with the threat of insta-kill--would be a challenge instead of just straight up frustrating and tedious? This game just has complete lack of polish. The exploration is also pretty boring, sure the areas look nice, and they have a good atmosphere, but there's nothing cool to discover or look at, just huge waves of enemies to kill. I know the devs were looking to make the exploration Zelda-like but that involved the collection of different items, visiting villages, and obstacles more complicated than pits. This game just doesn't have that, so the exploration falls flat.
The combat is at least fun, it's simplistic but you can upgrade your gun and sword and you can buy bombs. I wish I could explain if the story is any good but I honestly don't know what it is or what my objective is. I'd give this game a pass overall, the concept was really nice--Zelda-style exploration with Diablo-style waves of enemies--but nothing was done to fuse these seamlessly, and all you're really ever doing is looking for the next wave of enemies to fight.

I played the original on the PSX. It was great for it's day. It still is. My issue with the game is more technical though.
First: This is a PSX to DOS port. The game literally starts it's own DOS prompt (using DOSbox) and launches. It does not run natively within windows. It's not a deal breaker, just annoying. In order to get the game into full screen or change any settings concerning graphics, input mapping, ect.... you have to alt+tab out of the game and get into DOSbox, change the settings you like, and then continue.
Second: DOSbox does not correctly recognize joysticks or controllers. I've been using my PS3 Sixaxis controller for playing many games. Almost all PC games I've played work just fine with the controller. Not so much with this game. In fact, only 4 buttons on my controller work.
Lastly: (And this is very important) There is no clear way that I have found to change the keyboard mapping. "WASD" can be set to move your character around, but you have to use buttons for the camera too! There is no mouse support for this game. (It runs in DOS) Which leaves you fumbling around just to make simple jumps. I never made it as far as any combat, though I'm sure that would have been a real pain in the rear.
To conclude: Skip this one. I got it as part of a bundle, so I don't feel too bad for grabbing it. But seriously, skip it. Find it elsewhere. Find a better port. Pull out that old grey PlayStation sitting in your closet and scrounge EBay for an origional disc. Just whatever you do, do not willingly buy this game.

A nice little point-and-click adventure, or the first episode of it anyway. While it isn't anything groundbreaking either in story, writing or character design, it isn't bad at any of those either.
1. Writing is decent to good, with some endearing humour and enough detail to line out the characters. Hopefully subsequent episodes will build on that and build good, well-defined and multi-dimensional characters on this foundation.
2. The story is good, some tiny twists and turns... I like that the background music forshadows the events to unfold. Subtle, but good.
3. Characters have a good foundation, but no depth so far. That is to be expected from such a very short game.
4. The sound design is a tad bit lacking in quantity, but what is there fits the game very well.
5. Mechanically the game is very well done, for the most part. This, fortunately, isn't one of those pixel-hunting adventures - all interactables are pretty easy to find and interact with. The mouse controls seem to be a bit weird, don't really know why, but they feel slightly choppy and imprecise. Also, the game starts in windowed mode for whatever reason. Due to the nature of the game, this are just tiny annoyances, but would be nice to see them disappear in future episodes/complete release.
6. The "puzzle" part of the game is shallow, but enjoyable. Most things are really easy to figure out, so far nothing to really strech your braincells. Simple but effective... it might be boring for veterans of this genre, but for relative newcommers like me, it was good enough.
All in all, a good game, well-worth the price. I sure hope the follow-up episodes will be this good, or better as well.

TL:DR; This game is awesome.
Alright so writing this review at 13 hours playtime, about 50/50 co-op/solo.
Do you want a semi-arcade vehicle combat game with interesting mechanics than isn’t an F2P grindfest? If yes, then Heliborne is worth a look.
THE GOOD
There’s a lot to like about this game. The map design is good. The whirlybird choice is good. The soundtrack -while a bit generic- fits the mood. Graphics won’t be winning any awards these days but they’re not terrible by any means.
The flight model, IMO, is spot on. It’s a great blend of arcade vs. realistic. Choppers drift and react to yaw, pitch, and roll in a realistic fashion. At low speeds they’re not nimble. They're sitting ducks that take a bit of coxing to get moving. You won't be playing the "peek from cover" game in Heliborne. You have to think ahead a bit, plan your maneuvers and approach. The different choppers perform differently, so you have to learn a bit how to use each one. Default “simple” controls with the KB/M are fairly intuitive and easy to pick up. It might be a little complicated for someone very unfamiliar with helicopter controls (for example, pitch forward to accelerate) but the game even has basic WSAD control for the complete rookie.
Kick it over to Advanced Controls and use a HOTAS, and the brilliance of the simucade flight model really shines through. It takes some time to get comfortable with, but my enjoyment of this game has increased 10 fold learning how to independently control the collective and cyclic. The lighter, nimble helis really shine with it. If you don’t want to use a HOTAS, you can still play it simple mode using a KBM no problem. I find both have their advantages.
Co-op play is a lot of fun. Game settings provide a variety of options to tweak the match to your preferences. Get 4 people in a game with multiple simultaneous objectives and team co-ordination is a must.
The different roles -scout, transport, and attack- are well defined and even the mundane “transport” role can be vitally important for deploying troopers, MANPADs, and RPGs to interfere with the opponent. Big twin-rotors are actually FUN to fly in this game.
Because this isn’t an F2P game, progression is fine. I’ve got about 15 hours and already unlocked most Gen I and Gen II helis, playing just co-op. You get enough points in one or two matches to actually do something with. So far the most expensive things to equip are the cool camo patterns. The different maps actually have different objectives and play differently. It’s not the same “capture these points” on every single map. Cool.
Very active devs. They respond to player feedback (hence why we even have a co-op mode).
So far DLC is exclusively limited to cosmetic items.
THE BAD
The interface needs a lot of work. It’s functional but unintuitive. Official documentation is also sorely lacking and hard to find. It took me 20 minutes to figure out how to host a co-op game and have a friend join. Most parts of the interface, to the squadron management, server list, aircraft hangar, etc. are all unintuitive.
There’s a few problems with some maps. The Tonkin map especially will see you blow up numerous times because you’ve flown outside the map boundaries (which are completely invisible) and have very little time to turn around before BOOM! This is made worse because some objectives can actually move outside these boundaries. Luckily the devs have acknowledged this as a problem and are planning on fixing it.
Other than that.. not much. For the cost this game is awesome.
CONCLUSION
If you’re looking for simucade game of a similar type to some of the F2P games out there, except without the massive grindfest and with devs who actually give a♥♥♥♥♥♥about their community, check out Heliborne. For the cost you can’t go wrong.

This "game" falls closer to a teaching program than entertainment.  Of course it has the major advantage of actually making you learn guitar, and can be a somewhat fun way to do it.  However it can also be frustrating at times.  First, the progression steps can seem too big.  At the beginning, I could play one note at a time ok, but suddenly it was throwing a bunch of successive 2-note chords at me instead of say 1 here and there, and I just couldn't do it without practicing a lot (with the repeater, slowed down).  I was expecting a much smoother learning curve where I could enjoy playing the songs, not constantly struggling so much.  Even after having gotten used to this, it means it's not as easy to keep motivated to practice regularly...
The game interface has been an annoyance for me.  It was poorly adapted to the PC: e.g. use O,P,9,0 instead of arrow keys, Esc doesn't always "go back", limited and awkward sorting of songs, etc.  It's just generally not very intuitive.  Another thing is the constant waiting on "transition screens".  So much unnecessary delays, things appearing one line at a time, 5 seconds wait here for no reason, oh look 2 more transition screens before you can do anything.  It's especially bad in the arcade games which sometimes last only a few seconds, you just want to restart right away but can't.  Even starting the game is painfully slow and you can't press anything to make it go.
There are bugs, especially in the Riff Repeater (reported, but likely ignored) and it doesn't look like there is any active development, apart from new songs (DLC) to purchase.  In multiplayer mode, somehow volume is unequal between guitars so using the mixer is needed.  Volume normalization is not perfect, songs from the original Rocksmith, when imported, have a different mix (song vs guitar) and you may need to use the mixer a lot switching between songs of different "sources".
All in all, I would recommend this "game" for people that want to spend time learning guitar in a more leisurly way than traditional lessons.  For me, it was a huge step up from just learning on my own.  One thing you won't learn with this game though is music theory (even basic).  It might be worth looking that up if you don't know it yet, though you can play without it.

Beautiful pixel art and stunning color schemes aside, this game is a giant mess. I read the info on the game and thought "Oh, no dialogue that sounds like an interesting approach" not knowing that there isn't a single line of text in the entirety of the game except the intro where it tells you how to check your HUD. Dropped into a game where nothing is explained, picking up random things and then given no explaination as to what they are for or what they do. This was a horrible approach. The controls using keyboard and mouse feel clunky and unfriendly for the user. Chaining together your dash (Which is essential to get to certain areas) is an unforgiving hell you're subjected to when using keyboard and mouse. To make feasible progress in the game one must find numerous hidden areas hinted to you by either little visual queues like marks on the floor or a little ring sound (not easily heard through the LOUD music) to collect these little golden ticket things to upgrade your abilities or life bar, or how much health packs you can carry. the game artificially adds hours of "play time" (DUBIOUS USE AT BEST) by forcing you to redo certain areas over and over to try and find the secret areas.
All said, the original concept of no dialogue seemed interesting in theory but the final execution of it seemed lazy, unintuitive keyboard and mouse controls makes the game hard to immerse yourself into as you are constantly fighting against the games poor controls to get the best out of it, dozens and dozens of secret areas might be an explorers dream, but the fact that they're required for game progression rather than being used to reward players who go the extra step is absurd and obnoxious. 2/10 just because the game is visually stunning.

Instead of focusing on what makes this game great, because that’s pretty much covered by the trailer and other reviews, this will mostly focus on what you should know before beginning to get the optimal experience.
While you are travelling, look around for little hidden paths and objects. If you aren’t aware you are supposed to pay attention to the subtle visual clues, you may (like me) have to spend time backtracking or traversing through an area multiple times- which can seem repetitive and boring. Especially look for marks on the ground near the edges of walls/trees that indicate openings and platforms that you might be able to reach by dashing.
Pay attention to the health system. This might solve itself if you follow my previous advice and find the health packs hidden around, but when I started the game I kinda missed how it worked and had to teleport home to heal a few times. You will generally do well if you use your health packs efficiently: only when your health is pretty low, don’t waste them for a few life points. Once I figured this out I had an excess of health packs and was able to focus on the awesomeness of the game.
Also be aware that the visionary and creator of this game has a heart condition, which inspired many of the themes throughout.
Why I loved this game: gorgeous visuals and music, smart combat system about balancing attacks and playing around the attack patterns of different enemies, understated but powerful storyline, and great unlockable late game content.
With these things in mind, I really doubt you could regret buying this game.

I'm writing my first review in a very long time because of how masterfully this game was designed.
Seriously, this game was a breath of fresh air that I haven't had from a game in what felt like forever. I'm by no means an expert on game design by any stretch of the imagination, but Hyper Light Drifter absolutely captivates me. The narrative, combat, and curious nature of the world that is strewn before you compliment each other in a wonderfully unique experience. The simple but unique aspects of this game are woven together to portray a narrative that, at least to this player, were reminiscient of other titles such as Journey, Dark Souls, and even Link to the Past.
The game is an experience. Below are two upstanding pros and a con of mine, short and sweet to keep spoilers at a minimum.
Pro) Combat.
The combat is akin to the perilous life-or-death nature of Dark Souls (although simplified for the top-down Zelda-esque nature), exemplifying the brutal, unforgiving world the Drifter finds themself. With limited tools, your own skill as a player will largely affect your traversal of the world.
Pro) Sense of discovery.
This game is crammed with more secrets than you can shake a stick at. Replayability is a given here, even I am still going strong. I highly advise the use of NO walkthroughs, at least for your first playthrough or two, just to come to appreciate the amount of meticulous craftmanship and beauty put into this aspect of the game. Hearkening back to my repeated Zelda example, this is where I feel the relationship is exemplified the strongest. I whole-heartedly felt as fulfilled searching for upgrades or secret passages or buttons (all the while, exploring a world with joyous eye-candy aplenty) in Hyper Light Drifter as I did playing Link to the Past or Minish Cap as a child. If you're a fan of that, this game will keep you entertained for ages (and have you crawling back for more.)
Con) Lack of Direction
Sometimes, the open nature of exploration is too overwhelming at first, and perhaps the learning curve could be too much for some players. I can recall several instances where slight frustration arose because I could not find "the last damn purple thingy" for a long stretch of time, effectively breaking the flow.
Ultimately though, the reward of finally succeeding was enough for me.
I honestly don't have much here. This was like pulling teeth for me, but I have to do my best to be fair and bring up at least one thing that may turn some players away.
9/10. I absolutely adore this game, and hope for more games to follow in it's footsteps.

I, on the other hand, recommend that you do not buy it. While the trailer and many positive reviews may make it seem like a great game, it has MANY flaws. Here are a few I've pointed out and explained:
-Sure, it may look nice in the trailers, but the color palette is all over the place and can be WAY too vibrant at times. Lots and lots of shaders and bloom are used to make the game look so much less bland and bare-bones than it actually is, which is good marketing but very misleading and can cause lots of angry reviews (*ahem*).
-It is much shorter than it seems. I beat 1/4th of the game in about an hour, meaning there's 4 hours of gameplay for a 20 dollar game. Sure, you could play it again, but there isn't any replayability or anything. Play it for 4 hours and leave it to rot in your Steam Library for the rest of eternity... totally worth 20 bucks.
-Most of the game is boring exploration, which is a huge downer with the awful bright colors in your face. There are many secrets that can be found while exploring, but searching for them can lead to you sacrificing health to dash off of a cliff, hoping there is a hidden platform to no avail.
-The music for the game is incredibly out of place at times, and will either be really quiet, or REALLY loud in your ears (headphone warning, no joke). I've only heard like 4 songs, by the way, and I know there are 28 total, so idk. The synth is nice sounding, but really boring music overall.
-Combat system is very poorly made. I don't know WHY people are comparing the combat in HLD to Dark Souls, as battles are not defined by skill (like in Dark Souls) but by ability to handle hordes of enemies all attacking you at the same time. The devs made the bad decision to make only a few different types of enemies, and instead of making harder enemies just putting lots of annoying, easy enemies in a small space. This is not fun, just tedious to overcome and proof of laziness. Oh, and you can get easily stunlocked... ♥♥♥♥ you.
-Hyper Light Drifter is really confusing. You get almost NO understanding of what is going on and why you are running around killing enemies. The game has no dialogue, and instead explains the story in pictures. This may sound creative and interesting, but it just makes the game confusing. The game breeds on this confusion by being an open world game, so half the time you don't even know if you are going in the right direction. Again, pictures only. Makes you wonder if there even IS a story.
I hope you take my advice and
.

Great game! It is always nice to go back to the classics and remember how all of this amazing series of games started. This is basicly what the whole game is about:
At a hotel in present day Calcutta, Lara Croft is approached by an American named Larson Conway, who works for the wealthy businesswoman Jacqueline Natla, owner of Natla Technologies. At Natla's request, Lara sets out on an expedition to recover a mysterious artefact called the Scion from the lost tomb of Qualopec, in the mountains of Peru. After successfully retrieving the object, she is attacked by Larson who attempts to claim it. She beats him then questions him, learning that the artefact she has is only a fragment and that a man named Pierre Dupont has been hired by Natla to collect the rest.
Lara breaks into Natla Technologies to find out Pierre's whereabouts. She discovers a medieval monk's journal, which reveals the depths of an ancient monastery of St. Francis in Greece to house the tomb of Tihocan, a ruler of Atlantis, along with a second piece of the Scion. Traveling to the monastery, Lara descends through an expansive underground complex, pursued and attacked throughout by Pierre Dupont. At the tomb of Tihocan, Lara recovers the second piece of the Scion and finally kills Pierre. An inscription inside the tomb states that Tihocan was "one of the two just rulers" of Atlantis.
When Lara joins the two pieces of the Scion, she receives a vision of the three Atlantean rulers and their respective pieces of the Scion. One of them utilises it to create a mutant breed, but the other two confront her, and take her piece of the Scion. Then Atlantis is struck by a fireball from the skies, and the three pieces of the Scion become scattered as the civilisation is destroyed. One of them goes to Egypt, Lara's next destination.
Lara travels to the City of Khamoon, a temple complex in Egypt that houses the final fragment. Here she battles the fierce mutants seen in her vision, and is once again confronted by Larson, this time in a battle to the death. She then takes the final piece of the Scion from the underground sanctuary. Upon leaving the tomb, she is ambushed by Natla and her henchmen, who steal the three artefacts and nearly kill her.
Having escaped, Lara stows away on their boat, which takes her to a remote island where mining operations of Natla Technologies have partially exposed the Great Pyramid of Atlantis. After making her way through the mines dispatching Natla's goons and the mutant-infested interior of Atlantis, Lara reaches the heart of the pyramid chamber, where the complete Scion has been fused together as a source of power. Touching it, Lara receives another vision, where Natla is revealed as the previously seen third ruler of Atlantis. She betrays her co-rulers by abusing the power of the Scion for genetic experimentation, and as punishment is locked in a stasis cell by Qualopec and Tihocan, her resting place until the prologue of the game.
Natla enters the chamber and confronts Lara; having reclaimed the artifacts, she attempts to restore her former power with an army of mutants. Lara attempts to shoot the scion, Natla tackles her through the observation window. "Thomas Was Alone" is an amazing experience in the form of a game. The music is beatiful, the graphics are simple yet captivating, the story is amazing. Oh, and Thomas, the 2D Rectangle, has more dimensions in his personality than many protagonists from AAA games. Seriously.

If anyone knows me or has read one of my reviews before, then you probably know that I am a sucker for great storytelling, and it's because of its storytelling that I can confidently claim that Thomas Was Alone is by far my favorite platformer of all time. After saying that I should mention that I don't play many platformers as it is, but still--this game is stellar.
The gameplay is about as basic as it gets. You control Thomas and other diversely shaped blocks you pick up along the way. Each block has their own name, personality and serves a specific function. None of these blocks are expendable. Not only because they're vital to many of the puzzles in the game, but because the narrator names them and tells their story when we meet them. It's mind-boggling to me, how Thomas Was Alone got me attached to a bunch of squares and rectangles. Each shape has their own little story to be told, and the narrator is more than willing to do the talking. It's adorable, really, as you hear the narrator talk of these shapes as if they're people with fleshed out personalities and quirks--exactly how you see them by the end of the game.
The plot of Thomas Was Alone is much more intricate than you may think. This game tells an interesting story that's driven by the characters (the shapes) and their curiosity. By the end of the game you will have grown attached to each of these characters and their mini story arcs. These shapes change, and it's not shown in anything but the dialogue of the narrator, and the steps the player takes to completing the game. There's not much else I can say as the game is so simplistic in nature. All I can do is urge you to Thomas Was Alone if you love a good story or you enjoy a solid platformer. Totally worth the cost.

This game. This game is what introduced me to the RE series. From the general reviews, MANY RE fan hate this game. They  said that it was a departure from the main series by a long shot, third person camera, duck and weave motions, clonky controls etc. There are many.
This game is not friendly when you boot and play it for the first time. Unskippable tutorial mission, instant death from QTEs (which some will appear without warning), mobs appearing to be bullet sponges, accidental action due to control overlap, odd camera angle adjustments etc. Some may hate this game because of it (heck many of the hardcore RE fans hate this game due to the above reasons above).
I had that feeling as well. "Why are I climbing a deck repeatedly, when I wanted to climb and then sprint?", as I thought when I died due to time running out trying to escape. However I thought "Hey, maybe instead of holding down the Space button (which is used for both sprinting and context action), why not I press it once I am far away from the prompt?" Guess what? It worked.
As I played it longer, all the above reasons were overlooked (though occasionally I still mess up the context actions). This game benefit more the longer you played it. You will know by then what will happen next, where to move, how to properly get rid of a mob etc, which will make the campaign mode less of a hassle.
In a brief overview of the campaign, it's divided into 4 parts, each are having their own backstory, atmosphere and mobs.  There is the classical campaign aka Leon's, RE 5-esque (or shall I call it, the COD bros campaign) of Chris, Jake's (or Sherry's, if you know who she is) campaign, which is a less actiony version of Chris's , and finally, the more stealth based campaign of none other than Ada Wong. Even though they ara their own campaign, in the end they overlapped which each other, with some part of the campaign even replayable on another campaign (e.g. Chris 2 with Sherry 1).
Control wise, it's not like the old RE that you know. You will get to sprint, duck, roll, strafe and slide, unlike the old RE controls, which is more limited to tank controls. Your default movement is a jogging based motion, so everything here is a bit faster paced. The cover system also returns here as well. You won't be using it much, maybe except for Chris's campaign (and to a much, much lesser extent, Sherry's). Item management wise is much simpler than RE 5 one, just press Delete if you want to remove them. However, you cannot contorl what weapon you will like to use. By default, you will wield them all.
QTEs make a return here as well (meh), though in an excessive manner. Granted you can make it automated, but this option will only appear once you have completed the game. But the biggest part of the prompt action comes in two ways:
a) Melees and c'oup de grace
b) Counters
Counter prompts appear for a brief period of time, but if you can get the timing down, you will receive 0 damage in total, in fact you may outright kill the attacker. Melee prompts appear during certain circumstances (headshots, few light melee blows) while c'oup de grace will appear when the enemies are stunned heavily (flash grenades especialy). If you can master this, the campaign will be a cakewalk, since you will be avoiding nearly all source of damages (except bullets and missiles, screw those).
After the campaign there are many other type of minigames you can play. Depending on whether you bought the DLC or not, by default, you get 3 modes:
a) A mode which is similar to L4D versus, where you invade other people's game as a monster.
b) Mercenaries make a return here from RE 5.
c) No Mercy as well.
Note that I won't cover the DLC modes, since I don't have them.
In my opinion, the true highlight of this game is not the campaign or the characters, but the Mercenaries mode. With the enhanced mobility, this mode is a must play mode of RE 6. Being surrounded by non-stop wave of enemies while keeping the time and combo counting is truly fun. No Mercy ramps it up by spawing even more mobs at you, Your whole screen will be covered by them.
Another additional highlight are the asses. There are section where you get to crawl as the female characters. My God, Ada's tight pants are to die for, though Sherry is overall the all rounded one. The trophy for the best booty, however have to go to Helena. Did I mention that all the pants the character are wearing are really, really tight? :3
Overall, I would really recommend this game. Some may not agree with me since I am a newcomer to the series, but to each their own. However, like fine wine, it will take a while for you to truly enjoy this game, since at the start, everything will always go south. Experience and memory of what will happen will help you on subsequent playthrough.

This game is an incredibly enjoyable Hearthstone-Like game.
It adds another layer of strategy as you place your minions on the battlefield and controle them. Your general is also Controllable.
There are different factions with some cards exclusive to their factions but there are also a big number of neutral cards.
In addition to regular daily quests like "play 4 games as Faction X", "Deal X damage in one game", "Kill X minions in one game" etc. It also offers a daily challenge, which is a scenario in which you have to defeat the enemy in one turn with the cards available to you. There are also a number of Challenges that serve as an "advanced" tutorial, teaching you some mechanics.
I found it rather easy to get the gold for Spirit orbs, which contain 5 cards each and at least one rare. But I also got a number of epics and just this morning(although that was big luck probably? 2 Legendaries in one Orb. Averaging out on about 4 legendaries in the roughly 20 orbs I opened so far.
Some epics will be awarded to you for the beginner quests and upgrading your faction ranks. Upgrading your faction will also award you some of the basic cards of that faction, as well as an additional Commander at level 10.
What I don't like is that there is the regular pvp mode is also the Ladder mode. This means if you want to try out a new deck you can only try it against the rather easy AI or risk your season ranking(I dont really mind but some people might).
It could use some more optimization options but so far Duelyst has been a blast to play.

So yea....lets look at Jazzpunk. I will do my reviews on a pro/ con style.
Pro:
