Hyper Light Drifter is an absolutely amazing game for anyone who wants a good challenge. I will go in depth with details down below.

-Art style
Simplistic yet effective. The game art is style is nothing too complex or very busy and difficult to see what exactly is going on. The colors are rich and vibrant and really captures the 16 bit look.

-Controls/Mechanics
My god, they are absolutely great. Dashing around the world feels very satisfying and the combat is excellent. It’s one of those cases where it is easy to pick up, yet difficult to master. Throughout the game, you will encounter large waves of enemies and having such tight controls really makes you strategize on what techniques for survival will work best. You will never die from the controls acting up on you or the game being completely unfair to you, it is always your fault and learning from those mistakes is makes dying a satisfying learning experience.
A complaint I have heard a lot about from HLD is the game’s map and how vague it is. Sure it may not be the best map in the world and at first glance you may not find it all that useful and also very confusing. The more you play the game You just have to give yourself some time to get used to it and the overworld shouldn’t be so difficult to navigate through.

-Soundtrack
It’s not really something that is catchy and you will want to listen to it every now and then, but it does an outstanding job creating the feel of being isolated and lost in its huge world. Disasterpiece’s work of art is truly a masterpiece.

-Plot
The way the plot is told is very debatable. Some will like it and some won’t. The plot is told in a way where it only uses still images and no dialogue to display what happened during those events and leaves the player to determine what happened. At first I wasn’t very fond of this style, but it eventually grew on me once I started to piece everything together. It will make more sense to you the more you progress through the game.

The Classic Tomb Raider games are a breed that have died out, for better or for worse. For that, Tomb Raider is a different kind of game than most others that has it's niche. The best points for a recommendation are the games enjoyable atmosphere and lack of direction. The environments are open with no true goal, which for many can kill the experience, however traveling around dangerous and precarious tombs in the search for the unknown can be very satifying to many. The controls are cumbersome and might cause for the game to be needless precise, but it could be rewarding once you really get a grasp on your environments and positioning.
The story sort of difficult to comprehend, not to mention awkwardly presented. Some of the characters are enjoyable (Particularly Lara) but they're mostly cartoonish in goofy ways. Combat is very basic and monotonous, I'd argue it's the least involving part of the game. This is not a direct port of the PS1 version, so you may want to look into mods if you want more music cues and the expansion pack that was released. If you're into quieter, slow-paced games, I'd recommend this, but if clunky-controls, dated graphics, (expected for the time) no direction, and subpar combat all sound like too many bad things to justify the time put in, then stay away.

I know its very late to post a review, but i think this game needs the attention. I will only be referencing the multiplayer aspect of the game because that is where i have spent the most time. Black Ops 3 at first was poorly optimized but over the past year the game has gotten a lot of love, and i think at this point it is one of the best PC ports for the CoD franchise. It has stunning visuals that leave the console versions of the game far away in the dust. The only thing this game is missing is a larger community that plays other game modes other than TDM(Seiously, its basically impossible to find anybody in Free For All or any other game mode).
Now, no game is perfect and BO3 definitely has its flaws. Some of the specialists characters like the Firebreak and Spectre are overused, and they award basically free kills to the user, which can feel unfair to others at times but there are ways around it. The melee weapons are definitely a nuisance. Why are there so many? Sure, they're nice to look at sometimes, but I'd prefer to get more useful weapons than melee weapons. The supply drop system is also an annoyance. Putting weapons behind a barrier and forcing players to grind or pay money to get a chance at the weapon is extremely unfair. I just want my darn FFAR, Treyarch.
Even though the game has flaws, ive enjoyed every minute that I've been playing it on PC. The game feels great and a lot of the maps are designed very well. Most of the weapons in the game are viable and each have their advantages and disadvantages, and the added weapons aren't overpowered either. Each of the specialist characters have interesting personalities, and its funny to hear them take jabs at each other throughout the game. There's also many challenges for the guns and specialist characters to keep you occupied.

Space Pilgrim Episode One: Alpha Centauri is a decently made, low budget, low price RPG Maker title.
It is Episode 1 of several episodes to be released one after the other, (Episode 1 consisting of three acts, which equaled about 1-1.5 hours play time for a single playthrough.)
The environments have an appealing look to them.
The ship is laid out fairly logically, and the mapping of the rooms did not annoy me.
Objectives are pretty straight forward and simple; more of manual playing than difficult puzzles.
There is not much back and forth walking, which is great. You can tell they tried to make the game engaging, and not a boring fetch quest repetitive game.
There is complete mouse support, which is great because there are also alot of things to interact with.
The inventory could really use some work, such as making item merging more highlighted during crafting, (I had to click guess my way through item customization first time, but it was easy after the initial guess work.)
There is a journal, which I found useful as a reference point, (noticed some lag switching between journal tabs.)
The music is immersive, with a nice Mass Effect type feeling, although slightly more retro sounding.
The writing is quite solid and humorous at times too, however there were a few spelling errors and points that made me think, "Now why would a character say/do that?"
I forsee the writing being just as good and better throughout the next episodes, and their future work.
The writing quality ties in with characters and character interaction; the characters are pretty cliched, but not in a bad way. You can have several conversations for minor character developement.
There are a few amusing one liners and situations the characters get themselves into.
I enjoyed the pacing of the story. A few times I found myself interested enough to be guessing what happens next, who is who, what looks suspicious and so on, which means I was engaged, contrary to my first assumptions about an RPG Maker style episodic game, which usually makes many people iffy to want to invest in.
All in all, I enjoyed my experience playing this first episode and was grinning as the game transitioned to the credits.
If I were to describe this, I would compare it to watching an episode of Firefly; the episode has its introduction, then problems arise, then the characters aim is to fix those problems or mysteries and it all interestingly unfolds infront of your eyes. By the end of the acts, and the episode, things are wrapped up, leaving you wondering what mysteries and problems will happen next episode.
Thanks for a decently designed, written and enjoyable game.

As Gail Pilgrim you embark on yet another voyage ferrying passengers through space: this time though what started as a milk run will soon become an unexpected and dangerous adventure.
The first episode of a planned tetralogy offers a decent story and simple puzzles in a short yet quite enjoyable adventure.
-decent story is, most of the time, quite cheerful but also sports some more serious twists
-there's a good amount of humor to be found and while most of it is pretty silly it's still decent enough to elicit a few chuckles
-while part of a series and finishing with a "to be continued" this chapter has a self-contained story with a proper ending
-the soundtrack is pretty nice and gives a good sci-fi vibe
-being part of a series means we won't have the full 10 hours story arc until all the chapters are released
-puzzles are quite easy, don't expect your brain to be challenged
-fully linear, short at about 1 hour to complete
-while decent the story won't win any awards for originality so far, the characters are effective in their roles but come out as pretty cliched
Space Pilgrim Episode One: Alpha Centauri was pretty good considering its price and low budget, while the story and characters aren't that original they're still good enough to keep the narrative going: the often present humor also adds a certain charm to the game and results in a few funny scenes.
The resulting game is quite basic in its plot and gameplay but still enjoyable if you're ok with this lighter fare: within its limitations it still does basically everything right with a tale featuring a few twists and puzzles requiring you to sometimes combine items together.

Right now it seems to be a stripped down uninspired reskin of Theme Hospital.
It's a nice idea, and there's definitely potential to build some interesting gameplay on what's there, but right now it doesn't have enough going on.  The interesting fantasy/medieval theme isn't really anything more than superficial - everything from the music, to the "inspections" (tavern inspectors with top hats and suits really clash with the setting), to the bank loans and worker pay rises just feels lifted from Theme Hospital without much thought.
There aren't a huge number of bugs, which is something.  But there's definitely some nonsensical stuff, and some really maddening design choices (like having to wait over a minute for an unskippable slow-motion performance of a man being hit by a turkey when you lose).
There's a lot of interesting things that the developer could do with the fantasy tavern setting.  For example, having external/random threats come and disrupt the tavern, and then being able to offer quests to visiting adventurers in order to fix/resolve them (for a price).  Thieves and drunks that need to be handled by security (who, too, could be hired adventurers).  I mean, just take a look at a tavern from an old school RPG - there are plenty of ideas to draw from.
Will keep an eye on the game and update review later on if things change.

I'd say I've given this game a good run for my money, and let me say, it's very good.
However, I do have some gripes about it, which I will get to momentarily. But, what did I like?
+ The game has amazing atmosphere and ambiance. The worldbuilding and story, though minimalistic at times, were very well put together, and I will forever praise this game for being gorgeous and having a fantastic backstory.
+ Combat feels tight and fun, especially boss fights. Some were frustrating, but in general, once you learn the patterns, they're all well designed and very rewarding to play through and defeat. Even combat with lesser enemies feels great, especially once you upgrade your sword and general arsenal.
+ Finding secrets feels fantastic, and you're oftentimes rewarded well for going out of your way to hunt them down. Rewards generally consist of some sort of tokens, with which you can upgrade and buy new abilities, which is always fun, as it makes the player feel like they're growing stronger.
Despite these, though, the game has issues.
- Some enemies are annoying or tedious to fight, and at times there are moments where the player might feel that a death was unfair or uncalled for. This issue in particular is emphasized in the Arena minigame in the endgame, where you can fight waves of enemies. These enemies can immediately attack you once they spawn in, adn considering many of their attacks death 2 "hearts" worth of damage, this can kill you instantly if you aren't expecting it. Additionally, enemies can knock you back, and around the area that you're fighting in, which may seem fun at first, but it can very easily lead to you getting accidentally knocked into a terrain hazard and instantly dying, or getting combo'd by other enemies.
- There are a LOT of ways for the player to immediately or near immediately die. I played in Standard mode, and there were still plenty of situations where I was getting killed near instantly, particularly in the Western forest area with the crystals.
- Chain Dashing. Oh my goodness Chain Dashing. This mechanic is something that I feel people sort of suck up and say is alright, when it's actually fairly tricky, and requires a rediculous amount of precision to pull off. This is made worse by the fact that many of the areas in which you must use Chain Dashing feature instant-death hazards or hazards that will respawn you at the start of the course, forcing you to struggle over and over again to get the timing of the dashes perfect, essentially forcing players to beat their heads against a wall until they break through. At the end of 15 hours, I hadn't mastered it, and I doubt I ever will.
Additionally, dashing in general is normally fairly responsive, but there are points where, if you don't chain dash, you'll stop dashing and take a second to "recharge" which is REALLY bad during combat if you're trying to avoid a large number of enemies or projectiles.
- Healing in the game takes a few seconds, during which you can be interrupted and killed. This feature, while making combat more tense, also means you oftentimes can't reliably heal in the thick of battle, which, in conjunction with dashing being an issue at times, frequently caused me to die.
Despite the issues, I'd still recommend the game (maybe try the easiest difficulty for a more relaxed experience). Just be aware that it may be frustrating at times.

Braveland is a casual strategy RPG which follows the incredibly standard plot of Dude's Village Is Pillaged -> Go Revenge It. I'm going to start off by saying that I played through the entire story campaign on Hard Mode; I recommend doing this because it feels like the best way to get a decent challenge out of this game.
Combat in the game takes place as turn-based tactical skirmishes on small hexagonal battlefields, with a particular emphasis on troops. That is to say, each character on the battlefield is actually made up of multiple people of the same class, with their stats stacking on top of each other. As these troops take damage and lose bodies, so too do their stats dwindle, similar to Advance Wars, and probably a lot of other games I haven't played because I am a huge scrub. This creates an interesting dynamic where it's not always the correct option to focus damage on one enemy troop at a time, but rather spread damage out enough to make enemy attacks feeble rather than fatal. Additionally, there's a long-term concern in the form of gold: You have to pay a penalty out of your gold reward at the end of combat to recover lost allies, and there's no way to grind for extra gold, so keeping losses to a minimum is paramount.
Progression is semi-linear. You go across a three-region map from skirmish to skirmish, picking up new allies and abilities along the way. There are short side paths to turn onto which end with treasure, stat upgrades, and shops to purchase additional units for troops as well as equipment to put on your main character — who inexplicably, despite being a warrior's son and built like such, doesn't have any actual presence in battle, instead preferring to radiate his stats onto his troops from the sidelines I guess. The early game can be pretty brutal due to the lack of troops and gold to enhance them with, though this gradually becomes less of an issue as income outpaces expenses. It isn't exactly clear how the stats on your main character affect your troops either, so to be honest I just didn't bother with equips until the best were available for purchase. Upgrading troops directly seems to be the best use of money anyhow — a massive clump of one-star Peasants can be surprisingly effective!
Graphically, the game is colorful and the environments are nice enough to look at, though the character models are a bit too reminiscent of a high school Flash animation for my taste. On the other hand, the music, while inoffensive, only consists of two tracks: The one used for travel and the one used for combat. Not even the final boss gets a different song, which I found quite disappointing.
Overall, Braveland was an enjoyable experience for a rather unassuming casual title. The campaign lasted around 4-5 hours for me to clear it 100%, which is a decent length for the $2 it tends to go for on sale. There's also a Survival mode where you just play battles and spend gold on upgrades in-between, which to be frank I didn't bother with too much.
Unfortunately, I've heard that the sequel, Braveland Wizard, adds the ability to grind for gold and apparently makes it feel necessary to do. Kind of ruins the need for strategic planning at that point.

The line between 'flash/casual game' and 'real game' is a blurred one, but Braveland clearly favors the first category.
Taking 'King's Bounty' style tactical combat and party-building, Braveland simplifies the formula to its most basic components, and then presents it in a simple, colorful, node-based design.
PROS
* Easy to pick-up, play for a couple minutes, and put down.
* Art style is simple, but appealing in its colorfulness
* Very stable, didn't notice any bugs or issues
*If you're looking for a palate cleanser between heavier fare, a mindless but well-presented time-killer, or an introduction to strategy games, this game is ideal.
NEUTRAL
* Very easy. Anyone with prior strategy experience ought be able to manage the hardest difficulty with no problems- in fact, even if you do suffer a lost battle, you suffer no penalties and get extra gold for your efforts.
* Very short. This game won't take you more than 5 hours for a full run-through, and you can likely manage it in 3 if you're motivated.
* There's a few 'wait till you're strong enough' side paths, but the game is essentially entirely linear.
* Minimal character building (just straight stat level-ups that end up not being overly significant) and swapping army formation is incredibly limited due to a mix of limited unit selection and limited army building points.
* Weird dialogue blurbs. This game has no story worth mentioning, but the developers did implement a basic plotline, with occasional npc dialogues. And each one of those comes across as an oddly mistranslated garble.
* By its very nature of being a casual stripped down version of meatier titles, the game doesn't offer anything new to the genre.
* Game has a survival mode that benefits from being able to offer characters from the subsequent games, but really doesn't offer much reason to play it past initial novelty.
CONS
* The interface is often clunky and underdeveloped, making things more of a hassle than it ought be [or than is usual for more modern games in the genre]. And sometimes trying to get info on a game component isn't near as simple a matter as it ought be.
* If you're looking for a strategy game of any depth, involvement, complexity, challenge, or a game with any story elements, this is not the game for you.
Summary:
If you go into this with the same mindset as playing a game of minesweeper, solitaire, etc, the game is quite enjoyable- and while it won't leave any lasting impression on you, it's a nice way to burn time when you've got no energy for anything too involved, or only have a few minutes to kill.
If you go into this with the mindset of a typical strategy gamer, you're going to be itching to use that steam refund option.
Casual Game perspective: 3.5/5
Strategy Game perspective: 2/5

All the sudden exploding zombies, giant-flying-zombie-mummy-whatever-the heck things and a massive supernaturally engineered torso zombie start attacking you and your puny guns are nearly useless. The shooting is frustrating because it is auto-aim only and the game completely lacks any stealth gameplay that I love. It is a fun time, but will test your self-control as it taunts you into self destruction.
Jump, jump, jump, and jump some more... Oh wait, not that far.... Ha, too short... Nope, only this jump works. The jumping mechanic was quite frustrating sometimes. Each platform jump sequence (which is most of the gameplay) has set jumping requirements that each only work for a certain gap. The running jump can easily overshoot a smaller gap, come up inches too short from a ledge and ultimately lead to multiple thudding demises. Every running jump must have one full "block" to make the jump (i.e. if you start a running jump just inside a block, you will be unable to jump before the ledge), this can be quite frustrating when blocks are lined up like paver stones: you think you can just run and bound off each one holding the jump button, sorry this does not work. SAVE AFTER EVERY LITTLE ACCOMPLISHMENT. The standing jump can either go forward, up, or to either side; these jumps are used for very specific jumps as well. For vertical jumps, Lara must slam her face into the wall or dangle her toes on the edge of the platform to successfully grab the ledge above. The side jumps are fantastic for fighting enemies from a slight distance because you take less damage and continue shooting even upside-down.
Possibly the worst part about this game is the camera. Lining up a jump when the third person perspective camera is cockeyed looking at the front of the character and unable to be moved in favor of a more comfortable viewing angle can be quite frustrating and lead to more deaths from simply missing a jump. The "Look" function is also quite clunky as the camera continues to be affected by walls and objects.
Oh, and another major critique of this game is DosBox emulator itself is trash (Again Save, save, save again, and don't forget to save), it will crash dozens of times.
All-in-all worth the playthrough and I am looking forward to the rest of the games since the newer one was quite good. Save twice, jump once.

What most people remember from this ancient relic of a title - fast approaching its twentieth anniversary at the time of writing - is an unassuming level called the Lost Valley. Ms Croft, far from the first female video game protagonist but arguably the most influential, runs through a short cave system not dissimilar to that of the opening levels, and gracefully swan dives into a pool from the very top of a waterfall. As Lara, you indiscriminately kill a few wolves, and then you find yourself in this expansive, jungle-like environment. The pitch black darkness above - the result of hardware limitations at the time - was intended to imply an outdoor, night time environment. It doesn’t quite pull it off, and you might feel like you’re still in a cave, miles underground, shrubs and trees inexplicably growing all around you. One thing’s for sure, though - you’re entirely alone.
But not for long. Two creatures attack, on top of you so quickly you hardly have time to register it. You push on, hoping there’s not more of them - the earlier Tomb Raider games had a genuine fear factor to them, a genuine sense of vulnerability - and just as you’re about to pass under a broken bridge, wondering what might have caused such destruction, the screen starts to shake. The tense musical cue kicks in*, and then it appears. A huge polygon monstrosity roars at you with not-quite CD quality sound, and then it’s up to you - fight or flight.
What makes this so notable a moment in the present day is that the Lost Valley was the third level of a fifteen level game. The Tyrannosaurus Rex does not act as a bookend for the game, or even for the level itself. It is not part of some grand set piece, or even an epic boss fight - provided you can avoid the damn thing’s jaws, a gunfight will last about twenty seconds, and yes, you can even beat the level without killing it at all.
What we have here is game design from an era where things weren’t focus-tested into banality, when developers implemented outstandingly memorable moments without basing an entire game around it. A T-Rex in Level Three suggests a time when developers could, in short, do close to whatever they wanted. Dinosaurs wandering around Peru? Well, sure, why the hell not? Jurassic Park had come out three years prior, and dinosaurs were the next big thing in entertainment. It didn’t necessarily make a lot of sense for Tomb Raider, from a contextual standpoint or a gameplay standpoint, but somehow, it worked. And Tomb Raider’s full of moments like that - our heroine’s making her way through a mutant-infested Atlantis, complete with fleshy, pulsating walls, and then she enters what appears to be… an underground skateboard park? And sure enough, someone’s riding towards her, skateboard under his feet, twin Uzis in his hands, spitting out a remark that seem to be an almost-quote from Taxi Driver (“You firing at me? You firing at me?!”).
These days are long gone. If you’re going to put dinosaurs in a game, dinosaurs have to *make* the game. You certainly can’t go putting a T-Rex in the third level. And forget murderous skaters altogether. You’d have half your audience scratching their heads. For better or for worse, consistency and logic are cornerstones of modern gaming - triple A and indie alike, I’d argue - and the times when developers could truly put an idea in their game “just because” are over. For those who can handle the archaic controls and dated visuals**, Tomb Raider remains well worth playing today. More recent Tomb Raider titles provide the same exotic locations and eclectic blend of platforming, exploration and combat as the original, but they often feel like you’re strapped into the seat of a rollercoaster - it's frequently breathtaking, but you're very much on a set path. For that reason, it’s the original 1996 release that has me coming back whenever I want a fix of the exotic, the surreal, and the often downright bizarre.
Tomb Raider. Come for the dinosaurs. Stay for the gun-totting skateboarder.
*Strangely, this Steam version of Tomb Raider seems to lack musical cues such as the one signalling the appearance of the Tyrannosaurus Rex. I’m not sure if this is my setup, but other cues, such as Lara’s voiceovers during the tutorial in her mansion home, play fine.
**The Steam version of Tomb Raider provides the smoothest graphical setup I’ve seen for the game, providing texture qualities not far removed from late-generation PS1 games, or even early Dreamcast titles. Unfortunately, it also introduces occasional screen tearing, clipping and pop-up/draw distance issues.

Horrible Piece of Crap
First of all, while this game has excellent graphic, the rest of the system is just abysmally horrible. The controls are severely over-complicated for PC, with multiple actions that require pressing at least three keys at once. Players are limited to using only a few and can barely touch its potential. The game has a truckload of keys to press in game, but the list is outside, in the first welcome screen instead of being accessible in the game. If you forget anything on that list while playing, then screw you. You have to quit the game to access that list in the key config. The tutorial, if you can call that pathetic excuse of a prelude one, are AWFUL and barely teach anything of the mechanics. I was hoping that the game would teach you more when you pick up things, but no. The game doesn't teach you ANY-FREAKING-THING. If you need any in-depth key combinations, you find it online. It's not even in the damn manual. This is how responsible CAPCOM has become.
The pathfinder system of your partner's AI is also god-awful. Your partner often finds yourself stuck near the edge of a door without being smart enough to walk an inch sideways and clear the obstacle. It is one of the case when artificial intelligence completely beats genuine stupidity. To make matters worse, sometimes you cannot cancel a command issued to your partner, and if the AI can't clear a door, it ends up getting stuck there forever, requiring you to restart from the check point. If your partner has no way of reaching you when you call, you end up watching him trying to get to you forevermore without being able to cancel it. Makes you wonder if the AI of your partner is controlling a BSAA Agent or a monkey. In fact, a monkey might be smarter than this game's AI.
The menu interface is also terrible. It is not intuitive and instead making things accessible in one place for easy access, it splits every bit of everyhing everywhere. There's a weapon in one menu, grenades and health items in another. Oh, and herbs have specific method of using them too. You have to mix them in the menu, put it in capsules, and use it outside the menu using a specific key. When you throw a grenade, if you have 10, you can't just throw 10. You have to throw one, and the game "intelligently" switch to your guns, and you have to swith the menu to grenade menu, find the grenade, select the grenades, and use another. If you want to use 10 grenades, you do that 10 times. If this is not called horrible, I don't know what is. You also have to do all this IN REAL TIME, WHILE FIGHTING.
There are over-abundance of quick-time event. One mistake, and you're dead. You also cannot skip cutscenes. NONE of them. Many of them are minutes long. If the quick-time events are specially difficult, the torture of watching the cutscenes over and over might be more of a challenge than the actual gameplay.
I certainly hope that despite all the heavy sales, this piece of crap doesn't get your money. If you want to know the story, just watch people play this game on YouTube and save yourself the frustration.

Big fan of the series since the beginning, and never have I liked a Resident Evil game so little. The combat is inconsistent, and firearms feel ineffectual and useless against enemies. The majority of the damage you take is from unavoidable "surprise" events, reducing any feeling of accomplishment or control. The game is packed with quick-time events as well, and they are poorly integrated into the flow of the action.
I did not have the feeling that my actions or skill level, good or bad, actually had anything to do with the progression of the game. Death is hardly a failure, as dying actually gets you some life back and and a refill of ammo. When it takes between 3 and 10 shots to the head at close range to kill a standard zombie on standard difficulty, you are going to run out of ammo. I defaulted to running around zombies and using melee attacks against them, which feels clunky and unsatisfying.
Buy this if you are a hardcore fan looking to continue the series. The story is not bad, the gameplay is poor and unsatisfying. Many other modern games have taken the old RE formula and done it better (Evil Within, Dead Space and Alan Wake come to mind).

Do you like to die?  Well, RE6 will grant your wish.  I've never played a game where it was so easy to get killed.  Not just through the typical action but from the generously peppered "reflex events" or whatever you call them where you have to mash buttons at specific times or suffer dire consequences.  The visuals and big-world feel are all there, even though you are mostly on rails the whole time from point to point.  The monsters definitely feel dangerous and the environments are classic RE, just scaled up.  The plot is decent and easy enough to follow, though neophytes to the series may be lost on who some of these people are and why they should care.  Even still, there's lots of action to be had and the ability to control your character in agile ways keeps things exciting, especially in fast paced, close-quartered combat.  And the dying again.  As frustrating as it is to get killed (which happens 1000x more when playing multiplayer) the death scenes are fairly gruesome and well done, actually worth watching.

Rebuild 3: Gangs of Deadsville combines turn based strategy, roleplaying, and simulation gaming into a delightfully addictive challenge.
There are a few things to bear in mind:
1). The difficulty level is high. This game is as challenging, as the graphics are simple. It catches you up into its storyline and before you know it you find the play as challenging as any hardcore game. Rebuild 3 is not casual!!!
2). This game is balanced. Rebuild 3 is not a game where you can concentrate on one area of developement. Neglecting one area of the game will have consequences. The game is not linear, and you can't get through with a linear strategy.
3). The theme is a whimsical countercultural romp with cartoonish noir graphics. I read one conservative Christian complain about how two of the "bad guy factions" were a fundamentalist motorcycle gang and the government. One of the "good guy" factions gets their name from combining the luddites with the hippies. This game was not meant to venerate Mom, Apple Pie, and America. This is a game where dressing up in "Free Tommy Chong" T shirts, and chowing down on a pint of Ben & Jerry's is a fun evening. I'm not going to knock the pledge of allegiance, but this is not the game to start with that.
If you don't like your funny games with a dash of hardcore play, or you can't enjoy post apocalypse games that don't espouse traditional American values. This game is not for you. Those of us who enjoy this game are freethinkers, who like playing with a sense of accomplishment. If you like your "funny" games casual, or think that the zombie apocalypse must reaffirm "traditional" values, This game will not make you happy!
If you like doing your own thing, playing a game that gives you a sense of achievement when you win, and poking fun at "The Man." This is your game dude(tte).

A visual treat of a follow-up to Crysis, the sequel completely changes direction and almost suffers from it, if not for its otherwise excellent game-play.
Whilst Crysis and Warhead did very little truly interesting in the narrative department (with Warhead at least trying to do something about addressing that) the sequel quickly puts you into an entirely new environment and situation with very little explanation into a world that is a mess. Being ferried from one set-piece to the next on a strictly linear and far narrower path, I quickly realised that I was losing focus on what was going on with a conflict that seemed to spring out of nowhere and whilst there are obviously connections to the original, they seem tenuous at best. Crysis 2's narrative is a mess and whilst Crysis got away with its minimalist approach as it didn't shove it right up your face, it's hard to ignore the silliness going on in 2 as it, unfortunately, does shove it in your face.
The plus of all of this is that the core game is still very fun, if not severely reduced in scope and potential variation. Replacing open objectives are checkpoints along a trail that mostly replaces the how you approach an encounter with where you approach it from; the game does at least provide different routes for you to approach fights from that can give eager travellers an upper hand. This is particularly important given that the nature of your enemies have changed and whilst you're still fighting a lot of humans, you also have various alien enemies to take out, from foot soldier equivalents to large walking annoying bosses.
The removal of island openness does at least make way for some truly fun set-pieces though as the further you get into the game, the more interesting they become culminating in an extremely fun final level. As memorable as some of them may be though, there is an inherent reduction in the replayability in the game; you can only approach encounters in so many ways, set-pieces are only unique the first time and weapon variation (both in what's available and how many you can carry) limit the empowering craziness of the original and Warhead.
Ultimately, 2 feels very much like an extension of the ideas in Warhead, but at double the length and losing what made Warhead a fun in-between point of Crysis' openness and general FPS linearity. By the end of this game though, whilst I had felt satisfied, I was in no rush to play it again, nor even consider how I would attempt to go back to that particular set-piece and try completing it in a different manner. Essentially, there's one good run here before the game feels like it has expired.
Whilst Crysis 2 does look fantastic and has a great sound-track to boot, it lacks much of the uniqueness that its predecessors had whilst only providing minor boosts to the things that already made it a great shooter. Fun overall, but a greatly reduced experience overall.
Multiplayer: There's a greater push for the MP component in 2, but it essentially plays out like many small map-based shooters. A few interesting quirks here and there, particularly in your suit-enabled movement, but otherwise an extended feeling from the main game, that of competency and not much else.

This game made me attached to geometric shapes. To greatly simplify the experience of this game, it's a 2D puzzle platformer, narrated in generalizations, which are occassionally interrupted with journal entries. It's worth noting that gameplay doesn't stop for this dialogue - it's melded into the actual gameplay. As you play, you meet and acquire different shapes, who all have their own personalities, character strengths, weaknesses, and quirks. As you play, these personalities are expanded as you solve the game's puzzles, and without really noticing, you find yourself enthralled by the personalities of these shapes, and their quest to escape an oppressive, cruel world.
To expand on the game further:
Gameplay: 8. The puzzles are fun. Some of them are challenging, and some of them are easy. None of them can honestly be described as 'hard'. This said, I have played puzzle games before, and several friends I played this game with got stuck occassionally - so if you're new to puzzle games, expect a bit of a challenge! The puzzles become more complex towards the middle and end of the game, as each new shape possesses a new ability (like the ability to float on water, acting as a boat, the ability to fall upwards, double jump, etc.).
Graphics (appearances): 9. I put 9, but put appearances in brackets, just because this game is intentionally minimalalist, so it's important to know that YES, this game looks NICE. It has shadows, light play, visually pleasing animations. But please don't expect a perfectly rendered 3D skyrim adventure, it's not that kind of game! My favourite animation in this game is the jump animation. It's just cute, I don't have any other word for it.
Story: 10. The story in this game is progressive, and pulls you in as you play. The characters all have strong personalities, and it's easy to find yourself thinking: "I've grown so attached to these characters! And they're just rectangles!". You'll be happy when they succeed, sad when they fail, and you'll be angry at the cruelity of the world they find themselves in. And, at the end of the game, you'll be left with deep philosophical questions, about a future that might not be too far away.
Music/sound: 7. The music in this game is FANTASTIC. It's soothing, it's immersive, and it blends into the backround as you play the game. I rated the music a 7 only because some tracks seem to blend with the main track incorrectly, causing the music to sound like a jumbled mess. For example, at one part of the game, a darker undertone was added to the main track that plays. I liked both of these tracks... separately, but together they clashed and sounded jumbled. I'm not sure if this was a glitch, an unpleasant side effect of not using headphones, or the way the game sounds at some points, but it's the reason I didn't rate the music 10/10.
Conclusion
This game is excellent. It has good gameplay and a good story. It's hilarious because it makes you attached to geometric shapes. But it's also thought provoking and at times sad, because of that. My only real gripe about this game, is that there aren't any plans for a sequel.

I'd say I've given this game a good run for my money, and let me say, it's very good.
However, I do have some gripes about it, which I will get to momentarily. But, what did I like?
+ The game has amazing atmosphere and ambiance. The worldbuilding and story, though minimalistic at times, were very well put together, and I will forever praise this game for being gorgeous and having a fantastic backstory.
+ Combat feels tight and fun, especially boss fights. Some were frustrating, but in general, once you learn the patterns, they're all well designed and very rewarding to play through and defeat. Even combat with lesser enemies feels great, especially once you upgrade your sword and general arsenal.
+ Finding secrets feels fantastic, and you're oftentimes rewarded well for going out of your way to hunt them down. Rewards generally consist of some sort of tokens, with which you can upgrade and buy new abilities, which is always fun, as it makes the player feel like they're growing stronger.
Despite these, though, the game has issues.
- Some enemies are annoying or tedious to fight, and at times there are moments where the player might feel that a death was unfair or uncalled for. This issue in particular is emphasized in the Arena minigame in the endgame, where you can fight waves of enemies. These enemies can immediately attack you once they spawn in, adn considering many of their attacks death 2 "hearts" worth of damage, this can kill you instantly if you aren't expecting it. Additionally, enemies can knock you back, and around the area that you're fighting in, which may seem fun at first, but it can very easily lead to you getting accidentally knocked into a terrain hazard and instantly dying, or getting combo'd by other enemies.
- There are a LOT of ways for the player to immediately or near immediately die. I played in Standard mode, and there were still plenty of situations where I was getting killed near instantly, particularly in the Western forest area with the crystals.
- Chain Dashing. Oh my goodness Chain Dashing. This mechanic is something that I feel people sort of suck up and say is alright, when it's actually fairly tricky, and requires a rediculous amount of precision to pull off. This is made worse by the fact that many of the areas in which you must use Chain Dashing feature instant-death hazards or hazards that will respawn you at the start of the course, forcing you to struggle over and over again to get the timing of the dashes perfect, essentially forcing players to beat their heads against a wall until they break through. At the end of 15 hours, I hadn't mastered it, and I doubt I ever will.
Additionally, dashing in general is normally fairly responsive, but there are points where, if you don't chain dash, you'll stop dashing and take a second to "recharge" which is REALLY bad during combat if you're trying to avoid a large number of enemies or projectiles.
- Healing in the game takes a few seconds, during which you can be interrupted and killed. This feature, while making combat more tense, also means you oftentimes can't reliably heal in the thick of battle, which, in conjunction with dashing being an issue at times, frequently caused me to die.
Despite the issues, I'd still recommend the game (maybe try the easiest difficulty for a more relaxed experience). Just be aware that it may be frustrating at times.

Pros: nice graphics and pretty easy to pick out, this game reviews well so I won't elaborate too much here.
Cons:
1) The PC price discrimination: See this time and time again, this game is $3.49 on Google/Apple store and almost double the price on Steam. When this title is on sale, it is about the same price as the normal price for the mobile version.
2) No PC optimizations: #1 would be ok if the developers actually put effort into the port, but as it stands there are little to no improvements. There are very basic features that the game lacks due to lack of will/laziness. One example is that you cannot find out the movement zone of enemy units - in typical strategy games you mouseover a unit to see how far it can move so you can stay outside the range, in this game, you need to look up its movement, and manually count squares. You cannot 'mouseover' on a phone, so why implement it on a PC? Right?
3) Lack of strategy: This game, despite being a strategy game, has almost no strategy. The two small figments of strategy is that most enemies have only one counter, so double teaming them saves one counter hit; also, you can block enemies with your troops to prevent them attacking your back line. Staples such as combo attacks are non-existent. So most battles are just a slapfest where your troops and enemy troops will stand toe to toe slugging it out until one stack dies.
Bottom line: Maybe acceptable for a kid, but for anyone who likes the strategic aspect, Braveland is a pass.

Duelyst is a game that takes the CCG (collectible card game) and adds a tactical element to create a game that feels more rewarding to skilled players.
Players have access to more tools to create consistancy in play, such as reducing the effects of poor draws by granting a system of replacing a card once a turn. The addition of a game board also gives players more tools to preserve resources, such as avoiding enemy minions to conserve health or protecting minions by body blocking or repositioning.
Recommend if:
- you enjoy turn-based tactics and M:tG/Vanilla HS-style games
- you enjoy being rewarded for skilled play and understanding of mechanics
- you like drawing multiple cards a turn

I really wanted to like this game, I spent a ton of time trying to force myself to like it. The problem is, it isn't all that bad of a game. It has really some really fun to play characters and a great combat system in general, in my opinion the best in the genre. Here's where the problems start.
See, every season 2 new characters are added. And they start out ridiculously over powered. Season 1 introduced the Centurion and the Shinobi. At launch both were top tier and almost guaranteed to win any match up. Shinobi featured an opening attack that guaranteed damage or could be used in a mix up to guarantee more damage. Centurion featured near infinite stamina with an infinite combo that could almost 100-0 characters with the most health, and could guarantee a 100-0 on weaker characters. Shinobi was fixed in a week or so. Centurion took months and months since Season 1 to get fixed.
Season 2 featured the Highlander and the Gladiator. Highlander, while being fun to play with amazing animations, isn't a superb character, which isn't the issue here. The issue was Gladiator, another horribly broken character at launch. I haven't played the game much since season 2 launched so I'm unsure of the current state of these 2 characters.
In summary, this is a fun game. If you don't care about game balance, then sure pick this up. It has a fantastic combat system. But I can't reccomend this game when they hold competetive tournaments with cash prizes while it's so unbalanced like this and participants will literally utilize glitches to win games.

The game concept in itself is amazing, and the way they have laid out the UI for you is simple but visually pleasing. The queue times could be quicker, but other than that this game is great. So to start this review off , I started playing guitar 6 months ago and I bought Rocksmith roughly 5 months ago I suppose. So this review is by an actual beginner guitar player.
Rocksmith really is a great tool if you want to learn how to play e-guitar , more speficially said it helps you play your favorite songs. There are technique lessons in there that you can tune in to and it might help you get better at the overall guitar playing techniques. the different scales are also included, so if you want to deeply delve into stuff like that , it gives you the most basic informations, but I guess further research is requiered.
But now the most important part about Rocksmith. Does it help, wil you get better at guitar and just as important , is it even fun?
Yes, Yes and Yes.
It helps- It's just TAB's made into a graphic game basically. You play it kinda like the Guitar Hero games , hit the notes/acc/bendings/etc when they hit your screen.
One of the biggest benefits for a beginner is the visualization of the Rhythm. It's much easier to memorize the rhythm when you kinda see when , which and how often you have to hit each strings.
Furthermore there are quests that help you to be diversive, which brings us to the next point....
It helps you to get better at your guitar playing.
Even in the standard game there's a good bunch of songs that range from country to metal , from very easy beginner friendly songs too songs that are for more experienced players.
The quests kinda motivate you to try out songs that you normally would'nt have touched and this will not only broaden your horizon in terms of music , it will also help you too see and use techniques that you wouldn't have used otherwise.
I can only give you the advice to try a majority of the songs. Even if you dont like them , they might be fun to play and since you bought the game anyways you own them.
And ofc , yes it is fun. It's fun because it is an easy and kinda "fast" way to learn the guitar. Is it the fastes like Ubisoft describes it? I doubt it , since every human being learns different. But alongside the song's you also have funny little minigames that are educational and let your train your chords , bendings , scales etc.
It's also just a fantastic feeling to rock out your favorite songs and learning them, until you can play them without Rocksmith with your home equipment.
What brings me to my last point , the sound of the ingame Amps.
The guys that decipher the songs note for note and try to get the tone for the song as real as possible , they do a great job. On all the songs I own , the sound is very close to the original.
But on the otherhand , the ingame amp sound without the original tones from the songs is not the best in my opinion , I would not want to use this for any kind of playing besides Rocksmith.
But there's also a major problem with the game that I don't think will be ever fixed.
Some of the bendings in some particular songs track very horrible and playing with a very low tuning like Drop C can be frustrating , some notes , strings and chords get veeeerrrry poorly detected.
You can still learn the rhythm and tabs however.
A quick summarize.
Positive
+ It helps you start your guitar hobby and helps you to continuesly get better at it
+ You can very easily learn your favorite songs and discover new bands/tracks that you never heard off
+ You can learn probably the majority of the most important techniques and scales
+ The tone of the songs is very close to the original tone , on the other hand....
Negative
- .... the standard ingame amp seems to lack a good tone. might be only my configs though.
- Bendings get sometimes very badly recognized
- If you want to play in low tunings like Drop C , be prepared to be frustrated. I would recommend getting thick strings , they tend to help the real-tone cable to recognized your chords better when tuned down.
- CARE THERE ARE SONGS OUT THERE THAT REQUIRE A CAPO. (ex. "WONDERWALL")

Genre: Tactical Role Playing Game.
Time to complete: About 6 hours for me to 100% the game.
Braveland is a TRPG that comprises of fairly standard hiring of soldiers to do battle while collecting gear (for your main character only who doesn't fight but provides support buffs) and defeating enemies in a very linier final fantasy tactics styled map.
Each unit you gain is comprised of a certain number of units in which you can hire more of in order to boost that units power / health.  In combat when you lose a health bar you lose 1 unit from that group and are forced to pay a penalty at the end of the mission. (The unit lose is temporary)
The main issue I find with this game is the lack of depth and that gold can be very limited because there is no way to grind or farm anything.  When a battle is done it is over.  You can choose to lose fights in order to gain gold and xp but that is extremely tidious and often not worth it.
Braveland is also very easy,  on the hardest setting I personally only ran into one small wall and that was trying to get the end game sword a bit early.
Pros
-Simple, easy to pick up and play.
-Fun to kill a quick night and get a 100% game without a ton of effort.

Cons
-Short and a bit to bare bones.
-No ability to grind for cash or exp other than losing fights.
I had a blast playing it and will more than likely play the next game in the series.
If you don't have a lot of time or just want a simple TRPG to kill a night of time this is a great buy.
However if you want more depth or are looking for a new RPG to sink your teeth into this might be disapointing.
Make up your own mind about it but it was worth my money.

An enjoyable little adventure, but don't expect too much of it. Basically, it is a short, kind, may be somewhat naive, fairy tale with not over-complicated tactical battles.
It took me just three evenings to complete the game, and it doesn't make much sense to replay it as I played on the hard difficulty, and although there is a survival mode as well, the core game is just a one-time trip, during which one sees pretty much everything of it. Even though the game can't be technically called absolutely linear, there is not much real freedom of exploration or choice.
I really liked the cute and positive art style (think HoMM1/2), although I would say that the interface is somewhat coarse and make one think about casual/mobile games. Oh, wait... it is a casual mobile game, after all.
The story (which is presented via short dialogues) is simple and not particularly deep, but exactly suits the general style of the game.
The global map reminds me of Puzzle Quest, where you travel between fixed points, to fight a fight or/and get the next piece of story, which is a fine format for me.
The tactical battles can be obviously described like HoMM-lite, and it is clear, that the encounters were designed so that they don't last more than few minutes. Some might like it, yet some might find them lacking complexity and depth. But again, the game does not pretend to be hardcore strategic. Having said that, certain design choices are still rather strange, +1% troop defense for a hero attribute point, seriously?(you hardly have 10 by the end of the game, so, basically, neither your hero's 'build', nor equipment really matters).
So, to sum up, Braveland offers an enjoyable relaxed experience for some 6 hours, maybe little more. It is a little game, but it is nice and fun.

With the rise of 8/16-bit nostalgia (did Deus Ex / Metal Gear Solid ever go away?), and the rising popularity of indie games such as NEON STRUCT with its stylized blockiness, Tomb Raider - which is approaching 20 years old now - doesn't really seem THAT out of place really.
Apart from the graphics, another hark-back to the golden era of 16-bit gaming is the lack of hand-holding. The levels can be huge, the puzzles daunting and without a map, the game can be a formidable challenge to the novice gamer - as it was even 20 years ago.
Looking at Tomb Raider 1 in 2015 things like door switches can seem wholly illogical, even nonsensical. But approach each game level as a conceptual puzzle set-piece, and one can see it has more in common with games like The Talos Principle than the Tomb Raider reboot.
The player controls, considering the games age, have arguably aged well once you've mastered them. Compared to TR1's contemporaries such as Deathtrap Dungeon, Syphon Filter and Soul Reaver, Lara Croft's animations - to be able to somersault and shoot simultaneously (and later 360 degree turns in the air), were incredibly underrated and advanced for the time.
Tomb Raider 1 is a Classic in every sense. Gameplay, music and yes, the graphics, will always hold a special place in the hearts of adventure gamers the World over.

The original Tomb Raider hasn't aged well. It's still playable but the pace is plodding and actions are slow and clunky. It's best to stick with the newer iterations like the remake Tomb Raider: Anniversary and the latest reboot of Tomb Raider.

TR:I, when you put it in the context of 1996 gaming, is okay. But if you only care about modern games [nothing to be ashamed of], you likely won't enjoy this game. I will do my best to review this game from the former point of view.
Putting aside the ridiculously "top-heavy" player model for Lara Croft, the game's graphics are okay. A bit polygonal, but not bad overall. I had some issues with DOSbox misplacing renders of non-world objects [e.g. health packs being visible behind walls], but nothing to make it unplayable.
The design of the levels is ok as well, but many of the jumping puzzles can end up being rather frustrating. This is because often the required key sequence will not always do what you intended [Trying to run and jump might cause a leap from a standing start, and vice versa]. However, the levels as a whole are generally rather extensive for the era, and there is usually a lot to explore.
The game controls primarily with keyboard only, but it can be configured to use a gamepad. I would very seriously recommend not using a gamepad, as it felt very sluggish and unresponsive.
The gameplay surrounding gunfights can be ridiculous at times, with both enemies and yourself soaking up bullets like
concrete. The game does auto-aim, and doesn't require reloading, so you can run around the map shooting everything with no difficulty whatsoever. Beware bats though, if one gets on top of you and you get stuck in a corner, you're done for.
To summarize, this game has flaws. It isn't completely terrible, so if you want to play this game for nostalgic purposes then go ahead, but otherwise don't bother.

Its a reasonably good game with plenty of potential. I think it has been released from Early Access prematurely. Basic gameplay is still somewhat embryonic and lacks variety, something that could of been improved following further feedback and development during Early Access.
A "campaign" has been unveiled upon full release, but there isn't much too it. Still very embryonic and a bit of a token gesture.  I would like to see a few more missions here, again with some more variety. The campaign feels a lot like an after-thought and was only introduced because the playerbase requested it, and the devs thought that it would shut us up for a while. I would rather efforts were focused on polishing the multiplayer element of the game instead.
Multiplayer (and the main focus of the game) shows the most promise but lacks replayability right now. The co-op / PvE gameplay mode is the most enjoyable way to play for myself. The limited development pathway hinted at by the devs includes ai helos that will make gameplay much more interesting. I have no time for PvP in this game since there is no balancing, servers claim to have chopper generations selected, yet I join a supposed Rank 1 server and get taken out from across the map by a player with a Rank 2 / 3 chopper using heat seeking missiles? Something isn't quite right here. Whats more is that the player base is somewhat limited in numbers at present.
Graphics are reasonable, clearly allowing players on lower spec machines to play, of which I have no issue with, partly because the player base drastically needs increasing.
Yes, the UI quite frankly needs improving. Its a bit of an amateur "lets just put square boxes with text in all over the screen". Some screens do overload the player with information, while some lack information altogether. Odd colour schemes also, Blue means enemy and Orange means friendly? Ever played Battlefield?
I find no issues with the controls, I use mouse and keyboard and picked it up reasonably quickly. Having support for flight sticks is a nice feature. The lack of a real tutorial segment (even text based) strikes me as a major hole. You are actually forced to leave the game and watch a YouTube video in your browser for any sort of tutorial. Even a video played with the game would improve on this. Forcing a user to leave your game is just poor software design in my opinion.
Overall, tl;dr, an embryonic, generic, and under-cooked game in its current state. Lacking replayability right now, with some odd design and functionality decisions. Some bugs as expected, but none that I have found game breaking, just mere annoyances. The game holds great promise and the devs show some direction, despite a lack of roadmap, but as of this moment, I would say keep your eye on it and come back at a later date. I will be.

Here's the deal with Resident Evil 6. It is the worst campaign in the series. Bizarrely bad writing even for Resident Evil, bad campaign design decisions, tons of poor scripted sequences, janky vehicle segments every half hour, not much in the way of actual gameplay. Very "cinematic", but the cinematics are bad, and it's very clear that several different teams worked independently on the different campaigns.
However, the game engine itself is quite possibly the best third person action game ever made. When given room to breathe in mercenaries mode, it reveals its true potential for adrenaline-pumping John Woo gunplay and rad wrestling moves against insane monster designs, with beautiful graphics and performance. Resident Evil 6 is an incredible game, and it's a shame that its name has been dragged through the mud by virtue of being Resident Evil 6, because that means that Capcom will probably abandon that line of gameplay in the future and try to stick closer to boring, cludgy survival horror mechanics.
Resident Evil 6 is worth it for mercenaries mode alone. You don't even need to play the campaign, it comes unlocked from the start on PC.

Get ready to strap that Nanosuit on again, because it's time to go to the jungle of New York.
Crysis 2 brings the beloved Nanosuit back into action, and improved in some ways. The suit's new look is fantastic, and the upgrades that are available gives the player more flexibility on how to use their suit. Whether it is for more stealth-like gameplay or more straight up shooting with a lot of armor, the suit gives the player a lot of fun customizable options that were not available in the first game.
As for the story and setting, Crysis 2 takes place three years after the first game's horrific first contact with the alien race known as Ceph. Rumor has it that the Ceph built an underground hatch millions of years ago, and it is up to you how to save New York. The story is fun, although could be confusing since many of the pieces between the 1st and 2nd game are never explained. Rather, they are implied through dialogue. The setting is fun and interesting, and New York looks astonishing in Crytek's game engine.
The gameplay is more linear, which is a big drawback since the first game prided itself on the open maps that gave players flexibility. In Crysis 2, you always move in a linear path and that's a shame really, since it doesn't allow the player to explore other interesting looking locations in New York. Yet, you still have some choices in certain areas, and the vast array of weapons at your disposal makes the gameplay quite fun. The AI is somewhat improved over the first game, but don't expect Einstein here, they will still make laughable mistakes. The game also becomes a bit challenging towards the end, which is a nice change from most FPS games these days. Last, some of the nanosuits functions such as sprint and strength from the first game are now automatic. Rather than improving those abilities from the first game, Crytek opted for a lazy removal of those abilities and made them automatic.
The graphics are, just as the first game, fantastic. Yet I cannot help but notice that they did hold the engine back because it was marketed towards consoles. This sadly put the game behind its potential. Make no mistake, the game still looks great.
The soundtrack is perhaps the best part of the game. Hanz Zimmer made the soundtrack and this automatically makes it awesome. But no, seriously, it's a fantastic and emotional soundtrack that makes you feel the desperation people feel in New York. Overall sounds are also great.
There is a multiplayer mode in the game, but hardly anyone plays it today. In fact, almost no one played it when the game came out. The multiplayer is bad in most respects, and tried too much to mimic Call of Duty. They should have focused entirely on the single-player aspect of the game, not the multi-player aspect.
Overall, if you want an FPS shooter with a crazy good soundtrack, fantastic graphics, and enjoyable story, then I see no reason for why you should not try Crysis 2.

So to start this review off , I started playing guitar 6 months ago and I bought Rocksmith roughly 5 months ago I suppose. So this review is by an actual beginner guitar player.
Rocksmith really is a great tool if you want to learn how to play e-guitar , more speficially said it helps you play your favorite songs. There are technique lessons in there that you can tune in to and it might help you get better at the overall guitar playing techniques. the different scales are also included, so if you want to deeply delve into stuff like that , it gives you the most basic informations, but I guess further research is requiered.
But now the most important part about Rocksmith. Does it help, wil you get better at guitar and just as important , is it even fun?
Yes, Yes and Yes.
It helps- It's just TAB's made into a graphic game basically. You play it kinda like the Guitar Hero games , hit the notes/acc/bendings/etc when they hit your screen.
One of the biggest benefits for a beginner is the visualization of the Rhythm. It's much easier to memorize the rhythm when you kinda see when , which and how often you have to hit each strings.
Furthermore there are quests that help you to be diversive, which brings us to the next point....
It helps you to get better at your guitar playing.
Even in the standard game there's a good bunch of songs that range from country to metal , from very easy beginner friendly songs too songs that are for more experienced players.
The quests kinda motivate you to try out songs that you normally would'nt have touched and this will not only broaden your horizon in terms of music , it will also help you too see and use techniques that you wouldn't have used otherwise.
I can only give you the advice to try a majority of the songs. Even if you dont like them , they might be fun to play and since you bought the game anyways you own them.
And ofc , yes it is fun. It's fun because it is an easy and kinda "fast" way to learn the guitar. Is it the fastes like Ubisoft describes it? I doubt it , since every human being learns different. But alongside the song's you also have funny little minigames that are educational and let your train your chords , bendings , scales etc.
It's also just a fantastic feeling to rock out your favorite songs and learning them, until you can play them without Rocksmith with your home equipment.
What brings me to my last point , the sound of the ingame Amps.
The guys that decipher the songs note for note and try to get the tone for the song as real as possible , they do a great job. On all the songs I own , the sound is very close to the original.
But on the otherhand , the ingame amp sound without the original tones from the songs is not the best in my opinion , I would not want to use this for any kind of playing besides Rocksmith.
But there's also a major problem with the game that I don't think will be ever fixed.
Some of the bendings in some particular songs track very horrible and playing with a very low tuning like Drop C can be frustrating , some notes , strings and chords get veeeerrrry poorly detected.
You can still learn the rhythm and tabs however.
A quick summarize.
Positive
+ It helps you start your guitar hobby and helps you to continuesly get better at it
+ You can very easily learn your favorite songs and discover new bands/tracks that you never heard off
+ You can learn probably the majority of the most important techniques and scales
+ The tone of the songs is very close to the original tone , on the other hand....
Negative
- .... the standard ingame amp seems to lack a good tone. might be only my configs though.
- Bendings get sometimes very badly recognized
- If you want to play in low tunings like Drop C , be prepared to be frustrated. I would recommend getting thick strings , they tend to help the real-tone cable to recognized your chords better when tuned down.
- CARE THERE ARE SONGS OUT THERE THAT REQUIRE A CAPO. (ex. "WONDERWALL")
I hope my review might help you guys

Thomas was the little quadrilateral that could Hm.
As I'm sure many others have said, don't let the looks fool you. This game is a splendid puzzle platformer about an enticing cast of quadrilaterals that will compel you to finish it in a single sitting (at least, they did for me). It isn't
challenging so if you're hoping for that, I wouldn't recommend this, though that isn't a mark against the gameplay. The game grows increasingly complex as you play and requires you to rethink how you play as you come across new characters and new abilities, however its strongest element by far is its writing.
Without the narrative, this game wouldn't stand out, end of story. It would be another slick looking game that blends into the background of slick looking puzzle platformers, of which there are many and each are lovely in their own way, I'm sure, but without a story to breathe character into your actions and the game's artistry, there's little enjoy on a deeper level. Thomas Was Alone tugs at you on a deeper level, not through some highminded brainmelting ideas or anything like that, but through distinct characters that gradually grow together despite their differences.
That's not all that novel, admittedly, but in games, especially puzzle platformers, it's a fairly rare find. If you enjoy light stories with fun, interesting characters and solid gameplay, you could hardly go wrong with Thomas Was Alone. It's an excellent demonstration that any game can be enriched by fascinating characters, so long as the effort and interest is put into it, without needing walls of text or drawn out cutscenes and days worth of gameplay.

Imagine a universe in which chess, Hearthstone, and Heroes of Might and Magic clash together.
It's a turn based strategy game, with the objective to kill your opposing general.  However, you can only move 2 spaces up, down, right or left, and 1 square diagonally.  It's up to you to use your wits to defeat your opponent, using cards that power up your general or your minions.  You start the game with 2 mana, which increases by 1 (just like hearthstone) until the cap at 9.  The spheres in the middle grant extra mana.
This game has "orbs," which are essentially card packs that are really, really easy to gain compared to Hearthstone.  This game is not at all pay to win as long as you keep playing.  Play the daily challenges, complete your quests and you should be fine.  There is a lot of similarity to other card games, but the element of controlling your minions in squares adds another layer of skill and tactics that hearthstone doesn't have.
All in all, if you love card games, and you love TBS games, then pick this game up!  it is truly free, and I have no problems getting orbs.  I know people are hesitant because card games reward people who buy packs.  No worries here.  The developers here truly know what "free to play" means, and I've opened up 3 packs in 90 mins of game time, compared to like 1 in Hearthstone.

Originally played this on the PS, so decided to try this one out on the PC.  Essentially the same great game if you previously played the PS version.  There are a few small cons with the PC Steam version, but they are nothing too big.
Cons:
*Missing background music.  The original sounds are there such as gunfire, enemies, ambient, but it is missing the short musical background scores that would usually play during certain moments that would signal danger or caution that would keep you alert and ready for battle.  While nothing to fuss over, it is a bummer.
*Resolution.  This one is hardly anything to get upset over since this game was never meant to be played in HD or widescreen resolution, so it does take a bit of messing around with the game settings to find the perfect resolution and to make the game fit onto the screen. (Even after setting it to my native 1080p resolution, the right side of my monitor would be black).  So you have to find what eventually will work for you.
Despite this, the PROS are that this is a fantastic game (which for its time) has great level design, challenging puzzles, good story, a power-hungry antagonist, and will keep you immersed till the end.  Also, I'd say the PC version is much easier since you can save whenever you like vs the PS version where you needed to find save crystals.
If you are a Tomb Raider fan, you will definitely love the original if for some reason you have never played it, but played any other installment of the series.

Crysis 2 is a game which puts you into a futuristic universe from the viewpoint of a soldier relying on technology to survive. As true with all Crysis games, the visuals are phenominal. Playing essentially as a supersoldier, you're put right into the heat of multiple conflicts. Even in times of crisis, humanity retains its selfish traits. You're up against an idiotic and unruly army, aliens, and even your own body, sometimes.
Gunplay is fantastic with the variations you can create using the weapons and multiple accessories for each available. Not to mention, it's got a pretty nice cover system which allows you to aim precisely over a bit of protection just enough to get a shot in at an enemy.
For an FPS, the AI was surprisingly good, I felt. Sometimes they coordinate attacks against you, while others, they may sit back behind cover and wait for you to approach.

Go save our world from aliens again as Alcatraz who got Prophet's suit from him.
Story reminds me War of the worlds where aliens were burried on Earth for quadzillion years long time before humanity appeared, waiting for their time to come. And time has come.
Played Crysis 1 and Warhed, so i was a bit stunned when i hop into Grysis 2. In bad way. Really small levels divided into even smaller sectors. In some moments game gave me heavy corridor-like feeling. For me huge downside after large open levels of previous two games in series. I really couldn't wait for finishing Warhead and moving to Crysis 2 for its city setting instead of jungle on carribean isle, but it was huge disappointment for me.
Anyway - after finishing game i must say game is still good. Yes, levels are much smaller than before, but good old is still here - really depends only on you how you will get through levels. But it gives really different gameplay when levels are so small. It can be much more harder if playing stealthy to avoid enemies.
Not bad AI, definitely one of smarter, they can hear you very well and they can see you even if you are cloaked if they come too close (they see 'something', not exactly you, but they will go investigate etc.).
Badass super hi-tech nano-suit with previous four modes was simplified into main two:
- cloak - sneak through almost anywhere unseen
- armor - withstand much more damage to your suit like from enemy bullets or simply drop down from large heights
Which can be limiting on one side, because there is no 'power' or 'speed' modes. Suit itself switches to speed/power mode while running/doublejumping. Anyway no more super-faar throwing of grenades in power mode like in previous games :(.
On the other side you can easily do double jumps or run fast and stay cloaked or armored, just your suit energy drains much faster.
Pros:
- even more epic story and storytelling (much more cutscenes and context-clicking scenes than before) about saving humanity from alien race's raid again, but in New York
- smart AI
- even with linear story you still have small sandboxes (levels) to solve goals only on your own
- beautiful graphics, but Crysis 1 and Warhead are still better with their trees and foliage, here is everything limited (visibility, levels surrounded by buildings etc.)
- tuning possibility of your nanosuit
- scout every area for ammo crates, enemies and points to hide
- Maximum Edition includes DX11 patch together with HD textures pack (over 2GB of data)
Cons:
- more bugged than previsou games which had none - very often stuck/repeating sound of NPC's (both human and alien) or i  saw a lot of AI stucked behing doorway on corner trying to go through
- definitely smaller levels with less possibilities
- worse graphics than in previous games (mostly noticeable on grass/trees/foliage)
- four suit vanilla modes simplified into two (less freedom during gameplay)
Conclusion
Beside my unavoidable comparison with previous games in series - game is still very nice and good and fun to play. Overall very good game (yet typical scenario 'go save our world'). I had wait some years to play it in desired quality, but waiting was worthy :). If you like sci-fi and stealth possibilities with sandbox play i'd definitely recommend it to you.

A horror/zombie action game with all the wants and needs of a good experience. Characters and story arcs that entice you to love and hate characters. Blooming unlikely love story. Unexpected partnership based on mutual trust. Unresolved and mysterious love interest. PTSD hero, who loses more than he wanted, and gains much more only to lose some. Deceit and disillusionment. Downside is the ANNOYING camera angles, that though you could get used to after a while, certain campaigns force camera angles that keep changing and warping into almost unworkable conditions that result in your death. QTEs are a pain sometimes but are exciting - thought it depends on you. An overusage of it - in my opinion - but there is an option to turn them off, so that's good. (I'm looking at you Chris/Piers)
Bottom line a product worth its blood and gore. There's a million ways to die and so satisfying when finished - not only cos of the action element, but also the story element. Graphics ain't half bad either, and is plenty reliable as compared to other franchises that are trying to up their game. This Resident Evil has done it in the most balanced way.

When you load the game for the first time who are greeted with a main menu that all you can pretty much do is load mods and create a new save. Once you click the new game button who are greeted with another menu that shows several differnt maps each with their own pros and cons, click a map and perpare for a loading screen. Better than Sim City:
This game is miles ahead of sim city by several reasons. First, you can place districts on areas of your cities. Draw out a section of your city, name that district, and apply rules that only that part of the city follows. DLC:
