Thomas Was Alone is a superlative game with the most joyous cast of characters I have ever seen. And they're all quadrilateral shapes. It is a beautiful, happy, simple game that will make anyone smile. Overall it is one of my favourite games of all time, and it is SO worth buying.

Thomas Was Alone looks like a basic, minimalist puzzle platformer with shapes at first glance, but it shines through with a well written story with character, a high quality and soothing soundtrack, and gameplay that is fun and simple.
As a puzzle platformer, the goal of each level is to bring each colored block to a portal by aligning them to the correct outline. To reach the portals, each shape has different abilities to help them get through the levels. In addition, multiple characters tend to appear together in each level, requiring players to use the characters together and help all the shapes out. The puzzle difficulties are not too hard to figure out, and on occasion there are levels needing some reflexes to evade obstacles. As the game continues, more mechanics are given which expand more abilities and level designs to play through and figure out.
Believe it or not, Thomas Was Alone has a story, and a really good one as well. Basically, these shapes seen in the game are AI, and scattered throughout the game are quotes from humans about the AI and their progression. The game is voiced by a narrator who tells the story, going into the events of the AI, their thoughts, and some humor in as well. The British narrator is one of the strong parts of the game by having a likable voice and interesting lines. In addition to a strong narrator, the AI have distinct personalities and character, which help drive the story. Most people who look at the game at first don't know it has a story or strong characters, but it actually does and makes for an excellent story.
The art style is composed of simple shapes, giving the game a minimalist flair. However, the game isn't all just flat shapes and colors, as there are finer details thrown in along with shading and other non geometric things in the game to give depth. The art design works well to get the point across and looks sharp and stylized without being hard on the eyes.
The music is another one of the best parts of the game. The songs use a mix of electronic and traditional instruments for a laid back and soothing experience. In addition, there are some procedurally generated sounds and ambient influences for the soundtrack as a whole. With a blend between electronic and traditional, along with using procedural generation and ambient music, the music is both relaxing and memorable to drive the game and its story forward.
Many people will look at images and some video of Thomas Was Alone and think there isn't much to this minimalist game. The puzzle platformer gameplay is simple, but gets more complex and interesting as the game goes on. Story plays a big role in Thomas Was Alone, as the AI have character to them and the story is explained with an excellent narrator that talks about the events that have happened, thoughts each character has, and some entertaining lines. Lastly, the music is rich with electronic and traditional influences, and makes for a well crafted soundtrack that goes hand in hand with the story. Thomas Was Alone should be given a play even though first impressions may seem otherwise, for it holds a great but simple set of puzzles along with a captivating story and an uplifting soundtrack.

A fun successor to what used to be a mobile-only game, Rebuild 3 starts off fairly easy to manage and claim your territory and survivors, but as you progress and unlock the survivor management research, it can get fairly overwhelming to start keeping track of each individuals happiness and their friends/enemies that should be taken into account before sending them on any mission, or even just letting them relax somewhere.
The event system is just as interesting as it was in the mobile games I had played previously, with a need to carefully figure out if the risk is worth potential rewards, as the same event could end with either good or bad results. The need for some buildings that you would think are unimportant, due to having no visible benefits to them, such as a 8-12 Mart, or a fire station, can sometimes save your proverbial bacon or give you extra options for events, or quests to improve relations with the other factions.
When I first found a fire station, I initally built a farm over it, due to assuming it was one of the numerous useless buildings. This was shortly realized to be a mistake when a event happened shortly after that caused one of my more important buildings (a hospital, in this case) to burn to the ground. This could have been avoided, obviously, if I had kept my fire station intact.
The factions are all fairly amusing stereotypes for the most part, and some you can figure out things about them just by the dialogue. *cough*PigFarmers*cough* And depending on the map seed, it might be more beneficial to form an alliance or trade frequently with a few of them to obtain resources you might be sorely lacking in, due to location and luck of the draw, so to speak.
The writing for the game itself is fantastic, in my opinion. Although after a little while, reading the survivors stories gets tedious and repetetive. And really, the only other thing that seemed to be in need of addressing was that explosives only worked on zombies, and zombie infested tiles. Upon trying to use some upon some invading Government faction soldiers, I was perplexed that it was not allowed by the game, which makes no sense whatsoever.
Other then that minor issue though, the game as a whole is overall a very fun and engaging game, and I would certainly recommend it to people who enjoy strategy games.

If you have a friend and you want to have a laugh together with a generic co-op zombie shooter loaded with problems, this game isn't too bad. I got it on sale for $7.50 and it's worth about that much. It's competent enough to function while being bad enough to laugh at.
As a Resident Evil game, though, it's TERRIBLE and because it's actually SUPPOSED to be a Resident Evil game, it deserves the negative review. The last great RE game, IMO and not counting remakes, was RE4. This game takes everything good about the older RE games and throws it out the window while taking all the bad stuff and amplifies it 100 fold. It also throws in all the garbage gaming conventions that modern AAA devs think games need that drive me crazy like QTEs, excessive cutscenes, QTEs, taking control away from the player in the middle of gameplay segments, QTEs, gamey button prompts that ruin immersion, have I mentioned QTEs?
Let me compare the beginning of this game to a great RE game like RE2. In RE2 you had an FMV cutscene (with zero QTEs) followed by a wonderful gameplay intro that was so memorable I could paint a picture of each scene from memory. Between the end of the FMV cutscene and finding the police station, there was only one short cutscene that used the in-game engine at a gun shop. Aside from that short cutscene it was all normal gameplay allowing the player to get used to the game and immerse themself in the world. In RE6 you're being shot at by a helicopter right off the bat, but wait, you have to open the options menu because you're dropped into the game without a main menu. The heli shoots constantly without hitting anything while you mess with settings, a real immersion killer. Then you have to drag Helena away from the heli but you don't press the movement keys to do so, you mash the spacebar for a garbage QTE. Then you're in an alley for an on-rails segment where any direction you press has Leon lumber forward. Up/down/left/right all progress him down this rail. The player has extremely limited control. In the next part you're finally free to walk around but that's it. You can't check the weapon controls or even run. You can only walk. Then the game expects you to learn the weapon controls in 0.25 seconds as they throw a zombie at your face and flash QTE style prompts on the screen (although this isn't a QTE, it just has the immersion-destroying prompts as a kind of tutorial). Failing to shoot the zombie because you weren't simply allowed to play with your gun to get used to it before the zombie shows up, you die and go back to a checkpoint. As the tutorial segment continues you jump over cars as part of a QTE, you fly a helicopter as part of a QTE, you run from an explosion as part of a QTE, you shoot zombies as part of a QTE, etc... It's all very exciting gameplay... NOT. Devs, how about you let ME play the goddamn game?
The co-op is generic, as I said. In a Resident Evil game I expect to poke around, click on environmental stuff to read little descriptions of things, pick up files, search for ammo/herbs, solve puzzles, etc. Aside from picking up the odd ammo/herb none of that is present. Also, 90% of your items come from enemy drops so searching for environmental pickups isn't even that important. It's streamlined for co-op, in other words. Devs these days seem to think that a co-op experience has to be FAST to be playable. Can't stop to read descriptions! Can't stop to admire the scenery! Can't stop to solve puzzles! Gotta blaze through the game ASAP! You want a puzzle? How about Player A helps Player B access a co-op accessible area, and then Player B presses a button/unlocks a door/pushes a box/etc to allow Player A to follow? Great puzzle, right? There are also dual pickups meaning both players can pick up each item once meaning there's no real communication aside from "ammo/herb over here". You won't have to discuss how much ammo/herbs of each type each player has and who should get what.
I could go on. There are many factors that make this a terrible RE game or just a sub-par generic co-op game but we'd be here all day. Overall, the game is playable. If you're playing with a friend, it's actually not bad to play through and laugh at the problems the game has so if that sounds like something you'd enjoy, I can honestly recommend picking it up on sale. For the many reasons stated, however, I feel this game falls way, way, way short of it's potential and isn't a fitting entry in the RE franchise and that's where the negative review comes from.
Final Edit: Finished the main campaign and while I have a number of new complaints, the one that really needs to be added here is the dynamic difficulty. In other games that have dynamic difficulty, after you die at the same spot a few times the game might get a little easier to help you get past that part. Here, though, you die once and it  switches to Baby Mode. You'll never die in the same place twice (unless it's due to some janky QTE). Not only is this very insulting to the player but it's also a huge flaw in game design philosphy to think that nothing in the game should take more than 2 attempts.

Score 9/10

Monster chess at its finest! We've all seen the scene in Star Wars aboard the Mellenium Falcon.. probably why many of us game in the first place.. but by the grace of Counterplay Games studios in association with my vivid imagination a turn based tactical deck builder arises with animated avatars of brutality to slake the bloodthirsty compulsion for pixelated slaughter.
Duelyst allows access to all cards for free by accruing in-game currency, (exhorbitant prices charged for cosmetics).  In game currency is plentiful with completion of daily quests.  So if you login, get a win and play your quests, which is about eight games  30-60 min, its worth a booster pack. The in-game crafting system also allows you to burn undesirable cards to get the ones you want.  It doesn't take long to build a fun deck and once you do you'll be thinking about the next one.  The pixel art is impressive and adds plenty of flavor to the proceedings. The positional element afforded by the 9x5 grid makes this much more tactical and enjoyable than similar games like Hearthstone. Highest recommendation.

BUT! The frames do drop quite a bit, down to about ~40 FPS when I play PvP with an almost full match.
A single player campaign for the US and the Soviets is included. Multiplayer matches can be Co-op or PvP. Co-op can be played on 4 different maps, a map for each tier of helicopter. PvP can be played on 6 maps (4 of the Co-op maps, 1 night time version of the Kosovo Co-op map, and 1 extra Afghanistan map). Although it only has 2 different game modes, they feel fun and original. Starting at the Vietnam conflict all the way to Kosovo and Afghanistan. Unlike some other WORLD games we'd like to compare this one to, it is nation against nation. So no Mi 24s fighting alongside Apaches. I like it, but it does lead to some issues as almost every player seems to go down the US line and finding Soviet/Russian opponents can be difficult.
The best way to enjoy this game is to play with friends. Get on comms and coordinate different helo classes together and there is some good fun to be had. Scouting out a base with recon helos and then softening it up with mortars and gunships, allowing the transport helos to come in and take and reinforce the base is pretty satisfying for me.
50 helicopters to choose from spanning 2 nations and 4 in game tiers, including those from the US (26) and USSR/Russian Federation (24) dating all the way from the 1950s to modern day AH 64s, UH60s, and Mi28s. Including paint jobs for most of them, some of which you can buy for in game EXP/credits (The game seems to just mix the 2 into one) and some others you have to pay actual currency for. You can also change the loadout on helicopters and purchase defensive upgrades like flares and upgraded door guns for transport helos.
There are 3 classes of helicopters. Each to fulfill their own special niche in the game. All 3 coming together to support each other, as not 1 single aircraft can accomplish every task needed to win a match. You can bring 3 helos into a match of any type.
Fast, small, and agile helicopters, not allowing for much in terms of weaponry. Can spot enemies for their team and act as a forward observer for mortar teams. Some can even carry a couple of troops to allow them to capture a base, but not reinforce it as well against enemy attack.
Probably the most diverse class in the game in terms of size. An almost essential class for every match as they are needed to capture bases with infantry. They can range from a small Huey carrying a squad (10-11) to the size of the Sea Stallion, able to deploy a platoon of soldiers (32). Some are equipped with forward firing weapons that can be controlled by the pilot. Although, most of them at the very LEAST can be loaded up with door guns. Ranging from heavy machine guns to mini guns and even grenade launchers.
My personal favourite class in the game, but I might just be a weirdo that enjoys menial tasks like being a glorified taxi. *shrug*
Includes some of the most iconic aircraft in the game and the class that most of us are here to play. Varying from fast and nimble, purpose built helos for tank busting and infantry suppression like the Apache, to more multipurpose and lumbering gunships like the Soviet built Hind. Loaded for bear with machine guns, cannons, grenade launchers, rockets, ATGMs; all are here and can be swapped around if the helo could support it historically. Capable of dealing as much destruction as you deem necessary.
Now if you haven't gotten a Wargame vibe from playing yet, this might do it. You can carry and deploy infantry on the map that makes it feel almost like you are a helo deploying troops in Wargame (The minimap in game also reminds me of Wargame). There are 4 different types of infantry units to aid in defeating the enemy.
'Infantry' (as it is referred to in game) can capture and hold bases. Bases that receive fire can take casualties, lowering the combat effectiveness of that base and will eventually lead to the loss of all soldiers on that base rendering the base neutral. At which point the AAA on that base will no longer be manned and can be captured by either side again. Infantry can only be deployed at bases.
'MANPAD.' Soldiers that carry 3 shoulder-launched surface-to-air missles that can pose a real threat to any helos in the vicinity. Can be deployed anywhere on the map.
'RPG.' Soldiers armed with 4 AT rockets. Are a threat to both land AND air targets, so don't hover around too slowly when these buggers are around. Can be deployed anywhere on the map.
'Mortar team.' 2 man mortar team. Their fire must be directed on target by a friendly recon helo. Can be deployed anywhere on the map.
The details on the helicopters and environments are pretty neat. Flares actually eject from their casing even when they are placed asymmetrically on the fuselage of the helo. Textures don't appear to be mirrored, a fault that even some AAA game devs are guilty of. So no 'Danger ɿǝϱnɒꓷ' lazily appearing on helos. Helicopter armament is historical from what I've seen. Armour thickness and angling actually works... for tanks though. So hitting an angled BMP will result in no damage, but steepen(?) that angle so you're firing straight on to the armour and you could actually do damage. Just little things that you might not think are in a game so arcadey and made by such a small dev team. Really shows how much work they put into this game.
As of the current date of this review (14OCT2017), the game is not grindy at all. You can get to the top tier of a nation in a day if you really wanted to, but I don't know if that would change or not in the future.
For any criticisms? The novelty of it wore off a bit 'quick' for me. After about 9 hours of playing I was already getting a bit bored, but a bit of that might be the result of playing alone for the most part. Having team mates that don't talk in chat a lot, or at all leads to the feeling of playing alone... with a bunch of headless chickens running around. Desync was a bit of a problem at times regarding hits registering on the enemy helo you were engaging. I once hit a team mate because I was firing and stopped WAY before he crossed my sights, but I still hit him somehow, even though the rounds were about 50 or so yards in front of him.
The main menu UI feels like there is a little TOO much going on at times; a little too cluttered and leads to you misclicking on things. I think it would be worth more like $10 or $15, maybe, or somewhere in between $10 and $20. $20 just seems like a LITTLE too much for most of my friends after seeing me stream it for them.
TL;DR: It's a great little game with lots of potential and fun to be had if even for a day or two alone. It is MUCH more fun when you have a group of friends on comms to play with or else it will probably get boring rather quickly. A little pricey IMO, but I got my Soviet Strike (♥) fix out of it. Fun and original game mechanics that are new to ME at least. Lots of accurately modeled helicopters. Some desync issues here and there with hits not registering on enemy helos. Neat details here and there. Has a Wargame(y) vibe along with some nostalgic Soviet Strike memories and similar to Apache: Air Assault, but less... crappy...? Devs seem to have done a pretty good job for being such a small team.
So if you liked Soviet Strike on the PS1 or Apache: Air Assault or if you're weird like me and like to look at tiny little Abrams and Humvees puttering along the road and want to support small dev teams that put some hard work into their game...
Then yes, I highly recommend it.

I've been playing guitar on and off for some years now and what I find the most disheartening after a long break is returning to the instrument and experiencing skill decay from the lack of practise. This is where Rocksmith 2014 comes in! If it were not for my puny callus-less fingers, I'd probably spend all day practising riffs, revising chords and working on general technique. The game keeps track of my progress and keeps throwing new stuff to do in my face. And before you know it a couple of hours have passed. Always new goals and song specific advice. I get to start out softly with a new song and I have different tools for learning the full versions at my own pace. I simply don't notice how much I am flubbing around because the game keeps me focused on progress and goals.
There's also a bunch of the mini games I haven't tried yet, but I can see many nice additions since the first edition of Rocksmith. The session mode is also a decent addition, in that you get to use all your hard earned skills more freely with backing instruments.
I find that the main draw of RS2014 is the motivational aspect, it gets you playing, it gets you practising. The game is not a replacement for a music teacher, since it cannot correct bad finger placement or perfectly detect the notes you play each time. It also lacks things in the music theory department, but you can find supplemental resources online easily these days. Maybe in ten years time, when the technology is there, we'll have a perfect artificial guitar teacher in RS.
The current RS2014 is one of the better education games out there, I'd say.

An absolutely unique and excellent game... program... teacher?
Rocksmith makes good on its promises of being a efficient, fast and (extremely) fun way of learning guitar (or bass). I have been playing for roughly 10 days and making more consistent, noticeable progress that I could ever hope for with a paid, limited-hour teacher, or the myriad of unorganized videos and programs around the Internet. Rocksmith has an unique edge on them by providing you with dynamic tracking of your progress, adjusting difficulty and providing many suggestions and options for you try to improve your skills, having easy to understand lessons on multiple techniques and aspects of playing guitar, a good and varied number of songs (which you can greatly increase with cheap official DLC, or free community-made ones), as well as unique and interesting minigames and oppotunities for focused, efficient learning. After all, practice doesn't make perfect, perfect pratice makes perfect.
Still, Rocksmith is far from perfect. There are a couple of glitches and incosistencies here and there, some weird mechanics, a lack of variety for some of its more unique features, and the game fails to specifcally recognize some more specific nuances when recognizing notes, like harmonics. It also doesn't do much in the way of teaching you music theory or how to improvise. Session Mode feels like a novelty more than anything, and a beta implementation at the most. In the end, even playing actual licensed songs is little more than having a tab coming at you in pretty graphics, since the game has, unfortunately, no multitrack options, and you merely hear the sound of your guitar "over" the original recording. I mean, this was something even Guitar Hero was capable of doing (however there are some custom DLC that allow for this). Nonetheless, it is still extremely satisfying.
My biggest gripe, though, comes from the fact that RS doesn't fully utilize the possibilities of modern gaming. We have seen many games on Steam which ranged from mediocre to downright bad on launch, only to be progressively improved with each update and DLC, free or not. Rocksmith 2014, however, limits itself to launching new songs as DLC (which it has been doing with excellent frequency!), there are no new features, new Guitarcade games or obvious refinements (like a search function) coming our way; testament to this game being published by Ubisoft, which has never been very fond of supporting their games for a long time. Perhaps in Rocksmith 2017?

I'll skip the whole novel-stating-why-I-♥♥♥♥ing-love-Tomb-Raider, and instead give you just a brief rundown of what you should expect from Tomb Raider I.
Backstory: Tomb Raider was a PS1 launch title that BLEW UP because of how amazing it was- no joke. Lara Croft became infamous for her "triangle ♥♥♥♥♥♥s" because her breasts were mere triangles instead of the round jiggly thingies we have today. Tomb Raider is an ongoing franchise that features Lara Croft as the protagonist who either struggles to survive, or go on a massive search for some artifact.
Storyline: You are Lara Croft- a world known archeologist on a search for something called "The Scion" which a mysterious person named "Natla" has informed you about. Lara Croft is a bad♥♥♥♥♥ dual pistol wielding girl who lives for adventure.
Gameplay: Okay, now you have to take into account that this game was made in 1996- a PS1 launch title to be fair, so the gameplay functionality is going to be on-par with these next generation titles. Tomb Raider is a 3D platform-adventure game with gun mechanics that actually work. Tomb Raider also integrates puzzles into this platforming-adventure experience, so not only do you have a compelling story, but also a great genre scheme.
Sound: Since this is an outdated game, the sound effects can come out quite poor at some times due to the lower files not being supported by newer tech. If you have high teir headphones, you will know what i'm talking about.
Graphics: I keep going back to the topic of it being from the 90s, but it's true and it's age really puts a show on it's graphics, sounds, and just gameplay in general. The textures can be a bit bad and look unrendered to it's full potential at times, but it still works and looks... ok.. for it's time. Lots of elements found on the ground are sprites including the pickups like health packs, ammo packs, and artifacts. Overall, it's not TOO BAD, but it's nowhere as good as the sequals.
Conclusion: If you haven't found out already- Tomb Raider is AMAZING. If you have not played it, what is wrong with you? Stop reading this, scroll up, and click "Add to Cart".
Do not buy this, it is a terrible port. Get the anniversary edition.

A good start for the Tomb Raider franchise and truly a great game on its own, successfully incorporating exploration, adventure, platforming and shooting!
The game makes you really feel like an explorer, a female Indiana Jones of sort, as the levels are really vast for a ~300MB game, quite a feat actually. Some levels were so big that I got lost a few times, made worse by the fact that there is no in-game map! Many secret areas are available as well.
The weapon arsenal isn't really that huge (pistols with unlimited ammo, shotgun, magnums and Uzis), but it's fine for this type of game, which focuses on exploration more than shooting. Not having a weapon reload function also helps concentrate more on that.
There are many enemies as well, from wolves and evil henchmen to raptors (and a lone T-Rex! Felt really good fighting it!) and supernatural monsters.
As for the graphics, which also brings me to recommending or not this game, I have to say that they are good enough for a 1996 game, but, having said that, modern gamers accustomed to today's graphics will probably not like this (the gameplay also feels obsolete for today's standards).
An expansion pack was also made available for PC (called Unfinished Business, which features 4 additional levels), but is not present in the Steam version, as well as the original Playstation game's music (which is a letdown, since the Steam version's in-game music is almost non-existent, while the Playstation one added a lot to the atmosphere), but thankfully I found
which fixes both those issues. I advise new players to read it before starting the game.
Having said all that, I fully recommend this game for fans of exploration, adventure and a bit of shooting, taken with a grain of retro salt!

This is probably one of the best sci fi fps games ever. It has a great storyline: a marine name Alcatraz (your character) is going to NYC on a humanitarian mission, when his transport is attacked. Alcatraz has to get past special forces who have the city on lockdown in order to prevent people from spreading a deadly and contagious virus, which isn't easy because the soldiers are under orders to shoot anyone attempting to escape in order to contain the virus. The goal is to get to a special lab, where the nanosuit can be tested, because the nanosuit is so advanced that it is actually collecting virus samples as the virus attacks, disabling the virus, and developing a vaccine. Unfortunately, the plan doesn't workout do to unforseen occurences and new enemies. My favorite parts of the game were using a sniper rifle, HMG, and even a tank. The tank is absolutely awesome since it has unlimited, powerful ammo. I also enjoyed walking unperturbed through  a storm of bullets in armor mode and strangling victims in melee. If you want a long gameplay, this game has it. The game does have a few bugs, but not many and not serious. The only thing I felt was lacking was realistic ballistics.

I've always wanted a zombie apocalypse game where you actually rebuild instead of just survive. This game is the beginning of my hopes for that game. The structure is basic: you start out with a few buildings and a couple of survivors and you have to slowly conquer back the zombie wastelands and build a new start for humanity. The survivors have specializations which allow them to do different things for your settlement and as it grows people end up in relationships, end up in fights, or end up dead. Your leadership determines how well your settlement does. I never played the first two Rebuild games, but I was very satisfied with this one. My only gripe is that 3 missions into the campaign and I'm already getting swarmed with 2 or 3 zombie hordes every couple of minutes, which makes trying to establish a settlement near impossible since you have to keep sending all of your people off to fight the horde or guard your turf. There's also no real way to tell where a zombie horde or enemy faction group is going until they're already there (or if you just keep placing guards at every building in the vicinity until the danger meter changes color). It's also fairly basic with only a few building types to construct, a few technologies to research, and a few specialties for the survivors. I really kind of hope the devs (who I think are a husband/wife team) get bigger and make an expanded version of this game with 3-D graphics and expanded mechanics. If this is the quality of their games at a small level, I would only wonder what they could accomplish with EA's resources.

I don't have alot of playtime on this game, but I'll try to go through it properly.
First of, I loved Rebuild 1 and 2. When I heard there was a third game coming up, I was excited. When I heard it was going to cost? No so much, but I decided to give it a go, if only to support the devs for their two previous games. I expected it to be at least as great as Rebuild 2. My opinion? Deadsville is far, far greater, and worth every penny. Now to the review itself.
Let's begin with the zombies. What's a zombie game without zombies, eh?
In Rebuild 1 and 2, zombies surrounded your fort all the time. They could attack out of nowhere, anytime, and the risk of injuries/areas of the fort depended on the surrounding zombies - the defense of the fort, which was survivors on duty/idling + some buildings like marts and police stations.
In Deadsville, the zombies still surround your fort. But here, they can only attack once they have "massed", similiar to a Zombie Horde, which will be marked on a location around your fort. They won't attack as soon as they're formed, but you will need to station some to prepare once they have. You can also attack the massed zombies if you have the strenght for it, but it's generally a better idea to wait for them to come to you.
Zombie Hordes are still in this game, fullfilling the same purpose like in Rebuild 1 and 2, and just like with "massed" zombies, you can attack them instead of waiting for them, but you REALLY should wait for them to attack instead, much safer that way.
Now, let's talk about survivors.
In Rebuild 1 and 2, you'd have alot of survivors. You generally didn't bother remember their names or faces, since you'd eventually have too many at once. There would be so many to recruit, that if 4-5 died, you wouldn't give a damn.
In Deadsville, you have slightly fewer survivors, but they feel abit more important and personal. You most likely won't see 12-16 surrounding your fort at once, so each one you see will give you the feeling "I have to recruit him/her".
Also, now you will see where they are and what they are doing, similarly to how you could see where the Zombie Horde was in Rebuild 1 and 2, in the form of a marker. Placing a survivor in the fort randomly will NOT add to it's defense. Instead, you must place survivors inside the fort next to zombies markers, so they will defend the fort once the zombies decide to attack.
Next: factions. You remember the Riffs, the Last Judgement Gang and Gustav? They're all here and more, each their own faction.
In Rebuild 1 and 2, the Riffs, LJG and Gustav where all events that happened, the Riffs killing zombies randomly, the LJG trying to attack/rob you, and Gustav appearing to trade among other things.
In Deadsville, the three mentioned above have returned, with a few other, newer groups, and they all have forts on their own (I'm unsure about Gustav, I think he's a nomad(wandering trader)). You can either ignore them, trade with them, ally with them or destroy them. Destroying is dangerous, obviously, but it's faster should you have alot of trained soldier-survivors. Allying takes time, but it's safer, if a bit costly, but it will be more worth it in the long run.
Almost at the end are we? Let's look at resources.
In Rebuild 1 and 2, there was food and happiness. Few and Simple.
In Rebuild 3, there's those two and materials, ammunition, medicine and fuel.
Materials is used in building barricades (that is, expanding your fort.) or re-building a useless building to something... well, usefull. You can get more materials by scavenging, trading, destroying a building or chopping wood(will be explained later).
Ammunition is pretty self-explanatory isn't it? It's used during events (mostly defense where you more than 0% danger) or if your survivor is equipped with a gun and uses it while attacking/defending. It can be acquired by scavenging, trading or crafting (will be explained later)
Medicine and fuel is used mainly in events, and can be acquired through scavenging and trades, and used in events and trades.
Finally, let's talk about Survivor Classes.
In Rebuild 1 and 2, there were Soldiers, Scavengers, Researchers, Builders and Leaders, each with their own, obvious purpose. In Rebuild 2, you could train each and everyone in all the fields, making them all-around epic units (jack of all trades and master of all).
In Rebuild 3, Researchers have become Engineers. They still research mind you, but they, like the others, fulfill more than just one purpose. In the Engineers case, they also "manafacture" items, ammo and more, depending on how much you have researched.
Soldiers I think hasn't changed any.
Scavengers were pretty damn useless after early game, when you got food through farms, when your survivors had maxed stats so giving them items were pointless, so that all they could do was sit around or help out with the fighting. Now, they have two new reasons to live.
First is hunting. On some specific places, there are "fields" where wild animals live. You can send a scout to "hunt" regardless if the field is in your fort or not, to acquire food. Like farming, bartering etc, this is a "endless" job that only ends if a Zombie Horde gets too close, or you tell the Scavenger to come back.
Second is stealing. As said earlier, there are factions with their own forts. A Scavenger can be ordered to steal from them, the greater his scavenging ability, the more likely he is to succeed. Do note that the faction will like you less (duh).
Builders have changed alot aswell. They, too, have two new reasons to live aside from expanding the fort and re-building usless stuff.
First is chopping wood. You know materials? Send a builder to a forest or a place with trees in general, and he will go on an "endless" mission to get more materials. The higher his builder-level, the more he will get each day.
Second is farming. Yes, farming. Anyone can farm, but a builder nets a greater result.
Leaders helped recruit new survivors. Well, now they also hang out in the bar or church for the sake of increasing happiness or talk with other factions.
Firstly, they can be stationed "endlessly" in a bar or church to increase happiness in the fort, just like in Rebuild 1 and 2. Exactly how it works I'm unsure of in Deadsville, since I've stationed a level 10 leader in a church to "preach" but happiness wasn't visibly affected...
Secondly, sending an experienced leader to another faction will make it easier to befriend them (you may find out if they need something, or get better options when talking with them (for example, one faction wanted 5 traps, but my leader was high level enough so he could convince them 1 was enough))
There are also alot of events surrounding your survivors, which can grant them various perks, but I won't go into that. Don't want to spoil the fun now, eh?
All in all, it's a great game. If you enjoyed Rebuild 1 and 2, you can and WILL enjoy this.

So a review for the game.
I remember this when it first started as Rebuild 1 at flash sites like Newgrounds and it was a very nice game there. I see that from a simple format it has evolved by now taking the advice its sequels produced to good use.
On this game both story and sandbox modes are enjoyable. I am willing to look past the plot of the story and facts like the faction's memory or carrying over research. I assume every city has its own branches of factions and people that need to be taught. I am also going to be kind and assume that when I complete a mission and I leave my city with one injured builder at the moment 17 zed hordes are threatening my walls, he finds some sort of militia to deal with the threat and ensure my empire stays prosperous.
After this little sacrastic intro, on the actual parts of the game. The time management system as well as the neutral/faction AI is satisfactory. The difficulty levels are fine and so far I have not encountered any bugs. The items have a nice variety and the events, while you may encounter the same event once or twice do well to adapt to the names of different survivors. The biggest positive impact I have from the game is the addition of factions, especially the cult and such religions. I am willing to overlook the extreme complexity of the policies regarding the cult because of the fact its cool to have these aspects in a zombie survival strategy game.
On top of that all the small details of things you expect, like buildings, bars, churches, workshops, labs etc are as they should be. The resources of the game are few so its not confusing and you can quickly pick it up. Props to the autosave system that saves every minute, although some people may prefer to save at important points in game so they can get back if things get rough. Finally on a more advanced dive to the AI, the factions expand in an ok manner and they are not the same behavior with a reskin which is good as well.
However some things in the game could be improved. First of all the inaccuracies I mentioned at the start of this review are overlookable but annoying none-the-less. I understand for example the research carrying over part is not easily integratable because of game balance, but factions having a set memory on you, even if it punishes some players is a realistic change that would add to the game. Remember that difficulty can be a positive part of a game, while some people make difficulty the defining part of their game and make money out of that (cough cough dark souls).
After that I searched a bit and found some people experience bugs with the trade missions, and survivors never recovering from injury but stuck at guarding the building they were recovering. These have not happened to be but should be referenced.
And finally, my biggest complaint, the game music. I swear I never thought I would have ever said a game doesn't have a nice track since its really easy to find a simple mix for any sort of game. There are games out there with incredible soundtracks yes but here I am not talking about quality. In my opinion it is almost garbage. Half the tracks that play during the game are just static on different pitch. At first I thought it was on my end, went as far as to order a new sound card since mine was from christmas of 2014 because I couldn't believe how annoying it was. Specifically all the tracks refered to as the future postcards and the one track called pistolero something are dubstep radio static. I can only recall two tracks that were normal tracks you would expect to see in the game(the one with orange in its name and the intro) everything else was either various degrees of what mentioned above while one very specific one was static on pause and play, meaning it would stop every 3 seconds making it even more annoying.
Now I am aware half the people dont care about sound and play the game on mute, windowed with their own music or shows in the background. That's why I still recommend this game, would give it a 3.8 / 5 despite being a boosted flash one because it is genuinely a good purchase and worth your time and money.
But when your game sound is downright repulsive, I believe that is something the devs should be aware of.

It would be easy to write off Floors of Discomfort (FoD) within the first few minutes of game play, as I almost did (my first thought: "This feels like it belongs on Kongregate."). That would be unfair though, because there really is more to it than first meets the eye.
The Overview: FoD is a platformer only inasmuch as you walk left or right killing things, and occasionally jump. That's it, really. The challenge comes with the sheer numbers of enemies thrown at you from the very start. For example, you can enter a new game and literally be overwhelmed with mobs in a matter of seconds (including one beastie who opens a portal through which other beasties can come). The more you play, however, the more you realize that some strategy is necessary to ensure your survival.  Running away from (or jumping over) mobs is a viable option. Some mobs (and crates strewn about the levels) drop coins, which can be used in an in-game store to purchase power-ups. Treasure chests also might provide help (pray for the Speed Boost). The longer you survive, the more powerful you can become, but proper management of your extremely limited money is essential.  The "Rogue-lite" aspects of the game refer to the random item and mob placement, the platform surface (although it might as well be designed, as it doesn't feel any different from one game to the next) and sorta-kinda permadeath.
The Finer Points: The first thing I usually do in an Indie game is to turn off the music, but it's actually above par here; I enjoyed the combination of atmospheric/dub/pop present in FoD (it also played continuously for me, but there is at least one report of it playing intermittently). The power-ups are also creative and fun. The character models are interesting to look at, and the hand-drawn art can be charming; at its  best, it's reminiscent of The Binding of Isaac. I love the look of the shop, for example, although in higher resolutions (which cap out at 1600x900) items float above the shelves they should be resting on.  Unfortunately, the rest of the play field (such as the background and platform surface) is dull and uninspired, and the tiled patterns used don't gel with the hand-drawn art, bringing down the overall look of the game.  The character animations are fairly fluid, though.
A couple of other things to consider: The controls cannot be remapped, and gamepads don't seem to be implemented which, in a platformer, seems a bit of an oversight. Finally, there is only one character unlocked at the start of the game, which means no choice for the player (a rarity in "Rogue-like" games).
Things I'd like to see in a patch: Steam overlay integration. Trading cards and (especially) achievements; in a game this difficult, with this few player options, achievements would go a long way to making it feel worth playing. I'd also like to see a crouch option, but I suspect the entire enemy is hitboxed, and not just the weapon it uses. Another character option at the start of the game would be great, too; make the rest unlockable.  Different heights and gaps in the platform would definitely increase replay value, although I'm sure that would involved re-coding enemy AI as well as the play field, so I wouldn't really expect it.
All that said, however, the game is pretty much complete, and I enjoyed it once I realized it was deeper than it first appeared. It's something to pick up and play for short bursts when you want to beat the crap out of things and push yourself to do better "just one more time." It's priced about a buck too high, but FoD is simple and fun, and, at its current price of $5.99, less than the cost of a matinee ticket. Recommended.

I just bought this game earlier today, and so far it seems great. As a background, I'm a helicopter pilot IRL with about 300 hours, and I play a lot of helicopters in DCS and X-Plane. I've also played a lot of World of Tanks and other similar games, which you can SOMEWHAT compare this game to.
This game seems really great. It's very well made, and has very fun objectives. It is not a grind fest and there is no pay to win. If you would be interested in a game like World of Tanks but WAY better and with helicopters, I highly recommend this.
I have only two complaints, but both are being addressed. The first is that pvp matches are relatively small and hosted by a player, rather than a larger battle setup by a matchmaker. From what I understand the devs plan to implement larger battles with matchmaker in the future. It also seems like there's a relatively small player base but the game did just release yesterday and the number of players is skyrocketing even just in the last few hours. The second issue I have is the flight model. It's not bad by any means, it's actually rather good for a non-simulation game. It's just restricting, especially for someone like me who is very familiar with how a real helicopter handles. However, the devs also said they plan to increase the fidelity of the flight model.
The devs appear to be a very small team who are very responsive to their player base, and have done an incredible job considering how small they are. I can see them doing great things, especially once more people start playing
TLDR: Kinda like World of Tanks but way, way better, more in depth, and with helicopters. If you're curious, get it, it is worth it.

Standard, straightforward strategy game with turn-based squad battles in a cartoon presentation. Choose and upgrade several units, much like Might & Magic games. Leaders can equip enhancing gear as well. Nothing groundbreaking, but it certainly does the trick and has some close encounters.

While this game is very short, as you can tell by my total play time of 6 hours, it's a nice little strategy game to play if you're either new to this hex-based strategy game, or if you just don't have the time or commitment to play other games like Blackguards. Very nice to play in short bursts.
My gripes with Braveland is because it's too short. I suppose I was expecting some 20 hour game, more side-missions, or anything to prolong my play time, other than the Survival mode. Also, I'm not usually very good at strategy games, but I was able to beat Braveland on Hard my first time around, just to give a general idea how easy this game can be.
My verdict: Check it out if you got some spare change and want a very casual strategy game to play. If you're looking for something with a bit of a challenge though, I'd try something else.

Cute little turn based tactical game. Fairly basic tactics and quite repetetive but it's fairly brief and it warranted getting to the end. There's a little scope for varying your army build, you basically get 15 points with each unit type being worth from 1 to 5, and there being 7 units to choose from once you've unlocked them all. Over the course of the game as you level up you can purchase extra forces, and basic items that improve your skills. Again this is very simplified and you may as well just buy the most expensive (i.e. best) stuff. I found the heaviest tank unit to be woefully underpowered compared to the crossbow unit, especially with the power up triple shot action that the crossbow guys have, and the tank is also very slow, and can be tricky to position to get the best from his power up skill of attacking all surrounding hexes.
I'm pointing out what could be considered flaws here but I did enjoy playing it, and it was never intended to be a heavy thinking game anyway. The quick battles are neat and the constant stream of new stuff being just a few minutes away keeps you interested. This is a casual, easy playing game that you could easily beat over the course of a week on your lunch break.

It has been a while since a game has had me 'wtf'ing' all over the place, but Pony Island brought it back to life. This game is genius.
Basic breakdown is that you are trapped within some funky arcade machine that has gone vicious thanks to the devil himself deciding to be a programmer. Take the cover of the game.. Take what you expect the game to be and throw them out the window. Already as you begin, it's clear that something isn't right - Having to fix a broken and glicthy menu from the get go before you're able to commence the gameplay is a sign that the devil may not be as good of a programmer as he likes to think.
As the cursed player of this hellish demon-game, you get whisked around from a chaotic, glitchy, broken world to a cutesey, diabetes-inducing pastel nightmare, with random logic puzzles thrown in, to fix Satan's buggy code. As you guide your pony through the devil's glitchy game, you can catch brief glimpses of who your character used to be before they were killed and trapped in the game. The story is gritty, blurred and as twisty as the day is long. Basically, it's fantastic.
I feels as though I had to make an extra section *just* for gameplay because it's honestly that damn good. The ingenuity of the puzzles, the level designs and the text communication alone make it note worthy. Pony Island as a whole is magnificent and shows incredibly unique ideas put together insanely well. When something like this, running on such simple mechanics can set an atmosphere so well, it raises the bar for many other games to do the same.

This game is not what it seems to be, a game about ponies quickly evolves into a point and click adventure with gameplay interspersed in between, you come across a soul that's trapped just like you and you resolve to find a way to shut down this miserable game for good to free everyone and yourself from the eternal torment of endlessly playing and endlessly testing Pony Island. Meanwhile, the programmer, who is referred to as Lucifer here, does everything in his power to get you to stop breaking his game and asks you on many occasions to give up your soul to him. Nice.
It's really well put together and while the story is relatively simple, it feels like it goes much deeper than what you see on the surface, and it certainly well does as you delve into the game's coding and do everything you can to find out more about these secrets. Who is the Hopeless Soul? Who am I? What's going on? All that and more will be answered as you play on in this fourth-wall breaking adventure that attacks not only the protagonist but you, yourself.
So, good job, 'Daniel Mullins Games', you did good. Is this game worth the price tag at the moment? Perhaps, it's about £3.99 or your regional equivalent. I highly recommend you seek out the Game Jam version of this first as that version is sort of like a demo and will give you an idea of what goes on in there.

As a bit of a zombie game nut, I was glad to spot that the Rebuild series was coming on Kickstarter, so it didn't take much convincing for me to back this one.
Having finished the game's campaign, here's a quick summary of what I thought:
PROS:
+ Interesting setting with a humorous twist, clever writing
+ Solid, yet simple city management and tactical gameplay to counter the threat of the ever-growing undead horde, starvation, disease, hostile factions and crazy loners.
+ Multitude of random events with various outcomes
+ Loads and loads of characters to rebuild your post-apocalyptic utopia. Nice little personal touches with random background stories, perks and familial ties, feuds and friendships that form during gameplay.
+ Persistent retinue in the campaign. You can usually take 3 followers with you to the next map.
+ Factions are nicely unique from each other and sport different goals and motivations, which can be used to your advantage or depending on your gameplay, stir trouble with them and make them hate your guts.
+ Long campaign with various subplots
+ Research tree
+ Personal equipment to every character to customize them.
+ Nice illustrated graphics and clear interface and UI.
+ Replayability with the random map gen function.
CONS:
- Some game functions are not necessarily instantly apparent or even explained to the player. For example, the loss of stats on your retinue members for balancing reasons between maps in the campaign.
- The soundtrack gets a bit repetitive after a few hours.
- After every map, you have to research everything again and again and again...
- Turn-Based gameplay seems to work much better as opposed to the RTS timer, in which you have no idea when anybody is going to make a move and when.
- The factions have no memory of your previous engagements with them, be it in alliance, indifference or bloody warfare
- The last mission of the campaign can be a bit unrewarding storywise, considering the difficulty spike.
Overall, I'd say the game is definitely worth a look for anybody who enjoys city management and zombie games, a dash of humour and reliance on your judgement to make best out of all the resources you have at your disposal.
I also found the persistent retinue feature and survivor micromanagement very satisfying, although after the number of survivors climbs to dozens, it becomes quite hard to track the right people you're looking for without organizing the survivors into work gangs.
However dissatisfied I may have been by the outcome of the story, it was still a good journey, eventful and at times lots of fun, despite the ever-looming aspect of dying of starvation, zombie bites or having your neighbouring gang turn you into a link of sausages. The side quests and writing made it certainly worthwhile- fresh in memory is one event in my early campaigning, when I lost my treasured top hat of office to domestic intrique. Good times.
They make this game with their hearts, while they balance it with their toes.

If You Love City Games you need this Game...

Seeing where Sim City is going this is the light in the dark we needed. City Skylines is the perfect game for any  city-sim lovers.
Overview:
When you load the game for the first time who are greeted with a main menu that all you can pretty much do is load mods and create a new save. Once you click the new game button who are greeted with another menu that shows several differnt maps each with their own pros and cons, click a map and perpare for a loading screen. Once it is done loading you are now looking at your soon to be beautiful city. All you have is a simple highway connection a few thousand dollars and a small area to begin with. This game is hard in the management aspect. Mainting governmant services and keeping a postitive income will be leaving you with failed city after failed city till you get it just right.
Better than Sim City:
This game is miles ahead of sim city by several reasons. First, you can place districts on areas of your cities. Draw out a section of your city, name that district, and apply rules that only that part of the city follows. For example you can have it to where every building will have smoke alarms but it will cost you alot, or you could ban heavy trucks so no indusrtial veichles pass through you nice and preety neighborhodd. Next you can buy plots of land. You can buy 8 tiles of land making your building area 9 plots of land which is prettry huge in game. The buildings in this game is smaller in scale so you can fit more in a a even alrger map which leads to larger cities that can get out of control.
Mods and the Steam workshop:
Almost like every game on steam, this one has mods. Now when you buy the game it comes with two mods that you can enable. These are pretty much the sandbox mods, since there is no sandbox mode. They are unlimted money and unlock all buildings. Also the Steam workshop has shown continued support for the game which is a nice added bonus for content. These items in workshop can range from momunemts to how your houses get built.
DLC:
This game I has four DLC packs and they all do their own thing. One is about the snow, other the dark, or  you want a high tech city, or just like to see you city be completly destroyed by mother nautre they all unique. Now the price tag on some of them are little too much and I kinda wish we got them as free updates but what can we do we have the workshop.
Overall if you are looking for a good city-sim game this is the one, you are bound to have hours of fun and fustraton becuase citizens will die becuase they can not find the hospital that was built across the street from their house.

As you progress further into the game, you begin to realize that a story isnt really there. Instead, JazzPunk turns into a walking art gallery. This is my review for Braveland ; (6.5/10)
Storyline: The storyline is dull and unintresting (atleast for me) it's one of those turn-based basic games, where it's focused on the combat and character elements rather than on the levels of story.

Gameplay: Unlike the aspect of the story, the gameplay itself is enjoyable for a turn-based strategy game.  (8/10)
1- Character Elements -
@You can view each character's information which include: health, damage, defence , range of movement and number of turns. There is also a description of character abilities and what it's capable of (stunning/magic damage/healing etc)
@Level System: You level up by getting exp (obviously) by defeating and winning enemies.
@Main Character: You buy more units or upgrades with the coins you get, you can't upgrade your units and however, you cannot fight with your main character (you only fight with your 'squad' aka your units)
2- Combat-
The combat is fun and easy. You get tips in the start of the game to understand the basics, and then you will just get used to the combat and know what to do.
There are some points however, where you will have to move forward and fight weaker enemies instead of trying to beat an overwhelming enemy squad because your squad is not strong enough (which makes the game challenging.)
Gameplay Styles: (5/10)
3 Difficulties (Set to Easy/Normal/Hard)
Easy is too easy , Normal is challenging enough and Hard oh well, it's for those of you who want to hit your head in the computer in order to win each match even if you have for example 5 units and your enemies have 500.

hours of gameplay either so it's just for fun for your free time) - (4/5)

Ah, Braveland. It's hard to know what to say about it. It is not a bad game. I'm tempted to call it good. But I'm not going to do that, and I wouldn't recommend it to people.
At $4.99, Braveland seems reasonably priced. On sale, it might even sound like a steal. But you're going to get a few hours out of it, and there's nothing remarkable about those few hours.
There's nothing really awful about Braveland. The graphics are slightly unnervingly Fisher Price, but they're effective and the backgrounds look nice. There are only a few songs, and they sound competent and appropriate. The interface is fine. The mechanics are... well, balanced and kind of standard for this kind of game.
So what's the problem?
There's not much depth to the battles, and there's not much to it besides battles. You pick up a modest variety of classes, and can bring up to five with you: archers, healers, knights, scouts, etc. Their roles are fairly obvious and they do them well enough. But you can really use whatever combination you want, and the gameplay won't change much at all.
The story is... well, the dialog is spelled and formatted correctly and does tell a pretty straightforward story about soldiers, bandits, villagers and the like. No one really says anything very interesting, but the conversations are short and inoffensive. The most personality you get out of the game is that bandits are dime-a-dozen jerks, and your peasant friend is a bit of a coward. There's a hero, who doesn't actually fight, and annoys me a little to look at him strutting around the world map as though he's helping. Technically he provides stat bonuses to the rest of the team by leveling up, but he mostly just speaks for the team and collects power-ups.
There's no real replay value to the campaign, but there's a Survival mode where you can play battle to battle, losing characters and buying new ones, and see how far you get. I played around with it a little, and it might add a bit of life to the game if you wind up loving it. So, there's a bit of hope for getting more play out of the game at least.
I have played a lot of Flash games in my days, on sites like Newgrounds - RPGs, tower defense, strategy games, action, etc.. Braveland feels very much like one of those games. The look, the feel, the length, the design choices and the options the player is given. Indeed, I feel like I've played Bravelands many times already. Except usually, when I play this kind of game, it's free. Often, it's also got something more novel or fun about it.
Normally, it's probably not good to get lost in the weeds talking about free vs. paid gaming in a review like this. I guess all I'm saying is, Bravelands is a dime a dozen kind of game that you see all over the internet, and even if it's got a bit of polish and isn't awful, it's hard for me to justify anyone spending their money on it. For a few dollars more, there are lots of really unique, memorable games on Steam.
If you just want to blow through some clean and simple RPG battles for a few hours, you probably won't hate this game. If it looks like it might be really awesome, it's not. It's just not. Look at the other reviews. A lot of the positive reviews say that it's short, it's easy, there's not a lot to it, it would be good for kids, etc.. Hardly ringing endorsements. If this game were getting 1 to 10 ratings instead of Yes or No, I don't imagine they'd be all that high. Nobody really loves this game. Everyone just agrees it's okay. If you want an okay game, buy Bravelands.

Overall crysis 2 makes up for most of the crysis 1 & warhead short comings. Controls are smoothed out making the annoying radial menu obsolete. We're no longer killing north koreans which feels a lot better. And gameplay can really allow you to play how you like.
There are chavets though. Although I can't blame this game directly, Krytek simply dropped the ball on picking up where Crysis 1 left off. That massive cliffhanger at the end of Crysis 1 was never even addressed. Moreover, only one of the characters from Crysis 1 even returns at all and he isn't one you got to play as. Its like they decided to scrap almost all the story progression and start over. You never hear about the marines you played as in either crysis 1 or warhead, and the giant battle they are about to embark on at the end of that game (but is subsequently cut) is never even mentioned. You know that Prophet survives it, because he is in this game. But really thats all there is. At the very least we could have had an epic cutscene that wraps up that hanging storyline.
But instead we start this game with nothing properly resolved. I found that to be extremely annoying as the best part of Crysis 1 was actually this (late to bloom) antogonist of an mysterious alien race. In this title almost all the rules are changed as to what these aleins are or what they do. The only thing left in common is the ice shard bullets they use. However, they are minimized and the whole frost/ice thing is replaced with a locus spore/disease cloud. This felt a lot like trying to pander to the zombie fanboys just to get them to buy the game. There are still the big questions hanging out there on why these aliens are now squids but maybe that will get resolved in the next installment. Given the history of the franchise, i'm not holding my breath. They are squids just because.
Crysis 2 did a few things right as far as the story goes, this time around. There was a point where you see the final alien hive thing and you're in a helicopter flying towards it. This was the exact moment Crysis 1 abruptly ended, so I was expecting the credits to roll here... but to my surprise we actually got to land and have this last level. Even better you have the option to playing this last area as you see fit. I decided to do a stealth approach and only killed the 4 aleins you absolutely have to to trigger the final cutscene. If i went in guns blazing the whole area was crawling to the teeth with huge guns and huge aliens. The option to play it either way was pretty great. The ending was a bit odd but felt fairly well rounded. They wrapped up the NYC storyline and opened up the game to sequels with other "infected" areas around the globe. What was important is that at the end you felt like the whole game you were battling to save NYC and you accomplished that goal. That was a feel-good ending.
I did find the changes to the aliens acceptable, but annoying. To expand... The aliens in the first game were very interesting, very dramatic and really quite unique. Although some aleins resembled things from matrix and other popular culture, these designs were tried and true. I found this fact charming, not bothersome in the first game. In this game it seems like there was an executive decision to make Crysis a sci-fi story that stood on its own feet. Although the end result was pretty good in the end, it didn't improve anything from the original. The whole "squid" theme really seemed forced. I felt like the fact that everything had tenticles from the aliens themselves to their guns and buildings...felt too much like the designers were like "SEE THIS IS UNIQUE! WE ARE UNIQUE" and I wasn't feeling it. To understand what this actually is... imagine if humans didn't drive cars but instead moved around in these crawling contraptions that looked like hands. Buildings weren't cubes, but instead all looked like human heads. This is what we get from these aleins here. Its too much.
I feel like this game was over all leaps and bounds better than Crysis 1, even if it wasn't as awe-inspiring. Controls were great, upgrades felt meaningful and weapons ramped up in great ways. The story feels self contained and ends with the feeling that you've accomplished something, even if it is very obvious that it was trying really really hard to be a unique franchise.
Over all: its a great game. Who knows about the next one, but its better than the first two.

TL:DR – First person shooter with limited RPG elements. The gameplay is more linear than the 2 previous Crysis games and you may actually find it a lot easier because of the new nanosuit upgrades. Excellent game 9/10.
If you’ve played Crysis and/or Crysis 2, you’ll know that millions of years ago, an alien race placed a huge amount of war machines deep underground with tunnels leading all over the world. After an elite team of nanosuited soldiers explored the alien presence on an remote island, the only character to return is Prophet, the team leader who kind of went crazy at the end. Now you find out that Prophet wasn’t actually crazy, but had a secret mission to gather as much info as possible about the aliens now known as the Ceph. Unfortunately for Prophet, his extreme exposure to the Ceph has contaminated him with the Spore, a kind of bio weapon that the Ceph have unleashed on New York to wipe out all the humans.  You take on the role of Alcatraz, a Force Recon marine sent into the quarantined New York City to help Prophet, and you end up taking on Prophet’s nanosuit when he falls.
Unlike the first couple Crysis games, the nanosuit isn’t just a tool; it’s a major plot point. The suit’s super advanced computer software is working on a way to combat the spore and save the world, not just kick alien♥♥♥♥♥ Your main nanosuit powers have been streamlined since the previous games and now have 2 main “modes” (armor and stealth). Instead of having Speed and Strength modes, those powers are now integrated into your actions. For example, you can pick up a large object and toss it without switching to strength, or you can use stealth (cloak) and speed at the same time. By the way, the stealth mode is probably overpowered in the single player campaign. You can turn invisible and sneak past about 90% of the enemies in the game if you want (no reason not to sneak past the human enemies unless you like gunning people down).
However, when it comes to alien enemies, the best solution is peace through overwhelming firepower. There are more than a dozen different weapons to choose from, and you can carry 2 of them at once (5 if you count the “disposable” weapons). Like in the previous Crysis games, you can customize nearly all of the main weapons with attachments such as silencers, scopes, and extended magazines. If you want to do things quietly though, just sneak up behind the enemy and do an instant stealth kill with your melee. It’s not only silent, it’s also a good way to pick up the nano catalyst that aliens leave when they die. The nano catalyst is like money that you can use at any time to buy upgrades for the suit. There aren’t many upgrades to choose from, but they can be quite a boost (and they carry over to your next playthroughs, so future campaigns are a lot easier).
Pros:
+Excellent graphics, and the game is actually less demanding than the previous Crysis games in terms of hardware requirements. The game is taking place in the city, so there’s no waving grass and tree foliage to stress your graphics card.
+The story is decent though I know a bunch of people didn’t like it. You get a nice variety of enemies and a large variety of ways to dispose of them. Crysis 2 isn’t open world, so the story and gameplay is pretty linear. You don’t need to drive all over an island like in Crysis 1.
Cons:
-Like I mentioned earlier, the stealth mode is probably too good. You can stay invisible for about 20 seconds and just run past all the enemies. This is especially true after you’ve beaten the game at least once because you won’t need to fight aliens for nano catalyst (you’ll already have bought all the upgrades).
-It’s a hefty installation size (about 14 gb) for a game that I beat in about 7 hours.
Overall, the game is great fun and you can replay it a few times before you really get bored of it. Online multiplayer requires an additional sign up (it’s not through Steam).

Crytek Studios Continues the series optimizing the interface and mixing up the story with its third extension to the Crysis experience. Crysis 2 Maximum Edition is a great example of a first person shooter that mixes up traditional style FPS with amazing dynamics.
Crysis 2 Maximum Edition starts off with a group of marines in flight to New York City in order to support military operations against alien invaders. The mission goes horribly wrong as submarine is blaster out of the water almost immediately leaving the entire crew marooned without communications; yet, it’s shortly lived because as soon as the crew emerges all but one are destroyed by an alien aircraft. It is up to you Alcatraz (a name they chose for obvious reasons) to continue on with a mission handed down to you as a legacy. You must push through the bowels of New York City fighting against humans and aliens alike in order to succeed! With the Nano Suit there is nothing that can truly stand in your way.
Crysis 2 is a relatively long campaign depending on your gameplay style and difficulty preferences. The game has a mediocre difficulty curve at best making the hardest game mode relatively easy for a seasoned gamer. Regardless if you decide for a slower paced game knock the difficulty up to Post-Human Warrior otherwise take a lower difficulty and just enjoy the ride. The campaign has an amazing depth in the level varieties and methods of completion. There are about eighteen levels which vary in how you can play them as well as the various opponents, options, and surprises within; although, there are actually only a few different enemies the way they are mixed and how they are placed make them seem like new posing challenges every step of the way. The game is played with a combination of sequences where you are either alone in the dark or surrounded by marine allies. Overall the campaign is relatively fun and definitely has high replay value due to the dynamics of the gameplay.
The controls are relatively simple which makes this game easy and entertaining to play. There were no points during the game where I was annoyed with gameplay elements, such as camera angles or controls. Hiding behind cover is very useful as you can pop over without having to stand up simply by using your sights. Unlike in the first Crysis there are really only two suit modes: Armor and Stealth. Power takes up both strength and speed and activates automatically when you hold space to jump or shift to run. This makes those abilities a lot more useful as I noticed in the first Crysis I never used super strength or speed just because of how inconvenient it was to switch mid battle then switch back. Just like the original there are loads of customizations for each weapon, but they’ve pushed it even further offering way more weapon choices and tons of different gameplay strategies; although I didn’t grab them all I believe there are about 20 weapons ranging from pistols, assault rifles, light machine guns, rockets, sniper rifles, explosives, and more. So depending on your gameplay you can either sneak with stealth and use silenced weapons or run and gun with light machine guns and armor. One of the major additions to Crysis 2 is the Nano Suit upgrades which allow you to optimize the suit and enhance your gameplay strengths. There are four different brackets which each contain three upgrades, but you can only have one active in each slot meaning if you buy all three for Armor you can only use one of the upgrades at a time.
Crysis 2 Maximum Edition was a fantastic game with loads of dynamics offering high replay value. If you are a fan of FPS this is a great game to buy and play. I honestly buy all my games at 75% off, but this would have been worth spending the whole $29.99 on, which is rare for me to say the least. One of the great things about Crysis is you can choose your play style, you can go in quietly and assassinate your enemies like Sam Fisher or you can run in like Space Marine and gun down your foes like hordes of orcs. The campaign has a large number of levels which provide a great experience.
Pros:
+Loads of weapons to choose from with dynamic customizations: Grenade launchers, shotgun attachments, silencers, semi/full fire, red dot, reflex, sniper, laser attachment, and more.
+Awesome levels which are semi-destructible; use an HMG to blast up a wall near an opponent in order to flank them out (does not apply to all walls).
+Cool vehicles, although you don’t use them much the tank missions and the Humvees are a fun aspect of the game.
+Awesome suit customization, take your suit and make it for your gameplay strategy by purchasing armor enhancement augmentations or optimizing your stealth.
+Suit strength and speed are auto activated rather than require a special mode to use.
+Loads of different levels which take you all over New York City taking you through buildings, underground, through streets, under water, or into parks.
+Good enemy AI, unlike the first one where the enemies would let you stealth shoot one and then stealth and walk two steps to the left and repeat these ones are a bit smarter. They will detect you and even flank you if they are high enough in numbers.
+Good story although I have a con about this as well the story is great and is highly intriguing.
Cons:
-Although I did enjoy the story my major con is how it doesn’t continue with the elements from Crysis, and Crysis Warhead. In fact it kind of transforms into something else, not necessarily worse but just different. In the original the enemies were robotic and manufacturing themselves through a facility on an uncharted island. Yet in Crysis 2 the enemies were organic and creating themselves from the living tissue of infected humans. This completely changes how the story even seems logical, in the first Crysis they were in hibernation deep underground while in this one it seems to be the same yet they are organic and sentient?
-Checkpoints were few and far between at some points. This was more a nuisance than anything, there were points where you’d fight for about 20-30 minutes and then die on the last enemy before a checkpoint. Resetting you back thirty minutes earlier and making you go “ugh”.
-Some checkpoints were triggered before cinematics, this meant if you died you were launched back prior to a cinematic and had to watch it again without being able to skip.
-Apparently multiplayer does not work for this game – I personally don’t play multiplayer but if you do then this may be a deal breaker for you.

What I liked:
- Good progression where you choose which path you take (even thou it's limited for no real good reason). Same goes for the skills & stuffs you buy which I loved.

- Good and simple boss fight.

What I disliked:
- The gameplay is sometimes annoying (even thou it's almost there). The multi dash is just a bit too slow and too tight where sometimes you'll miss it while you are sure you did it well. The dash doesn't allow you to go through ennemies so you get often stuck in them failing your dodge. It also does not have invincibility frames even thou there is a skills to block projectiles while dashing, nothing exist melee or ranged non-projectile attakcs.This is a important point because the fun of fighting in this game resolve a lot around dodging, which is great, but failed at it by constrainting its players into a unresponsive and lack utility behind it. It was probably done this way for balancing purposes but I think it's a mistake to prioritze balance over the player experience if it's really the reasoning behind the dash mechanics.
- The lack of originality. There is very few moments where I was astonished, intrigued or appricated the ingenuity of the game.
- The level design was in some part intresting but for the most part it wasn't really above average. There was too much of those moments where you are locked into a small rooms and a bunch of ennemies spawn to attacks you. The game was crying for more geniously designed levels and a smarter ennemies placements and diversity.
- Lack of contents. 17 hours and I almost did everything in the game says it all. The game is too short and lack contents. I was at least hoping for a game double its size when I think of a 2D action game like that.
