Rebuild 3 is a true sequel to Rebuild Mobile and Rebuild 2 (Flash game). If you really want to know what this game is about go to any number of flash sites and try Rebuild 2 or download Rebuild for IOS. This is basically the same game but with a lot more elements. It added a degree of polish, factions, multiple cities, a campaign, a more fleshed-out RPG system and more. I think this game is a ton of fun as it lets you manage a group of survivors in a simulation/4x style game. The diplomacy is very weak but the other portions of the game are fun. You basically assign your survivors on a mission and based on their skills, equipment and team they may succeed or fail.
Be warned this game is a massive time sink and the entire game does take place on a map screen (similar to CK2 or EU).

An honest improvement from Rebuild 2. Graphics are phenomenal, the events are sparse and diverse enough that I don't encounter the same three or four through every playthrough, and there is some pretty interesting character development and storywriting. The games a bit unbalanced and easy to beat if you know how to work the system (example: stack all your soldiers onto one stack and wreak havoc on any enemy factions to eliminate them), but that just adds to some of the zaniness of the game.
I have to add that there was a very interesting story arc involving the Pig Farmers when (SPOILERS AHEAD) one of my citizens was captured in an ice cream truck. After some investigation, I found my way to the pig farmer's pig house. What followed was an actually interesting and well-written event about how my leader went all the way back to the freezer section, found the missing citizen, and discoverd that the PigFarmers were cannibals. My leader then threw a knife at the main leader of the Pig Farmers and the other captives attacked while my leader and several others escaped. It was completely unexpected, but it was so engaging that it basically embodied Rebuild's ability to tell a story, which is something I look forward to in games.
Recommendation: Buy the hell out of this game. It is a 100% solid investment.

This game, from a competative, online fighting-genre perspective, is purely amazing. The simple, yet rich and varied combat system (utilising an analogous "rock-paper-scissors" design), compliments the wide variety of selectable characters well, and results in some of the most engrossing and intense online matches I have ever had in the genre.
While the primary game mechanics work almost flawlessly together, this game does have its negative aspects. The character progression, particularly at higher levels, is slow and somewhat arduous. A similar comment can be made for the rate at which you acquire loot, gear and in-game currency, and obviously this is to encourage the purchase of in-game currency. Additionally, when new characters are introduced, there are typically teething periods and the game needs minor to moderate rebalancing from time-to-time, however the combat system can overcome these issues if you know your character well enough.
While there are some notably negative aspects to this title (such as an extremely weak single player campaign with which, quite frankly, they just shouldn't have even bothered), these really are made almost irrelevant due to the fact that what works well, works almost perfectly. To top it all off, the graphical fidelity and sound design are second to none, and setting up a round so that you can end the round by performing one of the many, amazingly animated executions at your characters disposal is extremely addictive - followed up by a taunt or two... and you just feel bad♥♥♥♥♥
This game will reside on my Steam Favorites list for some time... I just love it.

This is probably the worst Resident Evil game, tied with ORC.
Starting with the gameplay. It's a mess, you can slide, make jumps to the right or left, roll over and throw yourself on your back. Besides the slide move I've never used any of these moves during my first playthrough, because they feel so unnecessary and out of place. Gunplay is downright horrible. You have a crosshair with a dot inside, which will jump all over the place after you shot your gun. The problem is that the dot will stay at a random position inside the crosshair, it won't be at the center. The recoil of a shot only pushes your crosshair upwards, guns feel like toys without any force.
Did I mention it doesen't have licensed guns? Capcom said that fans of RE4 requested more realistic guns, That is why RE5 had so many awesome realistic guns (except for the upgrades of course). In RE6 we get guns called "Bear Commander" or "Wing Shot". Resident Evil was always fairly realistic when it came to guns.
QTE's everywhere, you can disable most of them but why did they even add them in the first place then?
The vehicle segments are horrible aswell. There's too many of them and the controls are super awkward. Fyling a jet or helicopter feels like playing table hockey.
Now for the graphics. Yet another step backwards from RE5. The only thing that looks decent are the character models, everything else ranges from 2002 to 2008 level graphics. Gun models are super low-poly, same goes for most texture resolutions.
Don't believe me? Check these out:

I don't want to bash a game due to it's graphics, but considering that RE5 had much better graphics...there's no excuse for that, Capcom.
Furthermore, we get some
, like pillars in front of consoles (see pic) or corridors that lead to nowhere.
Now for the worst part...the plot. Seriously, you thought RE5's plot was bad with Jill's mind control and Wesker becoming some god complex villain? Trust me, this game puts "bad writing" on a whole new level. The dialogue, the cutscenes, the characters...just everything. It's not even "funny" bad like the voice acting of the first game, it's just plain bad. Chris is now a drinker who talks about nothing but Ada and Leon's voice seems halfway faded. I miss the "No thanks, bro." kind of guy. I think the character that stayed the most true to it's former self was HANNIGAN, and she has like 4 minutes of screen time.
Now I'll talk about the decent parts of the game.
The best part of the game is the mercenaries mode. There you just aim for the highest score possible, without the stupid plot being constantly showed into your face or dumb vehicle segments.
Personally, I still prefer RE5's and even Mercs3D (yep, that game for the Nintendo 3DS) mercenaries modes over RE6's because of the basic gameplay, but from a mechanical standpoint (like killing a specific amount of enemies in a specific time window will trigger a boss to spawn) you can't deny that RE6's mercs is the most developed one (thanks to Dfactor for some explanation).
Next thing is the melee system. Now, I'm not saying that it's good, I'm saying that it's okay-ish.
While it can be fun to throw an enemy at another one and seeing them both smashing into a table, it just feels out of place and even overpowered. You can melee ANYTIME, which is my biggest point of criticism on the melee system. It's just way too focused on melee combat overall, which makes me think "Resident Fighter VI" would have been a more appropriate name.
Lastly, the amount of content. My first playthrough of all campaigns took me about 20 hours. Now that would be a big + if the game itself wasn't bad, and if I didn't have to force myself through the last two campaigns.
That's the end of this review. If you really want to try this game, then get it during a sale.

Getting into Rocksmith, I never touched a guitar before.  Those instructional DVD's out there don't help you learn at all, really.  Neither do YouTube videos.  How does the video know if you're doing it right or not?  It's such a passive experience.  And paying for lessons requires scheduling stuff, paying somebody, etc.
So that's where Rocksmith comes in.  Starting out, it assumes you know nothing about guitars at all, which I really liked.  Which I liked, because I didn't.  So I went out and bought a cheap beginners guitar.  Starting out, you are going to be your own limitation, not your guitar.  So spending big bucks doesn't make sense if you're just learning the strings like I was.
I got myself a $100 Dean Vendetta XM, it has pretty good reviews on Amazon and people on YouTube seem to really rock out with them using proper amps and stuff.  To play Rocksmith though, you need the Rocksmith 2014 Real Tone Cable (avail on Amazon) to connect your guitar to your PC which costs about $47, on top of the price of the game on Steam.  So if you already have a guitar, this game is about a $80 investment @ full price.
I know, the price of this game is really starting to add up if you don't already own any of this stuff.  But on the upside, the Rocksmith Cable also works in other applications for PC, and works on console too.  So if you're like me and you don't even have an amp yet... between this app and other software like Guitar Rig (the Rammfire plugin is pretty awesome!) you can have alot of fun learning and playing electric guitar at the fraction of the price of paying for a Guitar, Lessons, and an amp.  But hey, hobbies in general... whether it's automotive, homebrewing, whatever... are never cheap.
When you first start out in Rocksmith 2014, it will show you graphically how to tune your guitar for the specific song you're playing, and test string to verify it's good to go.  It'll have you play the easiest song on the lowest difficulty... which is usually 1 note at a time all played on one string, typically the fat one at the top since it's easiest to hit.  As you play, if you don't make mistakes, it'll gradually increase the difficulty of the song until you start to screw up.  Then it knows where to start with you.
For each song, it has a "Riff Repeater" which is basically a feature where it selects a small portion of the song, and slows it down for you so you can get used to moving around on the fretboard and hitting the right notes.  Once you start getting it right, it speeds up, and as you get better at that... it adds extra notes, then extra strings and chords and stuff.  Then it starts getting into harmonics, bends, etc.
But what's really cool about Rocksmith 2014 on PC in particular is that you can download custom songs called CDLC (Custom DLC) from
.  These are user-made songs that you can add to the game for free.  Don't get the wrong idea though... this isn't a way of pirating the extensive DLC library this game has on Steam.  You won't find the official DLC songs on that website, it just has a huge library of songs that
.  So if you're like me and you're a huge Rammstein fan, but you're disappointed that they aren't in this game even as a DLC option, that's where you go if you want to rock out with their songs.  Just be careful setting off pyro in your living room.
Hobbies, regardless of what they are... aren't cheap.  But this is the cheapest and most fun way of learning how to play the electric guitar, even though it is more expensive than your typical videogame ($80 assuming you have a guitar already).  If you already know how to play guitar, I think this is a much more fun and interactive way of playing music than using tabs.  The built-in distortion effects (which vary by song, and in some cases - within parts of the same song) are certainly awesome too and you'll get closer to sounding like the real thing in a way that's more economical and easier than getting amp setups with pedals and stuff.
Definitely worth the money even though it costs more than Call of Duty.

"Crysis 2," where Master Chief travels to New Vegas and encounters The Flood.
I swear, that's what this game felt like.
"Crysis 2" borrows a number of tropes from sci-fi and sci-fi gaming, and that's not necessarily a bad thing. It feels like Crytek was pretty appreciative and respectful about how they borrowed from other stories, and that's something I can appreciate.
In terms of visual design, this offering is really quite impressive. The environments are huge and detailed, even though your traversal of those environments can be a bit limited at times. (Much like "Crysis" and "Crysis Warhead," where there was a sprawling island in front of you...and lots of mountains or cliffs which prevented you from going too far afield.) What's even more jaw-dropping is the impression that all of the hugeness probably had to be built (largely) by hand. A natural environment lends itself to certain kinds of procedural generation, whereas a ruined city is something that demands much more manual crafting.
Where the game does not truly impress is in how it all knits together as a whole.
The story is actually a pretty good "yarn," but the telling of it is a little clumsy and not quite paced in the right way. The acting tends to be wooden, and what really ought to come out "in game" tends to be rendered instead as exposition over "cheap" cutscenes. I call them cheap because most of them are just "tactical overview" videos or "nanosuit rebooting as it struggles with alien strangeness" sequences. In a certain way, the presentation ends up giving a person the impression that it serves mostly to cover up the bulk of loading the next level. It all ends up being a little disjointed, and there's no emotional core. Even when you do meet up with the actual characters in the game, they quickly go back to being little more than voices with Internet connections.
The basic gameplay is pretty good, with you having to balance your suit's limited power with what you're trying to achieve. The stealth energy management returns to good effect, with you having to think about where you can get to before your cloak drops and you become easy to spot. The ability to customize the suit's upgrades to your preferred playstyle is a nice touch.
However, the gameplay is only "pretty good." It's not stellar. The weapons generally lack punch, especially against the aliens. While this does encourage you to think tactically, it also tends to punish you disproportionately for when you inevitably do get into a full-on fight. Further, the overall lack of hitting power combines with the long spaces between checkpoints in an unfun way. Combat tends to be a relatively slow-paced, repetitive, hit-n-hide grind...which, if you screw up, affords you the opportunity to do that grind ALL OVER AGAIN. AGAIN.
It's not like the "Halo" series, where combat was dynamic and entertaining - and even dying had an element of fun, because it tended to be so over the top. In comparison to that experience, "Crysis 2" feel like a chore. To be brutally honest, I was tired of the game by the end.
I also have to ding the "stealth kill" mechanic. Coming from "Far Cry 4" and "Blood Dragon" to the "Crysis" series, I definitely felt that not having a takedown system subverted the stealth aspects of the game. When I saw that "Crysis 2" had added its own brand of takedowns, I was initially elated. That elation quickly faded, though, as I experienced how finicky and unforgiving the stealth kill system is. The radius for it to work is miniscule, with a very sharp "falloff." That is, it's easy to find yourself in the transition range where a tiny bit of movement is all it takes to change "stealth kill" to "melee." It's far too simple to end up doing something you didn't expect to do, and even if you do end up initiating a stealth kill, your cloak drops for the duration of the animation. It turns out that stealth kills aren't all that stealthy at all. You are very likely to be seen and "lit up" by the unfortunate enemy's buddies, which is a pretty dangerous situation.
I DO recommend the game because, for its flaws, it's still an interesting way to spend about 10 hours or so. It's not a bad game at all - it just isn't a genre defining title, because it sometimes gets in its own way. I say, give it a shot when it's on sale, and enjoy the enjoyable bits.

Note that I'm not big on multi-player for fps games, so this review will pertain primarily to the story and technical aspects of Black Ops 3. Though I will get around to updating about the zombie horde mode. That said.
One belief I have is a game should be able to stand up on just it's single player alone. Black Ops 3 manages this, a bit wobbly in some spots, but stands solid for the most part. The story picks up some time after the events of Black Ops 2 and contains story content from the first two games that feel organic to the story, if the story made any real sense. The pieces all fit like a warped jigsaw puzzle, with funky exposition the player can feel lost for a majority of the story. Whether this is intentional or not, I leave to the subjective side of things. But otherwise the game continues the underlying narrative of how the mind is affected in warfare and the advantages and disadvantages of technologies role in both the public and private worlds. Though cliche, the story manages to not lose itself entirely to entire levels set in a surreal reality muddled with pseudo-science.
On the technical side, the game performed quite well. With only two real hiccups which consist of an entirely random ctd and one game breaking glitch which in which the AI seemed to forget just what it was doing. Frame drops only occured in a small handful of areas which quickly stopped after seconds. However the user interface feels very much designed for console without being reworked for a mouse and keyboard setup which ruins the pacing throughout the game. The in combat menu to select your special abilites is designed for analog stick controllers, wasting precious seconds in the heat of combat to choose an ability. As for combat itself, this honestly feels like a game that just happens to have the Call of Duty IP attached to it.

Talking about other aspects, a lot of people say that the game is clunky, and that the game's controls are bad, but I'm willing to look past that, as 1. For its time, the original installment of the Tomb Raider series was a revolutionary game that not only helped cover more ground for the action-oriented genre, but also provided a paradigm shift for the games that feature a female protagonist as the lead, if not sole character. Lara Croft, in essence, is the Indiana Jones of the do-or-die relic hunter's world, prior to Indy's golden spotlight being usurped by Nathan Drake of the "Uncharted" series.
The game elements of the original still provide exceptional nostalgic value for those who have played and beaten the game before, whether for only a rented fling or a repetitive display of skilled prowess. Pushing onward through Incan ruins only to discover a hidden world complete with a showdown with a Tyrannosaurus Rex is certainly enough for an action-seeking gamer to polish the edge of his/her seat and say, "that's pretty awesome. What's next?"
Although this catalyst of the series is not exactly education friendly, since somehow the names of Neptune and Thor show up in Greek ruins, the focus of the game overall is utilizing puzzle solving skills and preparation techniques as a means to survive the perils and pitfalls, find the artifacts, and inadvertently save the world from an ancient power-hungry demigod.
Despite the archaic quality of the graphics, when compared to more modern games, Tomb Raider I still has yet to ever lose its overall value. The Tomb Raider series still runs strong, even with the most recent installment unnervingly having the exact same name as the first installment with no alteration (which would certainly explain Steam's decision to label the first three titles with Roman numerals). The series maintains its streak of popularity because of how groundbreaking the very first game actually was when it was first released in 1996. Lara Croft became one of the many bright-shining stars in the gaming universe, and playing this game will easily exhibit why.

It's difficult to criticize this game but I'm going to try.
We have fallen in love with the mechanics of gaming history and the interfaces used to navigate designed worlds. This game is about the narrative and its mechanic conceived together. Springing from the long flat fellow reminds me of the springs in Sonic.
Here, levels create chapters of narration about the inner psychology of shapes with different traits. The world contains little live-and-learn mechanics to advance the plot at a bookish pace. For me, I'd have preferred a tighter story. It went on. And on. Eventually I played through out of spite.
Thomas Was Alone is a successful experiment with the Unity engine, a kind of test of the engine if I understand interviews with the publisher correctly. A course study, then, that we needn't put on our essential lists. What's more promising is what's next from Mike Bithell.
I hesitate to 'not recommend' this game, but if it helps to balance the average on Steam than I side with not purchasing it for the purpose of utility.

TLDR: Fun game worth being in your library, great mental exercise, requires patience.  Chess + CCG, will have a few bad matches every now and then (just ignore them).
REVIEW:
Pros:
-In general, fast paced matches that don't last as long as Hearthstone and can be friendly for those who are on the go or only have 20-30 minutes to spare.
-Collectable Card Game + Grid-based turn tactics provides a worthwhile and lasting fun game
-The pace to get gold is almost 100 a day, so basically a booster a day, so you don't have to shell out money.
-Crafting system to craft the cards you want, although it may be slow to get "spirit" at first.
Cons:
-While not pay to win, you may be stuck in the lower divisons while people who have better cards sift to their respective ranks.  I'm personally fine by it, but after your initial fun runs out, it may be better to just be patient and grab your daily gold rewards from quests and slowly get booster packs (aka spirit orbs).  So while this game is a quick pick-up game, if you get tired of slowly getting new cards it may not be your cup of tea.
Overall a nice free game that'll maybe satiate your fix on CCG or turn based tactics for a while.
Further insights:
This game is not only a CCG but the other half is a chess game, which helps to equalize what deck you make.  Patience is not only needed in fighting, but also in:
-acquiring knowledge of what other decks are out there
-Learning the mechanics (for example dispelling can be very important but what you bring in your deck to dispel (silence/nullify minions etc.) can really matter, as minions can dispel or you can cast a spell.  Some minions require you to physically move near the enemy you want to dispel to work hence the chess aspect while others can be casted and ignore the chessboard.)
-Acquiring spirit to craft.  What really helps is every now and then you'll get a "prismatic" (foil/holographic) card that may not be useful, so you can salvage it and get more spirit than a normal card
-All in all, to address the negative reviews, yes, it'll take a while to acquire some much needed cards, but counterplay makes this game doable so that you can casually complete quests to acquire about a booster in a day or two.  Very casual friendly so it doesn't hurt to add this game into your library.
-As for the cards you start out with, learning not only each faction's uniqueness but also the neutral faction that all factions can use really is important.  For example, when I started out I noticed I'd get whooped by huge threats or an opponent would summon a seemingly OP card.  Using a dispelling minion or a removal card can equalize it especially if you manage your mana and board space right.  While you do lose to obviously someone with better cards, the fun is in the fights with someone who may only possess a few cards better than you (the fight is still doable).

At first glance, it seems like a complete rip off of hearthstone. it has the same mana mechanic, it has the same card system, it has the same shop, except bigger. And it has foil cards, which serve no real purpose as I've seen yet, except to be disenchanted for more dust... i mean spirit...
Yes, at first glance, this review might also seem skewed to be against this game, you would be wrong.
While as of this moment, Songhai faction is very strong, the game does seem to try to be balanced. A bit 'more' balance would be nice, as well as some other avenues to utilize cards that I can only assume will be implimented later on.
This game actually draws more from Fire Emblem. For those commanders out there who, like me, enjoyed spending an hour on one mission, to do a 'perfect' run, where backstabs reigned supreme and the rock paper scissors of spears swords and so on got our blood boiling in all the good ways.
Well... you may not be disappointed too much by this game. While it is still 'early' since so far, as of this review, there's only one expansion to the 'Core' set of cards, which I call Shurima~ There is a backstab mechanic, opening mechanics like in hearth, spells and special abilities like in FE and Hearth.
Overall, it does have a lot to offer, and it 'DOES NOT LIE' when refering to itself as a ccg with a strategy spin, I would greatly reccomend this game to anyone who likes card games, or strategy. The pixel art is not too bad honestly. it reminds me a lot of the Undertale attempts. So far, the only frustration new players might face, is asking themselves if they should save up for packs from the shop, or use gold for Gauntlet Runs (Gauntlet is basically Arena) the rewards are not too bad, in that you get Spirit for crafting, and usually a core pack along with gold.
As long as the people behind this game pay attention to community feedback, and keep adding things for us to buy, and new cards for us to test strategies with, I can see this game lasting quite a while.
My one big wish for this game, would be cooperative play, with a friend. 2v2... that would be so amazing if they could pull that off. Perhaps doubling the board size, or something. But if they did that, I would be so happy.

The melee units are all on the same spectrum, with fast, weak units on one end and slow, strong units on the other.  The ranged units are similar, and it seems like the designers went out of their way to make the game completely balanced so that there are no wrong choices.
Which means there are no right choices either; nothing you do deployment-wise or unit management-wise has any real effect on the battles.  I suppose you could decide to intentionally damage your chances (ie: not buying/equipping new items, not upgrading when you have the option), but there's no advantage to be had by making that choice.  So, for each choice you're presented with in the game, either all answers are equivalent (and therefore it doesn't matter what you decide) or one answer is clearly better than the others (at which point, why even ask the player?).
Combat itself, the heart of the game, is similarly weak. There's no real tactical or strategic interest in the battle system. Melee characters bash things in the next hex, ranged characters are weak against melee, but can hit any hex on the map. There's no cover or line of sight, so there's nowhere to hide from the ranged units.  There's no zone of control, so there's no preventing the melee units from running straight up to the ranged units and pounding on them. None of the hexes has any intrinsic value (other than the occasional chest, of which I think there were two in the entire game?), so you almost never need to be anywhere in particular on the map.
So really, it's just a brawl in an empty parking lot.  Over and over.
There are some special abilities (one per unit), but there's no tradeoff for using them.  The crossbowman, for instance, gets a super shot.  He has to sacrifice a turn to use it, but does triple damage the next round. There is no reason not to use this power every time it comes available; the enemies aren't variable enough to make it worth banking (especially since there are no reinforcements), and it means that in two turns you do three turns worth of damage.  It's simply more effective than just using the regular attack.
There's a global set of spells you can cast any time, but you accrue spell points by your units taking hits, so you can't really contrive to earn them more quickly.  They come in at the rate they come in, and you can spend them on (by the end) one of five spells.  Two of which are "hit enemy" and "hit random enemies", one of which makes a unit faster, and two of which I can't remember because I never needed them and they weren't interesting enough to try.  So, much like the unit powers, the spells wind up being an attack you get to throw for free once in a while. There's never a good reason not to do so when you have the chance.
A total absence of interesting choices (tactically, strategically, plot-wise...) is the defining experience of the game.  With some minor changes to combat (ZOC!  How did they manage to make a hexmap game without zone of control?  What were they thinking?  And where are the tradeoffs for the specials?  Why isn't your hero on the field somewhere?) it could be really good, but as it stands it's weak and unsatisfying.

As the highly anticipated sequel to Crysis, this game definitely exceeds expectations. Leaving the island setting established in the first game, this one brings the player into a post-apocalyptic New York City filled with aliens and other enemies around every corner. The plot is similar to the first game, but the scope of it has changed dramatically. The player not only has to save the city, but the entire world too.
The terrain has completely reshaped the gameplay. For starters, there is a lot more room to room combat. Secondly, the player will encounter a lot of street combat where checking the rooftops is necessary for survival. Lastly, the weaponry is pretty much the same, but how it's used has also changed a lot. For example, the player may need to rely on their pistol a lot more during a close firefight.
For any PC gamer out there wanting to play a beautiful looking game along with great gameplay, this is definitely worth checking out.

Wow! It is everything it promises to be. I've tried learning guitar in the past, but got discouraged by the difficulty curve and the tedium of practicing. This software makes all of it enjoyable! From the beginning you're playing along with great songs. The notes are presented on a Guitar Hero-like note highway and the dynamically adjusting difficulty adds or removes notes depending on how well you're doing. Naturally, you can scale the difficulty and speed to your level, either in sections or for the whole song. Each song has its preset guitar sounds -- modeled after the original song -- but the software allows you to customize the sound of your guitar by setting up virtual amplifiers and pedals. You can have jam sessions with a vitual band. The lessons seem to cover pretty much everything you need to know and are well presented. The mini-games for practicing guitar techniques are all fun, excpet for Gone Whaling (which is about controlling the volume of your playing).
I first got a cheap guitar just to see if I can remain motivated using this software and after a month -- averaging a bit over an hour a day playing -- upgraded to a much better guitar. I'm also buying a bunch of the DLC songs. Do remember that it takes a lot of time and effort to learn to play an instrument. Maybe this software speeds up the process somewhat, but it most definitely makes it fun!

Note that I'm not big on multi-player for fps games, so this review will pertain primarily to the story and technical aspects of Black Ops 3. Though I will get around to updating about the zombie horde mode. That said.
One belief I have is a game should be able to stand up on just it's single player alone. Black Ops 3 manages this, a bit wobbly in some spots, but stands solid for the most part. The story picks up some time after the events of Black Ops 2 and contains story content from the first two games that feel organic to the story, if the story made any real sense. The pieces all fit like a warped jigsaw puzzle, with funky exposition the player can feel lost for a majority of the story. Whether this is intentional or not, I leave to the subjective side of things. But otherwise the game continues the underlying narrative of how the mind is affected in warfare and the advantages and disadvantages of technologies role in both the public and private worlds. Though cliche, the story manages to not lose itself entirely to entire levels set in a surreal reality muddled with pseudo-science.
On the technical side, the game performed quite well. With only two real hiccups which consist of an entirely random ctd and one game breaking glitch which in which the AI seemed to forget just what it was doing. Frame drops only occured in a small handful of areas which quickly stopped after seconds. However the user interface feels very much designed for console without being reworked for a mouse and keyboard setup which ruins the pacing throughout the game. The in combat menu to select your special abilites is designed for analog stick controllers, wasting precious seconds in the heat of combat to choose an ability. As for combat itself, this honestly feels like a game that just happens to have the Call of Duty IP attached to it.
Overall, the single player campaign feels good. Not entirely worth a full price of $60, but good enough to catch on sale if multi-player isn't your bag and you want a good fairly solid shooter. At first glance, it seems like a complete rip off of hearthstone. it has the same mana mechanic, it has the same card system, it has the same shop, except bigger. And it has foil cards, which serve no real purpose as I've seen yet, except to be disenchanted for more dust... i mean spirit...
Yes, at first glance, this review might also seem skewed to be against this game, you would be wrong.
While as of this moment, Songhai faction is very strong, the game does seem to try to be balanced. A bit 'more' balance would be nice, as well as some other avenues to utilize cards that I can only assume will be implimented later on.
This game actually draws more from Fire Emblem. For those commanders out there who, like me, enjoyed spending an hour on one mission, to do a 'perfect' run, where backstabs reigned supreme and the rock paper scissors of spears swords and so on got our blood boiling in all the good ways.
Well... you may not be disappointed too much by this game. While it is still 'early' since so far, as of this review, there's only one expansion to the 'Core' set of cards, which I call Shurima~ There is a backstab mechanic, opening mechanics like in hearth, spells and special abilities like in FE and Hearth.
Overall, it does have a lot to offer, and it 'DOES NOT LIE' when refering to itself as a ccg with a strategy spin, I would greatly reccomend this game to anyone who likes card games, or strategy. The pixel art is not too bad honestly. it reminds me a lot of the Undertale attempts. So far, the only frustration new players might face, is asking themselves if they should save up for packs from the shop, or use gold for Gauntlet Runs (Gauntlet is basically Arena) the rewards are not too bad, in that you get Spirit for crafting, and usually a core pack along with gold.
As long as the people behind this game pay attention to community feedback, and keep adding things for us to buy, and new cards for us to test strategies with, I can see this game lasting quite a while.
My one big wish for this game, would be cooperative play, with a friend. 2v2... that would be so amazing if they could pull that off. Perhaps doubling the board size, or something. But if they did that, I would be so happy.

Hopefully someone will see this and read it before spending money on the game.
On the surface it is a great game, there appear to be layers of strategy and mechanics that attempt to minimize RNG and coming from HS that is just huge.
After a few hours playing the game you begin to realize that is mostly just smoke and mirrors though.  The draw of the "board" and interaction between the different mechanics starts to fade into the background as you realize the designers for all of their apparent good intent don't have a terribly solid grasp of card game design.
As of now in the post expansion meta there are 4 different decks that can reliably put 14+ damage on your life total out of hand with no real way to counter it.  The worst offender is Songhia, the so called meld deck is just like playing against miracle rogue back in the early days of HS.  Not only can they just win without any input from you(no, positioning tricks and praying RNG puts the second boar in a bad spot does not count, at all) even if they don't win the match is incredibly boring.  There are other examples of poor design that is rapidly leading to a stale and boring meta devoid of any fun what so ever but I think the worst example is the best and will leave it at that.
I struggle to find positives about this game but for the sake of fairness I will say the art is great, really tickles that pixel itch you may or mat not get on occasion.
I really wanted to like this game and I hope they will go back to the drawing board on at least most of these issues but I don't see that happening any time soon.  So for now it is a very sad thumbs down from me.
Update 11/6/16
So, they did a balance pass.  One of the big ones was they nerfed a card that everyone has access to and can be played around, and didn't touch the insane out of hand damage half the factions are capable of.
I have a theory the out of hand damage (ei, the damage you can not stop or interact with at all) was such a bedrock of the game core that altering it or taking it out would destroy any ability the devs have to push the game forward and as a result they aren't doing anything at all.
At this point any faith I had that things would be fixed or get better are gone.
Note this review and update are here because at one point I thought the game had a lot of potential to be something special in the otherwise god awful electronic CCG market.  But turns out it isn't.  So please, avoid this thing and if you do decide to try it out (after all it starts out free) please do not spend a dime on it.  Learn from my mistake.

, I really can't think that someone was actually testing it.

Wind Child is another excellent addition to my growing library of the classic style rpg games that is driven by a well crafted and interesting story that is character driven and quickly draws the player into the events.
Driven to rescue an innocent girl who is wrongly kidnapped at the beginning of the story, the heroes face many circumstances of peril, weather, evildoers whose agendas are unknown, and, of course, monsters of all sorts in a complex and labyrinthine setting where searching carefully for gold, items, and other treasures is a must.
The game is carefully laid out so you don't find yourself wondering what the objectives are, but there are choices to make as you move along ---- just the right mix.
The characters are all important, and you need to follow all the conversations pretty closely so as to get a good feel for the story as it unfolds. A lot of humor, as well.
The graphics are unique, and nicely done ---- both in the overworld, and in the battle scenes.
Music is excellent, and is very appropriate to the events occurring as you play.
This one is a steal at the price being asked, and is a must have for any fan of these classic games ---- very much recommended.

10/10 Will fly UH-1B "Huey" to fortunate son whilst blowing up AA guns again
No seriously get this game, granted I've only played 2 hours or so but the gameplay alone is enough to keep me going. The controls are a little difficult to understand to begin with but thankfully the devs have put in a training map with enough to room to swing your helo around and even gives you targets to shoot at as well as providing tutorials through the career page. Once you get the hang of it though it is a blast to play and immensely satisfying doing sweeping runs on enemy infantry/boats/AA with rockets and machine guns.
And that's just the singleplayer/co-op side, the PVP is quite intense as you not only have to worry about the AI shooting you down you even have enemy players to contend with which further increases the tension and satisfaction once you blow an unsuspecting player out of the sky or engaging in an intense dogfight and coming out on top.
The progression system is alright so far but the game has only just been released officially so I'm giving it the benefit of the doubt. It's way to easy to just sit in singleplayer and farm points, I managed to unlock 3 helo's and fully upgrade (as far as you can go anyway, not everything is unlocked) them within just 2 hours of play just doing medium difficulty missions so whilst it isn't as grindy as most games of its genre it doesn't feel as rewarding working your way up if the aircraft you want is handed to you inside 2 missions. Granted the higher tier helo's are harder to get but right now it is too easy to work your way past tiers 1-3.
The class sytem feels right and makes you tactically think, you can't just jump into a gunship and fly around expecting to win with just that one aircraft. The game makes you choose between scouts, gunships and dedicated troop transports and it is imperative that you become familiar with each of their styles as the game throws you into different objectives. One minute you're tasked with destroying AA installations which the gunship is built for to suddenly having to capture a landing zone which is where the troop transport comes in, something the gunship isn't built for forcing you to either die or flying back to your spawn to change helo's (I'd recommend doing that instead of dying, it's better to learn how to land as there will be times when you're going to have to as the higher tiers take longer to repair if shot down whereas simply landing only takes under 30 seconds to a minute)
All of that aside I'd definitely recommend getting this game, it was made by a very small dev team and they're in constant contact with their fan base as well as providing updates frequently. It's £11 (or $15 for you Yankees) which quite frankly is underdoing it considering the potential it has, I'd happily pay up to £18-£20 for a product like this as it is well worth the price.
To sum it up, if flying helo's is your thing, you like doing a bit of grinding like you find in WOT and Warthunder and you like tactical arcady style flying games then this is the one for you. Though don't be discouraged if you prefer something a bit less arcady, they do include an option for more "realistic" flight via joystick. Now hurry up and get in here, there's a war on son and that Huey ain't gonna fly itself!

I bought this game having thoroughly enjoyed the original Crysis - which was the right mix of tense espionage thriller, intense action, and open world exploration to make it one of my favourite shooters of all time.
Crysis 2 seemed to have lost that touch.
Although there were different paths through the environments of ruined New York, gone was the sense of freedom. The urban setting felt claustrophobic, repetitive and limiting - you could no longer go where you wanted, and I often felt that the designers funnelled me down set pathways with little scope for any creative approach.
The story felt like nothing more than a series of stylish but linear set-pieces which you plodded through in order. Although there were moments of wonder, the plot held no surprises. I felt little attachment to the forgettable one dimensional characters who did little more than relay orders to you.
The action was the only thing that I liked about this game. The Nanosuit v2.0 interface was streamlined and intuitive, the weapons were varied and well-balanced, and there were plenty of things to shoot and blow up in spectacular fashion. The ability to upgrade and specialise the capabilities of the Nanosuit was a nice touch as well, and imparted a little depth to the game.
Sadly beyond that there is little else to recommend this glorified shooter. For those in the Call of Duty generation, this might appeal, but those looking for a little more depth might be disappointed.

A decent 4x-esque zombie apocalyspe simulator, where you travel from city to city looking for the cure. Suffers from a some major flaws, though.
+Captures the "just one more turn feeling" very well.
+More backstory, items, and equipment than the first two games.
+Amusing cartoony graphics.
-+An attempt at a story, though rather half-heartedly.
-Game lacks polish: spelling errors, incorrect character portraits, characters don't stay married from town to town, etc.
-Hard to find a happy medium in difficulty. It's is either too hard early on or far too easy late game.
-Characters must specialize. You can't just put people where they're best anymore.
-Campaign mode is far too long. It takes 10-12 cities to tell a story that could be done in 5. And you won't even learn the story if you choose to fight the other factions, rather than ally with them.
-The optional cities are sometimes not skippable due to glitches.
-Goals never change. The only way to win is to either destroy everyone, ally with everyone, or fix the plane.
-Surprise twist ending!!1! in the last level is so awful it made me quit playing.

Not the most difficult puzzler out there, but it doesn't need to be.
'Thomas Was Alone' features well-designed characters (that are rectangles), a narrator that clearly knows what it's like to be a quadrilateral, puzzles that can be puzzling at times but never enough to discourage you, and a story that's as likely to give you a giggle as it is to rouse a flaming passion for geometry you that you never thought possible.
Easily recommendable.

Guide a group of rectangles through a series of obstacles, using their different skills together to get to the end of each environment.
In the meantime, enjoy clever puzzles, beautiful music, and a powerful story about a group of very different characters with very different personalities and capabilities.
Note the use of the word "characters", because that's exactly what this ragtag bunch of quirky quadrilaterals are. They interact with each other physically in order to solve puzzles, but perhaps equally as important is the way they interact with each other emotionally, developing relationships, romances and rivalries like the most human characters could.
Do not be deceived by the brevity in this game's description. Like Portal and Cave Story, the simple gameplay, neatly summed up in a few quick, concise comments, hides a gripping narrative that perfectly humanizes a bunch of... rectangles. As many reviews before mine have accurately expressed, you'll find yourself getting more attached to geometry than you ever did in math class.
The game is fairly short, a few hours from start to finish, but appropriately so. While puzzle games like this one lend themselves to infinite possible configurations that can be solved using the unique properties of the tools at hand, Thomas Was Alone finds just the right number of configurations to keep the game interesting and thought provoking -- and, perhaps even more importantly, just the right number to keep the narrative, and the relationships between your group of characters, moving at an approachable, human pace. By the time the game is over, you will have revelled in the story, but you won't be left wanting more; just those few hours, those few wonderful hours with your jumping, bouncing rectangles are so immeasurably satisfying that you'll immediately set about writing a gushing review like this one.
In short, a quick little bite of skilful puzzle platforming gameplay with a masterful story that will keep you glued to your seat right to the very end.

The Secret Order 4: Beyond Time is a casual H.O. Game where Artifex's signature can be easily sensed, even though they are only publishing this one.
I liked the storyline, the pace of the game, as well as the ambiance/atmosphere and the art style. Prepare yourself to meet a polymath, a great navigator, a priest and other astonishing and eclectic characters all along a fantastic journey.
I didn't like the music very much but it didn't bother me either. Voice acting is good enough.
Regarding the difficulty it's not a hard game, more of an easy casual one. Puzzles are somewhat easy and the main game causes no trouble to advance in the story.
I did like H.O.Puzzles. They are some sort of dynamic H.O. Scenes with no objects list, where you have to interact with certain objects of the scene (which then interact between them) in order to find something useful for the main game. It's less mind-numbing than classic H.O. Scenes.
There is a bonus chapter which makes the game lifetime quite fair.
It's not hard to beat and it's possible to get all the achievements in a unique playthrough, if you pay attention to details.
Though I liked the art style and the graphics to some extent, i'd like to specify that there are 2 resolution related messes.
1/ The 1st issue that stroke me affects all collectibles. In this game there are 3 kinds of hidden statuettes you need to find to get 3 achievements. They are not very visible, they may be hard to make out. Sure, you're not supposed to spot them immediately but that's not the problem. Even when you notice them and look at them it's difficult to see what it is really.. Is it a pile of leaves? are those branches? is that a fire burning over there? Oh no! Of course it's a statuette !! Seriously, if it weren't for the colour I would never have spotted them and when I did, I clicked on them most of the times with no certainty, since I couldn't make head or tail of what i was staring at ! This is no big failure but it's nevertheless a pity.
2/ The 2nd problem is more serious and almost leads me to put a thumb down to The Secret Order 4: Beyond Time. At some point there's a puzzle/mini-game with spinning cogs and it's definitely bugged on some screens/resolutions. I had to play from another computer because there is no way to change the game resolution in the game options menu and though you're suposed to be able to switch from window mode to full screen mode I couldn't do it either (the game wouldn't allow it on my screen resolution! What does this mean?). I didn't want to skip this mini-game because there is an achievement depending on it (no mini-game skipping), so I waited for an opportunity to play elsewhere than on my desktop. That's why I'm not happy about that and I think the devs should do something about it. It's not fair to anyone who bought the game. As you may see in discussions topics related to this game, I'm not the only one experiencing this..
In conclusion, some good ideas and a nice entertainment. Not a bad game if you have the adequate resolution ;)

Ah, Crysis. An Instant classic in my book. Gamebreaking visuals of 2007 that even some of the best PCs found to be a bit of a challenge. Amazing visuals, stunning environments - particularly the alien space ship, and every level that was completely snowed out and frozen. Great alien concept, though apparently there were people ♥♥♥♥♥ing that they resembled War of the Worlds aliens too much (as if that really matters? It was a great enemy in-game).
**** TL;DR at Bottom of this Review ****

I have great memories with Crysis 2 when I bought it on xbox360 the week it came out. Stunning visuals, Still a pretty good story.
While I recently purchased C2 on steam for nostalgia purposes (although it seems I am unable to use the crysis 2 login feature for multiplayer atm..), I must say that I still have my disappointments with the game.
I'm going to go head-on with what I consider to be the CONS of the game.
Unlike the original Crysis and Crysis Warhead, Crysis 2 (and 3) change up the overall HUD/viewpoint. Crysis 1 felt more realistic to me. In Crysis, your weapon was lowered and, visually, it looked further away from your head. In Crysis 2 and 3, your weapon feels like you are hugging it with your face 24/7.
I preferred how the weapon was positioned in the first installment. It felt more realistic to me, and therefore helped immerse me.
To add to that, while they still look killer, I much prefer the original look of the weapons in the first game. The Scar looks a little too futuristic in comparison to the original Crysis 1 scar which still looked futuristic (like an updated M8 Assault Rifle) while maintaining that solid modern look. The weapon designs in Crysis 1 and 2 do look great, but my preference, flat out, is the weapon design of Crysis 1.
Again, visually, I also dislike the changes they made with the nanosuit powers. The first Crysis had a "Maximum Speed" power, which was completely removed as a standalone feature, and instead, sprinting drains your energy. While this feature still works well for the game, I miss the overall individuality of Max Speed, and the other abilities. In addition, Crysis features a color changing effect when those abilities are activated.
Using Max Strength empowered your nanosuit with a red glow, a glow that my eyes seriously enjoyed to look at. It just looked great.
And using Max Speed surged your nanosuit with a vibrant yellowish glow that as described, surged through your suit. It looked astonishing even from the fiew parts of your body you could see in the first person view.
Max Armor had no effect, and of course stealth made you stealth. These two maintained between both Crysis 1 and 2.
Visually the nanosuit looked better with abilities in use, and overall more realistic from my perspective. Whereas in Crysis 2 and 3, it seems almost like Alcatraz / Prophet is too buff. The muscles of the suit are almost exaggerated, and it just bugs me, the suit still looks iconic and great.
Previous statements involve cosmetic differences between the first and second game. However, my biggest complaint with Crysis 2 is the change in alien design.
Crysis 1 featured blue-lighted robotic aliens (with pilots inside) that flew around the sky with tentacles flailing about, as the aliens shot ice projectiles and ice beams. Their entire premise was freezing the environment while flying around. This was iconic and part of why Crysis 1 is and always will be in my mind a classic. Crysis 2 features red-colored robotic aliens with a premise of basically biological warfare instead of ice-age warfare. While the premise is just as, if not more effective story-wise for mass homicide, I cannot help but dislike this change. I much prefer Crysis 1's enemies to Crysis 2.
If you're still reading this, I give you a thumbs up.
These CONS of course are personal CONS, and probably do not settle the same way with most other players as they do with me.
That being said, despite my biases, I do love Crysis 2, because I am open-minded and won't hate a game just because it isn't quite what I prefer.
That and the game still maintains a lot of traditional Crysis feel to it.
The game feels great, and the multiplayer was a blast.
I definitely recommend this game, but I INSIST that anyone who considers Crysis should purchase the first Crysis game first.
TL;DR Buy Crysis 1 (If you already have played it then GREAT!) THEN play Crysis 2.

Pros:
Rocksmith 2014 is a tremendously efficient guitar tutor masked cleverly as enjoyable entertainment.  If you have any desire to learn guitar or bass you owe it to yourself to pick this up.  Even at full retail price it is bus fare compared to one-on-one guitar training at a music store.  You'll learn the same stuff, perhaps not the nitty gritty theory, but certainly the techniques as you would from a professional tutor but at a fraction of the cost... easy peasy decision.
You will Rock out... oh yes, you will.
The Steam version doesn't come with the cable but it can be sourced through Amazon and other retailers.  Be aware that it 'could' cost more than just buying the physical box with the game DVD and cable when they're bought seperate.
The only Con:
Cost of DLC.  Most songs are 3 bucks a piece, gets expensive fast.  Buy packs where you can, and wait for Steam sales.
Edit (March 2017) -
250+ hours in, time for an update...
I've found that I get the best experience playing Rocksmith if I use pedals, not effects, just pedals to get a better line signal.  I have a buffer, a compressor, and a noise gate and they are all set to be mild to medium in their attack and release.  I find this tightens up the dynamics enough that notes I'm clearly playing that didn't register with the game engine, now do.  It has meant song scores going way up and a near ♥♥♥♥♥♥ic level of joy playing the tunes I like to play... okay maybe that last bit was too far.
For anyone that might be interested, here's the rig:
Gretsch/Strat -> Boss NS2 -> Friedman SirCompre (omg so cherry) -> TC Bonifide Buffer -> RealTone Cable -> Profit???
I've actually got an A/B switcher in place so I can push my pedal board to either the RealTone cable or to my audio interface.
So yeah, if you're reading this thinking I like the idea of the game but half of what I play it ignores?  Get a cheap compressor at the minimum, or borrow one to try first before investing that it does indeed work for you, but I think you'll find it does.
I mean, I got 'Eye of the Tiger' up to 99.9% and I totally suck!
Cheers!

This game is completely addicting.  I love it.  It comes with a lot of songs already, but if you get bored with those, there are around 700+ more available.  I don't think anyone would quit the guitar if they use this to learn to play.  You get to play along with your favorite bands!
There are so many aspects to this game.  First, it really is a learning tool.  It includes lessons, arcade games for building real skills, a tone designer by which you can mix and match effects, amps, and cabinets and just play the guitar and also a jam session mode by which you can practice scales and soloing with a band that intuitively follows your lead.
In addition to all of this, the main part of the game are the songs you can learn.  When you choose a new song to play, the game starts you out with root notes and the more you play it, the game fills in the gaps with chords, riffs and runs.  You learn progressively and get progressively better.  It's really amazing.
There is a feature called riff repeater that let's you choose a section or sections of a song you want to work on and then slow it down as much as you'd like to.  It will loop the section over and over so you can master it at your own rate.  You'd be amazed at how you can progress using this tool.  Sometimes, when I choose to play a new song that is particularly easy, I'll go into the riff repeater and choose the entire song and slow it down to 85% and just inch up the speed until I master the whole thing.
After you master a song, you can play for a score in score attack mode by which your performance is ranked against every other player.  It makes you want to compete to become better at each song.  It's really motivating.
There is also a multi-player mode by which another player can plug in a real tone cable and play along with you.  I have not tried this as of yet.
Just about every song includes a rhythm, lead, and bass part.  I set up two profiles so far; one for lead and one for bass.  I will eventually learn rhythm as well, but I have plenty to keep me busy for years to come.
Some people say they have issues when connecting their instruments, but I haven't encountered anything I haven't been able to work through quickly and easily.  I have a Gibson Les Paul Standard guitar, Ernie Ball Music Man Cutlass guitar, Ernie Ball Music Man Sterling Bass, and Ernie Ball Music Man Sting Ray Bass (Ernie Ball makes amazing intruments!!!).  They all work with this game.  You have to "Calibrate" each guitar through the game's calibrate tool to get the appropriate level for each because each has difference in how hot the pickups/signal are.  I've found you have to mute the strings when dealing with noisy strat-style pickups (as on my Cutlass) when you start up the game or you'll have issues with signal noise and note tracking.   As a result, I just make a practice of muting the strings when starting the game and it seems to eliminate any signal noise issues.  I've had no problems with my Les Paul at all.  When I turn the volume up too loud with my basses (both use active EQ and really hot pickups), my bass pickups will start feeding back (sound you're playing looping out of the speakers and into the pickups) and it confuses the tracking.  Sometimes just turning the pickups away from the speakers in this case does the trick.  But if I turn the speaker volume down enough, all is well.  I think you might experience this with any hot pickups though.  At any rate, its easy to get any guitar you plug in working with minimal and often no tinkering.
Every once in a while, the game dings me when I've actually played the correct note and it can be frustrating at times (especially when competing for a score), but it doesn't take away my ability to learn the songs.  You just play through it.
All in all, this is an amazing piece of software.  It really shouldn't be called a game, but it combines the fun of a game with the seriousness and fun of learning guitar.  It is among the best kept secrets in the music instruction world.  They should have a game for any instrument you can mic up too (trumpet, sax, drums, etc...).  I personally think it's worth way more money than they charge because of how much there is to it.  You can actually become a great player using this software.
Update...
The more I play the more I find this game does better with a signal that's less "hot".  Passive electronics/eq is the easiest config with this game.  Les Paul is best.  "Silent Circuit" on the Cutlass is problematic.  Active EQ is sometimes a little too hot on the Sting Ray and Sterling, but not bad at lower volumes.  Seems like they could make this a little less aggravating.

P E R F E C T I O N

– A beautiful, lovingly crafted game with challenging, yet satisfying mechanics and a unique experience to offer. Easily a 10/10 in my book.
- - -
The game's art, in addition to its soundtrack, is where Hyper Light Drifter really shines. Every area, cutscene, and character is rendered beautifully; each section of the game's world feels truly unique, with it's own atmosphere and personality; animations are fluid and incredibly satisfying; and the game's use of light and color makes the entire experience a visual treat. Visual cues for abilities, hidden secrets, UI elements, and other aspects of gameplay never feel out of place. What more is there to say? My heart is full of praises that my mind simply can't put into words.
The gamplay itself, at its core, isn't anything
unique. You explore a ruined world while fighting off varieties of different monsters in waves, all with their own distinctive movement and attack patterns. What the gameplay does offer, however, it handles superbly well. The key to combat is a good sense of timing; sword strikes, dashes, abilities, long-range attacks, and even healing must be timed well to be effective. Getting hurt slows you down (some attacks even stun you for a short time)—in addition to having a relatively small health pool from the beginning, this means you'll have to avoid taking damage as much as possible as charge attacks, bullets, and other hazards come at you from all directions. It can potentially be a bit of a learning curve (it took me a little while to get the hang of it), but once you get it down, combat feels extremely fun and satisfying.
The game doesn't hold your hand. The beginning tutorial is short and minimal, quickly and neatly teaching you only the very basics you'll need to get by, forcing you to figure the rest out as you play. Because of this, it's quite fun learning to string together combos, or how to best utilize your abilities and upgrades as you get them, or just figuring out how to effectively combat that one enemy or boss that always gets the better of you.
On the topic of bosses, the boss fights are fairly short and simple. They all have two or three mechanics to look out for, and you can likely think of a few different strategies for dealing with each, but once you've done that, there's not too much to worry about. If you can keep your rhythm under pressure, you'll get on just fine. Bosses don't have multiple "phases" like in some other games, and they don't have a whole lot of HP, so if you're doing particularly well, you can likely take them all out in under a minute. They're a fun challenge, but in the grand scheme of things, they might also feel a bit anticlimactic. Whether the minimal approach is a pro or a con will depend upon your outlook—I didn't really mind it, but I know some may wish for bigger, longer battles.
Regardless, odds are you will die.
. What's more, since dying puts you back at your last save point, you'll often be put back at the very beginning of a room or encounter if you happen to croak partway through, possibly losing anything you might have found along the way (don't forget to go back and get that collectible!). This has the potential to be a little frustrating, but don't lose hope, as no challenge is impossible!
Puzzle elements here and there will make you think and keep the gameplay feeling fresh throughout. For the achievement hunters and completionists out there, there's a lot to be had in the way of little secrets, collectibles, and achievement challenges, and a few different difficulty settings should appease those looking for a relatively easy ride as well as those seeking a more masochistic (for lack of a better word) gameplay experience.
There's not much I can say about the game's soundtrack, really, aside from that it's beautiful beyond words and entirely fit to accompany Hyper Light Drifter's unique and immersive world. The music and art work hand in hand to make everything feel truly alive.
In the beginning, I didn't really know what I was doing or why. To be clear, this isn't a bad thing—the game made it easy to tell that whatever I was doing was important, and thus I was intrigued, and set out into its vast world to learn more.
Hyper Light Drifter is a bit different in the 'story' department. It won't dump exposition in the form of dialogue or text—instead, it opts to let its beautifully crafted world speak for itself. The few characters you can speak to do so through pictures rather than words, leaving it up to the player to make connections and inferences, and the circumstances of your own drifter are hinted through the world, its inhabitants, and your character's actions as you play. Cutscenes, though always wonderfully done, are few and far between, and friendly faces are a rare sight. The end result is that if you're not interested in the game's lore, you won't really have to pay attention to it at all (and indeed you might think there simply isn't much to be had), but if you care to look into and engage with the beautiful world you're thrust into, there's a lot of fun to be had in just trying to put together the puzzle pieces. The developers have taken immense attention to detail, and you can truly learn a lot just by exploring and taking it all in.
I believe this approach really works in the game's favor. Hyper Light Drifter hands you a unique and intriguing setting and the tools with which to learn quite a bit about it, and then it allows you to choose whether to dig deeper or to remain on the surface. Those looking for a story that unfolds neatly right in front of you may be in for a slight disappointment, but Drifter's relatively minimal approach to exposition makes the experience one of exploration and discovery—and that, in my humblest of opinions, is all too rare and immensely satisfying.
Regardless of how you may feel about the game's lack of neatly packaged exposition, by the time you reach the end, you will find yourself having grown fond of this drifter after watching him overcome challenge after challenge to reach the story's climax. It's a simple, but effective bond that has left quite an impression on me; I know for certain that I'll remember this game fondly for long after I've seen all it has to offer.
I haven't enjoyed a game this much in a long, long time. My already high expectations going into this experience were completely shattered; the game goes above and beyond and really, truly shines. I've never been moved to write a review on Steam—until now, that is. I write this in the hope that my words can help a few more people to discover the veritable masterpiece that is Hyper Light Drifter.

Beyond Time is a little too enthusiastic about gimmicky hidden object scenes, but it is still a fun adventure through a time-displaced Mesoamerican civilisation, and a strong entry in the series.
The fourth Secret Order game, Beyond Time, moves a bit closer to the time-travelling roots of the series: instead of battling maleficent wizards, we team up with a bunch of random historical figures to thwart the plans of an evil Cortéz in a time-displaced Central American jungle.
This realistic scenery helps to create a sense of some classic adventure better than any standard magical fairy tale kingdom, even if the cute animal sidekick doesn’t really belong in this picture (it is a reborn baby Anubis, who for some reason knows how to use Aztec magic).
While Beyond Time is technically a HOG, it puts too much emphasis on the simplistic point ‘n’ click mechanics and puzzles. Even most of the hidden object scenes are more like single-screen puzzles instead of the usual item searching. This means that the game relies more on the created atmosphere than the content, but the writing is enjoyable, the game lasts longer than most modern HOGs, and it is just fun to play.

Before I go any further, I highly suggest that anyone considering playing
first play the other titles in this series. While this game does a good job of getting players up to speed on what happened, the games happen in chronological order and focus on the same main character so playing all the games helps the player understand her and how the story has been going so far. That being said, even if you haven’t played any of the previous
games you’ll probably enjoy this one if you’re a fan of hidden object adventure games. The story is fun and well written, supplement by beautiful art and solid gameplay.
Once again we are put in the role of Sarah Pennington who, after her last adventure, is stuck in a magical land trying to get back home. She is a member of the Secret Order of the Griffin and enemy to the evil Dragon Clan. Despite being about time travel there are many liberties taken here so be ready to suspend your disbelief. The story is mainly about Sarah trying to return home, but along the way the Dragon Clan traps her in a land outside of the time stream where she meets others who are time displaced. I enjoyed the story, but it’s best not to think too hard about the ramifications of time travel and magic. My only issue is that there isn’t much sense of urgency in the game. There’s a sense of urgency at first, when the Dragon Clan goes after Sarah but after that I didn’t feel very worried about the other villain in the game at all, especially near the end when you easily solve the major problem and send everyone home. I did enjoy having Nubi, who is a young version of the god Anubis, helping out throughout the game. His story is explained in the main game and concluded in the bonus chapter.
As mentioned earlier, this is a hidden object adventure game. Everything is point and click so you only need a mouse if playing this title on your computer. You interact with other characters to progress the story while also solving puzzles and collecting items as needed. Despite being a hidden object game there aren’t that many to be had, sadly, rather there are more puzzles than hidden object scenes. That being said, the puzzles are fun and offer a decent amount of challenge and the hidden object scenes aren’t all the traditional worded list of items to find. Adding to the gameplay is Nubi who has four special abilities though only two of them are used often. He’s a nice addition to the game and also very cute. You’re also given a standard map that allows you to teleport, making travel easy. The game has three difficulty settings and a tutorial if you need one.
The graphics are lovely. Bright colors, appropriate shading and a general mystical feel as you travel through time and space. My main issue is the animation of the character’s faces when they talk, often times the lips just don’t look right and their expressions are blank. Other than that, though, I had no issues with this game aesthetically speaking. The hidden object scenes are well-rendered so no need to squint and hurt your eyes. The music in the game is fine and there is also full voice acting. The voices are alright for the most part but some of the acting isn’t very good, expect Leonardo Da Vinci to talk with a horrible stereotypical Italian accent.
While I would have liked more hidden object scenes in the game and the story could have expanded on Sarah’s character and backstory more, I wholly enjoyed playing
. There is a main game as well as a bonus chapter plus the game has collector’s edition content like concept sketches and more. Playing this title on Steam will reward you with trading cards as well achievements that aren’t too difficult to collect. I recommend this games for new players as well as veterans of the genre, it's well balanced and fun. The ending left me wanting more, I eagerly await Sarah’s next journey.

The very good 4th entry in a series of perfectly balanced, satisfying hidden-object games. Gameplay is fair and diverse, not too easy and not too hard. Finally, thank you, devs, for supporting Linux!

Dear Artifex Mundi, while I'm happy to see that you're publishing on Steam The Secret Order and that it's a fun ride since the Masked Intent, I do hope that you have the right for New Horizon, which is the first game in the series and which may be interesting for Sarah's background.
As you understand, while Beyond Time is the third game of the series to be published on Steam, the first entry, introducting our heroin in a corrupt world (because I've read the description), is still missing (a matter of rights perhaps). Having a full series would be great as the fifth game was published not long ago.
Let's dive into Beyond Time.
After being stuck in Aeronheart, Sarah managed to find a way to come back to her era. But in the same time, she's taking care of Nubi, a little creature that was hidden by Cleopatra. However, her enemy managed to send her and Nubi in another dimension, where Cortez is the ruler and where inventors are captive, having been themselves abducted from their eras. Can Sarah come back to her present?
To remind you, Sarah Pennington is the daughter of a powerful master of a secret order that was attacked. Sarah had to find mystical objects to beat her enemy, however, they were unstable and Sarah found herself sent back in time, in the mythical kingdom of Aeronhart, to save the future. Beyond Time is beginning at that moment, when Sarah is trying to find a way home, as the Royal Griffin, the time-travelling ship, is destroyed.
While I liked the story, after a moment, it can be a little confusing: I mean, you're in an ancient time but apparently, a merchant was time travelling too and was in contact with Cleopatra, who hid Anubis, in his form of Nubi, in order to protect him from Romans. And after travelling to Ancient Egypt, Sarah got caught by an enemy with the Royal Griffin, before its destruction, and sent into another dimension with Cortes being a tyrant, Da Vinci, Tesla and even... Cleopatra being prisoners. The three local tribes need your help to restore the harmony of the world. If you're still following, I must say that it's beginning to have a lot of past altering or time travelling in the whole universe of The Secret Order.
Anyway, the gameplay is standard: hidden objects scenes, puzzles, items to find and to use. However, I liked the whole idea to progress in three tribes, to help each representant and to hunt down masks related to these (which isn't vital to the story as it's collectibles). Besides, Nubi, if you prefer Anubis in his ritual of rebirth, is cute and helpful: he can grab stuff that you can't. But during the course of the game, he will acquire new powers: levitation, electricity (fire) and invisibility. It's just a shame that the game isn't using more Nubi.
Graphically, the game is a beauty in itself: I loved the background and how the people were represented. From mines to a night camp without forgetting Ancient Egypt and Aeronheart, it's sufficient to feel like you're really travelling.
The soundtrack was good, as the voice acting.
If anything, the game is a good entry to the series, however, too much time travelling can be quite confusing after a while, mainly if you didn't play the rest of the series (New Horizon apart). Masked Intent, Ancient Times and Beyond Time are needed to be played in order if you want to have a real understanding of the universe (even if it's confusing).
Anyway, dear Artifex Mundi, I'm waiting for the fifth game. And the first if possible. I'm really curious about it. You'll tell me that I can get it elsewhere but I love playing on Steam with your titles (published or developed)...

Overall, this is a thoroughly enjoyable HOG.
Pros:
- Custom difficulty (love this).  Allows you to turn on/off all the "helper" features to suit your exact play style.

- Helper pet with 4 different special abilities.
- Many of the HOP's were of the type where you need to interact with object A to make object B, which reveals object C, etc., until you get the final object.  I love these interactive puzzle type HOP's much more than the standard ones of just finding a list of objects.
- Object use was intuitive.  I never had to use hints for anything.
- Very good bonus chapter at the end.
- All achievements can be done with one play through (although I did do the standard "finish a HOP in 60 seconds" in a separate run).
Cons:
- As someone else mentioned, the game just kind of ends before you expect it.  However, the bonus chapter was a nice additional story.
- I have played a lot of Artifex Mundi games, and the mini-games all seem to be re-skinned versions of the same puzzles in every game.
If you like HOG's, then I definitely recommend this one.
