Thomas Was Alone is a rather simple puzzle game that involves different characters who each hold unique skills that allow them to reach their goals... If the player can figure out how to get them there. Although the general play-by-play is simple, the game itself is quite cute, the graphics smooth and the colors pleasing to the eye in a way where they capture your attention where it's needed and doesn't strain them, thanks to the darker backdrop.
The only issue I really had with the game was that if too many tabs were open or the internet connection became choppy/ was being too focused on some other programme, there was a tendency for there to be a bit of lag. Rather subtle, really, but it was quite frustrating during levels where timing and speed were key. Aside from that though, I suppose they could have made the challenges a bit more difficult, longer or more of them. However, a sense of satisfaction was gained upon completion and any more to either aspect may have ruined its simplicity charm.
Overall though, the game is somewhat charming and captivating with its own backstory, and is a game open to all ages. It may seem too simple for those who might consider themselves to expertise in puzzle and problem solving games. It's refreshing though, in my opinion, and a good way to relax. Especially with the music that they choose to play throughout the levels. It's calming, simple chords of piano that truly do help to keep those of us who may have a shorter temper or are not so skilled at puzzles, feel calm and not so under pressure.
I think anyone would enjoy Thomas Was Alone, even if they don't play it all in one go (as my brother had after my finishing it). Maybe it can be used as something for younger audiences which can be found as cute and entertaining for a week or two; a way to pass the time at work; or between homework assignments. I don't deny though my enjoyment and the feeling of being absorbed when I did play longer than 15 minutes at a time. Anywho, it's a game I certainly don't regret playing and I hope everyone will give it a chance.

With the release of this game, I'm finally able to recommend it to other players. Personally, I hate Wargaming products, so much so that I was pushing my grievences with those games, onto this one in my first review, which I apologize for.
Some people are saying that "this game is World of Tanks with helicopters", which I disagree with. Everything that World of Tanks has done wrong, Heliborne has done right. Firstly, the gameplay. This game is both PvP and PvE, with both features being fleshed out and not feeling like an afterthought, tacked on in order to pull in a specific crowd. In PvP games, it feels like a tug of war as you fight for control of bases, pushing your units across the map to claim victory, and this is the first thing the game gets right: The three classes you play as, recon, attack, and transport, actually work together in a balanced way, with some helicopters being hybrids of two of them, allowing an interesting playstyle.
Attack helicopters have the most firepower and health, good at attacking other copters and things on the ground, however you'll be unable to see many targets that are in the trees, seemingly taking fire from knowhere; this is where the recon class comes in, able to fly fast, spot targets, and use the mortar crews setup by the final class, the transport. If you enjoy logi trucking in foxhole, this is your class; it's the job of these slow gunships to capture bases by putting boots on the ground. If you see one, it's best to help out by flying escort or clear defenses so it can capture the base safely. All three of these classes belong in this game, and each play an important part to your team.
When you get into the game, you can select three vehicles to take into combat with you, and when you die, your vehicle is on a repair timer. This is the second thing the game does great. While your mistakes can be punished, you aren't out of the match, allowing you to try different strategies and take risks.
The controls in this game are great, and while they are arcadey, each chopper feels different, and you need to issue commands slightly early. Even though it may feel weird at first, it's never daunting, and after you slam into the ground a few times while trying to land, you'll get the hang of it.
The PvE mode has interesting content. You're able to play both alone and with other people, completing objectives around the map before the time runs out.
And perhapse most importantly, there's very little grind. You aren't going to be outmatched because of a helicopter's supperier stats, and you aren't going to need to force yourself through a horrible vehicle in order to get to something you actually want to play.
Heliborne is a fantastic game, and while its playerbase is small, the game is still very fun. Each class is interesting to play and caters to all playstyles: If you want to attack helicopters and defend your team as they take objectives, do it. If you like pushing resources across the map and aren't that interested in the fighting, that's okay too. No matter what you like to do, there's a way for you to help the team. If you are tired of World of Tanks and other arena shooters, give this game a try; even if you don't like PvP, the PvE game mode is actually well developed, and you won't be sacrificing progression by playing it.
This game does still need work, but there's a very passionate team behind this project and they not only deserve, but completely earn the support.

TL;DR - Hyper Light Drifter is like watching Evangelion muted and with no subtitles.
It's very easy to look at Hyper Light Drifter and think "Man, what an awesome game!". It's a gorgeous game on the surface, with vibrant colors and beautiful animations. However at the core of the game, beautiful graphics, okay combat, anticlimactic boss fights, and mediocre exploration make for a product that is substantially less than the sum of its parts.
A major gripe I have with HLD is that other than a few tutorial messages and the main menu, the game is totally devoid of written text. Every character with which you can interact communicates with you via images. In some circumstances, this system works efficiently. With upgrade vendors, it's easy enough to understand via images that one upgrade lets you dash more, one upgrade lets you charge up a powerful sword swing, etc. etc. But with regards to story, allowing characters only to communicate via pictures did not create a world of mystery and grandeur as I feel the devs had intended. Instead, it left me feeling detached from the world, the story, and the main character (who, despite his silent demeanor, I was beginning to like).
The game opens with a cutscene in which some sort of cataclysm throws the world into ruin. Our protagonist, struggling against the forces of darkness, confronts a small army of titanic creatures who are suddenly stripped of their life and thrown about the map, presumably by the aforementioned cataclysm. Setting off to restore the world to its former state, our hero sets off on a journey. At least I think so. That's my best guess in lieu of an actual explanation.
The combat in HLD seems to require a sense of timing from the player in order to function smoothly. The player can purchase an upgrade allowing consecutive dashes as opposed to one single dash, which must be stringed together with rhythm. Based on my playtime (I beat the game like 20 minutes ago at the time of writing this) it seems that sword swings after dashes must also be timed to some degree. Whether this aspect is intended, side effects of careless game development, or completely made up in my head, it can either be very rewarding or very frustrating depending on the type of player you are. Additionally, from start to finish (barring any deaths), boss fights in Hyper Light Drifter seem to take about 45 seconds to a minute and a half. I was sad to see such underwhelming boss fights, as this game has enormous potential for very good ones.
Despite calling it mediocre earlier, I have very little to say about navigating the game's areas. For me, the in-game map functioned as more of a loose guideline than an essential tool. Were it not for the objective markers as well as needing the map to teleport, I likely wouldn't have used it at all.
There are many hidden objectives within the game, though I will admit that I uncovered few of them. Perfectionist players are likely to have a field day exploring all the hidden content.
Overall, Hyper Light Drifter is a decent title that is as easy to overestimate as it is difficult to enjoy.

Beautiful graphics, crisp controls and a moving story thats conveyed without language.  This game deserves way more press and attention.  The best indie game I've ever played.  Simply amazing and there are all sorts of nooks and crannies and unlocks to pursue in addition to the main story and quests.  The art style is stunning and its complimented by a beautiful soundtrack that reminds me somewhat of the Blade Runner score.

By far the best things about HLD are the combat and the art style.  HLD has some of the best pixel art out there, with goergous backgrounds and enemy sprites.  There are lots of minor details in various designs that you might not have thought possible with pixel art, and everything has incredibly fluid animation.  The music is also fairly decent, and greatly complements the art style.  The combat is what I remember best, though.  It's simply dashing, slashing, and shooting.  You dash towards the enemy, attack with your sword to charge your gun, dash away to dodge an attack, and shoot from the distance.  Everything was designed around this attack and retreat strategy, including your health, as you have very little, but can replenish it with health backs as long as you aren't being hit.

The original Tomb Raider is one of my favourite Action/Adventure games ever. It could have something to do with the fact it was the first game i bought for the Playstation though.
Well let's get this out of the way then; The graphics were amazing at that time when it launched on the Playstation, let alone the PC version. But most games that came out in the Playstation era did not age well, this is no exception. The graphics look blocky, just like most Playstation games.
Tomb Raider's gameplay didn't change much over the years so there's nothing special on that front. Lara shoots & jumps and that's about it. She's not able to crouch in this game yet, but she can switch levers!
The protagonist of Tomb Raider is ofcourse Lara Croft, I don't think there's anyone that doesn't know who that is. The other characters in the game are quite interesting too. The voice acting wasn't great but it didn't bother me much.
I won't say the game's story will blow your mind but it's pretty decent and makes you want to play on.
Most of the game takes place in Ancient buildings, Ruins, Tombs and Caves with lots of references to mythical gods. Obviously one of the things that made this game so great.
One of the reasons why Tomb Raider is such a memorable game. I know Music or sounds doesn't make a game but it sure can make it stand out from the rest. The sounds themselves are nothing special but the music is something special. Beautiful Ambient tracks and Orchestrial tracks will be played whenever you enter a new location and it instantly sets the mood.
There are only a few weapons in the game but I don't think this game needs a lot of weapons.
Tomb Raider has a big variety of enemies. Most of the time you will be shooting animals, some of them are endangered species or even extinct. Aside from animals you will be battling monsters and a few humans.
As I already said before; Tomb Raider will always be one my favourite games and I would recommend anyone, who isn't afraid of outdated graphics, to try this game.

So I've played the original Rebuild games on Kongregate back in the day and found I really enjoyed them, considering that was at a time when zombie genre games were all the rage.
Now I've gotten a bit sick of zombie games as of late as they are now pretty much everywhere (the games, not the zombie themselves, otherwise I'd doubt I'd be able to make this review). So I was a bit skeptical buying this; the only reason I ended up buying it was because of the name.
The game is very familiar to the older games, just with much better graphics, runs a lot smoother and has a decent enough story about it. Characters have more personality than before, and actually encourages you to get to know them better as you progress through the game. The game offers a significant challenge, with the difficulty swerving all over the place. At some points you will be doing very little as you try to expand your little community, while others you will be desperately holding on for dear life as you try to push back the hordes that are coming to nobble on your googlies. This isn't necessarily a bad thing, as I can imagine this is how a zombie horde would play out.
This game though, is not without fault. The game feels very mobilesque especially in the UI. Of course, I don't know if it was designed with mobile gaming in mind, but based on initial impressions it feels that way. Also, I must say rather reluctantly I don't feel there has been enough improvement over the original F2P games online. It's certainly better than them without argument, but you may find yourself asking is it worth paying money for it?
My answer to that question would be: yes, solely for the fact the originals were good enough to pay money for.
Overall, the game is still good to play and is fun to delve into the midst of zombie hordes, and does take a slightly different direction in an overly saturated genre. Bare in mind though, if you are unsure whether to buy it, there are alternatives in the form of the prequels.

of" - this is an actual PC game, even if it doesn't look like one on the surface.
The mechanics are simple & straightforward, and the learning curve is deceptive.  It seems childishly simple
but once you've sunk an hour or two into you start to see the much deeper strategy game hidden just behind that "casual" image.  Running side-by-side with your
game element of juggling food, materials, ammo, fuel and (most importantly) time, all while playing the risk-management game alongside when choosing missions... there is also an above-average
riding sidecar with it as well.  People have relationships - friends, enemies, lovers, spouses and children.  Those relationship are dynamic, and true mastery of this game means not just tossing the people with the best skill stats at a problem but also making sure that your team actually functions as such.
Another nice, yet simple, feature that the game gets right is the difficulty scale.  Put it on Easy and yeah, a chimp can beat it, but put it on Impossible and you better have a jar of lube ready.  Maps can be anywhere from tiny hamlets to a city so large & vast it would make Judge Dredd do a double-take.  While you can't customize the map generation per se, it is seed based.  So if you've got a map that you really like you can duplicate it for replay simply by jotting down that number for later use.
This game would be complete as it is even if all you had to do was deal with zombies, but of course you can - at your own discretion - crank it up another notch by adding a dozen different factions into the game.  They can become allies, trade partners, or (most likely) enemies to further assail your little fort on a daily basis.
Now don't let this praise fool you - it's still got bugs, and it does have it's flaws.  I'd rate the "price-to-entertainment" ratio of this game as Good.  Meaning it's got the quality level of a $20 to $25 game but only costs $15.  And as of this writing it's on sale, so even better.

And to keep this review honest, I kickstarted Duelyst back in 2014. I was hoping to get a Fire Emblem-esque game but PvP. And I was greatly impressed back then as I am now. Actually, even moreso now.
Now for the review:
Pros:
-It's a wonderful iteration of tactics style rpg combat made for a MMO audience. That is pretty darn rare considering the best PvP scenario with this type of gameplay was Fire Emblem or Advance Wars, and that was uncommon outside of Japan.
-Easy to get into. Harder to master. That's right, there's depth to the combat mechanics!
-The art was as beautiful and charming. It's a blend of pixel and something akin to cellshading. The music is also soothing and I find that the summon blips, swings, grunts to be spot on.
-The devs are faithful, the devs work hard, and the devs listen. It's come a long way since alpha and beta back in the day. The new factions are balanced and the additional heroes to the factions are different enough to twist a general gameplay style.
-F2P? Casual? No problem. The game is very generous with giving out gold and thus, cards (and it was a lot easier getting legs here than it was in Hearthstone)
-Legs are not as influential as they are in HS. Most of them are not as efficient in terms of value as are lower cards. Plus, they tend to be higher mana cost cards, meaning you won't see 2 drops giving a good chunk of momentum with effects you can't mirror unless you own those cards.
-Once a day daily puzzles. Do you remember "checkmate in one turn" puzzles? I do. I loved them as a kid. Still do now. And if you don't have the patience for it, then someone can easily give you the solution. But where's the fun in that?
-Tight knit community. I find this a plus: if you need help, you can easily find it on the official forums as well as the subreddit.
-The game feels balanced compared to other TCGs I've mingled with, IRL and online.
-Disenchanting a leg for much needed dust early in the game to make basic decks is not as painful as it is in Hearthstone. For most, it's actually recommended.
Cons:
-It's still a collectible card game. If you tire of collecting packs then it's not your cup of tea.
-There's a crate system in the game. You'll have a random chance of finding said crates after a game but you'll have to pay money in order to open them. It's only for cosmetics though so you're not missing much by not being able to open them.
-UI seems a little clunky at first. I'm being nitpicky, but it bugs me when I have to buy cards in a different window in order to open said packs.
Tips:
-The Duelyst subreddit has a list of the hidden achievements available. Google it, thank me later.
-Get all the factions to level 10. Don't focus on one. When you'll need to branch out later, you'll be hard pressed to compete with others of your ranking since you didn't get the second general unlocked or the extra copies of the common (and usually necessary) cards of the typical budget deck.
And of course, hope to see more people join the ranks! I hope you guys enjoyed this review!

Overall, a fantastic experience, a big thumbs up!

The game is inspired by so called "vehilcular games" but this time helicopters, this mean movement and orientation form 3rd person and most of the shooting from 1st person.
Its has in it current state some PvP balance issues.
But you can enjoy its PvE games.
Make no mistake while the game has its realistic flightmodel approaches the game wants to acceable, so looking for a hardcore simulation is the wrong approach.
In the future there will be more realism but i dont see it turning into a simulator (there is an advanced control mode maybe it can statisfy your simulation needs).
While its more arcade it is not a brainoff game, i see a lot of player dying from carelessly flying around.
But that is a good thing!
Bring a bit of brain and you can enjoy the game.
The game lacks atm ingame tutorials there are community tutorials but you have to look for them. (press F1 for the controls if you are ingame)
Matches in this game are an hour long if the victory conditions are not reached, so compared other game there is more commitment needed.
Overall its runs fine, but atm during the desync the hitdetection has its problems.
At the moment the game has 5 maps 3 with the "Frontline" mode: You drop infantry at Landing Zones to capture it, tanks will move up this LZ and reinforce it and pave the way to the next one in the direction of the enemie base.
The other mode is a "Domination" like mode also here LZ get captured by the infantry dropped from your helos and try to hold more than the other team long enough to fullfill their victory condtions.
In both modes players fight with their helos over this LZ, But only helos which have infantry loaded can capture them.
Attack helis like the AH-64 Apache will deliver destruction but they will not be able to win the game alone.
Also there are atm three additional infantry types to deploy on the map which can support you and your team.
OK thats it have fun!

Until this title came up in the sale I hadn't really paid much attention to it as I have been a long term fan of the grand-daddy of the genre - Sim City - right from its early days on my old trusty Commodore Amiga.  The last decade or so have been spent living in Sim City 4  which with countless mods has become the game I'd always wanted - albeit now a little dated.  So when the sale price for Skylines grabbed my attention the first thing I went off and searched about t'interweb was 'Sim City 4 vs Cities: Skylines'.  The results you will find are pretty much unanimously that it is the natural successor starting where SC4 is now with all its mod base... so I bit the bullet - and I am VERY pleased I did.  Move over SC4 - your crown has well and truely been usurped.  Skylines is FANTASTIC.  It provides the full 3D experience of your city in stunning quality and variety from which ever angle you desire with the same game play area of its more successful predecessor.  And when it starts to get stale or you want a feature from a mod in SC4 just go look on the workshop - there are a country load of quality mods - and if not you can build your own.  So I am going to agree with all the reviews I saw and shout from the tallest rooftop I can build that Cities: Skylines is well worth its title.  Its aiming high and not far off being there.
Definately a recommended game from a long term fan of Sim City 4 - SC4 is dead - long live Sim City 4 - Cities: Skylines now rules the roost on this PC...

Rocksmith 2014 has been the biggest help with me improving my guitar and bass skills. While basic guitar class gave me the fundamental, Rocksmith helped me play a lot better. The lessons are a great for beginners and even more experienced players. Guitarcade is an interesting way to teach various techinques such as fret movement, chords, scales, and more all through mini-games. Duelyst is a beautiful amalgamation of classic card games like Magic: The Gathering and Hearthstone and hex-based strategy games such as Final Fantasy Tactics and less specifically, the newer XCOM games. Developed by Counterplay games, smooth animations and a crisp and pleasing pixel art style give Duelyst a level of polish that very few free-to-play games have. The game has been available through an individual launcher up until yesterday when it was released on Steam, hopefully giving this game a much deserved boost in the player base.
Being free-to-play hopefully won't turn off many collectible card game players because, well, most digital CCG's are free-to-play. Unlike most, however, Duelyst is very generous with its booster packs, called Spirit Orbs. I received tons of them when I started playing that gave me a great collection of cards to build off of. Single Orbs will cost you 100 gold, which is plentiful as like as you complete all of your daily quests and can win a couple of games against real players every now and then.
You have your traditional Hearthstone style mana system, gaining one permanent mana every turn. Combat is as smooth as a whistle. After your summoned minions, that can be summoned within a few tiles of your general (think as if your Hearthstone hero was a 2/20 card itself), are rid of their summoning sickness, they can attack in any direction within a certain tile radius. minions who are attacked, counter attack just like almost any other CCG out there.
Duelyst truly sets itself apart from these other CCG's with the added strategy and almost puzzle like layer. Ranged minions, who can attack anything from any spot on the board, are just one of the ways the game uses the play field in an effective and fun way. Provoke is another mechanic that does such a thing, adding a taunt-like mechanic in which no minions in the minion with provoke's radius can move or attack without first destroying said minion. Teleporting minions to any spot on the board is yet another way Duelyst creates fun and different ways to use it's mechanics.
I mentioned earlier a puzzle aspect that Duelyst presents. While regular PVP games don't seem to give you the feeling of a puzzle game, the daily challenge, as well as Solo Challenge mode, is absolutely, in and of itself, a puzzle. The board is set the same every time you retry the challenge and your goal is to move minions and use mechanics in a certain way and order to kill the opposing general in one turn. Solo Challenge mode includes 6 sets of 5 challenges, each one more difficult than the last. This mode is sure to give even the sharpest of players at least a few hours of gameplay.
Card rarity will look familiar to any CCG player: Common, Rare, Epic, and Legendary. With each orb containing 5 cards, with at least one rare, you will find yourself with more rare or better cards than normal. Epic cards tend to show up every two orbs and legendaries one in every four. This may seem high, but when you can have 3 copies of a legendary in a deck, along with 3 copies of any other card, it's easy to see why Duelyst is so generous with its rare cards. Deckbuilding is very fun with tons of mechanics you can build around. A Golem based deck built around Golem Vanquisher, which gives your other golems provoke, ranged decks that buff your ranged minions to ping down the opposing general, or a deck that is designed to try and OTK (one turn kill) your opponent, are just a few of the near infinite decks you can build, provided you have the cards for it.
With 10% of the proceeds of all pre-orders of the upcoming expansion Denizens of Shim'zar, which will add more than 90 new cards to the collection, going towards the prize pool for the Duelyst World Championship, I'm sure the pro scene is about to bustle and explode.
While I just spent the last 700 words or so gushing over the game, I struggle to play more than 4 or 5 games at a time. I would love to lose an entire day or weekend to this game as I do to other CCG's, grinding out gold and wins on the ladder, I just can't. The game is mentally exhausting, which is absolutely not a bad thing. It makes you think more than most games which is a definite plus to most people. It's my weak mind that's the problem.
With it's recent release on Steam, coupled with the fact that it is free-to-play, I would be on the look out for this game to explode in popularity very soon. Counterplay Games seem to have their priorities set straight and have content lined up for a while, including a second expansion in the works and four new cards added to the core set every month. Give Duelyst a try. You will not be disappointed. Plus, its free, so why not give it a chance?

In-depth game that requires skill and tactics. Pretty much Hearthstone chess, but without the bull of Hearthstone. Cards are easy to obtain. You can quickly build a deck in the timespan of a week or two. Thats about the time it takes to learn the ins and outs of the game.
Also unlike Hearthstone, there is a movement system, which allows for much greater usage of tactics and diversity. Even halfway decks can compare to the stronger decks, as long as good strategy is used. Also very different to Hearthstone, which is full of RNG bull and meta decks.
There are so many ways to play this game. Every faction has two Generals (similar to HS classes, but with TWO :D ). Each has their own ability to help their minions or themselves. Or hurt the enemy. Factions have specific cards and abilities unique to them, each with their own strengths and weaknesses. There are also neutral cards that anyone can use.
Deck building is very creative. You can do anything (mostly) and get away with it. Do you wanna make a deck focusing on taking out the enemy general with the pure brute force of yours? Maybe you want to play dirty and lure enemies into well placed traps. Or you could just make a giant army of 1/1 minions. Possibilities are endless. Unlike Hearthstone...

Absolutely stunning visuals, a lovely soundtrack, and a story that might not say much but tells so much more in text. Hyper Light drifter is a treat to the eyes, the ears, and the brain! It's also tough as nails and quite a challenge to beat.
There's so much to do and see in the game, including several collectibles, some of which I haven't even seen. The bosses are a treat and remind me of older games like Megaman, following interesting patterns that allow for learning as you watch them.
Your limited health pool and amount of medkits make this journey to heal yourself and the world quite an arduous one, but it's worth it in the end, especially with all the abilities you can find. All four areas are teeming with life and character, and there are even alternate outfits if you're so inclined as to find them.
I still haven't finished the game 100%, and I doubt you will either without a walkthrough, but there's a lot of detail in the environment and a lovely plethora of entertaining locales, so even if you aren't a completionist there's most definitely something for you.

After my first playthrough I was almost about to return it. Reasons being that : Cant unlock more aircraft yet, lack of game modes, lack of maps, lack of users at times. However, I had a second thought that this game is just in EARLY ACCESS so therefore many more features and improvements will come in the future (Hopefully) so I stuck with it.
After getting to used to whats available now, im kinda glad I kept this game instead of returning it. Im playing it on a borrowed Macbook Air and so far so good under custom low settings (I keep my textures and detailing Medium to High depending) also if youre not too into or willing to bear with it, the framerate is decent for my laptop. The game however is a bit challenging, its not simply fly around and kill everyone thats not on your side, youre basically playing the support role that most of these helicopters to, from landing troops and special troops in cap points to supporting other team mates when theyre doing the same to attack or defending. You gotta strategize and work with your team mates to win the day....when your playing against other human players lol (No bots just yet)

I wont go that much into negative details (Its tough to fly these things but then again, im willing to learn hahaha) but if youre more into arcade fast action stuff this wont be your cup of tea but if you are into military stuff then this might be up your alley. *8/31/15 Update - Revisiting the game and doubling my game time*
I put 20 hours in the game in the past two weeks, doubling my game time, as the game has been fully completed.
The core of the gameplay is still the same, and if you liked the first two Rebuilds, you'll enjoy this one. That being said, the reason why Rebuild 3 is so addicting because it plays exactly the same as the first two Rebuilds. Building a strong community of survivors while reclaiming buildings for your base was the reason why the first two Rebuilds were addicting and it is the same for Rebuild 3. The new faction addition doesn't add much to the enjoyability of the game because it's repetitive and the novelty fades away faster than you'd like.
This game introduces factions, which you have to befriend or destroy, and the premise is exciting. Learning how to befriend these factions for trading and security bonuses for your base is very satisfying. However, forging alliances is formulaic - as long as you have a high level leader, craftable trading goods, and agree to all the demands of the faction leaders - you'll have an alliance before long. There are meaningful interactions with the faction leaders which make the faction system unique and interesting, but there aren't nearly enough of these. Each map in story mode is the same as the one before it and there isn't much variation to the gameplay. The result is an alliance system doesn't really add much to the game and Rebuild 3 falls short as a paid sequel.
In conclusion, Rebuild 3 is an addicting game that is a polished version of its predecessors. For what it is, Rebuild 3 is a fun game - a fantasy zombie survival. However I ask that you try the free prequels on Kongregate before you purchase, because the fun part of Rebuild 3 hasn't been changed since the first Rebuild. Had I known what I know now, I probably would've skipped this title.

TL;DR: Rebuild 3: Gangs of Deadsville is a light, zombie themed 4X game. It's fantastic and you should buy it.
I am a huge fan of Civ. I love the exploration, the gradual expansion, the sense of progress and increasing power.
As a Civ player I tend to turtle, that is, I like to build a solid and impenetrable perimeter before I expand further. Eventually, I'll push out to nab a bit of territory here, a strategic resource there. Over time, I'll get bigger and bigger, with every gain hard fought and locked down. Rebuild 3 might be my perfect game.
Another thing about Civ is that it is
intended to be a realistic government or historical simulator, I like the fact that Chairman Mao is fighting with Abraham Lincoln. I like the bright colours and the slightly irreverent tone. I don't need the game to include 'realistic' details like racism and slavery, and I don't mind the fact that swordsmen can occasionally kill a tank.
Rebuild 3: Gangs of Deadsville is not a realistic zombie simulator, it contains cartoonish graphics, cannibalism, and over the top stereotypes. You can convert a field of rubble into a tower apartment block with a single builder. It's
. Obviously, however, if what you're after is something dark, brooding and 'realistic', this game is not for you.
One more thing. The prequel, Rebuild 2 (AKA Rebuild Mobile, or just "Rebuild"), was a popular game on iOS and Android and Rebuild 3: Gangs of Deadsville has also now been released on the same platforms. The mobile version is identical in every way to the PC version, and the game plays really well on the mobile. If you want your mobile games to stay on mobile then feel free to buy it there. But I'm mostly a PC player and I like my big screen and mouse control.
Regardless, Rebuild doesn't
like a mobile game in that it's not particularly 'clicky', menus work like PC menus and the interface works like a PC interface. Still, it doesn't have infinite tech trees or massive worlds or complex animation and that's a huge part of its appeal.
Basically, if you're after a light 4X game with a very strong sense that you're always making progress, that doesn't become overwhelming towards the end game, that doesn't have dead time following an initial expansion/exploration rush, that strips out a lot of tedious micromanagement, and if you like your 4X games to completely play out in a couple of hours each, then this is your game.

Wind Child is a unique type of RPG Maker game, which doesn't fall into the pile of rubbish RPG Maker games which just want to take your money. This one on the other hand looks like the developers have taken some care and attention to their game. There is a interesting story line, and great opening cutscene that just makes you ask "what the hell is going on?" The characters are really nicely done and the mapping is fairly decent, of course there are some flaws with the game which I will talk about as well.
Wind Child is a fun and great RPG Maker game that really does look like they have taken some care and consideration to this game. This game isn't a cash grabber like some other RPG Maker games are. According to the developer, the game is approximately 20 hours long, if this is true then this game really has been worked on well. The opening cutscene ireally pulled me into the story, I wasn't really sure what was going on and why I was these people I was playing as but it was intriguing none the less. As the story begins to unfold, the game really shows off what you can do with RPG Maker. The characters that you come across are very well done, it's not like other games where you have a character added to your party for no specific reason to do so. Wind Child really makes sense for this person to help you along your journey as you play through the game. Upon entering new towns and cities you come across, you will find people to talk to. They aren't all just welcome to the city, some of these characters give you some background information about the story or about themselves.This draws away to the basic defult character saying things like "hello" and such that just really aren't that interesting. Another thing that the developers dide very well is the custom start menu and the mission log. The mission log is rather helpful if you have taken a break fro the game and when you come back in you are not sure what to do. The mission log will tell you what your missions are. Although I have explained a lot of positives about the gameplay itself, there are also some negatives that I feel like I must cover. First off, some of the tiles don't work the way that they should. What I mean by this is that you can walk through a tile that you aren't suppose to normally, either because you aren't on the right level, or because the block is meant to be impassable. A example of this is when you enter your home town, upon entering you will have to walk under a bridge to get across, although you walk over the bride. If you then walk forwards you will then be on the next height part of the world. This kind of brings down the game a little, as I found a couple of tiles that weren't exactly acting like they where suppose to. Another thing that slightly annoyed me whlist playing this game is the text that breifly describes the mission you are currently doing. Sometimes a line of text will be bold and the other lines will just be in normal font, this slightly annoyed me as this game is really fun to play.
The developers really went all out with the custom tilesets that they created for their game specifically. This really makes it look different from the other RPG Maker games that only use the default tiles with minimum editing. Wind Child really takes the game and makes it their own, this just makes the game more unique and well presented. There is also a very nice transition whenever you enter a new town or city, with the name of the town that appears on the screen. The mapping (which I guess is part of graphics) is really well done, although I found that in some places it did seem a little bit empty like there was just too much space. Also in my personal opinion I didn't like some of the designs of the houses, they looked weird and out of place. Most of the outside mapping was done really well, there wasn't overcrowding trees or anything that really didn't make the map look natural.
When it comes to the music and sound of this game, I feel like th developers really got it right. There is fast paced music when something happens, when you have to chase that guard. It's then very calm and collective when you are in town or city. Something that I didn't like is that some of the houses didn't have any sound at all, and that really was a little dull. I also didn't like the way that the music carried on from outside to the inside of the houses. To me that kinda lowers the game a little.
Wind Child is a very unique type of RPG Maker game. For the price that it's asking for this is definitely worth picking up. The game is approximately 20 hours long according to the developer, and that is well worth the money the game is asking for. The story is very interesting as are some of the characters you meet along the way.

Impressions & Score:

Story: 9.5 out of 10
The story in part II of Crysis has improved by a lot, although you do have a feeling that's copying Half-Life 2 on some aspects. There is a lot of work put into this new story, videos before every mission, information about characters and enemies, in-game cutscenes etc., most of the work is of good quality and there are some surprises throught the story, but not many. I liked how the aliens have been changed but at the same time I would have prefered to see a mix of old aliens and new ones, so that there's a logic why they changed aspect (they upgraded some of their units, etc.) otherwise you'll have the impression that there aren't the same as those from Crysis I, even though the story tries to tell you that they are. There are many captivating moments throught the story and I like the fact that it isn't too predictable, meaning that you won't know what will happen exactly. The end leaves room for many sequels to come, so be ready to continue buying Crysis.
Graphics: 10 out of 10
Crysis 2 continues it's legacy of excellent graphics that it started in 2007, improving on every aspect. The lights, weapon effects, character design, environments are all top notch, the only thing I'm dissapointed is the fact that they removed vehicule interiors, which were not only great in the first Crysis but gave more realism to the game. There are some bad graphics on certain objects, but you'll ignore them easily  when you evaluate the whole game. Crysis 2 graphics still manage to impress me and I'm playing this game in 2015, so that's why I gave it the maximum score.
Gameplay: 8 out of 10
Gameplay is great, many features added (ledge grab, power kick, combined nano powers etc.) but other were removed (vehicule interiors - which would have been great on the streets of New York, no flight vehicules, no boats, no tanks, no freezing effect etc.). Some removed features, I can understand, others not, since they would have made the gameplay better. Also, I've mentioned earlier the bug with some spawn locations, which can remove some realism from the game.  The good thing is that some of the features added work very well, in the ruined New York environment. Many players complained for the fact that the game became too linear, you don't have the freedom to roam around on huge map like in Crysis 1, but I understand the producers for making the game more linear, since many of the cool effects (buildings, bridges falling etc.) wouldn't have been possible on a  free-roam map, also the level of details wouldn't have been the same. Overall the gameplay is quite cool when combined with the great story.
Audio: 10 out of 10
The music in Crysis 2 is just awesome, especially the music in the menu, the other sound effects are also of high quality. How can I give it less than 10 when sometimes I was starting the game just to listen the music, I wasn't even playing.
AI Behavior: 8.5 out of 10
The AI is quite good, not awesome, but it handles itself pretty well. I've played the game on the max difficulty (Post-Human Warrior) and I didn't find the game too hard, the AI shoots very well but if you use corectly the nanosuit powers, you'll manage to finish each mission after just a few tries (you'll need a few, since the enemies are unpredictable).  The Human AI soldiers will try to flank you and use grenades, while the Aliens AI will jump on you, deactivate your suit and even cloak (at end of the game). The bad part is that sometimes the AI acts stupid, for example you kill an enemy AI on cloak right in front of his friends and they don't react at all, like nothing happened. Also sometimes the AI gets stucked behind certain boxes or in certain areas. Over 75 % of my kills were stealth kills (mostly with the knife), actually if you play on the max difficulty, most of your kills will be stealth also, since the enemy can kill you easily even with armor mode on. Still even after those bugs, the AI is quite good and dynamic, for which it deserves a good score.
Multiplayer: not tested
I've played this game during a month that I had no internet at all, so I couldn't actually test anything that involved multiplayer. But I've red that the suits powers are diminished considerably, in order to be able to kill other players faster, and not wander around in a stalemate. I'm not a multiplayer gamer, so I mostly prefer single-player campaigns, but I think that Crysis 2 would have deserved at least an 8 or a 9 for the multiplayer (mostly because of many removed features).
Overall: 9.2 out 10
The new Crysis 2, really improves on everything that the last one did except gameplay. I didn't gave the maximum score because I didn't liked the fact that they removed a lot of cool stuff from the previous Crysis, like a lot of vehicules and boats and other things. But even after this Crysis 2 definitely is worth the money, the story is very well done for a shooter, you'll spend many hours of good gameplay, the environments are awesome, the aliens are great, the audio is cool, what more can I say. I bought the game on a sale for less than 4 EUR, but if you don't want to wait for a sale, go and buy it right away cause it deserves full price.
PS:
Enemies in Crysis do have the same amount of health and deal the same amount of damage regardless of difficulty. Difficulty only affects their A.I.; i.e. reaction time, awareness, accuracy, and duration of burst fire.
On the highest difficulty setting(Post-Human Warrior there's no split-second invincibility after you're hit, allowing you to be damaged by each consecutive bullet in a spray of automatic fire. As a result, you die a LOT faster against automatic fire when not in Armor Mode. In Armor Mode, however, your durability seems pretty much the same. Source:
2 Weapons-Enemies Guide
Important: After finishing the game I only got 12 out 13 weapons attachments, which gave me a 99.76 % completion. I was a bit disappointed that I couldn't get 100 % completion and started to look online for tips. I found out that you actually cannot get the 13 weapons attachments because of a bug (they decided that ironsights isn't an attachment, but then they forget to update the list to contain 12 not 13) that the producers forgot to remove, so at least try to get at least 12 if you want to have the game completed 100 %.

Short summary of review:
A charming game which is surprisingly fun to play, although you have to do the toturial each time. If you're experienced with these type of games the tutorial is painfully slow anyhow as the mechanics of this game is not different enough from most other games like it to make it necessary to explain the combat and workings of the game in detail to anyone but the less experienced players. Also the combat doesn't really change much hence it's not very replayable and to be honest i didn't find even the hardest difficulty noticably more challenging than normal (didn't try easy).
Still. If it's on sale it is a good time once you get past the tutorial and start playing the game.
Pro:
- Charming graphics
- Easily learned battle mechanics that, although somewhat easy, still can throw you if you don't get rid of the right enemy first (as an example: leaving the poison dealing archers till last while dealing with a slow moving, heavy hitting boss may make you lose the battle). These should however be things that come naturally to more experienced players.
- Good balance of difficulty throughout the game as the middle part is not the most difficult part of the game as in so many other games.
- Choices matter - chances are you will not earn enough gold to focus both on having a full army, all skills unlocked AND all the best equipment, you may have to choose unless you're insanely good at not taking damage and healing your own units (the gold won from each battle depends on how many of your units died).
- Some resemblence of a storyline throughout the game despite the fact that it's a small one that took me only a few hours to play through. The current time on my profile is two playthroughs, and the second was much shorter than the first. Although it's generic and has the almost clichéd throwback that most RPGs have where you - upon beating your sworn arch enemy - realize that who you that who was portrayed at the main villain was just someone's pawn afterall aaaand you have to defeat them to. And their armies. And their pets. And their wife. Possibly. Also sully the honour of their daughter in in the nude.. waitwhat. No. Nevermind.
Cons:
- Music got really annoying to me (granted, i find myself unable to listen to game music most of the time).
- The different difficulty settings were really not that different to me.
- You're forced to play through the tutorial as it's integrated in the story of the game (First three moves or so on the map).
- Not really challenging at all, even on the hardest difficulty.
(- For the achievement junkies like myself: you have to check out their twitter online in order to obtain all achievements. What the h*** is that about? For someone who doesn't even have a twitter account that was just a nuisance. In fact. It'd probably be a nuisance even if I did have an account.)
Conclusion: See summary (top of the post).

Braveland is a simple mobile strategy game that was ported to PC. For the price, this game is a winner! Overall, the turn-based battles are the classic type of battles that games like “Heroes of Might & Magic” uses. It follows a linear campaign where the main character is a poor farmer who sets out to find the evil king and gets revenge for losing his village and family.
In addition, to the campaign mode, Braveland also has a survivor mode. Survivor mode provides a more challenging battle environment than the campaign mode. Also, survivor mode places healing and combat limitations on certain units so the battles get tricky as additional thinking is required to survive to the next battle.
In conclusion, Braveland is nothing of a surprise, but it a good game to both beginners of turned-based strategy games and to veterans as well. Although it does lack replay value, the simple and easy gameplay is family friendly and it provides a few hours of quick enjoyable moments.

TL;DR: Rebuild 3: Gangs of Deadsville is a light, zombie themed 4X game. It's fantastic and you should buy it.
I am a huge fan of Civ. I love the exploration, the gradual expansion, the sense of progress and increasing power.
As a Civ player I tend to turtle, that is, I like to build a solid and impenetrable perimeter before I expand further. Eventually, I'll push out to nab a bit of territory here, a strategic resource there. Over time, I'll get bigger and bigger, with every gain hard fought and locked down. Rebuild 3 might be my perfect game.
Another thing about Civ is that it is
intended to be a realistic government or historical simulator, I like the fact that Chairman Mao is fighting with Abraham Lincoln. I like the bright colours and the slightly irreverent tone. I don't need the game to include 'realistic' details like racism and slavery, and I don't mind the fact that swordsmen can occasionally kill a tank.
Rebuild 3: Gangs of Deadsville is not a realistic zombie simulator, it contains cartoonish graphics, cannibalism, and over the top stereotypes. You can convert a field of rubble into a tower apartment block with a single builder. It's
. Obviously, however, if what you're after is something dark, brooding and 'realistic', this game is not for you.
One more thing. The prequel, Rebuild 2 (AKA Rebuild Mobile, or just "Rebuild"), was a popular game on iOS and Android and Rebuild 3: Gangs of Deadsville has also now been released on the same platforms. The mobile version is identical in every way to the PC version, and the game plays really well on the mobile. If you want your mobile games to stay on mobile then feel free to buy it there. But I'm mostly a PC player and I like my big screen and mouse control.
Regardless, Rebuild doesn't
like a mobile game in that it's not particularly 'clicky', menus work like PC menus and the interface works like a PC interface. Still, it doesn't have infinite tech trees or massive worlds or complex animation and that's a huge part of its appeal.
Basically, if you're after a light 4X game with a very strong sense that you're always making progress, that doesn't become overwhelming towards the end game, that doesn't have dead time following an initial expansion/exploration rush, that strips out a lot of tedious micromanagement, and if you like your 4X games to completely play out in a couple of hours each, then this is your game.

The Good: Charming narration (both in voice acting and in writing), great soundtrack, nice (if simple) visual aesthetic, concept of blocks with different skills helping each other through puzzles is both interesting and directly mirriors the story this game is trying to tell.
The Less Good: Though there are a lot of cool ideas and interesting puzzles in this game, overall I felt this game under utilizes its coolest ideas in favor of simple platforming.  Yes, there are plenty of levels where you use your blocks together to achieve your goals but there are also many levels even later in the game that are just platforming.  Also, the difficulty from level to level fluctuates greatly with no real curve.  A lot of this comes from the game not always building off of what you've learned in previous levels, even in the late game.  If you are good at platforming, you may not notice but if you're more interested in the puzzles than simple jumping, you might have a hard time at certain points.
Summary: Thomas Was Alone is a charming game that made me care about colored rectangles but a combination of an inconsistant difficulty curve and not doing as much with its ideas as I hoped it would keeps me from wholeheartedly recommending this game, especially if platforming is difficult for you.

Transformers Devastation is a different beast, it’s a game that wears nostalgic influence not on its sleeve but in its core. To this game, nostalgia is the Matrix of leadership. This is evident from the boxart alone. This isn’t one of the newer series of Transformers or the films; we’re talking original Generation One. Even the opening menu evokes an old-school feel with a sparse screen crackling with static, while showcasing its options. It’s like an old DVD menu screen and really adds to the overall experience.
In-game the character models look stunning, I’ve never seen cel-shading look quite this good before. Chunky outlines surround beautifully bright colours as metallic style shading cascades across the panels, and it’s all animated beautifully. This is some exceptional design work that’s completely wondrous to behold. The environments, while quite bland early on, at least make some use of verticality with fights taking place on rooftops and skyways with the city below. As the game progresses Platinum ramps the spectacle up, with oodles of large, moving background artifacts, lightshows and particle effects giving later areas a real epic feel.
You can choose from five selectable Autobots, each with their own fighting style to bring to the table. Optimus Prime is the usual “good at everything” character; Bumblebee is small and nippy; Wheeljack has a shield; Sideswipe has good range, and Grimlock is a grappler. The styles are quite distinct with certain advantages applied to each, but you can easily complete each chapter regardless of your choice. If you decide you don’t like a particular one then you can switch between them before each chapter, or at select points in at an Autobot logo.
Regardless of length, Transformers Devastation is a wonderful blend of pure 90s nostalgia and one of the best fighting systems in games. It truly feels like a Transformers videogame should, and one that fans have always wanted. Whether or not you’re a fan of the original Transformers or not, this is a great game. The fan service will obviously make it more enjoyable for some, but anyone will derive enjoyment from this.

After like week of “playing” songs I decided that it is time for next step “Lessons”. Rocksmith covers like 80-90% of all you need to know about guitar playing only questions I had\have are about my better posture\picking\sitting\guitar holding methods\thumb position.
I played every day for 1 hour minimum. Whole month I played lessons and after I finished all to 80-100% “score” I thought “Now I am ready to Rock \m/!”. RS2014 have very interesting thing - “Session mode” where you can play along selected instruments, learn scales or use metronome. So after I “finished” lesson mode - I launched Session mode to Rock like hell.  I hit strings and instead of epic music heard nothing even close to what normal people call “music” that was random note pickings\bends. “I suck”, “Time to uninstall and die”, “60 day challenge”...
So what was wrong with me or is it game? -nothing is wrong here, you can’t play like Slash after 2 months in Rocksmith, sorry. Then where is problem, why I felt so badly? I could play some songs like to 90%, but when I try session - almost nothing (I can play some parts from songs but no improvisation). Main reason for that is - game teach you how to play Guitar, but almost nothing about how to play music. You can learn how to drive a car, but how you will ride if you don’t know any rules? And that was the answer for my suffering - game gives you good start, then you must walk by yourself - and here comes youtube, books, lessons etc. After Rocksmith you will feel more comfortable with guitar, you will understand what that cool guy on youtube says about technique.
And I continued to practice, even more every day. I watched many videos on youtube, read forums about techniques (how I hate my boney fingers when I practice bar chords). Next I decided to buy new guitar and amp to practice without RS.
2 months after that (5 total in RS) I hear some melodies and clean sound when I play , I still can’t play good improvisation, but I can see progress - from someone who picks string, then looks at monitor and picks next one, to someone who can play some songs to 90-100% and play without RS2014. With all my progress I still think that I suck - and that is normal too, it is called “Learning”. More you play more critical you become to yourself. I still play RS everyday, downloaded many DLC’s - some easy, some hard. With time you will play better, you will see mistakes what you are making (wrong finger placement, wrong hand position) and understand how to fix them - for example now I more and more try to place my fingers correctly and mute strings that aren’t used when I play, month ago I hadn't even thought about it.
Worst thing in all this is when I start comparing time wasted on other games and time I played Rocksmith.

Black Ops III is, unsurpisingly, not very good. I only played the game's multiplayer, because I only had the multiplayer pack because of Humble Monthly's chubby cheeks.
To start off, I've played a good amount of Call of Duty games in my brief existence on this hellish plane of reality that we choose to call Earth. When I was a console peasant, I kind of enjoyed the games, particuarly MW2 and Black Ops. I've played both of these games on PC, and they still hold up a little bit. The games had consistant tone, they had alright map design, they had robust customization systems for classes and a large array of weapons to put in them. The voice acting was decent, in both English and Russian. People will spray♥♥♥♥♥♥all over COD games, and to be honest, there are way better FPS choices on PC. They were good games for their time.
As you might have guessed, Black Ops III does not do this. Let's start with the characters I noticed while playing the multiplayer.
The game has a wide scale of characters, they're all equally stupid. They have voice lines that are horribly acted in the English version, and acted rather nicely in the Russian version. Sometimes the translation is a little odd, but it holds up pretty well, I'd say. The characters have very little personality, which would be reasonable if they weren't individual. This game, much like R6 Seige, brings in a hero system, every operator is equally different and equally inconsequential. Their weapons are one-shot kills, some have little traps, others have lousy abilities. A big part of the game, and in my opinion the best part of the game, is when the matches end. There's a victory scene where the top 3 players on the winning team do emotes, such as the Gangnam Style dance and the infamous "Dab". This brings me to my next part of the review...
This game's tone is all over the place. Your character can get set on fire and scream terribly as their faces melt, and can also go into a dab at the end of a match. Your character can get dismembered by flesh eating nanobugs, crying in absolute pain, all while dressed as a power ranger. The game couldn't really make up its mind on whether to be a wacky fun shooter where everyone has jet packs strapped to them and dance in goofy ways, or to be a sad, melodramatic game where people are dismembered and disfigured by technology.
Tone and interesting character, however, aren't all that makes a game, what about the gameplay. It's not good, it feels really odd, to be frank. 400 hours of CSGO have made me an FPS god when it comes to COD, but I'm not very good at BOIII. The shooter doesn't really make any sense, there isn't really any tactics to it. The game gave players jet packs and wall running, but didn't increase the players movement speed. You're in Exosuits, sure, but you still feel like a regular dude with a jump jet. The guns are boring, the only one's I liked was the Gorgon LMG and the Pump Shotgun, and I didn't use the shotgun very much because I'd get cussed out by other people for using, well, a shotgun. The maps are not made to be played with jetpacks, and it feels really clumpy and misplaced. The maps aren't very well made, at least the ones that come with the game. I'm not spending the money I stole from a homeless man on COD DLC, I'm not 13.
I think.
Many guns are locked behind the "Black Market", a system which makes this lousy, somewhat toleratable game horrendous and grindy. Microtransactions aren't that bad if they only include cosmetics, because then they don't affect the gameplay. Microtransactions that sell amazing weapons that look more interesting than the ones you're currently using is really bad design. If you want the gun that shoots miter saws, buy a pack for 3 bucks and hope that you don't get another cosmetic outfit for a character you haven't unlocked yet. This is reason enough not to buy the game, if it weren't already bad enough.

Hyper Light Drifter is, flat out, just a good game. It doesn't stand out in one particular aspect but the whole game is just well rounded and enjoyable.
The combat the game is based around is admittedly a little repetitive once you get into it, but new enemies and areas keep fights different and challenging. Game mechanics are basic enough to be grasped quickly but take time to master. I have to say the game will warn you it's best played on a controller, and it most certainly is, but it can be done with mouse/keyboard as well. Be prepared for a challenge.
The visuals and soundtrack for the game are stunning, they nail the 16bit style. The UI is good and easy enough to navigate though it could be a bit more straight forward.
The story is... odd, and a bit hard to follow. There's no dialogue so figuring out what's going on in this world you're thrown into takes time and a lot of piecing together but the journey is fun.
Overall 8.5/10, great game.

I really like the concept of this game but I feel there's quite a few things that just aren't quite there yet. For one the singleplayer mode is simply a multiplayer lobby in which you are the only player able to connect. This means that while there are AI ground units there are no AI helicopters which makes the matchs feel very empty. some what realated to this is the extreme effectiveness of enemy AAA. The moment you stray into range, often well before you have the enemies marked on your HUD they open up on you and they're incredibly accurate. capabale of shooting you  down in a matter of seconds reguardless of how hard you manuever or how fast you're moving. This makes it very difficult and frustrating to do anything in singleplayer, even when playing Gen 1 aircraft you'd expect the AAA to be balanced for you decressed speed, agility, and survivability but it's not it's just as powerfull. The final big issue I see with the game as it is, as I mentioned this eariler, is how poor your spotting range is. While ground units will render much further away you won't actually get a HUD marker for them untill you're literally on top of them, well within AAA ranges and far too close for you to be effective with any of your own weapons. The one exeption to this seems to be scout helicoptors which have increased spotting range, which makes sense, but something like an AH-64D should be perfecrtly capable of detecting and identifying an enemy from a safe distance so as to make use of its missiles. All in all I think Heliborne has potential but there's a lot of work that needs to be done before it can be considered finished and before I could in good concience recomend it.

While I wish my Crysis and Warhead games were on Steam instead of DVD so i could review those more publically, all we get is Crysis 2.
Since I have not finished C3 I can only work any comparisons to C1 and WH. I know the tech is older, but guess what, C1 and WH are better than C2 in some ways.
Now, while C2 starts out pretty awesome, because were I ever dying, that would be the only cool way to be saved, and it continues to build into the story and unknown environment with some nice suspense, as you proceed you will start to be dragged around a bit. This means you start by working your way into yourself, building prowess and skills, and get to making some friends. But then, your new pals start to tell you what to do, how to do it, when to do it, etc. Which is fine for a bit, "Sure I'll help you out, grab that latte, make a copy of that document...", but drags on in such a manor for a length of time that starts to get agggrevating. Am I not practically a superhuman? Can I not kick a car into your face from 20 yards? If you give the marine grunt spec-ops mentality a leeway, you can at least cover your lack of independence there. No worries though. Towards the end, you will still be told some things you need to do, but you will have more of a freelance, superhero feel gathered with your actions. And the only issue is the realization that someone has been able to know the dirty things you were thinking about that CIA vixen.
*Notes:
The custom 1912x1076 resolution some players needed for C1 and WH does not seem to be necessary for C2.
If you have experience with C1 and WH, you likely had performance issues. This is the old poorly optimised engines. Crysis 2, even though a heavier engine, with better graphics, ran much better on my system. Which is exactly the same as it was when I completed C1 and WH.*
Pros.
Nice environments/Better graphics than C1 and WH
Great audio/Soundtrack
Lots of pointless collectibles
Except for a point at the beginning in the city, ran much better than C1 and some better than WH
More viable/easy to work with Nanosuit, let's hope they didn't fubar NS 3.0 eh?
Decent arsenal and modifications/easier to work with and access
Decent storyline
Completely different alien enemies
Cons.
More linear gameplay than C1 and WH
Some suit upgrades are pointless, others ar used for less than 1 minute
Weapons dont seem quite as moddable as in C1 and WH
Pretty much no vehicle utility or availablility, a staple for C1 and WH
Much of the game you play a mindless drone, I mean a marine....
Lots of pointless collectibles
New suit setup requires more attention so you don't get ROFLStomped
At first the human enemies make sense, but as time passes, you begin to wonder why they are such ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s to you, and you never really find out why. So you are required to assume its Epeen envy
Less fun and challenging aliens, literally a pushover, if you get my meaning....
Overall.
A graphically enhanced, tighter gameplay, non-story-bridging game that provided me 21 hours of what I feel is time decently spent. After all, what else is there to do when you have the flu.

Ultimately, I could've gone either way on this one, but since I'd rather kill myself than play this again, I think it's safe to say this review leans in towards the negative.
Thomas Was Alone is nice and quirky - one of those titles that could probably be considered an "experience" - but it's just not a very good GAME.
The controls are okay, but far from great, and the way the puzzles handle (i.e., being more tedious than difficult) makes it so frustrating you want to put the game down at times despite its relatively short length.
The narration was another cool idea, but ultimately falls flat and doesn't really deliver in any satisfying way.
Then there's the myriad characters. Yet again, cool idea, but switching between them is such a pain and a bore, that I feel relieved whenever there's a level with only two or three of them. Nor are they essential; there have been entire levels where I thought their interactions were required to progress, but nope, they were just there because why not. Perhaps I used some underhanded method without realizing it, but either way, I can't count that as good level design.
Honestly, though I'm sure many would disagree, this is a game I'd label as "pretentious." I'm glad it had great music, nice ideas, and pleasing visuals - but it's just not functioning on some level - and far, far from the level of something like Braid.
But hey, I'd still say play it if you like puzzle platformers, or if you just want to get some quick achievements.

I first played Thomas Was Alone way back when it was a short online Flash game. Then, it was a fairly simple puzzle game notable for how it humanized and made you care for the characters even though they were just coloured, rectangular blocks. Now it's a full game that takes that core idea and expands everything a thousand-fold. The puzzles still aren't too difficult but there's lots more with lots of variation and new mechanics to keep things interesting. But most importantly the story has become a mini-epic with about a dozen different characters joined by soothing and humorous narration to tell the tale of AI's struggling to survive. I was amazed how protective I am became of my little blocky friends, how eager I was to see them succeed, and yes I absolutely cried over these coloured pixels. Heartily recommended!

When I was child- first playing this game didn't seem so much of a big deal- there were a ton of other games that were a lot more colourful and brighter looking. After playing the newest edition of Tomb Raider i decided to go back, and as an adult- I've fallen in love with the parts my younger self could not. I love the audio, I love the levels, I love the puzzles, I love the visuals but most of all I love the adventure.
Me and my brother both purchased the game and played it side by side- and we figured out all the puzzles together. There's this one puzzle that literally doesn't give you any clues except a name. It took me and my brother 3 hours to figure this one puzzle out- it wasn't until I remembered a song with the particular myth they were speaking of that we solved it.
Visually- yea the graphics are clunky and dated- but as well as adding charmful nostaglia- I felt that the game overall was much much better than the newer edition! I loved that I didn't get much help- I loved the fact that I had to ration my supplies and I felt that everytime I found a new gun or solved a puzzle or found a secret- I was a Tomb Raider!
The audio- isn't the best and while some of the voice actors are okay, some are obviously just the best they could get at the time. The music for what little there is- is nice- but most of the time your left with only the sound of your footsteps or what's around- which REALLY works as you have to use your ears to know what's coming or what lies beyond the path.
If you really wanna sink your teeth into an adventure that has your thinking and on your feet- then your looking at the right game. Visually it's not the best and yea it can be glitchy- but it's a classic and still really holds up!

There isn't much to actually say about this game. It's basically Rock Band (or Guitar Hero) with an ACTUAL guitar! Your six strings are color coded so you can easily find the string to strum (for example, the red string is the thickest string on the guitar, yellow is next, blue after that and so on). Next is the fretboard in the game, it shows numbers on the interface (3, 5, 7, 9, 12 and the other dot places). It also comes with an in game tuner for many different setups (unlike the original 2). Also something I chose this game over the original was the official songs (songs that come with the game, not DLC), it has AWESOME tracks, not just stuff by bands that got famous by these games (with a few exceptions), it's got Bat Country by Avenged Sevenfold, Say It Ain't So by Weezer (side note, I've spent the most time here because it's good practice for chords), My Own Summer by Deftones and many more!
There is one BIG downside to this game though, the way the game's programmed, you need a pretty good guitar with brand new strings, and not too many pickups and stuff. I don't know why but, sometimes the game reads your tuning as right in the tuner then says you're tuning is completely off during a song. Here's a good example, you tune your guitar as close to the 0 mark as you can get (in this one, that's near impossible to do), then you strum the right note at the right time, and it says you either didn't hit it or you hit it late. All because of the way it's programmed. If you don't have a $5,000 guitar, I recommend you get the original Rocksmith as it isn't as picky with your tuning...

You liked Heroes of Might & Magic? Or perhaps King's Bounty or Age of Wonders? Stripped of all city management, you basically just have the turn-based combat. Braveland takes this and adds a big, friendly smile on every creature.
It presents you a cute, classic storyline: a happy farmer boy loses his family and farm to bandits and sets out on a bold journey for revenge, but it turns out there is something more sinister going on and the happy guy wants to deal with it. He travels around and beats up the bad guys who take the hits with permanent crooked smiles on their faces. At first the dialogue attemps some meme-based humour (arrow in the knee anyone?), but they are quickly discarded for cheerful, repetitive greetings and taunts.
Travelling happens on a board with enemies, stores and events in each tile. It's linear, though you can (and should) check every branching road for bonus items, gold and experience points. Gold gets you more troops and items, experience gives small bonuses to creature stats and increases the cap on troops.
While I only played the hard mode, combats are easy for a player familiar with turn-based strategy games. Combat AI does not offer surprises in neither good nor bad ways, so it's okay. There are only 7 different types of troops to buy and around the same number of different enemies with upgraded versions of the usual ones coming later into the game. Basically all of them also smile all the time.
Why, I even lost one battle! Being vastly out-numbered, my troops collected their pocket money and gave it to me to hire more troops for another try. Happyland would have been a more appropriate name for the game.
In conclusion, Braveland would probably be a nice introduction to turn-based strategy games for children or people not acquainted with the genre. For the rest of us it's just a small snack (it lasted ~4 hours for me) that gets a dusty taste towards the end. Get it on sale.

Braveland is a strategy game where you lead a band of fighters on a quest to stop the person that wrecked your village.
Battles take place on a hexagonal grid where a single cell can contain any number of units of a specific class. So if you have an active party of 76 farmers and 24 archers you'll see 2 units on the field. One for the farmers, one for the archers.
Units take turns based on their speed stat and will move up to and/or attack the enemy.
This all sounds quite nice, and tactical turn based combat was what drew me to this game in the first place.
However, the game is very limited in scope.
There are ~12 classes in the game, of which ~6 are recruitable. They're almost all human, and rather lacklustre. It doesn't help that the art style makes everybody look bland and uninterested/uninteresting, truly like Playmobil figurines.
Progression happens on a world map, where each node is an event or a battle, and these progress roughly linearly (there are short branches that lead to minor upgrades every now and then). Battles can not be replayed.
All in all the whole game seems to lack passion.
None of what it presented managed to surprise or engage me.
The plot went nowhere, the upgrades, spells and allies you gain don't really change the basic formula in any way.
There's nothing
with the game, but I don't think you should play it.
